sections.heading: Introduction: What, Exactly, Is the Revival We Long For?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we are going to face together a word that is both familiar and strange — “revival”.

Familiar, because hardly any word is spoken in church more often than “revival”. We pray for revival, fast for revival, organise conferences for revival, and sing for revival late into the night. Strange, because if someone handed you a microphone right now and asked, “Tell me in one sentence: what is revival?” — how many of us could answer straight away, clearly and plainly?

Many people talk about revival without really understanding what revival is.

And so, without our noticing, the word “revival” has been quietly “translated” into something else.

Is it more people? We count Sunday attendance, see every seat filled and extra chairs set out in the aisles, and say, “God is at work among us!”

Is it a fiery atmosphere? We see people raising their hands, weeping and leaping in worship, lingering long after the meeting has ended, and say, “Today really had the feel of revival!”

Is it an impressive event? We see the lighting, the sound, the speakers, record-breaking registrations, posts shared everywhere on social media, and say, “This meeting was truly a sign of revival!”

Brothers and sisters, I want to be very honest: more people is good, a fiery atmosphere is good, impressive events are good too. None of these is a sin; often they even accompany God’s grace. But — none of them is revival itself. They are the thermometer, not the fire; they are the spray of the waves, not the sea; they are the outer skin of the fruit, not the life in the roots.

A picture often comes to my mind. You can point a hairdryer at a pot of water and make the sides of the pot feel hot; or you can light the burner and make the water boil from the bottom up. From the outside both pots are “hot”, but only one is changing.

Thank God, the Bible doesn’t leave us guessing on this question. It gives us an exceedingly clear answer:

Revival has only one essence — life change.

Not a bigger venue but a renewed life; not louder sound but a renewed life; not more programmes but a renewed life.

And true revival never stays with the individual alone. When a person’s life is truly changed by Jesus, that change will always flow outward — into the family, into the church, into the workplace, into the whole of society. This is how revival has happened in every generation: God first changes people, and people then change the world.

In the vision of Kingdom 321 we express this order in one phrase: life first, then relationships, then ministry. This is not a slogan. It is the Bible’s consistent order, and the path church history has confirmed again and again.

In today’s lesson we will open up “the definition of revival” in five parts:

First, the heart of revival: life change.

Second, the result of revival: influencing society.

Third, the true mission of the church.

Fourth, the source of life: Jesus and the word of God.

Fifth, the key to receiving life: humility and repentance.

May the Holy Spirit himself speak to us this morning. As we leave this Morning Devotion, may we not simply know one more definition, but have a real fire lit in our hearts — and the name of that fire is “no longer I, but Christ”.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: One Sentence, Two Pictures
sections.html:
Today we have two theme passages, one in the Gospel of John and one in the Gospel of Matthew; to receive them rightly, we first need to know their background.

The first: John 12:32.

The Gospel of John was written by John, the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved — the son of Zebedee and the brother of James. The church’s history consistently testifies that the book was written around AD 80 to 90, when the elderly John was shepherding the churches in and around Ephesus. By then most of the first-generation apostles had been martyred; outside, the church faced persecution from the Roman Empire, and inside, heretics were denying that Jesus had truly come in the flesh. John’s purpose in writing is perfectly clear — he spells it out himself: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:31)

Notice those last words — “have life”. The key word of the whole Gospel of John is “life”. It appears over thirty times in the book, far more than in the other three Gospels. So if we want to ask “What is revival?”, the Gospel of John is the very textbook the Holy Spirit has prepared for us: revival is people receiving the life of God.

Now look at the context of John 12. This chapter marks the end of Jesus’ public ministry; the cross is only days away. In verses 12 to 19, Jesus rides a donkey into Jerusalem, the crowds wave palm branches and shout “Hosanna”, and the Pharisees say among themselves, “See how you accomplish nothing. Behold, the world has gone after him.” (John 12:19) Then in verses 20 and 21 comes a vitally important interlude: “Now there were certain Greeks among those that went up to worship at the feast. These, therefore, came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying, ‘Sir, we want to see Jesus.’”

Brothers and sisters, this is the Gentile world knocking at the door formally for the first time. What they say is, “We want to see Jesus.” Yet Jesus’ answer is unexpected. He doesn’t arrange an audience at once. He says: “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:23–24)

Only then comes our theme verse: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” Immediately the Holy Spirit, through John, adds an explanation: “But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die.” (John 12:33)

That nails the whole saying to one place — the cross. “Lifted up from the earth” does not mean rising in reputation or a stage being raised; it means being hung on a tree. The reason all people are drawn is not that Jesus put on a spectacular event, but that Jesus laid down his life for sinners. Only when a grain of wheat dies does it bear many grains. The source of revival is at the cross, and the method of revival is life through death.

The word “draw” in the original Greek is ἑλκύω (helkuō), meaning “to pull, to drag”. It carries a strong, forceful action, like hauling a fishing net out of the water onto the shore. The same word appears in John 6:44: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” So this “drawing” is not a marketing technique but God’s own initiative. Revival is never us pulling people into church; it is the lifted-up Jesus pulling people to himself.

The second: Matthew 16:18.

The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, a former tax collector, chiefly for Jewish readers, between AD 50 and 70. One theme runs through the whole book: Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament — he is the King.

Chapter 16 is set in Caesarea Philippi, a city full of pagan temples, with a massive rock face where the locals believed a cave was the entrance to the underworld. In just such a place Jesus asks his disciples, “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answers, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:15–16) Jesus at once declares: “I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.”

There is an important distinction in the original here. “Peter” is Πέτρος (Petros), a masculine noun meaning “a stone”; “rock” is πέτρα (petra), a feminine noun meaning “a great bedrock”. Jesus is not building his church on a man who would grow weak and deny his Lord three times, but on the faith Peter confessed — “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” The foundation of the church is Christ himself.

The Greek word for “church” — the “assembly” — is ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia), formed from “out” and “call”, meaning “the congregation called out”. Notice what the word means: the essence of the church is a people whom God has called out of the world, set apart for himself and transformed. The church is not a building, not a programme unit, not a religious-services company. The church is a community made up of changed lives.

Brothers and sisters, put these two verses together and we see the full panorama of “revival”: Jesus on the cross draws people (John 12:32); those he draws form a community transformed by God (Matthew 16:18); and against that community not even the gates of Hades can prevail. That is revival. Now let’s go through it, one key point at a time.

sections.heading: 1. The Heart of Revival: Life Change
sections.html:
Revival is not an outward phenomenon; it is the renewal of the inner life.

This is the most important sentence in this lesson — please write it on the tablet of your heart: outward phenomena pass away, but the inner life endures for ever.

What does the Bible say?

“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

One verse speaks of a renewed standing, the other of a renewed way of living; one is a fact God has already accomplished, the other a process we experience every day.

Look first at the original. The word “transformed” in Romans 12:2 is the Greek μεταμορφόω (metamorphoō), the same word used in Matthew 17:2 to describe Jesus’ transfiguration on the mountain. It is not changing into a different set of clothes; it is a change of form from the inside out — the biological term “metamorphosis” comes straight from it. “Renewing” is ἀνακαίνωσις (anakainōsis): not renovating something old, but a change of nature.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the essence of revival: not the old self being redecorated to look a little better, but the old self being crucified and the new self coming alive in Christ.

The Old Testament uses the same picture. The prophet Habakkuk prays: “Yahweh, … Renew your work in the middle of the years. In the middle of the years make it known.” (Habakkuk 3:2) The word rendered “renew” here — “revive” in the Chinese Union Version — comes from the Hebrew root חָיָה (chayah), which simply means “to live”. Brothers and sisters, in the Bible the word “revival” never meant “excitement” in the first place; it means “to make alive again”. On the plain of dry bones Ezekiel heard God say: “The Lord Yahweh says to these bones: ‘Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and you will live.’” (Ezekiel 37:5) God’s revival makes the dead live — not the cold lukewarm.

So what will revival look like in a person? The lesson gives us three very clear marks.

First, people become more like Jesus. Not more like some spiritual giant, not more like some kind of religious persona, but more like Jesus. Paul says God’s purpose is this: “For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.” (Romans 8:29) Revival has only one measuring rod — Jesus.

Second, life turns from the self-centred life to selflessness. This is the very core of Kingdom 321. The root of humanity’s fall is the self-centred life; the root of the problem is pride. At the moment Adam and Eve sinned, it was not because the fruit tasted good but because the words “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5) moved them — they wanted to leave their originally intended position, seize rights and take God’s place. Revival is that process turned around: from the self-centred life back to selflessness, from leaving our originally intended position back to it — let man be man and let God be God.

Third, living out Christ, not living out ourselves. Paul offers his own life as testimony: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) Brothers and sisters, notice: selflessness is not “having nothing”; selflessness is “entering into the limitless”. I hand over my limited self, and Christ’s limitless life is lived out in me. This is no loss — it is the best exchange under heaven.

Let me use an example from nature. A caterpillar does not become a butterfly by having wings added to it. Scientists have found that inside the chrysalis most of the caterpillar’s tissues are broken down by enzymes, almost into liquid, leaving only clusters of cells called “imaginal discs”, which reorganise into an entirely different creature. The old must dissolve before the new can take shape. Brothers and sisters, inside the chrysalis there are no lights and no applause — all is quiet — yet it is the most dramatic change in the story of that life. Revival often happens in just such a place — in the quietest, most hidden place within us.

Psychology bears this out from the side as well. The American researchers Prochaska and DiClemente (Prochaska & DiClemente, 1983) proposed the “transtheoretical model of the stages of change”, showing that genuine behavioural change passes through precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance; a brief emotional high that never moves on into action and maintenance will almost inevitably spring back. This reminds us from the other direction: if the tears shed at a conference don’t lead to following Jesus day by day, the tears will dry and the life will not have changed. Psychology cannot replace Scripture, but it can remind us not to mistake being moved for being changed.

This is where revival begins.

Without life change, every revival is only surface excitement.

God does not despise our zeal, but he values our life far more.

So true revival always begins with “me”.

Not “Lord, revive this church”, but “Lord, begin with me.” 321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When I stop staring at how others ought to change and start letting Jesus change me, revival has already begun its work in me. In 321’s fivefold change, these are the first two steps: change the mindset and you change the life.

sections.heading: 2. The Result of Revival: Influencing Society
sections.html:
When lives are changed, the influence will always spread.

This is certain, not merely possible. For the life of God by its very nature spreads — just as light cannot be shut up inside the lamp, and salt cannot help being salty.

The Lord Jesus said: “You are the salt of the earth, but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will it be salted? It is then good for nothing, but to be cast out and trodden under the feet of men.” (Matthew 5:13) And again: “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.” (Matthew 5:14) And he explained the purpose: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16)

Neither salt nor light exists for itself. Salt has value only in the food; light has meaning only in the dark. People whose lives have been changed are destined to be placed by God right in the middle of the world.

The lesson points to three levels of this spreading.

First, families are changed. The first place revival is put to the test is not the pulpit but the dinner table. Whether someone has truly met God, their spouse knows best, and their children know best. If a person worships loudly in the meeting but goes home still irritable, cold and controlling, we have to admit honestly: that life has not yet been changed.

Second, the church is renewed. When one person in a family truly lives out selflessness, the atmosphere in the small group changes, the tug-of-war in the co-workers’ meeting lessens, and serving is no longer about competing for position but about washing one another’s feet. 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. The renewal of a church often begins with one person willing to humble themselves first.

Third, society is shaken. In Thessalonica the people dragged Jason out, crying, “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also” (Acts 17:6). Brothers and sisters, these were not people who ran events; they were people whose lives had been turned upside down, who weren’t even afraid of death. They had no media and no budget, yet they stirred up the Roman world.

History proves this order again and again. In eighteenth-century Britain, society was corrupt, drunkenness was rife and the slave trade was rampant. God raised up John Wesley (1703–1791), George Whitefield and others, who preached the gospel at pit-heads and in open fields, and thousands upon thousands of miners repented and turned to the Lord. That revival did not stay inside church buildings. Among those changed by the gospel was a young Member of Parliament, William Wilberforce (1759–1833), who after his new birth poured his whole life into the fight to abolish the slave trade. Parliament finally passed the act abolishing the slave trade in 1807, and in 1833 passed the act abolishing slavery itself — the very year Wilberforce died.

Brothers and sisters, see this order: it is not that social movements come first and faith follows; changed lives come first, and then a changed society.

The Welsh Revival at the beginning of the twentieth century (1904–1905) was the same. God used a young man in his twenties, Evan Roberts (1878–1951), to bring a great wave of repentance to the mining districts; it is recorded that about a hundred thousand people turned to Christ within a few months. Newspapers of the day reported that the pubs’ trade fell sharply and that outstanding debts were being paid off unprompted. This was not the fruit of a moral reform movement; it was the result of hearts touched by the Holy Spirit and sin being dealt with.

Modern science also offers side evidence for this “spreading”. Christakis and Fowler, in a 2008 study published in the British Medical Journal (BMJ), analysed twenty years of social-network data from the Framingham Heart Study in the United States and found that “happiness” spreads through social networks, reaching even the friends of friends of friends — the so-called “three degrees of influence”. Brothers and sisters, if even emotions can spread like that, how much more the life of God?

This is what the revivals of every generation have in common: people are changed, and the world is influenced.

And the order must never be reversed: not changing the world first, but changing lives first.

One of the greatest temptations of our generation is to skip over life and go straight to changing the world — to change society with methods, change the church with strategies, change our families with techniques. But 321 reminds us: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. And the priority of relationships must not be jumbled either — first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

Here there is a very practical exercise: 321’s “920 practice”. Every person I have a relationship with is my “2” — my spouse, my children, my colleagues, my neighbours. Before them I practise living out the “0” of selflessness, and let the Holy Spirit bear his fruit in all nine of its expressions in me — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, this is the most real pathway by which revival spreads: not broadcasting but contact; not shouting slogans but walking alongside.

sections.heading: 3. The True Mission of the Church
sections.html:
“I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.” (Matthew 16:18)

Brothers and sisters, notice the verb the Lord uses: “build”. Building is slow; it is stone laid upon stone. The Lord did not say, “I will get my church up and running,” nor “I will whip my church into a frenzy.” He said: I will build.

Notice too that the Lord says “my assembly” — my church. The church belongs to the Lord, not to the pastor, not to the co-workers. Since it is the Lord’s church, the purpose of its existence must be defined by the Lord, not by the market.

The lesson lists three “nots”, very directly.

The church does not exist to make people happy. Happiness is good, but if the church’s highest aim is to make people happy, the pulpit won’t dare to preach repentance, the pastors won’t dare to speak the truth, and the members will never grow up.

The church does not exist to entertain people. If people come to church to be entertained, we have to keep raising the stakes, because entertainment has diminishing returns — this year’s wow becomes next year’s ho-hum.

The church does not exist to satisfy people. What is meant here is self-centred satisfaction. If the church is just a company providing religious services, people come to consume, not to offer themselves.

Then what does the church exist for? The lesson says it emphatically: for people’s lives to be changed, for people to become more like Jesus.

Paul wrote this mission out most fully: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:11–13). Look at the final destination: “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ”. Every office, every gift and every meeting exists to bring people there.

Elsewhere Paul puts it even closer to each of us: “We proclaim him, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus” (Colossians 1:28). Notice that the words “every man” appear three times. The church’s mission is not to process crowds but to walk alongside people one by one.

The lesson then gives us a very sharp contrast between two kinds of church.

The first is the entertainment-style church. It draws people with events; what people see is people — the speaker’s eloquence, the band’s standard, the scale of the occasion; and the result is that lives are not changed. When the meeting ends, people take away a few photos and a little emotion.

The second is the life-giving church. It draws people with Jesus; what people see in it is Christ; and the result is that lives are renewed. When the meeting ends, people take away repentance, forgiveness and the courage to stand up again.

Hear this clearly: this does not mean events are necessarily wrong. An event can be a tool, but a tool can never replace the purpose. When the tool becomes the purpose, the church begins to slide downhill; when Jesus is the purpose, every tool finds its proper place.

Psychology offers some side evidence here that is worth pondering. Self-determination theory, developed by the American psychologists Deci and Ryan, distinguishes between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation. Deci’s classic experiment (Deci, 1971) went further and found that when something people had been doing out of interest was paired with an external reward, once the reward stopped their willingness to engage actually fell below where it had been before. Set that finding in the church, and what a sobering reminder it is: if people come to church because they are drawn by external stimulation, when the stimulation stops they will leave; only those who have truly received life will follow for a lifetime.

The Lord himself gave the final answer:

“And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” (John 12:32)

We have already seen that this saying refers to the cross. So the logic of revival is this: lift up Jesus, and people are drawn; lift up ourselves, and people only see us.

What draws people is not events; it is Jesus.

John the Baptist summed up this spiritual principle in one sentence: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) Brothers and sisters, these words ought to be engraved on the heart of everyone who serves.

This is exactly 321’s Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The church’s real crisis has never been too few resources or too little talent; it is that Jesus is not on the throne, that something else has sat down in that seat — perhaps tradition, perhaps numbers, perhaps one person’s face. When Jesus reigns as King again, the church has power again.

321’s Path of Serving is Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the Holy Spirit is my guide, the Bible is my standard, Jesus is my role model, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. A church that walks this path naturally becomes a life-giving church, because it is not building itself; it is establishing God’s system.

sections.heading: 4. The Source of Life: Jesus and the Word of God
sections.html:
Since the essence of revival is life change, the next question is crucial: where does this life come from?

The lesson’s answer has only two outlets — and the two are in fact one and the same Person.

First, Jesus is life.

“Jesus said to him, ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.’” (John 14:6)

Notice the Lord’s wording. He did not say, “I point out a way” or “I bring life.” He said, “I am.” The Greek uses that most solemn “I am” (ἐγώ εἰμι, egō eimi), echoing God’s self-designation to Moses in Exodus 3:14, “I AM WHO I AM”. Jesus is not the best of many life coaches; he is life itself.

John declared it at the very opening of his Gospel: “In him was life, and the life was the light of men.” (John 1:4)

The word “life” here is the Greek ζωή (zōē), which refers to God’s eternal, incorruptible life, entirely different from another word, βίος (bios), which refers to physical livelihood and the business of living. Brothers and sisters, a person can have an excellent bios — good health, a thriving career, a comfortable living — and have no zōē at all. Revival is not upgrading bios; it is being connected to zōē.

Second, the word of God is life.

“It is the spirit who gives life. The flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life.” (John 6:63)

The background of this verse is important. In John 6, Jesus had just fed five thousand with five loaves and two fish, and the crowd was eager to make him king; yet he turned and preached an extremely hard message — “I am the bread of life”. The text then says: “At this, many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.” (John 6:66) That day the numbers fell from five thousand to twelve. The Lord did not run after them to keep them, nor did he adjust his message to please the crowd. He simply asked the Twelve, “You don’t also want to go away, do you?” (John 6:67) Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.” (John 6:68)

This is the watershed between the entertainment style and the life-giving way. After the five loaves and two fish there were five thousand; after the word of life there were twelve left. But it was those twelve who changed the world.

The letter to the Hebrews describes God’s word like this: “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” (Hebrews 4:12) “Living” in the original is ζῶν (zōn), simply “alive” — God’s word is a word that has life in it, and once it enters a person it goes to work.

So the lesson reminds us of three things, and they are vital: it is not people who change people; it is Jesus who changes people; it is the word of God that changes people.

Brothers and sisters, for those who serve, this is both a great release and a great warning.

It is a release, because at last we can lay down a burden that was never ours. How many nights have we lain awake over family members we cannot change, or blamed ourselves for a small group we cannot get off the ground? Changing people was never our job in the first place.

It is a warning, because we must lay down a power that was never ours. When we think we can change people, we begin to control them, manipulate them and push them with pressure. That is precisely the self-centred life — leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place.

The Lord Jesus explained this with the simplest of pictures: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) The branch’s job is not to produce fruit; the branch’s job is to stay connected. The fruit is the inevitable result of the connection.

Let me use an example from the body. Scientists estimate that an adult human is made up of about thirty-seven trillion cells (Bianconi et al., 2013, Annals of Human Biology). Each cell stays alive because the blood keeps bringing oxygen and nutrients right to it; cut off the blood flow for just a few minutes, and however healthy it used to be, it dies. Brothers and sisters, our relationship with the Lord is just like that. The question is not whether you finished reading the Bible this year, but whether, this morning, the source of life has flowed in.

So the lesson says: our responsibility is not to “manufacture life” but to “bring people to meet Jesus”.

Andrew brought Simon to Jesus (John 1:42); Philip said to Nathanael, “Come and see.” (John 1:46) They didn’t argue, they didn’t persuade — they simply brought people to see Jesus.

This is the practical application of 321’s Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — as I see him act, so I act. The Bible is my standard — I go not by feelings, not by experience, not by majority opinion, but by the word of God alone. The Holy Spirit is my guide — not relying on the brain and ourselves, but relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit. 321 has a very vivid saying: rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. For “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

sections.heading: 5. The Key to Receiving Life: Humility and Repentance
sections.html:
We have seen that revival is life change, and that the source of life is Jesus and the word of God. The final question is: how can I receive this life?

The lesson’s answer is just two words: humility and repentance.

“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

“Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.” (James 1:21)

Look at the verbs in these two verses. John says “confess” — the Greek ὁμολογέω (homologeō) literally means “to say the same thing”: no longer defending myself, but saying about my sin exactly what God says about it. James says “putting away” — the original ἀποτίθημι (apotithēmi) is the action of taking off clothes; and the word behind “humility”, πραΰτης (prautēs), meekness, was often used of a wild horse that had been broken in — not lacking strength, but with its strength wholly yielded to its master’s hand.

So the lesson says that the entrance to life is humility plus repentance.

Humility: laying ourselves down.

Repentance: turning to God.

The Greek word for “repentance”, μετάνοια (metanoia), is made up of “change” and “mind”, meaning a complete turnaround of thoughts and intentions; the Hebrew uses שׁוּב (shuv), meaning “to turn back, to turn around”. Brothers and sisters, repentance is not just feeling sorry; it is turning around. A person can weep bitterly over their sin and still keep walking in the same direction. True repentance is turning round.

Peter said to the people: “Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out, so that there may come times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord” (Acts 3:19). “Times of refreshing” are the days of revival, and they come after repenting and turning again. The order cannot be reversed.

The Old Testament promise is exactly the same: “if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” (2 Chronicles 7:14) Four conditions — humble themselves, pray, seek, turn; three promises — hear, forgive, heal. The healing of the land begins with the people humbling themselves.

The two negatives the lesson warns of are just as important: without humility, we cannot receive life; without repentance, we cannot change.

Why can’t we receive without humility? Because “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) This is a law of the spiritual world. Peter says too: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6).

Let me use a simple picture. If a cup is upside down, you can pour a whole river over it and it will still be empty inside. It isn’t that there isn’t enough water; it’s facing the wrong way. Pride is a life lived with the cup upside down — it isn’t that such a person has no opportunity; they simply can’t receive. And repentance is turning the cup the right way up.

God himself says: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.” (Isaiah 57:15) Brothers and sisters, “revive” — that is revival. God dwells in two places: the high and holy place, and the hearts of the contrite and humble. If we want God’s presence, we don’t need to climb up; we only need to go down.

David learned in his deepest failure: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (Psalm 51:17)

Psychological research on “humility” has advanced considerably over the past twenty years. The American psychologist June Price Tangney (2000), writing in the Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, pointed out that humility is not self-deprecation; it includes an accurate view of one’s own abilities and limitations, the ability to admit mistakes, openness to new ideas, an appropriate appreciation of the worth of others, and a capacity to “forget oneself”. Brothers and sisters, how close that last one is to what 321 calls “selflessness”! True humility is not constantly thinking “I’m so bad”; it is no longer thinking about oneself at all, because one’s eyes have already been captured by Jesus.

Paul says of Jesus: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8) Brothers and sisters, “emptied himself” is the supreme role model of selflessness. If the Lord of the universe was willing to empty himself, what reason do we have to cling to ourselves?

This is 321’s most central message: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan’s very nature is pride — “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God!” (Isaiah 14:13) Satan cannot overcome a truly selfless person, because he can find nothing in them to take hold of. The Lord Jesus said: “the prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me.” (John 14:30)

Every revival begins here.

Brothers and sisters, this is why every truly great revival in history has begun not on a stage but with confession of sin.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: Revival Is Letting Jesus Be King
sections.html:
Set the five key points of this lesson alongside the vision of Kingdom 321, and a complete picture appears.

First, the Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — the standard of revival is not other people; it is Jesus. The Bible is my standard — the definition of revival is decided not by trends, not by feelings, but by the word of God. The Holy Spirit is my guide — it is not people who change people; it is the Holy Spirit who changes people through the word of God. Our responsibility is to obey, not to manufacture.

Next, the Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — if a church lets Jesus be King, it doesn’t need entertainment to keep people; if a person lets Jesus be King, they no longer need to prove themselves before others. Let Jesus receive all the glory — “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” (John 12:32) The reason others are drawn must be that Jesus is lifted up in us.

Last, the Goal: establish God’s system. This is exactly what Matthew 16:18 is about. God’s system is not an organisation but a connection of lives; not an institution but the body of Christ. The ultimate goal of revival is the fulfilment of the Lord’s Prayer: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)

Then look at the main thread running through the whole lesson: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless.

The lesson says “life turns from the self-centred life to selflessness” — that sentence is the heartbeat of this lesson. What is pride? It is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. What is humility? It is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. So the “humility plus repentance” of the fifth key point is the concrete path of “returning from the self-centred life to selflessness”.

And selflessness is not having nothing. Selflessness is not erasing yourself, not having no personality. Selflessness is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless — I hand over my limited “self”, and what I receive is Christ’s limitless life. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20) — this is the most glorious exchange under heaven.

Then look at the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Today’s Morning Devotion is doing precisely the first change — mindset. When our mindset about revival turns from “excitement” to “life”, the change has already begun. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; once daily living changes, relationships change; once relationships change, ministry has a real foundation.

Brothers and sisters, this is also the order of the lesson’s first and second key points: first life change, then social influence. We often try to use ministry to drive life and events to drive change, and the result is busy people, empty hearts and little fruit. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

We also need to see the shift in perspective. Revival, in the end, is a complete move to a new vantage point:

From man’s perspective to God’s perspective — man looks at numbers; God looks at lives.

From an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective — earth looks at the spectacle; heaven looks at the altar.

From a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective — the temporary looks at tonight’s emotion; the eternal looks at the fruit ten years from now.

From a worldly perspective to a godly perspective — the worldly asks, “Does it work?”; the godly asks, “Is the Lord pleased?”

These four shifts answer exactly the three questions of the introduction: Is it more people? Is it a fiery atmosphere? Is it an impressive event? From the human, earthly, temporary and worldly perspective, those three things are revival; from God’s, the heavenly, the eternal and the godly perspective, only one thing is revival — life change.

Finally, there are the 920 practice and the 235 relationships — two tracks for working this lesson out in real people.

The 920 practice: every person I have a relationship with is my “2”. I don’t need to wait for the church to hold a big evangelistic rally before I take part in revival; this morning’s phone call, this apology, is where revival is happening. Before my “2” I practise the “0” of selflessness, and the Holy Spirit bears his fruit in all nine of its expressions (Galatians 5:22–23). The fruit is not something we manufacture; it is borne by the Spirit. All we need to do is remain in the Lord.

The 235 relationships: revival is not a one-person affair. Become a “2” with someone who is also pursuing selflessness, keeping honest watch over each other; build a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, so that life is passed on; and then join with co-workers of the fivefold ministry to form a “5”, a team of spiritual comrades. This echoes Ephesians 4:11–13 exactly — the purpose of the fivefold ministry is to bring everyone to “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ”.

Revival has never been a firework display; it is a chain of life passed down from one to another.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Walking It Out through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will use 321’s “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to walk each of them out, one by one.

Practice 1: Examine your focus — am I pursuing an atmosphere, or life?

Don’t be drawn by the outward; come back to whether your inner life has truly changed.

Information: Today I have received the Bible’s definition of revival — life change (2 Corinthians 5:17; Romans 12:2).

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to turn this information into personal light for me. Be still for three minutes and ask God, “Lord, this past year, have I been pursuing an atmosphere, or life?” Don’t defend yourself; wait for him to speak.

Conviction: When the Holy Spirit points something out, I admit it and stop arguing. This is “confessing” — saying the same thing as God (1 John 1:9).

Implementation: Change the question you ask after a meeting. In the past I asked, “Was I moved today?” From this week on, ask instead, “Which of my mindsets did God correct today? How will I act on it?”

Evaluation: At the weekend, spend ten minutes looking back and write down the real changes of this week, even if there is only one.

Correction: If you find you are still chasing feelings, don’t lose heart. Repentance is turning around, and it is never too late to turn around.

Repetition: Keep this practice up for at least four weeks in a row. Spiritual muscle grows through repetition.

Multiplication: Find a brother or sister, pass this question on to them, and invite them to practise it with you. That is your “2”.

Practice 2: Connect with Jesus every day

Through prayer and reading the Bible, let the source of life keep flowing in, rather than relying on your own effort to change.

Information: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Revelation: Ask the Lord to let me truly see that “apart from me you can do nothing” is not a polite turn of phrase but a spiritual fact.

Conviction: Admit that much of my past weariness came from doing God’s work in my own strength.

Implementation: Set a practice you can actually keep. I suggest fifteen minutes each morning: five minutes of quiet praise, five minutes reading God’s word (this week you might read John 12–15), and five minutes of prayer in response — praying the very sentence you read straight back to God.

Evaluation: Each day write one line in a notebook: “The one sentence God spoke to me today.” After a week, look back over those seven lines.

Correction: If you miss a day, don’t try to catch up and don’t condemn yourself — simply reconnect from today. Connection matters more than performance.

Repetition: Let it become a habit. The power of habit is that it keeps life’s bloodstream flowing without interruption.

Multiplication: Send that one line from your notebook each day to a spiritual companion. You will find that the words you pass on come back to feed you.

Practice 3: Practise a life of humility and repentance

Open yourself to God every day, acknowledge your true condition, and let God’s word renew your life.

Information: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9) “Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.” (James 1:21)

Revelation: Each night before sleep, let the Holy Spirit search the day. Not raking over old accounts, but letting the light shine in.

Conviction: Say the same thing to God, without explanations, without blaming others, without blaming circumstances.

Implementation: Make it specific to a person. If today I was proud, angry or judgemental towards someone, go and apologise tomorrow — a sincere “I’m sorry, I was wrong” is enough. 321 says: humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Evaluation: After a week, ask yourself: has the atmosphere at home changed? Has my “2” responded to me differently?

Correction: If the other person doesn’t respond after you apologise, don’t retreat into pride. Our humility is not a transaction; it is worship.

Repetition: Let confession become your daily breath, not an annual conference.

Multiplication: When your children and colleagues see someone who knows how to apologise, they see the gospel. Humility is contagious.

A Gentle Reminder

Revival is not things heating up on the outside; it is coming alive on the inside.

Brothers and sisters, please take this sentence home with you. Heating up on the outside may be nothing more than stage lighting; coming alive on the inside — that is the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call: Letting People See Jesus Living in Us
sections.html:
True revival does not begin with a crowd; it begins with one heart.

Brothers and sisters, we often think revival needs a great crowd of people, but God often needs only one person. What he wants is not ten thousand half-hearted people, but one person wholly surrendered.

When one person is changed by Jesus, they will influence another; when a group of people is changed by Jesus, a whole generation will be turned around.

History confirms this again and again: from one Peter to three thousand (Acts 2:41), from one Wesley to the whole of Britain. God has never lacked resources; God is looking for vessels.

What is revival? In one sentence: revival is letting people see — Jesus living in us.

Not letting people see our gifts, not letting people see our growth curve, not letting people see our events — but letting people see Jesus. “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to issue three calls to you.

First, let Jesus be King. Make a concrete handover in your heart: that seat you have been clinging to — control at home, control over a certain relationship, the right to plan your future — hand it back to the Lord now. Let man be man and let God be God.

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. From today on, when someone praises you, pass it on to the Lord in your heart; when someone wrongs you, entrust it to the Lord in your heart. The glory goes to the Lord, and so does the burden.

Third, begin with me. Stop waiting for others to change first. Today, let revival begin with you — begin in your prayers, begin at your dinner table, begin in the phone call you are going to make today.

When the Lord Jesus was lifted up, he drew all people to himself. Today we ask the Lord to be lifted up in our lives as well, so that the people around us, because of us, will see Jesus.

Matthew 16:18

prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We thank you that this morning you have used your word to correct our mindset about revival. We confess that in the past we often took excitement for revival, numbers for fruitfulness, and being moved for being changed. Lord, forgive us.

Make us truly come alive. You are the way, the truth and the life; apart from you we have nowhere to go. Pour your life into us, turn us from the self-centred life to selflessness, from living out ourselves to living out Christ.

Lord, we hand our seat back to you. Reign as King in our homes, reign as King in our church, reign as King in our workplaces. Humble us, so that every day we confess, every day we repent, every day we are renewed by your word.
Make us people who have been changed, so that those around us are influenced; make us people who see Jesus, and people through whom others see Jesus.
May all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Read 2 Corinthians 5:17: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” Looking back over the past year, what is the most real “become new” that God has done in your life? Did it happen in an exciting meeting, or in quiet, even difficult, days?

Read 1 John 1:9: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” In the relationships closest to you right now (spouse, children, parents, co-workers), is there something the Holy Spirit is reminding you today to confess or apologise for? When and how do you plan to do it?
l114.title: What Revival Is
l114.subtitle: True Revival Is a Life Changed by Jesus
l114.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

blog.title: Revival Is Not Things Heating Up on the Outside

blocks.x: It Is Coming Alive on the Inside
If someone handed you a microphone right now and asked, “Tell me in one sentence: what is revival?” — how would you answer?
We pray for revival, fast for revival, organise conferences for revival. Yet without our noticing, the word “revival” has often been quietly “translated” into something else.

Is it more people? Is it a fiery atmosphere? Is it an impressive event? When every seat is filled, worship is on fire and registrations break records, we say, “God is at work — this is truly a sign of revival.”

I want to be very honest: these things are all good, and often they even accompany God’s grace. But none of them is revival itself. They are the thermometer, not the fire; the spray of the waves, not the sea.

You can point a hairdryer at a pot of water and make it feel hot to the touch, or you can light the burner and make the water boil from the bottom up. From the outside both pots are hot, but only one is changing.
The Heart of Revival: Life Change
The Bible gives us an exceedingly clear answer: revival has only one essence — life change.
“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

Not the old self being redecorated to look a little better, but the old self being crucified and the new self coming alive in Christ. Revival leaves three marks on a person: they become more like Jesus; they turn from the self-centred life to selflessness; and they live out Christ, not themselves.

A caterpillar does not become a butterfly by having a pair of wings added. Inside the chrysalis most of its tissues are broken down by enzymes, almost into liquid, leaving only the “imaginal discs”, which reorganise into an entirely different creature. Inside the chrysalis there are no lights and no applause, yet it is the most dramatic change in the story of that life.
Revival often happens in just such a place — in the quietest place within us. And it always begins with “me”, not with someone else.
The Result of Revival: From the Dinner Table to Society
When lives are changed, the influence will always spread. Families are changed, the church is renewed, society is shaken.

In eighteenth-century Britain, society was corrupt and the slave trade was rampant. God raised up John Wesley to preach the gospel in the open fields. Among those changed by the gospel was a Member of Parliament, William Wilberforce, who after his new birth poured his whole life into abolition; Parliament finally abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery itself in 1833.

See this order clearly: not changing the world first, but changing lives first. This is exactly what Kingdom 321 means by “life first, then relationships, then ministry”. And the first place revival is put to the test is not the pulpit but the dinner table — whether someone has truly met God, their spouse knows best, and their children know best.
Where Is the Entrance? Humility and Repentance

Where does life come from? There is only one answer: Jesus. He said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.” (John 14:6) He also said that the words he speaks are spirit and are life. So it is not people who change people; it is Jesus who changes people. Our responsibility is not to manufacture life but to bring people to meet Jesus.

The entrance to this life comes down to two words: humility and repentance. If a cup is upside down, you can pour a whole river over it and it will still be empty inside; it isn’t that there isn’t enough water — it’s facing the wrong way. Repentance is turning the cup the right way up. Without humility, we cannot receive life; without repentance, we cannot change. Every truly great revival in church history has begun not on a stage but with confession of sin.
Three Practices You Can Begin Today
1. Examine your focus: after a meeting, don’t just ask, “Was I moved today?” Ask instead, “Which of my mindsets did God correct today? How will I act on it?”
2. Connect with Jesus every day: fifteen minutes each morning of quiet praise, reading God’s word and prayer in response, so that the source of life keeps flowing in.
3. Practise humility and repentance: each night let the Holy Spirit search the day; if you have wronged someone today, go and apologise tomorrow.

True revival does not begin with a crowd; it begins with one heart. When one person is changed by Jesus, they will influence another; when a group of people is changed by Jesus, a whole generation will be turned around.
Revival is letting people see — Jesus living in us.
Reflection Question
If revival means “life change”, what is the most real change God has made in you over this past year? Did it happen in a lively meeting, or in quiet — even difficult — days?
