script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we are going to look together at a topic called “What Revival Is”. It is a word we use all the time, yet one of the hardest to explain clearly. We pray for revival, fast for revival, hold conferences for revival. But if someone asked you right now, “Tell me in one sentence: what is revival?” — how would you answer? Today’s theme verse is John 12:32, where the Lord Jesus says, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” Please remember these words; we will come back to them shortly.

Brothers and sisters, we often translate revival into something else. Is it more people? Is it a fiery atmosphere? Is it an impressive event? I want to be very honest: more people is good, a fiery atmosphere is good, an impressive event is good too. But none of them is revival itself. That is the thermometer, not the fire. You can warm a pot with a hairdryer, or you can bring the water to the boil over a flame; from the outside both are hot, but only one is changing. The Bible gives us an exceedingly clear answer: revival has only one essence — life change.

Let’s look first at the background. The Gospel of John was written around AD 80 to 90, and the key word of the whole book is “life”. In John 12, some Greeks came to Philip and said, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.” The Lord Jesus didn’t grant them an audience at once. He said: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. Then he said, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” And Scripture explains straight away that he said this signifying by what kind of death he should die. Brothers and sisters, “lifted up” is not a stage being raised; it is the cross. The source of revival is at the cross.

The first key point: the heart of revival is life change. Revival is not an outward phenomenon; it is the renewal of the inner life. People become more like Jesus, life turns from the self-centred life to selflessness, and we live out Christ, not ourselves. Paul says, “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” A caterpillar does not become a butterfly by having wings added; inside the chrysalis it almost entirely breaks down and is put together again. Brothers and sisters, inside the chrysalis there are no lights and no applause, yet it is life’s most dramatic change. So true revival always begins with “me”.

The second key point: the result of revival is influencing society. Once lives change, the influence will always spread. Families are changed, the church is renewed, society is shaken. In eighteenth-century Britain, God raised up John Wesley to preach the gospel in the open fields; among those changed by the gospel was a Member of Parliament, Wilberforce, who gave his whole life to abolition, and Britain finally abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in 1833. Brothers and sisters, see this order clearly: not changing the world first, but changing lives first. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

The third key point: the true mission of the church. The Lord Jesus said, “On this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.” Notice that the Lord’s verb is “build”, not “get up and running”. The church does not exist to make people happy, to entertain people or to satisfy people; it exists for lives to be changed, for people to become more like Jesus. Paul says that every office is given “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving”, until we attain “to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ”.

Brothers and sisters, there are two kinds of church here. The entertainment-style church draws people with events; what people see is people, and lives are not changed. The life-giving church draws people with Jesus; what people see is Christ, and lives are renewed. I’m not saying events are wrong; events are tools, but tools can never replace the purpose. The psychologist Deci found that when external rewards stop, people’s willingness to engage actually falls lower than before. Those who come for stimulation leave as soon as it stops. That is why the Lord said, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” What draws people is not events; it is Jesus.

The fourth key point: the source of life. Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life”; and he also said, “The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life.” Brothers and sisters, it is not people who change people; it is Jesus who changes people, it is the word of God that changes people. This is a great release, and also a great warning. A release, because we can lay down a burden that was never ours; a warning, because we must lay down a power that was never ours. The Lord said, “Apart from me you can do nothing.” So our responsibility is not to manufacture life but to bring people to meet Jesus.

The fifth key point: the key to receiving life is humility and repentance. John says, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins”; James says, “Receive with humility the implanted word.” Humility is laying ourselves down; repentance is turning to God. If a cup is upside down, you can pour a whole river over it and it will still be empty inside. It isn’t that there isn’t enough water; it’s facing the wrong way. Brothers and sisters, without humility we cannot receive life; without repentance we cannot change. Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Every revival begins here.

Now we come to the practices. First, examine your focus: am I pursuing an atmosphere, or life? From today, after a meeting don’t just ask, “Was I moved today?” Ask, “Which of my mindsets did God correct?” Second, connect with Jesus every day: fifteen minutes each morning — quiet, the Bible, prayer — and let the source flow in. Third, practise a life of humility and repentance: each night let the Holy Spirit search you, and if you have wronged someone, go and apologise tomorrow. Brothers and sisters, please remember this sentence: revival is not things heating up on the outside; it is coming alive on the inside.

Finally, brothers and sisters: true revival does not begin with a crowd; it begins with one heart. When one person is changed by Jesus, they will influence another; when a group of people is changed by Jesus, a whole generation will be turned around. So today I want to issue three calls to you. First, let Jesus be King — hand that seat you have been clinging to back to him. Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. Third, begin with me — stop waiting for others to change first. Revival is letting people see — Jesus living in us.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, thank you that this morning you have used your word to correct our mindset. We confess that in the past we often took excitement for revival. Lord, forgive us. Make us truly come alive; turn us from the self-centred life to selflessness, so that we live out your likeness and become people who influence this generation. Reign as King in our homes; reign as King in our church. May all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless you and keep you until the day we see him face to face.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. The topic we are going to look at together today is called “What Revival Is”. It is a word we use all the time, yet one of the hardest to explain clearly. If someone asked you right now, “Tell me in one sentence: what is revival?” — how would you answer? Today’s theme verse is John 12:32, where the Lord Jesus says, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” Please keep these words in your heart. Today we will walk through five key points: the heart of revival, the result of revival, the mission of the church, the source of life, and the key to receiving life.

Brothers and sisters, many people talk about revival without really understanding what revival is. And so the word “revival” has been quietly translated into something else. Is it more people? We see every seat filled and extra chairs in the aisles, and we say, “God is at work!” Is it a fiery atmosphere? We see people raising their hands and weeping in worship, and we say, “Today really had the feel of revival!” Is it an impressive event? We see record-breaking registrations, and we say, “This is truly a sign of revival!” I want to be very honest: more people is good, a fiery atmosphere is good, an impressive event is good too — often they even accompany God’s grace.

But brothers and sisters, none of them is revival itself. They are the thermometer, not the fire; the spray of the waves, not the sea. You can point a hairdryer at a pot of water and make it feel hot to the touch, or you can light the burner and make the water boil from the bottom up. From the outside both pots are hot, but only one is truly changing. Do we want something that feels hot, or something truly coming alive inside? Thank God, the Bible doesn’t leave us guessing: revival has only one essence — life change. And true revival never stays with the individual alone; it always flows into the family, the church and society. This is exactly what 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Let’s look first at the background. The Gospel of John was written by John, the disciple whom the Lord loved, around AD 80 to 90, so that people might have life in his name; the key word of the whole book is “life”. In John 12, Jesus has just ridden a donkey into Jerusalem, and some Greeks come to Philip and say, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.” The Lord doesn’t grant them an audience at once. He says: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. Only then does he say, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” And Scripture explains straight away that he said this signifying by what kind of death he should die. Brothers and sisters, “lifted up” is not a stage being raised; it is the cross. The source of revival is at the cross.

The first key point: the heart of revival is life change. Revival is not an outward phenomenon; it is the renewal of the inner life. Paul says, “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” And again, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” The original word for “transformed” is the same word used for the transfiguration on the mountain — not changing into a different set of clothes, but a change of form from the inside out. The Old Testament paints the same picture. Habakkuk prays, “Yahweh, … Renew your work in the middle of the years. In the middle of the years make it known.” On the plain of dry bones Ezekiel hears God say, “I will cause breath to enter into you, and you will live.” God’s revival makes the dead live.

So what will a changed life look like? The lesson gives us three marks. First, people become more like Jesus. Second, life turns from the self-centred life to selflessness. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position. Third, living out Christ, not ourselves. Paul says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is entering into the limitless. A caterpillar does not become a butterfly by having wings added; inside the chrysalis it almost entirely breaks down and is put together again. There are no lights and no applause in the chrysalis, yet it is life’s most dramatic change. In 1983 the psychologists Prochaska and DiClemente proposed the stages-of-change model, showing that a brief emotional high that never moves on into action and maintenance will almost inevitably spring back. So true revival always begins with “me”.

The second key point: the result of revival is influencing society. Once lives change, the influence will always spread, because light cannot be shut up inside the lamp, and salt cannot help being salty. The Lord Jesus said: you are the salt of the earth; you are the light of the world. This spreading has three levels. First, families are changed; the first place revival is tested is not the pulpit but the dinner table. Second, the church is renewed; when one person truly lives out selflessness, the tug-of-war among the co-workers lessens. 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Third, society is shaken. In Thessalonica the people dragged Jason out, crying, “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also.” They were not people who ran events; they were people who weren’t even afraid of death.

History proves this order again and again. In eighteenth-century Britain, society was corrupt, drunkenness was rife and the slave trade was rampant. God raised up John Wesley to preach the gospel in the open fields, and thousands upon thousands of miners repented and turned to the Lord. Among those changed by the gospel was a Member of Parliament, Wilberforce, who after his new birth poured his whole life into abolition; Parliament finally abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in 1833. Brothers and sisters, see it clearly: not changing the world first, but changing lives first. This is how 321’s 920 practice is worked out — everyone I relate to is my “2”; before them I practise selflessness, and the Holy Spirit bears his ninefold fruit.

The third key point: the true mission of the church. The Lord Jesus said, “On this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.” Notice that the Lord’s verb is “build”, not “get up and running”; building is slow — stone laid upon stone. Notice too that the Lord says “my church”, so its purpose must be defined by the Lord, not by the market. The original word for church means “the congregation called out”. So the church does not exist to make people happy, to entertain people or to satisfy people; it exists for lives to be changed, for people to become more like Jesus. Paul says God gave the fivefold ministry for the perfecting of the saints, until we attain to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.

Brothers and sisters, here is a sharp contrast. The first is the entertainment-style church: it draws people with events, what people see is people, lives are not changed, and when the meeting ends people take away only a few photos. The second is the life-giving church: it draws people with Jesus, what people see is Christ, lives are renewed, and people take away repentance, forgiveness and the courage to stand up again. Hear this clearly: I’m not saying events are wrong; events are tools, but tools can never replace the purpose. In a 1971 experiment the psychologist Deci found that when something people did out of interest was paired with an external reward, once the reward stopped their willingness to engage actually fell. Those who come for stimulation leave as soon as it stops.

So the Lord himself gave the final answer: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” The logic of revival is simple: lift up Jesus, and people are drawn; lift up ourselves, and people only see us. What draws people is not events; it is Jesus. John the Baptist summed up the principle: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” These words ought to be engraved on the heart of everyone who serves. This is exactly 321’s Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The church’s real crisis is not too few resources or too little talent; it is that Jesus is not on the throne. When Jesus reigns as King again, the church has power again.

The fourth key point: the source of life. Where does this life come from? First, Jesus is life. The Lord said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.” He didn’t say, “I point out a way”; he said, “I am.” The Greek uses that most solemn “I am”, echoing God’s self-designation to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM”. The original word zōē is God’s eternal life, entirely different from bios, physical livelihood. A person can have an excellent bios and no zōē at all. The Lord said, “Apart from me you can do nothing.” An adult is made up of about thirty-seven trillion cells, and every one of them stays alive by the blood supply; cut off the blood flow, and in a few minutes it dies. Our relationship with the Lord is just like that.

Second, the word of God is life. The Lord said, “The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life.” The background matters. In John 6, Jesus had just fed five thousand, and the crowd was eager to make him king; yet he turned and preached an extremely hard message. The text then says, “At this, many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.” That day the numbers fell from five thousand to twelve. The Lord did not adjust his message to please the crowd. But it was those twelve who changed the world. So the lesson reminds us: it is not people who change people; it is Jesus who changes people; it is the word of God that changes people. This is a great release, and also a great warning. Our responsibility is not to manufacture life but to bring people to meet Jesus.

The fifth key point: the key to receiving life comes down to two words — humility and repentance. John says, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” James says, “Receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.” The original word for “confess” means “to say the same thing” — no longer defending ourselves. The original word for “humility” was often used of a wild horse that had been broken in: not lacking strength, but with its strength wholly yielded to its master’s hand. Peter says: repent and turn again, so that there may come times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord. The times of refreshing come after repenting and turning again.

So the entrance to life is humility plus repentance. Humility is laying ourselves down; repentance is turning to God. The Greek word for “repentance” means a complete turnaround of the mind; the Hebrew means “to turn back, to turn around”. Repentance is not just feeling sorry; it is turning round. A person can weep bitterly over their sin and still keep walking in the same direction. If a cup is upside down, you can pour a whole river over it and it will still be empty inside; it isn’t that there isn’t enough water — it’s facing the wrong way. Repentance is turning the cup the right way up. The Old Testament promise is the same: if God’s people humble themselves, pray, seek his face and turn from their wicked ways, he will hear, forgive, and heal their land.

The two negatives the lesson warns of are just as important: without humility, we cannot receive life; without repentance, we cannot change. For “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” God says, “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.” Brothers and sisters, “revive” — that is revival. If we want God’s presence, we don’t need to climb up; we only need to go down. In 2000 the psychologist Tangney pointed out that humility is not self-deprecation but an accurate knowledge of our own limitations, together with the capacity to “forget oneself”. How close that is to 321’s “selflessness”! Paul says of Jesus that he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

Now we come to the practices for daily life. First, examine your focus: am I pursuing an atmosphere, or life? From today, after a meeting don’t just ask, “Was I moved today?” Ask instead, “Which of my mindsets did God correct today?” Then at the weekend spend ten minutes looking back and write down the real changes of this week, even if there is only one. Second, connect with Jesus every day: through prayer and reading the Bible, let the source of life keep flowing in, rather than relying on your own effort. I suggest fifteen minutes each morning: five minutes of quiet praise, five minutes reading God’s word, five minutes of prayer in response. If you miss a day, don’t try to catch up and don’t condemn yourself — simply reconnect from today.

Third, practise a life of humility and repentance: open yourself to God every day and acknowledge your true condition. Each night before sleep let the Holy Spirit search the day — not raking over old accounts, but letting the light shine in. Then make it specific to a person: if today I was proud, angry or judgemental towards someone, go and apologise tomorrow; a sincere “I’m sorry, I was wrong” is enough. Brothers and sisters, walk these three practices out through 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Spiritual muscle grows through repetition.

Let’s bring the 3-2-1 vision together. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. The main thread is this: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Our perspective must shift too: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. And there are the 235 relationships: becoming spiritual companions with someone pursuing selflessness, building spiritual parents and children, and then becoming a team of spiritual comrades in the fivefold ministry. Revival is not a firework display; it is a chain of life passed down from one to another.

Finally, brothers and sisters: true revival does not begin with a crowd; it begins with one heart. We often think revival needs a great crowd, but God often needs only one person. When one person is changed by Jesus, they will influence another; when a group of people is changed by Jesus, a whole generation will be turned around. From one Peter to three thousand, from one Wesley to the whole of Britain. God has never lacked resources; God is looking for vessels. So this morning I want to issue three calls to you. First, let Jesus be King: hand that seat you have been clinging to back to the Lord. Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. Third, begin with me — stop waiting for others to change first. Revival is letting people see — Jesus living in us.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you that this morning you have used your word to correct our mindset about revival. We confess that in the past we often took excitement for revival, and being moved for being changed. Lord, forgive us. Make us truly come alive; you are the way, the truth and the life, and apart from you we have nowhere to go. Turn us from the self-centred life to selflessness, from living out ourselves to living out Christ. Lord, we hand our seat back to you; reign as King in our homes, reign as King in our church. Make us people who have been changed, and people through whom others see Jesus. May all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless you and keep you until the day we see him face to face.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Seed That Slept for Two Thousand Years
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to ask you first to come back with me to the wilderness of Judea.

On the western shore of the Dead Sea stands a mountain fortress built by King Herod, which later became the Jews’ last stronghold. It is called Masada. In the 1960s an archaeological team digging in its ruins unearthed a batch of Judean date palm seeds. Carbon-14 dating showed that the seeds came from somewhere between the first century BC and the first century AD. For nearly two thousand years they had lain quietly in the dry cracks of the rock.

In 2005 an Israeli research team did something bold: they took a few of those seeds, soaked them, fertilised them and planted them in soil. Eight weeks later, one of them actually sprouted. The team named the little tree “Methuselah”, after the man in the Bible who lived to the age of nine hundred and sixty-nine. The research was later published in the journal Science in 2008 (Sallon et al., 2008).

Brothers and sisters, think about it: for two thousand years that seed had always been a real seed. Inside it was the complete code of life, the full potential to sprout. It had “existed” for two thousand years — but it had not “lived out” those two thousand years.

Only when someone placed it in the soil and gave it water, light and warmth did that sleeping life truly unfold.

This morning I want to set this question gently in your heart and mine: you have received the life of Jesus — has that life sprouted?

Salvation Is Not the Finish Line but the Starting Line

Many Christians think that once they are “saved”, it’s all done. They raise a hand to make a decision, get baptised, have their name written in the book of life — and then what? Then they stop right there. Year after year we attend meetings, year after year we sing the same songs, yet year after year we don’t grow. We treat salvation as the final station, when in fact salvation is the starting line.

In God’s heart, receiving life is only the beginning, not the end.

Just as the purpose of an egg is not to exist but to hatch; the purpose of a seed is not to stay buried but to grow; the purpose of a baby is not to be born but to grow up.

No mother says on the day her child is born, “Right, job done, I can clock off now.” At the moment of birth, what fills a mother’s heart is this: next I’ll feed him, hold him, teach him to walk, walk with him as he grows. Birth is not a full stop; birth is the beginning of a whole new journey.

In the same way, we have received the life of Jesus in order to live out the life of Jesus.

In the vision of Kingdom 321 we often say: life first, then relationships, then ministry. But notice: “life first” does not mean “life only”. Life is the foundation, not the destination; life is there to be lived out, to grow, to bear fruit and to multiply. A seed kept in a glass jar for people to admire, however genuine it is, is only a specimen, not a harvest.

The Lord Jesus once said: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) Notice, he says “it remains by itself alone”. A grain of wheat doesn’t turn into two grains because it’s been kept a long time. If life is not lived out, it stays “one grain” for ever.

In today’s lesson we will look together at four things: the purpose of life is to live out Christ; the process of life is moving from receiving to growing; the key to life is cultivating, not waiting; the mission of life is to multiply life.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Secret of the Word “Perfect”
sections.html:
The theme verse of this lesson is Matthew 5:48. To understand this verse rightly, we must first understand its context.

The Gospel of Matthew was written by Matthew, also called Levi, who had been a tax collector in Capernaum — a traitor in the eyes of his fellow Jews. The Lord Jesus walked past the tax booth and said just two words to him: “Follow me.” (Matthew 9:9) And he got up and followed him. A man society had written off as “beyond saving” became the author of a Gospel — and that in itself is the best footnote to this lesson: once life has been received, it is meant to be lived out.

Most evangelical scholars believe Matthew was written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish Christians scattered in many places. That also explains why the book quotes the Old Testament so heavily, showing again and again that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament.

Matthew chapters 5 to 7 contain the most famous sermon in the history of the church — the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus went up the mountain, his disciples came to him, and he opened his mouth and taught them. This sermon is not a moral lecture for unbelievers; it is the charter of life for the citizens of the kingdom of heaven.

And Matthew 5:48 is the conclusion of the six “antitheses” that run through chapter 5. Six times Jesus says, “You have heard that it was said … But I tell you …” (Matthew 5:21, 27, 31, 33, 38, 43). He is not abolishing the law; he is bringing the law back from outward behaviour to the inner life.

The last antithesis is about loving our enemies: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.” (Matthew 5:43–45) Then verse 48 rings out like the stroke of a bell: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.”

The Meaning of the Greek Word for “Perfect”

The word “perfect” here is the Greek teleios (τέλειος), whose root is telos (τέλος), meaning “purpose, end, goal, the target to be reached”.

So the basic meaning of teleios is not the moral perfectionism of “zero defects, without blemish” that the word so easily suggests to us. Its core meaning is: having reached the purpose for which it was made, having grown into what it ought to be — mature, complete, fully there.

A fruit that is teleios is not one without a single spot on its skin; it is one that is ripe and ready to eat. A person who is teleios is not someone who will never be weak again; it is someone who has grown into what God made him to become.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The word the Lord Jesus uses in this verse has “purpose” at its root. That is exactly the theme of this lesson: the purpose of receiving life. God gave you life with a telos — with a purpose, with a goal. He wants you to grow into the likeness of his Son.

Paul states this very clearly: “For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.” (Romans 8:29) The purpose of predestination is not merely to get you into heaven, but for you to be “conformed to the image of his Son”.

The background of this lesson’s other three passages also needs a brief word. Genesis 1:28 is the first blessing God spoke after creating humankind, and also the first commission humanity received; the setting is the Garden of Eden. Acts 1:8 is the last thing the Lord Jesus said to his disciples before his ascension, written by Luke to an official named Theophilus. 1 Corinthians 11:1 is what Paul wrote from Ephesus to the church in Corinth around AD 55; the preceding passage is about how a mature believer lays down his own rights for the good of others.

Four passages, one thread: God gives you life so that you will grow into the likeness of Christ, live it out, and pass it on.

sections.heading: 1. The Purpose of Life: Living Out Christ
sections.html:
“Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)

We Receive Life Not to Possess It but to Live It Out

The Bible speaks of “receiving life” in the most decisive terms: “He who has the Son has the life. He who doesn’t have God’s Son doesn’t have the life.” (1 John 5:12) When it comes to being saved, there is no middle ground: either you have it or you don’t.

But when the Bible speaks of “living out life”, it uses a different tone. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Notice the difference between these two statements. 1 John speaks of “having” — ownership; Galatians speaks of “living” — experience. The first is our standing; the second is our condition. The first is what God has already accomplished in me; the second is what God wants to bring about in me every day.

Paul has an even shorter, weightier saying: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” (Philippians 1:21) “To live is Christ” — not “I live for Christ”, but “to live is Christ”. Christ was not only the one he served; Christ had become the very content of his life.

So we receive life not to “possess” it but to “live it out”; it is not only “believing in Jesus”, but “living out Jesus”.

John puts it even more directly: “he who says he remains in him ought himself also to walk just like he walked.” (1 John 2:6)

The Danger of Stopping Halfway

Many people stop right here: received life — tick; lived out life — cross.

What happens to such a life? The lesson uses a vivid and rather piercing comparison: an egg that isn’t hatched goes rotten, and a baby that doesn’t grow cannot survive.

Let’s look at a little natural science. A fertilised hen’s egg kept at around 37.5 degrees Celsius with the right humidity will produce a chick breaking out of its shell in about twenty-one days. But the very same egg, if it is neither incubated nor refrigerated, just left on a table at room temperature, will have its proteins broken down by bacteria, producing hydrogen sulphide and other gases — the pungent smell of a rotten egg.

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: the same egg, hatched, becomes life; not hatched, it becomes a stench. There is no third way. An egg doesn’t automatically get better because you leave it a bit longer.

The saddest sight in the church is not someone falling, but someone just sitting there, “neither foul nor fragrant”. Twenty years a believer, and still the same temper, the same face, the same scheming as twenty years ago. It isn’t that there is no life; it’s that the life has never been hatched.

The Lord Jesus said: “Therefore by their fruits you will know them.” (Matthew 7:20) James said: “Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.” (James 2:17) These words do not tell us we are saved by works; they remind us that real life will always show itself, just as a living seed will always sprout.

The “Why” Deep in the Human Heart

Psychology offers an interesting piece of side evidence here. Viktor Frankl was an Austrian psychiatrist, a survivor of the Nazi concentration camps and the founder of logotherapy. In his book Man’s Search for Meaning he set out a central observation: humanity’s deepest drive is not the pursuit of pleasure or of power, but the search for meaning in life; anyone who knows “why” they live can bear almost any “how”.

In the camps Frankl saw that those who collapsed first were often not the physically weakest, but those who had first lost their purpose inwardly. Once a person feels their existence has no purpose, life withers fast.

The Bible said this thousands of years before psychology did. God made humankind with a purpose; there is a place in the human heart that no one but God can fill. Augustine put it superbly in the prayer that opens his Confessions, quoted down the ages: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.

Brothers and sisters, if you find that since becoming a believer the days feel dull, meetings feel like routine and prayer feels like ticking a box, the problem is often not that you aren’t busy enough, but that you have forgotten why you live. Once the purpose of life grows blurred, the warmth of life will always drop.

Applying the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness

The core message of Kingdom 321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem.

Why do so many people receive life yet fail to live it out? The greatest obstacle is not circumstances, not gifts, not time — it is the “self” that has never been dealt with.

“It is no longer I who live” in Galatians 2:20 is the most precise definition of selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is not becoming an empty shell, a person with no thoughts and no feelings. Selflessness is “‘I’ no longer live, but Christ lives in me”. I make room by giving up my limited self, and the limitless Christ comes to live within — so selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless.

321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When our focus is right, the purpose of our life is right. Matthew 5:48 calls us to be “perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect” — a standard so high it would drive us to despair, unless you understand that it is not asking you to imitate, but to let the Perfect One live within you and live himself out through you.

The first of the Three Foundations says: Jesus is my role model. A role model is not an idol far out of reach; it is footprints we walk in day by day. The purpose of life is to let Jesus live his life again in me.

sections.heading: 2. The Process of Life: From Receiving to Growing
sections.html:
“as newborn babies, long for the pure milk of the Word, that with it you may grow” (1 Peter 2:2)

Life Is Not Completed in an Instant

The lesson puts it exactly: life is not completed in an instant; it is a process.

Receiving life is the beginning; cultivating life is the process; living out life is the result.

The Lord Jesus himself described this process through a farmer’s eyes: “For the earth bears fruit: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.” (Mark 4:28)

First the blade, then the ear, then the full grain. The growth of God’s kingdom within a person has an order and has stages; you can’t skip a grade. You can’t lose your temper with a freshly sprouted wheat seedling and say, “Why haven’t you produced an ear yet?” All you can do is give it time, water and light.

Many people misunderstand this: the moment you believe, you ought to be perfect. So they make demands of themselves and of others. When they see a brother or sister being weak, they shake their heads: “He’s been a believer so long — how can he still be like this?” When they see themselves fail, they lose heart: “Maybe I’m not really saved.”

But the truth of Scripture is this: we have “already begun to be like Jesus”, and we are “becoming more and more like Jesus”.

Three Tenses in Theology

Evangelical theology states this very clearly: salvation has three tenses.

First, salvation already accomplished — justification. This happens in an instant; it is a change of standing. “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

Second, salvation in progress — sanctification. This is a lifelong process; it is a change of life. “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” (2 Corinthians 3:18)

“From glory to glory” means, in the original, moving from one glory into another. It is the present continuous, not the perfect tense.

Third, salvation still to come — glorification. “Beloved, now we are children of God. It is not yet revealed what we will be; but we know that when he is revealed, we will be like him; for we will see him just as he is.” (1 John 3:2)

So, brothers and sisters, the fact that you are not yet perfect today is not proof of failure; it is proof of a process. But notice: a process is not marking time. A process has direction and progress. Paul said of the Galatian believers: “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). What he wanted was “Christ formed”, not Christ in name only.

Development Is a Lifelong Lesson

The psychologist Erik Erikson, in Childhood and Society, published in 1950, set out his theory of psychosocial development, dividing the human lifespan into eight stages, from trust versus mistrust in infancy all the way to integrity versus despair in old age. One of his most important contributions was to break the old idea that “personality is fixed in childhood”, showing that human development is lifelong, and that each stage has tasks that must be completed — what is not dealt with in one stage is carried into the next.

Spiritual life is the same. The writer to the Hebrews rebuked a group of long-time believers: “For everyone who lives on milk is not experienced in the word of righteousness, for he is a baby.” (Hebrews 5:13) Years of seniority are not maturity; sitting for a long time is not growing tall.

The theological benchmark is in Ephesians: “until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13). Notice the phrase: “the stature of the fullness of Christ”. What God expects of you is not that you’re a little better than the brother next to you, but that you attain the full stature of Christ.

C. S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity, gave a famous illustration: you are like a living house, and God comes in to rebuild it. At first you think he is just going to fix the leaking roof and stop up the draughty windows — the places you yourself knew needed repairing. But then he starts knocking down walls and shifting beams, and it hurts in ways you can’t make sense of. It turns out that the blueprint in his heart is a palace — because he intends to come and live in it himself.

Brothers and sisters, if lately you feel that the work God is doing in you is rather big and rather painful, perhaps it is precisely because his blueprint is bigger than you thought.

Applying the 321 Vision: The Fivefold Change

Kingdom 321 speaks of the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry.

This fivefold change is exactly an ordered path of growth. You can’t skip the mindset and go straight to changing ministry — that’s just busywork; nor can you skip life and go straight to changing relationships — that’s just socialising.

Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) “The renewing of your mind” is a change of mindset; and “transformed” in the original is the very same word as “transformed into the same image” in 2 Corinthians 3:18, and also the word used in the Gospels for Jesus’ transfiguration.

Once the mindset changes, life changes with it. This is what 321 stresses again and again: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. If you turn the order upside down — rushing into ministry first, then talking about relationships, and only thinking of life at the very end — the work will leave you exhausted and empty.

Growth takes time, and it also takes cultivation. Time, God will give; cultivation is something you and I must do. That brings us to the third key point.

sections.heading: 3. The Key to Life: Cultivating, Not Waiting
sections.html:
“Exercise yourself toward godliness. For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come.” (1 Timothy 4:7–8)

Spiritual Life Needs Feeding Too

The body needs nourishment, and spiritual life needs cultivating. That sounds obvious, yet in spiritual matters we often do things we would never do with our bodies.

No one says, “I ate last month, so I don’t need to eat this month.” Yet we easily say, “I read through the Bible last year.” No one says, “Since I gave birth to my child, he’ll grow up by himself.” Yet we easily say to our own spiritual life, “I’m saved anyway — God will take care of it.”

The lesson puts it exactly: it doesn’t grow naturally; it is deliberately cultivated.

The word “deliberately” is the key to this lesson.

Paul’s command to Timothy is: “Exercise yourself toward godliness.” (1 Timothy 4:7) “Exercise” in Greek is gymnazō (γυμνάζω), the very root of the English word “gymnasium”. In the Greco-Roman world it described athletes stripping off their outer garments and training, drenched in sweat, in the arena. It is a thoroughly unromantic word; it smells of sweat, repetition and discipline.

The letter to the Hebrews uses the same root: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” (Hebrews 5:14) “Exercised” is also gymnazō. Spiritual discernment is not something you get by praying once; it is “exercised” into you day after day.

The Tree by the Stream and the Tree in the Wilderness

The Bible has two famous trees that express this beautifully.

“but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night. He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.” (Psalm 1:2–3)

Jeremiah also says: “Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh. For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit.” (Jeremiah 17:7–8)

Notice that neither passage says this tree is more capable than other trees. Its only difference is where it stands — planted by the streams, its roots spread out by the river.

Brothers and sisters, spiritual growth is not a contest of who has the strongest willpower; it is about who is standing in the right place. Cultivating life, when it comes down to it, is one thing: placing yourself every day beside the channels of grace.

This explains the phenomenon the lesson points out: some people have been believers for many years yet haven’t changed; others have believed only a short while yet are very like Jesus. Where is the difference? The difference is whether life has been cultivated.

In my years as a pastor I have seen far too many contrasts like this. One sister, a believer for just a year, read the Bible for fifteen minutes every morning, wrote down one sentence, then did one thing in obedience to it. A year later her whole bearing had changed; even her husband, who had opposed her becoming a Christian, said, “That Jesus of yours seems to be real.” Another brother has been a believer for twenty years and has risen from deacon to co-worker, but if you ask him when he last wept over a verse of Scripture, he can’t tell you. The years don’t make people mature; practice does.

Deliberate Practice and the Science of Habit

Psychology offers two solid pieces of side evidence here.

The first is “deliberate practice”. In a study published in Psychological Review in 1993, the psychologist K. Anders Ericsson and his colleagues observed violin students at the Berlin music academy and found that the real dividing line between the top group and the next-best group was not talent, nor simply total hours, but the amount of “deliberate practice” they put in — the kind of practice that has a clear goal and immediate feedback, specifically targets weaknesses, and is not enjoyable. Malcolm Gladwell later popularised it as the “ten-thousand-hour rule”, but Ericsson himself disagreed with that simplification, insisting again and again that how you practise matters more than how many hours you practise.

Brothers and sisters, that is a portrait of spiritual practice. Not “how many years I have spent in church”, but “in which specific weakness the Lord is dealing with me every day”.

The second is habit formation. In a study published in the European Journal of Social Psychology in 2010, Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London followed ninety-six participants as they formed a new daily habit, and found that it took an average of sixty-six days for the behaviour to become automatic, with wide individual variation, anywhere from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days.

This figure gives us two comforts. First, forming a habit takes longer than we imagine, so wanting to give up on day five is normal — it is not spiritual failure. Second, habits really do form, as long as you don’t stop.

Not Striving to Be Better, but Letting Christ Live Out

Having come this far, we must be especially careful of one danger: misunderstanding “cultivating life” as “trying hard to become better by our own effort”.

Paul rebuked the Galatians sharply: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” (Galatians 3:3) Beginning in the Spirit, yet seeking completion in the flesh — this is the pit believers of every generation fall into most easily.

The Lord Jesus said: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Notice that the Lord does not tell the branches to “try hard to bear fruit”; he tells them to “remain in me”. The branch’s job is not production but connection. The fruit is a by-product of the connection.

So the lesson puts it exactly: not striving to “become better”, but letting Christ “be lived out”. When you focus on cultivating life, living out life will happen naturally.

This is what 321 means by: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. Proverbs says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) The wellspring of life flows out of the heart, not out of the brain.

Applying the 321 Vision: The 920 Practice

Kingdom 321 has a very practical exercise called 920.

Every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before every “2” we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life; and the result is the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions, the “9”.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Notice that the Bible says “fruit”, not “product”. A product is manufactured; fruit grows. You can’t grit your teeth and manufacture patience; you can only let the Holy Spirit grow patience in you.

And what culture dish does the Holy Spirit most often use? Your “2” — that difficult colleague, that family member who never appreciates anything, that brother who once hurt you. The 920 practice is this: before him, “I” no longer live.

So please decide one thing this very morning: identify one of your “2”s, and with that person practise the one fruit you most lack. Cultivating life never happens in a vacuum; it happens in relationships.

sections.heading: 4. The Mission of Life: Multiplying Life
sections.html:
“God blessed them. God said to them, ‘Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.’” (Genesis 1:28)

The Instinct of Life Is to Multiply

God’s heart is not only that you receive life, but that life multiplies.

Genesis 1:28 is the first blessing humanity received, and also the first commission. Notice that the very first words of this commission are “be fruitful, multiply”. The Hebrew is פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ (peru urevu), literally “bear fruit, increase”. The root of “bear fruit”, parah, is related to the word for “fruit”.

This is a law God has placed in every created life: whatever has life will multiply. Cells divide, seeds scatter, dandelion down rides the wind for kilometres. When a life stops multiplying, there are usually only two reasons: either it isn’t mature yet, or it is already sick.

Spiritual life is the same. A church that doesn’t bear children, a believer who never brings anyone along — this isn’t some heinous crime; it is that they haven’t yet grown up, or something somewhere is sick.

Before his ascension the Lord Jesus handed this commission to the church afresh: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” (Acts 1:8)

The Greek word for “witness” is martys (μάρτυς), which later became the English “martyr”. Why? Because the believers of the early church discovered that a true witness is not a matter of a few fine words but of proving it with your whole life. The weight of a witness has never lain in eloquence but in the cost.

Multiplying Life Is Not Giving but Making People Long

Here the lesson makes a very important correction, worth chewing over slowly.

What is multiplying life? It is not “I give life to others” — in fact, I have no life to give anyone; life is only in the Son of God.

Rather, it is “I live out life, and make people long for Jesus.”

This distinction is crucial. The first is called selling; the second is called witnessing. The first makes people weary; the second makes people hungry and thirsty.

When people see Jesus in you, they will long to receive this life.

The Lord Jesus said: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16) Notice, light doesn’t need to shout, “I am light!” Light only needs to shine, and the darkness naturally retreats.

He also said: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” (John 13:35) Know — not hear it, but recognise it. It is something seen.

Church history has a beautiful example. Acts 11:26 records: “The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.” The name “Christian” means, in the original, “those who belong to Christ, Christ’s followers”, and was very likely first given to them as a nickname by the Gentiles of Antioch. In other words, the name was not self-chosen by the disciples; outsiders saw it in them. They lived so much like Christ that a whole city had to invent a new word to describe them.

Brothers and sisters, what we need today is not Christians who talk better, but Christians who are more like Christ.

Be Imitators of Me, Even as I Also Am of Christ

Paul said something extremely bold: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1)

Some people find this saying proud. In fact it is exactly the opposite. Paul dared to say “imitate me” because he immediately added “even as I also am of Christ” — he is not the goal but a signpost. He is not asking people to look at him, but to follow his line of sight and see Christ.

This is the heart of spiritual parents. True spiritual elders don’t say, “You must listen to me,” but, “Follow me — I am walking towards Christ.”

The psychologist Albert Bandura, in his social learning theory, showed that people learn mainly not through lectures but through observation and imitation. In his famous 1961 “Bobo doll” experiment he found that children who had watched an adult attack an inflatable doll were markedly more likely than the control group to behave aggressively when later left with the doll themselves. This research laid the foundation of “observational learning”, and it reminds us of something sobering: for children, newcomers and seekers, seeing how we act is far more powerful than hearing what we say.

Our families don’t grow up listening to our sermons; they grow up watching how we live.

Paul handed this chain of life on to Timothy: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)

Count them: there are four generations in this verse — Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others. The gospel is not a one-generation affair; it is a matter of four generations, forty generations. This is the life of a disciple; this is how life carries on.

Applying the 321 Vision: The 235 Relationships

Kingdom 321 speaks of the 235 relationships, which are the most concrete pathway for multiplying life.

The “2” is a spiritual companion: find a brother or sister who is also pursuing selflessness, and support one another, remind one another and pray for one another. Ecclesiastes says that two are better than one.

The “3” is spiritual parents and spiritual children: you need spiritual parents, and you need to begin having spiritual children — like Paul with Timothy, like Barnabas with Saul.

The “5” is a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers” (Ephesians 4:11). God never wants lone rangers; he wants teams.

And the last of the eight stages of changing our mindset is precisely “Multiplication”. If a mindset stops with you, it isn’t finished yet; it must keep being passed on through you.

This is exactly 321’s Goal: establish God’s system. A system is not an organisation but a network of life; it is held up not by institutions but by people, one by one, who live out Christ and are connected together.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s set the four key points of this lesson within the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations correspond exactly to this lesson’s three needs. Jesus is my role model — this is the benchmark for living out life: Matthew 5:48 says to be perfect as the Father is perfect, and 1 Corinthians 11:1 says to imitate Christ. The Bible is my standard — this is the food for cultivating life: Peter says to long for the pure milk of the Word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — this is the power for growing life: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” (Galatians 5:25)

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. What does it mean to live out life? Living out life is letting Jesus truly reign as King in the person that I am — reigning over my time, money, emotions, tongue, family and workplace. What does it mean to multiply life? Multiplying life is letting Jesus receive more glory. The Lord said: “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples.” (John 15:8)

The Goal: establish God’s system. One person living out Christ is a witness; a group of people living out Christ is a system; a generation living out Christ is revival.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The obstacle to all four key points of this lesson is, in the end, one and the same: “self”. The self-centred life treats salvation as part of its own collection; selflessness lives out salvation as a display of Christ.

Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Paul says: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:5–7) “Emptied himself” is selflessness; the Lord himself is the role model of selflessness.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The four key points of this lesson walk exactly this path: receiving life and living out Christ is life; bearing fruit in the 920 practice is relationships; multiplying life and building the 235 is ministry. The order cannot be reversed; people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The first thing this lesson sets out to change is one mindset — salvation is not the finish line but the starting point. If that one mindset changes, your life will change, your daily routine will change, your family relationships will change, and in the end your service will change too.

The shift in perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. From man’s perspective, believing in the Lord is for peace and smooth sailing; from God’s perspective, believing in the Lord is for growing into the stature of Christ. From a temporary perspective, whether or not I read the Bible today makes little difference; from an eternal perspective, each day’s cultivation is sculpting the self that will one day see the Lord face to face.

The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. First let the Holy Spirit guide (Spirit), then let the Bible open your eyes (Understanding), then life is shaped (Life), and only then do you enter service (Service), with the glory going to God in the end (God). Many people skip the first three steps and go straight to “Service”, and end up serving themselves dry. This lesson reminds us to return to the order.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take each one deeper, one by one.

Practice 1: Examine your life — am I “receiving life”, or “living life”?

The lesson says: ask yourself every day, did I live out Jesus today?

Information: First know the truth. Today’s lesson is the information — receiving life is only the beginning; living out life is the purpose. Copy Matthew 5:48 onto a small card.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to turn this information into personal light for you. Pray: “Lord, show me which part of my life I have received but not lived out.”

Conviction: Not just knowing, but truly yielding in your heart. Admit before God: in the past I treated salvation as an insurance policy, not as life.

Implementation: From today, spend three minutes each night before sleep asking three questions. In what did I live out Jesus today? In what did I live out myself today? In what will I entrust myself to him afresh tomorrow?

Evaluation: Every Saturday evening, leaf through the record of the past seven days and see what keeps recurring.

Correction: For the weakness that keeps recurring, ask the Lord for a verse to be your standard for the coming week.

Repetition: Don’t give up because you forgot on day three. Lally’s research tells us that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a habit to become automatic. If you forget, start again — don’t condemn yourself all over again.

Multiplication: After a month, teach this practice to another brother or sister.

Practice 2: Deliberately cultivate habits of life

The lesson says: establish a steady life of prayer, Bible reading and obedience to the Holy Spirit, so that your life is fed.

Information: Spiritual life doesn’t grow naturally; it only grows deliberately. 1 Timothy 4:7 says “Exercise yourself toward godliness” — and that is the word for an athlete’s sweat.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to show you which root in your life is most short of water. Is it prayer? Bible reading? Or obedience?

Conviction: Admit a fact — in the past it wasn’t that I had no time; it was that I hadn’t put it in my schedule.

Implementation: Set three small, concrete things you can sustain. First, a fixed time — for example, twenty minutes every morning. Second, fixed content — for example, reading one book of the Bible, a chapter at a time, copying out one verse. Third, a fixed response — after reading, write one sentence: “Today, the one thing I will do in obedience to this verse.”

Evaluation: Each week, check how many days you managed — just record it, don’t judge it.

Correction: If you only managed two days in a week, don’t raise the target — lower the threshold. Better ten minutes for seven days than a resolution of an hour kept for zero days.

Repetition: Let it become like brushing your teeth — something that needs no willpower.

Multiplication: Find a companion and report to each other once a week. That is the “2” in 235.

Practice 3: Become a witness — let people see Jesus in me

The lesson says: in the family, the church and the workplace, live out love, humility and obedience, and become a role model for others.

Information: Witness is not selling; it is living out. People are not argued into the kingdom of heaven; they are drawn into it.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to let you see that the hardest person to love near you is the very best practice ground God has given you.

Conviction: Honestly face the question — if they watched my life, would they want to know my Lord?

Implementation: This week, do one thing out of love in your family, one thing out of humility at church, and one thing out of obedience at work. And none of them needs explaining.

Evaluation: At the weekend ask yourself: how many of those three things did I do? As I did them, was my heart willing, or reluctant?

Correction: If it was reluctant, don’t stop doing them; go back to the Lord and ask him to renew your motives as well.

Repetition: Keep it going through the 920 practice. Every person you have a relationship with is your “2”; before them, live out selflessness.

Multiplication: When someone asks you, “How come you’re different from before?” — that is the door opening. At that moment, introduce Jesus to them.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, at the end the lesson gives us a short but powerful gentle reminder: life is not something to possess; it is something to live out.

Receiving life is grace; living out life is response.

Grace comes first; response follows. God never wants us to trade our response for his grace, but neither is he ever content for his grace to stop halfway in us.

When you begin to live out Jesus, your life will never be the same; when many people live out Jesus, revival truly comes.

Revival has never been a special meeting; revival is a group of people beginning to be truly like Jesus. The revival in Antioch began with a group of people who lived like Christ. Today’s revival must begin with you and me too.

So let us make this declaration of faith together: Lord, I don’t only want to receive your life; even more, I want to live out your life. Make me more like you day by day, and let people see you in me, so that I become a witness to life and a blessing.

Let us not only receive life, but live out life, and let life be multiplied.

Let Jesus reign as King within us; let Jesus receive all the glory through us.

That seed which slept for two thousand years sprouted within eight weeks once it went into the soil. Brothers and sisters, the life within you has never lacked power; it lacks only one decision: today, I will place myself in God’s hands.

keyVerses: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)
practices: Deliberately cultivate habits of life
Become a witness — let people see Jesus in me
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.
Thank you for giving us your own life — a grace we can never repay.

Lord, forgive us. We have often treated salvation as a collector’s item, put away in a drawer, without letting it be lived out in us. We have life, yet we have not lived out life; we have your name, yet not your likeness.
Lord, we ask you to work in us yourself today. Deal with the “self” within us, so that we can truly say: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
Give us a longing heart, to place ourselves every day before your word and your Spirit — to be fed by you, cultivated by you, pruned by you.
And make our lives a blessing to others, so that our families, colleagues and friends see you in us, and so long for you, seek you and receive you.
Lord, we place ourselves in your hands. Reign as King within us; may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48) The original word for “perfect”, teleios, means “having reached the purpose for which one was made; mature”. Think honestly: which area of your life have you “already received, but not yet lived out”? With what specific small thing will you begin to let it be hatched?

Question 2: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1) If someone were watching your life right now, which side of Christ would they be most likely to see in you? And which side of you would be most likely to make them stumble? Name one person you are willing to begin walking alongside with your life, and pray for them.

blog.title: The Seed That Slept for Two Thousand Years

blocks.x: Salvation Is Not the Finish Line but the Starting Line

In the ruins of the ancient fortress of Masada on the western shore of the Dead Sea, archaeologists unearthed a batch of Judean date palm seeds. Carbon-14 dating showed that they came from somewhere between the first century BC and the first century AD — in other words, they had lain quietly in the dry cracks of the rock for nearly two thousand years.

In 2005 an Israeli research team did something bold: they took one of them, soaked it, fertilised it and planted it in soil. Eight weeks later, it sprouted. The team named the little tree “Methuselah”. The research was published in the journal Science in 2008.

Think about it: for two thousand years that seed had always been a real seed. Inside it was the complete code of life, the full potential to sprout. It had “existed” for two thousand years — but it had not “lived out” those two thousand years.
1. The Purpose of an Egg Is Not to Exist but to Hatch

Many Christians think that once they are “saved”, it’s all done. They make a decision, get baptised, have their name written in the book of life — and then they stop right there. We treat salvation as the final station, when in fact salvation is the starting line.

The purpose of an egg is not to exist but to hatch; the purpose of a seed is not to stay buried but to grow; the purpose of a baby is not to be born but to grow up. No mother says on the day her child is born, “Right, job done.”
The Lord Jesus’ words in our theme verse are beautiful: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)

The word “perfect” here is the Greek teleios, whose root is telos, meaning “purpose, goal”. So being perfect is not the perfectionism of zero defects; it is maturity — growing into what we were made to be.
2. It Doesn’t Grow Naturally; It Is Deliberately Cultivated
Why do some people stay unchanged after many years as believers, while others, believers only a short while, are very like Jesus? There is only one difference: whether life has been cultivated.

The body needs nourishment, and spiritual life needs cultivating. Paul said to Timothy, “Exercise yourself toward godliness.” (1 Timothy 4:7) The original word for “exercise” is gymnazō, the root of the word “gymnasium”, describing athletes training in the arena drenched in sweat. It is a word that smells of sweat, repetition and discipline.

Psychological research nods along from the side. In 2010 Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London followed ninety-six participants and found that it took an average of sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become automatic.
This figure gives us two comforts: first, wanting to give up on day five is normal — it is not spiritual failure; second, as long as you don’t stop, change will certainly come.

But beware of one danger: cultivating is not trying hard to become better by our own effort. The Psalm says the blessed person is like a tree planted by the streams of water. The Bible doesn’t say this tree is more capable than other trees, only that it stands in the right place. Spiritual growth is not a contest of who has the strongest willpower; it is about who is standing in the right place.
3. The Purpose of Life Is to Multiply
The first blessing God spoke to humanity, and also the first commission, was “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28). Whatever has life will multiply.

But notice: multiplying life is not “I give life to others” — I have no life to give anyone. Multiplying life is “I live out life, and make people long for Jesus.” The first is called selling; the second is called witnessing. The first makes people weary; the second makes people hungry and thirsty.

Acts records: “The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.” (Acts 11:26) The name “Christian” was very likely first given to them as a nickname by the Gentiles of the city — they lived so much like Christ that a whole city had to invent a new word to describe them.
What we need today is not Christians who talk better, but Christians who are more like Christ.
Receiving life is grace; living out life is response.
When you begin to live out Jesus, your life will never be the same; when many people live out Jesus, revival truly comes.
That seed which slept for two thousand years sprouted within eight weeks once it went into the soil. The life within you has never lacked power; it lacks only one decision.
Reflection Question
Which area of your life is one you have “already received but not yet lived out”? What specific small thing will you start with, so that it can be hatched?
