script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 116 of Morning Devotion 321. Our title is “Nurturing Life”, and our subtitle is “The growth of life lies in nurturing life”. The Lord Jesus said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.” (John 4:34) May the Holy Spirit, this morning, plant that one word, “nurture”, in our hearts.

Brothers and sisters, picture this. In a nursery lie babies only a few days old, who can do nothing at all. Thirty years later, one has become a doctor, another a mother, another a preacher. What happened in between? In between lie more than ten thousand days of feeding. No child in the world grows up naturally. We long to receive life, and we long to live it out, yet we often overlook the most crucial step — nurturing life. Without nurture, there is no growth; without growth, there is no living it out. A baby who is not fed cannot grow; a sapling that is not tended cannot bear fruit. Spiritual life is just the same.

Today’s theme verse comes from John chapter 4. The Lord Jesus, weary from the journey, sat down by Jacob’s well outside the town of Sychar. A Samaritan woman came to draw water; her life was renewed, and she left her water jar and ran back into the town. The disciples came back with food and urged the Lord to eat. The Lord Jesus said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.” (John 4:34) In the disciples’ hands was bread; on the Lord Jesus’ lips was the will of God.

The first point: the key to growth in life is not demands but nurture. Brothers and sisters, many people think that living out life depends on effort, and that becoming like Jesus depends on willpower. And the result? The harder they try, the more it hurts; the more they strive, the more they fail. There is only one reason: they have overlooked nurturing life. If we only demand results without the process of nurture, life will wither. But brothers and sisters, when you begin to nurture life, growth becomes natural, change becomes easy, and living it out becomes joy.

The Lord Jesus said, “For the earth bears fruit: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.” (Mark 4:28) The farmer sows, sleeps, rises and waits; the one thing he does not do is pull the shoots up taller. Mencius records a man from the state of Song who thought his rice shoots were growing too slowly and pulled each one up a little higher — and every shoot withered. Brothers and sisters, have we done too little of that kind of shoot-pulling in our spiritual lives? Paul says, “But God gave the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:6) It is not forcing ourselves to change, but letting life grow.

The second point: the environment of life is the spiritual family. Paul says, “God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.” (1 Timothy 3:15) The original word for “house” means “a household”, not a building. Fish need water, seeds need soil, babies need a family; spiritual life needs the church. Life cannot grow on its own; it must have an environment. Spiritual life needs spiritual parents, spiritual companions and a spiritual community.

How did Paul shepherd the church? He said, “But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.” (1 Thessalonians 2:7) He gave not only the gospel but his own life. Brothers and sisters, leave the spiritual family, and life stops growing. And it isn’t only about being shepherded; we must also learn to shepherd others. The Lord said to Peter, “Feed my lambs.” (John 21:15) Educational psychology has found the “protégé effect”: people who learn in order to teach others learn more deeply. Those who feed others are fed first themselves.

The third point: the food of life is doing God’s will. Many people think spiritual food is reading the Bible, prayer and meeting together. These are very important, but they are not yet complete. Reading the Bible and praying put the food on the table; doing God’s will is eating it. If we only hear the word and do not do it, it is like eating without absorbing. James says, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) When the crowd asked what they must do to work the works of God, the Lord Jesus said, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.” (John 6:29) Doing God’s work is not doing tasks; it is believing in Jesus. The more we trust in Jesus, the more our life is fed.

The fourth point: the five steps for nurturing life — See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do. See means reading God’s word and letting the truth come in through your eyes; Listen means hearing God’s voice and letting the Holy Spirit speak to you; Think means meditating on God’s word and letting the truth enter your heart; Speak means declaring and sharing, letting the truth come out of your mouth; Do means living it out in practice and letting the truth become life. Brothers and sisters, only “doing” is true feeding. The more times these five steps go round, the faster life grows. Psychologists have long found that what we repeatedly retrieve and say out loud is remembered more firmly than what we repeatedly read. God’s word is the same: what you have read you may forget; what you have spoken is hard to forget; what you have done becomes life.

Today we have three practices. First, establish a daily rhythm of nurturing life: read the Bible, pray and meditate at a set time. Second, deliberately practise doing the word: today, choose at least one thing God has moved you to do and carry it out — don’t stop at knowing. Third, enter into spiritual relationships: connect with a spiritual companion and with spiritual parents, and at the same time begin caring for and shepherding others. Research shows that a new habit takes on average sixty-six days to become automatic, so don’t pronounce yourself a failure on day five. Please remember this sentence: life does not grow up naturally; it grows up by being nurtured.

Brothers and sisters, the lesson’s closing words say: the change of a life is not a miracle of a moment, but a nurture that continues. God never does instant; God nurtures. He took forty years to nurture one Moses, and three and a half years to nurture twelve disciples. No apple tree has to grit its teeth to produce apples; as long as it is joined to its roots, the fruit comes. When you begin to nurture life, you will discover: living out Jesus is no longer hard, and being a blessing becomes natural. For a life that is truly growing will naturally live out Christ. May we be not Christians who try harder, but Christians who are better fed. None of the growth belongs to us; all the glory goes to Jesus.

Let us declare together: Lord, I am willing to nurture the life you have given me — not stopping at receiving it, but being continually fed and renewed. Let me see, listen, think, speak and do your word every day, so that your life in me keeps on growing. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Yahweh bless you, and keep you.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 116 of Morning Devotion 321. Our title is “Nurturing Life”, and our subtitle is “The growth of life lies in nurturing life”. Our theme verse is something the Lord Jesus said himself: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.” (John 4:34) This morning we will look at four things together: the key to growth in life, the environment of life, the food of life, and the five steps for nurturing life. May the Holy Spirit plant that one word, “nurture”, deep in our hearts.

Brothers and sisters, first picture something with me. In a hospital nursery there is a row of little cots, and in them lie babies only a few days old. They can do nothing at all — they cannot walk, they cannot talk, they cannot feed themselves. Thirty years later, one of them has become a doctor, another a teacher, another a mother, another a preacher. What happened in between? Not one baby grew up by waking up one morning. In between there were more than ten thousand days: a mother getting up in the middle of the night to feed, a father’s hand steadying the baby walker. We often say children just grow up naturally, but in fact no child in the world grows up naturally.

The twentieth century left us a heartbreaking testimony. In Romania’s orphanages, thousands of babies had beds, blankets and food, but no one held them and no one talked to them. Later, the Bucharest Early Intervention Project, led by the American researchers Nelson, Zeanah and Fox, followed them over many years and found that children who were merely kept alive lagged markedly behind in language, cognition and emotional development, while those placed in foster families, with someone caring for them one to one, improved markedly. Brothers and sisters, this states a piercing truth: merely being alive is not the same as growing up. We long to receive life, and we long to live it out, yet we overlook the most crucial step in between — nurturing life. Without nurture, there is no growth; without growth, there is no living it out.

Our theme verse comes from John chapter 4. John’s Gospel was written around AD 80 to 90, and its theme is “life”. That day the Lord Jesus was going from Judea to Galilee, and he needed to pass through Samaria. Weary from the journey, he sat down by Jacob’s well outside the town of Sychar; it was about noon. A Samaritan woman came to draw water, and the Lord Jesus talked with her, from a bucket of water to living water, and at last revealed to her that he himself was the Christ. The woman left her water jar and ran back into the town to tell everyone. The disciples came back with food and urged the Lord Jesus to eat. But he said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.” In the disciples’ hands was bread; on the Lord Jesus’ lips was the will of God.

The first point: the key to growth in life is not demands but nurture. Brothers and sisters, many people think that “living out life” depends on effort, and that “becoming like Jesus” depends on willpower. So they grit their teeth, draw up plans and make vows: I will not lose my temper; I will read the Bible every day. And the result? The lesson is very honest: the harder they try, the more it hurts; the more they strive, the more they fail. Why? There is only one reason — they have overlooked nurturing life. If we only demand results without the process of nurture, life will wither.

The Lord Jesus told a parable we often overlook: “God’s Kingdom is as if a man should cast seed on the earth, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should spring up and grow, though he doesn’t know how. For the earth bears fruit.” (Mark 4:26–28) The farmer sows, sleeps, rises and waits; the one thing he does not do is pull the shoots up taller. Mencius records a man from the state of Song who thought his rice shoots were growing too slowly, pulled each one up a little higher, and went home very pleased with himself; his son ran out to the field, and every shoot had withered. That is “pulling up shoots to help them grow”. The “Biosphere 2” experiment of the last century is fascinating too: the trees inside the glass dome grew fast and tall, but one after another they fell before reaching maturity — because there was no wind inside. A tree without wind has height but no resilience.

But the lesson then gives a beautiful promise: when you begin to nurture life, growth becomes natural, change becomes easy, and living it out becomes joy. Paul says, “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it.” (Philippians 1:6) And again, “But God gave the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:6) The Lord Jesus said, “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit.” (John 15:5) A branch never bears fruit because the branch strains; it bears fruit because it is joined to the vine. Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what 321 reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Trying to become better by our own effort is in fact just another face of the old self’s self-centred life.

The second point: the environment of life is the spiritual family. Paul said to Timothy, “God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.” (1 Timothy 3:15) At the time Timothy was in the church at Ephesus, facing the troubles stirred up by false teachers. Paul told him how to behave in God’s house. Notice that the word Paul uses is “house”, which in the original means “a household”, not a building. Fish need water, seeds need soil, babies need a family; spiritual life needs the church. Life cannot grow on its own; it must have an environment.

How did Paul shepherd the church? He said, “But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children. Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls.” (1 Thessalonians 2:7–8) Brothers and sisters, notice that Paul gave two things: the gospel, and his own life. True nurture is not merely passing on information; it is handing over a life. He also said, “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you.” (Galatians 4:19) Today many people receive a great deal of information yet are seldom truly accompanied by anyone, so their knowledge has grown while their life stays where it was.

The lesson says: not only being shepherded, but also learning to shepherd others; in the process of feeding others, your own life will grow faster. The risen Lord said to Peter on the shore, “Feed my lambs.” (John 21:15) Educational psychology has a phenomenon called the “protégé effect”: when students learn in order to teach someone else, they put in more effort and learn more deeply than when they learn to pass their own exam. The Bible said it long ago: “He who waters shall be watered also himself.” (Proverbs 11:25) This is exactly 321’s “235 relationships”: becoming a “2”, spiritual companions, with someone selfless; establishing a “3”, spiritual parents and children; and becoming a “5”, a team of spiritual comrades in the fivefold ministry.

The third point: the food of life is doing God’s will. If you ask what spiritual food is, most people will say: reading the Bible, prayer, meeting together. The lesson says: these are very important, but they are not yet complete. Reading the Bible, praying and meeting together put the food on the table; doing God’s will is actually eating it. The Lord Jesus did not say, “My food is to study the will of God, to discuss the will of God, to pray about the will of God”; what he said was “to do”. The original word for “food” means real food that goes into the mouth and sustains life — not a snack, not a nibble.

In medicine there is a condition called malabsorption. It’s not that the patient doesn’t eat — he may eat more than anyone — but his gut cannot absorb it, so he grows weaker day by day. Brothers and sisters, spiritual malabsorption is not rare in the church. Some people hear a hundred sermons a year and fill notebook after notebook, yet their lives make no progress at all. The lesson puts it vividly: if we only hear the word and do not do it, it is like eating without absorbing. James says, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) Psychology also tells us honestly: even when people’s intentions are successfully raised, the change in actual behaviour is limited. Between “I really want to” and “I go and do it” lies a gulf that is all too real.

But here we must be careful, so that we don’t hear “doing God’s will” as “doing twice as many tasks”. The crowd asked the Lord Jesus, “What must we do, that we may work the works of God?” The Lord Jesus answered, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.” (John 6:29) Brothers and sisters, the crowd asked “what to do”; the Lord Jesus answered “whom to believe”. They wanted a job list; the Lord Jesus gave them a person. So doing God’s work is not doing tasks; it is believing in Jesus. The more we trust in Jesus, the more our life is fed. This is the first of 321’s Two Core Values: let Jesus be King. When I let Jesus be King, my perspective shifts from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal.

The fourth point: the five steps for nurturing life — See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do. Step one, See: read God’s word, and let the truth come in through your eyes. The psalmist says, “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.” (Psalm 119:18) Research has found that when people know information can be looked up at any time, they remember the content itself less well. Brothers and sisters, we know where to find God’s word, but we have not let God’s word dwell in us. Step two, Listen: hear God’s voice. The Lord Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice.” (John 10:27) The boy Samuel said, “Speak; for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:10) Listening can be learned.

Step three, Think: meditate on God’s word, and let the truth enter your heart. “But his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.” (Psalm 1:2) The Hebrew word for “meditate” is also used for the low moaning of a dove and the low growl of a lion — to meditate is to murmur and chew over God’s word again and again in your heart. Ebbinghaus’s forgetting curve tells us that material we don’t review is quickly lost, and spaced review is far more effective than cramming everything in at once. Meditation is spiritual spaced review. Step four, Speak: let the truth come out of your mouth. Paul says, “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” (2 Corinthians 4:13) A passage you have read, you may forget; a passage you have spoken out even once, you will find hard to forget.

Step five, Do: let the truth become life. The Lord Jesus said, “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17) The lesson says: only “doing” is true feeding. Research shows that for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit takes on average sixty-six days — eighteen days for some, two hundred and fifty-four for others. So, first, don’t imagine you can change yourself in three days; and second, don’t imagine you can never change. Doing the word leads to new seeing, new listening, new thinking, new speaking. The lesson says: the more times these five steps go round, the faster life grows.

Today’s first practice: establish a daily rhythm of nurturing life. Settle the time, the place and the reading plan, and read the Bible, pray and meditate at a set time every day. Ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes so that one verse leaps out; copy it out, carry it into today’s schedule, and spend three minutes looking back in the evening. If you can’t get up, move the time later; if you can’t finish the reading, cut it down. Only a plan you can keep up is a good plan. The second practice: deliberately practise doing the word. Today, choose at least one thing God has moved you to do and carry it out; shrink it until it is too small to fail — make a phone call, say a word of apology, send a message of greeting, make an offering. Do it today; don’t leave it until tomorrow.

The third practice: enter into spiritual relationships. Connect with a spiritual companion and with spiritual parents, and at the same time begin caring for and shepherding others. The Bible says, “Two are better than one.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9) The coast redwoods of California can grow to nearly a hundred metres, yet their roots are not deep. How do they stay standing? Because the roots of one redwood interlace with the roots of the redwoods beside it. When the wind comes, it is not one tree bearing the load; it is the whole forest. The Harvard Study of Adult Development, running since 1938, has also found that what makes people healthier and happier is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

Brothers and sisters, let’s put today’s four points back into the framework of 321. Seeing and thinking let the Bible be my standard; listening lets the Holy Spirit be my guide; doing lets Jesus be my role model. Doing God’s will is letting Jesus be King; when life grows and bears fruit, all the glory goes to Jesus. The old self, self-centred, wants to complete even its own sanctification; the new self, selfless, lets God be God in everything. Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; and change is fivefold — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Once the mindset changes, life begins to change.

The lesson’s closing words say: the change of a life is not a miracle of a moment, but a nurture that continues. One of the greatest temptations of our generation is wanting things instant. But God never does instant; God nurtures. He took four hundred years to nurture a nation, forty years to nurture one Moses, three and a half years to nurture twelve disciples. When you begin to nurture life, you will discover: living out Jesus is no longer hard, and being a blessing becomes natural. Why? Because a life that is truly growing will naturally live out Christ. No apple tree has to grit its teeth to produce apples.

So this morning I want to extend three invitations to you, brothers and sisters: come back to nurture, come back to the spiritual family, come back to the real food. Let us declare together: Lord, I am willing to nurture the life you have given me — not stopping at receiving it, but being continually fed and renewed. Let me see, listen, think, speak and do your word every day, so that your life in me keeps on growing. Lord, may your will be our daily food, until Christ is formed in us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Yahweh bless you, and keep you.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Why Do We Know So Much, Yet Fail to Live It Out?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I want to begin by asking you to be still for thirty seconds and answer one question honestly.

How long have you believed in the Lord? Three years? Ten years? Thirty years? In all that time, how many chapters of the Bible have you read? How many sermons have you heard? How many revival meetings, special conferences and discipleship trainings have you attended? How many recorded sermons are saved on your phone? How many memory verses are copied into your notebook?

Then please answer a second question just as honestly: over these years, how much has your life really changed because of all this?

I once met a brother whose Bible had been thumbed so much that the pages were coming loose, and whose flyleaf was crammed with notes. He could recite whole chapters of Romans, rattle off the theme of every book of the Pentateuch, and explain the features of the seven churches of Revelation with complete fluency. But his wife said to me with red eyes, “Pastor, at church he’s the Bible expert, but at home he doesn’t have one gentle word for me.”

I also met a sister who had been to more than thirty special conferences, and every time she wept in repentance and raised her hand to make a commitment. Yet after more than thirty of them she was still bound by the same bitterness, still unwilling to forgive the person who had hurt her twenty years before. She asked me, “Why, after hearing so many sermons, is my life still the same?”

Brothers and sisters, this is not just the problem of these two people. It is the most common, and the most painful, problem in the church today:

Why do we know so much, yet fail to live it out? Why have we heard so many sermons, yet our lives have not grown?

We often think the problem is that “we haven’t received enough”. So we go and hear more sermons, read more books, attend more meetings, follow more speakers. We keep upping the dose, only to find our lives are like an engine idling — the accelerator pressed to the floor, yet the car stays where it is.

Today’s lesson tells us a truth that cuts deep yet sets us free: the problem is not that we “haven’t received”, but that — we have not gone through the complete process of “nurturing life”.

The growth of life follows a complete process that God has designed. This process has five links, and not one can be missing:

See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do.

Miss any one link and life gets stuck; go through all five and life flows. Today, let’s look together at this process of life that God has designed.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The Pillar and Ground of the Truth
sections.html:
Our theme passage today comes from 1 Timothy 3:15.

The writer, the recipient, the time of writing

The author of 1 Timothy is the apostle Paul. The recipient is Timothy — Paul’s spiritual son, a young man whose mother Eunice and grandmother Lois both had sincere faith (2 Timothy 1:5). After his third missionary journey and his release from his first Roman imprisonment, Paul wrote this letter some time between AD 62 and 64. Paul had left Timothy in Ephesus to deal with problems in the church: “As I urged you when I was going into Macedonia, stay at Ephesus that you might command certain men not to teach a different doctrine” (1 Timothy 1:3).

Ephesus was then the capital of the Roman province of Asia, with a population of about 250,000, one of the most important ports and religious centres in the eastern Mediterranean. In the city stood the Temple of Artemis, counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world and four times the size of the Parthenon in Athens. This city lacked neither religion, nor knowledge, nor philosophical debate — and it was precisely in such a city, one that “knew a bit about everything”, that Paul wrote to tell Timothy: the church is not a lecture hall; the church is God’s household.

The picture of “pillar and ground”

Paul says: “which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15).

“Pillar” in Greek is στῦλος (stylos), a stone column that holds up a roof; “ground” in Greek is ἑδραίωμα (hedraiōma), meaning a firm base, a support. Both are building terms, and both are “load-bearing” elements.

Notice which way this picture runs: it is not the truth holding up the church, but the church holding up the truth. The truth itself will not fall, but if the truth has no people who live it out to carry it, the world cannot see it. The job of a pillar is not to store the roof away, but to lift it up and hold it high, so that everyone in the city can see it.

So truth is not something to be stored away; it is meant to become the foundation of life. It is not something to be put on display; it is meant to be lived out and lifted up.

And let us not forget the very next verse: “Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great: God was revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16). The one the pillar holds up is Christ, “revealed in the flesh”. God did not merely write the truth down in a book and leave it at that; God lived the truth out as a person. This is the ultimate “doing” — the Word became flesh.

The context

What is the earlier part of 1 Timothy 3 about? It is about the qualifications of overseers and deacons. Read 3:1–13 and you will find something astonishing: Paul lists a dozen or more qualifications, and only one of them has to do with “whether he can speak” — “apt to teach”. All the rest test “can he live it out?”: without reproach, the husband of one wife, temperate, sensible, modest, hospitable, not a drinker, not violent, gentle, not quarrelsome, not covetous, one who rules his own house well.

In other words, when God chooses the pillars that carry the truth, he looks not at how much they know but at how much they live out. This is exactly the theme of today’s lesson.

We should also look at the other two theme passages. Matthew 5:48, “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect,” is the conclusion of the section of the Sermon on the Mount about loving your enemies — Jesus does not want us to “understand” being perfect but to “live out” being perfect. In Philippians 4:9, “The things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me: do these things,” Paul lists all four — learning, receiving, hearing, seeing — and then closes with one phrase: do these things.

Brothers and sisters, this is today’s message. See, Listen, Think, Speak — all of them point towards the same exit: Do.

sections.heading: 3. The Key to a Changed Life: The Complete Spiritual Cycle
sections.html:
Scripture

“which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.” (1 Timothy 3:15)

“Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words were to me a joy and the rejoicing of my heart, for I am called by your name, Yahweh, God of Armies.” (Jeremiah 15:16)

Life is changed not by “knowing” but by “being fed”

Brothers and sisters, think about this: how does a baby grow?

Not because he has studied nutrition, not because he has memorised the food pyramid, and not because he can name every vitamin. A baby grows for one reason only — he is fed, and he really swallows the milk, digests it and absorbs it.

Spiritual life is the same. Jeremiah puts it beautifully: “Your words were found, and I ate them” (Jeremiah 15:16). Notice that the verb he uses is not “read”, not “study”, but “eat”. When the Lord Jesus was tempted, he too quoted Deuteronomy: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth” (Matthew 4:4).

God’s word is food. Food set out on the table does not satisfy anyone; only food taken into the body satisfies.

Five links, three stages

See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do — these five actions actually form three stages:

The first stage is “taking in”: seeing and listening. This is bringing the food in.

The second stage is “digesting”: thinking and speaking. This is breaking the food down into nutrients the body can use.

The third stage is “absorbing”: doing. This is letting the nutrients truly enter the bloodstream and the bones and become part of you.

Let’s look at them one by one; for every link, the Bible has clear teaching.

“See” — John 5:19: “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.” Jesus’ own ministry began with “seeing”. Paul also says: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). What you look at, you become.

“Listen” — Luke 8:18: “Be careful therefore how you hear.” Notice the Lord did not say “be careful what you hear” but “be careful how you hear”. The Hebrew for “hear” is שָׁמַע (shāma‘), a word that carries both meanings, “to hear” and “to obey”. The Shema prayer, which Israelites recite every day, begins with this word: “Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). In Hebrew thinking, hearing without obeying is not “hearing” at all.

“Think” — Joshua 1:8: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it.” The Hebrew for “meditate” is הָגָה (hāgâ), whose basic meaning is “to murmur in a low voice, to mutter over and over”; the same word is used for the low growl in a lion’s throat as it holds its prey (Isaiah 31:4). Meditation is not zoning out with an empty mind; it is clamping on to God’s word the way a lion clamps on to its prey, turning it over and over until you have chewed the flavour out of it.

“Speak” — Romans 10:10: “For with the heart, one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation.” The Lord Jesus said: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34). Speaking squeezes out what is inside; only when you put a truth into words do you find out whether you have actually understood it.

“Do” — James 1:22: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”

Five links, one lifeline. Seeing and listening bring the truth in; thinking and speaking chew the truth up; doing sends the truth into the bloodstream.

Stop at the early links, and life becomes “malnourished”

There is a phenomenon in modern medicine that fits this remarkably well. The World Health Organization calls micronutrient deficiency “hidden hunger”. People suffering from it are not thin, nor are they hungry; they eat three meals a day and may even look well fed. But because their bodies lack key nutrients such as iron, iodine and vitamin A, their immunity is low, their development is delayed and their eyesight is damaged. Reports from the World Health Organization and UNICEF indicate that more than two billion people worldwide are affected by micronutrient deficiency.

Brothers and sisters, there is “hidden hunger” in the church too. Such believers never miss a meeting, never fall behind in giving, know the hymns and can recite the memory verses; they look “spiritually very well fed”. But because the truth has never gone the whole way into their lives, they fall down the moment trials come, turn bitter the moment someone offends them, and panic the moment they suffer loss. It isn’t that they haven’t eaten; it’s that they haven’t absorbed.

The writer of Hebrews diagnosed this disease long ago: “For although by this time you should be teachers, you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God. You have come to need milk, and not solid food” (Hebrews 5:12). Then he names the cause: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil” (Hebrews 5:14). “Exercised” in Greek is γυμνάζω (gymnazō), meaning “gymnastic training”; the English word “gymnasium” comes from this very word. Spiritual maturity is not something you hear your way into; it is something you train your way into.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
In the 321 vision we speak of “fivefold change”: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry.

Have you noticed? This fivefold change corresponds exactly to the complete cycle of See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do. Seeing and listening bring in new information, thinking renews our mindset, speaking confirms the new mindset, doing truly turns our life around, and in the end there flows out new daily living, new relationships and new ministry.

Put the other way round: why does so many people’s spiritual life get stuck? Because they get only as far as the first level and stop. They collect a great pile of mindsets, yet their life doesn’t move an inch. That isn’t called change; that’s called hoarding.

321 also reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you are troubled, rely on the heart and you are glad. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). The destination of See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do is not one more folder in our heads, but a little more of the likeness of Christ in our hearts.

sections.heading: 4. A Picture of Spiritual Growth: How a Meal Is Eaten
sections.html:
Scripture

“The things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me: do these things, and the God of peace will be with you.” (Philippians 4:9)

Buying the food, cooking it, eating it

Brothers and sisters, let me use a picture everyone understands to make these five links clear.

Seeing and listening are “buying the food”. You walk into the market, pick out the freshest greens and the best fish, and carry home two big bags full.

Thinking and speaking are “cooking the food”. You wash, you chop, you season, you put it in the pan, and the aroma fills the whole kitchen.

Doing is “eating the food”. You pick it up with your chopsticks, put it in your mouth, chew it, swallow it, and let it go into your stomach and your bloodstream until it becomes your own flesh and bone.

A very simple picture, yet it hides a truth that cuts deep. Let’s look at three situations.

The first: only buying the food

There is a kind of person who only sees and listens. He buys food every day and his fridge is crammed full, yet he never cooks a meal.

He has plenty of knowledge, but no life. His bookshelf is full of spiritual books, his phone is full of sermons, his notes are neat and tidy — and then what? The food in the fridge rots day by day, and he goes hungrier day by day.

That sounds absurd, but psychology gives us a very sobering figure. The nineteenth-century German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus, in his work On Memory, published in 1885, used himself as the subject of his experiments and recorded the famous “forgetting curve”: without any review or application, within just one day of learning something a person forgets more than half of it, and the forgetting is fastest in the first few hours.

Brothers and sisters, what does that mean? It means that the wonderful sermon you heard on Sunday — if you don’t think about it, speak it or do it — by Tuesday it has most likely gone from you. You think you bought the food, but in fact it fell out of the bag on the way home.

The Lord Jesus told us long ago how such a person ends up: “Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand” (Matthew 7:26). Notice: this man did “hear”. It wasn’t that he didn’t buy the food; he bought the food and starved to death in his own kitchen.

The second: buying the food and cooking it

The second kind of person goes a step further: he sees, he listens, he thinks, and he speaks too. He buys the food and he cooks it, and the whole house is filled with a wonderful aroma — but he doesn’t eat it.

This kind of person can share, can teach, can explain the truth with complete fluency, can lead deep discussions in a small group, can move people to tears from the pulpit. But he has not lived it out, and so his life is still unchanged.

There is a passage in Ezekiel that sends a chill down the spine. God said to the prophet Ezekiel: “They come to you as the people come, and they sit before you as my people, and they hear your words, but don’t do them; for with their mouth they show much love, but their heart goes after their gain. Behold, you are to them as a very lovely song of one who has a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument; for they hear your words, but they don’t do them” (Ezekiel 33:31–32).

“A very lovely song of one who has a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument” — they enjoyed God’s word like a concert. When it was over they applauded and cheered; out the door they went, and life carried on as before.

Brothers and sisters, aren’t we often just the same today? After a good sermon we say, “That was so good,” “So moving,” “Amen” — and then we go home and carry on treating our spouse the way we always have, carry on with the same attitude to money, carry on wearing the same face towards the person we don’t like. The food is cooked and smells delicious, and we haven’t taken a single bite.

The third: buying the food, cooking it and eating it too

The third kind of person goes the whole way. He sees, he listens, he thinks, he speaks, he does. He buys the food, cooks it, and eats it too.

And so the truth enters his life, and his life truly grows.

Physiologically, absorption is far more intricate than we imagine. The inner wall of the human small intestine is covered with folds, villi and microvilli, which multiply its absorbing surface to an astonishing degree. According to a measurement study by Helander and Fändriks published in the Scandinavian Journal of Gastroenterology in 2014, the absorptive surface of the adult small intestine is about thirty square metres — roughly half a badminton court. God designed the human body with an interface the size of half a badminton court for one purpose alone — to turn food into you.

Brothers and sisters, God has designed just such an interface in your life too, and it is called “doing”. Doing is the moment the truth enters your bloodstream.

The Lord Jesus said: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock” (Matthew 7:24). Notice: the wise man and the foolish man heard the same sermon and met the same storm; the only difference was one thing — doing.

The key is not how much you know, but how much you live out

The great German writer Goethe wrote in Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years: “Knowing is not enough; we must apply. Willing is not enough; we must do.”

And the German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer put it even more sharply in The Cost of Discipleship: “Only he who believes is obedient, and only he who is obedient believes.” When he wrote these words, he was walking a road of obedience that would take him to the gallows. On 9 April 1945 he was martyred in Flossenbürg concentration camp, only thirty-nine years old. He did not just cook the word until it smelled good for others; he ate it himself and digested it with his life.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The 321 Path of Serving is: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God — the Holy Spirit is my guide (Spirit), the Bible is my standard (Understanding), Jesus is my role model (Life), let Jesus be King (Service), let Jesus receive all the glory (God).

You see, this path also runs from “receiving” to “living out”, and finally gives the glory to God. Stop at “Understanding”, and you have only bought the food and cooked it; only when you reach “Life” and “Service” have you really eaten it.

321 also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people have the order reversed — ministry first, then relationships, and life only as an afterthought. The result is “a lifetime spent cooking for others, while starving to death in the kitchen”. Brothers and sisters, remember: people matter more than tasks, and life matters more than ministry.

sections.heading: 5. Why Do So Many People Fail to Grow?
sections.html:
Scripture

“But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)

“For indeed we have had good news preached to us, even as they also did, but the word they heard didn’t profit them, because it wasn’t mixed with faith by those who heard.” (Hebrews 4:2)

Two common stopping points

Why do so many people fail to grow? The answer is actually very simple: they have stopped. And they usually stop in one of two places.

The first stopping point is at “seeing” and “listening”. These people are great at hearing sermons. Wherever there is a special conference, they rush there; whichever speaker is popular, they listen to him. They have a collector’s passion for truth, but no heart to practise it.

The second stopping point is at “speaking”. These people are great at sharing. In the small group they talk the most, in the prayer meeting they pray the longest, and they have an answer for everyone else’s problems. But when it comes to their own lives, not one of those answers gets used.

Great at hearing sermons, great at sharing, but not doing the word — a life like that is spiritual malnutrition.

“Mixed”: one crucial word

Hebrews 4:2 gives us the most precise diagnosis: “the word they heard didn’t profit them, because it wasn’t mixed with faith by those who heard.”

“Mixed” in Greek is συγκεράννυμι (synkerannymi), which originally means to pour two liquids together and stir them until they are thoroughly blended — like mixing wine, like making a soup — so blended that you can no longer tell them apart.

Brothers and sisters, this word tells us that once the word has entered you, it must be stirred together with your faith, stirred together with your real daily life; otherwise it floats on top, like oil on water — visible, but unable to get in.

That is exactly what happened to the generation of Israelites who came out of Egypt. They heard the promises, saw the Red Sea part, saw manna come down from heaven, saw the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire — when it comes to “seeing” and “hearing”, few generations in all of human history have been richer than they. Yet they fell dead in the wilderness, because the word was not mixed with faith.

Deluding your own selves

James 1:22 uses a very severe expression: “deluding your own selves.” The Greek is παραλογίζομαι (paralogizomai), which literally means “to deceive yourself with a false calculation”, like someone who has added up his accounts wrongly and thinks he is rich.

What kind of self-deception is this? It is miscounting “I’ve heard it” as “I’ve got it”, miscounting “I agree” as “I’ve changed”, miscounting “I was moved” as “I’ve obeyed”.

James then uses a brilliant picture: “For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was. But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets, but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does” (James 1:23–25).

What is a mirror for? It is for showing you what needs adjusting, so that you go and adjust it. If a man looks in the mirror in the morning, sees that his hair is a mess and his collar is crooked, and then turns and walks away without doing a thing — what use is that mirror to him?

God’s word is that mirror. Look in the mirror without lifting a hand, and however clearly it shows you, the looking was for nothing.

Psychology confirms it: the gap between knowing and doing

In 2006 the psychologists Webb and Sheeran published a meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin, bringing together a number of experimental studies, and its conclusion is well worth our reflection: even when experiments succeeded in raising participants’ “intention” to act by a medium to large amount, the change in actual “behaviour” was only small to medium. Researchers call this phenomenon the “intention–behaviour gap”.

In other words, resolve is not the same as action. This is a fact of human nature that has been confirmed again and again.

Brothers and sisters, this explains exactly the sister who went to more than thirty special conferences and wept and made a commitment every time. Each time her “intention” was raised to the highest pitch, yet her “behaviour” never took that step. The stirring in the meetings was real, the tears were real — it’s just that being moved is not obeying.

Another psychologist, Peter Gollwitzer, put forward the concept of “implementation intentions” in the journal American Psychologist in 1999: when someone does not merely resolve, “I will do such-and-such,” but sets a concrete plan — “If situation A arises, I will do action B” — the rate at which the behaviour is actually carried out rises significantly.

This is exactly the wisdom of “doing”. Don’t say vaguely, “From now on I’ll love my family more.” Say concretely, “Tonight, as soon as I come through the door, I’ll go into the kitchen and give my wife a hug.” Vague resolutions evaporate; concrete actions land.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 speaks of the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Those who stop at “seeing and listening” have reached only the first stage, “Information”. Those who stop at “speaking” may have reached the second and third stages, “Revelation” and “Conviction” — they understand, and they agree — but they have not stepped into the fourth stage, “Implementation”.

And if the truth never enters “Implementation”, then “Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication” after it never get the chance to happen. The eight stages are like a chain, and the fourth link is the crucial one; if the fourth link isn’t joined, the whole chain breaks off in mid-air.

321 also reminds us: the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. Many people won’t do the word because their focus has slipped — their eyes are fixed on “I can’t do it”, on “nobody else is doing it either”, on “my circumstances won’t allow it”. Brothers and sisters, turn your focus back to Jesus, and you will find that he never commands anything without preparing the grace for you to accomplish it.

sections.heading: 6. Action Is the Doorway into Life
sections.html:
Scripture

“Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)

“If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17)

“Doing” is not the last step but the most crucial step

We tend to put “doing” at the bottom of the list, as if it were a finishing touch. Wrong. Brothers and sisters, “doing” is not the last step; “doing” is the most crucial step.

Because without “doing”, nothing that came before counts as finished.

It’s like an operation. The surgeon’s diagnosis is precise, the scans are clear, the team is in place, the instruments are all ready, the theatre lights are bright — but if that incision is never made, the patient is not healed. All the preparation was for that one incision.

Or it’s like a seed. Breeding, choosing the ground, turning the soil, fertilising, watering — all of it done; but if the seed is never put into the ground, it will never sprout. “Doing” is the act of putting the seed into the soil.

The Lord Jesus said: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” (John 13:17). He said this just after washing the disciples’ feet. He did not say, “Since you know these things, you are blessed.” What he said was, “if you do them”. The blessing is not in knowing; the blessing is in doing.

The Lord also asked a question no one can sidestep: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46)

“Perfect” comes not by knowing, but by living it out

Matthew 5:48 says: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.”

“Perfect” in Greek is τέλειος (teleios), from τέλος (telos, purpose, end). It means not “without any flaw” but “having reached the purpose for which it was made, grown into the maturity it should have”. A fruit that is fully ripe and ready to be picked is called teleios.

So the Lord is not telling us, “You must become sinless, flawless people.” He is saying, “You must grow into what you are meant to grow into — grow until you love the way your heavenly Father loves.” Notice the verses just before this one: the Lord has just said, “love your enemies … and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you” (Matthew 5:44), and then says the Father “makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust” (Matthew 5:45).

The Father’s perfection shows itself in his “action” — continually, unceasingly showing grace to the undeserving. The sun shines every day, the rain falls year after year — this is the Father’s perfection.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Perfection is not a state of knowledge; it is a pattern of action. Perfection comes not by knowing, but by living it out.

Once or twice is not enough — keep on doing it

The lesson has one very precious sentence: doing the word once or twice is not enough; we must keep on doing it. What is done becomes habit, and habit becomes life.

This is exactly the teaching of the Bible. Paul says to Timothy: “Exercise yourself toward godliness. For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come” (1 Timothy 4:7–8). “Exercise” in Greek is that same word again, γυμνάζω (gymnazō) — training in the gym. No one builds muscle from one visit to the gym, and no one grows character from reading the Bible once.

Modern research supports this too. Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London, in a study published in the European Journal of Social Psychology in 2010, followed participants as they formed new daily habits and found that it took on average sixty-six days for a behaviour to become “automatic”, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days.

Sixty-six days. Brothers and sisters, this gives us two reminders. First, don’t rush — if you’ve done it for three days and feel nothing, that is normal; don’t give up. Second, don’t stop — real change happens on day forty, day fifty, day sixty, in those days that seem to show no progress at all.

Neuroscience also tells us that repeated practice gradually thickens the myelin sheath around neural circuits, making signals travel faster and more reliably. This is why an accomplished pianist can play scales without thinking. Spiritual life is the same: at first you have to grit your teeth to forgive someone; keep doing it long enough, and forgiveness becomes a reflex.

What is done becomes habit; habit becomes life.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Why can’t we live it out? Because that “self” is stuck in the middle. “I can’t do it” is “self”; “I’ll lose face” is “self”; “Why should I be the first to back down?” — that is “self” too.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. The first act of doing the word is very often laying down that “self”.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). When you move the “self” out of the way, what is lived out is no longer your effort but the life of Christ.

Brothers and sisters, if you can’t live it out, it may well not be because you aren’t trying hard enough, but because you are trying too hard — you keep relying on the brain and yourself instead of relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit. 321 says: rely on the heart and you are glad; rely on the brain and you are troubled. Hand over the “self”, let the Holy Spirit be your guide, and you will be able to take that step.

sections.heading: 7. True Disciples: Not Just People Who Preach
sections.html:
Scripture

“but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected.” (1 Corinthians 9:27)

“My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” (1 John 3:18)

Those who preach may also fail to grow

Brothers and sisters, this is the point today that takes the most courage to hear, and the most humility to receive.

The lesson gives us a very important reminder: those who preach may also fail to grow.

Why? Because they are only “cooking the food”, not “eating the food”.

Being able to speak doesn’t mean being able to live; being able to teach doesn’t mean having life.

This is not a jibe at anyone; it was the apostle Paul’s deepest warning to himself. He said: “but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected” (1 Corinthians 9:27).

“Beat” in Greek is ὑπωπιάζω (hypōpiazō), literally “to strike under the eye”, a term from the boxing ring — to hit your opponent until his eye is bruised black. Paul used such a violent word to describe how he governed himself. This apostle, who wrote thirteen letters, founded countless churches and received visions in the third heaven, still said soberly: I am afraid that after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected.

Brothers and sisters, if even Paul needed to be this watchful, how much more do you and I?

The Lord Jesus’ sternest rebukes were for “people who could talk”

Read the four Gospels and you notice something: the Lord Jesus was gentle with tax collectors, gentle with prostitutes, gentle with lepers, gentle with the Canaanite woman. His sternest rebukes he kept for the group of people who could talk about the Scriptures best of all.

He said: “The scribes and the Pharisees sat on Moses’ seat. All things therefore whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do, but don’t do their works; for they say, and don’t do” (Matthew 23:2–3).

“They say, and don’t do” — these few words are the Lord Jesus’ diagnosis of the religious professionals.

He also said: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 7:21). What follows is even more startling: on that day many will say, didn’t we prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name? But the Lord will say to them: “I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity” (Matthew 7:22–23).

Prophesying, casting out demons, doing mighty works — these are the very peak of “speaking” and “working”. Yet what the Lord looks at is not the results on the platform but the reality in the life.

The picture of a chef

I know a head chef at a restaurant. Every day he prepares meals for hundreds of guests, perfect in colour, aroma and taste. But he has one habit: at the end of the rush he just shovels down a couple of mouthfuls of cold rice and calls it a meal. After a few years, the guests who eat his cooking glow with health, while he himself has developed stomach trouble.

Brothers and sisters, doesn’t this picture look a lot like some preachers, small-group leaders, Sunday school teachers — perhaps even ourselves? We prepare a lavish spiritual feast for others, while for years we ourselves eat cold rice. We study the Bible in order to lead Bible studies, we read Scripture in order to write sermons, we pray because it’s on the order of service — the truth passes through us but never gets into us.

True spiritual influence has never come out of the mouth; it shines out of the life. When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, the skin of his face shone, and that light was not because of anything he had said but because he had been with God (Exodus 34:29).

True disciples are people who live out the truth

The Lord Jesus defines a disciple very clearly: “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples” (John 8:31).

“Disciple” in Greek is μαθητής (mathētēs), from the verb μανθάνω (manthanō, to learn). But in the Jewish rabbinic tradition, “learning” was never copying the teacher’s knowledge into a notebook; it was living with the teacher and imitating his every move. A disciple watched how the teacher prayed, how he ate, how he treated people, how he faced his enemies — and then did the same.

So in the biblical sense, a “disciple” was always a “person who lives out the truth”. Someone who could recite but would not imitate would not even have counted as a disciple in the rabbinic tradition.

That is also why the last line of the Great Commission is worth chewing on all our lives: “teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you” (Matthew 28:20). The Lord did not say “teaching them to know”; the Lord said “teaching them to observe”.

The goal of discipleship training has never been to produce more people who know a lot, but to produce more people who can live it out.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 has a very practical exercise called “the 920 practice”: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; with each “2” we are to practise living out a selfless life (0) and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, notice this: fruit is not spoken into being; fruit grows. No tree ever grew apples by giving a speech.

The 920 practice is the training ground for “doing”. It nails abstract truth to one concrete person. Who is your “2” today? Your spouse, your child, your colleague, that neighbour who gives you headaches. If the truth doesn’t enter your relationship with them, the truth is still in the kitchen and hasn’t yet reached your bloodstream.

321 also speaks of “235 relationships”: becoming a “2”, spiritual companions, with someone selfless; establishing a “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; becoming a “5”, spiritual comrades in a fivefold-ministry team. The role of a spiritual companion is precisely to support each other, evaluate each other and correct each other at this checkpoint of “doing”. One person easily deceives himself; two people find it much harder.

321 also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. True disciples have the order right. They first let the truth happen in their own life, then let it flow out in their relationships, and only then does it become ministry. Reverse the order, and the bigger the ministry, the emptier the life.

sections.heading: 8. Integrating the 321 Vision: See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do and 3-2-1
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today’s five actions in fact correspond perfectly with the 321 vision. Please keep this in your heart.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

“See” — Jesus is my role model. The Lord said: “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). The Lord himself was the one who acted by watching the Father. We too must look to him every day. What we look at, we become.

“Listen” — the Bible is my standard. We hear too many voices: the voice of the world, the voice of public opinion, the voice of our own desires. Only God’s word is the standard. “Be careful therefore how you hear” (Luke 8:18).

“Think” — the Holy Spirit is my guide. Thinking is not reasoning with the brain; it is letting the Holy Spirit shine his light in the heart. “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2).

“Speak” — let Jesus be King. Confessing with our mouth that Jesus is Lord is the very declaration that hands over the throne. “For with the heart, one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation” (Romans 10:10). Revelation also says: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony” (Revelation 12:11).

“Do” — let Jesus receive all the glory. For the Lord said: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). What people see is not our doctrine but our deeds; and the glory goes to the Father in heaven.

Finally, all of this flows together into the Goal: establish God’s system. A community that sees together, hears together, thinks together, proclaims together and acts together is exactly what 1 Timothy 3:15 speaks of — the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.

A shift in perspective

321 says: we must move from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from what is of the world to what is of God.

Man’s perspective says, “Knowing is enough — why take it so seriously?” God’s perspective says, “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” (John 13:17).

The earthly perspective says, “First show some results.” The heavenly perspective says, “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2).

The temporary perspective says, “Let it go this time; we’ll see next time.” The eternal perspective says: those sixty-six days, those small, unremarkable acts of obedience one after another, are forging a life that will last for eternity.

The worldly perspective says, “If you can talk, you’ll have influence.” God’s perspective says, “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15:22).

sections.heading: 9. Putting It into Practice: Eating the Truth
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take them deeper, one by one.

Practice one: Examine yourself — at which stage have I stopped?

Face your spiritual condition honestly: do I only see and only listen? Or have I already begun to do?

Information: today you have received the five links, See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do. Copy them onto the first page of your notebook.

Revelation: be still and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: “Lord, please show me which link I am stuck at.” Don’t guess for yourself; let the Holy Spirit speak.

Conviction: when the Holy Spirit points it out, don’t argue. Admit it: “Lord, it’s true — I’ve stopped at speaking and haven’t gone on to doing.”

Implementation: write it down today, on a piece of paper you will see every day.

Evaluation: at the end of this week, look back: did I actually move, or do I merely know I ought to move?

Correction: if you didn’t move, don’t condemn yourself; adjust your method — shrink the goal until it is something you are sure you can do.

Repetition: examine yourself once a month, so that self-examination becomes a habit.

Multiplication: explain these five links to someone, and invite them to examine themselves too.

Practice two: Put at least one truth into practice every day

From the word you hear today, choose the simplest thing and do it, so that the truth enters your life.

Notice that word “simplest”. This is not lowering the standard; it is spiritual wisdom. Remember Gollwitzer’s research mentioned earlier: concrete, clear plans are far more likely to be carried out than vague resolutions.

So don’t say, “From now on I’ll be more loving.” Say, “At lunchtime today I’ll phone that older friend I haven’t been in touch with for three months.”

Don’t say, “I want to be better at forgiving.” Say, “Tonight I’ll pray for three minutes, by name, for the person who hurt me.”

Don’t say, “I want to read the Bible more.” Say, “Tomorrow at half past six in the morning I’ll sit in this chair and read Mark chapter 1.”

Information and Revelation: after your morning devotion each day, ask yourself one question — “What does this passage want me to do today?”

Conviction: believe that this small thing is a big thing in God’s eyes. “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10).

Implementation: do it the same day; don’t let it sit overnight.

Evaluation and Correction: spend one minute before bed going back over the day. If you did it, thank God; if you didn’t, make it smaller and more concrete tomorrow.

Repetition: forty days in a row. Remember that sixty-six-day study — habits take time to grow.

Multiplication: find a spiritual companion, and each day report to each other in one sentence: “Here’s what I did today.”

Practice three: Build the complete cycle of See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do

Don’t just read the Bible; meditate on it, share it, and finally be sure to live it out, so that your life is fed.

Here is a suggested way to arrange each day:

See and Listen: in the early morning, do your morning devotion — read a passage of Scripture and listen to a message. This is buying the food.

Think: after reading, be still for five minutes. Chew one verse over and over, like the lion that clamps on to its prey and won’t let go (the “growling” in Isaiah 31:4 is the very same Hebrew word as “meditates” in Psalm 1:2). Ask three questions: What does this passage say about what kind of God he is? What does it say about what kind of person I am? How does it want me to act today?

Speak: write down what you have received and send it to a spiritual companion, or share it in your small group. This is cooking the food.

Do: set one concrete action and complete it that day. This is eating the food.

Evaluation, Correction, Repetition: look back once a week, adjust once a month, and keep going without stopping.

Multiplication: bring someone along to do this cycle with you. When you bring someone onto this road, you will find you walk it more steadily yourself — because “Multiplication” is itself the strongest form of “Repetition”.

A Gentle Reminder

It isn’t how many sermons you have heard, but how much of the word you have lived out.

sections.heading: 10. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the growth of life is not a change in an instant, but “living it out” one time after another.

No one is changed in a single special conference. People are changed in one small, unremarkable act of obedience after another: in the harsh word you held back and never said, in the phone call you made first, in the moment when you could have kept score but chose to let it go, in that early morning when you wanted to stay in bed but got up and knelt down instead.

When you begin truly to do it, you will discover — the truth is no longer just knowledge; it becomes life.

One day you will be surprised to find that you no longer have to grit your teeth to forgive, because forgiveness has become your nature; you no longer have to force yourself to love, because love has become your breath. That is being “perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect”.

So this morning I want to issue you a call.

Not a call to hear more sermons, not a call to buy more books, not a call to attend more meetings.

I want to call you — to do one thing.

Just one. Today. Something concrete.

Let Jesus be King in that one thing. Let the “self” step down in that one thing. Let the truth, in that one thing, move from your head into your bloodstream.

Then tomorrow, one more. The day after, one more.

Once you’ve bought the food, cook it; once it’s cooked, eat it. Let us go through the whole process, live a life that is truly like Jesus, and give all the glory to him.

For the Lord said: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

keyVerses: but if I wait long, that you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth. (1 Timothy 3:15)
Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect. (Matthew 5:48)
The things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me: do these things, and the God of peace will be with you. (Philippians 4:9)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, please declare with me:
Lord, I don’t only want to hear your word — I want to live out your word! Help me to move from “knowing” to “doing”. Let your truth become my life, and make me more like you day by day!
practices: Put at least one truth into practice every day
Build the complete cycle of See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

You have given us your word, not for us to store away, but for us to eat and live out. Lord, we confess that we often buy a great deal of food and cook a great deal of food, yet never eat it. We know so much, and live out so little. Please forgive us.
Holy Spirit, shine your light on me, and show me which link I am stuck at. Have I stopped at seeing and listening? Have I stopped at speaking? Give me courage to take that step.

Lord Jesus, reign as King in me. Move my “self” out of the way, so that it is no longer I who live, but you who live in me. Give me perseverance — not to do it once or twice, but day after day, until the truth becomes my habit, and the habit becomes my life.
Make me a pillar and ground of the truth — not in word, but in deed and truth — so that people, seeing my good works, will give the glory to you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Of the five links — See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do — at which do you most often stop? What makes you stop there? Share a specific example with your group. (James 1:22: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”)

Write down one specific thing you “can go and do today” — the smaller the better — and arrange with a spiritual companion to ask each other about the result in a week’s time. How do you think living it out consistently will change your relationship with God and with others? (John 13:17: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.”)

blog.title: You Bought the Food and Cooked It — But Did You Eat It?

blocks.x: Why do we know so much, yet our lives don’t change?
How long have you believed in the Lord? Three years? Ten years? Thirty years?
In all those years, how many chapters of the Bible have you read, how many sermons have you heard, how many memory verses have you copied out?
And then comes the hardest question of all: how much has your life really changed because of it?

I know a brother whose Bible has been thumbed so much that the pages are coming loose, and who can recite whole chapters of Romans. But his wife said to me with red eyes, “At church he’s the Bible expert, but at home he doesn’t have one gentle word for me.”
This is not just his problem. It is the most common, and the most painful, problem in the church today.

We often think the problem is that we haven’t received enough, so we keep upping the dose: more sermons, more books, more special conferences. Only to find our lives are like an engine idling — the accelerator pressed to the floor, yet the car stays where it is.
The problem is not that we haven’t received, but that we have not gone through the complete process of “nurturing life”.
Buying the food, cooking it, eating it
The process of life that God has designed has five links: See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do.
Seeing and listening are taking in; thinking and speaking are digesting; doing is absorbing.
To put it in a picture everyone understands: seeing and listening are buying the food; thinking and speaking are cooking it; doing is eating it.
And so there are three kinds of people.

The first kind only buys the food. The fridge is crammed full, yet he never cooks a meal. As far back as 1885 the psychologist Ebbinghaus found that, without review or application, within one day of learning something a person forgets more than half of it. That wonderful sermon you heard on Sunday — if you don’t think about it, speak it or do it — by Tuesday it has most likely gone from you.

The second kind buys the food and cooks it too. The whole house is filled with a wonderful aroma, yet he doesn’t take a single bite. He can share, he can teach, yet his life is unchanged. Through the prophet Ezekiel God spoke of such people: “Behold, you are to them as a very lovely song of one who has a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument; for they hear your words, but they don’t do them” (Ezekiel 33:32). They enjoy God’s word like a concert: when it’s over they applaud and cheer, and out the door life carries on as before.
The third kind buys the food, cooks it, and eats it too. The truth enters his life, and his life truly grows.
The key is not how much you know, but how much you live out.
“Doing” is not the last step, but the most crucial step
We tend to put “doing” at the bottom of the list, as if it were just a finishing touch. Wrong.
Without “doing”, nothing that came before counts as finished.

It’s like an operation: however precise the diagnosis, however complete the instruments, however bright the lights, if that incision is never made, the patient is not healed. All the preparation was for that one incision.

After washing the disciples’ feet, the Lord Jesus said: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” (John 13:17). He did not say, “Blessed are you if you know.” The blessing is not in knowing; the blessing is in doing.

And once or twice is not enough. A 2010 study by Lally and her colleagues at University College London found that it takes on average sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become automatic. That gives us two reminders: don’t rush, and don’t stop. Real change very often happens in the days that seem to show no progress at all.
What is done becomes habit; habit becomes life.
From knowing to doing
So stop asking, “What did I learn today?” Ask one question instead: “What does this passage want me to do today?”

Then shrink it down until it is as small and as concrete as possible. Don’t say, “From now on I’ll be more loving.” Say, “At lunchtime today I’ll phone that older friend I haven’t been in touch with for three months.” Don’t say, “I want to be better at forgiving.” Say, “Tonight I’ll pray for three minutes, by name, for the person who hurt me.”
Vague resolutions evaporate; concrete actions land.

The growth of life is never a change in an instant, but “living it out” one time after another. No one is changed in a single special conference; people are changed little by little — in the harsh word they held back and never said, in the phone call they made first.
When you begin truly to do it, you will discover — the truth is no longer just knowledge; it becomes life.
May we all become people like that: not only hearing, but living it out; not only cooking the food, but eating it too. So that people may see our good works, and glorify our Father who is in heaven.
Question for reflection
Of the five links — See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do — where do you most often stop? Today, what one small, concrete thing are you willing to do about it?

Key points:
1. Background: Paul wrote around AD 62–64; Timothy was in Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:3).
2. “Pillar” stylos and “ground” hedraiōma are both load-bearing building terms.
