script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 119, and the theme is “Seeing Rightly”.
Our theme verse is Psalm 119:18: “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.”
Brothers and sisters, he didn’t ask God to change his circumstances; what he asked was — open my eyes.
Today’s lesson comes down to one sentence: when the eyes are opened, life is turned around.
In December 1995 some astronomers made a bold decision. They pointed the Hubble Space Telescope at a tiny patch of night sky that seemed to contain nothing at all, and exposed it for ten days.
And the result? That “empty” patch was crammed with some three thousand galaxies.
Brothers and sisters, did the sky change that night? No. The galaxies had been there all along. What changed was the ability to see.
We often think the problem lies in our circumstances, in other people, in what has happened to us. But the real key is this — how we see.
The same event, seen differently, leads to completely different lives.
So we haven’t come today to trade in our sky for a different one. We’ve come to ask the Lord for a new pair of eyes.
Our theme verse comes from Psalm 119 — the longest chapter in the whole Bible, with a hundred and seventy-six verses.
The writer was derided, persecuted and weary with sorrow. Brothers and sisters, it was in circumstances like these that he prayed: “Open my eyes.”
In the original, “open” means “to lift off a covering”. Lord, it isn’t that your word isn’t wonderful enough; it’s that there’s a cloth over my eyes.
Paul, in prison in Rome, prayed the same way for the believers in Ephesus — asking God to enlighten the eyes of their hearts.
Brothers and sisters, there is a pair of eyes within us. If those eyes have not been enlightened by the Holy Spirit, we see nothing at all.
The Bible tells us that human beings have two kinds of eyes.
The first is worldly eyes. Genesis 3:7: “Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked.”
Brothers and sisters, these weren’t physical eyes. They could already see. What was opened was a way of looking that had turned away from God.
When those eyes opened, the first thing they saw was not God’s glory, but their own nakedness.
Seeing their own inadequacy, their own shame, their own lack.
And the result? Genesis 3:10: “I was afraid… so I hid myself.”
Fear, then distance from God, then covering themselves by their own efforts. That is worldly eyes — they make people live in “self”.
The second is spiritual eyes. Ephesians 1:18: “having the eyes of your hearts enlightened”.
The subject of “enlightened” is not us; it is God. Brothers and sisters, we have no way of opening our own eyes; it is the work of the Holy Spirit.
What do spiritual eyes see? They see God’s glory, they see God’s promises, they see God’s heart.
Luke 24:31: “Their eyes were opened and they recognized him.”
On the road to Emmaus, Jesus walked with them the whole way, yet they couldn’t recognise him. Brothers and sisters, the Lord has been there all along; it is our eyes that are clouded.
When spiritual eyes are opened, people recognise Jesus. The focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.
The fall of humanity began with a single word: “saw”.
Genesis 3:6: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise…”
Wrong seeing has three layers: looking at the appearance — a delight to the eyes; looking at the gain — good for food; looking at self — to be desired to make one wise.
And they have only one essence: self-centred seeing.
What is the result? Wanting to be our own master, no longer relying on God, living in the system of the self-centred life, and finally ending up in fear and separation.
Brothers and sisters, each of our eyes has a physiological blind spot, and the brain fills it in automatically, so we think we see perfectly clearly.
The most frightening thing about wrong seeing is not that it sees wrongly, but that it sees wrongly and still thinks it’s right.
So what is right seeing?
Psalm 119:18: “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.”
Right seeing does not look at ourselves or at our circumstances; it sees God, sees the truth, sees heavenly reality.
Elisha’s servant saw the Syrian army and was terrified. Elisha prayed: please open the young man’s eyes.
He looked — and the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire. Brothers and sisters, the chariots and horses of fire had been there all along; he just hadn’t seen them.
Acts 26:18: “to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God.”
The starting point of it all is eyes being opened.
Paul is the clearest example.
He knew Scripture thoroughly and served zealously, yet he went out to arrest those who believed in the Lord. It wasn’t that he didn’t read Scripture; he read it and still couldn’t see Jesus.
When the light shone down on the road to Damascus, his eyes were open, yet he could not see, and for three days he neither ate nor drank.
Brothers and sisters, God had to shut down his worldly eyes before he could open his spiritual ones.
Then, Acts 9:18: “Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight.”
Outwardly, it was the restoring of sight; in essence, it was the opening of spiritual eyes.
From persecuting Jesus to living for Jesus; from opposing God to complete obedience to God.
One change in “seeing” brought about the change of an entire life.
Brothers and sisters, the key truth comes down to one sentence: as you see, so you live.

Look at yourself, and you’ll have inferiority, shame and fear. Look at your circumstances, and you’ll have anxiety, unease and pressure. Look at other people, and you’ll have comparison, envy and hurt.
Peter sank on the water not because the wind grew stronger, but because he “saw” that the wind was strong.
The ten spies said: we were in our own sight as grasshoppers. Brothers and sisters, once you’ve seen yourself as a grasshopper, the whole world will see you as a grasshopper too.
But — look at Jesus, and you’ll have peace; look at the truth, and you’ll be free; look at God, and you’ll overcome.
The problem isn’t out there; it’s in your eyes.
So this week we have three practices.
First, discern where your way of seeing is coming from. When you’re feeling emotional, ask yourself: am I looking at this right now with worldly eyes, or with spiritual eyes?
Second, deliberately shift your focus. When you start looking at the problem or at yourself, practise turning: look at Jesus, look at the promises, look at what God is doing.
Third, pray every day for your eyes to be opened. Pray using Psalm 119:18: Lord, open my eyes, that I may see your truth.
Brothers and sisters, remember: it isn’t your circumstances that determine your life; it’s how you see that determines your life.
When the eyes are wrong, life goes off course; when the eyes are right, life lights up.
The man born blind said: one thing I do know — though I was blind, now I see.
Brothers and sisters, may this become our testimony too.
Let us no longer look with the eyes of “self”, but with eyes the Holy Spirit has opened — seeing Jesus, fixing our eyes on Jesus, living out Jesus.
This is the beginning of entering the victorious life.
Let us pray together.
Dear Lord Jesus, we confess that we often think the problem lies in our circumstances and in other people. Today you have shown us that the key is how we see.
Please open our eyes, remove the scales from our eyes, and enlighten the eyes of our hearts.
In every circumstance, let us see you, trust you and follow you.
Reign as King in our lives, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, may the Lord himself open your eyes today. See you tomorrow.
Brothers and sisters, good morning. May the grace and peace of the Lord be with us this early morning.
Today we come together to Lesson 119, and the theme is “Seeing Rightly”.
Our theme verse is Psalm 119:18: “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.”
Brothers and sisters, please notice: he didn’t ask God to change his circumstances, nor to destroy his enemies. What he asked was — open my eyes.
Today’s lesson comes down to one sentence: when the eyes are opened, life is turned around.
Let me begin with a story.

In December 1995 astronomers pointed the Hubble Space Telescope at a tiny patch of night sky that seemed to contain nothing at all — about the size of a grain of sand held at arm’s length. They kept the shutter open, building up exposure over ten days.
When the image came out, the whole world was stunned. That darkness was crammed with some three thousand galaxies.
Brothers and sisters, did the sky change that night? No. Those galaxies had been there for billions of years.
What changed was not the sky; it was the ability to see.
Our lives are just the same.
We often say: if only my husband would change a bit; if only the children were a bit more sensible. Brothers and sisters, we spend half our lives trying to rearrange the sky outside.
But the real key isn’t out there; it lies in how we see.
In the same wilderness, ten spies saw giants, while two spies saw the promise. In the same city surrounded by the enemy army, the servant saw the enemy, while Elisha saw chariots and horses of fire.
Proust said: the real voyage of discovery consists not in seeking new landscapes, but in having new eyes.
So today we haven’t come to trade in our sky. We’ve come to ask the Lord for a new pair of eyes.
Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the whole Bible, with a hundred and seventy-six verses; it is an acrostic poem in twenty-two stanzas.
Who wrote it? The Bible doesn’t tell us. But he was derided by the proud, persecuted by princes without cause, and his soul was weary with sorrow.
Brothers and sisters, it was in circumstances like these that he prayed: open my eyes.
The basic meaning of this word “open” in the original is “to lift off a covering”. He is saying: Lord, it isn’t that your word isn’t wonderful enough; it’s that there’s a cloth over my eyes.

Paul, in prison in Rome, prayed the same way for the church in Ephesus. The Reformer Calvin said that Scripture is like a pair of spectacles. God has already given us the spectacles; the question is whether we are willing to let the Lord first heal our eyes.
Brothers and sisters, from the very beginning Scripture reveals that human beings have two completely different ways of “seeing”. Worldly eyes are wrong seeing; spiritual eyes are right seeing.
The difference isn’t sharpness of sight but direction: one is turned towards self, the other towards God. One makes people leave God and hide; the other lets people recognise Jesus.
In the language of 321: one is self-centred eyes, the other is selfless eyes.
Genesis 3:7: “Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked.”

Brothers and sisters, these weren’t physical eyes being opened. Before he sinned Adam wasn’t blind; he had even given names to all the animals. What was opened was a way of looking that had turned away from God.

This is exactly what the serpent had promised. Genesis 3:5: “in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” Satan never blinds people directly; he gives you a pair of eyes that are “like God” — putting yourself at the centre and judging good and evil for yourself.
When those eyes opened, the first thing they saw was not God’s glory, but their own nakedness.
Genesis 3:10: “I was afraid… so I hid myself.” Fear, distance from God, and then covering themselves by their own efforts.
We don’t sew fig leaves any more. We sew academic degrees, job titles and performance figures, to cover up the self we don’t dare to face.
Thank God, Scripture doesn’t stop at Genesis chapter 3. Ephesians 1:18: “having the eyes of your hearts enlightened”.

The subject of “enlightened” is not us; it is God. Brothers and sisters, we have no way of opening the eyes of our own hearts by gritting our teeth and straining; it is the work of the Holy Spirit. This is exactly the third of 321’s foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide.
What do spiritual eyes see? They see God’s glory, they see God’s promises, they see God’s heart.
Luke 24:31: “Their eyes were opened and they recognized him.” On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus walked with them the whole way, yet they couldn’t recognise him.
The Lord has been there all along; it is our eyes that are clouded. The focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.
The second point: wrong seeing leads people away from God.
Genesis 3:6: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise…”

Brothers and sisters, the fall of humanity began with a single word: “saw”. She passed that tree every day and nothing had ever gone wrong; what went wrong was this particular act of seeing — because this time she was looking with the serpent’s words in her head.

Our eyes are always shaped by the words we listen to. Listen to the serpent, and you’ll look at that tree with the serpent’s eyes; listen to God, and you’ll look at life with God’s eyes. That is why 321 says: the Bible is my standard.
Wrong seeing has three layers: looking at the appearance — a delight to the eyes; looking at the gain — good for food; looking at self — to be desired to make one wise.
These three layers have only one essence: self-centred seeing.

Look at Genesis chapter 13. Lot lifted up his eyes and saw that all the plain of the Jordan was well-watered — he saw water and pasture, rich land and prospects; and step by step he moved his tent until he was living in Sodom.
But God said to Abram: lift up your eyes and look northward, southward, eastward and westward, for all the land which you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.
Lot lifted his eyes and chose for himself; Abram lifted his eyes because God told him to look. Lot saw a plain; Abram saw forever.
Self-centred seeing results in wanting to be our own master, no longer relying on God, living in the system of the self-centred life, and finally ending up in fear and separation.
Brothers and sisters, each of our eyes has a physiological blind spot with no light-sensitive cells at all; yet the brain fills it in automatically, so we think we see completely.
We all have blind spots, and our minds even tell us: you don’t have any blind spots.
So what is right seeing?
Psalm 119:18: “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.”
Brothers and sisters, please notice: this is a prayer. Right seeing is not a technique; it is a grace. It isn’t “I must try harder to think positively”; it is “Lord, please open my eyes.”
This is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.
That is humility. Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.
In 2 Kings chapter 6, the Syrian army surrounded the city of Dothan by night. Elisha’s servant got up early, took one look and was terrified.

Verse 17: “Elisha prayed, and said, ‘Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.’ Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.”

Brothers and sisters, Elisha didn’t ask the Lord to remove the army; he asked, “open his eyes”. At that moment the chariots and horses of fire weren’t suddenly created — they had been there all along.

Here is another scientific fact: the visible light the human eye can see lies only between about three hundred and eighty and seven hundred and fifty nanometres — a minute fraction of the whole electromagnetic spectrum.
2 Corinthians 4:18: “For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.”
This is the 321 shift in perspective: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal.
The fourth point: once the eyes are opened, the life is turned around. Paul is the clearest example.

Who was Saul? A star pupil of Gamaliel, a Pharisee of the Pharisees. He knew the law thoroughly, served zealously, and believed he was burning with zeal for God — yet he took letters from the high priest and went to arrest those who believed in the Lord.
Brothers and sisters, it wasn’t that he didn’t read Scripture. He read Scripture and still couldn’t see Jesus.
Acts 9:8: “Saul arose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened, he saw no one.” His eyes were open, yet he was blind, and for three days he neither ate nor drank.
Those three days of blindness were one of the greatest graces God ever gave Paul. God had to shut down his worldly eyes before he could open his spiritual ones.
Three days later Ananias came and laid his hands on him. Acts 9:18: “Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized.”

Brothers and sisters, outwardly it was the restoring of sight; in essence it was the opening of spiritual eyes. The hard crust over Paul’s eyes, formed of legalism, religious zeal and self-righteousness, fell away.
Please notice: God used Ananias. God often uses one obedient person to open another person’s eyes. Today, you too may be someone’s Ananias.
Once the eyes are opened, what is the result? From persecuting Jesus, he became a man who lived for Jesus; from opposing God, he became completely obedient to God.

Philippians 3:8: “Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ.”
Brothers and sisters, his education was the same education, his pedigree the same pedigree. The things hadn’t changed; the eyes that valued them had.
In the 1960s the psychiatrist Beck developed cognitive therapy. He found that people’s emotional distress is often caused not by events themselves, but by the way they interpret those events.
But psychology can only describe the phenomenon; it has no way of giving anyone a new pair of eyes. Who can make those scales fall away? Only Jesus.
321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Paul was first baptised — that is life; then came Barnabas — that is relationships; and only last the missionary journeys — that is ministry.
The fifth point, and the key truth of this lesson: as you see, so you live.

Matthew 6:22: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.” Jesus didn’t say the eye is a window; he said it is a lamp. A window only lets light in; a lamp decides whether the whole house is light or dark.
Look at yourself, and you’ll have inferiority, shame and fear — that was Adam’s condition in the garden.

Look at your circumstances, and you’ll have anxiety, unease and pressure. Matthew 14:30: “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink.” Peter sank not because the wind grew stronger, but because he “saw” that the wind was strong.

Look at other people, and you’ll have comparison, envy and hurt. Numbers 13:33: “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.” Did the sons of Anak ever say anything of the kind? Scripture never records it — the spies imagined it themselves.
Once you’ve seen yourself as a grasshopper, you’ll assume the whole world sees you as a grasshopper too.
But, brothers and sisters, the reverse is also true.

Look at Jesus, and you’ll receive peace. Hebrews 12:2 tells us to be “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith”. In the original, “looking to” means turning one’s gaze away from everything else and looking intently at one thing — to look to him, you first have to stop looking at certain other things.
Look at the truth, and you’ll receive freedom. John 8:32: “the truth will make you free.”
Look at God, and you’ll receive victory. Facing a powerful enemy, Jehoshaphat prayed: our eyes are on you.

In 1999 Simons and Chabris published a study in the journal Perception: participants watched a video and counted how many times the people in white shirts passed a ball; partway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the scene, beat their chest and walked out again — about nine seconds in all. Almost half of them never saw it at all.
This is called “inattentional blindness”. What people see depends on what they are paying attention to.
Brothers and sisters, all our lives we’re busy counting our own passes — counting our results, counting our grievances — and so God’s works pass right in front of us, and we don’t see a thing.
The problem isn’t out there; it’s in your eyes.
So how do we practise this week?

First, discern where your way of seeing is coming from. When you’re feeling emotional or under pressure, stop and ask yourself: am I looking at this right now with worldly eyes, or with spiritual eyes?

Emotions are an excellent alarm system: anxiety usually means you’re looking at your circumstances, envy usually means you’re looking at other people, shame usually means you’re looking at yourself. First use the emotion to find out where your eyes are pointing.

Second, deliberately shift your focus. The key word is “deliberately” — just as those people counting passes didn’t automatically see the gorilla. You have to say it out loud: Lord, I am taking my eyes off this matter; I want to look at you.
One practical way: prepare three verses to turn your eyes, and the moment emotions rise, read them out loud.
Third, pray every day for your eyes to be opened. Pray using Psalm 119:18: Lord, open my eyes, that I may see your truth.
Let’s also go deeper using the eight stages of changing our mindset.
Information: today’s lesson is the information — people have two kinds of eyes. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to point out which matter, which person, I am looking at with worldly eyes right now.
Conviction: no excuses; the first words are “Lord, you are right.” Implementation: this week, choose one person and deliberately look at them with new eyes — how does Jesus see this person?

Evaluation: every evening, spend three minutes keeping an honest record, without condemning yourself. Correction: find the moments when your focus is most easily stolen, and prepare one action for turning.
Repetition: Paul’s scales fell off all at once, but he spent his whole life practising not looking at the things which are seen. Multiplication: pray for your “2” — Lord, open the eyes of his heart.
Brothers and sisters, let’s set this lesson within the picture of 321.
The Three Foundations are the three focal lengths of a new pair of eyes: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

The Two Core Values: wherever the eyes look, that is where the throne is. When my eyes are fixed only on myself, I am my own king. When spiritual eyes are opened, what they see is glory — and that glory doesn’t belong to me.
The Goal: establish God’s system — God is God and man is man; people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things.

Going from the old self to the new self is exchanging self-centred eyes for selfless eyes. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into fullness; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
Brothers and sisters, a tiny coin held right up against your eye can block out the whole sky. “Self” is that coin — it isn’t big; it’s just too close to you.
The 920 practice: which pair of eyes you look at your “2” with determines whether you can bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit towards them.

Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the sky we began with. Those three thousand galaxies had been there all along; the chariots and horses of fire had been there all along; the risen Lord had been walking with his disciples all along.
When the eyes are wrong, life goes off course; when the eyes are right, life lights up.
The man born blind, after he was healed, answered his questioners with one most powerful sentence. John 9:25: “One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.”

This morning I want to invite you to make a decision: take off that pair of glasses you’ve been wearing for so long. Perhaps they’re called “I’m not good enough.” Perhaps they’re called “He’ll never change.” Put them in the Lord’s hands, and then say: Lord, please open my eyes.
Let us no longer look with the eyes of “self”, but with eyes the Holy Spirit has opened — seeing Jesus, fixing our eyes on Jesus, living out Jesus.
Let us pray together.

Dear Lord Jesus, we confess that we often think the problem lies in our circumstances and in other people; today you have shown us that the key is how we see. We also confess that there are many blind spots within us that we cannot see for ourselves.
Lord, as you opened the eyes of Elisha’s servant, open our eyes; remove from our eyes the hard crust formed of self, pride and fear.
Enlighten the eyes of our hearts, so that we see your glory, your promises and your heart.
When we are about to look at ourselves, let us see you; when we are about to look at our circumstances, let us see you; when we are about to look at other people, let us see them through your eyes.
Lord, open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.
Reign as King in our lives, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, may the Lord himself open your eyes today. See you tomorrow.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Gorilla in the Middle of the Picture
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Before we open the Bible, I’d like you to join me in a small experiment.

In 1999 two psychologists, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris, published a paper called “Gorillas in Our Midst” in the journal Perception. They asked volunteers to watch a very short video: two teams passing basketballs in front of the camera, one team in white shirts, the other in black. The researchers’ instruction was very simple — just one sentence: please count how many passes the white team makes.

The volunteers concentrated hard. Their eyes stayed glued to the ball, darting back and forth with it, not daring to miss a single pass. Halfway through the video, a person in a gorilla suit strolled in from the right of the screen, walked to the very centre, stopped, turned to the camera and thumped its chest — staying there a full nine seconds — and then ambled unhurriedly out to the left.

When the video ended, the researchers first asked: how many passes did the white team make? Almost everyone answered quickly and accurately. Then came the second question: tell me, did you see a gorilla?

Nearly half of the volunteers — about 46 per cent in the experiment — stared back wide-eyed and asked blankly, “What gorilla?”

Brothers and sisters, notice this: their eyes were fine, their sight was normal, the lighting was bright, and the gorilla stood right in the middle of the picture thumping its chest for a full nine seconds. Yet they truly did not see it. Psychology has a name for this: “inattentional blindness.” It means that when your attention is completely taken up with one thing, you become entirely blind to something else that is right in front of you.

The most startling thing about the experiment isn’t that “some people didn’t see the gorilla.” It is this — every one of those who missed it was convinced they had seen perfectly clearly. They’d even argue with you: there was no gorilla in that video at all.

In our last lesson we saw a truth together: people have two kinds of eyes — worldly eyes and spiritual eyes. Today we’re going to take one step further and face a truth that is even more decisive, and even more piercing —

These two kinds of eyes cannot be open at the same time.

If you’re counting passes, you won’t see the gorilla; if you’re fixed on the world, you won’t see God. Whether your life is full of light or full of darkness is, most of the time, not decided by your circumstances, but by which kind of “seeing” you choose. Your circumstances are only the video; what really decides the ending is what you’ve been told to count.

This morning, may the Holy Spirit himself speak to us, rescue us from “thinking we see,” and enable us truly — to see God.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Lamp in the Sermon on the Mount
1. Author, Date and Readers
sections.html:
The Gospel of Matthew was written by Matthew, one of the Lord Jesus’ twelve disciples, also called Levi, who had been a tax collector in Capernaum. Before the Lord called him, he looked at people, at money and at profit every day with eyes well trained in keeping accounts; once the Lord called him, he left the tax booth behind and followed Jesus with a brand-new pair of eyes. That a man who once could see nothing but silver later wrote down “the lamp of the body is the eye” is a testimony in itself.

Matthew’s Gospel is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish Christians scattered in many places. These people had just come out of the traditions of Judaism and were facing a hard question: what is true righteousness, really? Is the righteousness the Pharisees could see the righteousness God wants? Matthew answers them with his whole book: Jesus is the King who brings the kingdom of heaven, and the righteousness of the kingdom begins on the inside.

sections.heading: 2. The Surrounding Context
sections.html:
Matthew 5 to 7 is the familiar “Sermon on the Mount,” the rule of life for the people of the kingdom. Our theme passage sits right in the middle of chapter 6, with a clear context on every side.

In Matthew 6:1–18 the Lord Jesus speaks about three religious disciplines: giving, prayer and fasting. These three sections share a common refrain: don’t do your good deeds before people in order to be seen by them; “your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” (Matthew 6:4). Right from the start the Lord Jesus is dealing with one question: whose eyes are you living for?

In Matthew 6:19–21 the Lord Jesus speaks about treasure: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth … but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven … for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:19–21).

Matthew 6:22–23, our theme passage, says that the eye is the lamp of the body.

Matthew 6:24 says no one can serve two masters.

Matthew 6:25–34 says do not worry, but seek first God’s kingdom and his righteousness.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Treasure, the eye, two masters, worry — these four passages aren’t four separate sermons; they are one chain, link fastened to link. Where your treasure is, there your heart is; where your heart is, there your eyes look; where your eyes look decides which master you serve; and which master you serve decides whether you worry every day or rest every day. The eye is the link in the middle of the chain.

sections.heading: 3. Laodicea, Ephesus, Dothan
sections.html:
Today we’ll also step into the setting of three other passages, so let’s prepare a little.

Laodicea, in Revelation 3, lay in the Lycus valley in Asia Minor and was a famous, wealthy city of its day. It was a centre of banking and finance; after an earthquake in AD 60 the Laodiceans even refused help from the Roman Empire and rebuilt their homes with their own money. It was known for a glossy black woollen cloth. It also had a well-known medical school that produced a salve for treating eye disease. But it had one fatal weakness: the city had no good water source of its own, so water had to be piped in from far away, and by the time it reached the city it was lukewarm. So every word the Lord spoke to them — lukewarm, buy white garments, buy eye salve — was nothing casual; each one pierced precisely the thing they were proudest of.

The letter to the Ephesians was written by the apostle Paul around AD 60–62, during his first imprisonment in Rome. Ephesians 1:15–23 is a great prayer. Paul didn’t pray about their circumstances; he didn’t pray for their health, their careers or their safety; he prayed for their “eyes.”

The setting of 2 Kings 6 is the northern kingdom of Israel in the ninth century BC, in the days of the prophet Elisha. The king of Aram sent out raiding parties against Israel again and again, and Elisha, by revelation from God, kept telling the king of Israel where the Aramean ambush lay. The king of Aram was furious and sent a great army by night to surround Dothan, the city where Elisha was. At daybreak a young servant pushed open the door and saw horses, chariots and soldiers all around the city.

Three places, three kinds of people, one shared problem: the eyes.

sections.heading: 1. The Eye Is the Lamp of the Body
sections.html:
“The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23)

Here the Lord Jesus sets out an enormously important principle — simple enough for a child to understand, deep enough that a theologian could never finish preaching it:

If the eye is clear, the whole body is full of light; if the eye is dim, the whole body is full of darkness.

sections.heading: 1. The Key Word: Not “Eyesight” but “Single”
sections.html:
The word translated “sound” is the Greek haplous (ἁπλοῦς). Its literal meaning isn’t “perfect twenty-twenty vision” but “single, simple, unfolded, undivided.” In the New Testament and in Jewish writings of the time, the word was also often extended to mean “generous, not grudging.”

Its opposite is ponēros (πονηρός), which literally means “evil.” In everyday Hebrew speech, “a bad eye” was an idiom for someone stingy, envious and greedy. Proverbs 28:22 says, “A stingy man hurries after riches, and doesn’t know that poverty waits for him” — the Chinese Union Version renders it “a man with an evil eye.”

So, brothers and sisters, what the Lord Jesus is talking about here is never, from start to finish, a problem for the eye doctor; it is a problem of the heart. He isn’t asking, “Can you see clearly or not?” He is asking, “Are your eyes fixed on one single direction, or are they split in two?”

A divided eye is a divided heart. And a divided heart brings a divided life.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Lamp Is Not the Light Source but the Window
sections.html:
Some people read “the lamp of the body is the eye” and mistakenly think the eye gives off light. In fact, in the imagery of the ancient world, the saying means this: the eye is to the body what a window is to a house. The house itself gives no light; whether it is bright or dark depends entirely on which way the window faces, how big it is and how clean it is.

That is why the Lord Jesus’ next sentence is so frightening: “If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:23) He didn’t say “it is dark outside”; he said “the light that is in you is darkness.”

Brothers and sisters, please hear this distinction clearly:

It isn’t dark outside; it’s dark inside.

It isn’t the world that shapes you; it’s “how you see” that shapes you.

Solomon says in Proverbs 4:23, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” The heart is the source; the eyes are the floodgate. Whichever way the floodgate opens, that is the water that fills the source; and whatever fills the source, that is what flows out of your whole life.

sections.heading: 3. Science and Life: One Lens Can Change the Whole World
sections.html:
The human eye is a breathtakingly precise piece of work. The retina of a single eye holds about 120 million rod cells and about 6 million cone cells. These cells turn light into electrical signals and send them through the optic nerve into the brain. But notice this: put just one thin tinted lens in front of so precise a system, and the whole world instantly changes colour.

Put on a pair of yellow-tinted sunglasses, and the blue sky turns khaki, the white clouds turn cream, your wife’s face looks sallow, and you can’t help asking her, “Are you feeling unwell?” The problem isn’t the sky, and it isn’t your wife; it’s the two pieces of plastic on the bridge of your nose.

The Reformer John Calvin, in Book One of his Institutes of the Christian Religion, used a beautiful image: the eyes of the human heart have grown dim through sin, and Scripture is like a pair of spectacles God has given us; put them on, and a world that was blurred and confused shows its clear outlines. Calvin reminds us that the question has never been “Should I wear lenses or not?” — everyone looks at the world through some kind of lens. The question is which pair you are wearing.

sections.heading: 4. A 321 Insight: Change the Mindset and You Change the Life
sections.html:
The 321 vision says the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. That order cannot be reversed, and the first link is mindset.

What is a mindset? A mindset is “how you see.” Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living; change your daily living and you change your relationships; change your relationships, and only then is there genuine ministry.

So, brothers and sisters, if today there’s a place in your daily living where you’re stuck, a relationship that won’t open up, a corner of your service that is dry and powerless, don’t rush to repair the ministry, and don’t rush to change other people. 321 tells us: life first, then relationships, then ministry. And the door to life opens with one key — the mindset.

The second of the Three Foundations says: the Bible is my standard. That standard is the pair of glasses that corrects our sight. When you open your Bible every morning, it isn’t just to “finish the reading plan”; it is so that God can correct the lenses you’ll be wearing today.

sections.heading: 2. The Two Kinds of Eyes Cannot Coexist
sections.html:
“No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)

Notice that this verse follows straight on from “the lamp of the body is the eye,” in one breath. The Lord Jesus speaks first about the eye and then about two masters, because these are really two sides of the same thing.

sections.heading: 1. Who Is Mammon?
sections.html:
“Mammon” is a transliteration of the Greek mamōnas, a word borrowed from Aramaic, and the Chinese Union Version adds a small note here: “Mammon: meaning wealth.” What’s interesting is that the Lord Jesus personifies wealth and calls it a “master.” Money itself is not a master, but once money becomes the focus of your eyes, it automatically takes the master’s seat and starts giving orders — deciding what time you get up, whom you spend time with, what you fear and what you chase.

The Lord Jesus didn’t say “you may not have money”; he said “no one can serve two masters.” Because the eye has only one focal length. You can own two things at once, but you can’t focus on two things at once.

sections.heading: 2. Light and Darkness Cannot Coexist
sections.html:
At the very beginning of Genesis 1, the first separation God makes is to divide light from darkness: “God saw the light, and saw that it was good. God divided the light from the darkness” (Genesis 1:4). Light and darkness can’t be mixed; they can only take turns. In the same way:

When the worldly eyes open, the spiritual eyes close; when the spiritual eyes open, the worldly eyes close.

The apostle Paul says it even more directly: “for we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7). And again: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

Moses’ life is a footnote to those words: “By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible” (Hebrews 11:27). Brothers and sisters, Moses wasn’t unafraid of Pharaoh because he didn’t see Pharaoh, but because he saw Someone greater.

sections.heading: 3. Science Bears It Out: Dark Adaptation Is a Long Wait
sections.html:
The human retina has two systems. The cone cells work in bright places and handle colour and detail; the rod cells work in dim places and are far more sensitive. These two systems aren’t fully switched on at the same time: when you walk out of blazing sunlight into a pitch-dark room, at first you can’t see a thing, and you have to wait while your eyes slowly “dark-adapt.” The cones adapt fairly quickly, but the rods need roughly twenty to thirty minutes to reach full dark adaptation.

But — and this is the crucial sentence — if someone suddenly switches on a lamp, or you glance down at your phone screen, within a few seconds all twenty minutes of hard-won dark adaptation is reset to zero, and you have to wait all over again. That’s why serious astronomers, whether in an observatory or stargazing up a mountain, use only red-light torches and never switch on a white light.

Brothers and sisters, how much this picture looks like our spiritual life. To grow quiet before God and see the One who is unseen takes time, takes waiting, takes an early morning that isn’t interrupted. Yet a single blast of worldly glare — a news item, a bit of gossip, a comparison, a scroll through your phone — can wreck half an hour of stillness in a few seconds.

This isn’t saying how strong the world’s light is; it’s saying how precious our spiritual eyes are, and how much they need protecting.

sections.heading: 4. Psychology Bears It Out: Attention Is Zero-Sum
sections.html:
As early as 1953, the British cognitive scientist Colin Cherry carried out his famous “dichotic listening” experiments and discovered what later came to be called the “cocktail party effect”: at a noisy party a person can focus on hearing one speaker clearly, but the price is that they hear almost nothing of what’s being said on the other side. Attention is like a spotlight: light it up here, and over there goes dark.

The gorilla at the start is exactly the same principle. Human attention is limited; it is zero-sum. You cannot “look at everything.” You think you’re keeping everything in view, but really you’re only switching; and every time you switch, something is going dark.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: You Must Choose a Side
The first of the 321 vision’s Two Core Values is this: let Jesus be King.
sections.html:
Being King is an exclusive position. A country can’t have two kings, and a heart can’t have two focal points. People’s deepest pain often isn’t “I don’t love God” but “I love God, and I can’t let go of Mammon either,” and so they live as divided people: on Sunday they look like spiritual people, on Monday like worldly people; with their mouths they speak of faith, in their hearts they go by sight.

321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. When we insist on keeping both sets of eyes under our own control, that is the self-centred life; when we are willing to close one of them and let God reign, that is selflessness.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, which side will you choose?

sections.heading: 3. Wrong Seeing: Thinking You See, When You Are Actually Blind
sections.html:
“Because you say, ‘I am rich, and have gotten riches, and have need of nothing;’ and don’t know that you are the wretched one, miserable, poor, blind, and naked.” (Revelation 3:17)

These are words the risen Lord spoke personally to the church in Laodicea, in the revelation generally held to have been received by the apostle John on the island of Patmos around AD 95.

sections.heading: 1. The Most Frightening Distance: Our Self-Assessment and God’s Assessment
sections.html:
Compare the two assessment reports in this verse.

Laodicea’s self-assessment: rich, have gotten riches, need nothing. Three descriptions, each more satisfied than the last.

The Lord’s assessment: wretched, miserable, poor, blind, naked. Five descriptions, each more desolate than the last.

The same church, at the same moment — how far apart are those two reports? Brothers and sisters, the most dangerous place in a person’s spiritual life isn’t being very weak; it’s being very weak and feeling very strong.

Then the Lord prescribes three remedies: “I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, that you may become rich; and white garments, that you may clothe yourself, and that the shame of your nakedness may not be revealed; and eye salve to anoint your eyes, that you may see” (Revelation 3:18).

Laodicea was proud of its banking and finance; the Lord says, buy real gold from me. Laodicea was proud of its black woollen cloth; the Lord says, buy white garments from me. Laodicea was famous for its eye salve; the Lord says, buy the real eye salve from me. What they held in their hands was precisely what they lacked most on the inside. They could heal the eyes of all Asia, but they couldn’t heal their own.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Those Who See Become Blind
sections.html:
John 9 records that after the Lord Jesus healed the man born blind, he said, “I came into this world for judgment, that those who don’t see may see; and that those who see may become blind.” Those of the Pharisees who were with him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?” Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, ‘We see.’ Therefore your sin remains” (John 9:39–41).

Brothers and sisters, these are some of the most piercing words in the whole Bible. The one who admitted he was blind was healed; those who insisted they could see — their sin remained. It wasn’t that God wouldn’t open their eyes; it was that they never felt any need for them to be opened.

Paul says too: “in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelieving, that the light of the Good News of the glory of Christ … should not dawn on them” (2 Corinthians 4:4). There are two kinds of spiritual blindness: one is being blinded by deception, the other is refusing to look. The second is harder to heal.

sections.heading: 3. Science: You Really Do Have a Blind Spot
sections.html:
Here is a solid physiological fact. In each of your eyes there is a place on the retina where the optic nerve passes out, called the optic disc. That spot has no light-sensitive cells at all; it is a real, physical blind spot. In other words, there is already a hole in your field of vision.

But have you ever noticed a black hole in your field of vision? No. Why not? Because your brain automatically “fills in” that hole with the surrounding image, so you think you’re seeing one whole, complete picture.

Brothers and sisters, please take this to heart: not only do you have a blind spot, but your brain will invent a picture that “looks complete” to cover it. The most dangerous thing has never been a blank; it’s an illusion.

sections.heading: 4. Psychology: Those Who Know Least Are Most Confident
sections.html:
In 1999, David Dunning and Justin Kruger of Cornell University published research in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology showing that the people who did worst on tests of grammar, logic and humour tended to rate themselves far above their actual scores. The reason is simple, and cruel — to recognise that you’re doing badly requires exactly the ability you lack.

Laodicea’s problem was a spiritual version of this kind of self-overestimation. They “looked at the outside and thought they were fine; looked at the world and thought they were rich.” Worldly eyes create an illusion: they make people think they’re doing well when they have actually drifted away from God.

This is the condition of many people today: they have Jesus but don’t know Jesus; they have a faith but no life; they have meetings but no encounter. Why? Because they’re still looking at spiritual things with worldly eyes.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: The Self-Centred Life Keeps Us from Seeing Our Own Poverty
The 321 vision says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.
sections.html:
Pride’s most powerful move isn’t making you bad; it’s making you unable to see that you are bad. A self-centred person has a home-made mirror that reflects only the image he wants to see. Laodicea wasn’t without a mirror; its mirror was broken.

321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. Only when our focus returns to Jesus do we see our true selves — not a self that is condemned, but a self lit up by grace and able to be healed.

That is why, after the rebuke, the Lord says, “As many as I love, I reprove and chasten. Be zealous therefore, and repent” (Revelation 3:19). When the Lord points out our blindness, it is never to humiliate us; it is to heal us.

sections.heading: 4. Right Seeing: We Need God to Open Our Eyes
sections.html: “having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints.” (Ephesians 1:18)

sections.heading: 1. Spiritual Sight Is Not Learned; It Is Revealed by God
sections.html:
Look at the verse just before this part of Paul’s prayer: “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him” (Ephesians 1:17).

“Enlightened” is phōtizō in the original, meaning “to give light, to illuminate”; “the eyes of your hearts” is a literal rendering. Paul knew very well that the Ephesian believers were not short of brains, information or teaching — Ephesus was a great city, and the church there had had three whole years of Paul’s teaching. What they lacked was the light of revelation.

So, brothers and sisters, remember: spiritual sight isn’t something people learn; it is something God reveals. You can build up knowledge by reading books, but you can’t manufacture revelation by reading books. The psalmist says, “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). He didn’t say, “Give me more law”; he said, “Open my eyes.” The Word was there all along; it was the eyes that needed opening.

sections.heading: 2. Morning in Dothan: Three Parties, Three Ways of Seeing
sections.html:
“When the servant of the man of God had risen early, and gone out, behold, an army with horses and chariots was around the city. His servant said to him, ‘Alas, my master! What shall we do?’ He answered, ‘Don’t be afraid; for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.’ Elisha prayed, and said, ‘Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.’ Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.” (2 Kings 6:15–17)

The same morning, the same city, the same hills.

What the Aramean army saw: one prophet, one small town, victory in the bag.

What the young servant saw: horses, chariots and soldiers surrounding the city — and so he cried out “Alas!”, trembling from head to foot.

What Elisha saw: the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire — and so he said, perfectly calmly, “Don’t be afraid.”

Pay special attention to Elisha’s prayer. When his servant was afraid, Elisha didn’t pray, “Lord, drive the Arameans away,” nor did he say, “Lord, let us escape safely today.” His prayer was a single sentence: “Please open his eyes, that he may see.”

God answered. And then? Did the Aramean army withdraw? No. The horses were still there, the chariots were still there, the soldiers were still there; not one piece of the siege had gone.

The circumstances didn’t change, but the “seeing” did. And so fear turned into faith.

Brothers and sisters, what a great comfort this is. The way God most often answers our prayers isn’t by moving the mountain at once, but by first opening our eyes, so that we see, on the other side of the mountain, whole ranks of horses and chariots of fire.

sections.heading: 3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Moment the Eyes Are Opened
sections.html:
The Bible has several moments when “eyes are opened,” and each one is a turning point in a life.

The two disciples on the road to Emmaus walked the whole way with the risen Lord and listened to him explain the Scriptures the whole way, yet they didn’t recognise him. Not until, at the table, the Lord took the bread, gave thanks, broke it and handed it to them — “Their eyes were opened and they recognized him” (Luke 24:31).

Saul of Tarsus was struck down by a blazing light on the road to Damascus and could not see for three days; after Ananias laid his hands on him, “Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight” (Acts 9:18). A Pharisee who thought he saw better than anyone first had to be truly blind for three days before he learned what seeing means.

sections.heading: 4. Science: Even the Best Eyes Need Light
sections.html:
How sensitive is the human eye? Modern vision research tells us that, when fully dark-adapted, a single rod cell can respond to just a handful of photons — clear evidence of the Creator’s precise design.

But, brothers and sisters, think about this: put someone with perfect eyes and better-than-perfect vision into a room with absolutely no light — what can he see? Nothing at all. Because seeing has never been only a matter of the eye; it is even more a matter of light. Without light, the best eyes are blind.

The psalmist said it long ago: “For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light” (Psalm 36:9).

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: The Holy Spirit Is My Guide
sections.html:
The third of 321’s Three Foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Of the eight stages of changing our mindset, the first is Information and the second is Revelation. Information you can find for yourself; Revelation you must ask God for. Many brothers and sisters are rich in Information — they’ve heard hundreds of sermons and read dozens of books — yet they’ve stayed stuck at stage one, because they’ve never once knelt down and said, “Lord, please open my eyes.”

321 also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. The young servant relied on his brain and did the arithmetic: a great Aramean army against two men, and the answer came out as “Alas!” Elisha relied on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and the answer he saw was “Don’t be afraid.” The same problem, different eyes, different answers.

sections.heading: 5. The Key to Opening Spiritual Eyes: Humility
sections.html: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” (James 4:6)

sections.heading: 1. Spiritual Eyes Are Grace, and the Entrance to Grace Is Humility
sections.html:
If spiritual sight is God’s revelation and God’s grace, then the next question is a very practical one: to whom does God give grace?

The Bible’s answer is entirely consistent from the Old Testament to the New. Proverbs 3:34 says, “Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.” James quotes it, and Peter quotes it too: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (1 Peter 5:5).

Notice the word “resists.” In Greek it is antitassomai, originally a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against.” God isn’t merely a little cool towards the proud; he draws up his ranks and stands against them. How serious that is.

sections.heading: 2. Four Passages, One Promise
sections.html:
“He will guide the humble in justice. He will teach the humble his way.” (Psalm 25:9) The humble are guided and taught.

“The humble have seen it, and are glad. You who seek after God, let your heart live.” (Psalm 69:32) The humble see — and seeing, they are glad.

“For the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy, says: ‘I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.’” (Isaiah 57:15) The God who dwells in the high and holy place has a second address: the heart of the humble.

“At that time, Jesus answered, ‘I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants.’” (Matthew 11:25)

Look carefully: the very same “these things” are hidden from the wise and understanding and revealed to infants. It isn’t that God plays favourites; it’s that the posture is different. When someone holds his chin up, the light can’t get into his eyes; when someone bows his head, the light comes in.

So the conclusion is very clear: the humble have their eyes opened by God; the proud have their eyes covered by God.

sections.heading: 3. The Marks of an Infant
sections.html:
The word “infants” in Matthew 11:25 is the Greek nēpios, meaning a little child who can’t yet talk. Why does the Lord Jesus single out infants? Infants have three marks:

First, simplicity. An infant doesn’t listen to you while calculating your motives in his heart.

Second, dependence. An infant never thinks, “I can manage on my own.” When he’s hungry he cries; he knows he has nothing.

Third, not being self-opinionated. An infant has no position to defend, no face to save, no foregone conclusion to prove.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the selfless life. Selflessness isn’t childishness, and it isn’t having no thoughts of your own; the Lord Jesus himself said, “be wise as serpents, and harmless as doves” (Matthew 10:16). Selflessness is this: I no longer treat my own opinion as the final verdict.

sections.heading: 4. Psychology: Only the Humble Can Tell True from False
sections.html:
In recent years psychology has developed a field of research called “intellectual humility,” meaning a person’s willingness to admit that their beliefs might be wrong. In 2017 Mark Leary of Duke University and his colleagues published research in the Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin showing that people higher in intellectual humility were better at telling strong arguments from weak ones when evaluating them, and more willing to revise their position in the light of new evidence.

In other words, even at the natural level, science has observed the same principle: humble people see more accurately. How much more in spiritual things.

sections.heading: 5. An Illustration and a Famous Saying
sections.html:
In ancient times there was often a small door beside the city gate, low and narrow; a man leading a camel couldn’t get through until he had unloaded the goods and made the camel kneel and lower its head. Spiritual sight is like that: if you don’t put down your load and bend your knee, the door is right there, but you simply can’t get in.

The English writer C. S. Lewis, in his 1944 address “Is Theology Poetry?”, said something that is often quoted: “I believe in Christianity as I believe that the sun has risen: not only because I see it, but because by it I see everything else.”

Brothers and sisters, this is the essence of spiritual eyes. It isn’t that you study the sun; it’s that the sun lights up your whole field of vision.

sections.heading: 6. A 321 Insight: Humility Overcomes Pride
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. It also says: pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility inspires humility and both sides win.

This holds not only in our relationships but even more in this matter of “seeing.” Proud people argue with others over who sees rightly, and in the end neither of them sees; a humble person says, “I may have seen it wrongly — Lord, open my eyes,” and in the end both are lit up by the light.

321 says the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Humility is the password for all four layers of relationship. Humble before God, I can see God; humble before myself, I can see my true self; humble before others, I can see the worth of my brothers and sisters; humble in the things I do, I can see God’s timetable rather than my own.

sections.heading: 6. A 321 Insight: Only Selflessness Can See Rightly
sections.html: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

sections.heading: 1. Two Equations
sections.html:
Having come this far, we can gather the whole lesson into two simple equations:

Pride equals the self-centred life, and the self-centred life means wanting to see with my own eyes.

Humility equals selflessness, and selflessness means letting God lead my seeing.

And so: in the self-centred life, the worldly eyes stay open; only in selflessness can the spiritual eyes be opened.

This is also the truth behind the first tragedy in the whole Bible. The serpent said to the woman, “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). Humanity really did eat, and their eyes really were “opened” — “Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked” (Genesis 3:7). Satan didn’t lie; he just didn’t finish the sentence: their eyes were opened, but it was the worldly pair that opened. Humanity gained the right to see for itself, and the price was losing the ability to see God.

From that day on, humanity’s problem has always been the same one: I want to see for myself.

sections.heading: 2. Selflessness Is Not Having Nothing; It Is Entering into the Fullness
The 321 vision puts it very precisely: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out.
sections.html:
Selflessness doesn’t mean wiping yourself out, or becoming someone with no opinions, no feelings and no worth. Selflessness means letting Jesus become my eyes.

No longer seeing with myself, but letting Christ see in me.

The apostle Paul says it like this: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Notice that Paul didn’t disappear. He went on writing letters, travelling, shepherding and suffering. What he lost was not himself, but that “self-centred way of seeing.”

sections.heading: 3. The Most Fitting Illustration: The Lens of a Telescope
sections.html:
You’re looking at the stars through a telescope. Tell me — do you see the lens, or the stars?

If what you see is the lens — dust, fingerprints, scratches — then the telescope has failed. The greatest achievement of a good lens is to make you forget it exists altogether, so that you see only the stars.

Our eyes are more wonderful still. You can go a whole day with healthy eyes and never be aware of them at all. When do you become keenly aware that you have eyes? When they’re inflamed, when there’s grit in them, when they’re dry and sore.

Brothers and sisters, “selflessness” works the same way. The healthiest state of the self isn’t self-inflation, nor self-destruction, but a self that is no longer in the way. When I’m no longer intensely aware of “me,” I begin to see “him” clearly.

This is exactly what the Lord Jesus said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). A pure heart is haplous — a single heart, an undivided heart, a lens with no fingerprints and no scratches.

sections.heading: 4. Jesus Is Our Role Model of Selflessness
sections.html:
The first of 321’s Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model.

Paul says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

“Emptied himself” is the most perfect definition of selflessness. And how did the Lord Jesus “see” while he ministered on earth? He said, “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19).

Listen: even the Son of God, on earth, didn’t see by himself, but looked at what the Father was doing. How much more should we?

sections.heading: 5. Seeing from Four Perspectives
sections.html:
321 says that our perspective must shift from the human to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, and from the worldly to the godly.

Seen from the human perspective, the young servant saw only an army with horses and chariots surrounding the city; seen from God’s perspective, Elisha saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.

Seen from the earthly perspective, Laodicea saw banks, wool and eye salve; seen from the heavenly perspective, the Lord saw the wretched, the miserable and the poor.

Seen from the temporary perspective, the world sees only what is seen; seen from the eternal perspective, Paul looked at the things which are not seen.

Brothers and sisters, these four pairs of perspectives are four pairs of glasses that today’s lesson wants to give you.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From Seeing to Being Built Up
1. The Three Foundations Are Three Lights
sections.html:
Jesus is my role model — he is the Lord who “emptied himself,” and the Son who didn’t see by himself. To see rightly, first look at how he sees.

The Bible is my standard — Scripture is the pair of glasses God has given us, correcting all our sight that sin has distorted. Any “seeing” that doesn’t fit the Bible, however beautiful, moving or reasonable, doesn’t count.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — revelation isn’t the result of human effort; it is the work of the Holy Spirit. So every day we must pray: Lord, enlighten the eyes of my heart.

sections.heading: 2. The Two Core Values Are One Focal Point
sections.html:
Let Jesus be King — the eye has only one focal length, and the heart can have only one King. Whom you choose to let reign as King today decides which eyes you’ll use to look at the world today.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when our spiritual eyes are opened, the first reaction isn’t “How wonderful I am, I have spiritual gifts,” but falling down in worship. Job said, “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you. Therefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:5–6). Anyone who has truly seen God will give the glory to God.

sections.heading: 3. The Goal: Establish God’s System
sections.html:
Why does God want to open our eyes? Not just so we’ll feel a little better and a little less anxious. God opens our eyes in order to establish God’s system.

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Only a group of people whose eyes have been opened, gathered together, can establish God’s system; a group of people who only think they see, gathered together, will just build another Tower of Babel.

sections.heading: 4. The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships
sections.html:
The 920 practice says: every person we’re in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions.

Brothers and sisters, this is the very training ground for “seeing.” How do you see your spouse? How do you see the co-worker who is always late? How do you see the person who once hurt you? Look with worldly eyes, and what you see is faults, debts and unpaid bills; look with spiritual eyes, and what you see is someone for whom Christ laid down his life. Galatians 5:22–23 says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” Only when you see rightly can the fruit be borne.

The 235 relationships say: become a “2” with a selfless person — your spiritual companion; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Notice Elisha’s relationship with that young servant. Elisha didn’t laugh at him for being a coward, didn’t scold him for unbelief, and didn’t show off with “I saw it long ago.” He did what a spiritual father ought to do — he prayed for his son and asked God to open his eyes.

Brothers and sisters, is there a “servant” beside you, standing at the city gate in the early morning, trembling? The best thing you can do for him isn’t to analyse the situation for him; it’s to pray for him: Lord, please open his eyes, that he may see.

sections.heading: 5. The Fivefold Change
sections.html:
A change of mindset: I no longer believe “seeing is believing”; I believe that faith is my evidence.

A change of life: from fear to faith, from complacency to humility.

A change of daily living: the first thing in the morning is no longer scrolling my phone, but asking God to enlighten the eyes of my heart.

A change of relationships: I begin to look at every “2” around me with heaven’s eyes.

A change of ministry: I no longer work out of my own zeal; I see what the Father is doing, and then I do it.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Three Practices, Eight Stages
sections.html:
This lesson has three practices for daily living. We keep the practices from the lesson text and use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take them deeper.

Practice 1: Make one choice every day — which eyes will I use?

Look at your circumstances? Or look at God? In the first three minutes after you open your eyes each morning, you have to make this choice.

Information: first fix today’s truth firmly in your memory — the two kinds of eyes cannot be open at the same time. Copy the theme verse somewhere you’ll see it.

Revelation: don’t stop at knowing. Kneel down and pray: Lord, let these words become light inside me, not just knowledge in my head.

Conviction: say one honest sentence to God in your heart: I admit that for most of my days I’ve been living with worldly eyes.

Implementation: start today. Change your first words on waking to: “Lord, today I want to see with your eyes.”

Practice 2: Practise “closing the worldly eyes”

Compare less, worry less, judge by feelings less; don’t let the world’s values take charge of you.

Implementation: this week, pick one specific thing to close off. For example: no social media in the hour before bed; or whenever you catch yourself comparing in your heart — income, children, the fruit of your ministry — stop at once and quietly recite 2 Corinthians 5:7: “for we walk by faith, not by sight.”

Evaluation: every evening take three minutes to look back: at what moment today did my worldly eyes suddenly snap open? What was I looking at?

Correction: identify your own personal “glare.” Just as astronomers know they mustn’t switch on a white light, you need to know what most easily wrecks your dark adaptation, and then set a boundary against it.

Practice 3: Practise “humbling yourself so God can open your eyes”

Pray every day: “Lord, I won’t rely on my own seeing; let me see what you see.”

Repetition: 321 says a change of mindset isn’t a one-off event; it is a matter of repetition. This prayer isn’t one you pray once today; you pray it every day for forty days, a hundred days. God often doesn’t open our eyes all the way at once; it’s like the blind man at Bethsaida, who the first time saw people “like trees walking,” and only when the Lord laid his hands on him again did he see everything clearly (see Mark 8:24–25). Don’t give up because you can’t see clearly yet.

Multiplication: learn from Elisha. When someone near you is trembling with fear, be the one who prays for them and asks God to open their eyes. Anyone who has truly learned to see will bring others to see as well.

A Gentle Reminder

It isn’t that you can’t see; it’s which eyes you choose to use.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: You Will Begin to See God
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we’re nearly at the end. Let me distil today’s message into one sentence:

The spiritual life doesn’t lie in how much you know, but in how much you see.

Those who know a great deal but cannot see are Laodicea; those who see and are glad are the humble of Psalm 69. Knowledge can be piled up; sight has to be given. And from creation until now, God’s condition for giving sight has been only one — humility.

When you’re willing to lay yourself down and let God open your eyes, three things will happen:

Darkness turns to light — because when the eye is sound, the whole body is full of light.

Fear turns to faith — because what you see is no longer horses, chariots and soldiers, but a mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.

Confusion turns to clarity — because you no longer serve two masters; your heart has become single.

This morning the Lord’s invitation is very concrete. He doesn’t want you to become cleverer; he wants you to let him reign as King. He doesn’t want you to try harder to see; he wants you to humble yourself and let him become your eyes.

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. When one day we truly see, we will never say, “I’ve finally figured it out.” We will only fall down like Job and say: I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.

Brothers and sisters, you will no longer just look at the world — you will begin to see God!

declarations: Lord, I choose to humble myself before you and lay down my own views and judgements! Open my eyes, and let me see your truth, your works and your glory! Let me live in the light and no longer in darkness!

Practise “closing the worldly eyes”
Practise “humbling yourself so God can open your eyes”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you that this morning you have shone on us through your Word. Lord, we confess that we are often like Laodicea, thinking ourselves rich when we are poor, thinking we see when we are blind. And we are often like that young servant: the moment we open our eyes we see only the horses, chariots and soldiers surrounding us, and we begin to be afraid.

Lord, enlighten the eyes of our hearts. Give us a spirit of wisdom and revelation, so that we truly know you. Take away the pride and the self-centred life within us, and make us like infants — simple, dependent and not self-opinionated. Teach us to close our worldly eyes, so that our spiritual eyes can be opened.

Lord, from today on we will no longer see by ourselves. Would you see in us and live in us. Reign as King in our homes, reign as King in our workplaces, reign as King in our church. May all the glory be yours, for ever and ever. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” Take three minutes of quiet and think honestly: this week, what specific thing is your “Mammon” using to steal your focus? How do you plan to close that eye?

2 Kings 6:17 says, “Elisha prayed, and said, ‘Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.’ Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.” Share a time when “your circumstances didn’t change, but what you saw did.” Right now, is there someone near you who is afraid, someone God wants you to pray for, asking him to open their eyes?
