blog.title: It Isn’t That You Can’t See — It’s Which Eyes You Choose

blocks.x: There is one experiment that startled the whole world.

In 1999 the psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris published “Gorillas in Our Midst” in the journal Perception. They asked people to watch a short video: two teams passing basketballs to each other, with just one instruction — count how many passes the white team makes.

Everyone counted accurately. But halfway through the video, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the very centre of the picture, thumped its chest for a full nine seconds, and then strolled unhurriedly out. The researchers asked, “Did you see a gorilla?” Nearly half of them looked blank: “What gorilla?”

Their eyes were fine, the gorilla was right in the middle, and yet they truly did not see it. Psychology calls this “inattentional blindness.” The most piercing part is this: every one of those who missed it was convinced they had seen perfectly clearly.
1. Two Kinds of Eyes Cannot Be Open at Once

In the Sermon on the Mount the Lord Jesus said: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23)

The Lord didn’t say “it is dark outside”; he said “the light that is in you is darkness.” The Greek word for “sound” is haplous, which doesn’t mean good eyesight but “single, undivided.” So the Lord isn’t asking whether you can see clearly; he is asking: are your eyes split in two? In the very next verse he says it even more directly: “You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24).
People have two kinds of eyes: worldly eyes and spiritual eyes. And the even more decisive truth is this — these two kinds of eyes cannot be open at the same time.

Even science bears witness to Scripture. When you walk into a dark room, your eyes need roughly twenty to thirty minutes to adapt fully to the darkness; yet if someone switches on a lamp, it is all reset to zero in a few seconds — which is why stargazers up a mountain use only red-light torches. Spiritual seeing is the same: it takes stillness and waiting, yet it can be wrecked within seconds by a news item, a bit of gossip or a single comparison.
2. The Most Frightening Thing Isn’t Blindness, but Thinking You See

The risen Lord said to the church in Laodicea: “Because you say, ‘I am rich, and have gotten riches, and have need of nothing;’ and don’t know that you are the wretched one, miserable, poor, blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17).

Laodicea was a banking and financial centre of its day, famous for its black woollen cloth, and home to a medical school that produced eye salve. They could heal the eyes of all Asia, but they couldn’t heal their own.

There is a physiological parallel too: each of your eyes has a real blind spot where the optic nerve passes out, with no light-sensitive cells at all. Yet you never feel there’s a hole in your field of vision — because your brain automatically “fills it in.” The most dangerous thing isn’t a blank; it’s an illusion.
This is the condition of many people today: they have Jesus but don’t know Jesus; they have a faith but no life. Because they are still looking at spiritual things with worldly eyes.
3. Humility Is the Door Through Which God Opens Your Eyes

2 Kings 6 records one early morning. The Aramean army had surrounded the city of Dothan by night, and when the young servant pushed open the door and saw horses, chariots and soldiers, he cried out in terror, “Alas!” Elisha prayed just one sentence: “Please open his eyes, that he may see.” God answered, and the servant saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire. Notice: Elisha didn’t ask God to drive the enemy away; after the prayer the horses were still there, the chariots were still there, the soldiers were still there. The circumstances didn’t change, but the “seeing” did — and fear turned into faith.

Spiritual seeing is grace, and the entrance to grace is humility. “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). The Lord Jesus also said, “you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants” (Matthew 11:25). It isn’t that God plays favourites; it’s that the posture is different: hold your chin up and the light can’t get into your eyes; bow your head and the light comes in.

The vision of Kingdom 321 puts it precisely: pride is the self-centred life, wanting to see with my own eyes; humility is selflessness, letting God lead my seeing. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is letting Jesus become your eyes — no longer seeing by yourself, but letting Christ see in you.
Three Small Things You Can Do Today
1. Make one choice every morning: which eyes will I use today? Will I look at my circumstances, or at God?
2. Practise closing the worldly eyes: compare less, worry less, judge by feelings less; find the one “glare” that most easily wrecks your stillness, and set a boundary against it.
3. Practise humbling yourself so God can open your eyes. Pray this one sentence every day: “Lord, I won’t rely on my own seeing; let me see what you see.”

The spiritual life doesn’t lie in how much you know, but in how much you see. Knowledge can be piled up; sight has to be given, and there is only one condition — humility. When you’re willing to lay yourself down and let God open your eyes, darkness turns to light, fear turns to faith, and confusion turns to clarity.
You will no longer just look at the world — you will begin to see God.
Reflection question: This week, what specific thing is stealing the focus of your eyes? How do you plan to close that eye?
