brief12.title: Cover
notes: What We See, We Receive
What We See, We Shall Surely Receive (Part 1)
The things which are seen are temporal
the things which are not seen are eternal
(2 Corinthians 4:18)
Open with the theme verse, 2 Corinthians 4:18, reading it slowly, word by word.
State the core of the lesson: not receiving first and then seeing, but seeing first and then receiving.
Reminder: what needs changing today isn’t our circumstances but a pair of eyes.
Speak warmly; invite the brothers and sisters to grow quiet and get ready to receive.

brief12.title: Introduction
notes: What are you actually looking at?
Not receiving first, then seeing
but seeing first, then receiving
What you see, you pursue
What you pursue, you receive
Opening question: over this past week, where have your eyes rested most often?
Example: Genesis 13:10–15 — Lot lifted his eyes and saw water and pasture; Abram lifted his eyes and saw the promise.
Psychology: Simons and Chabris’s 1999 “gorilla experiment” in the journal Perception — about half the participants never saw the gorilla; this is called “inattentional blindness.”
Application: people don’t see everything in front of them; they see only what they pay attention to.
The key isn’t how much you own, but what you are looking at.

brief12.title: Theme Verse and Background
notes: Paul’s Watchtower
“while we don’t look at the things which are seen,
but at the things which are not seen”
(2 Corinthians 4:18)
Treasure in clay vessels — so we don’t lose heart
Background: Paul wrote to the church in Corinth around AD 55–57; Corinth was a rich, licentious commercial city.
Situation: Paul was criticised — “his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised” (2 Corinthians 10:10) — yet he said the treasure is held in clay vessels (4:7).
Original language: “look at” is σκοπέω (skopeō) — to fix your gaze on, to take careful aim; the root of the English word “scope.”
Contrast: “light affliction, which is for the moment” against “more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory” (4:17).
Conclusion: the circumstances didn’t change; the way of seeing did.

brief12.title: Point 1
notes: Two Kinds of Seeing
What can be seen is temporary
What cannot be seen is eternal
Body, money and status pass away
Life, relationships and reward last for ever
The Bible divides everything into two kinds — not good and bad, but short-lived and lasting.

Science: visible light for the human eye lies only between 380 and 700 nanometres; data from the European Space Agency’s Planck satellite in 2013 show ordinary matter makes up only about 5 per cent of the universe.
Scripture: Hebrews 11:1 and 27; 1 John 2:17.
Example: 2 Kings 6:17 — Elisha’s servant had his eyes opened and saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire. They had been there all along.
321 application: the four shifts of perspective — from the human to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

brief12.title: Point 2
notes: Wrong Seeing: Living for Zero
Birth certificate, diplomas, payslips
Title deed, savings — then a death certificate
Every number ends up at zero
“All is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2)
Scripture: 1 Timothy 6:7; Ecclesiastes 1:2.
Original language: “vanity” is the Hebrew הֶבֶל (hebel), originally breath, a puff of white mist — impossible to grasp.
Illustration: life’s papers — from birth certificate to death certificate; every earlier one has numbers, and in the end they all go to zero.
Example: the rich fool in Luke 12:16–21 — in two short verses “I” and “my” come up eight times.

Psychology: Kahneman and Deaton’s 2010 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences — beyond an annual income of about 75,000 US dollars, emotional well-being clearly levels off; the Harvard Study of Adult Development, following more than seven hundred men since 1938, concludes that good relationships keep people healthy and happy.

brief12.title: Point 3
notes: Invest the Temporary in the Eternal
“Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven”
(Matthew 6:20)
Money isn’t the problem — how you see it is
Use time to love, money to bless
Jesus never rejected earthly resources; what he teaches is how to use them.
Scripture: Matthew 6:19–21 — moth, rust and thieves: three kinds of wealth, three fates.
Scripture: 1 Timothy 6:17–19 — giving isn’t a loss; it is transferring your savings to heaven.
Quotation: the missionary Jim Elliot’s journal, 28 October 1949: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.”

Psychology: Walter Mischel’s “marshmallow experiments” at Stanford — the way to overcome temptation isn’t gritting your teeth but taking your eyes off it; this echoes Hebrews 12:2, where Jesus saw the joy that was set before him.

brief12.title: Point 4
notes: Your Eyes Decide Your Master
“The lamp of the body is the eye”
(Matthew 6:22)
What you look at, you love
What you love, you serve
Scripture: Matthew 6:22–24 — treasure, the eye and masters belong together.
Original language: “sound” is ἁπλοῦς (haplous) — single, undivided in devotion; in Jewish idiom the “evil eye” meant greed (Proverbs 28:22).
Jesus personifies “Mammon” as a master that will never say to you, “That’s enough.”
Illustration: every driver knows the car goes where your eyes look.
Key point: it isn’t that you have no master; you are choosing who will be master. 321 says: let man be man and let God be God.

brief12.title: Point 5
notes: Trading the Fleeting for the Eternal
“Faithful in a very little”
Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness
God meets your needs; you seek his kingdom
Scripture: Luke 16:10–11 — the very little things are the entrance exam for God’s kingdom.
Three practices: use money to bless people, use resources to build people up, use your life to glorify God.
Example: Mark 12:44 — the widow’s two small coins; God counts the proportion, not the amount.
Scripture: Matthew 6:33 — “first” is πρῶτον (prōton), first in value; “given as well” means added on as an extra.
321 application: the 920 practice — everyone I relate to is my “2”; towards them I live out the “0” and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.

brief12.title: Point 6
notes: A 321 Insight
Look at yourself, live out yourself
Look at the world, live out the world
Look at Jesus, live out Christ
Self-centred sees the temporary; selfless, the eternal
Scripture: 2 Corinthians 3:18 — first seeing, then transformed.
Example: Numbers 13:33 — ten spies saw themselves as grasshoppers; Numbers 14:24 — Caleb had another spirit.
Forty-five years later, at eighty-five, Caleb still took hold of that mountain (Joshua 14:12).
321 core: the self-centred life is the root of the fall; selflessness is not having nothing — it is entering into the fullness and living it out.
The selfless don’t live for themselves, but for Jesus, for others and for God’s kingdom.

brief12.title: Putting It into Practice
notes: Practices for Daily Living
Re-examine your “seeing”
Do one eternal thing every day
Put God’s kingdom first
Everything else follows naturally
Practice 1: a three-minute “eye inventory” every evening — note the three things that took most of your attention today.
Practice 2: ask the Lord for one name, and today do one thing of eternal value for that person.
Practice 3: write “God’s kingdom” into your diary and your budget, so the real order shows.
Go deeper with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Reminder: knowing isn’t the same as changing; repeat it until it becomes life, then multiply it into others.

brief12.title: Closing and Call
notes: What you see is what you receive
It isn’t that you haven’t received
You haven’t been looking at the right thing
See the temporary, get the temporary; see the eternal, get the eternal
Let Jesus be King and receive all the glory
Recap: Abram, Caleb, Moses, Stephen — each saw first, then received.
Scripture: Acts 7:55 — Stephen looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
Scripture: Colossians 3:2 — set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.
Three calls: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory; do one thing of eternal value today.
Speak firmly and warmly; invite the brothers and sisters to respond on the spot.

brief12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Prayer of Response
Lord, adjust the way I see
Let me see what has eternal value
Let me live my whole life for your kingdom
May the Lord bless and keep you. Amen
Lead the brothers and sisters in speaking the lesson’s declaration of faith together.
Pray that the Lord would open our eyes as he opened the eyes of Elisha’s servant.
Ask the Lord to take away the self-centred life and make us selfless people.
Ephesians 1:18: ask the Holy Spirit to enlighten the eyes of our hearts.
Send out with a blessing: may the brothers and sisters go out today living with an eternal perspective.

brief21.title: Cover
notes: What We See, We Receive
What We See, We Shall Surely Receive (Part 1)

the things which are not seen are eternal
(2 Corinthians 4:18)
Open with the theme verse, 2 Corinthians 4:18, reading it slowly, word by word.
State the core of the lesson: not receiving first and then seeing, but seeing first and then receiving.
Explain that this is the first talk in the series “What We See, We Shall Surely Receive.”
Reminder: what needs changing today isn’t our circumstances but a pair of eyes.
Speak warmly; invite the brothers and sisters to grow quiet and get ready to receive.

brief21.title: Introduction 1
notes: What are you actually looking at?
Not receiving first, then seeing
but seeing first, then receiving
What you see, you pursue
What you pursue, you receive
Opening question: over this past week, where have your eyes rested most often? Your phone? Your bank account? What other people think of you?
Point out that people usually assume the order is receiving first, then seeing; the Bible’s order is exactly the opposite.
The chain: what you see, you pursue; what you pursue, you receive.
Conclusion: the key isn’t how much you own, but what you are looking at.

brief21.title: Introduction 2
notes: Both lifted their eyes — different ends
Lot lifted his eyes and saw water and pasture
Abram lifted his eyes and saw the promise
(Genesis 13:10–15)
People see only what they pay attention to
Example: Genesis 13:10 — Lot lifted up his eyes, saw that all the plain of the Jordan was well-watered, and chose Sodom.
Contrast: Genesis 13:14–15 — Abram looked northward, southward, eastward and westward, and God said, all the land which you see I will give to you.

Psychology: in 1999 Simons and Chabris published “Gorillas in Our Midst” in the journal Perception; about half the participants never saw the gorilla that walked into the picture for nine seconds — “inattentional blindness.”
Application: people don’t see everything in front of them; they see only what they pay attention to.
Spiritual reminder: it isn’t that God isn’t there; it’s that we aren’t looking.

brief21.title: Theme Verse and Background
notes: Paul’s Watchtower
“while we don’t look at the things which are seen,
but at the things which are not seen”
(2 Corinthians 4:18)
Treasure in clay vessels — so we don’t lose heart
Background: the author is the apostle Paul, writing to the church in Corinth around AD 55–57, probably from Macedonia.
Situation: Corinth was the capital of Achaia, rich and licentious; Paul was criticised — “his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised” (2 Corinthians 10:10).
Scripture: 2 Corinthians 4:7 — treasure in clay vessels; the original, ostrakinos, means the cheapest earthenware.
Original language: “look at” is σκοπέω (skopeō) — to fix your gaze on, to take careful aim; the root of the English word “scope.”
Contrast: “light affliction, which is for the moment” against “an eternal weight of glory” (4:17) — the circumstances didn’t change; the way of seeing did.

brief21.title: Point 1a
notes: Two Kinds of Seeing
What can be seen is temporary
What cannot be seen is eternal
Body, money and status pass away
Life, relationships and reward last for ever
The Bible divides everything into two kinds — not good and bad, but short-lived and lasting.
What can be seen: the body wastes away, money disappears, status changes (Matthew 6:19).
What cannot be seen: spiritual life, our relationship with God, heavenly reward (1 John 2:17).

Science: visible light for the human eye lies only between 380 and 700 nanometres; the 2013 Planck satellite data from the European Space Agency show ordinary matter makes up only about 5 per cent of the universe, the rest being dark matter and dark energy.
Scripture: Hebrews 11:1 and 27 — Moses endured “as seeing him who is invisible.”

brief21.title: Point 1b
notes: Lord, Open My Eyes
“Please open his eyes”
(2 Kings 6:17)
The horses and chariots of fire were there all along
Look at the temporary, live in it; look at the eternal, live it out
Example: 2 Kings 6:15–17 — Elisha’s servant got up early, saw the enemy surrounding the city and panicked.
Elisha said: those who are with us are more than those who are with them.
Key point: the horses and chariots of fire were there all along; all that changed was a pair of eyes.
Prayer: Psalm 119:18, “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.”

321 application: the four shifts of perspective — from the human to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly; we change our eyes through the Three Foundations.

brief21.title: Point 2a
notes: Wrong Seeing: Living for Zero
“We brought nothing into the world,
and we certainly can’t carry anything out”
(1 Timothy 6:7)
“All is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2)
Scripture: 1 Timothy 6:7; Ecclesiastes 1:2.
Original language: “vanity” is the Hebrew הֶבֶל (hebel), originally breath, vapour, a puff of white mist.
“Vanity of vanities” is the Hebrew way of expressing the superlative, like “King of kings.”
Illustration: the white breath you puff out on a winter morning — reach out to grab it, and all you catch is air.
Reminder: naked we came from our mother’s womb, and naked we shall return.

brief21.title: Point 2b
notes: Life’s Papers All End Up at Zero
Birth certificate, diplomas, payslips
Title deed, savings — then a death certificate
Every number ends up at zero
Worldly eyes can see only the present
Illustration: life’s papers — birth certificate, diplomas, payslips, title deed, savings book, and finally a death certificate.
Every earlier one has numbers written on it; the last one has no numbers at all.
Example: the rich fool in Luke 12:16–21 — in two short verses “I” and “my” come up eight times.
321 diagnosis: this is the self-centred life; Genesis 3:6 — Eve’s fall began with “seeing.”

Psychology: Kahneman and Deaton’s 2010 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences — beyond an annual income of about 75,000 US dollars, well-being clearly levels off; the Harvard Study of Adult Development, following more than seven hundred men since 1938, concludes that good relationships keep people healthy and happy. This echoes 321: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

brief21.title: Point 3a
notes: Invest the Temporary in the Eternal
“Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven”
(Matthew 6:20)
Jesus never rejected earthly resources
What he teaches is: how you use them
Jesus never rejected earthly resources; what he teaches is how to use them.
Scripture: Matthew 6:19–21 — moth, rust and thieves: three kinds of wealth, three fates.
Illustration: there is a bank in heaven that no pest can get into, that rust cannot touch, that no thief can break into.
Scripture: Matthew 6:21, “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Reminder: the question isn’t whether you have it, but for whom you have it.

brief21.title: Point 3b
notes: For Yourself or for God
Money isn’t the problem — how you see it is
For yourself, it becomes vanity
For God, it becomes eternal
Use time to love, money to bless
The key comes down to just two words: “for whom.”
Use your time to love people (Matthew 25:40), your money to bless people (Proverbs 19:17), your life to serve God (Luke 9:24).
Scripture: 1 Timothy 6:17–19 — giving isn’t a loss; it is transferring your savings into an account that can never go bankrupt.
Quotation: the missionary Jim Elliot’s journal, 28 October 1949: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” He was martyred in Ecuador in 1956, aged just twenty-eight.

Psychology: Walter Mischel’s “marshmallow experiments” at Stanford — overcoming temptation doesn’t come from gritting your teeth but from taking your eyes off it; this echoes Hebrews 12:2, where Jesus, for the joy that was set before him, despised the shame.

brief21.title: Point 4a
notes: Your Eyes Decide Your Master
“The lamp of the body is the eye”
(Matthew 6:22)
What you look at, you love
What you love, you serve
Scripture: Matthew 6:22–24 — treasure, the eye and masters are tightly linked.
Original language: “sound” is ἁπλοῦς (haplous) — single, undivided in devotion; its opposite is “divided.”
In Jewish idiom the “evil eye” meant greed and stinginess (Proverbs 28:22).
The chain: what you look at, you love; what you love, you serve; what you serve becomes your master.
Illustration: every driver knows the car goes where your eyes look; stare at the barrier and you’ll hit the barrier.

brief21.title: Point 4b
notes: You Are Choosing Your Master
“You can’t serve both God and Mammon”
(Matthew 6:24)
Look at money, and money is master
Look at Jesus, and Jesus is King
Original language: “Mammon” is μαμωνᾶς (mamōnas), from Aramaic, meaning wealth; Jesus personifies it as a master.
Reminder: once money takes the throne, it becomes a brutally harsh master that will never say, “That’s enough.”
Quotation: Augustine, Confessions — “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
Key point: it isn’t that you have no master; you are choosing who will be master. The throne of the heart never stays empty.

321 application: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

brief21.title: Point 5a
notes: Trading the Fleeting for the Eternal
“Faithful in a very little”
God doesn’t value “how much”
but “how you use it”
Scripture: Luke 16:10–11 — the very little things are the entrance exam for God’s kingdom.
“The unrighteous mammon” literally reads “the mammon of unrighteousness,” meaning the money of this present age; only when we pass this quiz does God entrust us with “the true riches.”
Three practices: use money to bless people, use resources to build people up, use your life to glorify God.
Example: Mark 12:44 — the widow’s two small coins; God counts the proportion, not the amount.
Scripture: Galatians 2:20, “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

brief21.title: Point 5b
notes: Seek First His Kingdom and His Righteousness
“All these things will be given to you as well”
(Matthew 6:33)
God takes care of your needs
You take care of God’s kingdom
Scripture: Matthew 6:33. “First” is πρῶτον (prōton) — not only first in time but, even more, first in value.
“Given as well” is προστίθημι (prostithēmi), meaning added on as an extra — God isn’t asking you to choose one or the other.
A beautiful division of labour: God takes care of your needs, and you take care of God’s kingdom.
The result: earthly provision plus heavenly reward, all given to you as well.

321 application: the 920 practice — everyone we relate to is our “2”; towards them we live out the “0” and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23); and from there we enter the 235 relationships.

brief21.title: Point 6a
notes: A 321 Insight
Look at yourself, live out yourself
Look at the world, live out the world
Look at Jesus, live out Christ
Scripture: 2 Corinthians 3:18 — with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image; first seeing, then transformed.
Example: Numbers 13:33 — ten spies said, “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers.”
They looked at themselves and saw grasshoppers; seeing grasshoppers, they lived like grasshoppers; living like grasshoppers, they died in the wilderness.
Contrast: Numbers 14:24 — Caleb had “another spirit.”
Joshua 14:12 — forty-five years later, eighty-five-year-old Caleb said, “give me this hill country”; what he had seen back then, he later truly received.

brief21.title: Point 6b
notes: Self-Centred or Selfless
Self-centred sees the temporary; selfless, the eternal
The selfless don’t live for themselves
but for Jesus, for others
and for God’s kingdom
Diagnosis: the self-centred person will always look at the temporary, because the “self” lives in time; its field of vision and capacity are limited.
Only the selfless can see eternity, because the centre of their circle is God, and God is eternal.
Clarification: selflessness isn’t erasing yourself or becoming a zero; it is the limited centre stepping aside so that the infinite God becomes the centre.
321 core: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and living it out — no longer I, but Christ lives in me.
The three “fors” match 321: living for Jesus, for others and for God’s kingdom — let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive the glory, establish God’s system.

brief21.title: Practice 1
notes: Examine Your “Seeing”
What do I pay most attention to each day?
Money? Achievement? God’s kingdom?
Do one eternal thing every day
Care for, share the gospel with, serve someone
Practice 1: a three-minute “eye inventory” every evening — note the three things that took most of your attention, and review the proportions at the weekend.
Practice 2: ask the Lord for one name, and today do one thing of eternal value for that person.
Scripture: Luke 16:10, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.”
Reminder: don’t wait until you’re more mature, better off or less busy — do it today.
This is the 920 practice brought down to earth — living out selflessness towards every “2.”

brief21.title: Practice 2
notes: Adjust Your Priorities
Put “God’s kingdom” first
Let everything else follow naturally
Eight stages: Information, Revelation,
Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
Practice 3: put “God’s kingdom” first — first schedule time with God, time for relationships and time for serving, and then everything else after.
Reminder: your diary and your accounts don’t lie; what is really “first” will show.
The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Core: don’t stop at “knowing.” Knowing isn’t the same as changing.
Only when it is repeated until it becomes life, and then multiplied into others, is the change complete.

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
notes: A New Pair of Eyes
Three Foundations: role model, standard, guide
Two Core Values: King, all the glory
The Goal: establish God’s system
Change the mindset and the life changes

The Three Foundations are three pairs of glasses: Jesus is my role model (how he sees), the Bible is my standard (discerning by Scripture), the Holy Spirit is my guide (Ephesians 1:18, the eyes of the heart enlightened).
The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — whatever you look at becomes king; let Jesus receive all the glory (John 3:30, “He must increase, but I must decrease”).
The Goal: establish God’s system — a group of people whose eyes are looking in the same direction.
The fivefold change begins with mindset: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.
Satan’s strategy is to zoom the lens in until only the self is left; the way to break it is to zoom out, to the cross and the throne. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: What you see is what you receive
It isn’t that you haven’t received
You haven’t been looking at the right thing
See the temporary, get the temporary; see the eternal, get the eternal
Let Jesus be King and receive all the glory
Recap: Abram, Caleb, Moses, Stephen — each saw first, then received.
Scripture: Acts 7:55 — Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
Scripture: Colossians 3:2, “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.”
Three calls: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory; do one thing of eternal value today.
Speak firmly and warmly; invite the brothers and sisters to respond on the spot.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Prayer of Response
Lord, adjust the way I see
Let me see what has eternal value
Let me live my whole life for your kingdom
May the Lord bless and keep you. Amen
Lead the brothers and sisters in speaking the lesson’s declaration of faith together.
Pray that the Lord would open our eyes just as he opened the eyes of Elisha’s servant.
Ask the Lord to take away the self-centred life within us and make us selfless people.
Declare: you are our King, and we will seek first your kingdom and your righteousness.
Send out with a blessing: may the brothers and sisters go out today living with an eternal perspective.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 121 of Morning Devotion 321. The title is “What We See, We Receive,” and the subtitle is “What We See, We Shall Surely Receive.” Our theme verse is 2 Corinthians 4:18: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” Brothers and sisters, this morning God may not change your circumstances; what he wants to change is your eyes.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask a question first: over this past week, where have your eyes rested most often? On your phone? On the figures in your bank account? Or on God’s kingdom? We often think we have to receive first before we can see. But the Bible says: first you see, and then you receive. What you see is what you pursue; what you pursue is what you receive. In Genesis 13, Lot lifted up his eyes, saw the rich, well-watered pasture and chose Sodom; Abram lifted up his eyes, saw God’s promise and received the whole land of Canaan for ever. Both of them lifted their eyes, but they looked in different directions, and their ends were completely different.

Paul spoke this verse in the midst of suffering. He was whipped, imprisoned and criticised for his “weak bodily presence,” yet he said, we have this treasure in clay vessels. The word “look at” is skopeō in the original, meaning to fix your gaze on, to take careful aim; the English word “scope,” as in telescope, comes from it. Brothers and sisters, Paul’s scope wasn’t trained on his circumstances but on eternity. That’s why he said our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us an eternal weight of glory. The circumstances didn’t change; the way of seeing did.

Our first point: two kinds of seeing. The Bible divides everything into two kinds. What can be seen is temporary; what cannot be seen is eternal. The body wastes away, money disappears, status changes. But spiritual life is eternal, our relationship with God is eternal, and heavenly reward is eternal. Brothers and sisters, did you know? Scientists tell us that the ordinary matter we can see makes up only 5 per cent of our universe. If even the natural world is like that, how can you say that what can be seen is all there is? Elisha’s servant got up early, saw the enemy surrounding the city and was afraid. Elisha prayed, please open his eyes. God opened his eyes, and he saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire. The horses and chariots of fire had been there all along; he just hadn’t seen them before.

Our second point: wrong seeing is living for “zero.” 1 Timothy 6:7 says we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out. Brothers and sisters, think about the pieces of paper in your life. At birth, a birth certificate; at school, certificate after certificate; at work, payslip after payslip; half a lifetime of hard work, and you get a title deed and savings. But the last piece of paper is a death certificate. Every earlier one was full of numbers; on the last one there are no numbers at all. If all our lives we live only for those numbers, we are living for “zero.” That is what worldly eyes are like: they can see only the present, never eternity.

Our third point: invest the temporary in the eternal. Jesus said, “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven.” Brothers and sisters, notice that Jesus never rejected earthly resources; what he teaches is how to use them. Money isn’t the problem; the problem is how you see it. For yourself, it becomes vanity; for God, it becomes eternal. Use your time to love people: eternal. Use your money to bless people: eternal. Use your life to serve God: eternal. The missionary Jim Elliot once wrote: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.”

Our fourth point: your eyes decide your master. Jesus said, the lamp of the body is the eye; if your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. He also said, you can’t serve both God and Mammon. Brothers and sisters, this is a chain: what you look at, you love; what you love, you serve. Look at money, and money becomes master; look at the world, and the world becomes master; look at God, and God becomes Master. Anyone who has driven a car knows that the car goes where your eyes look. So it isn’t that you have no master; you are choosing who will be master.

Our fifth point: trading the fleeting for the eternal. The Lord said, he who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. What God values isn’t “how much,” but “how you use it.” Use money to bless people, use resources to build people up, use your life to glorify God — that is serving God. The Lord also said, “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” Brothers and sisters, there is a beautiful division of labour here: God takes care of your needs, and you take care of God’s kingdom. Earthly provision, plus heavenly reward, will all be given to you as well.

Our sixth point is today’s light from 321: what you see is what you live out. Look at yourself, and you’ll live out yourself; look at the world, and you’ll live out the world; look at Jesus, and you’ll live out Christ. Why do people see wrongly? Because of the self-centred life. The self-centred can see only the temporary, because the “self” lives in time; only the selfless can see eternity, because the centre of their circle is God. Brothers and sisters, selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is entering into the fullness and living it out. The selfless don’t live for themselves, but for Jesus, for others and for God’s kingdom.

Now for the practices. First, re-examine your “seeing.” Every evening, for three minutes, ask yourself: what did I pay most attention to today? Money, achievement, or God’s kingdom? Second, invest deliberately in eternity. Ask the Lord for one name, and today do one thing of eternal value for that person — caring for them, sharing the gospel, serving them. Third, adjust your life’s priorities. Put God’s kingdom first, and let everything else follow naturally. Brothers and sisters, knowing isn’t the same as changing. Keep practising until it becomes life, and then multiply it into others.

Brothers and sisters, the most important thing in life isn’t how much you own, but what you see. Look at the temporary, and you’ll receive the temporary; look at the eternal, and you’ll receive the eternal. So it isn’t that you haven’t received; it’s that you haven’t been looking at the right thing. Abram saw the promise and received the whole land; Caleb saw that mountain, and at eighty-five could still take hold of it; when Stephen was being stoned, he looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God. When you begin to see God’s kingdom, your life will no longer be reset to zero; it will enter into eternal value and glory. Today, let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Let’s pray together. Lord, adjust the way I see, so that I no longer see only fleeting things, but see what has eternal value. Open our eyes, as you opened the eyes of Elisha’s servant. Take away the self-centred life within us, so that we live our whole lives for your kingdom and live out eternal meaning in this fleeting life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you and keep you. What you see is what you will receive.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come to Lesson 121 of Morning Devotion 321. The title is “What We See, We Receive,” and the subtitle is “What We See, We Shall Surely Receive.” Our theme verse is 2 Corinthians 4:18: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” Notice that the verse doesn’t say the things which are seen are bad; it says they are temporal. This morning God may not change your circumstances; what he wants to change is your eyes.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask a question first: over this past week, where have your eyes rested most often? On your phone? On the figures in your bank account? On what other people think of you? Or on God’s kingdom? We often think we have to receive first before we can see. Once I have money, I’ll be able to see a future. But the Bible’s order is exactly the opposite — first you see, and then you receive. What you see is what you pursue; what you pursue is what you receive. So the key isn’t how much you own, but what you are actually looking at.

In Genesis 13, Abram and Lot part ways. Lot lifted up his eyes, saw that all the plain of the Jordan was well-watered, and chose that land. But God said to Abram: lift up your eyes and look northward and southward and eastward and westward, for all the land which you see I will give to you and to your offspring for ever. Both lifted their eyes; Lot saw water and pasture, Abram saw the promise, and their ends were completely different. In 1999 the psychologists Simons and Chabris asked people to watch a video of players passing a ball; halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the picture and stayed for nine seconds, and half the viewers never saw it at all. This is called “inattentional blindness.” Brothers and sisters, people see only what they pay attention to. It isn’t that God isn’t there; it’s that we aren’t looking.

The author of this verse is the apostle Paul, writing around AD 55 to 57 to the church in Corinth — the richest and most licentious commercial city of its day. Some criticised Paul, saying his bodily presence was weak and his speech despised, yet Paul said: we have this treasure in clay vessels. Clay vessels are the cheapest earthenware, the kind that breaks the moment you drop it. “Look at” in the original is skopeō, meaning to fix your gaze on, to take careful aim; the English word “scope,” as in telescope, comes from it. Paul’s scope wasn’t trained on his circumstances, only on eternity. That’s why he said our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us an eternal weight of glory. The circumstances didn’t change; the way of seeing did.

Our first point: two kinds of seeing. The Bible divides everything into two kinds. What can be seen is temporary; what cannot be seen is eternal. The body wastes away, money disappears, status changes. But spiritual life is eternal, our relationship with God is eternal, and heavenly reward is eternal. Brothers and sisters, the naked human eye can see only light with wavelengths between 380 and 700 nanometres. Data released in 2013 from the European Space Agency’s Planck satellite tell us that ordinary matter makes up only 5 per cent of this universe; the rest is invisible dark matter and dark energy. If even the natural world is like that, how can you say that what can be seen is all there is?

In 2 Kings 6 the Aramean army surrounded the city by night. Elisha’s servant got up early, looked out and was terrified. Elisha prayed, “Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.” God opened his eyes, and he saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire. Brothers and sisters, notice: the horses and chariots of fire had been there all along; he just hadn’t seen them before. The circumstances didn’t change; all that changed was a pair of eyes. This is exactly 321’s four shifts of perspective: from the human to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. If you look at the temporary, you’ll live in the temporary; if you look at the eternal, you’ll live out the eternal.

Our second point: wrong seeing is living for “zero.” 1 Timothy 6:7 says, “For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out.” Ecclesiastes 1:2 says: all is vanity. “Vanity” in the original is hebel, which originally means breath, a puff of white mist. On a winter morning you puff out a white breath and reach out to grab it, and all you catch is air. Solomon says that is what everything people chase under the sun is like. Naked we came from our mother’s womb, and naked we shall return.

Brothers and sisters, think about the pieces of paper in your life. At birth, a birth certificate; at school, certificate after certificate; at work, payslip after payslip; half a lifetime of hard work, and you get a title deed and savings. But the last piece of paper is a death certificate. Every earlier one was full of numbers; on the last one there are no numbers at all. If all our lives we live only for those numbers, we are living for “zero.” In the rich fool Jesus spoke of, “I” and “my” come up eight times in just two verses. That is what 321 calls the self-centred life. Harvard’s Study of Adult Development, which has followed more than seven hundred men since 1938, reaches one conclusion: what keeps people healthy and happy isn’t wealth, but good relationships. That echoes 321: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Our third point: invest the temporary in the eternal. Jesus said, “but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal.” Brothers and sisters, notice that Jesus never rejected earthly resources. What he teaches isn’t about “having or not having” but about “how you use it.” In those days grain was eaten by pests, clothing by moths, and gold and silver were stolen — three kinds of wealth, three fates, and not one of them could be kept safe. But Jesus says there is a bank that no pest can get into, that rust cannot touch, that no thief can break into, and that bank is called “heaven.”

So money isn’t the problem; the problem is how you see money. The same hundred dollars, if it’s for yourself, goes to zero along with you; if it’s for God, it goes into eternity along with God. The watershed comes down to two words: for whom. Use your time to love people, and that time enters eternity; use your money to bless people, and that money enters eternity; use your life to serve God, and that life enters eternity. Paul says, charge them to be willing to share, laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come. So giving isn’t a loss; it’s a transfer. The missionary Jim Elliot said: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.”

Our fourth point: your eyes decide your master. Jesus said, “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.” “Sound” in the original is haplous, meaning single, undivided in devotion. Brothers and sisters, there is a chain here: what you look at, you love; what you love, you serve. Anyone who has driven a car knows that the car goes where your eyes look. Driving instructors say: when you take a bend, never stare at the barrier. Life is the same: stare at what you lack, and you’ll drive into lack; look up to Jesus, and your life will turn towards him.

Jesus goes on: “You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” Mammon comes from Aramaic and means wealth. Notice that Jesus treats Mammon as a “master.” Once money takes the throne, it is no longer a tool but a master — and a brutally harsh master at that, because it will never say to you, “That’s enough.” Brothers and sisters, you are not “without a master.” If you don’t let Jesus be King, something else will certainly be king. Augustine said: Lord, our heart is restless until it rests in you. 321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place; humility is returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Our fifth point: trading the fleeting for the eternal. The Lord said, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” Promotion in God’s kingdom works differently from the world. The world looks at how big the things you’ve achieved are; God looks at whether you are faithful in the very least of things. The Lord goes on: if you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches? So money is a quiz, and what it tests is faithfulness. So: use money to bless people, use resources to build people up, use your life to glorify God. The widow put in two small coins, and the Lord said she gave all that she had to live on. In God’s ledger, what counts isn’t the amount but the proportion.

Jesus condenses all of this into one overarching principle: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” “First” in the original is prōton — not only first in time, but even more, first in value. “Given as well” means added on as an extra. God isn’t asking you to choose one or the other; God is saying: take care of that “first,” and he himself will add on the rest. Brothers and sisters, this is a beautiful division of labour: God takes care of your needs, and you take care of God’s kingdom. Earthly provision, plus heavenly reward, will all be given to you as well. This is exactly the 920 practice: everyone we relate to is our “2”; when we live out the “0” towards them, we bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.

Our sixth point is today’s light from 321: what you see is what you live out. Look at yourself, and you’ll live out yourself; look at the world, and you’ll live out the world; look at Jesus, and you’ll live out Christ. Paul says that with unveiled face, seeing the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image. Notice the order: first seeing, then transformed. In Numbers 13 the ten spies said: we were in our own sight as grasshoppers. They looked at themselves and saw grasshoppers; seeing grasshoppers, they lived like grasshoppers, and in the end they died in the wilderness. But Caleb had “another spirit,” and forty-five years later, at eighty-five, he said: give me this hill country. What he had seen back then, he later truly received.

Why do people see wrongly? 321 gives the deepest diagnosis: because of the self-centred life. The self-centred person will always look at the temporary, because the “self” lives in time; the self’s lifespan is limited, its field of vision is limited, its capacity is limited. Only the selfless can see eternity, because the centre of their circle is no longer themselves but God. Brothers and sisters, please hear this clearly: selflessness isn’t erasing yourself or becoming a zero. Selflessness is that small, limited centre stepping aside, so that the infinite God becomes the new centre. Change the centre, and the circle goes from finite to infinite. So the selfless don’t live for themselves, but for Jesus, for others and for God’s kingdom.

Now for the practices. First, re-examine your “seeing.” Spend three minutes every evening taking an “eye inventory”: which three things took most of my attention today? Money? Achievement? Or God’s kingdom? Second, invest deliberately in eternity, and do one thing of eternal value every day. Brothers and sisters, I suggest you pray like this: Lord, give me a name — the person you want me to love today. Then do it today; don’t put it off until tomorrow. A phone call, a prayer for someone, some time spent with someone — any of these will do.

Third, adjust your life’s priorities. Put God’s kingdom first, and let everything else follow naturally. Brothers and sisters, your diary and your accounts don’t lie. This month, first block out time with God, time for relationships with people and time for serving, and schedule everything else after that. 321 has a precious tool called the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. These eight stages have only one core: don’t stop at “knowing.” Knowing isn’t the same as changing. Only when it is repeated until it becomes life, and then multiplied into others, is the change complete.

Let’s place today’s message within the framework of 321. The Three Foundations are the three pairs of glasses for our seeing: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — because whatever you look at becomes king; let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system — a group of people whose eyes are looking in the same direction. Brothers and sisters, what Satan is best at is zooming the lens in, so close that all you can see is your own grievances and your own face. The way to break it is simple: zoom the lens out — out to the cross, out to the throne. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Change the mindset, and the life changes.

Brothers and sisters, we began with a question: what are you actually looking at? Now we finish with an answer: the most important thing in life isn’t how much you own, but what you see. Look at the temporary, and you’ll receive the temporary; look at the eternal, and you’ll receive the eternal. So the lesson says: it isn’t that you haven’t received; it’s that you haven’t been looking at the right thing. Abram saw the promise and received the whole land; Caleb saw that mountain and at eighty-five still received it; when Stephen was being stoned, he looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God. When you begin to see God’s kingdom, your life will no longer be reset to zero; it will enter into eternal value and glory. So today I give you three calls: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory; and starting today, do one thing of eternal value.

Let’s pray together. Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you. Lord, we confess that our eyes are often filled up with the things right in front of us. We see the bills, but not your provision; we see the difficulties, but not the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire. Open our eyes, as you opened the eyes of Elisha’s servant. Take away the self-centred life within us, so that we no longer live for numbers that will all end up as zero. Teach us to use our time to love people, our money to bless people and our lives to serve you. We declare: you are our King, and we will seek first your kingdom and your righteousness; all glory be to you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you and keep you. What you see is what you will receive.

sections.heading: Introduction: What Are You Looking At?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. This morning, let’s first be still for three seconds, and then open our eyes and look at the room in front of us.

What do you see? Some see a table not yet cleared, dishes not yet washed, a pile of bills. Others see a lamp left on for them, an open Bible, a new morning given by God. The same room, the same light, the same twenty-four hours — and yet we see completely different worlds.

In the last lesson we saw a key truth together: what you see is what you pursue, and what you pursue is what you obtain. A person’s eyes are, in fact, the steering wheel of his life. Today God wants to take us one layer deeper. He wants to tell us this: the “value you see” determines the direction and the ending of your life.

Please pay special attention to this sentence: it is not how hard you try, but what you treasure.

We often think the differences between lives come down to how much effort we put in, how much ability we have, how good or bad our opportunities are. But the Bible shows us a more fundamental fact: two people can work equally hard, be equally clever, stand in exactly the same place — and end up worlds apart. The reason lies not in the feet but in the eyes; not in the hands but in the heart. For what you chase in life will never exceed what you see, and what you gain will never exceed what you treasure.

There is a famous experiment in psychology that can help us understand this. In 1999, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris, then teaching at Harvard University, published a study in the journal Perception called “Gorillas in Our Midst.” They asked participants to watch a short video in which two teams were passing basketballs, and the task was to count the passes made by the team in white. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit strolled right through the middle of the screen, even stopping to beat its chest — nine seconds in all. And the result? About half of the participants never saw the gorilla at all.

Their eyes were fine, the light was good enough, and the gorilla was real. They didn’t see it simply because they were busy counting something else. The researchers gave this phenomenon a name: inattentional blindness. It isn’t that we cannot see; it’s that we “only see what we are paying attention to.”

Brothers and sisters, this is a true picture of the spiritual life of many Christians. God is right there among us, grace is right before our eyes, his works are made plain every day — but we are busy counting our own balls: counting our losses, counting what others owe us, counting the difficulties of our circumstances. And so we miss God.

So today’s lesson is not meant to rebuke our weakness but to renew our eyes. God wants to set six lights before us, to turn us from worldly eyes to spiritual eyes; from man’s point of view to God’s point of view; from what is earthly and temporary to what is heavenly and eternal.

Because what you see today determines what you receive tomorrow.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Histories of “Seeing”
sections.html:
The two main passages we are entering today are Genesis 13 and Exodus 14. According to the unanimous tradition of the Jewish people and the church for two thousand years, both books were written by Moses. Moses was writing for the people of Israel, who had just been brought out of the land of slavery in Egypt, were walking through the wilderness and were about to enter Canaan. What was the greatest problem of this people? Not a lack of miracles, but an inability to see. They had seen the ten plagues, seen the Red Sea part, seen the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire — and still in the wilderness they complained, drew back and were afraid. So Moses took up his pen and wrote first how their forefather Abraham “saw,” and then how they themselves “saw” at the edge of the Red Sea. This is a textbook about the eyes.

The background of Genesis 13 is a family dispute over property. Abram (God had not yet renamed him Abraham) came back from Egypt to Bethel, and the Bible says he “was very rich in livestock, in silver, and in gold” (Genesis 13:2). His nephew Lot had also grown rich. With so much wealth, the land was no longer enough. The text says: “The land was not able to bear them, that they might live together; for their possessions were so great that they couldn’t live together … The Canaanites and the Perizzites lived in the land at that time” (Genesis 13:6–7). Notice that last sentence: the Canaanites and the Perizzites lived in the land. In other words, this quarrel was taking place before the eyes of unbelieving outsiders. The family shame of God’s household was being watched by the world.

Abram was the elder, the one who had been called. By custom, by law and by seniority, the first choice was his. But he did something that in the world’s eyes was utterly foolish: he gave the choice to the younger man.

The background of Exodus 14 is a national crisis. Israel had only just come out of Egypt, yet God did not lead them by the short road through the land of the Philistines; instead, “God led the people around by the way of the wilderness by the Red Sea” (Exodus 13:18). God even told them to turn back and camp by the sea, in order to lure Pharaoh out in pursuit (Exodus 14:2–4). In other words, the dead end at the Red Sea was no accident; God himself had arranged it. Water in front, soldiers behind, wilderness on either side — a deadlock no human calculation could solve and no one could escape.

In both of these histories God is doing the same thing: he places two people, two groups of people, in exactly the same circumstances, and then lets us see how different ways of “seeing” lead to utterly different endings.

Brothers and sisters, this is also what God wants to do with us this morning. He may not change your circumstances straight away; first he wants to change your eyes.

sections.heading: 1. Two Ways to Live: For Yourself, or for God
sections.html:
“Abram said to Lot, ‘Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives. Isn’t the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me. If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left.’” (Genesis 13:8–9)

This is the most beautiful “giving way” in the whole Bible. Abram and Lot faced the same situation and the same choice — how to divide the gains. But they “saw” in different ways, and so their endings were completely different.

How Lot Saw: Worldly Eyes

“Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere, before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of Yahweh, like the land of Egypt, as you go to Zoar.” (Genesis 13:10)

“Lifted up his eyes, and saw” — Lot raised his eyes, but his eyes could do only three things.

First, he looked at the environment. He saw that it was “well-watered,” a fertile plain. The Hebrew word is “the whole plain” (kikkar) — a round, lush lowland. What he saw was water and grass, harvests, a place where livestock could grow fat.

Second, he looked at advantage. The question he asked was: which piece is best for me? He did not ask God, nor did he ask his elder, and the Bible records not a single prayer from him.

Third, he looked at the present. Here the Bible adds a very important aside: “before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.” When Moses wrote this, he already knew the ending. That land, which looked like the garden of Eden, became a scorched waste of sulphur and fire a few decades later. Lot saw what was in front of him; the Holy Spirit saw how it would end.

And the result? “So Lot chose the Plain of the Jordan for himself. Lot traveled east, and they separated themselves from one other” (Genesis 13:11). Then the Bible records his slide in one very quiet yet very frightening verse: “Abram lived in the land of Canaan, and Lot lived in the cities of the plain, and moved his tent as far as Sodom” (Genesis 13:12).

The Chinese Union Version puts it this way: he “moved his tent little by little” — words we should remember all our lives. Lot did not move into Sodom in a single day. First he gazed at it from afar, then he lived on the plain, then he moved his tent a little closer each time, and in the end he was sitting in the gate of Sodom (Genesis 19:1). Spiritual decline is never one leap off a cliff; it is a move of an inch a day.

And the next verse of the Bible coldly adds: “Now the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinners against Yahweh” (Genesis 13:13). Lot saw the pasture but did not see the sin. His eyes measured only altitude, never depth.

And the final ending? When God’s judgement came, Lot lost almost everything. His sons-in-law treated the warning as a joke (Genesis 19:14), and his wife “looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt” (Genesis 19:26). Later the Lord Jesus reminded his disciples in just three words: “Remember Lot’s wife!” (Luke 17:32)

Brothers and sisters, that “looking back” was not a movement of the neck; it was the direction of the heart. Where a person looks, the heart goes; where the heart goes, the person stops. Her body left Sodom, but her heart stayed in Sodom, and so she stopped forever halfway, a pillar of warning.

There is a famous experiment in psychology that can help us understand Lot. In the 1960s and 70s, Professor Walter Mischel of Stanford University in the United States carried out the “marshmallow test.” He put a marshmallow in front of a child and told the child that if they could wait until the researcher came back before eating it, they would get two. Some children ate it immediately; others tried every way they could to distract themselves and waited for the double reward. Mischel’s later follow-up studies found that the children who were able to delay gratification often did better in adolescence. And his key finding was this: the children who could wait did not have stronger willpower; they simply knew “not to keep staring at the marshmallow.”

What you see is what you crave; what you crave is what you grab. Lot’s tragedy was that he kept staring at that plain.

How Abram Saw: Spiritual Eyes

Abram did three things that were the exact opposite of Lot: he did not contend, he gave way, and he did not live for himself.

He did not contend — he said, “let there be no strife between you and me,” because what he saw was not a piece of land but the reputation of God’s testimony before the nations. He gave way — he handed over the right to choose first. He did not live for himself — he gave up the visible gain and held on to the invisible God.

And the result? How beautifully the text puts it: “Yahweh said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him, ‘Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward, for I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever’” (Genesis 13:14–15).

Brothers and sisters, please notice two details.

First, the time when God spoke was “after Lot was separated from him.” Abram let go first, and only then did God speak. While our hands are still clenched tight, God often says nothing; when we let go, heaven opens.

Second, the action God spoke of was the same as Lot’s: “lift up your eyes, and look.” Lot lifted his own eyes and saw one plain; Abram was told by God to lift his eyes and saw the whole land, north, south, east and west. Lot used his own eyes to pick the best piece; God used his eyes to give Abram all of it. The very land Lot chose was later included within the borders God promised to Abram.

This is the great dividing line between the worldly and the spiritual: those who live for themselves lose; those who live for God gain everything.

The Lord Jesus put this principle even more plainly: “For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 16:25).

The 321 vision tells us: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. What is pride? It is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. What is humility? It is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Lot seized the right to choose; he sat in God’s seat and made himself lord of his own life. Abram laid down the right to choose; he returned to his originally intended position as a creature and let God be Lord for him. One grasped, one let go; one contended, one gave way. Looking back thirty years later, the man who grasped lost everything, and the man who gave way became a blessing to all nations.

Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. This is not a slogan; this is the history of Genesis 13.

sections.heading: 2. The Value You See Is the Life You Live
sections.html:
“The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23)

These words of the Lord Jesus come in the Sermon on the Mount, and the surrounding context is about “laying up treasures in heaven” and “no one can serve two masters.” In other words, the “eye” the Lord is speaking of here is not eyesight but values. The original word for “sound” (haplous) carries the sense of “single, pure, undivided”; the word for “evil” (ponēros) carries the sense of “bad, wicked, greedy.” A person whose eye is single is full of light; a person whose eye is greedy is full of darkness.

So what the Lord is saying is this: whatever you see as valuable is what your whole being will be lit up by — or swallowed up by.

Let’s lay this principle out point by point.

Those who look at themselves live for themselves. Their world is very small, small enough to hold only one person, and everything revolves around “I feel, I need, I’ve been hurt, I’ve been short-changed.” It isn’t that they don’t work hard — they work very hard — it’s just that all that effort goes to feeding themselves.

Those who look at advantage live for advantage. Before doing anything they reach for the calculator; even in serving God they ask, “What’s in it for me?” It isn’t that they bear no fruit; it’s just that their fruit has no eternal weight.

Those who look at God live for God. Their world is very large, large enough to hold a kingdom. They know they are not the main character, and precisely because of that they have found true freedom.

The same principle applies between the church and the kingdom.

Those who look at “my church” will breed competition. Whose congregation is bigger, whose church building is larger, whose speaker is more famous — once the comparisons start, conflict follows. Those who look at “God’s kingdom” will move towards unity. Because the kingdom has only one King, and all the glory goes to him alone, there is nothing left for us to fight over.

Worldly seeing says, “I want to get”; spiritual seeing says, “I want to give.” Paul wrote the difference between these two kinds of eyes into a passage of great depth: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” (Philippians 2:3–4). Notice that in the Chinese Union Version Paul again uses the word “see”: each one sees others as better than himself. Unity is not something we grit our teeth to endure; it is something we learn to see.

Brothers and sisters, here we must say something very important: denying of self is not a loss; it is entering into a greater gain.

The Lord Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24). Many people hear “deny yourself” as a losing bargain, as if believing in Jesus means having things taken away again and again. But the 321 vision makes this very clear: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Paul bore witness to this himself: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Think about it: put a drop of water in the palm of your hand, and in half a day it has dried up; put a drop of water into the ocean, and it will never dry up — and from then on it has the power of the whole ocean. What has that drop lost? It has lost the shape of its own “self.” What has it gained? It has gained the ocean.

This is selflessness. Selflessness is not becoming zero; it is placing that “self” into the infinity of God.

From the standpoint of psychology, too, there is evidence for this. Viktor Frankl, the Austrian psychiatrist and a survivor of the Nazi concentration camps, recorded his observations in his book Man’s Search for Meaning: in an environment as extreme as the camps, those who held on were often not the physically strongest, but those who could still see a meaning in their hearts, who still had an unfinished mission, who still had someone waiting for them to come home. Frankl quoted Nietzsche, whose words are commonly taken to mean that a person who knows “why” he lives can bear almost any “how.”

People who see meaning have the strength to go on living. And the meaning a Christian sees is not some vague ideal, but a Lord who is true and living.

The fivefold change of 321 says: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. The first link in the whole chain is mindset — that is, how you see. That is why we say: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

This is exactly how Abram saw things in that dispute over the land: Lot the man mattered more than that pasture; the testimony of God’s household mattered more than my rights. He kept the relationship, and God gave him the land.

sections.heading: 3. Same Circumstances, Different Sight, Different Endings
sections.html:
“Moses said to the people, ‘Don’t be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of Yahweh, which he will work for you today; for you will never again see the Egyptians whom you have seen today.’” (Exodus 14:13)

Now we move from Genesis to Exodus, from the choice of one family to the crisis of a whole nation.

The scene is the Red Sea. In front, fathomless water; behind, Pharaoh’s six hundred chosen chariots. God’s people are caught in between. Notice that at this moment everyone’s situation is exactly the same: the same sea, the same pursuers, the same sand, the same night. Yet they “saw” differently, and so their endings were different.

How the Israelites Saw: A Dead End

“When Pharaoh came near, the children of Israel lifted up their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them; and they were very afraid. The children of Israel cried out to Yahweh.” (Exodus 14:10)

“Lifted up their eyes” — that phrase again. What did they see? The Red Sea in front, the pursuers behind. Their conclusion was perfectly reasonable: it’s over. So they said to Moses, “Because there were no graves in Egypt, have you taken us away to die in the wilderness? Why have you treated us this way, to bring us out of Egypt?” (Exodus 14:11)

Brothers and sisters, listen to those words — the day before they were cheering their freedom, and today they would rather go back and be slaves. That’s what the human heart is like: whatever we see, we speak; whatever we speak, we become. What they saw was a threat, and what they reaped was fear and complaint.

Psychology can explain this. In 1998 the psychologist Barbara Fredrickson, then at the University of Michigan in the United States, put forward the “broaden-and-build theory.” Her research shows that negative emotions, especially fear, “narrow” a person’s attention and range of possible actions, leaving only two roads — flight or fight; whereas positive emotions, such as joy, hope and gratitude, “broaden” a person’s field of attention and flexibility of thought, enabling them to see more possibilities.

That is why the frightened Israelites could think of only two options: drown, or go back to Egypt. Their eyes had been narrowed by fear. God’s third way was right in front of them, and they could not see it.

How Moses Saw: God

Moses stood on the shore of the very same sea. What did he see?

He saw the works of God — “see the salvation of Yahweh, which he will work for you today.”

He saw the promises of God — God had said, “I will bring you into Canaan,” so Moses knew this sea could not be the end of the road.

His conclusion was: God will save. And the result? A miracle happened.

“Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. The children of Israel went into the middle of the sea on the dry ground, and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left.” (Exodus 14:21–22)

Brothers and sisters, please take hold of this order — it is the most important sentence of today: the circumstances did not change first. The “seeing” changed first, and then the miracle appeared.

When did the sea part? After Moses had finished saying, “Don’t be afraid. Stand still.” When Moses made his declaration, the sea was still there. He did not have faith because he saw the sea part; he saw the sea part because he had faith.

We often get the order backwards. We say to God, “Lord, part the sea first, and then I’ll believe you.” God says to us, “Child, see me first, and the sea will part.”

There is a beautiful parallel passage here, the story of Elisha and his servant. The Aramean army surrounded the city of Dothan by night. The servant got up early in the morning, saw horses and chariots and soldiers besieging the city, and panicked. “Elisha prayed, and said, ‘Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.’ Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:17).

Notice that Elisha did not ask God to “drive the enemy away”; he asked God to “open his servant’s eyes.” The horses and chariots of fire had been there all along; the servant just could not see them. God did not change the circumstances. God changed the eyes — and for the servant, the circumstances were completely different.

From a scientific point of view, the human eye is itself a lesson in humility. Every eye of every person has a physiological blind spot on the retina — the place where the optic nerve leaves the eyeball. There are no light-sensitive cells there, so nothing at all is seen. The reason we don’t normally notice it is that the brain automatically “patches” the hole using the surrounding image. In other words, a small piece of the world we see every day is made up for us by our brain — and we are convinced it is the truth.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t our spiritual life just the same? Every one of us has blind spots, and our minds are very good at making up stories to cover them. That is why we need God to open our eyes. The psalmist prayed, “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). This should also become our very first prayer every morning.

The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. It also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you will worry, rely on the heart and you will rejoice. The Israelites relied on their brains and calculated all night, and what they came up with was a grave; Moses relied on the heart and looked to God, and what he saw was dry ground.

sections.heading: 4. A Spiritual Principle: What God Lets You See, He Will Bring to Pass
sections.html:
“By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible.” (Hebrews 11:27)

The first three points showed us how people see. The fourth point is to show us how God works.

There is a spiritual order that recurs again and again in the Bible: God first gives you “sight,” and then leads you into “experience.”

He first had Abram lift up his eyes and look north, south, east and west, and only then gave him the land. He first gave Joseph dreams, in which he saw the sheaves and the stars bow down to him, and only after thirteen years in the pit and the prison did he set him as ruler over Egypt. He first let Moses see at Horeb a bush burning with fire yet not consumed, and only then sent him to Pharaoh. He first let Joshua and Caleb see the fruit of the land, and only then gave the land into their hands.

Brothers and sisters, what a great comfort this is: you do not need to know “how” first. You only need to see, believe and obey; the responsibility for bringing it to pass lies with God, not with you.

Hebrews 11:8 says: “By faith, Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went.” Not knowing where he was going, he still went — because he had seen the One. What he saw was not a route map; it was God himself.

This is the essence of faith. The definition of faith that Hebrews gives is: “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). The original word for “assurance” (hypostasis) carries the sense of “base, foundation, substance”; the word for “proof” (elenchos) carries the sense of “evidence, credentials.” Faith is not shutting our eyes to the facts; faith is seeing a higher fact — that the invisible Lord is more real than the visible Red Sea.

So we must hold this firmly: faith is not a feeling; faith is seeing “what cannot be seen.”

Feelings rise and fall with blood sugar, sleep, the weather and a single remark from someone else; but God’s word never changes. Paul says: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

This is precisely the change of perspective 321 speaks of: from man’s to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly.

Here is a good picture of it. At the foot of a mountain, what you see is a wall blocking the way; ride the cable car to the summit, and you see a winding path that goes round the wall and straight on to the other side of the mountain. The wall was there all along, and so was the path. What changed was not the terrain but the height. Prayer is the cable car God gives us; God’s word is the height God gives us.

In 1948 the sociologist Robert K. Merton put forward the concept of the “self-fulfilling prophecy”: the way a person defines a situation affects his behaviour, and his behaviour in turn makes that originally false definition come true in the end. The ten spies saw themselves as grasshoppers, and they really did fall dead in the wilderness; Caleb “had another spirit with him” (Numbers 14:24), and at the age of eighty-five he really did receive the hill country of Hebron.

Of course, we must make a clear distinction here: this is not what the world calls the “law of attraction,” as though whatever a person imagines in his heart he can create. The Bible never says that human faith can create reality. What the Bible says is this: God speaks first, God gives the sight first, and our faith is our “Amen” to God’s word. It is God who brings things to pass, not our thoughts. We do not use faith to command God; we use faith to respond to God.

So, brothers and sisters, the question to ask this morning is not “Can I do it?” but “What has God said?” You don’t need to know how. You only need to see, believe and obey. God takes responsibility for bringing it to pass.

sections.heading: 5. Weakness Is Not the Problem — Seeing Wrongly Is
sections.html:
“He has said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.” (2 Corinthians 12:9)

Brothers and sisters, this part is for those of you who, this morning, feel in your heart that you are not good enough.

When Paul wrote 2 Corinthians 12, he was dealing with something very painful. There was “a thorn” in his flesh. The Bible does not say plainly what it was — perhaps an illness, perhaps persecution. Paul pleaded with the Lord three times to take this thorn away from him. God’s answer was not to remove the thorn, but to give him a word: “My grace is sufficient for you.”

The tone of the original is beautiful. “Is sufficient” (arkei) is in the present tense, meaning continually, unceasingly enough. God did not give Paul a one-off deposit of grace; he gave him a stream of living water supplied every day.

Then God spoke the sentence that turns everything around: my power is made perfect in weakness. “Made perfect” (teleitai) means “brought to completion, reaching fullness.” God’s power does not reach its fullness when we are at our strongest, but when we are at our weakest.

So please hear this sentence clearly today: God is not afraid of your weakness; God is afraid of your seeing wrongly.

Look at yourself, and you are weak; look at God, and you are strong. Paul goes on: “Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10).

This is not a trick of positive thinking; it is spiritual physics. A cup filled with itself has no room for anything else; only an emptied cup can be filled. Weakness is the empty space God clears in your heart.

Let’s look at an example. Gideon was threshing wheat in the winepress, afraid the Midianites would see him. The angel appeared to him and said, “Yahweh is with you, you mighty man of valor!” (Judges 6:12) Gideon immediately replied, “My family is the poorest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house” (Judges 6:15). You see, what the angel saw and what Gideon saw were completely different. The angel saw a Gideon of whom it could be said, “Yahweh is with you”; Gideon saw himself as “the least.” God did not argue with him. God simply said, “Surely I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man” (Judges 6:16).

The problem was never how small Gideon was, but whom he was looking at.

The psychologist Carol Dweck, a professor at Stanford University in the United States, has spent many years researching people’s “mindset.” Her research distinguishes between a “fixed mindset” and a “growth mindset”: people with a fixed mindset believe ability is fixed, so they treat failure as a verdict on their self-worth and tend to give up when they meet difficulties; people with a growth mindset believe ability can grow through effort and learning, so they treat failure as information and become more engaged when difficulties come. The same setback, two ways of seeing it, two different lives.
