Brothers and sisters, Christians have an even higher way of seeing than the “growth mindset.” We might call it “the eyes of grace”: I do not grow by my own strength; I am filled by grace. My weakness is not my sentence of condemnation; it is my letter of invitation — inviting the power of Christ to rest on me.

Helen Keller is commonly credited with saying something like this: the only thing worse than being born blind is having sight but no vision. Helen Keller herself was blind and deaf, yet she saw things that many people with bright eyes never see in their whole lives.

So the problem is not how strong you are; the problem is whom you are looking at. Stop staring at your thorn. Lift up your head and look at the Lord who says, “My grace is sufficient for you.”

sections.heading: 6. A 321 Insight: The Selfless See the Works of God
sections.html:
When we gather the previous five points together, we see a clear spiritual law:

The self-centred look at themselves, and the result is that they limit God; the selfless look at God, and the result is that they experience God.

This is not to say that God’s power can be limited by man — God is almighty. It is to say that a heart full of itself leaves no room for God to work; just as with the Lord Jesus in Nazareth, “He didn’t do many mighty works there because of their unbelief” (Matthew 13:58).

What is the self-centred life? The self-centred life puts “self” at the centre and measures everything by “me”: my face, my rights, my feelings, my plans. Self-centred people do not necessarily do evil; they may be hard-working, zealous, even very spiritually busy — but their eyes keep circling around themselves, and so the world they see all their lives is no bigger than themselves.

What is selflessness? Selflessness is not having no self-worth; it is not being negated or trampled on. 321 puts it very clearly: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Selfless people bear three marks:

First, they do not contend for themselves. They know their inheritance is in God’s hands, and no one can take it away. Abram was just such a person.

Second, they do not live for themselves. “For the love of Christ constrains us; … He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15).

Third, they do not gain for themselves. It is not that they receive nothing; it is that they do not treat what they receive as private property. They know they are stewards, not landlords.

So for whom do such people live? For three: for Jesus, for others and for God’s kingdom.

This is exactly the order 321 speaks of: the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

And such people experience three things: they see God, they experience God, and they gain God.

Notice that these three things form one line. Seeing is the starting point, experiencing is the process, gaining is the outcome. And what is gained is not “things” but God himself. What Abraham finally gained was not only the land of Canaan, but God himself saying to him, “I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward” (Genesis 15:1).

In the Sermon on the Mount the Lord Jesus said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). To be “pure in heart” is to be single-hearted, without impurity, without a divided mind — in other words, selfless. The pure in heart shall see God. This is the Lord’s promise.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s walk through today’s message once more, this time within the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Jesus is my role model — he is the Lord “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). What he saw was the Father’s will, not his own rights. Abram’s giving way is only a shadow of him.

The Bible is my standard — our eyes are far too easily deceived by our circumstances, so we need a standard that does not move. When the Red Sea is in front of you, the question to ask is not “What does this look like?” but “What has God said?” Let God’s word replace what the eye sees; let the promises replace feelings.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — it is the Holy Spirit who opens the eyes of our hearts. Paul prayed for the church in Ephesus: “having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints” (Ephesians 1:18). Only the Holy Spirit can enlighten the eyes of the heart.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

Lot’s problem was not that he chose the wrong land, but that he made the choice sitting on the throne himself. When Jesus reigns as King, we are set free from the burden of choosing — because the right to choose has been handed back to the Lord who is wisest and who loves us most. And when the miracle happened, Moses did not take the credit for himself; the glory of the Red Sea went wholly to Yahweh.

The Goal: establish God’s system.

When Abram gave up that land, it looked as though he had lost a round; in fact, God was using him to establish a new system — a family that did not rely on grabbing or on calculating, but trusted in God alone. Four thousand years later, we still call him “the father of faith.”

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Today’s lesson starts precisely with the first link. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. How you see determines what kind of person you become; what kind of person you become determines how you live your days; how you live your days determines your relationships with others; your relationships with others determine the fruitfulness of your service. That is why we say: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

If a person does not change in how he “sees,” then changing churches, changing positions or changing methods is only moving the same play to a different stage.

The 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” Before them we practise living out a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, think about it: the person you will face today — the colleague who often makes you uncomfortable, the stubborn elder, the rebellious child — the way you “see” them will determine your attitude towards them, and your attitude towards them will determine your relationship. If you look at them with Lot’s eyes, you will see a threat and a loss; if you look at them with Abram’s eyes, you will see someone God loves and wants to bless through you.

The 235 relationships: become a “2” with selfless people, as spiritual companions to one another; build a “3,” becoming spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. One person’s eyes tire easily; when a group of people remind one another, they can see further and walk longer. Elisha prayed for his servant, and the servant’s eyes were opened — this is the value of a spiritual companion.

The change of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

Paul says: “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:1–2).

Brothers and sisters, this is the summary of the whole lesson: lift your eyes a little higher.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will use the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive each of them deep, one by one.

Practice 1: When facing a choice, ask yourself, “What am I looking at?”

Information: First put the truth into your heart — Lot looked at the plain, Abram looked at God; one lost, the other gained the whole land.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine on you and bring to mind the most recent major choice you made. What was your real reason that time? Advantage, or God’s will?

Conviction: Say to God in your heart, “Lord, I believe your view is more reliable than my calculations.” Without conviction, knowledge is just data.

Implementation: Starting today, before making any choice that takes more than three minutes to decide, stop and ask one question: “Lord, how do you see this?”

Evaluation: Every evening spend three minutes thinking back over the day: was there a choice I made with Lot’s eyes?

Correction: If there was, confess it in prayer, and immediately think of a concrete action that can put it right.

Repetition: Practise this for forty days in a row. Psychology reminds us that forming a habit takes time and repetition; spiritual renewal all the more so — Paul tells us to “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2), and in the original this is an ongoing process.

Multiplication: Teach this question to your family, your companions and your small group, so that they too learn to ask God before they choose.

Practice 2: When facing difficulty, change what you see

Information: Remember Moses’ order — the circumstances did not change first; the “seeing” changed first, and then the miracle appeared.

Revelation: Write your greatest difficulty right now on the left side of a sheet of paper; then quietly ask God, and write his power and his promises on the right side.

Conviction: Acknowledge that your difficulty is real — but God is more real than your difficulty.

Implementation: Don’t look at the size of the problem; look at the power of God. Whenever you notice yourself replaying that problem over and over again, open your mouth and declare one of God’s promises.

Evaluation: At the end of the week, look at that sheet of paper: how many of the difficulties on the left were imagined, and how many were real?

Correction: Add one more promise on the right.

Repetition: Every time a difficulty comes, make the sheet again.

Multiplication: When God opens a way for you, tell that testimony, so that someone else standing at the edge of their own Red Sea can also stand firm.

Practice 3: Practise “the seeing of faith” every day

Information: Let God’s word replace what the eye sees; let the promises replace feelings.

Revelation: Each morning as you read the Bible, ask God to give you one verse as “today’s promise.”

Conviction: Copy that verse onto your phone’s wallpaper and onto a sticky note, and put it where you will see it ten times a day.

Implementation: Whenever you feel low, don’t analyse the feeling first; read that verse first.

Evaluation: In the evening, write down how God fulfilled it for you today, or how he comforted you.

Correction: If you didn’t think of that verse all day, move it somewhere more visible tomorrow.

Repetition: One verse a day, and in a month you will have thirty verses in your heart.

Multiplication: Each week share one verse with a friend who has not yet believed, or who is going through a weak time.

Brothers and sisters, there is one more little reminder — please keep it in your heart: it is not that you have no opportunities; it is that you have not seen God’s opportunities.

God’s grace is never absent; what is often absent is our eyes. Just like the half of the participants who could not see the gorilla — God is right there in the middle of the picture, and we are busy counting our own balls.

keyVerses: “Yahweh said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him, ‘Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward, for I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever. I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth, so that if a man can count the dust of the earth, then your offspring may also be counted. Arise, walk through the land in its length and in its width; for I will give it to you.’” (Genesis 13:14–17)
“By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible.” (Hebrews 11:27)
declarations: Let us declare together:
Lord, open my eyes! Let me no longer look only at myself and my circumstances, but see your works and your promises! Make me live by faith, obey your leading, and experience your wonderful power!
Brothers and sisters, let’s walk today’s road once more.
Lot saw the plain, and what he received was destruction; Abraham saw God, and what he received was the promise.
The Israelites saw the Red Sea and lived in fear; Moses saw God and experienced a miracle.
The same land, the same sea, the same day. The difference was not in the circumstances, but in the eyes.
So please take this sentence home with you: what you see today determines what you receive tomorrow.

When you choose to see with spiritual eyes, crisis becomes opportunity, weakness becomes power, and the impossible becomes possible. Not because you are capable, but because the One you see is capable. For what you see, God will surely bring to pass for you.

Dear brothers and sisters, this morning God wants to do something in your heart: he wants to take your eyes off yourself and set them on him. He wants you no longer to be Lot, clinging tightly to the plain, but Abraham, who opened his hands and lifted up his eyes to look. He wants you no longer to be the one at the seashore counting the pursuers, but the one who stands firm, declares, and sees the salvation of the Lord.
Let Jesus be King over your eyes, let Jesus be King over your choices, let Jesus be King over your weakness. May all the glory go to him.
practices: When facing difficulty, change what you see
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you. You are the God who opens the eyes of the blind, and the God who shows us your works every day.

Lord, please forgive us — so often, like Lot, we see only the advantage in front of us and do not see your heart; so often, like the Israelites at the Red Sea, we see only the pursuers and the great waters and do not see your arm.

Enlighten the eyes of our hearts, so that we may know the hope of your calling. Take away the “self” in our hearts, so that we no longer contend for ourselves, live for ourselves or gain for ourselves, but live only for Jesus, for others and for your kingdom.
Lord, today we hand the right to choose back to you, entrust our difficulties to you and offer our weakness to you. May your power be made perfect in our weakness.
May all that we see today be you; may all that we receive tomorrow be what you have promised.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Genesis 13:10–11: “Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere … So Lot chose the Plain of the Jordan for himself. Lot traveled east, and they separated themselves from one other.” Please share: in the most recent major choice you made, what did you “see” at the time? If you could do it again, what question would you want to ask God first?

2 Corinthians 12:9: “He has said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’” Please share: what is the one weakness you currently dislike most? If God wanted to display his power through this weakness, how do you think he might do it? What kind of prayer are you willing to pray about it this week?

blog.title: What You See Is What You Receive

blocks.x: Why Some See a Plain and Others See God

In 1999 the psychologists Simons and Chabris carried out a famous experiment. They asked people to watch a video and count how many passes the team in white made. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked right across the middle of the screen, even stopping to beat its chest — nine seconds in all. And the result? About half of the participants never saw the gorilla at all.
Their eyes were fine, the light was good enough, and the gorilla was real. They didn’t see it simply because they were busy counting their own balls.

That hits the mark about our spiritual condition. God is right there among us, grace is right before our eyes, yet we are busy counting our losses, what others owe us, the difficulties of our circumstances — and so we miss him.
1. The Same Land, Two Pairs of Eyes

When Abram and Lot had to part ways, Abram gave the choice to the younger man. Lot lifted up his eyes and chose the whole plain of the Jordan — well-watered, lush, and best for himself. The Bible coolly adds: “Abram lived in the land of Canaan, and Lot lived in the cities of the plain, and moved his tent as far as Sodom” (Genesis 13:12).
Lot moved his tent little by little — words worth remembering all your life. Spiritual decline is never one leap off a cliff; it is a move of an inch a day.

And only after Lot had left did God speak to Abram: “Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward, for I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever” (Genesis 13:14–15).
Both “lifted up their eyes and looked.” Lot used his own eyes to pick the best piece; God used his eyes to give Abram all of it.
Those who live for themselves lose; those who live for God gain everything.
2. The Circumstances Didn’t Change First — the “Seeing” Did

At the Red Sea there was water in front and the pursuing army behind. The Israelites lifted up their eyes, saw the Egyptians marching after them, were very afraid, and said they would rather go back to Egypt as slaves. Moses stood at the edge of the same sea, yet he said: Don’t be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of Yahweh, which he will work for you today.
Only then did the sea part.

Notice the order: Moses didn’t have faith because he saw the sea part; he saw the sea part because he had faith. We often say to God, “Part the sea first, and then I’ll believe you.” But God says, “Child, see me first, and the sea will part.”

It was the same for the prophet Elisha’s servant. With the city surrounded by enemy troops, Elisha didn’t ask God to drive the enemy away; he only asked God to open his servant’s eyes. The horses and chariots of fire had been there all along; he just couldn’t see them.
3. God Isn’t Afraid of Your Weakness — Only of Your Seeing Wrongly

Paul had a thorn in his flesh and pleaded with the Lord three times to take it away. God didn’t remove it; he simply said: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).
Weakness isn’t the problem; seeing wrongly is. Look at yourself, and you are weak; look at God, and you are strong. The problem isn’t how strong you are; it’s whom you are looking at.

A cup filled with itself has no room for anything else; only an emptied cup can be filled. So selflessness isn’t becoming zero; it is placing the “self” into the infinity of God. Put a drop of water in the palm of your hand and in half a day it has dried up; put it into the ocean and it will never dry up.

The self-centred look at themselves and limit God; the selfless look at God and experience God. They don’t contend for themselves, live for themselves or gain for themselves, but live only for Jesus, for others and for God’s kingdom. People like that will see God, experience God and gain God.
Take One Sentence Home

Lot saw the plain, and what he received was destruction; Abraham saw God, and what he received was the promise. The Israelites saw the Red Sea and lived in fear; Moses saw God and experienced a miracle.
The difference was not in the circumstances, but in the eyes.
What you see today determines what you receive tomorrow. When you choose to see with spiritual eyes, crisis becomes opportunity, weakness becomes power, and the impossible becomes possible.
For what you see, God will surely bring to pass for you.
Reflection question: Think of the thing that has troubled you most this week. If God opened your eyes right now, what do you think he would let you see first?

brief12.title: Theme Verse and Background
notes: Genesis 13:14–17, written by Moses
For Israel, newly out of Egypt
Two histories: the land and the Red Sea
God changes the eyes first, then the circumstances
1. The author is Moses, writing for the Israelites just out of Egypt and walking through the wilderness.
2. Background of Genesis 13: Abram and Lot had so many possessions the land couldn’t hold them, and they quarrelled in front of the Canaanites.
3. Background of Exodus 14: the dead end at the Red Sea was arranged by God himself (Exodus 14:2–4).
4. The main thread: God may not change the circumstances first; he changes our eyes first.

brief12.title: 1. Two Ways to Live: For Yourself, or for God
notes: Lot: circumstances, advantage, the present
Abram: no strife, gave way, not for himself
“If you go left, I will go right” Genesis 13:9
For yourself, you lose; for God, you gain all
1. Read Genesis 13:8–9 — Abram freely hands over the right to choose.
2. Lot’s three ways of looking: at the circumstances (the well-watered plain), at advantage, at the present — Genesis 13:10.
3. “Moved his tent as far as Sodom” (Genesis 13:12) — spiritual decline is an inch a day.
4. God spoke only after Lot had separated from Abram (Genesis 13:14): let go first, and heaven opens.
5. 321: pride is grasping power and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position.

brief12.title: 2. The Value You See Is the Life You Live
notes: Look at yourself, live for yourself
Look at God, live for God
“My church” breeds rivalry; the kingdom brings unity
Denying self is no loss, but a greater gain
1. Matthew 6:22–23 — the lamp of the body is the eye; “sound” in the original carries the sense of single, pure.
2. Three contrasts: looking at yourself, at advantage, at God; looking at the church versus at the kingdom.
3. Philippians 2:3–4, “each counting others better than himself” — unity is something we learn to see.
4. Illustration: a drop of water in your palm dries up; put into the ocean, it has the whole ocean.
5. 321: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness; Galatians 2:20.

brief12.title: 3. Same Circumstances, Different Sight, Different Endings
notes: Israel: sea in front, soldiers behind
Moses: God’s works and promises
“Made the sea dry land” Exodus 14:21
Not the circumstances first — the seeing first
1. Exodus 14:10–12 — the Israelites lifted their eyes, saw the pursuers, and would rather go back to slavery.
2. Barbara Fredrickson’s broaden-and-build theory (1998): fear narrows our attention.
3. Moses looked at God’s works and God’s promises — Exodus 14:13.
4. Exodus 14:21–22 — the sea became dry land; the key order: the seeing changed first, then the miracle appeared.
5. 2 Kings 6:17 — Elisha asked God to open his servant’s eyes; the horses and chariots of fire had been there all along.

brief12.title: 4. What God Lets You See, He Will Bring to Pass
notes: God gives sight first, then experience
No need to know how — just obey
“As seeing him who is invisible”
Hebrews 11:27
1. Hebrews 11:27, “as seeing him who is invisible.”
2. The Bible’s order: God gives sight first, then leads you into experience (Abram, Joseph, Moses, Caleb).
3. Hebrews 11:1, the definition of faith; faith is not a feeling, but seeing what cannot be seen.
4. 2 Corinthians 4:18 — the things which are seen are temporal, the things which are not seen are eternal.
5. Illustration: at the foot of the mountain you see a wall; at the top you see a path — what changed is the height.

brief12.title: 5. Weakness Is Not the Problem — Seeing Wrongly Is
notes: God fears not your weakness, but your seeing wrongly
Look at yourself: weak; look at God: strong
“My power is made perfect
in weakness” 2 Corinthians 12:9
1. 2 Corinthians 12:9 — Paul asked the Lord three times to remove the thorn; God gave him grace instead.
2. “Made perfect” means brought to completion; weakness is the room God makes in the heart.
3. Judges 6:12–16 — the angel saw a mighty man of valour; Gideon saw himself as the least.
4. Carol Dweck (Stanford University): the contrast between a fixed mindset and a growth mindset.
5. Helen Keller is commonly credited with saying: the only thing worse than being born blind is having sight but no vision.

brief12.title: 6. A 321 Insight: The Selfless See God
notes: Self-centred: looks at self, limits God
Selfless: looks at God, experiences God
Not contending, living or gaining for self
Only for Jesus, others, God’s kingdom
1. The self-centred life puts the self at the centre; selflessness is entering into the fullness and living it out.
2. Three marks of selflessness: not contending for yourself, not living for yourself, not gaining for yourself.
3. 2 Corinthians 5:14–15 — no longer living for ourselves, but for the Lord.
4. Matthew 5:8, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”
5. 321: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks.

brief12.title: Putting It into Practice
notes: When choosing, ask: what am I looking at?
In difficulty: look not at the problem but at God
Daily let God’s word replace what the eye sees
Let the promises replace feelings
1. Practice 1: before choosing, ask, “Lord, how do you see this?”
2. Practice 2: write the difficulty on the left and God’s promises on the right; look not at the size of the problem but at the power of God.
3. Practice 3: ask for one promise each day and put it where you’ll see it ten times a day.
4. The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
5. A gentle reminder: it is not that you have no opportunities; it is that you have not seen God’s opportunities.

brief12.title: Closing and Call
notes: Lot saw the plain and received destruction
Abraham saw God and received the promise
What you see today, you receive tomorrow
Let Jesus be King over your eyes
1. Contrast in review: Lot saw the plain and received destruction; Abraham saw God and received the promise.
2. Contrast in review: the Israelites saw the Red Sea and lived in fear; Moses saw God and experienced a miracle.
3. The difference wasn’t in the circumstances but in the eyes; what you see today determines what you receive tomorrow.
4. Call: let Jesus be King over your eyes, your choices and your weakness, and give him the glory.

2. Prayer focus: ask God to enlighten the eyes of our hearts (Ephesians 1:18).
3. Prayer focus: take away the self in our hearts, hand back the right to choose, offer up our weakness.
4. Blessing: may all you see today be God, and all you receive tomorrow be his promises.

2. Background of Genesis 13: both households had so many possessions that “the land was not able to bear them” (Genesis 13:6), and they quarrelled in front of the Canaanites.
3. Background of Exodus 14: God told the people to turn back and camp by the sea to lure Pharaoh into pursuit (Exodus 14:2–4); the dead end was God’s arrangement.
4. The main thread: God may not change the circumstances first; he changes our eyes first.

brief21.title: 1a: How Lot Saw
notes: Circumstances: the well-watered plain
Advantage: what’s best for me
The present: only what’s in front of him
“Moved his tent as far as Sodom” Genesis 13:12
1. Read Genesis 13:10 — Lot “lifted up his eyes, and saw” all the plain of the Jordan.
2. Three ways of looking: at the circumstances, at advantage, at the present; note the Holy Spirit’s aside, “before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.”
3. Genesis 13:12, “moved his tent as far as Sodom” — spiritual decline is an inch a day.
4. Genesis 13:13 — the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked; Lot saw the pasture but not the sin.
5. Walter Mischel’s (Stanford University) marshmallow test: the children who could wait didn’t have stronger willpower; they just didn’t keep staring at the marshmallow.

brief21.title: 1b: How Abram Saw
notes: No strife, gave way, not for himself
“If you go left, I will go right” Genesis 13:9
Only after Lot left did God speak
For yourself, you lose; for God, you gain all
1. Read Genesis 13:8–9 — Abram freely hands over the right to choose; three actions: no strife, giving way, not living for himself.
2. God spoke only “after Lot was separated from him”: let go first, and heaven opens.
3. Genesis 13:14–15 — God told Abram to lift up his eyes north, south, east and west, and gave him the whole land.
4. Matthew 16:25 — whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it.
5. 321: pride is grasping power and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position; humility inspires humility and both sides win.

brief21.title: 2a: What You See, You Live Out
notes: Look at yourself, live for yourself
Look at advantage, live for advantage
Look at God, live for God
“The lamp of the body is the eye” Matthew 6:22
1. Matthew 6:22–23 — the lamp of the body is the eye; “sound” in the original carries the sense of single, pure.
2. The context is laying up treasure in heaven and not serving two masters — so this is about values.
3. Three contrasts: looking at yourself, at advantage, at God.
4. Luke 17:32 — the Lord’s reminder, “Remember Lot’s wife!”; Genesis 19:26 — she looked back and became a pillar of salt.

brief21.title: 2b: Denying Self Is No Loss
notes: “My church” breeds rivalry; the kingdom brings unity
Worldly: “I want to get”; spiritual: “I want to give”
A drop in the ocean never dries up
“It is no longer I who live” Galatians 2:20
1. Looking at “my church” breeds rivalry; looking at “God’s kingdom” brings unity.
2. Philippians 2:3–4, “each counting others better than himself” — unity is something we learn to see.
3. Illustration: a drop of water in your palm dries up; put into the ocean, it has the whole ocean.
4. Galatians 2:20, “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”
5. Viktor Frankl, Man’s Search for Meaning: those who see meaning are the ones who hold on.

brief21.title: 3a: How the Israelites Saw
notes: The Red Sea in front, pursuers behind
Conclusion: it’s over — back to Egypt
Result: complaining and fear
Fear narrows our field of vision
1. Exodus 14:10 — the Israelites lifted up their eyes, saw the Egyptians marching after them, and were very afraid.
2. Exodus 14:11 — “Because there were no graves in Egypt…?”; yesterday they cheered, today they would rather be slaves.
3. Barbara Fredrickson’s broaden-and-build theory (1998): fear narrows attention and options.
4. Application: they were left with only two options; God’s third way was right in front of them, yet they couldn’t see it.

brief21.title: 3b: How Moses Saw
notes: God’s works and God’s promises
“Don’t be afraid. Stand still” Exodus 14:13
“Made the sea dry land” Exodus 14:21
Not the circumstances first — the seeing first
1. Exodus 14:13 — Moses looked at God’s works and also at God’s promises.
2. Exodus 14:21–22 — the sea became dry land, and the waters were a wall on their right hand and on their left.
3. The key order: the circumstances didn’t change first; the seeing changed first, and then the miracle appeared.
4. 2 Kings 6:17 — Elisha didn’t ask for the enemy to be removed, only for his servant’s eyes to be opened.
5. Science: everyone has a physiological blind spot, and the brain fills it in automatically; we need God to open our eyes. Psalm 119:18.

brief21.title: 4a: God Gives You Sight First
notes: Abram looked first, then received the land
Joseph dreamed first, then ruled
You needn’t know how first
See, believe, obey — God brings it to pass
1. The Bible’s order: God gives sight first, then leads you into experience.
2. Examples: Abram lifting up his eyes, Joseph’s dreams, Moses seeing the burning bush, Caleb seeing the fruit of the land.
3. Hebrews 11:8 — he went out, not knowing where he went.
4. Application: you don’t need to know how; you only need to see, believe and obey — God takes responsibility for bringing it to pass.

brief21.title: 4b: The Essence of Faith
notes: “Faith is assurance of things hoped for”
Hebrews 11:1
Faith is not a feeling
It is seeing the One who is invisible
1. Hebrews 11:1, the definition of faith; “assurance” in the original carries the sense of foundation, substance.
2. Hebrews 11:27, “as seeing him who is invisible.”
3. 2 Corinthians 4:18 — the things which are seen are temporal, the things which are not seen are eternal.
4. Illustration: at the foot of the mountain you see a wall; at the top you see a path — what changed is the height.
5. Distinction: this is not the “law of attraction”; it is God who brings things to pass, and we simply say “Amen” to his word.

brief21.title: 5a: God Isn’t Afraid of Your Weakness
notes: Paul asked three times for the thorn to go
“My grace is sufficient for you”
God didn’t remove it — he gave grace
Weakness is room God has made
1. 2 Corinthians 12:7–9 — Paul pleaded with the Lord three times about the thorn.
2. “Is sufficient” is in the present tense in the original — continually, unceasingly enough.
3. “Made perfect” means brought to completion; God’s power reaches its fullness at our weakest point.
4. Illustration: a cup filled with itself has no room for anything else; only an emptied cup can be filled.

brief21.title: 5b: It’s About Whom You Look At
notes: Look at yourself: weak; look at God: strong
Gideon: “I am the least”
God: “I will be with you” Judges 6:16
“When I am weak, then am I strong”
1. Judges 6:12 — the angel said “mighty man of valour”; 6:15 — Gideon said “I am the least.”
2. Judges 6:16 — “Surely I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites.”
3. 2 Corinthians 12:10 — when I am weak, then am I strong.
4. Carol Dweck (Stanford University): fixed mindset versus growth mindset; Christians have the even higher “eyes of grace.”
5. Helen Keller is commonly credited with saying: the only thing worse than being born blind is having sight but no vision.

brief21.title: 6a: Self-Centred or Selfless
notes: Self-centred: looks at self, limits God
Selfless: looks at God, experiences God
Selflessness is not having nothing
It is entering the fullness and living it out
1. The self-centred life puts the self at the centre and measures everything by “me.”
2. Matthew 13:58 — he didn’t do many mighty works there because of their unbelief.
3. Selflessness isn’t being negated; it is entering into the fullness and living it out.
4. 321: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan.

brief21.title: 6b: For Whom the Selfless Live
notes: Not contending, living or gaining for self
Only for Jesus, others, God’s kingdom
See God, experience God, gain God
“The pure in heart shall see God” Matthew 5:8
1. Three marks of selflessness: not contending for yourself, not living for yourself, not gaining for yourself.
2. 2 Corinthians 5:14–15 — no longer living for ourselves, but for the Lord.
3. Three results: seeing God, experiencing God, gaining God; Genesis 15:1, “I am your shield.”
4. Matthew 5:8, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”
5. 321: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, relationships more than things.

brief21.title: Practices 1 and 2
notes: When choosing, ask: what am I looking at?
Advantage, or God’s will?
In difficulty: look not at the problem but at God
Not the problem’s size, but God’s power
1. Practice 1: before making a choice, ask, “Lord, how do you see this?”
2. Evaluation for Practice 1: three minutes each evening — did I make any decision with Lot’s eyes?
3. Practice 2: write the difficulty on the left side of a sheet of paper and God’s promises on the right.
4. Implementation for Practice 2: whenever you notice yourself replaying the problem, open your mouth and declare a promise.

brief21.title: Practice 3 and a Gentle Reminder
notes: Daily let God’s word replace what the eye sees
Let the promises replace feelings
Eight stages: Information to Multiplication
Not no opportunity — you haven’t seen it
1. Practice 3: each morning ask God for one verse as “today’s promise,” and put it where you’ll see it ten times a day.
2. The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
3. Romans 12:2, “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” — in the original, an ongoing process.
4. A gentle reminder: it is not that you have no opportunities; it is that you have not seen God’s opportunities.

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
notes: Three Foundations: role model, standard, guide
Two Core Values: King, all the glory
The Goal: establish God’s system
Change the mindset and the life changes
1. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model (Philippians 2:6–7, he emptied himself), the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide (Ephesians 1:18).
2. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King (hand the right to choose back to the Lord), let Jesus receive all the glory.
3. The Goal: establish God’s system; Abram gave up a piece of land, and God built a family.
4. The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry; the 920 practice and 235 relationships.
5. Shifting perspective: Colossians 3:1–2, set your mind on the things that are above.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: Lot saw the plain and received destruction
Abraham saw God and received the promise
What you see today, you receive tomorrow
Let Jesus be King over your eyes
1. Contrast in review: Lot saw the plain and received destruction; Abraham saw God and received the promise.
2. Contrast in review: the Israelites saw the Red Sea and lived in fear; Moses saw God and experienced a miracle.
3. The difference wasn’t in the circumstances but in the eyes; what you see today determines what you receive tomorrow.
4. Call: let Jesus be King over your eyes, your choices and your weakness, and may all the glory go to him.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Lord, open my eyes!
Let me see your works and your promises
Crisis to opportunity, weakness to power
For what you see, God will bring to pass
1. Lead everyone in declaring together: Lord, open my eyes!
2. Prayer focus: ask God to enlighten the eyes of our hearts (Ephesians 1:18).
3. Prayer focus: take away the self in our hearts, hand back the right to choose, offer up our weakness.
4. Blessing: may all you see today be God, and all you receive tomorrow be his promises.

script: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. This morning let’s look together at a theme: what you see is what you receive. In Genesis 13 God said to Abram, “I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever.” Please keep these words in your heart. The land God promised begins with “seeing.” Your eyes are the steering wheel of your life.

In the last lesson we saw that what you see, you pursue, and what you pursue, you obtain. Today God wants to take us one layer deeper. Brothers and sisters, it is not how hard you try, but what you treasure. In 1999 Simons and Chabris ran an experiment in which people watched a video and counted passes. A gorilla walked across the middle of the screen for nine seconds, and half the people never saw it at all. Why? Because they were busy counting their own balls. Aren’t we just the same? God is right there among us, and we miss him.

Today’s passages come from Genesis 13 and Exodus 14. Both were written by Moses, for the people who had just come out of Egypt and were walking through the wilderness. These people had seen the ten plagues and the Red Sea, and still they were afraid. So Moses took up his pen and wrote first how their forefather Abraham saw, and then how they themselves saw at the edge of the Red Sea. It is a textbook about the eyes. Brothers and sisters, God often doesn’t change your circumstances first; he changes your eyes first. Today we’ll look at six lights, and may the Lord open our hearts to each one.

First, two ways to live: for yourself, or for God. Abram said to Lot, “If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right.” How did Lot see? He looked at the circumstances and saw a fertile plain; he looked at advantage and asked only which piece was best for him; he looked at the present and didn’t see how Sodom would end. The Bible says he “moved his tent as far as Sodom.” Spiritual decline is never one leap off a cliff; it is a move of an inch a day. And Abram? He didn’t contend, he gave way, he didn’t live for himself. And the result? Only after Lot had left did God speak, giving Abram the whole land, north, south, east and west. Brothers and sisters, those who live for themselves lose; those who live for God gain everything.

Second, the value you see is the life you live. The Lord Jesus said, “The lamp of the body is the eye.” Look at yourself, and you live for yourself; look at advantage, and you live for advantage; look at God, and you live for God. Look at “my church,” and there is rivalry; look at “God’s kingdom,” and we move towards unity. Worldly seeing says, “I want to get”; spiritual seeing says, “I want to give.” Brothers and sisters, denying self is not a loss. Put a drop of water in the palm of your hand and in half a day it has dried up; put it into the ocean and it will never dry up. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness. Paul says, “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Brothers and sisters, how will you see the person who often makes you uncomfortable today? If you look at them with Lot’s eyes, you’ll see a loss; if you look at them with Abram’s eyes, you’ll see someone God wants to bless through you.

Third, the same circumstances, different sight, different endings. At the Red Sea there was water in front and soldiers behind. The Israelites saw the pursuers and said: it’s over — we’d be better off back in Egypt. What did Moses see? He looked at God’s works, and he looked at God’s promises. He said: Don’t be afraid. Stand still! And then? He “made the sea dry land.” Brothers and sisters, remember this order: the circumstances didn’t change first; the “seeing” changed first, and then the miracle appeared. Moses didn’t have faith because he saw the sea part; he saw the sea part because he had faith. We often say to God, “Lord, part the sea first, and then I’ll believe you.” But God says to us, “Child, see me first, and the sea will part.”

Fourth, what God lets you see, he will bring to pass. God first gives you sight, and then leads you into experience. Abram lifted up his eyes first, and then received the land; Joseph dreamed first, and then became ruler. So, brothers and sisters, you don’t need to know “how”; you only need to see, believe and obey. Hebrews says that Moses endured “as seeing him who is invisible.” Faith is not a feeling; faith is seeing what cannot be seen. The responsibility for bringing it to pass lies with God, not with you.

Fifth, weakness is not the problem; seeing wrongly is. Paul had a thorn in his flesh and pleaded with the Lord three times to take it away, and God said, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Brothers and sisters, God is not afraid of your weakness; God is afraid of your seeing wrongly. Look at yourself, and you are weak; look at God, and you are strong. Gideon said he was the least, and God said, “I will be with you.” The problem isn’t how strong you are; it’s whom you are looking at.

Sixth, the light of 321: the selfless see the works of God. Self-centred people look at themselves and so limit God; selfless people look at God and so experience God. The selfless don’t contend for themselves, live for themselves or gain for themselves; they live only for Jesus, for others and for God’s kingdom. People like that will see God, experience God and gain God. The Lord said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

Brothers and sisters, today we have three practices. First, when facing a choice, ask yourself: what am I looking at? Advantage, or God’s will? Second, when facing difficulty, change what you see: look not at the size of the problem but at the power of God. Third, practise the seeing of faith every day: let God’s word replace what the eye sees, and let the promises replace feelings. All three practices should follow the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Doing it once isn’t practice; repeating it is. Please remember this little reminder: it is not that you have no opportunities; it is that you have not seen God’s opportunities. God’s grace is never absent; what is often absent is our eyes.

Brothers and sisters, let’s walk today’s road once more. Lot saw the plain, and what he received was destruction; Abraham saw God, and what he received was the promise. The Israelites saw the Red Sea and lived in fear; Moses saw God and experienced a miracle. The difference was not in the circumstances, but in the eyes. So please take this sentence home with you: what you see today determines what you receive tomorrow. Let Jesus be King over your eyes; let Jesus be King over your choices.

Let us declare together: Lord, open my eyes! Let me no longer look only at myself and my circumstances, but see your works and your promises! Make me live by faith, obey your leading, and experience your wonderful power! Dear Heavenly Father, enlighten the eyes of our hearts and take away the self in our hearts. May crisis become opportunity, weakness become power, and the impossible become possible. For what we see, you will surely bring to pass for us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. This morning we come together before God to receive a theme: what you see is what you receive. In Genesis 13 God said to Abram, “I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever.” Notice that the inheritance God promised begins with “seeing.” Your eyes are the steering wheel of your life; the value you see determines the direction and the ending of your life.

Brothers and sisters, let’s first be still for three seconds, and then open our eyes and look at the room in front of us. What do you see? Some see dishes not yet washed and bills not yet paid; others see a lamp left on for them, an open Bible, a new morning given by God. The same room, the same light, the same twenty-four hours — and yet we see completely different worlds. In the last lesson we learned that what you see, you pursue, and what you pursue, you obtain. Today we go one layer deeper. It is not how hard you try, but what you treasure.

Let me tell you about a real study. In 1999 Simons and Chabris published a paper in the journal Perception called “Gorillas in Our Midst.” They asked participants to watch a video and count how many passes the team in white made. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked across the middle of the screen, even stopping to beat its chest — nine seconds in all. And the result? About half the people never saw the gorilla at all. Their eyes were fine, the light was good enough, and the gorilla was real. They didn’t see it simply because they were busy counting their own balls. Brothers and sisters, aren’t we just the same? We are busy counting our losses, what others owe us, the difficulties of our circumstances — and we miss the God standing right in the middle.

Today’s passages — one in Genesis 13 and one in Exodus 14 — were both written by Moses, for the Israelites who had just come out of Egypt and were walking through the wilderness. The greatest problem of this people wasn’t a lack of miracles, but an inability to see. So Moses wrote first how their forefather Abraham saw, and then how they themselves saw at the edge of the Red Sea. The background of Genesis 13 is a property dispute; the Bible says “the land was not able to bear them,” and the quarrel took place in front of the Canaanites. The background of Exodus 14 is a national crisis, and that dead end was arranged by God himself. Brothers and sisters, God often doesn’t change your circumstances first; he changes your eyes first.

Let’s look at Lot first. The Bible says, “Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere.” Lot raised his eyes, but they could do only three things. He looked at the circumstances and saw lush water and grass; he looked at advantage and asked only which piece was best for him; he looked at the present and didn’t see the future. Here the Bible adds an aside: “before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.” Lot saw what was in front of him; the Holy Spirit saw how it would end. Then the Bible says, “Abram lived in the land of Canaan, and Lot lived in the cities of the plain, and moved his tent as far as Sodom.” Brothers and sisters, remember all your life that he moved his tent little by little. Spiritual decline is never one leap off a cliff; it is a move of an inch a day.

Now look at Abram. He was the elder, the one who had been called; by custom and by law the first choice was his. Yet he said, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me … If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right.” He did three things: he didn’t contend, he gave way, he didn’t live for himself. And the result? The Bible says, “Yahweh said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him, ‘Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward.’” Brothers and sisters, notice the timing — Abram let go first, and only then did God speak. While our hands are still clenched tight, God often says nothing; when we let go, heaven opens. Lot used his own eyes to pick one piece; God used his eyes to give Abram all of it. Those who live for themselves lose; those who live for God gain everything.

The second light: the value you see is the life you live. The Lord Jesus said, “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.” The context of these words is laying up treasure in heaven and not serving two masters, so the Lord isn’t talking about eyesight but about values. “Sound” in the original carries the sense of single, pure. Brothers and sisters, look at yourself, and you live for yourself, in a world so small it holds only one person; look at advantage, and you live for advantage, reaching for the calculator even in serving God; look at God, and you live for God, in a world large enough to hold a kingdom.

The same principle holds in the church. Look at “my church,” and there is comparison and rivalry; look at “God’s kingdom,” and we move towards unity, because the kingdom has only one King. Worldly seeing says, “I want to get”; spiritual seeing says, “I want to give.” Paul says, “each counting others better than himself.” So unity isn’t something we grit our teeth to endure; it is something we learn to see. Brothers and sisters, denying self is not a loss; it is entering into a greater gain. Put a drop of water in the palm of your hand and in half a day it has dried up; put it into the ocean and it will never dry up — and from then on it has the power of the whole ocean. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and living it out. Paul says, “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

The third light: the same circumstances, different sight, different endings. The scene is the Red Sea. In front, fathomless water; behind, Pharaoh’s chariots. Everyone’s situation was exactly the same. The Bible says, “When Pharaoh came near, the children of Israel lifted up their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them; and they were very afraid.” They said to Moses: because there were no graves in Egypt, have you taken us away to die in the wilderness? Brothers and sisters, listen to those words — the day before they were cheering their freedom, and today they would rather go back and be slaves. In 1998 the psychologist Barbara Fredrickson put forward the broaden-and-build theory; she found that fear narrows our attention, leaving only flight or fight. No wonder they could think of only two options: drown, or go back to Egypt.

Moses stood at the edge of the same sea, yet he saw something different. He looked at God’s works, and he looked at God’s promises. He said, “Don’t be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of Yahweh, which he will work for you today.” And then, “Moses stretched out his hand over the sea … and made the sea dry land.” Brothers and sisters, take hold of this order: the circumstances didn’t change first; the “seeing” changed first, and then the miracle appeared. Moses didn’t have faith because he saw the sea part; he saw the sea part because he had faith. It was the same with Elisha. His servant saw the city surrounded by enemy troops and panicked; Elisha didn’t ask God to drive the enemy away, only to open his servant’s eyes. The horses and chariots of fire had been there all along; he just couldn’t see them.

The fourth light: what God lets you see, he will bring to pass. There is an order that recurs again and again in the Bible — God first gives you sight, and then leads you into experience. He first had Abram lift up his eyes and look, and only then gave him the land; he first gave Joseph dreams, and only then set him in the place of ruler; he first let Moses see a bush burning with fire yet not consumed, and only then sent him to Pharaoh. Hebrews says, “By faith, Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out … He went out, not knowing where he went.” Brothers and sisters, you don’t need to know how first; you only need to see, believe and obey. The responsibility for bringing it to pass lies with God, not with you.

This is the essence of faith. Hebrews says, “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen.” The word “assurance” in the original carries the sense of foundation, substance. Faith isn’t shutting our eyes to the facts; faith is seeing a higher fact — that the invisible Lord is more real than the visible Red Sea. That is why the Bible commends Moses: “as seeing him who is invisible.” Brothers and sisters, faith is not a feeling. Feelings rise and fall with sleep, blood sugar, the weather and a single remark from someone else; but God’s word never changes. Paul says the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal. At the foot of a mountain you see a wall; climb to the top and you see a path. The wall was there all along, and so was the path; what changed was the height.

The fifth light: weakness is not the problem; seeing wrongly is. This part is for those of you who feel this morning that you’re not good enough. Paul had a thorn in his flesh, and he pleaded with the Lord three times to take it away. God didn’t take it away; he gave him a word instead: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” In the original, “is sufficient” is in the present tense — continually, unceasingly enough. God didn’t give Paul a one-off deposit; he gave him a stream of living water supplied every day. Brothers and sisters, a cup filled with itself has no room for anything else; only an emptied cup can be filled. Weakness is the empty space God clears in your heart.

So please hear this clearly: God is not afraid of your weakness; God is afraid of your seeing wrongly. Look at yourself, and you are weak; look at God, and you are strong. Gideon was threshing wheat in the winepress when the angel said to him, “Yahweh is with you, you mighty man of valor!” Yet Gideon said: I am the least in my father’s house. You see, what the angel saw and what Gideon saw were completely different. God didn’t argue with him; God simply said, “I will be with you.” The problem was never how small Gideon was, but whom he was looking at. Professor Carol Dweck of Stanford University has researched people’s mindsets, and she found that those with a fixed mindset treat failure as a verdict, while those with a growth mindset treat failure as information. And Christians have an even higher way of seeing — the eyes of grace: my weakness isn’t my sentence of condemnation; it is my letter of invitation.

The sixth light is the light of 321: the selfless see the works of God. Self-centred people look at themselves and so limit God; selfless people look at God and so experience God. It isn’t that God’s power can be limited, but that a heart full of itself leaves no room for God to work. The Bible says that in Nazareth the Lord Jesus “didn’t do many mighty works there because of their unbelief.” Brothers and sisters, the self-centred life puts the self at the centre and measures everything by “me” — my face, my rights, my feelings. Selflessness isn’t being negated or trampled on; selflessness is entering into the fullness and living it out. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Selfless people bear three marks: they don’t contend for themselves, because they know their inheritance is in God’s hands; they don’t live for themselves, because the love of Christ constrains them; they don’t gain for themselves, because they are stewards, not landlords. They live for only three: for Jesus, for others and for God’s kingdom. And such people experience three things: they see God, they experience God, they gain God. And what they finally gain isn’t things, but God himself. God said to Abraham, “I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.” The Lord Jesus said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” To be pure in heart is to be selfless.

Brothers and sisters, today we have three practices. First, when facing a choice, ask yourself: what am I looking at? Advantage, or God’s will? From today on, for any decision that takes more than three minutes to make, stop first and ask: Lord, how do you see this? Every evening spend three minutes looking back: did I make any choice today with Lot’s eyes? Second, when facing difficulty, change what you see. Write your greatest difficulty on the left side of a sheet of paper, quietly ask God, and write his promises on the right. Look not at the size of the problem, but at the power of God.

Third, practise the seeing of faith every day: let God’s word replace what the eye sees, and let the promises replace feelings. Each morning ask God to give you one verse as “today’s promise,” copy it down and put it where you’ll see it ten times a day. All three practices should follow the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Doing it once isn’t practice; repeating it is. Learning it yourself isn’t the finish; teaching it to others is Multiplication. Brothers and sisters, please remember this little reminder: it is not that you have no opportunities; it is that you have not seen God’s opportunities. God’s grace is never absent; what is often absent is our eyes.

Let’s walk through today’s message once more within the 3-2-1 vision. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — existing in the form of God, he emptied himself; the Bible is my standard — when the Red Sea is in front of you, the question isn’t “What does this look like?” but “What has God said?”; the Holy Spirit is my guide — only he can enlighten the eyes of our hearts. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — Lot’s problem wasn’t that he chose the wrong land, but that he made the choice sitting on the throne himself; let Jesus receive all the glory — the glory of the Red Sea went wholly to Yahweh. The Goal: establish God’s system. The fivefold change begins with mindset: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. Life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Brothers and sisters, let’s walk today’s road once more. Lot saw the plain, and what he received was destruction; Abraham saw God, and what he received was the promise. The Israelites saw the Red Sea and lived in fear; Moses saw God and experienced a miracle. The same land, the same sea, the same day. The difference was not in the circumstances, but in the eyes. So please take this sentence home with you: what you see today determines what you receive tomorrow. When you choose to see with spiritual eyes, crisis becomes opportunity, weakness becomes power, and the impossible becomes possible. Not because you are capable, but because the One you see is capable.

Let us declare together: Lord, open my eyes! Let me no longer look only at myself and my circumstances, but see your works and your promises! Make me live by faith, obey your leading, and experience your wonderful power! Dear Heavenly Father, forgive us — so often, like Lot, we see only the advantage in front of us, and so often, like the people at the Red Sea, we see only the pursuers and the great waters. Enlighten the eyes of our hearts and take away the self in our hearts, so that we live only for Jesus, for others and for your kingdom. May all that we see today be you; may all that we receive tomorrow be what you have promised. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Ending of a Life Begins with a Single “Look”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning.

Let me begin with a question. Picture the same heavy rain on the same morning. One person pushes open the window, frowns and says, “What a wretched day.” Another pushes open the very same window, takes a deep breath and says, “How clean the air is today.” The same rain, the same window, the same morning — yet two moods, two days, and as the days add up into months and years, two lives. The rain didn’t change; the window didn’t change. What changed was the pair of eyes.

We often think the outcome of our lives is decided by our circumstances. When the economy is good, things go well for me; when my health is good, I’m joyful; when people treat me well, I’m loving. Circumstances are the cause, life is the effect, and we are merely passive recipients. But the Bible shows us a deeper, truer spiritual path:

Seeing determines thinking; thinking determines doing; doing determines the outcome.

How you see determines how you think; how you think determines what you do; what you do determines how your life ends. These four links are like a chain, each link fastened to the next, with no break in between. You cannot spend years looking at everything through the wrong eyes and yet live the right life; nor can you fix your eyes on Jesus every day and find your life entirely unchanged. This is cause and effect in the spiritual world, more reliable than gravity.

So the key is not “how things happen,” but this: how you see what happens.

Humanity has in fact been groping towards this truth for a long time. As early as the first and second centuries AD, the Stoic philosopher Epictetus wrote in the fifth section of his Handbook (Enchiridion): “People are disturbed not by things themselves, but by their views about things.” In the twentieth century, in 1955, the American psychologist Albert Ellis put forward Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (REBT), the best-known part of which is the “ABC model”: A is the Activating event, B is the Belief — how a person interprets that event — and C is the Consequence, the emotions and behaviour that follow. Ellis pointed out that most people assume it is A that determines C — that event made me angry, that event made me depressed; but in fact it is B that determines C — it is my view of that event that makes me angry and depressed. Later, the cognitive therapy that Aaron T. Beck developed at the University of Pennsylvania was built on the same insight.

Brothers and sisters, psychology took a detour of nearly two thousand years to arrive where the Bible had long since been: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). However the heart sees, so the outcome flows.

And there is an even more piercing discovery. In 1999 the American psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris carried out an experiment at Harvard University that later became famous around the world, known as “the invisible gorilla.” They asked participants to watch a short video, and the task was simple: count how many times the people in white passed the ball to one another. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked in from the right of the screen, stopped in the very centre to beat its chest, and walked out on the left — nearly nine seconds in all. After the experiment the researchers asked, “Did you see the gorilla?” About half of the participants had not seen it at all. Their eyes were plainly open, the light had plainly entered their retinas, the image had plainly reached the visual cortex of the brain — but they “did not see.”

Psychology calls this phenomenon “inattentional blindness.” It turns out that seeing has never been only a matter of the eyes; it is a matter of attention, a matter of the heart. What you pay attention to, you see; what you see, you think about; what you think about, you do; what you do, you become.

Today’s lesson is to take this chain apart link by link, so that we can see: different ways of seeing bring completely different outcomes.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Eye and the Focus
1. Matthew 6:22–23
sections.html:
The author of Matthew’s Gospel is Matthew, also called Levi, who was originally a tax collector at the tax office in Capernaum. The Lord Jesus said to him, “Follow me,” and he left everything and followed the Lord (Matthew 9:9). It is generally thought that the book was written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish Christians, which is why the whole book quotes the Old Testament so heavily, showing again and again that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the Son of David, the King of the kingdom of heaven.

The saying “The lamp of the body is the eye” comes from the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7). We often read this passage as a stand-alone proverb, but in fact it sits between two very practical teachings. Before it, verses 19–21 say: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth … but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven … for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:19–21). After it, verse 24 says: “No one can serve two masters … You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24).

When the Lord Jesus places “the eye” between “treasure” and “Mammon,” he is not suddenly changing the subject; he is pointing out the hinge of the whole passage: where your treasure is, there your eye is; where your eye is, there you go.

The word translated “sound” is the Greek ἁπλοῦς (haplous), meaning “single, simple, undivided,” and in Jewish usage it also carries the sense of “generous, holding nothing back.” Its opposite, “evil,” is πονηρός (ponēros), whose basic meaning is “wicked”; in Jewish idiom “an evil eye” means greed, envy, stinginess. So what the Lord Jesus is talking about here is not a problem of eyesight at all but a problem of loyalty: are your eyes fixed singly on one Master, or are you glancing left and right, with a foot in two boats?

Notice also the picture of the “lamp.” Houses in ancient Palestine had very small windows and were dim inside all day long; the light or darkness of the whole house depended on one small oil lamp. If the lamp was bright, the whole room was lit; if the lamp went out, the whole room was dark. The eye is to a person what that lamp is to the whole house.

sections.heading: 2. 2 Corinthians 4:18
sections.html:
The author of 2 Corinthians is the apostle Paul. It was written in about AD 55–56, to the church in Corinth. Corinth was the capital of the Roman province of Achaia, a great, wealthy, proud seaport city that prized eloquence and appearances. At the time, some in the church were questioning Paul: he was unimpressive in person, crude in speech, persecuted everywhere, his body covered in scars — how could someone like that be a servant God was using mightily?

Paul’s answer is written in 2 Corinthians 4. He says, “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 4:7). He also says, “Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day. For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:16–17). Immediately after comes verse 18, the summing up.

The word translated “look at” is the Greek σκοπέω (skopeō), the very root of the English word “scope” (as in telescope or rifle scope), meaning “to aim at, to gaze at intently, to make one’s target.” Paul is not saying Christians shut their eyes to reality; he knew reality better than anyone. He is saying: what we aim at is not what is in front of us, but what is eternal. Wherever you aim the gun of your life, that is what you will hit.

Put these two passages together and you have the skeleton of this lesson: the eye determines the whole body, and the focus determines the ending.

sections.heading: 1. Wrong Seeing Brings Sin and Destruction
sections.html:
“At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to look at.” (2 Samuel 11:2)

Before the Fall Comes Slackness

When we read this verse, we often jump straight to “he saw,” and overlook the verse before it: “At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel; and they destroyed the children of Ammon, and besieged Rabbah. But David stayed at Jerusalem” (2 Samuel 11:1).

The Holy Spirit took care to record one sentence: David stayed at Jerusalem. When he should have gone out to battle, he stayed in the palace; when he should have been up, he was still in bed; only when the sun was going down did he get up. Brothers and sisters, a spiritual fall never happens suddenly. Before the fall comes slackness; before failure comes leaving one’s post. A person who has left his originally intended position will find his eyes beginning to wander.

The Chain Reaction of One “Look”

The Hebrew word for “saw” is רָאָה (ra’ah), and the original behind “very beautiful to look at” is טוֹבַת מַרְאֶה (tovat mar’eh), where mar’eh means precisely “what is seen, the outward appearance.” In other words, the Bible tells us with great precision: what David saw was “appearance.” He did not see God, nor did he see that behind this appearance was a married woman, the home of a loyal officer.

What follows is a clear downward chain:

He saw beauty — this step is not sin; a person’s eyes will inevitably fall on beautiful things.

He did not turn his eyes away — at this step, the door to sin opened.

He began to think — he sent to inquire about her (2 Samuel 11:3).

Desire arose — imagination turned into longing.

He put it into action — he sent messengers and had the woman brought to him.

The book of James describes exactly the same chain: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death” (James 1:14–15). John also says, “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s” (1 John 2:16). Notice that John lists “the lust of the eyes” on its own, because the eyes are the front door of the heart.

One wrong look brought a whole series of destruction: adultery, then murder by another’s hand — he wrote to Joab, “Send Uriah to the forefront of the hottest battle, and retreat from him, that he may be struck, and die” (2 Samuel 11:15). Finally, the breaking of his family — God declared through the prophet Nathan: “Now therefore the sword will never depart from your house, because you have despised me, and have taken Uriah the Hittite’s wife to be your wife” (2 Samuel 12:10). The later disgrace of Amnon, the rebellion of Absalom, the bloodshed within the family — all of it began with that one look from the palace roof.

Let’s set beside him a man who saw rightly. Job said, “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1) Job did not wait until he had seen before he struggled; before he ever saw, he had already made a covenant with his own eyes. What wisdom that is.

An Example from Daily Life: Where You Look, the Bike Goes

Anyone who has had motorcycle or racing training knows a term called “target fixation.” The instructor’s first lesson is often: don’t stare at the thing you’re afraid of. When a rider on a mountain road sees a large rock by the roadside and thinks, “Whatever I do, I mustn’t hit it,” yet keeps his eyes fixed hard on that rock, nine times out of ten the bike heads straight for it. That’s because the body unconsciously follows the line of sight. So the right thing to do is: look where you want to go, not at what you’re afraid of.

Psychology confirms this too. In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner and his colleagues published the famous “white bear experiment” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. The researchers asked participants not to think of a white bear for the next five minutes, and to ring a bell whenever they did. The result was that those told “don’t think of a white bear” actually thought of white bears more than those who had not been told. This is called the “ironic rebound effect.”

Brothers and sisters, this is why simply gritting our teeth and saying, “I won’t look, I won’t think about it,” nearly always fails. The Bible’s method has never been “don’t think about it”; the Bible’s method is “turn your eyes and fix them”: “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:2a). The way to overcome the darkness is not to glare at the darkness with all your might, but to switch on the light.

Thank God: Repentance Also Begins with a “Look”

But the story does not end in destruction. Nathan came and told a parable about a poor man and his little ewe lamb. David burned with anger, but Nathan said, “You are the man!” And so —

“David said to Nathan, ‘I have sinned against Yahweh.’ Nathan said to David, ‘Yahweh also has put away your sin. You will not die.’” (2 Samuel 12:13)

Brothers and sisters, please notice: David’s fall began with a wrong look; David’s restoration also began with a right look — at last he saw his own sin. In Psalm 51 he says, “For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me” (Psalm 51:3).

That is why he could pray like this: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24).

The Hebrew word for “search” is חָקַר (chaqar), whose basic meaning is “to dig deep, to explore,” like a miner with a lamp digging down layer by layer. David is asking God: Lord, I cannot see myself; please bring your light and dig down to the very bottom of my heart.

Only when we see ourselves rightly can we enter into repentance and restoration.

Applying the 321 Vision

In the light of 321 we say: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. David standing on the palace roof and looking down — this was precisely a look that had “left its originally intended position”: he was king, he had power, and whatever he saw he could take. When a person looks with his own eyes, the eyes become servants of desire; when a person lets Jesus become his eyes, the eyes become a window of worship.

When the focus is on ourselves, the ending is failure. Of the fivefold change, the first is mindset — because how you see is your mindset. Only a change of mindset can change the life, and only a changed life can change daily living.

sections.heading: 2. Wrong Seeing Brings Fear and Sinking
sections.html:
“But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” (Matthew 14:30)

The Background: The Sea in the Fourth Watch

This took place right after the miracle of the five loaves and two fish. “Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat, and to go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the multitudes away” (Matthew 14:22). The Lord himself went up the mountain to pray. Then “in the fourth watch of the night” — that is, between three and six in the morning, when the sky is darkest and people are most exhausted — “Jesus came to them, walking on the sea” (Matthew 14:25). The disciples thought it was a ghost and cried out in terror. “But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, ‘Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid’” (Matthew 14:27).

Then comes one of the bravest sentences in the whole Bible: “Peter answered him and said, ‘Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.’ He said, ‘Come!’ Peter stepped down from the boat, and walked on the waters to come to Jesus” (Matthew 14:28–29).

Brothers and sisters, please don’t be too quick to laugh at Peter. In that boat, he was the only one who got out; in all of human history, apart from the Lord Jesus, he is the only one who has walked on water. To begin with, Peter was this: looking at Jesus, he walked on the water.

What Changed Was Not the Circumstances but the Focus

Then the text says: “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid.” The word “saw” here is the Greek βλέπω (blepō), meaning seeing with the physical eye.

Here is a vitally important detail: the wind and waves did not arrive at that moment. The wind and waves had been there before he got out of the boat — indeed, even earlier, the disciples had been tossed about on them for most of the night. What changed was not the circumstances; what changed was the focus. At first he looked past the wind and waves and saw the Lord; now he let the wind and waves block his view of the Lord.

So Peter did not sink because his ability fell short, nor because his faith was too small to get out of the boat — he had already got out of the boat! He sank because he “saw wrongly.”

When the Lord pulled him up, he said, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matthew 14:31) The Greek word for “doubt” is διστάζω (distazō), whose root carries the idea of “two,” meaning “to stand on two sides, to have a heart split in half.” Half looking at the Lord, half looking at the wind — and a person sinks. This is exactly what the Lord Jesus said in Matthew 6:22: when the eye is not sound, not single, the whole body is full of darkness.

Supporting Evidence from Science and Psychology

Physiologically, our balance depends not only on the vestibular system of the inner ear but very heavily on sight as well.
