You can try it right now: stand on one foot, and many people can stay there for a long time; but close your eyes, and most people start wobbling within a few seconds. Where the eyes look, there the body steadies itself. That is why tightrope walkers never look down at their feet; they fix their eyes on one point on the far side.

Psychologically, research on anxiety has repeatedly confirmed a phenomenon called “attentional bias.” In 1986 Colin MacLeod, Andrew Mathews and Philip Tata published a study in the Journal of Abnormal Psychology which found that the attention of highly anxious people is involuntarily drawn to threatening information, whereas that of ordinary people is not. In other words, the more afraid people are, the more they stare at frightening things; and the more they stare, the more afraid they become — a vicious circle.

The Bible gave us the way out long ago. The word “looking” is the Greek ἀφοράω (aphoraō), made up of apo (away from) and horaō (to see). Its literal meaning is: first take your eyes off everything else, and only then can you fix them on the One. So the act of faith has two halves: first look away, then fix your gaze. If you don’t look away, you can’t fix your gaze.

Here is another picture. When Elisha was surrounded by the Aramean army, his servant got up early in the morning, saw horses, chariots and soldiers all around the city, and cried out: “Alas, my master! What shall we do?” “He answered, ‘Don’t be afraid; for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.’ Elisha prayed, and said, ‘Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.’ Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:16–17).

Brothers and sisters, please notice: those horses and chariots of fire were there all along. Elisha did not ask God to conjure up horses and chariots of fire; he only asked God to open his servant’s eyes. God’s resources are never lacking; what is lacking is our seeing.

Applying the 321 Vision

When the focus is on our circumstances, we waver. 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you will rejoice, rely on the brain and you will worry. The moment Peter stepped out of the boat, he was relying on the heart; the moment he began calculating amid the wind and waves, he was relying on the brain. As soon as he started calculating, he started sinking.

Look at your circumstances, and you are afraid; look at Jesus, and there are miracles. The key to faith has never been how hard you try, but this: whom you are looking at.

sections.heading: 3. Right Seeing Brings Promise and Blessing
sections.html:
“For I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever.” (Genesis 13:15)

How Abram Saw, and How Lot Saw

The background of this passage is a family dispute. Abram and his nephew Lot both had large flocks and herds, and their herdsmen quarrelled with each other. As the elder, as the one who had been called, Abram could easily have exercised his authority. But he said: “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives. Isn’t the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me. If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left” (Genesis 13:8–9).

What humility this is — laying down his rights and returning to his originally intended position; letting man be man and letting God be God.

Then Lot also “lifted up his eyes”: “Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere, before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of Yahweh, like the land of Egypt, as you go to Zoar. So Lot chose the Plain of the Jordan for himself. Lot traveled east, and they separated themselves from one other” (Genesis 13:10–11).

Brothers and sisters, Lot also lifted up his eyes and also saw, but what he saw was “well-watered” — immediate, worldly, temporary gain. Right after, in verse 13, the Holy Spirit adds a sentence: “Now the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinners against Yahweh” (Genesis 13:13). Lot saw the water and grass of Sodom, but did not see the wickedness of Sodom. And the result? He lost his property, lost his testimony, lost his sons-in-law, and in the end lost even his wife — “But Lot’s wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt” (Genesis 19:26). Even while fleeing for her life, she looked back at the wrong place.

And Abram? “Yahweh said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him, ‘Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward’” (Genesis 13:14).

Please notice two things. First, he gave way first, and only then did he see. Humility comes first; then comes spiritual vision. Second, it was God who told him to look. Human seeing is something we choose for ourselves; spiritual seeing is God opening your eyes. Lot’s seeing was his own choice; Abram’s seeing was God’s gift. Two kinds of seeing, two endings.

God also said: “Arise, walk through the land in its length and in its width; for I will give it to you” (Genesis 13:17). After seeing, you must step out — the seeing of faith inevitably brings forth the steps of faith.

Interestingly, Abraham never actually possessed that land in his lifetime. Stephen said before the Council: “He gave him no inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on” (Acts 7:5a). All he ever bought in the land of Canaan in his whole life was a single burial plot for Sarah. But Hebrews says: “For he looked for the city which has the foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Hebrews 11:10). And again: “These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13a).

What he saw was further and truer than the ground beneath his feet.

Elisha: To See Is to Receive

“Elijah said to Elisha, ‘Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.’ Elisha said, ‘Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.’ He said, ‘You have asked a hard thing. If you see me when I am taken from you, it will be so for you; but if not, it will not be so.’” (2 Kings 2:9–10)

Why was “seeing” the condition? This was not a magic show or an eyesight test. It was a spiritual verification. That day, fifty of the sons of the prophets stood watching at a distance (2 Kings 2:7), but only Elisha followed closely: from Gilgal to Bethel, from Bethel to Jericho, from Jericho to the Jordan. Three times Elijah told him to stay behind, and three times he answered, “As Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you” (2 Kings 2:2, 4, 6).

In other words, “seeing” was the fruit of following to the very end. You cannot stand at a distance watching and expect to receive a double anointing.

“As they continued on and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them, and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven. Elisha saw it, and he cried, ‘My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!’” (2 Kings 2:11–12a) He saw, and so he received. From that day on, the waters of the Jordan parted in his hands, and the sons of the prophets said, “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha” (2 Kings 2:15a).

See spiritual things, and you inherit spiritual power.

An Example from Science: That Seemingly Empty Patch of Sky

In December 1995 astronomers made a decision that many at the time thought was a waste: they pointed the Hubble Space Telescope at a tiny patch of sky in Ursa Major that appeared completely empty, and exposed it continuously for ten days, taking more than three hundred images in all. How small was that patch of sky? Roughly the area you would cover with the head of a pin held at arm’s length.

And the result? Out of that tiny patch of “nothing” emerged nearly three thousand galaxies. This is the famous “Hubble Deep Field.”

Brothers and sisters, what seems completely empty is in fact full of glory — it just takes a long enough, focused enough gaze. Does your situation today look like a blank? God’s glory may be right there, waiting for you to fix your eyes on it.

Applying the 321 Vision

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things. This is exactly what Abram did. He dealt with the relationship first — he would rather lose out himself than quarrel with his own flesh and blood; once the relationship was right, God gave him the inheritance. Lot did it the other way round, grabbing things first, and in the end he lost both the things and the relationship.

321 also speaks of the 235 relationships: become a “2” with selfless people, build a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, and become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Abram and Lot could have been each other’s “2,” but they were separated because of Lot’s way of seeing; Elijah and Elisha, on the other hand, became the most beautiful “3” in the Bible — a spiritual father and son. The first thing Elisha cried out was “My father, my father!” This was not the handing on of an office; it was the handing on of a life.

sections.heading: 4. The Seeing of Faith Brings Eternal Reward
sections.html:
“By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible.” (Hebrews 11:27)

Moses: Faith Is a Revaluation

Hebrews 11 has been called “the roll of honour of the heroes of faith.” About Moses, the writer says: “By faith, Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to share ill treatment with God’s people than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a time, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he looked to the reward” (Hebrews 11:24–26).

The word “considering” is the Greek ἡγέομαι (hēgeomai), meaning “to judge after weighing things up, to assess.” So please notice: faith is not blind; faith is a revaluation. It is not that Moses had never done the sums — he did them more clearly than anyone. He put the treasures of Egypt on one side of the scales and the reproach suffered for Christ on the other, and then said: the second weighs more.

“As seeing him who is invisible” is, in the original, ὡς ὁρῶν τὸν ἀόρατον — literally, “as seeing the unseeable.” The same root for “see” (horaō) is used twice in a single phrase, once positively and once negatively, forming a beautiful contrast. The essence of faith is to see, in an unseen way, the God who cannot be seen.

Supporting Evidence from Science: What We Can See Is Only a Tiny Part

Here I want to draw your attention to a wonderful fact, brothers and sisters. The visible light the human eye can see has wavelengths of only about 380 to 700 nanometres — an extremely small slice of the whole electromagnetic spectrum. Infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays, radio waves — we cannot see any of them, yet they are really there every moment, even passing through our bodies.

Even more staggering is the make-up of the universe. According to the observations published in 2013 by the European Space Agency’s Planck satellite, the universe is made up of roughly 68% dark energy and 27% dark matter, while the ordinary matter we can see accounts for only about 5%.

Brothers and sisters, even science is telling us: what can be seen is only a tiny part. How narrow, then, is a life that judges entirely by the naked eye; how poor is a person who believes only what he can see.

So Hebrews goes on: “But now they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them” (Hebrews 11:16). See eternity, and you will not be bound by this life. A person with a homeland in his heart will not quarrel himself red in the face over a scrap of land while he is a sojourner.

Paul: A Recalculated Profit-and-Loss Statement

“Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ.” (Philippians 3:8)

The Greek word for “refuse” is σκύβαλον (skybalon), meaning kitchen scraps, leftovers, rubbish and dung thrown out of the door. It is a very strong word.

But please notice that Paul is using the language of accounting here. In the previous verse he says: “However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ” (Philippians 3:7). Gain and loss — this is a profit-and-loss statement. Paul’s pedigree, education, zeal and righteous deeds had all been entered in the “assets” column; after he came to know Christ, he did the accounts again and moved every one of them to the “liabilities” column.

It was not that those things had gone bad in themselves; it was that he “looked” at them again, and their value was completely revised.

Because he saw rightly, he lived rightly.

The Crown: See Eternity, and You Gain Eternity

When Paul wrote 2 Timothy, he was in prison in Rome, about to be martyred for the Lord. He said, “For I am already being offered, and the time of my departure has come” (2 Timothy 4:6). And then he said:

“From now on, the crown of righteousness is stored up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give to me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all those who have loved his appearing.” (2 Timothy 4:8)

To the naked eye, it was a cold cell, a sword about to fall, an ending in failure. To the eye of faith, it was a crown of righteousness, a Lord who gives the crown in person, a glorious beginning. The same scene, two ways of seeing, two conclusions.

Help from Psychology: Seeing the Reward Not Yet in Hand

From the late 1960s to the early 1970s, the Stanford University psychologist Walter Mischel and his colleagues carried out the famous “marshmallow test.” The researcher put a marshmallow in front of a preschool child and told the child that if they could wait a while without eating it, they would get two when the researcher came back. Later follow-up studies (Shoda, Mischel and Peake, 1990) found that the children who had been better able to wait showed better self-control and academic results in adolescence. It should be said that a large-sample replication study by Tyler Watts and others in 2018 found that this link was weaker than originally reported and was influenced by family socio-economic background; but the basic principle — “those who can see a reward not yet in hand can let go of the immediate pleasure in their hand” — is still widely affirmed.

Brothers and sisters, faith is in fact the highest form of delayed gratification: because we see the unseen reward, we can let go of the temporary sweet in our hand. Moses let go of the throne of Egypt, Paul let go of his prospects in Judaism, and the Lord Jesus himself, “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame” (Hebrews 12:2b).

Helen Keller is commonly credited with saying: “The only thing worse than being blind is having sight but no vision.” A person can have excellent eyesight and yet see nothing at all.

Applying the 321 Vision

321 speaks of a change of perspective: from man’s point of view to God’s point of view, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. These four changes can be seen plainly in Moses and in Paul.

See eternity, and you gain eternity.

sections.heading: 5. Key Summary: Two Ways of Seeing, Two Ways of Living
sections.html:
Let’s gather these four parts together.

Worldly Seeing

Look at desire, and you sin — that was David.

Look at circumstances, and you fear — that was Peter.

Look at yourself, and you are weak — that was the ten spies.

The result: failure, destruction, sinking.

Spiritual Seeing

Look at God, and you have faith — that was Elisha.

Look at the promise, and you obey — that was Abraham.

Look at eternity, and you overcome — that was Moses and Paul.

The result: blessing, power, glory.

The Same Land, Two Reports

Numbers 13 is the most vivid example of this truth. Twelve spies explored the same land of Canaan, walked the same roads, looked at the same city walls, met the same descendants of Anak — and came back with two completely opposite reports.

The ten spies said: “There we saw the Nephilim, the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim. We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Numbers 13:33).

Brothers and sisters, please notice the second half of this verse — “and so we were in their sight.” They imagined that for themselves; the Bible never records a single descendant of Anak saying any such thing. A person who sees himself as a grasshopper will assume the whole world sees him as a grasshopper. A sense of inferiority is also a kind of seeing wrongly.

But Caleb and Joshua said: “Only don’t rebel against Yahweh, neither fear the people of the land; for they are bread for us. Their defense is removed from over them, and Yahweh is with us. Don’t fear them” (Numbers 14:9).

The same giants were, through one pair of eyes, a wall too high to scale; through another, “bread for us.” We all know the outcome: the ten spies and that whole generation aged twenty and over fell dead in the wilderness, and only the two who saw rightly entered the promised land.

Supporting Evidence from Psychology: The Frame Determines the Choice

In 1981 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman published their famous study of the “Asian disease problem” in the journal Science. The researchers told participants that a disease was expected to kill 600 people, and that there were two programmes to choose from. The first group heard it described this way: “Programme A will save 200 people; with Programme B there is a one-third chance that all 600 will be saved and a two-thirds chance that no one will be saved.” Most chose the cautious A. The second group heard it described this way: “With Programme A, 400 people will die; with Programme B there is a one-third chance that nobody will die and a two-thirds chance that all 600 will die.” This time most chose the risky B.

But brothers and sisters, the numbers for the two groups were exactly the same! The only difference was that one looked at it in terms of “saving” and the other in terms of “dying.” This is the famous “framing effect.” The facts were identical; only because the frame through which they were seen was different, the choices were completely reversed.

This is precisely what the Lord Jesus said: “The lamp of the body is the eye” (Matthew 6:22a).

sections.heading: 6. A 321 Insight: The Focus Determines the Outcome
sections.html:
Three Focal Points, Three Endings

When the focus is on ourselves, the ending is failure.

When the focus is on our circumstances, the ending is wavering.

When the focus is on Jesus, the ending is victory.

The self-centred look with their own eyes; the selfless let Jesus become their eyes.

Brothers and sisters, please notice that selflessness is not shutting our eyes, not looking at nothing. 321 puts it very clearly: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. It is the same with the eyes — it is not that we stop looking, but that we look with a different pair of eyes.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Asking God to Enlighten the Eyes of the Heart

Paul’s prayer for the church in Ephesus was for exactly this: “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints” (Ephesians 1:17–18).

So it turns out we also have a pair of eyes in our hearts, and those eyes need to be enlightened by the Holy Spirit. The physical eye is lit by light; the eye of the heart is lit by the Holy Spirit. This is the third of the Three Foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Humble Seeing and Proud Seeing

321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

David looking down from the palace roof was seeing from outside his originally intended position: I am king, and whatever I see I can take.

Abram saying to Lot, “If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right,” was seeing from within his originally intended position: I am not the owner of this land; God is.

And the result? Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. From then on the sword never left David’s house, while Abram’s offspring became like the dust of the earth.

Change Your Position, Change Your Life

In 1987 the writer Frank White coined a term, “the Overview Effect.” He interviewed many astronauts and found that the moment they looked back at the earth from space, their values were often permanently changed: there was a blue planet hanging in the darkness, without a single national border, fragile, beautiful, whole. Looking down from that height, many of the rivalries of the human world suddenly seemed very small.

Brothers and sisters, we too have a position. God “raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6). Our seat is not beside our problems; it is in Christ, in the heavenly places. That is why Paul says, “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2).

This is how the selfless see the heart of God, experience the power of God and receive the promises of God.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s string the light of 321 together from beginning to end.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — the Lord himself is the One who “saw rightly”: he, “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame” (Hebrews 12:2b). The Bible is my standard — “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path” (Psalm 119:105). The eyes need a lamp, and the lamp is God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — it is the Holy Spirit who enlightens the eyes of our hearts.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — where the King is, there the eyes are; where the eyes are, there the person goes. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when we look at Jesus alone, human glory naturally fades away.

The Goal. Establish God’s system — when a group of people who see rightly gather together, that is God’s system; when a group of people who each see their own way gather together, they are merely a crowd.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. This lesson works on precisely the first. How you see is your mindset. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. Many brothers and sisters want to change their daily living or their ministry directly, but are unwilling to change their mindset — and so after all their effort they are still going round in circles in the same place.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. David’s tragedy was that he turned this order completely upside down — he looked first at a “thing” (a beautiful appearance), and as a result he ruined his relationship with God, his relationship with himself and his relationship with others.

The 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” Brothers and sisters, think about it: when you look at your “2” with worldly eyes, what do you see? Their faults, their threat, what they owe you, how they have wronged you. But when you practise selflessness (0) and let Jesus be your eyes, you see someone God loves, someone for whom Christ laid down his life. Then the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit naturally grow: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23a).

How you see your “2” determines how many of those fruits you can bear.

The 235 relationships. Elijah and Elisha were the most beautiful “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children. Elisha was able to inherit a double anointing not because he had some outstanding talent, but because he followed all the way, kept his eyes fixed all the way, and in the end “saw.” Spiritual inheritance has never depended on courses; it depends on seeing.

The Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit guides me, the Bible enlightens me, Jesus is my role model, and so I rise up to serve, until in the end Jesus receives all the glory. Every step of this path requires a renewed pair of eyes.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very practical exercises. We’ll keep them, and deepen them using the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Check your “seeing” on the spot

Whenever your emotions surge, immediately ask yourself one question: What am I looking at right now? My circumstances? Myself? Or God?

Emotions are the most honest dashboard there is. When you’re angry, you’re looking at “my rights”; when you’re jealous, you’re looking at “how well others are doing”; when you’re anxious, you’re looking at “what hasn’t happened yet”; when you feel inferior, you’re looking at “this grasshopper that is me.” Behind every negative emotion stands a focal point.

A suggestion: put a small card on your phone’s home screen or on your desk with five words on it — “What am I looking at?”

Practice 2: Practise turning your eyes to Jesus

Whenever anxiety or temptation comes, don’t argue with it, don’t play tug-of-war with it; turn to the Lord at once, and let Scripture replace what your eyes see.

This is exactly the reminder the white bear experiment gives us: telling yourself “don’t think about it” only makes you think about it more. So the Lord’s method is “looking to” — first look away, then fix your gaze.

A suggestion: prepare three “turn-your-eyes verses” and learn them by heart, so you can say them at any moment. For example:

“looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:2a)

“Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2)

“while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen.” (2 Corinthians 4:18a)

Practice 3: Ask the Lord every day to search your sight

Every night before you sleep, use David’s prayer to ask God to shine his light on the way you see inside, and to correct the wrong ways of seeing.

“Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

Information: First fix the content of this lesson in your memory — seeing, thinking, doing and the outcome form a chain; David, Peter and Lot saw wrongly; Abraham, Elisha and Paul saw rightly. Information is the foundation; without the right information, there is no right seeing.

Revelation: Information is in the head; revelation is in the heart. Ask the Holy Spirit to turn “knowing” into “seeing,” just as God opened the eyes of Elisha’s servant. Pray: Lord, enlighten the eyes of my heart.

Conviction: Do you really believe that “I am not defeated by my circumstances; I am defeated by seeing wrongly”? Conviction means handing over sovereignty, admitting that your way of seeing needs to be governed by God. Without conviction, practice turns into performance.

Implementation: Starting tomorrow morning, put the three exercises above into practice. Don’t make ten resolutions at once; start with one — start with the question, “What am I looking at?”

Evaluation: Set aside three minutes every evening to review today’s “seeing.” At what moment today did I see wrongly? What was I feeling at that moment? What did I do afterwards?

Correction: Identify the situation in which you most often see wrongly — it might be when you open your phone, when you look at your bank account, or when you face a particular family member. Prepare a verse for that situation, like a soldier posting extra guards on the stretch of wall most easily breached.

Repetition: A habit is not formed all at once. Give yourself forty days, every day without a break. Spiritual sight is like a muscle: the more you use it, the stronger it gets; and like a mirror: the more you polish it, the brighter it shines.

Multiplication: Find one of your “2”s and practise together, asking each other one question every week: “What have you been looking at this week?” 321 says that if change does not multiply, it stops with us. Those who have received must become those who give.

A Gentle Reminder

You are not defeated by your circumstances; you are defeated by “seeing wrongly.”

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s look once more at what we have seen today:

David saw wrongly, and he sinned.

Peter saw wrongly, and he sank.

Lot saw wrongly, and he lost.

Abraham saw rightly, and he received the land.

Elisha saw rightly, and he received power.

Paul saw rightly, and he received the crown.

Different ways of seeing bring completely different outcomes.

This morning the Lord sets this choice before us. He has not promised us that there will be no wind and waves — on the night Peter stepped out of the boat, the wind was already strong. He has not promised us that there will be no temptation — every one of us stands on David’s roof once a day. He has not promised that we will receive the land straight away — to the day he died, Abraham bought only a burial plot.

But the Lord does promise: what you look at, you become.

So when you choose not to look at the world, not to look at yourself, but to look at Jesus alone, your life will never be the same again; instead it will enter into the victory and glory God has prepared!

Brothers and sisters, letting Jesus be King begins with letting Jesus be your eyes. When he reigns as King in your eyes, he reigns as King in your thoughts; when he reigns as King in your thoughts, he reigns as King in your actions; when he reigns as King in your actions, he reigns as King over your whole life.

On that day, everything we have received will be laid at his feet. Because we saw rightly, we lived rightly; because we lived rightly, all the glory goes to him.

May all the glory go to our Lord Jesus Christ alone.

keyVerses: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23)

“while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)
declarations: Lord, guard my eyes! Do not let me look at everything with worldly eyes, but with your eyes! In every choice, let me see you and walk in the way that pleases you!
practices: Practise turning your eyes to Jesus
Ask the Lord every day to search your sight
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we worship you before your face.

Lord, thank you for reminding us this morning that the outcome of our lives is no accident; it begins with a single “look.” Please forgive us — so often we are like David, seeing and yet refusing to turn our eyes away; so often like Peter, plainly walking on the water and yet letting the wind and waves steal our focus; so often like Lot, seeing only the well-watered plain in front of us and not the danger behind it.

Lord, guard our eyes. Do not let us look at people, at things or at ourselves with worldly eyes, but with your eyes. Just as you opened the eyes of Elisha’s servant, open our eyes, so that we see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire, and see that your presence has never left us.
We ask that the Holy Spirit would enlighten the eyes of our hearts, so that we may see the hope of your calling. Let us see you in every choice, and walk in the way that pleases you.
May the focus of our whole lives be not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances, but on Jesus alone. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Think back to the most recent event that sent your emotions surging. At that moment, where was your focus — on your circumstances, on yourself, or on God? If you had been able, like Peter, to cry out, “Lord, save me!”, how might things have turned out differently? Read Matthew 14:30–31 together.

Abram gave way first, and only then did God tell him to lift up his eyes and look (Genesis 13:8–9, 14–15). In your relationships at present, is there something in which God wants you first to lay down your rights and return to your originally intended position? What price are you willing to pay first, so that you can see further? Read Genesis 13:14–17 together.
l123.title: Different Seeing, Different Outcomes
l123.subtitle: Focus Decides the Outcome; Vision Decides the Life
l123.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

blog.title: How You See Decides How You Live

blocks.x: Subtitle: One change in how you see, and a completely different life
The Rain Didn’t Change — the Eyes Did

The same heavy rain on the same morning: one person frowns and says, “What a wretched day,” while another takes a deep breath and says, “How clean the air is today.” The rain didn’t change; the window didn’t change. What changed was the pair of eyes.

We often think the outcome of our lives is decided by our circumstances: when the economy is good, things go well for me; when my health is good, I’m joyful; when people treat me well, I’m loving. But the Bible shows us a deeper path —
Seeing determines thinking; thinking determines doing; doing determines the outcome.
How you see determines how you think; how you think determines what you do; what you do determines how your life ends. So the key has never been “how things happen,” but “how you see what happens.”

In 1999 the psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris carried out a famous experiment at Harvard University: participants concentrated on counting the passes in a video, while a person in a gorilla suit walked into the picture, beat its chest and stayed for nearly nine seconds — and about half of them didn’t see it at all. It turns out that seeing is not only a matter of the eyes; it is a matter of attention, a matter of the heart.
Three Who Saw Wrongly, Three Who Saw Rightly

On the roof of the king’s house, David saw a woman bathing, very beautiful to look at. He did not turn his eyes away, and so thought became desire, desire became action, and in the end came adultery, murder and a broken family. One wrong look brought a whole series of destruction.

Peter was walking on the Sea of Galilee, and all was well until, the text says, “when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink” (Matthew 14:30a). Notice: the wind and waves did not arrive at that moment; they had been there all along. What changed was not the circumstances but the focus. He did not sink because his ability fell short; he sank because he saw wrongly.
Lot lifted up his eyes and saw all the plain of the Jordan, well-watered everywhere — but he did not see the wickedness of Sodom, and in the end he lost everything.

But there were also those who saw rightly. Abram let Lot choose first, and only then did God say to him, “For I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever” (Genesis 13:15). Humility comes first; then comes spiritual vision. Elisha followed all the way to the end, and because he “saw,” he received a double anointing. Paul counted the world as refuse and Christ as his treasure, and in the end he received the crown of righteousness.
The Focus Determines the Outcome
In the light of 321 we say: when the focus is on ourselves, we fail; when the focus is on our circumstances, we waver; when the focus is on Jesus, we overcome.
The self-centred look with their own eyes; the selfless let Jesus become their eyes. Selflessness is not that we stop looking, but that we look with a different pair of eyes.

Interestingly, science says the same thing. The visible light the human eye can see is only a tiny slice of the whole electromagnetic spectrum; according to the data published by the Planck satellite in 2013, the ordinary matter we can see makes up only about 5% of the universe. What can be seen has only ever been a tiny part. A life that judges by the naked eye is bound to be narrow.
So how can we begin today?
1. Whenever your emotions surge, ask yourself one question: What am I looking at right now? My circumstances, myself, or God?
2. When anxiety or temptation comes, don’t argue with it; turn your eyes to Jesus at once, and let Scripture replace what your eyes see.
3. Every night before you sleep, use David’s prayer to ask God to search your sight and correct the wrong ways of seeing.

David saw wrongly, and he sinned; Peter saw wrongly, and he sank; Lot saw wrongly, and he lost. Abraham saw rightly, and he received the land; Elisha saw rightly, and he received power; Paul saw rightly, and he received the crown.
Different ways of seeing bring completely different outcomes. You are not defeated by your circumstances; you are defeated by seeing wrongly.

When you choose not to look at the world, not to look at yourself, but to look at Jesus alone, your life will never be the same again; instead it will enter into the victory and glory God has prepared.
Reflection Question
Think of the thing that stirred your emotions most this week. Where was your focus at that moment? If you had turned your eyes to Jesus then, how might the outcome have been different?
