script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 124 of Morning Devotion 321. Our theme is “Listening Rightly (Part 1): Right Listening and Wrong Listening.” Our key verse is Jeremiah 7:23: “Listen to my voice.” May the Lord himself open our ears this morning.

In our last lesson we thought about “seeing rightly.” Today we ask another question: what are you listening to? Brothers and sisters, what sets the direction of a life is not only the eyes but also the ears. How you listen shapes what you believe; what you believe shapes how you live. In 1912 the Titanic received six ice warnings in a single day. The wireless operator snapped back, “Shut up, I am busy.” Forty minutes later the ship hit the iceberg. It wasn’t that there was no warning; it was that no one listened. Many people’s problem is not that they don’t try hard enough; it’s that they are listening to the wrong voice.

Jeremiah was called around 627 BC, and he is known as the weeping prophet. Chapter 7 is the famous Temple Sermon. God told him to stand in the gate of the temple and speak to those coming in to worship. At that time the people offered sacrifices every day; with their mouths they said, “This is Yahweh’s temple,” but in their hearts they did not listen to God. So God said, “This thing I commanded them, saying, ‘Listen to my voice.’” Brothers and sisters, there is only one thing. Not seventy things, not seven things — one thing. The Hebrew word for “listen” is shama, and in itself it carries the sense of paying heed, responding, obeying. To hear without obeying is not to have heard at all.

First let’s look at three people who listened wrongly. Saul listened to the voice of the people and kept the best of the sheep and cattle — outwardly obedient, but rebellious at heart. He said himself, “I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.” Whomever we listen to is whomever we fear. Abram listened to Sarai and used a human method to bring about God’s promise, and it cost him family turmoil and long-running conflict. Rehoboam rejected the counsel of the old men and listened only to the young men who had grown up with him, and the nation was divided. In his 1951 conformity experiment, the psychologist Solomon Asch found that about 75 per cent of people went along at least once with an answer they knew was wrong. Brothers and sisters, none of these three was deaf; none of them asked God first.

So what does right listening look like? Samuel said, “Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” God doesn’t want a great deal of ministry from you; God wants you to listen to his word. Suppose you asked a decorator to paint your master bedroom off-white, and instead he painted the whole house navy blue and was dripping with sweat — would you be moved? It’s not about doing a lot; it’s about doing what is right.

Martha was distracted with much serving. The original word means “pulled off in every direction.” And Mary? She sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word. The Lord said, “One thing is needed.” Brothers and sisters, Martha wasn’t doing the wrong thing; she had it in the wrong order. Listen first, then act; align first, then move. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Right listening bears two fruits. The first is faith: “So faith comes by hearing.” Faith isn’t something you grit your teeth to produce; it’s something you hear your way into. The second is repentance: on the day of Pentecost, when the people heard Peter’s words, they were cut to the heart. The original word means “pierced through.” That day about three thousand were added. So true listening isn’t only the ears hearing; it is the heart being changed.

Some people say, “I want to listen, but I can’t hear.” On Mount Horeb, Elijah met a great wind, an earthquake and a fire, and God was in none of them; after the fire came a still small voice. The original means a thin, silent sound. Of course God can speak in thunder, but far more often he speaks in a still small voice, because a still small voice can be heard only by those who draw near. A father speaking to his baby never uses a loudspeaker. Brothers and sisters, very often the problem isn’t that God hasn’t spoken; it’s that we haven’t been quiet enough to listen. God doesn’t need to raise his volume; we need to lower the noise. Rely on the brain and everything is noise; rely on the heart and you hear.

Why do some people hear and others don’t? 321 gives us the answer: the self-centred listen to themselves and to other people; only the selfless can hear God. The proud already have the answer and don’t need to listen; the humble are willing to wait and willing to obey. Young Samuel said, “Speak; for your servant hears.” Whoever speaks is king.

Today there are three practices. First, check what you listen to every day — is it the voice of the world, or the word of God? Open your phone and look at your screen time, then count the time you spend reading the Bible and praying, and set the two numbers side by side. Second, build the habit of listening first, then acting: seek God before every decision. Saul decided in fear, Sarai decided when she couldn’t wait any longer, Rehoboam decided when he wanted to assert his authority — and all three times they were wrong. Third, set aside time every day to listen quietly to the Lord: pray, meditate, wait. Brothers and sisters, start with just ten minutes — same place, same time, with your phone in another room.

Saul listened wrongly and was rejected; Abraham listened wrongly and suffered; Rehoboam listened wrongly and the kingdom was divided. Mary listened rightly and received the good part; the disciples listened rightly and received life; the church listened rightly and received revival. Different ways of listening bring different outcomes. When you choose not to listen to the world, not to listen to yourself, but to listen to God alone, your life will enter a road that is clear, steady and victorious.

Let’s declare together: Lord, open my ears! Let me no longer listen to the voice of the world, nor to my own voice, but to your word alone! Through your word give me faith, and let me walk in the way that pleases you. Lord, we say: Speak; for your servant hears. May all the glory go to Jesus. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 124 of Morning Devotion 321. Our theme is “Listening Rightly (Part 1): Right Listening and Wrong Listening.” Our key verse is Jeremiah 7:23: “Listen to my voice.” We ask the Lord himself to open our ears this morning.

In our last lesson we thought about “seeing rightly.” The direction our eyes look is very often the direction our feet will walk. Today we take one more step: what are you listening to? Brothers and sisters, what sets the direction of a life is not only the eyes but also the ears. Let me begin with a story. Late on the night of 14 April 1912, the Titanic struck an iceberg. Many people think it was a disaster that came without warning. In fact, over the course of that day the wireless room received at least six ice warnings from nearby ships. That evening the wireless operator was busy sending private telegrams for passengers, and to the final warning he even snapped back: “Shut up, I am busy.” Forty minutes later the ship hit the iceberg. It wasn’t that there was no warning; it was that no one listened.

Brothers and sisters, please keep this order in mind: how you listen shapes what you believe; what you believe shapes how you live. Listening is the source, believing is the middle of the road, living is the outcome. Let the source be off by one degree, and by the end of the road you are a thousand miles astray. The Bible makes this plain from its very first pages. Humanity’s first fall did not begin with seeing; it began with listening. God said to Adam, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake.” The doorway of sin is the ear; and thank God, the doorway of salvation is the ear as well.

Jeremiah was called around 627 BC; his ministry spanned five kings, and he is known as the weeping prophet. Chapter 7 is the famous Temple Sermon. God told him to stand in the gate of the temple and speak to those coming in to worship. At that time the people kept chanting, “Yahweh’s temple, Yahweh’s temple, Yahweh’s temple, are these.” They treated the temple as a lucky charm. But God said, “This thing I commanded them, saying, ‘Listen to my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people.’” Brothers and sisters, look at the order: first we listen, and then there is relationship; once there is relationship, there is true blessing. The Hebrew word for “listen” is shama, which is also the first word of Deuteronomy 6:4, “Hear, Israel.” The word itself contains obedience. In the Hebrew mindset, to hear without obeying is not to have heard at all.

Now let’s look at three people who listened wrongly. The first is Saul. God’s command was crystal clear: strike the Amalekites and utterly destroy all they had. But the text says Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the sheep and cattle, and destroyed everything that was vile and refuse. What they kept was the best; what they killed was the worthless — he treated God’s command as a list of suggestions. When Samuel arrived, Saul said, “I have performed the commandment of Yahweh.” But Samuel asked, “Then what does this bleating of the sheep in my ears, and the lowing of the cattle which I hear mean?” Brothers and sisters, your mouth can dress things up, but your life makes its own sound. God said, “It grieves me that I have set up Saul to be king.” In the end Saul admitted, “I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.” Whomever we listen to is whomever we fear; and whomever we fear becomes our king. In 1951 the psychologist Solomon Asch carried out his famous line conformity experiment and found that about 75 per cent of participants went along at least once with the crowd in giving an answer they knew was wrong. Saul knew perfectly well what God had said; he just didn’t want to be shut out by the people.

The second is Abraham. The text says, “Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.” In the culture of the day Sarai’s suggestion was legal, understandable and reasonable; the problem was that it was a human method used to bring about God’s promise. As a result, when Hagar conceived she despised her mistress, and God said Ishmael would be like a wild donkey among men. Family turmoil and long-running conflict. The third is Rehoboam. The text says, “But he abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him, and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him, who stood before him.” Notice “who had grown up with him” — that was his echo chamber. In 1960 the psychologist Peter Wason put forward what came to be known as “confirmation bias”: the tendency to look for information that supports what we already think. Rehoboam wasn’t asking for advice; he was looking for people to endorse him. And so, around 931 BC, the kingdom split in two and never came back together. Brothers and sisters, none of these three was deaf; none of them asked God first.

So what does right listening look like? What God asks is actually very simple. He says, “This thing I commanded them, saying, ‘Listen to my voice … Walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.’” Listen, and obey. These two are really one. The Greek word for “obey” literally means “to listen from beneath” — placing ourselves beneath the word and listening. God doesn’t want a great deal of ministry from you; God wants you to listen to his word. I often use this illustration: you ask a decorator to paint the master bedroom off-white, but he very diligently paints the living room, the kitchen and the hallway all navy blue, then says to you, “Boss, I got so much done today!” Would you be moved?

That’s why Samuel left us one of the most important principles in the Old Testament: “Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” Notice that Samuel did not say sacrifice was bad; he was talking about order. It’s not about doing a lot; it’s about doing what is right. Isaiah 50:4 says, “He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what morning devotions mean. It isn’t that we wake God up every morning; it is that God wakes up our ears every morning. The Lord Jesus himself said, “As I hear, I judge.” Jesus is my role model — he listened first, then acted.

The third key point takes us to Bethany. The text says Martha was distracted with much serving. The original word means “pulled off in every direction.” Being frazzled isn’t having a lot to do; being frazzled is having your heart torn apart. And Mary? She sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word. That was the place of a disciple. Martha couldn’t hold back her complaint, and the Lord said, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

Brothers and sisters, the Lord did not rebuke Martha for serving. What he pointed out was this: she wasn’t doing the wrong thing; she had it in the wrong order. Listen first, then act; align first, then move. Bonhoeffer wrote in Life Together that the first service we owe our brothers is listening to them. In 1953 the scientist Colin Cherry described the “cocktail party effect”: in a noisy room a person can focus on and clearly hear one speaker. So “hearing” is not the work of the ears alone; it is a choice of attention. In 2012 Dalton and Fraenkel of Royal Holloway, University of London, ran an experiment in which a man walked through a soundtrack for nineteen seconds repeating “I’m a gorilla,” and about seventy per cent of those concentrating on a demanding task never heard him at all. God’s voice may also have walked through your life for nineteen seconds, and because you were frazzled, you didn’t hear a single word. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Right listening bears two fruits. The first is faith. Paul says, “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” Brothers and sisters, faith isn’t something you grit your teeth to produce; it’s something you hear your way into. So when your faith feels weak, the prescription isn’t to believe harder, but to listen more quietly. No one gets strength by frantically telling himself, “I must be strong”; he needs to eat. And the food of faith is the word of God.

The second fruit is repentance. On the day of Pentecost Peter preached, and the text says, “Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart.” The original word means “pierced through.” That day about three thousand were added. The same sermon — the difference was that those who heard received it. So true listening isn’t only the ears hearing; it is the heart being changed. James puts it bluntly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” The Lord Jesus also said that everyone who hears his words and does them is like a wise man who built his house on a rock. The wise man and the foolish man heard the very same sermon; the difference was in “does them.” This is exactly the fivefold change of 321: change the mindset, and the life changes; change the life, and daily living changes.

But some brothers and sisters say, “I want to listen, but I just can’t hear.” Look at Elijah. He had just won a great victory on Mount Carmel, and in the blink of an eye he was being hunted down; he fled to Mount Horeb and asked to die. And there God spoke to him: a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke the rocks, but Yahweh was not in the wind; after the wind an earthquake, but Yahweh was not in the earthquake; after the earthquake a fire, but Yahweh was not in the fire; after the fire, a still small voice. Three earth-shaking spectacles, and God was in none of them. God was in the still small voice. The original means a thin, silent sound.

Of course God can speak in thunder; he did so on Mount Sinai. But far more often he speaks in a still small voice. Why? Because a still small voice can be heard only by those who draw near. A father speaking to his baby never uses a loudspeaker. Engineers have a term, the signal-to-noise ratio: when the background noise is too loud, even the clearest signal is drowned out. God doesn’t need to raise his volume; we need to lower the noise. In 2022 the World Health Organization reported that more than a billion young people worldwide aged twelve to thirty-five are at risk of hearing loss from loud recreational sound; the human cochlea holds about fifteen thousand hair cells, and once damaged they never grow back. As it is in the body, so it is in the spirit. The psalm says, “Be still, and know that I am God.” The original word means “let go.” And the Lord says, “My sheep hear my voice.” Familiarity is the secret of hearing.

Why do some people hear and others don’t? 321 gives us a sharp answer: the key is whether we are self-centred or selfless. The self-centred person listens to his own voice, and to other people’s voices too, because he wants their approval; only the selfless person can hear the voice of God. The proud person already has the answer in his heart; he doesn’t need to listen, and when he asks your opinion he only wants you to agree. The humble person is different: he is willing to wait, willing to obey, because he knows he is not God. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Young Samuel gives us the most beautiful example. That night he said, “Speak; for your servant hears.” Brothers and sisters, notice the shape of that sentence. Not “Listen, for your servant will speak,” but “Speak; for your servant hears.” Whoever speaks is master. Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is entering into the fullness of Jesus. Paul says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” When my voice grows quieter, Christ’s voice grows louder. This is letting Jesus be King and letting the Holy Spirit guide. Only when we hear God can we live out God.

Today there are three practices. First, check what you listen to every day. Open your phone and look at your screen time, then count the time you spend reading the Bible, praying and listening to sermons, and set the two numbers side by side. Second, build the habit of listening first, then acting. Saul decided in fear, Sarai decided when she couldn’t wait any longer, Rehoboam decided when he wanted to assert his authority — and all three times they were wrong. Don’t make major decisions when you are exhausted, angry or impatient. Third, set aside time every day to listen quietly to the Lord: pray, meditate, wait. Start with just ten minutes — same place, same time, with your phone in another room.

321 has eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Please don’t stop at Implementation. Evaluate — how many days did you manage this week? Correct — not by condemning yourself, but by adjusting your method. Repeat — in 2009 Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London found that a new habit takes on average about sixty-six days to become automatic, so don’t give up because you failed on day five. And finally, multiply — find a brother or sister and hold each other accountable. What you share is what truly becomes your own. A gentle reminder: it isn’t that you don’t know what to do; it’s that you haven’t first listened to the right voice.

Let’s set what we have seen today within the picture of 321. All Three Foundations are tied to listening: Jesus is my role model — he said, “As I hear, I judge”; the Bible is my standard — faith comes by hearing; the Holy Spirit is my guide — your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, “This is the way. Walk in it.” The Two Core Values are the purpose of our listening: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal is to establish God’s system — a body moves in harmony because every member listens to the same head. The 920 practice begins with listening too, because the first act of love is listening; James says, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak.

Brothers and sisters, let’s walk today’s road once more. Saul listened wrongly and was rejected; Abraham listened wrongly and suffered; Rehoboam listened wrongly and the kingdom was divided. Mary listened rightly and received the good part; the disciples listened rightly and received life; the church listened rightly and received revival. The same ears, the same voices — different ways of listening bring utterly different outcomes. When you choose not to listen to the world, not to listen to yourself, but to listen to God alone, your life will enter a road that is clear, steady and victorious. Clear, because you no longer rely on guesswork; steady, because your foundation is the word of God; victorious, because a life that lets Jesus be King is, by its very nature, a victorious life. Seven times Revelation says: he who has an ear, let him hear.

Let’s declare together: Lord, open my ears! Let me no longer listen to the voice of the world, nor to my own voice, but to your word alone! Through your word give me faith, and let me walk in the way that pleases you. Dear Lord, take away the noise in our hearts, and let us recognise you in the still small voice. Work the selfless life in us, so that it is no longer we who live, but Christ who lives in us. Lord, we say: Speak; for your servant hears. May all the glory go to Jesus. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: Introduction: What You Hear Is Shaping You
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this early morning. Today let’s think together about something utterly ordinary and yet supremely important — listening.

Let me begin with a true picture. In 1953 Colin Cherry, a scientist at Imperial College London, carried out a famous experiment. He placed participants among a noisy crowd, with voices coming at them from every side, and asked them to concentrate on just one person speaking. What he found was that people have an astonishing ability: even with dozens of voices pouring into their ears at once, they can still lock on to one voice and push all the rest into the background. Researchers later called this phenomenon the “cocktail party effect.”

That experiment tells us something very important: the ear is not a passive radio receiver; the ear is an organ that chooses. Every day you are choosing whose voice to listen to. You think you’re “just half-listening,” but in fact you are selecting who gets to shape you.

We often think “listening” is just receiving information — a sound comes in, you know something, and that’s the end of it. Not so. Brothers and sisters, please keep this sentence in your heart this morning: listening is where a changed life begins.

Why? Because there is an invisible chain: what you listen to decides what you believe; what you believe decides what you become. No one changes first and then starts to listen; every person who has changed first heard, and then began to change.

So Paul says, “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” (Romans 10:17) Faith doesn’t sprout out of thin air; faith grows out of the ear. Wherever your ears lead, that is the shape your life will grow into.

This also explains a puzzling thing we see in the church. Many people have believed in the Lord for ten or twenty years. They can recite verses, sing the hymns, share in small group — and yet their lives have barely moved. The same temper, the same fear, the same bondage. Where is the problem?

The problem isn’t a lack of truth. If there is one thing this age doesn’t lack, it is information about the truth — sermons a tap away, verses a search away, more commentaries than any generation before us. The problem is that there is no “listening rightly.”

The truth goes into the ears but not into the heart; it is heard but not received; it is known but it doesn’t change us. It’s like someone who stands at the dining table every day reading the menu but never eats a mouthful. Of course he’s still hungry.

The Lord Jesus spoke very sternly about this. He said, “Be careful therefore how you hear. For whoever has, to him will be given; and whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he thinks he has.” (Luke 8:18) He didn’t say, “Be careful what you hear”; what he said was, “Be careful how you hear.” The same sermon, the same verse — one person hears it and receives life, another hears it and feels nothing. The difference isn’t in the word; it’s in “how you hear.”

The Lord also said, “Take heed what you hear. With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you, and more will be given to you who hear.” (Mark 4:24) However large the vessel you bring to listen with, that is the size of vessel God will fill for you. Small ears receive small grace; large ears receive large grace.

Brothers and sisters, in this lesson we will learn seven things together: true change begins with hearing God; right listening brings renewal of life; the key strategy of replacing the wrong with the right; right listening brings an expanding blessing; how to discern whom you are listening to; how you listen decides how you live; and finally a 321 insight — only the selfless can hear God.

May the Lord himself tune our ears this morning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Setting and Context of Ephesians 4
sections.html:
Before we come to the key points, let’s get clear on the background of our theme text. When a text has its background, the exposition stands on solid ground.

The author of Ephesians is the apostle Paul. The letter begins: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, to the saints who are at Ephesus, and the faithful in Christ Jesus.” (Ephesians 1:1) When Paul wrote this letter he was in prison; he calls himself “the prisoner in the Lord” (Ephesians 4:1). It is generally thought to come from his first Roman imprisonment, around AD 60–62. The same group of letters includes Philippians, Colossians and Philemon, which church tradition calls the “Prison Epistles.”

Ephesus, the city receiving the letter, was the capital of the Roman province of Asia and a great port on the eastern shore of the Aegean, with a population at the time of perhaps more than two hundred thousand. The city was most famous for the Temple of Artemis, which the ancients counted among the Seven Wonders of the World. Acts 19 records that Paul lived in Ephesus for more than two years, reasoning daily in the school of Tyrannus, “so that all those who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks” (Acts 19:10). Notice the verb — “heard.” The Ephesian church was a church born of listening.

And precisely because of that, the believers in Ephesus lived with an enormous tension. Most of them came from Gentile backgrounds, steeped from childhood in a culture of idol worship, sorcery and sensual indulgence. Acts 19:19 says that many who had practised magic brought their books and burned them, books worth “fifty thousand pieces of silver.” They had come to faith, but the old world still spoke in their ears every day — the hawkers in the marketplace, the music from the temples, the neighbours’ gossip, the memories of the past.

So Paul wrote Ephesians with its first three chapters on “who you are in Christ” — chosen, redeemed, reconciled to God, fellow members of God’s household — and its last three chapters on “how you should walk.” Chapter 4 is the pivot: “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called.” (Ephesians 4:1)

At 4:17, Paul begins to deal head-on with the problem of the “old life”: “This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that you no longer walk as the rest of the Gentiles also walk, in the futility of their mind, being darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of their hearts.” (Ephesians 4:17–18)

Notice Paul’s diagnosis: “darkened in their understanding,” “the hardening of their hearts.” The original uses νοῦς (nous), which means mind, understanding, mindset. The Gentiles’ problem was not outward behaviour but inward mindset; it wasn’t their hands that were sick, it was their thinking.

Then comes our theme text: “But you didn’t learn Christ that way, if indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man … and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man.” (Ephesians 4:20–24)

There are three actions here, each wonderfully vivid in the Greek. “Heard” is ἀκούω (akouō), simply hearing; “were taught” carries the sense of being personally instructed, of becoming a disciple; and “learned” Christ means being taught, being shaped. Paul is saying: true listening has layers — from hearing, to receiving, to being taught until you take shape.

The pair of verbs “put away” (ἀποτίθημι, apotithēmi) and “put on” (ἐνδύω, endyō) were originally everyday words for taking off and putting on clothes. Paul uses the most down-to-earth picture to teach the deepest truth: the old self is like a garment worn for decades and caked with filth; the new self is like a white robe. You don’t give the old clothes a wash and keep wearing them; you take them off, throw them away, and put on the new.

The sentence in the middle is the key: “be renewed in the spirit of your mind.” That is a literal rendering of the original — the renewal takes place not in behaviour but in the mind, in the mindset. This is exactly the starting point of the fivefold change the 321 vision speaks of: only when the mindset changes does the life change; only when the life changes does daily living change.

And where does mindset come from? From the ears. That is why Paul puts “hearing” first. Brothers and sisters, this is the logic of the whole passage: hearing → mindset → putting off the old self → putting on the new self → living out Christ.

sections.heading: 1. True Change Begins with Hearing God
sections.html:
“He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’” (Acts 9:4)

Let me begin with a man. Saul — later Paul.

Before he met the Lord, he was the most promising young man in the Judaism of his day. He says himself, “I advanced in the Jews’ religion beyond many of my own age among my countrymen, being more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers.” (Galatians 1:14) He was taught at the feet of Gamaliel, a Pharisee of the Pharisees. His zeal went so far that he personally hauled Christians off to prison and personally stood at the scene of Stephen’s martyrdom.

Acts 9:1 says he was “still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord.” He wasn’t a cold-blooded killer; he was a man full of religious passion, heading completely the wrong way. He thought he was burning with zeal for God.

Then, on the road to Damascus, everything was turned upside down.

“As he traveled, he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him. He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’ He said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ The Lord said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.’” (Acts 9:3–5)

Brothers and sisters, notice what the key to Saul’s turnaround was.

It wasn’t that his circumstances changed. He was still on the same road, still carrying the high priest’s letters, still the same man with the same standing.

It wasn’t that he gained more doctrine. Saul knew the Old Testament better than anyone else there. His problem was never a lack of knowledge.

It wasn’t that he met with setbacks. He was at the very height of his success; he wasn’t a failure, he was a winner.

The key was this — he heard the voice of the Lord.

One act of “hearing” changed a whole life. From persecuting Christ to following Christ; from opposing God to suffering for God. The Lord later said to Ananias, “For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.” (Acts 9:16) The man who once made others suffer for the Lord would from then on suffer for the Lord himself.

And this “hearing” has one very tender detail. In Acts 26:14, Paul himself adds, “I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language.” The Lord didn’t use Greek, didn’t use the official tongue; the Lord called him by name in his mother’s language, the language of his childhood. And he called him twice: “Saul, Saul!”

In the Bible, when God calls a name twice, it is often the most intimate and most urgent of calls. “Abraham, Abraham!” (Genesis 22:11) “Moses! Moses!” (Exodus 3:4) “Samuel! Samuel!” (1 Samuel 3:10) “Martha, Martha” (Luke 10:41). When God calls a person, he never calls out a number; he calls a name.

Science gives us a beautiful picture too. In 1980 the American researchers Anthony DeCasper and William Fifer published a study in the journal Science showing that newborns only a few days old can already recognise, and prefer, their own mother’s voice. Before a person can speak, before he can see clearly, he already knows the voice that loves him most. Brothers and sisters, this is the mark the Creator has placed within us: we are born to recognise the voice of the One who loves us.

The Lord Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27)

So if this morning you feel you are “hard to change,” let me say a word of comfort to you: what you need may not be more effort, but one true hearing of God.

The 321 vision says that the first of the Three Foundations is “Jesus is my role model,” and the third is “the Holy Spirit is my guide.” Where does guidance begin? With hearing. The Holy Spirit cannot guide a person who won’t listen; but for a person who is willing to listen, one word from God can turn his whole life around. The moment Saul fell to the ground was the moment Paul was established in heaven — because at last he was no longer the one doing the talking; instead he asked, “Who are you, Lord?”

sections.heading: 2. Right Listening Brings Renewal of Life
sections.html:
“If indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:21–24)

Brothers and sisters, Paul speaks of “listening” here with great precision.

He doesn’t say, “It’s enough that you’ve heard of it.” In the Chinese Union Version his words unfold as three progressive verbs: heard, received, learned. (The Greek of this verse has “heard” and “were taught”; “learned” comes in the verse before: “But you didn’t learn Christ that way.”)

The first layer is “heard” — the sound has entered the ears.

The second layer is “received” — the truth has entered the heart and become mine.

The third layer is “learned” — the life is shaped and grows into the likeness of the truth.

Many people get stuck at the first layer. Hearing is information; receiving is revelation; being shaped is life. In what the 321 vision calls the eight stages of changing our mindset, the first stage is precisely “Information,” the second is “Revelation,” and only the third is “Conviction.” Information stays in the head; revelation enters the heart; conviction grows into life.

So what does true listening bring? Paul makes it very clear: it brings three processes.

First, putting off the old self. “That you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit.” (Ephesians 4:22) Notice the words “grows corrupt.” The old self didn’t go bad in a day; it was deceived by desire day after day, eaten away bit by bit. Like clothes left in a cupboard — you don’t touch them, and they go mouldy all by themselves. So putting off the old self isn’t waiting until it has rotted through before dealing with it; it’s taking it off today.

Second, the renewal of the mind. “And that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind.” (Ephesians 4:23) The emphasis of the original is on νοῦς — mind, mindset. This is the most crucial sentence of the whole passage. Behaviour is the fruit; mindset is the root. If you change your behaviour without changing your mindset, that’s called suppression, and it won’t hold for long. Paul says the same thing in Romans 12:2: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.”

Third, putting on the new self. “And put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:24) The new self is not an improved version of the old self; it is created anew in the likeness of God. We take off in order to put on; we are emptied in order to be filled.

Psychology gives us a very apt confirmation here. In 1949 the Canadian neuropsychologist Donald Hebb proposed a principle later known as “Hebb’s rule”: neurons that fire together wire together. That is, the more often you repeat a particular thought or reaction, the thicker, faster and more automatic that neural pathway in the brain becomes. That’s why a habitual complainer hardly needs to think before complaining — that road has already been worn into a motorway.

But the same principle brings enormous hope: neural pathways can be laid down anew. This is called “neuroplasticity.” If you keep walking a new road, the new road will widen too. When God made us, he built “the capacity to be renewed” right into our design.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? Even your brain bears witness to being “renewed in the spirit of your mind.”

This is the very route of the fivefold change in the 321 vision: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. And the renewal of the mindset begins with “listening rightly.”

James says, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) “Deluding your own selves” — the greatest victim of a person who only hears and never does is himself, because he thinks he already has it.

So remember this sentence: listen rightly, and your life will change.

sections.heading: 3. The Key Strategy: Replace the Wrong with the Right
sections.html:
“Putting off the old self” sounds easy. Why is it so hard to do?

Because many people use the wrong method. Their method is — suppression. Grit your teeth so you won’t lose your temper; clench your fists so you won’t look at that website; tell yourself desperately, “Don’t think about it, don’t think about it.” And the result? The more you suppress it, the more you think about it; the more you think about it, the wearier you get; and in the end everything collapses.

Brothers and sisters, here is a vitally important strategy: putting off the old self is not straining to suppress; it is replacing the old with the new.

The Bible never just tells us “don’t.” In the Bible, “don’t” is always followed straight away by “but.”

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” (Romans 12:2)

“Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit.” (Ephesians 5:18)

“Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.” (Ephesians 4:29)

Do you see it? Every time, it is “don’t … but …” God’s method isn’t to create a vacuum; God’s method is replacement.

The Lord Jesus told a very sobering parable. An unclean spirit goes out of a man and wanders through waterless places, then says it will return to where it came from; “when he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order,” and so it brings along seven other spirits more evil than itself, and “the last state of that man becomes worse than the first” (Matthew 12:43–45). A house swept clean but left empty is more dangerous than one never swept at all. After being emptied, we must be filled.

So our practice is replacement on five levels:

Wrong seeing becomes right seeing.

Wrong listening becomes right listening.

Wrong thinking becomes right thinking.

Wrong speaking becomes right speaking.

Wrong doing becomes right doing.

These five levels form a chain. What you see affects what you listen to; what you listen to affects what you think; what you think decides what you say; what you say brings out what you do. If you only try to change the last link — behaviour — without touching the four before it, it’s labour in vain. Solomon says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

There is a widely told Native American fable about two dogs fighting inside a person’s heart, a white dog and a black dog. Someone asks: which one will win? The answer: the one you feed.

That picture fits here perfectly. The white dog is the spiritual life; the black dog is the self-centred life. What we must do is this — nourish the white dog, and starve the black dog.

Notice: not “beat the black dog to death.” You can’t kill it; the more you beat it, the fiercer it gets. What you must do is stop feeding it. What does it eat? Negative information, complaining conversations, accusing words, indulgent images. Cut off the supply, and day by day it grows thin.

And what does the white dog eat? The word of God, praise, thanksgiving, fellowship with spiritual companions. Keep up the supply, and day by day it grows strong.

Paul puts it even more positively: “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8) Paul doesn’t say, “Don’t think bad things”; Paul gives you eight good things to think about. When your mind is full of good things, there is no room left for the bad.

This is the practical outworking of what the 321 vision calls “selflessness.” Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is giving up the place the self-centred life has occupied and letting Christ fill it. Paul says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Not becoming empty, but changing masters.

Brothers and sisters, whatever you feed is what you will live out.

sections.heading: 4. Right Listening Brings an Expanding Blessing
sections.html:
“All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring, because you have obeyed my voice.” (Genesis 22:18)

This verse is the most glorious promise in the Bible attached to “listening.”

The setting is Mount Moriah. God said to Abraham, “Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.” (Genesis 22:2)

This is the heaviest command in human history. Isaac was the son of promise, the son awaited for twenty-five years, the very one of whom God himself had said, “For your offspring will be named through Isaac” (Genesis 21:12). It was as though God were tearing down his own promise.

How did Abraham respond? The Bible says, “Abraham rose early in the morning.” (Genesis 22:3) No arguing, no delaying, no bargaining. He heard, and he obeyed.

Three days’ journey. Three days is long enough for a man to change his mind a hundred times. Yet step by step he climbed. On the mountain, with the knife already raised, the angel of Yahweh called to him from heaven: “Abraham, Abraham!” (Genesis 22:11) — once again, a name called twice. Then God said, “Don’t lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him. For now I know that you fear God.” (Genesis 22:12)

And then comes that astonishing blessing: “All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring, because you have obeyed my voice.” (Genesis 22:18)

Brothers and sisters, notice the “because” clause: “because you have obeyed my voice.” The Hebrew literally reads, “because you listened to my voice.” The Hebrew word for “listen” is שָׁמַע (shama), which carries both senses at once — “to hear” and “to obey.” In the Hebrew mindset, to hear without obeying is not to have listened at all. That is why the confession of faith Israel recites every day begins with this very word: “Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.” (Deuteronomy 6:4)

That is why Samuel said to King Saul, “To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” (1 Samuel 15:22) King Saul kept back the sheep and cattle for sacrifice; it looked very spiritual, but it was really not listening. What God wants is not your offering; what God wants is your ear.

And how great is the result of one person obeying God? As great as “all the nations of the earth.”

When Abraham raised the knife on Mount Moriah, he did not know he was foreshadowing what would happen on another mountain two thousand years later — “For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son” (John 3:16). Nor did he know that Paul would one day say, “Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring … which is Christ.” (Galatians 3:16)

One man’s obedience became the blessing of the nations.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the 321 vision calls “Multiplication.” The last of the eight stages of changing our mindset is not “Repetition”; it is “Multiplication.” If your change truly comes from God, it will surely flow outward. When one person truly hears God, his home will be different, his small group will be different, his workplace will be different.

This is also the spirit of the 920 practice: every person connected to us is our “2.” When we live out the “0” of selflessness, the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23) — will grow in those relationships. And so the blessing spreads outward, ring after ring.

So right listening affects not only you but the people around you. The day you obey may be the day your children’s blessing begins.

sections.heading: 5. Discerning the Voices: Whom Are You Listening To?
sections.html:
“The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out.” (John 10:3)

There is deep meaning in the Lord Jesus comparing us to sheep. Sheep have poor eyesight, can’t run fast and have no claws or fangs; their only way to survive is to recognise the shepherd’s voice.

The Lord goes on: “They will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him; for they don’t know the voice of strangers.” (John 10:5)

Brothers and sisters, here is a fact we must admit: every one of us is listening to some voice at every moment. Nobody lives in a vacuum.

Broadly speaking, there are four voices in our ears:

The voice of God.

The voice of Satan.

Our own voice.

The voice of the world.

The question isn’t whether there are voices — the voices are always there; the question is which one you listen to.

So how do we tell them apart? The most practical way is to look at the results. A tree is known by its fruit, and so is a voice. The Lord said, “By their fruits you will know them.” (Matthew 7:16)

Listening to Satan’s voice produces four kinds of fruit: discouragement, condemnation, anger and despair.

One of Satan’s names is “the accuser.” Revelation 12:10 says, “The accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them before our God day and night.” His voice has one hallmark: it presses you down — down until you can’t lift your head, down until you feel you are beyond help, down until you don’t want to pray and don’t dare come before God. His aim is to “steal, kill, and destroy” (John 10:10).

Listening to God’s voice produces four kinds of fruit: humility, repentance, peace and change.

God will also point out our sin, but his correction brings hope, not despair. Paul draws the line very clearly: “For godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world produces death.” (2 Corinthians 7:10)

It’s the same words — “You are wrong.” When God says them, you want to run towards him; when the enemy says them, you want to hide from him. After Adam sinned he hid among the trees — that was the enemy’s voice in his ears. After David sinned he wrote Psalm 51 — that was God’s voice in his heart.

James gives us another measuring rule: “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.” (James 3:17)

There is one more principle of discernment: God’s voice will never contradict God’s word. The Bible is our standard. Any voice, however pleasant, however moving, however much it fits your wishes, is not from God if it goes against Scripture. The second of the Three Foundations is “the Bible is my standard.”

We also need to watch out for our own voice and the voice of the world. These two are often the hardest to discern, because they say exactly what we want to hear. Paul warned Timothy: “For the time will come when they will not listen to the sound doctrine, but having itching ears, will heap up for themselves teachers after their own lusts.” (2 Timothy 4:3) “Itching ears” — what a vivid phrase. People with itching ears aren’t looking for truth; they are looking for agreement.

And God’s voice is often quiet. On Mount Horeb, the great wind, the earthquake and the fire all passed Elijah by, and then? “After the fire, there was a still small voice.” (1 Kings 19:12) God doesn’t need to shout, because he isn’t competing with anyone. He waits for you to grow still.

“Be still, and know that I am God.” (Psalm 46:10)

Brothers and sisters, different voices bring utterly different results. This morning, whom are you listening to?

sections.heading: 6. How You Listen Decides How You Live
sections.html:
This is the most practical point of the whole lesson.

We have talked about “whom we listen to”; now we need to talk about “how we listen.” Because the very same sentence can be heard as two completely different voices.

Take the most common example: criticism from others.

Someone says to you, “You didn’t handle this very thoroughly.”

Listen with worldly ears, and what you hear is: he looks down on me, he’s got it in for me, he’s embarrassing me in front of everyone. The result: hurt, anger, defensiveness, a broken relationship.

Listen with spiritual ears, and what you hear is: perhaps God is using this person to show me something I can’t see. The result: growth, change, and a relationship that actually goes deeper.

One sentence, two kinds of ears, two kinds of life.

So the Bible says, “The ear that listens to reproof lives, and will be at home among the wise.” (Proverbs 15:31) And again, “Don’t reprove a scoffer, lest he hate you. Reprove a wise person, and he will love you.” (Proverbs 9:8) The difference between the wise and the scoffer isn’t who gets rebuked but how each one listens to rebuke.

David takes this to its very limit: “Let the righteous strike me, it is kindness; let him reprove me, it is like oil on the head; don’t let my head refuse it.” (Psalm 141:5) “Don’t let my head refuse it” — what humble ears those are.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: very often the problem isn’t the sentence itself but how you hear it.

Next I want to speak about a more hidden danger: “replaying.”

Wrong listening keeps replaying negative voices.

Have you ever had this experience? Someone says something unkind; the person who said it has long since forgotten it, but you have been playing it in your heart for three months. Lying in bed at night, that sentence starts up again by itself; you go over the scene again and again, and get hurt all over again each time. The person who said it hurt you once; you have hurt yourself a hundred times.

Aaron T. Beck of the University of Pennsylvania, the founder of cognitive therapy, put forward the idea of “automatic negative thoughts” in the 1960s. He observed that in people who are depressed, negative verdicts keep popping up automatically in their minds; these thoughts come uninvited and loop over and over, and in time they are taken as fact. His treatment was not to tell people “don’t think about it,” but to help them identify these thoughts and then replace them with thoughts that match reality.

Brothers and sisters, God’s method came earlier, goes deeper, and has more power.

Right listening means meditating on God’s word again and again.

“His delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.” (Psalm 1:2)

“This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.” (Joshua 1:8)

The Hebrew word for “meditate” is הָגָה (hagah), which originally carries the sense of murmuring under one’s breath and chewing over again and again. Some compare it to a cow chewing the cud — swallowing, bringing it back up and chewing slowly, again and again, until it is fully digested into its own flesh and blood.

Your heart is a player, and it will always be playing some recording. The only question is: which tape will you put in?

Paul gives us a very powerful picture: “throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.” (2 Corinthians 10:5) “Bringing into captivity” — that is the language of war. Your thought life is a battlefield; either it is occupied by the enemy, or it is taken captive for Christ.

So whatever you meditate on again and again, that is what you are shaped into.

This is what the 321 vision calls a shift of perspective: from the human perspective to God’s perspective; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly. Paul says, “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2) And again, “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

Listen from a new perspective, and you will live a new way.

sections.heading: 7. A 321 Insight: Only the Selfless Can Hear God
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, having come this far, we must ask the most fundamental question: why is it that some people simply can’t hear God?

The answer lies at the heart of the 321 vision: because of the self-centred life.

The self-centred person hears only what he wants to hear.

It isn’t that he has no ears; it’s that he has a sieve. Whatever suits him, he takes in; whatever doesn’t, he automatically filters out. When he listens to a sermon, he isn’t asking, “Lord, what do you want to say to me?” He is assessing, “Was that a good preacher or not?” When he reads the Bible, he isn’t looking for God’s heart; he’s looking for verses to back up his own position.

The self-centred person resists the voice of God.

Because God’s voice so often asks us to let go — let go of our rights, let go of our face, let go of our plans, let go of whatever we are clutching so tightly. And the instinct of the self-centred life is to hold on.

The 321 vision puts it very penetratingly: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Go back to Eden, and you will find that humanity’s first fall was precisely a case of “listening wrongly.” The serpent said, “For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) Eve listened. Afterwards God said to Adam, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you …” (Genesis 3:17) Notice the words: “Because you have listened …” Humanity’s catastrophe began with listening to the wrong voice.

And humanity’s salvation also began with one Man’s perfect listening. The Lord Jesus said, “I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me.” (John 5:30)

“As I hear, I judge” — this is selflessness at its height. The life of the Son of God on earth was a life of perfect hearing and perfect obedience. “Though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.” (Hebrews 5:8) “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:8)

Paul sets these two side by side with perfect clarity: “For as through the one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous.” (Romans 5:19)

One man would not listen, and all humanity fell; one Man listened, and all humanity was offered salvation.

So what does a selfless person look like?

The selfless person is willing to hear the truth — even when the truth stings.

The selfless person is willing to be adjusted — even when the adjustment is humiliating.

The selfless person hears God, obeys God and lives out God.

The Lord Jesus said, “He who is of God hears the words of God. For this cause you don’t hear, because you are not of God.” (John 8:47) Being able to hear God’s words is itself a sign.

Brothers and sisters, this is where the Two Core Values of the 321 vision come in:

Only selflessness can let Jesus be King. Because as long as “I” am still on the throne, Jesus can only stand at the side as an adviser. You can ignore an adviser; you cannot ignore a King.

Only selflessness can be led by the Holy Spirit. Because the Holy Spirit guides; he does not coerce. He speaks in a “still small voice,” and a noisy self cannot hear a still small voice.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

And selflessness is not having nothing. Selflessness is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) When you turn your own voice down, you hear the voice of the One who created the universe. That isn’t loss; that is the greatest gain of all.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s set what we have learned today within the framework of the 321 vision and look at it once more.

The Three Foundations are, in fact, three kinds of right listening.

Jesus is my role model — he said, “As I hear, I judge” (John 5:30). If we want to learn how he lived, we first learn how he listened.

The Bible is my standard — “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). Every voice must be brought before Scripture to be tested.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — “and when you turn to the right hand, and when you turn to the left, your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it.’” (Isaiah 30:21) The Spirit’s guidance is something received with the ears.

The Two Core Values decide how we listen.

Let Jesus be King — the King’s word is a command, not a suggestion. To hear and then go and do it: that is what it means for him to be King.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — we don’t listen to sermons to add to our knowledge or to our stock of conversation, but so that his name may be lifted high.

The Goal — establish God’s system. One person who listens to God will influence a household; one household that listens to God will influence a small group; and a community that listens to God is what God’s system looks like on earth.

The fivefold change can be seen especially clearly in this lesson.

A change of mindset: from “listening is receiving information” to “listening is where a changed life begins.”

A change of life: putting off the old self, being renewed in mind, putting on the new self.

A change of daily living: stop replaying negative voices, and start meditating on God’s word day and night.

A change of relationships: hear criticism with spiritual ears and rebuke with humble ears, and relationships move from breakdown towards repair.

A change of ministry: “All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring” (Genesis 22:18) — one person’s obedience becomes the blessing of the nations.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people’s service bears no fruit because they have skipped the first two steps. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Nor can the priority of relationships be jumbled: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. The order of listening is the same — first listen to what God says, then honestly listen to the voice in your own heart, then patiently listen to others, and only last deal with the task. Get the order right, and things will go right.

The 920 practice: every person connected to us is our “2.” When we live out the “0” — the selfless life — the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow in those relationships. Notice that not one of the nine graces is “eloquence,” yet several of them have to do with how we listen: patience, kindness, gentleness, self-control. A person who knows how to listen is bound to be a person who bears fruit.

235 relationships: with selfless people we become each other’s “2,” spiritual companions who remind each other, “Did I just hear that wrongly?”; we build “3,” spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing right listening down the generations; and we become “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, standing together on the truth.

Finally, the shift of perspective: from the human to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly.

Brothers and sisters, when all is said and done, to change your ears is to change your perspective, and to change your perspective is to change your life.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html: The lesson gives us three practices. We will use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to work them through, solidly and thoroughly.

sections.heading: 1. Build the Habit of “Right Input”: Listen to God’s Word Every Day (Scripture Reading, Sermons, Hymns).
sections.html:
Information: First, face a fact — on average, how much time do you spend each day listening to God’s word, and how much listening to other voices? Write it down honestly.

Revelation: Ask God to show you that the present state of your life is the result of what you have taken in over the past. This isn’t condemnation; it is light.

Conviction: Resolve to believe that Romans 10:17 is true — faith really does come by hearing.

Implementation: Make a plan that is concrete, small and doable. For example, every morning read a passage of Scripture, read it once aloud, and then be still for three minutes. 321 Morning Devotion itself is the best training ground.

Evaluation: After a week, look back. On which days did you manage it? On which days did you break off? Why?

Correction: Don’t make the penalties stiffer; make the threshold lower. If you can’t manage twenty minutes, start with five. The German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus’s research on the forgetting curve in 1885 showed that memory fades fastest at the beginning, but that if you review it again before it is forgotten, it can be kept for a long time. Little and regular beats a lot and broken off.

Repetition: Let it become as much a part of everyday life as brushing your teeth, so that you don’t have to decide afresh every day.

Multiplication: Bring someone along to do morning devotions with you. When you teach others, you yourself hear most clearly.

sections.heading: 2. Stop Feeding the Wrong Voices: Cut Down on Negative Information, Complaining and Accusation.
sections.html:
Information: Make a list of your “voices” — the channels you regularly watch, the social media you regularly scroll, the chat groups you regularly talk in.

Revelation: Ask God to point out which of them is feeding the black dog.

Conviction: Believe that “whatever you feed is what you live out” is not a slogan but a spiritual law.

Implementation: This week, cut off one of them first. Just one. At the same time, add a positive replacement — leave a complaining group and join a group that prays for one another. Remember: emptying must go hand in hand with filling.

Evaluation: After three days, have your emotions changed? Has your sleep changed?

Correction: If you can’t cut it off, find a spiritual companion to walk with you; don’t fight alone.

Repetition: Keep it up for four weeks, until the new pathway becomes the main pathway.

Multiplication: Share your experience so that others can be set free too.

sections.heading: 3. Practise “Listening with the Heart”: Not Just Having Heard, but Receiving, Meditating and Doing.
sections.html:
Information: Learn a simple method — after hearing a sermon or reading a passage of Scripture, write down three sentences: What did God say? What does God want me to change? What one thing will I do this week?

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into revelation. Without the Holy Spirit, Scripture is only words on a page; with the Holy Spirit, the words become living water.

Conviction: You must believe that God still speaks today, and that he wants to speak to you.

Implementation: This week choose one verse, say it aloud three times every day, and meditate on it whenever you can.

Evaluation: At the weekend ask yourself: did this verse help me in some specific situation?

Correction: If not, perhaps the verse you chose was too abstract; switch to one closer to where you are right now.

Repetition: Build up verse by verse. Fifty-two verses a year means that in ten years more than five hundred verses will be written on the tablet of your heart.

Multiplication: Share in your small group how this verse has changed you.

The 321 vision reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you rejoice, rely on the brain and you worry. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). Listening with the brain means analysing, comparing, judging; listening with the heart means receiving, surrendering, responding.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, please take this sentence home with you:

It isn’t that you can’t change; it’s that you haven’t kept on “listening rightly.”

It isn’t that you are weaker than others, or that your personality is especially stubborn, or that your circumstances are especially hard. It is a problem of input.

Change the input, and you change the output; change the input for long enough, and you change a lifetime.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Let’s walk today’s road once more.

Saul heard the Lord, and his life was turned around. The man who persecuted Christ became a man who suffered for Christ.

Abraham obeyed God, and the nations were blessed. One man’s obedience on a mountain became a blessing to the whole earth.

The sheep listen to the shepherd’s voice, and they have life. “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)

Three figures, three situations, one principle:

What you listen to is what you become.

So when you begin to listen to God’s word constantly — not now and then, but every day;

when you begin to listen to God’s word with the heart — not analysing it with the brain, but receiving it with the heart;

when you begin to obey God’s word — not hearing and leaving it there, but hearing and then doing;

your life will not merely change; it will enter into a life that is abundant, victorious and like Christ.

This morning the Lord Jesus still stands outside the door and knocks. “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him, and will dine with him, and he with me.” (Revelation 3:20) He doesn’t break the door down; he only knocks. He is waiting for someone who can hear, and who is willing to open the door.

And he is still speaking to the churches: “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies.” (Revelation 2:7)

Brothers and sisters, may each of us answer as the boy Samuel did: “Speak; for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:10)

May we be, every morning, like the one who is taught: “He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” (Isaiah 50:4)

Let us offer up our ears and let Jesus be King; let us offer up our changed lives and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Romans 10:17 (WEB):
“So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.”

Stop feeding the wrong voices — this week cut off one negative source, and add a positive replacement in its place.
Practise listening with the heart — afterwards write down three sentences: What did God say?
prayer: Lord, tune my ears.

Let me no longer listen to the wrong voices, nor let negative words linger in my heart. Lord, I confess that the reason my life has not yet changed is not that you have not spoken, but that I have not listened rightly.

Help me listen to your word alone. Cleanse my ears, and remove from me the self-centred life that hears only what it wants to hear. Make me humble, willing to be adjusted; make me selfless, able to be led by the Holy Spirit.

Lord, let your truth change my life. Teach me to put off the old self, to be renewed in my mind, and to put on the new self. Teach me to nourish the white dog and starve the black dog; teach me to replace everything wrong with right seeing, right listening, right thinking, right speaking and right doing.
May I, like Saul, turn to you as soon as I hear you; like Abraham, obey you as soon as I hear; like the sheep, recognise the voice of the Shepherd.
May my obedience become a blessing to my family, and a blessing to the people around me.

blog.title: It’s Not That You Can’t Change — You Haven’t Been Listening Rightly

blocks.x: Listen Rightly, and Life Changes
The Ear Is an Organ That Chooses

In 1953 Colin Cherry, a scientist at Imperial College London, carried out an experiment. He placed people among a noisy crowd, with voices coming at them from every side, and asked them to concentrate on just one person speaking. And people really could lock on to one voice and push all the rest into the background. Researchers call this the “cocktail party effect.”

The ear is not a passive radio receiver; it is an organ that chooses. You think you’re “just half-listening,” but in fact you are selecting — selecting who gets to shape you. Because there is an invisible chain: what you listen to decides what you believe; what you believe decides what you become.
Paul puts it plainly: “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). Faith doesn’t sprout out of thin air; faith grows out of the ear.
Why Believe in the Lord and Yet Not Change?

There is a puzzling thing we see in the church: many people have believed in the Lord for twenty years, can recite verses and sing the hymns, and yet their lives have barely moved. The problem isn’t a lack of truth — if there is one thing this age doesn’t lack, it is information about the truth. The problem is that there is no “listening rightly.”

The Lord Jesus said, “Be careful therefore how you hear” (Luke 8:18). He didn’t say, “Be careful what you hear”; he said, “Be careful how you hear.” The same verse — one person hears it and receives life, another hears it and feels nothing.

In Ephesians 4 Paul speaks of three progressive steps: heard, received, learned. Hearing is the sound entering the ears; receiving is the truth entering the heart; learning is the life being shaped. Many people get stuck at the first layer, like someone who reads the menu every day but never eats a mouthful — of course he’s still hungry.
True listening brings three processes: putting off the old self, being renewed in mind, and putting on the new self.
Nourish the White Dog, Starve the Black Dog

So how do we put off the old self? Many people’s method is suppression: grit your teeth and tell yourself desperately, “Don’t think about it.” And the result? The more you suppress it, the more you think about it, until in the end everything collapses.

The Bible’s method isn’t suppression; it is replacement. The Bible never just says “don’t”; “don’t” is always followed straight away by “but” — “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2). So we practise replacement on five levels: wrong seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing all become right seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing.

There is a widely told Native American fable: two dogs are fighting inside a person’s heart, a white dog and a black dog. Which one will win? The one you feed. The white dog is the spiritual life; the black dog is the self-centred life. So — nourish the white dog, and starve the black dog.

Notice: not “beat the black dog to death.” You can’t kill it; the more you beat it, the fiercer it gets. What you must do is stop feeding it. It eats negative information, complaining and accusation; cut off the supply, and day by day it grows thin.

In the 1960s Aaron T. Beck of the University of Pennsylvania described “automatic negative thoughts”: negative verdicts that come uninvited, loop over and over, and in time are taken as fact. His treatment was not to tell people not to think, but to replace those thoughts with ones that match reality. God’s method came earlier and has more power: “but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2).
Your heart is a player, and it will always be playing some recording. The only question is: which tape will you put in?
Only the Selfless Can Hear God

Why is it that some people simply can’t hear God? Because of the self-centred life. The self-centred person hears only what he wants to hear — it isn’t that he has no ears; it’s that he has a sieve. The selfless person is different: willing to hear the truth even when it stings, willing to be adjusted even when the adjustment is humiliating.
Only selflessness can let Jesus be King. As long as “I” am still on the throne, Jesus can only stand at the side as an adviser — and you can ignore an adviser, but you cannot ignore a King.

Saul heard the Lord, and his life was turned around; Abraham obeyed God, and the nations were blessed; the sheep listen to the shepherd’s voice, and they have life. What you listen to is what you become.
Starting This Morning
Three small practices:
First, build the habit of right input — read Scripture, hear sermons and sing hymns every day; just start with five minutes.
Second, stop feeding the wrong voices — this week cut off one negative source, and add a positive replacement in its place.
Third, practise listening with the heart — afterwards write down three sentences: What did God say? What does God want me to change? What one thing will I do this week?
It isn’t that you can’t change; it’s that you haven’t kept on “listening rightly.”
Reflection Question

This week, which kind of voice have you spent the most time listening to? What fruit has that voice produced in you — discouragement, condemnation, anger and despair, or humility, repentance, peace and change?
