Key points:
Illustration: Colin Cherry’s 1953 “cocktail party effect” experiment at Imperial College London — the ear is not a passive radio receiver but an organ that chooses.
Point out a common phenomenon: many have believed for years without changing — not for lack of truth, but for lack of right listening.
Quote Luke 8:18: “Be careful therefore how you hear.” The Lord speaks of “how” we hear, not “what” we hear.
Illustration: someone who reads the menu every day but never eats a mouthful is still hungry.

brief12.title: Key Text and Background
notes: Slide text:
“If indeed you heard him,
and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus”
(Ephesians 4:21)
A prison letter from Paul to the church in Ephesus
Key points:
Author: Paul, during his first Roman imprisonment (generally dated AD 60–62); one of the Prison Epistles with Philippians, Colossians and Philemon.
Ephesus: capital of the province of Asia, a great Aegean port, home to the Temple of Artemis; Acts 19:10 says all in Asia “heard the word of the Lord” — a church born of listening.
The preceding verses, 4:17–18, describe the Gentiles as “darkened in their understanding”; nous means mind, mindset — the problem is mindset, not behaviour.
“Put away” and “put on” were everyday words for taking off and putting on clothes; the key in the middle is “be renewed in the spirit of your mind”.

brief12.title: True Change Begins with Hearing God
notes: Slide text:
“Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
(Acts 9:4)
Not new circumstances — he heard the Lord
One hearing changed a whole life
Key points:
Saul’s background: Galatians 1:14 says he advanced in Judaism beyond many of his own age; he was taught at the feet of Gamaliel.
The key to his turnaround was not new circumstances, more knowledge or setbacks, but hearing the voice of the Lord.
Detail: Acts 26:14 says the Lord spoke to him “in the Hebrew language” and called his name twice — as with Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Martha.
Scientific support: Anthony DeCasper and William Fifer’s 1980 study in Science showed that newborns can recognise and prefer their mother’s voice.
Conclusion: what you need may not be more effort, but one true hearing of God.

brief12.title: Right Listening Renews Life
notes: Slide text:
Heard, received, learned
Put off the old self
Be renewed in mind
Put on the new self
Key points:
Read the full text of Ephesians 4:22–24.

Three steps: hearing is information, receiving is revelation, learning is the life being shaped — matching the first three of the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction.
“Grows corrupt” shows the old self didn’t go bad in a day; in “be renewed in the spirit of your mind” the emphasis is on nous (mind, mindset).
Psychological support: in 1949 the Canadian neuropsychologist Donald Hebb proposed that “neurons that fire together wire together” — repetition shapes pathways, and pathways can be laid down anew.
321 application: the fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

brief12.title: Key Strategy: Replace the Wrong with the Right
notes: Slide text:
Putting off the old self: replace, don’t suppress
Wrong seeing, listening, thinking, speaking, doing
become right seeing, listening, thinking, speaking, doing
Nourish the white dog, starve the black dog
Key points:
Suppression doesn’t work: the more you suppress, the more you think about it. The Bible’s way is “don’t … but …” — Romans 12:2, Ephesians 5:18, Ephesians 4:29.
Warning: Matthew 12:43–45 — the house swept clean but left empty; the last state is worse than the first. Emptying must go with filling.
Illustration: a widely told Native American fable — a white dog and a black dog fight in the heart; whichever you feed wins. The white dog is the spiritual life, the black dog the self-centred life.
Positive practice: Philippians 4:8 lists eight things to think about; Proverbs 4:23, “out of it is the wellspring of life”.
321 application: selflessness is not having nothing; it is a change of master — Galatians 2:20.

brief12.title: Right Listening Spreads Blessing
notes: Slide text:
“All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring,
because you have obeyed my voice”
(Genesis 22:18)
Abraham’s key: listen, and obey
Key points:
Background: the offering of Isaac on Mount Moriah (Genesis 22:2) — as though God were tearing down his own promise.
Abraham’s response: “Abraham rose early in the morning” (Genesis 22:3) — no arguing, no delaying.
Original language: Hebrew shama means both “to hear” and “to obey”; Deuteronomy 6:4, “Hear, Israel,” begins with this very word.
Contrast: 1 Samuel 15:22, “to obey is better than sacrifice” — God doesn’t want your offering; he wants your ear.
321 application: the last of the eight stages is Multiplication; the 920 practice — everyone we relate to is our “2”, and the selfless life bears the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.

brief12.title: Discerning the Voices: Whom Do You Hear?
notes: Slide text:
“The sheep listen to his voice”
(John 10:3)
Satan’s voice: discouragement, condemnation, anger, despair
God’s voice: humility, repentance, peace, change
Key points:
The sheep illustration: sheep have poor eyesight, can’t run fast and have no claws or fangs; their only way to survive is to recognise the shepherd’s voice (John 10:5, 27).
Four voices: God’s, Satan’s, our own, the world’s. The question isn’t whether there are voices, but which one you listen to.
Discern by the fruit. Satan is the accuser (Revelation 12:10), who comes to steal, kill and destroy (John 10:10).

2 Corinthians 7:10: godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation; worldly sorrow produces death. The same words, “You are wrong” — from God they make you run to him; from the enemy they make you hide.
2 Timothy 4:3, “itching ears” — people with itching ears aren’t looking for truth but for agreement. God’s voice is often a still small voice (1 Kings 19:12).

brief12.title: How You Listen Decides How You Live
notes: Slide text:
One sentence, two kinds of ears
Wrong listening: replaying negative voices
Right listening: meditating on God’s word
What you meditate on, you become
Key points:
Illustration: someone says, “You didn’t handle this very thoroughly.” Worldly ears hear contempt; spiritual ears hear a reminder.
Scripture: Proverbs 15:31 and 9:8; Psalm 141:5, “don’t let my head refuse it”.
The danger of “replaying”: the speaker has long forgotten, but you play it for three months and hurt yourself a hundred times.

Psychological support: in the 1960s Aaron T. Beck of the University of Pennsylvania described “automatic negative thoughts”; the treatment is not to stop thinking but to replace them with thoughts that match reality.
The right way: Psalm 1:2 and Joshua 1:8, “meditate day and night”; Hebrew hagah means murmuring and chewing over; 2 Corinthians 10:5, “bringing every thought into captivity”.

brief12.title: 321 Insight: Only the Selfless Hear God
notes: Slide text:
Self-centred: hears only what it wants
Selfless: willing to hear and be adjusted
Only the selfless can let Jesus be King
Only the selfless can be led by the Spirit
Key points:
The self-centred person has a sieve: whatever suits him goes in; whatever doesn’t is filtered out.

321 core: the self-centred life is the root of the fall; pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position.
Contrast: humanity’s first fall was listening wrongly (Genesis 3:5, 17); salvation came through one Man’s perfect listening (John 5:30, Romans 5:19).
Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into fullness — Galatians 2:20, “it is no longer I who live”.
Humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan; pride provokes pride and both lose, humility inspires humility and both win.

Build the habit of right input

Listen with the heart: receive and do

Key points:
Practice 1: read Scripture, hear sermons and sing hymns daily. Keep it concrete and small; Morning Devotion 321 itself is the best training ground.
Practice 2: make a list of your “voices”; this week cut off one, and add a positive replacement.

Go deeper with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Support: Hermann Ebbinghaus’s forgetting curve (1885) — little and regular beats a lot and broken off.

Ephesus: capital and great port of the province of Asia, home to the Temple of Artemis; Acts 19:10 says all in Asia “heard the word of the Lord”.
The preceding verses, 4:17–18, describe the Gentiles as “darkened in their understanding”; nous means mind, mindset — the sickness is in the mindset, not the behaviour.
“Put away” and “put on” were everyday words for taking off and putting on clothes; the key in the middle is “be renewed in the spirit of your mind”.
The logic of the passage: hearing → mindset → putting off the old self → putting on the new self → living out Christ.

brief21.title: Saul: One Hearing Changed a Life
notes: Slide text:
“Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
(Acts 9:4)
From persecuting Christ to following Christ
From opposing God to suffering for God
Key points:
Saul’s background: Galatians 1:14 says he advanced in Judaism beyond many of his own age; Acts 9:1 says he was “breathing threats and slaughter”.
He wasn’t a cold-blooded killer; he was full of religious passion, heading completely the wrong way.
Read Acts 9:3–5 to paint the full scene on the Damascus road.
Contrast: Acts 9:16 — the man who once made others suffer for the Lord would now suffer for the Lord himself.

brief21.title: The Key: Not Circumstances, but Hearing the Lord
notes: Slide text:
Not a change of circumstances
Not more knowledge
He heard the voice of the Lord
In Hebrew, calling his name twice
Key points:
Rule things out one by one: his circumstances didn’t change, his knowledge was already great, and he was not in a time of setback.
Detail: Acts 26:14 says the Lord spoke to him “in the Hebrew language” — calling him in his mother’s tongue.
Names called twice: Abraham (Genesis 22:11), Moses (Exodus 3:4), Samuel (1 Samuel 3:10), Martha (Luke 10:41).
Scientific support: Anthony DeCasper and William Fifer’s 1980 study in Science showed that newborns can recognise and prefer their mother’s voice.
Conclusion and comfort: what you need may not be more effort, but one true hearing of God.

brief21.title: Three Layers of Listening
notes: Slide text:
Heard: the sound enters the ears
Received: the truth enters the heart
Learned: the life is shaped
Information, Revelation, Conviction
Key points:
Read Ephesians 4:21 and point out the three progressive verbs.
“Heard” is akouō; “were taught in him” carries the sense of being personally instructed, of becoming a disciple; to “learn” Christ is to be taught and shaped.
These match the first three of the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction.
Warning: James 1:22, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”

brief21.title: Right Listening Brings Three Processes
notes: Slide text:
Put off the old self: lay down old habits
Be renewed in mind: the mindset changes
Put on the new self: live out Christ
(Ephesians 4:22–24)
Key points:
Read the full text of Ephesians 4:22–24.
“Grows corrupt” shows the old self didn’t go bad in a day; it was deceived and eaten away by desire day after day.
In “be renewed in the spirit of your mind” the emphasis is on nous; compare Romans 12:2, “transformed by the renewing of your mind”.
Psychological support: Donald Hebb (1949), “neurons that fire together wire together”; neuroplasticity shows that a new road also widens with use.
321 application: the fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

brief21.title: Putting Off the Old Self Isn’t Suppression
notes: Slide text:
Suppress it and you think of it more — then collapse
The Bible’s way: “Don’t … but …”
After emptying, we must be filled
Replace the old with the new
Key points:
Name the common mistake: gritting your teeth and telling yourself “don’t think about it” — the more you suppress, the more you think.
The Bible’s pattern: Romans 12:2, Ephesians 5:18 and Ephesians 4:29 are all “don’t … but …”.
Warning: Matthew 12:43–45 — the house swept clean but left empty; the last state is worse than the first.
A positive list: the eight things of Philippians 4:8 — when the mind is full of good things, there is no room for the bad.

brief21.title: Replacement on Five Levels
notes: Slide text:
Wrong seeing becomes right seeing
Wrong listening becomes right listening
Thinking, speaking and doing — replaced too
Nourish the white dog, starve the black dog
Key points:
Explain that the five levels form a chain: seeing affects listening, listening affects thinking, thinking decides speaking, speaking brings out doing.
Scripture: Proverbs 4:23, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.”
Illustration: a widely told Native American fable — a white dog and a black dog fight in the heart; whichever you feed wins.
Key: not beating the black dog to death but no longer feeding it; the black dog eats negativity, complaining and accusation; the white dog eats God’s word, praise and thanksgiving.
321 application: selflessness is not having nothing; it is a change of master — Galatians 2:20.

brief21.title: Abraham: Listen, and Obey
notes: Slide text:
“All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring,
because you have obeyed my voice”
(Genesis 22:18)
Not only he was blessed, but all the nations
Key points:
Background: the offering of Isaac on Mount Moriah (Genesis 22:2) — as though God were tearing down his own promise.
Response: “Abraham rose early in the morning” (Genesis 22:3); three days’ journey is long enough to change your mind a hundred times.
Original language: Hebrew shama means both “to hear” and “to obey”; Deuteronomy 6:4, “Hear, Israel”.
Contrast: 1 Samuel 15:22, “to obey is better than sacrifice” — God doesn’t want your offering; he wants your ear.
321 application: the last of the eight stages is Multiplication; the 920 practice — when the selfless “0” is lived out, the ninefold fruit of the Spirit grows in every “2” relationship.

brief21.title: Whose Voice Are You Hearing?
notes: Slide text:
“The sheep listen to his voice”
(John 10:3)
God’s, Satan’s, our own, the world’s
The key is which one you listen to
Key points:
The sheep illustration: poor eyesight, slow, no claws or fangs — their only way to survive is to recognise the shepherd’s voice.
Scripture: John 10:5, “They will by no means follow a stranger”; John 10:27, “My sheep hear my voice”.
Admit the fact: nobody lives in a vacuum; we are always listening to some voice.
Reminder: our own voice and the world’s are the hardest to discern, because they say exactly what we want to hear — 2 Timothy 4:3, “itching ears”.

brief21.title: How to Discern? Look at the Fruit
notes: Slide text:
Satan’s voice: discouragement, condemnation, anger, despair
God’s voice: humility, repentance, peace, change
God’s rebuke brings hope
The enemy’s accusation brings despair
Key points:
Principle: by their fruits you will know them (Matthew 7:16).
Satan is the accuser (Revelation 12:10), who comes to steal, kill and destroy (John 10:10).
2 Corinthians 7:10: godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation; worldly sorrow produces death.
Contrast: after sinning, Adam hid among the trees; after sinning, David wrote Psalm 51. The same “You are wrong” — completely different results.
Bottom line: God’s voice never contradicts God’s word — the Bible is my standard; God’s voice is often a still small voice (1 Kings 19:12).

brief21.title: One Sentence, Two Kinds of Ears
notes: Slide text:
When others criticise you:
Worldly ears — hurt and anger
Spiritual ears — growth and change
The problem isn’t the words, but how you hear
Key points:
Scene: someone says, “You didn’t handle this very thoroughly.” Two kinds of ears, two kinds of life.
Scripture: Proverbs 15:31, “The ear that listens to reproof lives, and will be at home among the wise”; Proverbs 9:8.
Example: Psalm 141:5, “let him reprove me, it is like oil on the head; don’t let my head refuse it”.
321 application: changed relationships begin with how we listen — humility inspires humility and both win; pride provokes pride and both lose.

brief21.title: What You Dwell On, You Become
notes: Slide text:
Wrong listening: replaying negative voices
Right listening: meditating on God’s word
“On his law he meditates day and night”
(Psalm 1:2)
Key points:
Point out the danger of “replaying”: the speaker has long forgotten, but you play it for three months and hurt yourself a hundred times.

Psychological support: in the 1960s Aaron T. Beck of the University of Pennsylvania described “automatic negative thoughts”; the treatment is not to stop thinking but to replace them with thoughts that match reality.
Scripture: Psalm 1:2 and Joshua 1:8; Hebrew hagah means murmuring and chewing over, like a cow chewing the cud.
The battle: 2 Corinthians 10:5, “bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ”.
321 application: a shift of perspective — from the human to God’s, the earthly to the heavenly, the temporary to the eternal, the worldly to the godly (Colossians 3:2; 2 Corinthians 4:18).

brief21.title: 321 Insight: Only the Selfless Hear God
notes: Slide text:
Self-centred: hears only what it wants
Selfless: willing to hear and be adjusted
Only the selfless can let Jesus be King
Only the selfless can be led by the Spirit
Key points:
The self-centred person has a sieve: whatever suits him goes in; whatever doesn’t is filtered out.

321 core: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man, let God be God.
Contrast: humanity’s first fall was listening wrongly (Genesis 3:5, 17); salvation came through one Man’s perfect listening (John 5:30; Romans 5:19).
Illustration: as long as “I” am on the throne, Jesus can only stand at the side as an adviser. You can ignore an adviser; you cannot ignore a King.
Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into fullness — Galatians 2:20, “it is no longer I who live”.

brief21.title: Practices 1 and 2
notes: Slide text:
Build the habit of right input
Scripture, sermons and hymns every day
Stop feeding the wrong voices
Less negativity, complaining, accusation
Key points:
Go deeper into Practice 1 with the eight stages: first honestly tally the daily time spent listening to God’s word and to other voices.
Keep implementation concrete and small: read a passage aloud in the morning, then be still for three minutes; Morning Devotion 321 is the best training ground.
Support: the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus’s forgetting curve (1885) — little and regular beats a lot and broken off.
Practice 2: make a list of your “voices”; this week cut off one, and add a positive replacement.
Reminder: emptying must go with filling; find a spiritual companion to walk with you — don’t fight alone.

brief21.title: Practice 3: Listen with the Heart
notes: Slide text:
Not just having heard
but receiving, meditating, doing
What did God say? What must I change?
What one thing will I do this week?
Key points:
Method: after hearing a sermon or reading a passage, write down three sentences.
Ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into revelation — without the Spirit, Scripture is only words on a page; with the Spirit, the words become living water.
This week choose one verse, say it aloud three times a day, meditate on it often; at the weekend check whether it helped in a specific situation.
321 reminder: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you rejoice, rely on the brain and you worry (Proverbs 4:23).
Multiplication: share in your small group how this verse changed you; bring someone along to do morning devotions with you.

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
notes: Slide text:
Three Foundations: role model, standard, guide
Two Core Values: King, all the glory
Fivefold change: from mindset to ministry
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
Key points:
The Three Foundations are three kinds of right listening: Jesus is my role model (John 5:30), the Bible is my standard (Romans 10:17), the Holy Spirit is my guide (Isaiah 30:21).
The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — the King’s word is a command, not a suggestion; let Jesus receive all the glory — we don’t hear sermons to add to our stock of conversation.
The Goal: establish God’s system. One person who listens to God influences a household; a community that listens to God is what God’s system looks like in embryo.

The fivefold change in this lesson: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry; then the 235 relationships — 2 spiritual companions, 3 spiritual parents and children, 5 a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.
The order of relationships: first with God, then ourselves, then others, last of all with things.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: Slide text:
Saul heard the Lord — his life turned around
Abraham obeyed God — the nations were blessed
The sheep hear the shepherd — and have life
What you listen to is what you become
Key points:
Three witnesses tie the lesson together; quote John 10:10, “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.”
The call in three steps: listen constantly, listen with the heart, obey.
Revelation 3:20 — the Lord stands at the door and knocks; he doesn’t break it down, he waits for someone willing to open.
Revelation 2:7, “He who has an ear, let him hear.”
Point to the Two Core Values: offer up our ears and let Jesus be King; offer up our changed lives and let Jesus receive all the glory.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, tune my ears
Let your truth change my life
“Speak; for your servant hears” (1 Samuel 3:10)
Reign as King, and receive all the glory
Key points:
Lead the brothers and sisters in praying together, reading slowly line by line so that all can follow and declare.
Prayer content: ask the Lord to cleanse our ears and remove the self-centred life that hears only what it wants, making us humble and willing to be adjusted.
Close with Samuel’s response: “Speak; for your servant hears” (1 Samuel 3:10).
Isaiah 50:4: “He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught” — the most fitting blessing for morning devotions.
Bless the congregation: may God let us hear his voice every morning, and may our lives enter into abundance, victory and Christlikeness.

script: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Today let’s think together about something supremely important — listening. Paul says, “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). Faith doesn’t sprout out of thin air; it grows out of the ear. Wherever your ears lead, that is the shape your life will grow into. The title of today’s lesson is: listen rightly, and life changes.

In 1953 the British scientist Colin Cherry carried out an experiment. In a room where dozens of people were talking at once, people could still lock on to just one voice. This is called the “cocktail party effect.” Brothers and sisters, this tells us that the ear is not a passive radio receiver; the ear is an organ that chooses. Every day you are choosing who gets to shape you. What you listen to decides what you believe; what you believe decides what you become. Many people have believed in the Lord for years without changing. The problem isn’t a lack of truth; it’s a lack of listening rightly. The Lord Jesus said, “Be careful therefore how you hear” (Luke 8:18).

Our key text is in Ephesians 4. When Paul wrote this letter he was in prison. Ephesus was a great port of its day, full of idols and sorcery; the believers had come to faith, but the old world still spoke in their ears every day. So Paul says, “if indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man … and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man” (Ephesians 4:21–24). Brothers and sisters, please remember this order: first we listen, then comes change.

First, true change begins with hearing God. Saul was a man who hauled Christians off to prison. But on the road to Damascus he fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). What was the key to his turnaround? Not a change of circumstances, not more knowledge, but hearing the voice of the Lord. From persecuting Christ to following Christ; from opposing God to suffering for God. Brothers and sisters, one act of “hearing” changed a whole life. What you need may not be more effort, but one true hearing of God.

Second, right listening brings renewal of life. Paul speaks of three steps: heard, received, learned. Hearing is the sound entering the ears; receiving is the truth entering the heart; learning is the life being shaped. True listening brings three processes: first, putting off the old self — laying down old habits and old thinking; second, being renewed in mind — the mindset changed by the truth; third, putting on the new self — living out the life of Christ. 321 says the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and the life changes. Brothers and sisters, listen rightly, and your life will change.

Third, the key strategy: replace the wrong with the right. Putting off the old self isn’t straining to suppress — the more you suppress it, the more you think about it; it is replacing the old with the new. Wrong seeing becomes right seeing; wrong listening becomes right listening; wrong thinking becomes right thinking; wrong speaking becomes right speaking; wrong doing becomes right doing. There’s a fable that says two dogs are fighting inside a person’s heart, a white dog and a black dog. Which one will win? The one you feed. The white dog is the spiritual life; the black dog is the self-centred life. Nourish the white dog, and starve the black dog. Brothers and sisters, whatever you feed is what you will live out.

Fourth, right listening brings an expanding blessing. God said to Abraham, “All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring, because you have obeyed my voice” (Genesis 22:18). On Mount Moriah God asked him to offer up his only son; he didn’t argue; he rose early in the morning. The Hebrew word for “listen” in itself carries the sense of obeying. To hear without obeying is not to have listened. Abraham’s key comes down to this: listen, and obey. And the result? Not only was he blessed, but all the nations too. Brothers and sisters, the day you obey may be the day your children’s blessing begins.

Fifth, discerning the voices: whom are you listening to? The Lord says, “The sheep listen to his voice” (John 10:3). We are all sheep, and we are always listening to some voice. There is God’s voice, Satan’s voice, our own voice and the world’s voice. The question isn’t whether there are voices, but which one you listen to. How do we tell them apart? Look at the results. Listening to Satan’s voice brings discouragement, condemnation, anger and despair; listening to God’s voice brings humility, repentance, peace and change. It’s the same three words, “You are wrong” — when God says them, you want to run towards him; when the enemy says them, you want to hide from him. Brothers and sisters, different voices bring utterly different results.

Sixth, how you listen decides how you live. The very same sentence can be heard as two different voices. When others criticise you, listen with worldly ears and you get hurt and angry; listen with spiritual ears and you grow and change. The problem isn’t the sentence; it’s how you hear it. Wrong listening keeps replaying negative voices — the person who said it has long since forgotten, but you’ve been playing it in your heart for three months. Right listening means meditating on God’s word again and again. “But his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2). Brothers and sisters, whatever you meditate on again and again, that is what you are shaped into.

Seventh, the light of 321: only the selfless can hear God. The self-centred person hears only what he wants to hear; the self-centred person resists God’s voice. Because God’s voice so often asks us to let go, and the instinct of the self-centred life is to hold on. And the selfless person? He is willing to hear the truth, willing to be adjusted. The selfless person hears God, obeys God and lives out God. Brothers and sisters, only selflessness can let Jesus be King; only selflessness can be led by the Holy Spirit. Because as long as “I” am still on the throne, Jesus can only stand at the side as an adviser. You can ignore an adviser; you cannot ignore a King.

Next come three practices. First, build the habit of right input: read Scripture, hear sermons and sing hymns every day, starting with five minutes. Second, stop feeding the wrong voices: this week cut off one negative source, and add a positive replacement in its place. Third, practise listening with the heart: not just having heard, but receiving, meditating and doing. Afterwards write down three sentences — What did God say? What does God want me to change? What one thing will I do this week? Brothers and sisters, please remember this: it isn’t that you can’t change; it’s that you haven’t kept on “listening rightly.”

Let’s walk today’s road once more. Saul heard the Lord, and his life was turned around; Abraham obeyed God, and the nations were blessed; the sheep listen to the shepherd, and they have life. What you listen to is what you become. When you begin to listen to God’s word constantly, to listen with the heart, and to obey God’s word, your life will not merely change; it will enter into a life that is abundant, victorious and like Christ. Let’s pray together: Lord, tune my ears. Let me no longer listen to the wrong voices, nor let negative words linger in my heart. Help me listen to your word alone; let your truth change my life and make me more and more like you. Reign as King, and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Today let’s think together about something utterly ordinary and yet supremely important — listening. Every day you are listening: to the alarm clock, to the news, to your family, to that voice in your heart. But have you ever considered that what you listen to is shaping you, day by day? Paul says, “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). Faith doesn’t sprout out of thin air; it grows out of the ear. Wherever your ears lead, that is the shape your life will grow into.

First, listen to an experiment. In 1953 Colin Cherry of Imperial College London placed people among a noisy crowd, with voices coming at them from every side, and asked them to concentrate on just one person speaking. And people really could lock on to one voice and push the rest into the background. Researchers call this the “cocktail party effect.” Brothers and sisters, this tells us that the ear is not a passive radio receiver; the ear is an organ that chooses. You think you’re just half-listening, but in fact every day you are selecting — selecting who gets to shape you.

We often think listening is just receiving information: a sound comes in, you know something, and that’s the end of it. Not so. Listening is where a changed life begins. Because there is an invisible chain: what you listen to decides what you believe; what you believe decides what you become. This also explains a puzzling thing: many people have believed in the Lord for twenty years, can recite verses and sing the hymns, and yet their lives have barely moved. The problem isn’t a lack of truth; it’s a lack of listening rightly. The Lord Jesus said, “Be careful therefore how you hear” (Luke 8:18). He didn’t say, “Be careful what you hear”; he said, “Be careful how you hear.”

Our key text is in Ephesians 4. When Paul wrote this letter he was in prison — generally thought to be his Roman imprisonment, around AD 60 to 62. Ephesus was the capital of the province of Asia, a great port on the Aegean, home to the Temple of Artemis, counted among the Seven Wonders of the World. Acts 19 says Paul lived there for more than two years, so that all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord. The Ephesian church was a church born of listening. Yet after they came to faith, the old world still spoke in their ears every day. So Paul says, “if indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man … and put on the new man” (Ephesians 4:21–24).

The first key point: true change begins with hearing God. Saul was the most promising young man in the Judaism of his day. He says, “I advanced in the Jews’ religion beyond many of my own age among my countrymen” (Galatians 1:14). He was taught at the feet of Gamaliel, and his zeal went so far that he was “breathing threats and slaughter” against the disciples. He wasn’t a cold-blooded killer; he was a man full of religious passion, heading completely the wrong way. Then, on the road to Damascus, he fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). From that moment he went from persecuting Christ to following Christ, from opposing God to suffering for God.

Notice the key to his turnaround. It wasn’t that his circumstances changed — he was still on the same road. It wasn’t that he gained more knowledge — he knew the Old Testament better than anyone. Nor was it that he met with setbacks — he was at the height of his success. There was only one key: he heard the voice of the Lord. And this hearing has one very tender detail. Paul says, “I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language” (Acts 26:14). The Lord called him in his mother’s language, and called him twice. In 1980 DeCasper and Fifer published a study in the journal Science showing that babies only a few days old can recognise, and prefer, their own mother’s voice. Brothers and sisters, we are born to recognise the voice of the One who loves us.

The second key point: right listening brings renewal of life. Paul speaks of three progressive steps: heard, received, learned. Hearing is the sound entering the ears; receiving is the truth entering the heart; learning is the life being shaped. Many people get stuck at the first layer. Hearing is information; receiving is revelation; only being shaped is life. In the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset, the first stage is precisely Information, the second is Revelation, and only the third is Conviction. James puts it bluntly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22).

True listening brings three processes. First, putting off the old self. The text says the old self “grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit.” Notice “grows corrupt” — the old self didn’t go bad in a day. Second, being renewed in mind; the emphasis of the original is on the mind, the mindset. Behaviour is the fruit; mindset is the root. Change the behaviour without changing the mindset, and that’s called repression. Third, putting on the new self. The new self is not an improved version of the old self; it is created anew in the likeness of God. In 1949 the Canadian neuropsychologist Donald Hebb proposed that neurons that fire together wire together. The more often you repeat a thought, the thicker that pathway becomes. That should make us wary, but it also gives us hope — walk a new road long enough, and it too will widen.

The third key point: replace the wrong with the right. Why is putting off the old self so hard? Because many people use the wrong method, and their method is suppression. Grit your teeth and tell yourself desperately, “Don’t think about it,” and the more you suppress it, the more you think about it. Brothers and sisters, the Bible never just tells us “don’t”; in the Bible “don’t” is always followed straight away by “but.” “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2). The Lord Jesus also warned that when an unclean spirit leaves a man and finds the house swept clean but empty, it comes back with seven spirits more evil than itself, and the last state of that man is worse than the first. After being emptied, we must be filled.

So our practice is replacement on five levels: wrong seeing becomes right seeing, wrong listening becomes right listening, wrong thinking becomes right thinking, wrong speaking becomes right speaking, wrong doing becomes right doing. These five levels form a chain. Solomon says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). There is a widely told Native American fable: a white dog and a black dog are fighting inside a person’s heart, and whichever you feed wins. The white dog is the spiritual life; the black dog is the self-centred life. So — nourish the white dog, and starve the black dog. Whatever you feed is what you will live out.

The fourth key point: right listening brings an expanding blessing. God said to Abraham, “All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring, because you have obeyed my voice” (Genesis 22:18). The setting is Mount Moriah, where God asked him to offer up his only son Isaac. How did Abraham respond? The Bible says just one thing: “Abraham rose early in the morning.” No arguing, no delaying. The Hebrew word for “listen” in itself carries the sense of obeying; to hear without obeying is not to have listened at all. That is why Samuel said, “To obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22). God doesn’t want your offering; God wants your ear. And how great is the result of obedience? As great as “all the nations of the earth.” This is what 321 calls Multiplication.

The fifth key point: discerning the voices — whom are you listening to? The Lord says, “The sheep listen to his voice” (John 10:3). There is deep meaning in the Lord comparing us to sheep: sheep have poor eyesight, can’t run fast and have no claws or fangs; their only way to survive is to recognise the shepherd’s voice. The Lord also says, “They will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him; for they don’t know the voice of strangers” (John 10:5). Brothers and sisters, nobody lives in a vacuum. We are always listening to some voice: God’s, Satan’s, our own, the world’s. The question isn’t whether there are voices; the question is which one you listen to.

How do we tell them apart? Look at the results. Listening to Satan’s voice produces four kinds of fruit: discouragement, condemnation, anger and despair. One of Satan’s names is “the accuser”; his voice always presses you down, until you don’t want to pray and don’t dare come before God. Listening to God’s voice produces four kinds of fruit: humility, repentance, peace and change. God will also point out our sin, but his correction brings hope. Paul says, “For godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). It’s the same “You are wrong” — when God says it, you want to run towards him; when the enemy says it, you want to hide from him. And there is a bottom line: God’s voice will never contradict God’s word. The Bible is my standard.

The sixth key point: how you listen decides how you live. The very same sentence can be heard as two different voices. Someone says to you, “You didn’t handle this very thoroughly.” Listen with worldly ears, and what you hear is: he looks down on me, he’s embarrassing me — and the result is hurt and anger. Listen with spiritual ears, and what you hear is: God is using this person to show me something I can’t see — and the result is growth and change. One sentence, two kinds of ears, two kinds of life. Proverbs says, “The ear that listens to reproof lives, and will be at home among the wise” (Proverbs 15:31). And David says, “Let the righteous strike me, it is kindness; let him reprove me, it is like oil on the head; don’t let my head refuse it” (Psalm 141:5).

Next comes a more hidden danger: replaying. Wrong listening keeps replaying negative voices. Someone says something unkind; the person who said it has long since forgotten, but you have been playing it in your heart for three months. The person who said it hurt you once; you have hurt yourself a hundred times. In the 1960s Aaron T. Beck of the University of Pennsylvania described “automatic negative thoughts,” and his treatment was not to tell people not to think, but to replace those thoughts with ones that match reality. God’s method came earlier and goes deeper. Right listening means meditating on God’s word again and again. “But his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2). The Hebrew word for “meditate” originally means murmuring under one’s breath and chewing over again and again, like a cow chewing the cud. Whatever you meditate on again and again, that is what you are shaped into.

The seventh key point, and the light of 321: only the selfless can hear God. Why is it that some people can’t hear God? Because of the self-centred life. The self-centred person hears only what he wants to hear — it isn’t that he has no ears; it’s that he has a sieve. The self-centred person resists God’s voice, because God so often asks us to let go, and the instinct of the self-centred life is to hold on. 321 puts it penetratingly: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position. Humanity’s first fall was a case of listening wrongly; and salvation began with one Man’s perfect listening. The Lord said, “As I hear, I judge” (John 5:30). Brothers and sisters, only selflessness can let Jesus be King. As long as “I” am still on the throne, Jesus can only stand at the side as an adviser. You can ignore an adviser; you cannot ignore a King.

Now for some practical exercises. First, build the habit of right input: read Scripture, hear sermons and sing hymns every day. First honestly count how many minutes a day you spend listening to God’s word, and how many listening to other voices. Then make a plan so small you are sure to keep it — even five minutes. In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus’s forgetting curve showed us that little and regular beats a lot and broken off. Second, stop feeding the wrong voices: make a list of your “voices,” and this week cut off one, adding a positive replacement in its place. Remember: emptying must go hand in hand with filling.

The third practice: listen with the heart. Not just having heard, but receiving, meditating and doing. Here’s a method: after hearing a sermon or reading a passage of Scripture, write down three sentences — What did God say? What does God want me to change? What one thing will I do this week? Then choose one verse and say it aloud three times every day. 321 reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you rejoice, rely on the brain and you worry. Listening with the brain means analysing, comparing, judging; listening with the heart means receiving, surrendering, responding. And finally, don’t forget the last of the eight stages — Multiplication: bring someone along to do morning devotions with you.

Let’s set what we have learned today within the framework of 321. The Three Foundations are three kinds of right listening: Jesus is my role model — he said, “As I hear, I judge”; the Bible is my standard — every voice must be brought before Scripture to be tested; the Holy Spirit is my guide — “your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it’” (Isaiah 30:21). The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — the King’s word is a command, not a suggestion; and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. The fivefold change can be seen especially clearly in this lesson: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. To change your ears is to change your perspective, and to change your perspective is to change your life.

Let’s walk today’s road once more. Saul heard the Lord, and his life was turned around; Abraham obeyed God, and the nations were blessed; the sheep listen to the shepherd’s voice, and they have life — “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly” (John 10:10). Three figures, one principle: what you listen to is what you become. When you begin to listen to God’s word constantly — not now and then, but every day; when you begin to listen to God’s word with the heart — not analysing it with the brain, but receiving it with the heart; when you begin to obey God’s word — not hearing and leaving it there, but hearing and then doing — your life will not merely change; it will enter into a life that is abundant, victorious and like Christ. Today the Lord still says, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock” (Revelation 3:20). He is waiting for someone willing to open the door.

Let’s pray together. Lord, tune my ears. Let me no longer listen to the wrong voices, nor let negative words linger in my heart. I confess that the reason my life has not yet changed is not that you have not spoken, but that I have not listened rightly. Help me listen to your word alone, and remove from me the self-centred life that hears only what it wants to hear. Make me humble, willing to be adjusted; make me selfless, able to be led by the Holy Spirit. Teach me to put off the old self, to be renewed in my mind, and to put on the new self. May I, like Saul, turn to you as soon as I hear you; like Abraham, obey you as soon as I hear. Reign as King in my life, and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord awaken your ear morning by morning, to hear as those who are taught. God bless you all!

sections.heading: Introduction: God Is Not Silent — We Have Gone Deaf
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning, let’s begin by being still for thirty seconds. Don’t do anything. Just listen.

What did you hear? Perhaps the low hum of the air conditioner, perhaps birdsong outside the window, perhaps your own breathing, perhaps a car passing somewhere in the distance. Those sounds were there all along. They didn’t appear in these thirty seconds; it was only in these thirty seconds that you “heard” them.

And that is the first spiritual fact we have to face today: the sound has been there all along. The problem lies with the one who is listening.

The human ear is a design of awe-inspiring precision. A healthy ear can pick up sound waves from roughly twenty hertz to twenty thousand hertz; inside the cochlea some fifteen thousand hair cells translate the vibrations of the air into nerve signals. And yet at this very moment countless waves are passing straight through your body — radio waves, mobile phone signals, the high-pitched song of insects — and you hear not one of them. Not because they don’t exist, but because your receiver isn’t tuned to that frequency.

In 1953 Colin Cherry, a cognitive scientist at Imperial College London, carried out a famous experiment; later generations would call what he found “the cocktail party effect.” He discovered that in a noisy banquet hall a person can focus on the friend in front of him and automatically filter out the conversations of dozens of people all around. Six years later, in 1959, Neville Moray of the University of Oxford found something more remarkable still: even while a person is concentrating on one voice, let someone at the far end softly mention his name, and he turns his head at once. What these studies tell us is this: we do not hear every sound; we hear the sounds we care about.

Brothers and sisters, please remember that sentence: we do not hear every sound; we hear the sounds we care about.

Our God has never been a silent God. From Genesis 1, “God said, ‘Let there be light,’” to the last chapter of Revelation, “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’” — the whole Bible is a book about a God who speaks. In Knowing God the theologian J. I. Packer points out that the very foundation of the Christian faith is this: God is a self-revealing God. He takes the initiative and speaks, and only so can anyone know him. If God did not speak, all human religion would be nothing but guesswork.

Yet many believers today live in a kind of spiritual dullness. They attend meetings, read the Bible, pray, even serve for years — and never once have they clearly sensed: God has just spoken to me. Their faith is knowledge about God, not conversation with God. They are like the Israelites in Samuel’s day, of whom Scripture says, “Yahweh’s word was rare in those days. There were not many visions, then.” (1 Samuel 3:1)

Notice that the verse says Yahweh’s word was rare — and yet in that very same chapter we see God calling, four times over, in a single night. God was not stingy with his voice at all. What was rare was not God’s word; it was people who heard it.

So in this lesson the question we ask is not “Is God speaking?” but “Am I listening?”

Here is an important 321 Insight; brothers and sisters, please take it to heart: it is not that God doesn’t speak — it is that we rely on the brain and not on the heart. It is not that God doesn’t guide — it is that we set our minds on the flesh and not on the Spirit.

Rely on the brain, and you worry; rely on the heart, and you rejoice. The brain is an organ of analysis; the heart is an organ of reception. When we spend our whole lives using our brains to calculate God, evaluate God and argue with God, we tune ourselves to a frequency on which God can never be received. God’s voice is not a puzzle waiting to be solved; it is the heart of a Father.

Today God wants to open our ears. May every one of us leave this lesson changed — from “someone who knows God can speak” into “someone who really hears God speak.”

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Night Servants Became Friends
sections.html:
Our key verse is John 15:15. To understand it we first have to stand in the place where those words were spoken.

John’s Gospel was written by John, the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved. It is generally dated somewhere between AD 85 and 95, very probably written in Ephesus in Asia Minor, to churches scattered across the Greco-Roman world. By then most of the first generation of apostles had been martyred, heresies were starting to rise, and believers needed to be reminded afresh that the Jesus they believed in is the Word who was with God from the beginning. That is why John opens his book with these words: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” (John 1:1)

“Word” in Greek is λόγος (logos), meaning “speech, a spoken word.” With this term John announces something astonishing: God does not merely speak — God himself is that Word. And this speaking God in the end became a Word that human beings could hear: “The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.” (John 1:14)

Our key verse falls within the long section of John 13 to 17. It is often called the Upper Room Discourse: the farewell words the Lord Jesus spoke to the eleven disciples on the night he was betrayed, after the Last Supper. Judas had already gone out, the cross was at the door, and the Lord had only a few hours left. What a man says in the last hours of his life is always what matters most to him.

What did the Lord say that night? He washed the disciples’ feet, he gave them a new commandment, he promised that the Holy Spirit would come, he told the parable of the vine and the branches. And then he said this: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.” (John 15:15)

There are two key Greek words here. “Servant” is δοῦλος (doulos), a bondservant, a slave. What marks a slave is not that he does little but that he is not told. A master owes his slave no explanation; the slave simply carries out orders. “Friend” is φίλος (philos), from φιλέω (phileō, to love dearly): someone the master holds in his heart, someone who is let into the master’s inner thoughts.

So what the Lord Jesus proclaims here is a revolution in relationship. He is saying: from now on I will not treat you as slaves who can only take orders; I will treat you as friends who can know my heart.

Pay special attention to the reason the Lord gives: “for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.” On what basis does the Lord call us friends? Not because we are so good, but because he has told us everything he heard from the Father. The evidence of friendship is speech.

Brothers and sisters, this is the Bible’s deepest definition of “God speaking to people”: God speaks not in order to issue commands, but in order to share his heart.

Look at how the Lord Jesus himself lived. He said, “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” (John 5:19) And again, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.” (John 7:16) Through his thirty-three years on earth the Lord Jesus was a man who listened to the Father every day and acted on the Father’s word every day.

This is exactly the first of the 321 vision’s Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model. We learn to hear God’s voice not in pursuit of some mystical experience, but in order to live the very life the Lord lived on earth — a life constantly connected to the Father, constantly hearing the Father’s heart.

From the Old Testament to the New there is a clear line of development in the way God speaks. Hebrews draws that line in its very first sentence: “God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son.” (Hebrews 1:1–2) “At many times and in various ways” — the phrase shows how astonishingly rich God’s ways of speaking are. He has spoken by a voice, by visions, by dreams, by the Law, by prophets, by nature, by the events of history. And in these last days he has spoken by his Son; and since the Lord’s ascension he has gone on speaking to everyone who belongs to him by the Holy Spirit and by the Scriptures.

In this lesson we will look at three of the most basic and most common ways: God speaking in person, God speaking through the Bible, and God speaking in our hearts.

sections.heading: 1. God Speaks in Person: He Is a God Who Will Speak to You
sections.html:
Scripture says, “Yahweh called Samuel. He said, ‘Here I am.’” (1 Samuel 3:4)

Scripture also says, “He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’” (Acts 9:4)

These two passages show us one and the same truth: God is able to speak to people directly, with a “voice.”

Take Samuel first. It was the close of the period of the judges, around the eleventh century BC, and the ark of the covenant rested in the tabernacle at Shiloh. Eli the high priest was old and his eyes were dim; his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were wicked men. All Israel lay in spiritual darkness, which is why Scripture says, “Yahweh’s word was rare in those days. There were not many visions, then.” (1 Samuel 3:1)

In just such an age, God spoke. And the one he called was not the seasoned high priest but a boy who “didn’t yet know Yahweh” (1 Samuel 3:7). Samuel was probably about twelve years old. At God’s first call he ran to Eli; at the second he ran to Eli again; at the third, once more he ran to Eli. It is a lovely detail, and a very true one — he heard the voice, but he didn’t know it was God.

Brothers and sisters, have you ever had that experience? A prompting comes, and you think you’re overthinking it. A word pierces you deeply, and you put it down to emotion. A burden weighs on you for days, and you call it stress. In fact it was God calling your name — you just didn’t yet recognise his voice.

The turning point that night came when Eli finally discerned what was happening. He said to Samuel, “Go, lie down. It shall be, if he calls you, that you shall say, ‘Speak, Yahweh; for your servant hears.’” (1 Samuel 3:9) And so, the fourth time, “Yahweh came, and stood, and called as at other times, ‘Samuel! Samuel!’ Then Samuel said, ‘Speak; for your servant hears.’” (1 Samuel 3:10)

“Here I am” in Hebrew is הִנֵּנִי (hineni). It is one of the weightiest words in the Bible. Abraham said “Here I am” on Mount Moriah (Genesis 22:1); Moses said “Here I am” before the burning bush (Exodus 3:4); Isaiah, in his vision in the temple, said “Here I am. Send me!” (Isaiah 6:8). The word is not answering a roll call; it is an act of surrender. It means: Lord, all of me is here before you — do with me whatever you will.

Now take Saul. Some time in the AD 30s the Pharisee Saul was on the road to Damascus, carrying letters from the high priest and breathing out murder. He was certain he was burning with zeal for God. Suddenly a light from heaven flashed all around him; he fell to the ground and heard the Lord say, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4)

Notice the Lord’s words. It was Christians that Saul was persecuting, yet the Lord said, “Why do you persecute me?” That one sentence overturned Saul’s entire theology at a stroke — the church is Christ’s own body, and to touch the church is to touch the Lord himself. Years later this same Paul would write, “Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually” (1 Corinthians 12:27), and the root of it lies in that one sentence on the Damascus road.

One word from God can rewrite a person’s whole life.

To Samuel that voice was as real as a person speaking; for Saul that voice shook the direction of his entire life. This tells us that it isn’t only prophets and apostles who can hear God’s voice. God is willing to speak to people — that has always been his heart.

But where is the key? The key is that Samuel said those words: “Here I am!”

That is the response of the heart, not the analysis of the brain. Samuel didn’t ask, Where did that voice come from? Could it be a hallucination? Is there any scientific evidence? He simply gave himself over completely.

I often use the radio as an illustration. Right now this room is full of the signals of dozens of stations: news, music, traffic — all of them here, without a moment’s pause. But you can’t hear them, because you have no receiver; and even with a receiver, if it isn’t tuned to the right frequency, all you hear is static. Tune it right, and you hear; tune it wrong, and there is nothing but silence.

What is God’s frequency? Humility.

Scripture says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) The Greek word for “resists” here is ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against.” In the spiritual world, the proud are people against whom God has drawn up his battle lines. It isn’t that they can’t pick up the signal; they are shut outside the door.

This is what the 321 vision means when it says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights — wanting to take God’s place. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. When someone says, “Here I am; speak, for your servant hears,” he has returned to his originally intended position: God is Lord and I am servant; God speaks and I listen. In that moment, heaven opens.

The proud, on the other hand, hear only themselves. In 1999 the Harvard psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris ran a famous experiment that later became widely known as “the invisible gorilla.” They asked participants to watch a video of people passing a ball and to concentrate on counting how many passes the players in white made. Partway through, someone in a gorilla suit strolled into the frame, beat his chest and walked out again — nine seconds in all. The result? Roughly half the participants never saw the gorilla at all.

The phenomenon is called “inattentional blindness,” and it reveals a sobering fact: when people are wholly absorbed in their own task, even the most obvious thing in front of their eyes gets automatically deleted. Brothers and sisters, the spiritual world has its own “inattentional deafness.” When we are wholly absorbed in our own plans, our own grievances, our own achievements, God can stand right in front of us and speak, and we will not hear.

So the first condition for hearing God’s voice is not technique; it is posture. It is that one sentence: “Lord, here I am.”

321 Insight: the humble hear God easily; the proud hear only themselves.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, will you say to the Lord, as Samuel did, “Lord, here I am. Speak, for your servant hears”?

sections.heading: 2. God Speaks Through the Bible: His Word Is Alive
sections.html:
Scripture says, “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” (Hebrews 4:12)

This is one of the most powerful verses anywhere in the Bible about the Bible itself. Notice its two descriptive words.

“Living” in Greek is ζῶν (zōn), quite simply “alive.” Applied to Scripture, it means that the Bible is not a finished ancient document, sealed and put away. It is a living thing. Open it today, and it will speak to you.

“Active” in Greek is ἐνεργής (energēs), the root of the English word “energy.” It means “at work, in operation, exerting its power.” The Bible is not an object lying there waiting for you to study it; it is a power actively at work in you.

And the most arresting part of the verse is its second half: “able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” The picture in the original is of a surgeon’s scalpel opening up the deepest places in a person. Brothers and sisters, when we read the Bible, the Bible also reads us. We think we are analysing the text, when in fact the text is laying us open.

Why, then, do some people read the Bible every day and never once hear God’s voice in it?

Paul gives the answer: “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” (2 Corinthians 3:6)

The word translated “spirit” here is πνεῦμα (pneuma), and the Chinese Union Version even notes in its margin that it may be rendered “the Holy Spirit.” Paul is not saying the words of Scripture don’t matter — his letters quote the words of the Old Testament from beginning to end. He is saying that words without the breath of the Holy Spirit are just letters carved on a gravestone; but words the Holy Spirit breathes into become God’s living word, spoken to you.

This is exactly what the 321 vision says: the Bible is my standard, and the Holy Spirit is my guide. These two foundations must be held together as one.

A standard without a guide turns faith into legalism — correct, but lifeless, like the Pharisees. The Lord said to them, “You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.” (John 5:39–40) What a frightening sentence: a group of people who knew the Scriptures inside out, and who walked straight past the very One the Scriptures point to.

A guide without a standard turns faith into mysticism — lively, but rootless, ready to be blown away at any moment. That is why Scripture says, “test the spirits, whether they are of God.” (1 John 4:1)

Standard plus guide — only that is truly hearing God.

So when God really does speak to us through the Bible, what are the signs?

Luke’s Gospel gives us the loveliest of answers. On the afternoon of the resurrection, two disciples were trudging dejectedly to Emmaus. The Lord walked with them and explained the Scriptures to them. Then, when he made himself known in the breaking of the bread and immediately vanished, they said this: “Weren’t our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32)

“Burning” in Greek is καιομένη (kaiomenē), “being on fire, ablaze.” And notice — they only understood afterwards. At the time all they felt was an inexpressible burning in their hearts; they didn’t know it was the Lord.

Brothers and sisters, this is the sign that God is speaking through the Bible: not merely “I understand,” but “my heart has been set on fire.”

Throughout church history this fire has blazed up again and again.

In the summer of AD 386 a North African named Augustine sat weeping in a garden in Milan. He was a man of brilliant learning and broken morals; at thirty-one he was bound by his own sin and could not break free. Suddenly he heard a child’s voice from a neighbouring house, chanting over and over, “Take up and read, take up and read.” He rushed back, picked up Paul’s letters, opened them at random and read: “Let’s walk properly, as in the day; not in reveling and drunkenness, not in sexual promiscuity and lustful acts, and not in strife and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts.” (Romans 13:13–14) In his Confessions he later wrote that as he finished that sentence, every shadow of doubt in his heart vanished at once. A passage he had read who knows how many times became, that day, God speaking to him in person.

More than thirteen hundred years later, on the evening of 24 May 1738, at a small meeting in Aldersgate Street in London, a discouraged English clergyman named John Wesley listened as someone read aloud Martin Luther’s preface to the Epistle to the Romans. In his journal he wrote the words still quoted today: “I felt my heart strangely warmed.” In that moment he was assured that Christ had taken away his sins. Wesley had been reading Romans for half his life, but that night the words became a voice.

I often put it like this: the Bible is like a letter, the Holy Spirit is like the one who reads the letter aloud to you, and your heart is the receiver. Without the Holy Spirit, the Bible is just print; with the Holy Spirit, the Bible becomes a voice.

That also explains a common experience. You have read the same verse twenty times and felt nothing, and then one morning it suddenly pricks your heart like a needle. The verse hasn’t changed. What has changed is that in that moment the Holy Spirit has aimed it squarely at your situation.

So the way we read the Bible has to change. Don’t read only with your brain; listen with your heart.

Church history has an ancient tradition called lectio divina, “sacred reading.” It had already taken shape among the Benedictines in the sixth century, and a twelfth-century monk later summed it up in four steps: read, meditate, pray, contemplate. Its spirit is very simple — reading the Bible is not gathering information; it is keeping an appointment.

We can turn it into an even simpler practice: as you read, stop at any point and ask the Lord, “Lord, what do you want to say to me today?” Then be still, and wait.

Here is a very practical reminder. Brain science tells us the human brain has a “default mode network,” proposed in 2001 by the American neuroscientist Marcus Raichle of Washington University. Research found that when people stop performing a task and become quiet, certain regions of the brain actually grow more active — and this is the crucial moment when people integrate meaning and arrive at insight. In other words, even physiologically, stillness is not wasted time; stillness is when deep understanding actually happens.

Brothers and sisters, when God made us he had already written “only in stillness can you hear” into our very bodies. No wonder the psalm says, “Be still, and know that I am God.” (Psalm 46:10) The Hebrew word here, רָפָה (raphah), means “to let go, to let your hands drop.” Let go first — and then you will know that he is God.

321 Insight: the Bible is the standard and the Holy Spirit is the guide; only when the two are one do we truly hear God.

From a 321 point of view, this is a change of mindset. The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. When your mindset about the Bible shifts from “a book to get through” to “a Lord to meet,” your daily habit of reading Scripture changes; when that habit changes, your life changes. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living.

sections.heading: 3. God Speaks in Our Hearts: The Holy Spirit’s Prompting Is the Most Common Way
sections.html:
Scripture says, “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14)

Scripture also says, “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:13)

Brothers and sisters, where does God speak most often? Not outside you, but inside you.

This is the greatest grace of the New Testament age. In Old Testament times the Spirit of God “came upon” certain people — upon judges, upon kings, upon prophets — and he could depart. That is why David prayed after his sin, “don’t take your Holy Spirit from me.” (Psalm 51:11) But in the New Testament the Lord promised, “he lives with you, and will be in you.” (John 14:17) From the day of Pentecost onwards, the Holy Spirit has come to live inside everyone who belongs to the Lord.

The Greek word for “led,” ἄγω (agō), is passive in Romans 8:14, meaning “to be brought along.” It is used of a shepherd leading his sheep and of a person being shown the way. It does not mean “to be pushed along” but “to be taken along” — a walking together that needs you to be willing to keep up.

The Greek for “works” is ἐνεργέω (energeō). Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? It shares its root with “active” (energēs) in Hebrews 4:12. The same divine energy is at work in Scripture and at work in your heart. The word outside you and the prompting within you come from the same God, and so they will never contradict each other.

So in what ways does God speak in our hearts? At least four: promptings, thoughts, conscience, and peace or the lack of it.

The first is promptings. While Peter, on the rooftop in Joppa, was still puzzling over his vision, “the Spirit said to him, ‘Behold, three men seek you.’” (Acts 10:19) That one prompting opened the door for the gospel to reach the Gentiles.

The second is thoughts. God often places a thought within us: call so-and-so, visit so-and-so, deal properly with a certain matter. These thoughts are often very light and unremarkable, yet they tend to be remarkably accurate.

The third is conscience. Paul says, “I tell the truth in Christ. I am not lying, my conscience testifying with me in the Holy Spirit.” (Romans 9:1) Notice Paul’s wording — his conscience bears witness “in the Holy Spirit.” Conscience in itself is not the Holy Spirit, but the Holy Spirit uses a conscience he has cleansed to speak.

The fourth is peace or the lack of peace. Paul says, “And let the peace of God rule in your hearts.” (Colossians 3:15) The Greek for “rule” is βραβεύω (brabeuō), originally meaning “to act as umpire, to arbitrate.” Like the referee in a match, peace blows the whistle in your heart: this step is fine, that one is not.

But here comes the question — the one more brothers and sisters ask me than any other: how do I tell whether this is God’s voice or just my own thinking?

Scripture gives us a clear measuring rod: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” (Romans 8:6)

The Greek for “mind” is φρόνημα (phronēma), the bent of a person’s thinking, the direction the whole person is facing. So this verse is not about a thought that occasionally flickers past; it is about the orientation of your whole self.

From this verse we can draw out three tests.

First, look at the fruit. God’s voice brings life and peace; the voice of the flesh brings confusion and unrest. Note that peace does not mean things going smoothly. When Jonah was running from God he found a ship, paid his fare and slept soundly; everything went smoothly all the way — but there was no peace in his heart. On the other hand, Paul was compelled by the Holy Spirit to go up to Jerusalem, knowing full well that chains were waiting for him, and yet he said, “nor do I hold my life dear to myself.” (Acts 20:24) Outside, a storm; inside, peace.

Second, see whether it agrees with Scripture. The Holy Spirit will never lead you to do what the Bible plainly forbids. Any “prompting” that goes against the clear teaching of Scripture, however strong it feels, is not the Holy Spirit. This is the standard standing guard.

Third, see whether it lifts up Jesus. The Lord said that when the Holy Spirit comes, “He will glorify me” (John 16:14). Any voice that puffs you up, that makes you feel more spiritual than others, that makes you want to control other people, is not from the Holy Spirit. This is precisely the second of the 321 Two Core Values: let Jesus receive all the glory.

Here I need to draw a very important distinction. The Holy Spirit lives in the “heart,” not in the “brain.”

Of course God has given us reason, and reason is good; God wants us to love him with all our mind. But the organ that receives the things of the Spirit is the heart, not the brain. Proverbs says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) A person’s life does not flow out of the brain; it flows out of the heart.

Rely on the heart, and things become clear; rely on the brain, and things become confused. The brain is forever calculating gains and losses, projecting risks, weighing advantages, and it can never work out the item called “God’s will.” But the heart is the altar God has placed within us, and there the Holy Spirit lights the fire.

The French mathematician and thinker Blaise Pascal wrote a famous line in his Pensées: “The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.” He also said that all of humanity’s unhappiness comes from one single thing — not being able to sit quietly alone in a room. An observation made more than three hundred years ago is even truer today. On average we unlock our phones dozens of times a day; we fear silence more than we fear busyness. Yet God’s voice is very often found in the very ten minutes we are least willing to give him.

Elijah’s experience at Mount Horeb gives us the best picture. “Behold, Yahweh passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains, and broke in pieces the rocks before Yahweh; but Yahweh was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake; but Yahweh was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake a fire passed; but Yahweh was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice.” (1 Kings 19:11–12) God was not in the wind, not in the earthquake, not in the fire. God was in that still small voice.

Brothers and sisters, God’s voice is not necessarily loud, but it is always clear. He usually doesn’t rush to speak; he waits for you to be still.

321 Insight: rely on the heart, and things are clear; rely on the brain, and things are confused — because the Holy Spirit lives in the heart, not in the brain.

This is also the lesson of what the 321 vision calls selflessness. The old self lives the self-centred life; everything revolves around “me,” so inside there is always one very loud voice talking, and that voice is “I.” When the voice of “I” is that loud, of course God’s still small voice is drowned out. The new self is selfless — not by reducing the self to empty nothing, but by giving up the throne so that Christ may reign as King within. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. When “I” fall silent, God’s voice becomes clear.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Hearing God Is a Road Back to Our Originally Intended Position
sections.html:
Let’s set today’s three key points within the 321 framework and look at them again; a complete picture will emerge.

The Three Foundations correspond exactly to the three ways God speaks. Jesus is my role model — the Lord himself is the Son of God who said, “everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you”; on earth he lived a life of constantly listening to the Father. The Bible is my standard — God speaks through Scripture, and every prompting must come back to this measuring rod to be tested. The Holy Spirit is my guide — God speaks in our hearts, turning the word outside us into life within us. Brothers and sisters, these Three Foundations are not three separate things; they are one and the same God saying one and the same thing to you on three levels.

The Two Core Values determine our motive for listening. Let Jesus be King — when we seek God’s guidance, it is not to get God to approve our plans but to hand over the throne and let him give the orders. Many people pray for God to speak when in their hearts they have already decided; they just want God to endorse it. That isn’t listening; that’s holding a vote. Let Jesus receive all the glory — every voice that truly comes from God will in the end give the glory to Jesus, not to the person who “heard” it.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. God has never spoken to people merely to soothe their personal feelings, but to build his kingdom. God spoke to Noah so that the ark would be built; God spoke to Abraham so that a nation would be founded; God spoke to Moses so that the tabernacle would be built; God spoke to Peter so that the door to the Gentiles would be opened. When God speaks to you today, it will surely have something to do with his kingdom on earth too.

Now look at the core message. The self-centred life and selflessness are precisely the watershed between not hearing and hearing. The old self is self-centred: the self sits on the throne within, so the loudest voices inside are its own desires, its own fears, its own face. The new self is selfless: it yields the throne to Christ, and then everything inside grows quiet, and God’s still small voice can be heard. So we say: only selflessness can hear God; only selflessness can let Jesus reign as King.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. This principle is especially true when it comes to listening. A proud person can’t even take in what his spouse, his children or his co-workers say — so how could he possibly hear what God says? Only someone who has learned to listen quietly before people will listen quietly before God. So the practice of listening to God begins with the practice of listening to people.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry.
