Many people are in a hurry to ask God, “What ministry should I be doing?” But God often asks first, “Will you be with me first?” God’s first purpose in speaking is to build a relationship with you, not to hand out jobs. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. God’s voice reaches us along exactly that order.

A change of perspective. When we truly hear God, our perspective is turned upside down — from man’s perspective to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. On the Damascus road Saul had all four perspectives overturned by a single sentence. He went from “zeal for his own religion” to “suffering for the name of Christ,” and from pursuing a position on earth to pursuing a reward in heaven.

The 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; live the life of “0” (selflessness), and you will bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Of the nine, the first is love, one is gentleness, and another is self-control. Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that these fruits all have to do with listening? Someone without self-control always has a mouth faster than his ears; someone without gentleness only wants to persuade, never to listen. So “hearing God” is not an isolated devotional technique; it bears fruit directly in your relationships with your family, your colleagues and your co-workers.

The 235 relationships. When you begin to hear God, you need a “2” — a selfless spiritual companion who can discern with you and confirm with you. For Scripture says, “Where there is no counsel, plans fail; but in a multitude of counselors they are established.” (Proverbs 15:22) God often puts half of what you have heard with someone else. Next come the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children — to pass on what you have heard; and then it widens into the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, establishing God’s system together.

Finally, there is the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. First the Holy Spirit’s guidance (Spirit), then understanding from Scripture (Understanding), then the life lived out (Life), then entering into service (Service), and at last giving all the glory to God (God). You see, the starting point of this whole road is listening. If you don’t listen, nothing happens.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Three Practices, Eight Stages
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. I want to take them deeper using the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Practise listening quietly for God’s voice every day

Set aside ten minutes every day. Don’t talk, don’t analyse; just be still before God and say to the Lord, “Lord, here I am; please speak to me.” Learn to turn from busyness to listening, and let your heart tune in to God’s frequency.

Information: first know a fact — God is a God who speaks, and he often speaks in a still small voice (1 Kings 19:12).

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to show you that part of your busyness over these years has really been a way of avoiding stillness.

Conviction: truly believe in your heart that “these ten minutes are not wasted; they are the most important ten minutes of my day.”

Implementation: starting tomorrow morning — a fixed time, a fixed place, a fixed posture, and your phone in another room. For the first five minutes do only one thing: breathe, and say to the Lord, “Lord, here I am.”

Evaluation: after a week, ask yourself — did I really become still? Or did I just move my thinking to a different place?

Correction: if ten minutes is too hard, start with three; if early morning is impossible, switch to bedtime. What matters is not the time slot but that you don’t break the chain.

Repetition: keep it up for forty days in a row. A study published in 2010 by the psychologist Phillippa Lally and her team at University College London found that a new habit takes on average sixty-six days to become automatic — and that missing a day or two along the way does not ruin the whole habit. So don’t give up just because you missed a day.

Multiplication: find a brother or sister and invite them to do these forty days of stillness with you, sharing with each other once a week.

Practice 2: Read the Bible prayerfully, and let Scripture become God’s voice

When you read the Bible, don’t just aim to understand the content; pray as you go: “Lord, what do you want to say to me?” Turn the text into a conversation, and let the Holy Spirit turn the words into life.

Information: know that the Bible is “living and active” (Hebrews 4:12); it will speak to you of its own accord.

Revelation: ask the Lord to show you that your Bible reading in the past has often stopped at “I understand” and never reached “my heart is on fire.”

Conviction: believe that reading the Bible is keeping an appointment, not handing in homework.

Implementation: read only a short passage each day, and when you finish, do three things. First, ask: what does this passage show me about who God is? Second, ask: Lord, what do you want to say to me today? Third, write down in a notebook, in a single line, the one thing the Lord said to you.

Evaluation: at the weekend, look back over those seven lines and see what theme God has been speaking to you about this week. You’ll be surprised how often it’s the same thing.

Correction: if a whole week goes by and you can’t write a single line, halve the amount you read. Hearing one sentence is better than finishing a whole chapter.

Repetition: let this way of reading replace your old method, and keep it up for three months.

Multiplication: share your “one-line notes” in your small group, and draw the whole group into reading the Bible this way.

Practice 3: Pay attention to the promptings of your heart and obey at once

When a peaceful leading, a reminder or a rebuke arises in your heart, don’t delay and don’t analyse — obey at once. Obey once, and it becomes easier to hear the next time.

Information: know that the Holy Spirit’s most common ways are promptings in the heart, thoughts, conscience and peace.

Revelation: think back over the past year. Was there a prompting you ignored at the time and regretted afterwards?

Conviction: believe that obedience is not a burden; it is the way we walk with God. The Lord said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27) Notice the order — first they hear, then they follow.

Implementation: begin with the smallest act of obedience. If today a thought comes telling you to phone someone, make the call within three minutes. Don’t put it off till the afternoon, and don’t analyse it first.

Evaluation: before you sleep at night, spend two minutes looking back: what did God say to me today? Did I obey?

Correction: if you find yourself delaying again and again, name the reason for the delay. More often than not it’s the fear of losing face, or the wish to control the outcome. Hand both of those over to the Lord.

Repetition: do this two-minute review every evening for a month.

Multiplication: as your stories of obedience start to pile up, tell them. Your testimony will become a doorway through which others hear God.

A Gentle Reminder

First, God is always speaking; the question is whether you are listening.

Second, God’s voice is not necessarily loud, but it is always clear.

Third, God’s voice is not confused; it brings life and peace.

That is why Scripture reminds us, “Don’t quench the Spirit.” (1 Thessalonians 5:19) The Greek word for “quench” is σβέννυμι (sbennymi), originally “to put out a fire by pouring water on it.” Brothers and sisters, the Holy Spirit’s prompting is like a candle flame just lit, easily put out by three things: delay, analysis, and other people’s idle talk. May the Lord guard that little flame within us.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Lord, Here I Am — I Am Willing to Listen
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, everything we have said today can really be gathered into one sentence: God is not a distant God; he is a God who speaks, who guides and who leads.

The question has never been whether God is speaking, but whether you are listening with your heart.

When you begin to rely on the heart, you will discover that the Bible is speaking to you, that the Holy Spirit is speaking within you, that God is speaking in every moment of your life. You will find that the things you took for coincidences were in fact arranged; that the promptings you dismissed as emotion were in fact a call; that the verses you have read for ten years suddenly open their mouths and speak to you.

Brothers and sisters, please remember our two sentences for today: only selflessness can hear God; only selflessness can let Jesus reign as King.

For as long as “I” sit on the throne, the voice of “I” will drown out everything else. When “I” step down and let Jesus take the throne, everything inside grows quiet. At that point it isn’t that you have become better at listening; it’s that you have finally returned to your originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

The purpose of all this is not to make us spiritual experts who can go and set others straight; it is to let Jesus be King and to let Jesus receive all the glory. Someone who has truly heard God won’t have “I heard him” written on his face, but “He is worthy.”

From today on, let’s learn one thing, and it comes down to a single sentence:

Lord, here I am. I am willing to listen.

prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you that you are not a silent God. You spoke at creation, you spoke on the cross, and you are still speaking this very morning.

Lord, forgive us. All these years we have been too busy, too noisy, too full. We have relied on the brain and not on the heart; we have set our minds on the flesh and not on the Spirit. We have often asked you to speak, yet we were not ready to listen.
Lord, open our ears, and open our hearts too. Remove the loud, talking “I” within us, and reign as King in us.
When we read your word, set our hearts on fire; when we are still, help us discern your still small voice; and whenever we are prompted, help us obey at once.
Make us people who hear your voice, understand your heart and obey your leading; and use us, we pray, to carry your voice to those who are still in darkness.
May all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

blog.title: God Has Always Been Speaking — But Are You Listening?

blocks.x: — The Ways God Speaks to People (Part 1)
Please do one thing first: be still for thirty seconds. Don’t do anything. Just listen.

What did you hear? The low hum of the air conditioner, birdsong outside the window, your own breathing. Those sounds didn’t appear in these thirty seconds; it was only in these thirty seconds that you heard them.

In 1953 Colin Cherry of Imperial College London discovered “the cocktail party effect”: in a noisy banquet hall you hear only the friend in front of you — yet let someone at the far end softly mention your name, and you turn your head at once. The conclusion is simple: we do not hear every sound; we hear the sounds we care about.
The spiritual world is just the same. The question has never been whether God is speaking, but whether we are listening.
1. He Has Always Been a God Who Speaks

On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus said to his disciples: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.” (John 15:15)

The difference between a servant and a friend is not how much they do, but whether they are told. God doesn’t want a crowd of servants who can only carry out orders; he wants friends who know his heart. God speaks not in order to issue commands, but in order to share his heart.

Samuel’s day is described with the words “Yahweh’s word was rare in those days. There were not many visions” — and yet in that very same chapter God called four times in a single night. What was rare was never God’s word; it was people who heard it.
2. He Speaks in Three Very Ordinary Ways

First, he speaks in person. Samuel heard his own name being called; Saul, on the Damascus road, heard the words, “Why do you persecute me?” The key is not how loud the voice was, but that Samuel answered, “Here I am!” In Hebrew, hineni — not answering a roll call, but an act of surrender.

Second, he speaks through the Bible. “For the word of God is living and active.” (Hebrews 4:12) The Greek word for “active” is the very root of the English word “energy”. Yet Paul reminds us, “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” The Bible is like a letter, the Holy Spirit is like the one who reads the letter aloud to you, and your heart is the receiver. Without the Holy Spirit, the Bible is just print; with the Holy Spirit, the Bible becomes a voice. The disciples on the road to Emmaus said, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us?” The sign of truly hearing is not “I understand” but “my heart has been set on fire.”

Third, he speaks in your heart — and this is the most common way of all. He speaks to you through promptings, thoughts, conscience, and peace or the lack of it. The measuring rod for discerning is clear: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” God’s voice brings life and peace; the voice of the flesh brings confusion and unrest. But remember: peace does not mean things going smoothly. When Jonah was running from God, everything went smoothly all the way — yet there was no peace inside him.
3. Those Who Hear Are Those Who Have Given Up the Throne

At Mount Horeb Elijah lived through a wind, an earthquake and a fire, and God was in none of them — “After the fire, there was a still small voice.” God’s voice is not necessarily loud, but it is always clear. He usually doesn’t rush to speak; he waits for you to be still.

This is exactly what the 3-2-1 vision calls selflessness. The old self is self-centred, and the loudest voice inside is “I” — my plans, my grievances, my face. When the voice of “I” is that loud, of course God’s still small voice is drowned out. The new self is selfless: it gives up the throne and lets Christ reign as King within, and then everything inside grows quiet.
Only selflessness can hear God; only selflessness can let Jesus reign as King.

So begin today with three small practices: ten minutes of stillness each day, saying to the Lord, “Lord, here I am”; one more question as you read the Bible — “Lord, what do you want to say to me today?”; and whenever a prompting comes, obey it within three minutes. Obey once, and it becomes easier to hear the next time.

Scripture says, “Don’t quench the Spirit.” (1 Thessalonians 5:19) In the original, it means: don’t pour water on the fire and put it out. The Holy Spirit’s prompting is like a candle flame just lit, and it fears three things most: delay, analysis, and other people’s idle talk.
Reflection Question
Think back over the past year. Was there a prompting that was really God speaking, which at the time you took for something else? If it happened again today, how would you respond?
