script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Our theme today is “Hearing God’s Voice” — the first part of “The Ways God Speaks to People”.
The Lord Jesus said, “But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.” (John 15:15)

Brothers and sisters, did you catch that? The reason the Lord calls us friends is this: he has told us everything he heard from the Father. God speaks not in order to issue commands, but in order to share his heart.
Let’s do one thing first. Please be still for thirty seconds. Don’t do anything. Just listen.
What did you hear? The air conditioner? Birdsong outside the window? Your own breathing?
Brothers and sisters, those sounds didn’t appear thirty seconds ago; thirty seconds ago you just weren’t listening.

In 1953 the British scientist Colin Cherry discovered “the cocktail party effect”: in a noisy banquet hall you hear only the person you care about. We do not hear every sound; we hear the sounds we care about.
So today’s question is not, “Is God speaking?” Today’s question is, “Am I listening?”
Our key verse was spoken on the night the Lord was betrayed. Judas had already gone out, and the cross was at the door.
The Lord said: the servant doesn’t know what his lord does — but I have called you friends.
Brothers and sisters, what is the difference between a servant and a friend? It isn’t how much or how little they do. It’s whether they are told.
God doesn’t want a crowd of servants who can only carry out orders; God wants friends who know his heart.
Today we’re going to look at three ways: God speaking in person, God speaking through the Bible, and God speaking in your heart.
First, God speaks in person.
Scripture says, “Yahweh called Samuel.” (1 Samuel 3:4)
And again, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4)
That was a dark age. Scripture says, “Yahweh’s word was rare in those days. There were not many visions, then.” And yet in that very same chapter God called four times in a single night.
Brothers and sisters, what was rare was not God’s word; it was people who heard it.
And the one God called was not the old priest but a boy. God is willing to speak to people — that is his heart.
But the key lies in one sentence. Samuel said, “Here I am!”
In Hebrew that is hineni. Abraham said it, Moses said it, Isaiah said it too. It isn’t answering a roll call; it’s an act of surrender. It means: Lord, all of me is here before you.

I often say the human heart is like a radio. Right now, in this room, the signals of dozens of stations are all here, without a moment’s pause. Tune it right, and you hear; tune it wrong, and there is nothing but silence.
What is God’s frequency? Humility. Scripture says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)
The humble hear God easily; the proud hear only themselves.
Second, God speaks through the Bible.
Scripture says, “For the word of God is living and active.” (Hebrews 4:12)
“Living” means it is alive. The word for “active” is the root of the English word “energy”; it means it is at work in you right now.
Brothers and sisters, when we read the Bible, the Bible also reads us. We think we are analysing the text, when in fact the text is laying us open.
So why do some people read the Bible every day and never hear God’s voice in it?
Paul says, “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” (2 Corinthians 3:6) The word there is simply “spirit”.
Without the Holy Spirit, the Bible is just print; with the Holy Spirit, the Bible becomes a voice.
The disciples on the road to Emmaus said, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us?” (Luke 24:32)
That is the sign: not merely “I understand”, but “my heart has been set on fire”.
Augustine read Romans in a garden, and one sentence set him free. Wesley listened to someone reading Luther’s preface and said, “I felt my heart strangely warmed.”
Third, God speaks in our hearts. This is the most common way of all.
Scripture says, “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14)
Brothers and sisters, where does God speak most often? Not outside you, but inside you.
He speaks to you through promptings, thoughts, conscience, and peace or the lack of it.
While Peter was still puzzling on the rooftop, “the Spirit said to him, ‘Behold, three men seek you.’” (Acts 10:19) One prompting opened the door to the Gentiles.
But how do I tell whether this is God or just me?
Scripture gives us a measuring rod: “the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” (Romans 8:6)

Three tests. First, look at the fruit — God’s voice brings life and peace; the voice of the flesh brings confusion and unrest. Second, see whether it agrees with Scripture. Third, see whether it lifts up Jesus.
Please notice: peace does not mean things going smoothly. Jonah ran from God and everything went smoothly all the way — yet there was no peace inside him.
On Mount Horeb God was not in the wind, not in the earthquake, not in the fire; God was in that still small voice.
Brothers and sisters, God’s voice is not necessarily loud, but it is always clear. Rely on the heart, and things are clear; rely on the brain, and things are confused.
So how do we practise this lesson? Three things.
First, ten minutes every day of listening quietly to God. Don’t talk, don’t analyse; just say to the Lord, “Lord, here I am; please speak to me.”
Second, read the Bible prayerfully. When you finish, ask, “Lord, what do you want to say to me today?” Then write down, in a single line, the one thing the Lord said to you.
Third, when a prompting comes, obey at once. No delay, no analysis — do it within three minutes. Obey once, and it becomes easier to hear the next time.
Scripture says, “Don’t quench the Spirit.” (1 Thessalonians 5:19) In the original, “quench” means to put out a fire by pouring water on it.
Brothers and sisters, today’s message can be gathered into one sentence: God is not a distant God; he is a God who speaks.
The question has never been whether God is speaking, but whether you are listening with your heart.
When you begin to rely on the heart, you will discover that the Bible is speaking to you, that the Holy Spirit is speaking within you, that God is speaking in every moment of your life.
Only selflessness can hear God; only selflessness can let Jesus reign as King.
For as long as “I” sit on the throne, the voice of “I” drowns out everything else. When “I” step down and let Jesus take the throne, everything inside grows quiet.
From today on, let’s learn just one sentence: Lord, here I am. I am willing to listen.
Let’s pray together.
Dear Lord Jesus, you are not a silent God; you are still speaking this very morning. Forgive us for being too busy, too noisy, too full — for relying on the brain and not on the heart.
Open our ears, and open our hearts too. Remove the loud, talking “I” within us, and reign as King in us.
Make us people who hear your voice, understand your heart and obey your leading. May all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, may God’s word be the voice you hear today. May you hear him all through this day.
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning let’s look together at a subject that touches our whole lives: hearing God’s voice.

The Lord Jesus said, “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.” (John 15:15)
Notice the reason the Lord gives. On what basis does the Lord call us friends? Because he has told us everything he heard from the Father.
So the evidence of friendship is speech. God speaks to people not in order to issue commands, but in order to share his heart.
Before we properly begin, let’s do one small thing. Please be still for thirty seconds. Don’t do anything. Just listen.
What did you hear? The low hum of the air conditioner? Birdsong outside the window? Your own breathing?
Brothers and sisters, those sounds didn’t appear in these thirty seconds; it was only in these thirty seconds that you heard them.

The human ear can pick up sound waves from roughly twenty hertz to twenty thousand hertz. At this very moment countless waves are passing straight through your body, and you hear not one of them. Not because they don’t exist, but because your frequency isn’t tuned to them.
Our God has never been a silent God. From Genesis, “God said, ‘Let there be light,’” to Revelation, “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’” — the whole Bible is a book about a God who speaks.

In 1953 Colin Cherry of Imperial College London discovered “the cocktail party effect”: in a noisy banquet hall you hear only the friend in front of you — yet let someone at the far end softly mention your name, and you turn your head at once.
Brothers and sisters, please remember this sentence: we do not hear every sound; we hear the sounds we care about.
So the question to ask today is not whether God is speaking, but whether I am listening. It is not that God doesn’t speak — it is that we rely on the brain and not on the heart.
Our key verse comes from John’s Gospel, generally dated somewhere between AD 85 and 95.

It falls within the Upper Room Discourse of chapters 13 to 17 — the Lord’s farewell words on the night he was betrayed. Judas had already gone out, and the cross was at the door. What a man says in the last hours of his life is always what matters most to him.
“Servant” in Greek is doulos; what marks a slave is not that he does little but that he is not told. “Friend” is philos — someone who is let into the master’s inner thoughts.

How did the Lord himself live? He said, “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” (John 5:19) This is exactly the first of the 321 Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model.
Today we will look at three ways. First, God speaks in person.
Scripture says, “Yahweh called Samuel. He said, ‘Here I am.’” (1 Samuel 3:4)
And again, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4)

One was a boy in the house of God; the other a Pharisee on the road, breathing out murder. Brothers and sisters, it isn’t only prophets and apostles who can hear God’s voice. God is willing to speak to people — that has always been his heart.

Take Samuel first. It was the close of the period of the judges; the ark of the covenant rested in the tabernacle at Shiloh; Eli the high priest was old and his eyes were dim, and his two sons were wicked men.
It was a dark age, which is why Scripture says, “Yahweh’s word was rare in those days. There were not many visions, then.” (1 Samuel 3:1)
And yet in that very same chapter God called four times in a single night. Brothers and sisters, what was rare was not God’s word; it was people who heard it.
What’s even more striking is that God called three times, and three times Samuel ran to Eli. He heard the voice, but he didn’t know it was God.
Have you ever had that experience? A prompting comes, and you think you’re overthinking it; a word pierces you, and you put it down to emotion. In fact it was God calling your name.
The turning point that night came when Samuel finally said those words: “Speak; for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:10)
“Here I am” in Hebrew is hineni. Abraham said it on Mount Moriah; Moses said it before the burning bush; Isaiah said it in the temple: “Here I am. Send me!”
The word isn’t answering a roll call; it’s an act of surrender. It means: Lord, all of me is here before you — do with me whatever you will.
Brothers and sisters, Samuel didn’t first analyse where the voice came from; he simply gave himself over. That is the response of the heart, not the analysis of the brain.

I often use the radio as an illustration. Right now the signals of dozens of stations are all here in this room, without a moment’s pause. Tune it right, and you hear; tune it wrong, and there is nothing but silence.

What is God’s frequency? Humility. Scripture says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) The Greek word for “resists” is a military term, meaning to draw up in battle array against.

In 1999 Simons and Chabris ran the “invisible gorilla” experiment: participants concentrated on counting passes, someone in a gorilla suit walked through the frame for nine seconds, and roughly half of them never saw it at all.
The spiritual world has the same kind of deafness. When we are absorbed in our own plans and grievances, God can stand right in front of us and speak, and we will not hear.
So the 321 Insight says: the humble hear God easily; the proud hear only themselves.
Second, God speaks through the Bible.
Scripture says, “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword … and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” (Hebrews 4:12)
“Living” in the original simply means “alive”. The Bible is not a sealed ancient document; open it today, and it will speak to you.
The Greek word for “active” is the root of the English word “energy”; it means “at work”.
Brothers and sisters, when we read the Bible, the Bible also reads us. We think we are analysing the text, when in fact the text is laying us open.
So why do some people read the Bible every day and never hear God’s voice in it?
Paul says, “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” (2 Corinthians 3:6) The word in the original is simply “spirit”.

I often put it like this: the Bible is like a letter, the Holy Spirit is like the one who reads the letter aloud to you, and your heart is the receiver. Without the Holy Spirit, the Bible is just print; with the Holy Spirit, the Bible becomes a voice.

The Lord once said to the Pharisees, “You search the Scriptures … Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.” (John 5:39–40) They knew the Scriptures inside out, and walked straight past the Lord.
So when God really does speak through the Bible, what are the signs?
The disciples on the road to Emmaus said, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us?” (Luke 24:32) “Burning” in the original means “ablaze, on fire”.
Brothers and sisters, that is the sign: not merely “I understand”, but “my heart has been set on fire”.

In the summer of AD 386 Augustine sat weeping in a garden in Milan when suddenly he heard a child next door chanting, “Take up and read, take up and read.” He opened Paul’s letters, read Romans chapter 13, and every shadow of doubt vanished at once.

More than thirteen hundred years later, on 24 May 1738, in Aldersgate Street in London, a discouraged clergyman named John Wesley listened as someone read Luther’s preface to Romans, and he wrote: “I felt my heart strangely warmed.”
The verses hadn’t changed. What changed was that in that moment the Holy Spirit aimed them squarely at these men.
So the Bible is my standard, and the Holy Spirit is my guide. These two foundations must be held together as one.
A standard without a guide turns faith into legalism — correct, but lifeless. A guide without a standard turns faith into mysticism — lively, but rootless.
The psalm says, “Be still, and know that I am God.” (Psalm 46:10) The Hebrew word for “be still” means “to let go, to let your hands drop”. Let go first — and then you will know that he is God.

In 2001 the neuroscientist Marcus Raichle proposed the brain’s “default mode network”: when people grow quiet, certain regions of the brain actually become more active — and that is the crucial moment when insight arrives.
So when God made us, he had already written “only in stillness can you hear” into our very bodies.
Third, God speaks in our hearts. This is the most common way of all.
Scripture says, “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14)
And again, “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:13)

This is the greatest grace of the New Testament. In Old Testament times the Spirit of God came upon people and could depart again; but in the New Testament the Lord promised, “he lives with you, and will be in you.” (John 14:17)

One more detail: the word “works” in Philippians shares its root with the word “active” in Hebrews. The word outside you and the prompting within you come from the same God, and so they will never contradict each other.
So in what ways does God speak in our hearts? At least four: promptings, thoughts, conscience, and peace or the lack of it.

The first is promptings. While Peter, on the rooftop in Joppa, was still puzzling, “the Spirit said to him, ‘Behold, three men seek you.’” (Acts 10:19) That one prompting opened the door for the gospel to reach the Gentiles.
The second is thoughts. God often places a thought within you: make a phone call, go and visit someone. The thought is very light, yet it tends to be remarkably accurate.

The third is conscience. Paul says, “my conscience testifying with me in the Holy Spirit.” (Romans 9:1) Conscience is not the same as the Holy Spirit, but the Holy Spirit uses a conscience he has cleansed.
The fourth is peace. “And let the peace of God rule in your hearts.” (Colossians 3:15) “Rule” originally means to act as umpire — peace blows the whistle in your heart.
But how do I tell whether this is God’s voice or just my own thinking?
Scripture gives us a measuring rod: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” (Romans 8:6)
First, look at the fruit. God’s voice brings life and peace; the voice of the flesh brings confusion and unrest.

But please notice: peace does not mean things going smoothly. Jonah ran from God, and everything went smoothly all the way, yet there was no peace inside him; Paul knew full well that chains awaited him in Jerusalem, and yet he said, “nor do I hold my life dear to myself.” Outside, a storm; inside, peace.

Second, see whether it agrees with Scripture. Third, see whether it lifts up Jesus. The Lord said that when the Holy Spirit comes, “He will glorify me.” Any voice that puffs you up or makes you want to control others is not from the Holy Spirit.
Brothers and sisters, the Holy Spirit lives in the “heart”, not in the “brain”.
Reason is good, but the organ that receives the things of the Spirit is the heart. Proverbs says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

Rely on the heart, and things become clear; rely on the brain, and things become confused. For the brain is forever calculating gains and losses, and it can never work out the item called “God’s will”.

What did Elijah hear at Mount Horeb? “But Yahweh was not in the wind … Yahweh was not in the earthquake … Yahweh was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice.” (1 Kings 19:11–12)
God’s voice is not necessarily loud, but it is always clear. He usually doesn’t rush to speak; he waits for you to be still.
So how do we practise this lesson? The lesson gives us three things.

First, practise listening quietly for God every day. Set aside ten minutes. Don’t talk, don’t analyse; just say to the Lord, “Lord, here I am; please speak to me.” A fixed time, a fixed place, and your phone in another room.

Second, read the Bible prayerfully. As you read, keep asking, “Lord, what do you want to say to me today?” Then write down, in a single line, the one thing the Lord said to you. At the weekend look back over those seven lines, and you’ll find God has been speaking about the same thing all along.
We can also take this deeper with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
The third practice: pay attention to the promptings of your heart, and obey at once.
Don’t delay, don’t analyse — obey at once. Obey once, and it becomes easier to hear the next time.
The Lord said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27) Notice the order — first they hear, then they follow.

In 2010 Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London found that a new habit takes on average sixty-six days to become automatic, and that missing a day or two along the way doesn’t ruin it. Brothers and sisters, if you miss a day, don’t give up.
Scripture reminds us, “Don’t quench the Spirit.” (1 Thessalonians 5:19) In the original, “quench” means to put out a fire by pouring water on it.
Let’s set today’s message within the 321 framework.
The Three Foundations correspond exactly to the three ways God speaks: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

The Two Core Values determine our motive for listening. Let Jesus be King — seeking God is not asking him to approve my plans, but handing over the throne. Many people pray for God to speak when in their hearts they have already decided; they just want God to endorse it. That isn’t listening; that’s holding a vote.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. God spoke to Noah so that the ark would be built, and to Moses so that the tabernacle would be built. When God speaks to you today, it will surely have something to do with his kingdom too.
And remember: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Don’t forget 235 either — God often puts half of what you have heard with someone else.
Brothers and sisters, everything we have said today can be gathered into one sentence: God is not a distant God; he is a God who speaks, who guides and who leads.
The question has never been whether God is speaking, but whether you are listening with your heart.

So let’s declare together: Lord Jesus, I believe you are a God who speaks. I am not someone who cannot hear; I am your sheep. I will learn to rely on the heart and not the brain; I will set my mind on the Spirit, not on the flesh.

Only selflessness can hear God; only selflessness can let Jesus reign as King. For as long as “I” sit on the throne, the voice of “I” drowns out everything else; when “I” step down and let Jesus take the throne, everything inside grows quiet.
From today on, let’s learn just one sentence: Lord, here I am. I am willing to listen.
Let’s bow our heads and pray together.
Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you that you are not a silent God. You spoke at creation, you spoke on the cross, and you are still speaking this very morning.

Lord, forgive us. We have been too busy, too noisy, too full; we have relied on the brain and not on the heart. Open our ears, and open our hearts too; remove the loud, talking “I” within us, and reign as King in us.

When we read your word, set our hearts on fire; when we are still, help us discern your still small voice; and whenever we are prompted, help us obey at once. May all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, may God’s word be the voice you hear today. May you hear him all through this day.

sections.heading: Introduction: You Heard It — You Just Weren’t Listening
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

In 1953 Colin Cherry, a cognitive scientist at Imperial College London, carried out a study of what would later be called “the cocktail party effect.” He discovered something remarkable: in a banquet hall full of voices, clinking glasses and loud music, a person can somehow pick out, from dozens of sounds, the one voice he is concentrating on. Six years later Neville Moray of the University of Oxford found something more remarkable still: even while you are deep in conversation with the person in front of you, if someone at the far side of the room calls your name, your ears turn towards it instantly.

These studies concluded that human hearing is never a passive radio; it is an active choice. It isn’t that we can’t hear; it’s that we aren’t listening.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what this lesson wants to say to us today.

In the last lesson we saw that God is a God who speaks. He spoke on the very first day of creation: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” (Genesis 1:3) And the first thing he did after making man was to speak with him. The sixty-six books of the Bible are, from beginning to end, the record of “God speaking to people.”

But today we want to see something further: God does not speak in only one way. He is the God who created heaven and earth and all things, and his speaking is rich, varied and beyond all limits. He speaks through prophecy, through visions and dreams, through angels, through circumstances, through an open Bible — and through a casual word of greeting.

The Bible shows us a truth of the utmost importance: God not only speaks — he speaks in all kinds of ways.

But the key has never been the method. The key is this — are you listening? Are you discerning?

A picture often comes to my mind. The radio is broadcasting, but the dial isn’t tuned properly, and the whole room fills with hissing static. The problem isn’t the station; the station has been transmitting all along. The problem is the reception. That is so often our condition: God is speaking all the time, but we are tuned to the wrong channel; we turn the volume right up, and all we hear is the echo of our own voice.

So in this lesson God wants to lead us deeper into two things: first, how God speaks to people in all kinds of ways; and second, how we can discern whether something really comes from God.

Here the 321 vision gives us its first ray of light: the focus is not the “method”; the focus is Jesus.

Some people spend their whole lives chasing dreams; some spend their whole lives chasing miracles; some spend their whole lives chasing one word from a particular prophet. But Jesus never told us to chase methods. He simply said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27) What the sheep recognise is not the shepherd’s gestures, nor the shepherd’s staff, but the shepherd’s voice. Recognising the voice is the fruit of a relationship, not the product of a technique.

And here is the second ray of light: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and things are clear; rely on the brain and ourselves, and things are confused.

The brain is an organ of analysis; the heart is an organ of reception. When we use the brain to take every prompting apart, it is like trying to grip a gust of wind with tweezers — the harder you try, the less you hold, until all that’s left is a heap of theories and a tired heart. When we rely on the heart and lean on the Holy Spirit, God’s voice comes like the light of early morning: it doesn’t dazzle, yet it makes everything plain. Scripture says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) Rely on the heart, and you rejoice; rely on the brain, and you worry. Brothers and sisters, this is not a slogan; it is a real road.

This morning, let’s ask the Lord together to retune the dial of our inner receiver to him.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: God Speaking in the Last Days, Men Moved by the Holy Spirit
sections.html:
Today we have two key passages, one from 2 Peter and one from Hebrews. To understand them, we first need to stand in the situation of the time.

2 Peter was written by the apostle Peter. From the tone of the letter, these are his last words, written before his martyrdom. He says, “knowing that the putting off of my tent comes swiftly, even as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me.” (2 Peter 1:14) The letter is generally dated to the mid-to-late AD 60s and was written to believers scattered in many places. The church at that time faced a serious problem: false teachers were arising, interpreting God’s word to suit themselves and using grace as an excuse for licence.

In chapter 1 Peter speaks of the Transfiguration, which he saw with his own eyes; he says they “were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2 Peter 1:16). But straight after that he says something unexpected: “We have the more sure word of prophecy” (2 Peter 1:19). Notice that Peter does not say, “My experience is more reliable than Scripture.” What he says is this — Scripture is more certain than my experience.

This is the foundation of today’s lesson. An apostle who had seen Jesus’ glory with his own eyes and heard the voice from heaven with his own ears turns round and hands the highest authority to the word God inspired. Brothers and sisters, if even Peter did that, how can we place one dream or one feeling of ours above the Bible?

Then Peter explains why: “For no prophecy ever came by the will of man: but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.” (2 Peter 1:21) The Greek word for “moved” here is pherō, meaning “to be carried along, to be borne.” In Acts 27:15 the same word describes a ship in a storm being “driven along” by the wind. It is a vivid picture: the prophet is like a ship and the Holy Spirit is the wind. The wind sets the course; the ship’s only task is to spread its sails. God’s word is reliable not because the one speaking is so clever, but because the one carrying him along is the Holy Spirit.

As for Hebrews, Scripture doesn’t name its author. It was written to Hebrew believers who were being persecuted, who were wavering, and who wanted to retreat into the old system of Judaism; it is generally dated before the destruction of the temple in AD 70. The book opens with a stunning declaration: “God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son.” (Hebrews 1:1–2)

“At many times and in various ways” is, in Greek, two adverbs: polymerōs (in many portions, piece by piece) and polytropōs (in many manners, through many different channels). This is exactly the theme of today’s lesson: the “amount” of God’s speaking has built up portion by portion, and the “ways” of God’s speaking are many and varied. He spoke through the Law, through the prophets, through history, through the altar, through visions and dreams, through the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire.

But Hebrews goes on to its summit: in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son. All the ways at last flow together into one Person — Jesus Christ. He is God’s most complete, most clear and most final Word.

So we can sum up the background like this: the ways God speaks are many, but the centre of God’s speaking is one. His channels are many; his focus is One alone. Revelation could not put it more plainly: “for the testimony of Jesus is the Spirit of Prophecy.” (Revelation 19:10)

Brothers and sisters, every voice that truly comes from God will bring you back to Jesus, to let Jesus be King and to let Jesus receive all the glory. Anything that takes you somewhere else — however moving, however overwhelming — calls for you to stop and discern.

sections.heading: 1. God Speaks Through Prophecy: He Entrusts His Heart to People
sections.html:
Scripture says, “For no prophecy ever came by the will of man: but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.” (2 Peter 1:21)

What is the essence of prophecy? As soon as many people hear the word “prophecy,” they think of fortune-telling, of predicting what will happen tomorrow. But the emphasis of prophecy in the Bible is not predicting the future; it is conveying God’s heart.

The Hebrew word for “prophet” is nabi, whose root has to do with “proclaiming, announcing.” The Greek prophētēs is made up of pro (before, on behalf of) and phēmi (to speak), meaning “one who speaks on behalf of another.” A prophet is not a futurologist; a prophet is God’s spokesman. What makes a prophet a prophet is not that he can tell fortunes, but that God says, “Surely the Lord Yahweh will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.” (Amos 3:7)

So the heart of prophecy is this — God entrusts his heart to people.

What an astonishing thing that is. The God who created the universe is willing to tell what is on his heart to people who grow weak, who fail, who run away. It is like a father crouching down to tell his child the family’s plans — not because the child is able to carry them, but because the father wants the child to have a share in them.

In the Old Testament God spoke chiefly through prophets. From Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Isaiah and Jeremiah down to Malachi, God chose a small group of people and put his words in their mouths.

But in the New Testament something even more stunning happened. On the day of Pentecost Peter stood up and quoted Joel: “‘It will be in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your young men will see visions. Your old men will dream dreams.” (Acts 2:17)

Notice the shift: from “a small group of people” to “all flesh.” From God’s prophets to all God’s children.

God does not use only special people; God is willing to use everyone who belongs to him.

That is what Paul says in 1 Corinthians: “But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” (1 Corinthians 14:3) Brothers and sisters, look closely at those three words — edification, exhortation, consolation. That is the function of New Testament prophecy. God wants to use your mouth to lift up someone who has lost heart, and your word to bring back someone who has lost their way.

I know of a very common kind of scene. Early one morning, as she reads the Bible, a sister finds a friend she hasn’t contacted for years coming to mind, so she sends a short message: “I prayed for you this morning. God hasn’t forgotten you.” The friend replies that only the night before she had been about to give up on everything. That is the essence of prophecy — God entrusts his heart to people, and people pass God’s heart on to people.

But precisely because the door has been opened so wide, discernment becomes all the more important.

Not every voice is God’s voice. Some people use the words “God told me” as a shield, packaging their own ideas, their own emotions, even their own ambitions, as the will of God. That is why Paul laid down rules: “Let the prophets speak, two or three, and let the others discern.” (1 Corinthians 14:29) And again: “Don’t quench the Spirit. Don’t despise prophecies. Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.” (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21)

Notice Paul’s balance: don’t quench, but don’t believe blindly either; don’t despise, but don’t swallow everything whole either. These two sayings are like a pair of chopsticks: lose one, and you can’t pick anything up.

So the key to prophecy is not the “speaking” but two things: does it come from the Holy Spirit, and does it agree with Scripture?

Psychology gives us a sobering reminder here. In 1960 the British psychologist Peter Wason found, in his famous “2-4-6 experiment,” that once people have a hypothesis in mind, they unconsciously look only for evidence that supports it and ignore the evidence against it. The phenomenon later became known as “confirmation bias.” In other words, when I already want something in my heart, it is very easy for me to “hear” God agreeing with me — in the Bible, in a sermon, in something someone says.

That isn’t God speaking. That’s me speaking — just using God’s voice.

The 321 vision puts it with great precision here: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred easily speak their own minds; only the selfless can become an outlet for God.

What is selflessness? Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) A truly selfless person is still before speaking; he is in no hurry to prove what he has heard, and he cares far more about whether God’s heart has been passed on accurately.

Brothers and sisters, the cleaner the pipe, the clearer the water. Our “self” is the rust on the inside of the pipe. May the Lord cleanse our pipes today, so that we become an outlet for God’s heart and not a loudspeaker for our own ideas.

sections.heading: 2. God Speaks Through Visions and Dreams: He Opens Our Spiritual Eyes
sections.html:
The Bible is full of visions and dreams.

At Troas, where Paul’s way forward had been blocked again and again, “A vision appeared to Paul in the night. There was a man of Macedonia standing, begging him, and saying, ‘Come over into Macedonia and help us.’” (Acts 16:9) That one vision carried the gospel from Asia into Europe and rewrote the direction of the whole of Western civilisation.

Jacob, on the run, fell asleep with a stone for a pillow, and “He dreamed and saw a stairway set upon the earth, and its top reached to heaven. Behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it.” (Genesis 28:12) When he woke he said something deeply moving: “Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn’t know it.” (Genesis 28:16)

After the wise men from the east had offered their gifts, “Being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own country another way.” (Matthew 2:12) A single dream saved the life of the holy Child.

All these accounts tell us the same thing: God speaks to people in “pictures.”

Sometimes it is in prayer, sometimes in sleep, sometimes even in a state wholly taken over by the Holy Spirit. Acts 10 records that while Peter was praying on the roof in Joppa, “he fell into a trance. He saw heaven opened” (Acts 10:10–11), and with a great sheet and all kinds of living creatures God overturned his deep-rooted mindset about the Gentiles. Ezekiel 8 records that as the prophet sat in his house with the elders sitting before him, “the Spirit lifted me up between earth and the sky, and brought me in the visions of God to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 8:3), showing him the abominations hidden in the temple.

The purpose of these experiences was never mystery for its own sake, but to lead people into God’s heart.

We could put it this way: a vision is like a video from God; a dream is like a message from God.

A video is moving and whole; it lets you take in a whole situation at a glance. A message is short and precise, and it often arrives at the most critical moment. But whether video or message, the point is never how overwhelming the picture is; the point is what God wants you to understand.

There is a very real danger here. Human nature loves excitement; it loves the “special.” An ordinary morning’s Bible reading won’t get anyone excited, but one strange dream can keep someone talking for three years. And so some people start chasing experiences, and hang the thermometer of their spiritual life on the number of visions they’ve had.

Science gives us a helpful reminder. In 1953 Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman of the University of Chicago discovered rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Later sleep research tells us that adults go through roughly four to six sleep cycles a night, each lasting about ninety minutes, and that most dreams happen during REM sleep. In other words, everyone dreams every night; most of the time we have simply forgotten by the time we wake.

This scientific fact reminds us of two things. First, dreaming is a normal physiological mechanism God built into us when he made us, so not every dream has spiritual significance; most dreams are just the afterimages of the day. Second, precisely because dreaming is so ordinary, the fact that God chooses to speak to people through such an ordinary channel actually shows his humility and tenderness — he stoops down to us and slips his heart in at the very moments when we are least on guard and least able to analyse with our brains.

So how do we discern?

The Bible itself gives us the standard. Jeremiah records God rebuking the false prophets: “The prophet who has a dream, let him tell a dream; and he who has my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the straw to the wheat?” (Jeremiah 23:28) God does not reject dreams; he simply ranks dreams and his word: the dream is straw, the word is wheat. Straw is not evil; you just can’t make a meal of it.

So please remember: every vision and every dream must be brought back to the Bible to be tested; every picture must point to Jesus.

sections.heading: What the 321 Vision Says Here: Don’t Pursue Experiences — Pursue God’s Heart.
sections.html:
This is exactly the change of perspective — from man’s perspective to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly. Pursuing experiences is earthly and temporary, because experiences pass and feelings cool; pursuing God’s heart is heavenly and eternal, because God’s will endures for ever.

Brothers and sisters, visions are for seeing God, not for being seen by people. If you have never had a vision or a dream from God, you have not one bit less than anyone else; if you often have visions and dreams, you are not one bit more spiritual than anyone else. True spirituality is this: whatever God says, I obey.

sections.heading: 3. God Speaks Through Angels and Circumstances: He Rules Over All Things
sections.html:
The Bible tells us that God has two other ways of speaking: one comes from heaven, and the other from the paths you and I walk every day.

First, angels.

An angel brought the news to Mary: “The angel said to her, ‘Don’t be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and give birth to a son, and shall name him “Jesus.”’” (Luke 1:30–31)

An angel made the announcement to the shepherds: “The angel said to them, ‘Don’t be afraid, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy which will be to all the people. For there is born to you today, in David’s city, a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.’” (Luke 2:10–11)

An angel led Peter out of prison: “And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side, and woke him up, saying, ‘Stand up quickly!’ His chains fell off his hands.” (Acts 12:7)

This shows us that God can send angels to deliver his word. In both Hebrew and Greek the word for “angel” itself means “messenger, one who is sent” (Hebrew malak, Greek angelos). Angels are not objects of worship; angels are couriers carrying a message. Hebrews puts it very plainly: “Aren’t they all serving spirits, sent out to do service for the sake of those who will inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14)

Notice two important boundaries in this verse. First, angels are “serving spirits”: they serve God and they do service for us, so the one we worship is always God, never angels. Second, the angels’ work is to be “sent out”: they don’t act on their own initiative; they faithfully deliver the word of the One who sent them.

Next, circumstances.

God also speaks through circumstances. Abraham took Isaac up Mount Moriah; the knife was already raised, and “Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and saw that behind him was a ram caught in the thicket by his horns. Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering instead of his son.” (Genesis 22:13) That ram was God speaking. So Abraham named the place “Yahweh Will Provide” (Genesis 22:14).

Lot lived in Sodom and couldn’t bear to leave. “But he lingered; and the men grabbed his hand, his wife’s hand, and his two daughters’ hands, Yahweh being merciful to him; and they took him out, and set him outside of the city.” (Genesis 19:16) Those hands that took hold of him were God speaking.

Brothers and sisters, sometimes the things that happen to you are God speaking.

A door that closes, an interview that fails, a sudden illness, a phone call from someone you haven’t heard from in ages, a stranger’s chance remark — God rules over all things, and he can speak through all things. Paul says, “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.” (Romans 8:28)

C. S. Lewis is generally credited with writing these words in The Problem of Pain: God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains; pain is his megaphone to rouse a deaf world. What makes the saying so profound is that it names a fact: it isn’t that God’s volume is too low; it’s that our ears are too hard.

But here we must be especially careful.

Not every circumstance is God’s guidance. Things going smoothly does not necessarily mean God has given permission, and obstacles do not necessarily mean God has forbidden something. When Jonah fled towards Tarshish there happened to be a ship in the harbour, and he happened to be able to afford the fare — everything went smoothly. But that wasn’t God’s guidance; it was the road he had chosen for himself (Jonah 1:3). When Paul was thrown into prison in Philippi, nothing went smoothly — yet it was God’s plan to bring the jailer and his household to salvation (Acts 16).

So circumstances need to be brought back to the Holy Spirit and the truth to be discerned. Circumstances are God’s megaphone, not God’s standard; the Bible alone is the standard.

Psychology also reminds us that human beings are born pattern-spotters. The brain looks for regularities in noise, a tendency psychology calls illusory correlation, first proposed and demonstrated experimentally in 1967 by the American psychologist Loren Chapman: people link two events that are in fact unrelated into cause and effect in their memory. So when we already want to do something, every green light on the way gets read as God’s permission.

sections.heading: What the 321 Vision Says Here: God Rules Over Circumstances, but Don’t Let Circumstances Carry You Along; Let the Holy Spirit Lead You in Reading Them.
sections.html:
This too is the practice of the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Circumstances are not a fourth foundation; circumstances are material that needs to be interpreted. Who interprets them? The Holy Spirit. With what? The Bible. And once interpreted, to whom do they point? To Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When circumstances become your lord, you start to worry; when Jesus is King, you can rejoice in any circumstance.

sections.heading: 4. How to Discern God’s Voice: Three Important Principles
sections.html:
When it comes to discernment, many people go to one of two extremes.

One extreme is not believing at all that God still speaks today. People like this shut God up inside a closed book; faith becomes a body of knowledge, and prayer becomes a monologue. The other extreme is treating every voice as God’s voice. A thought in the heart, a picture in a dream, a word on the street — everything is “God told me,” until in the end their lives are pulled this way and that by all kinds of voices, and the more they listen, the more confused they become.

God’s heart is neither of these extremes. God’s heart is this — truly to hear, and rightly to discern.

Paul says, “for God is not a God of confusion, but of peace.” (1 Corinthians 14:33) God’s voice will not send you spinning in circles. He will light you up little by little with the light of early morning, not dazzle you with a flash of lightning.

The Bible gives us three very practical confirmations.

(1) The confirmation of Scripture: God’s voice will never contradict the Bible

The first test is the test of truth.

“For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” (Hebrews 4:12)

Notice that last phrase: able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart. That is exactly what we need most. Our greatest difficulty is not telling God’s voice apart from the devil’s; it is telling God’s voice apart from our own. And God’s word is like a supremely sharp blade that can divide soul from spirit — divide “what I want” from “what God wants.”

The prophet Isaiah puts it even more directly: “Turn to the law and to the covenant! If they don’t speak according to this word, surely there is no morning for them.” (Isaiah 8:20)

Brothers and sisters, this verse is the bedrock of discernment. Every prompting must be brought back to the truth to be tested. If it conflicts with the Bible, it is certainly not God. No need to pray about it for three more days, no need to ask three more people — it is certainly not God.

Someone may say, “But my feeling is so strong.” A strong feeling does not mean it comes from God. Fear can make a feeling strong; desire can make a feeling strong; long-held grievance can make a feeling strong. When the devil tempted Jesus, he quoted the Psalms too (Matthew 4:6). Scripture can be quoted, and it can also be twisted, so we must not look at one verse alone; we must interpret Scripture by Scripture and look at the consistent witness of the whole Bible.

Here is a very practical checklist, all drawn from the Bible: Does this voice lift up Jesus (Revelation 19:10)? Does it bring edification, exhortation and consolation (1 Corinthians 14:3)? Does it bear the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23)? Does it make me more humble, more obedient, more loving?

Jesus said, “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak.” (John 16:13) The Holy Spirit and the Bible always agree, because the Bible was inspired by the Holy Spirit in the first place. The Holy Spirit will not overturn the book he himself wrote.

This is the second of the 321 Three Foundations: the Bible is my standard. A standard is not a reference; a standard is a measuring rod. When the measuring rod and my feelings disagree, it is the feelings that must be adjusted, not the rod.

(2) The confirmation of the body: if God is speaking to the church, he won’t let only one person know

The second test is the test of community.

Paul says, “At the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.” (2 Corinthians 13:1) The saying is originally a principle of the Law, quoted from Deuteronomy 19:15, and Paul applies it to the church’s judgements. From the very beginning God set up a safety mechanism: important matters are not decided by one person alone.

The church at Antioch is the finest example: “As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.’” (Acts 13:2) Notice that when the Holy Spirit spoke, it was a group of people serving and fasting together. The call that sent Paul out was not announced by Paul himself; the whole church received it together, laid hands on them together and sent them off together.

The Council of Jerusalem was the same. Faced with the problem of the Gentile believers, the apostles and elders gathered to debate, to listen and to search the Scriptures, and finally said, “For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things.” (Acts 15:28) “The Holy Spirit, and to us” — what a beautiful phrase. The Holy Spirit’s guidance is confirmed within a united community.

So please remember: what truly comes from God brings unity, not division.

When a “word you’ve received” makes you start to look down on the church, drift away from your spiritual companions and feel that only you understand God, that voice is already wrong in itself. Satan’s work has always been first to separate the sheep from the flock, and then to devour them one by one.

But the confirmation of the body also takes wisdom. There are two misuses to avoid here.

The first misuse is “making up the numbers.” Some people go round asking everyone until someone says “Amen.” That isn’t confirmation; that’s looking for allies.

The second misuse is “group pressure.” In 1951 the American psychologist Solomon Asch carried out his famous line-judgement experiment: when everyone else in the room deliberately gave an obviously wrong answer, about a third of the participants’ answers in the critical rounds went along with the majority and got it wrong too. The experiment reminds us that the group is not necessarily the truth; a group that has lost the standard of truth can go wrong together.

So the precondition for the confirmation of the body is this — the people in question must be people living in the truth. This is exactly what 321 calls the 235 relationships: become a “2” with someone selfless, a spiritual companion; nurture one another in the “3” relationships of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and stand together as spiritual comrades in the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team. When you have people like that around you, your discernment is no longer a lone battle.

Brothers and sisters, people matter more than tasks. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Someone without relationships has no confirmation; someone without confirmation easily goes astray.

(3) The confirmation of time: what God says will surely come to pass

The third test is the test of time.

“So is my word that goes out of my mouth: it will not return to me void, but it will accomplish that which I please, and it will prosper in the thing I sent it to do.” (Isaiah 55:11)

What God says will surely come to pass. That is God’s nature, and it is his faithfulness. So time will prove everything.

Moses gave Israel this standard in the Law long ago: “When a prophet speaks in Yahweh’s name, if the thing doesn’t follow, nor happen, that is the thing which Yahweh has not spoken. The prophet has spoken it presumptuously. You shall not be afraid of him.” (Deuteronomy 18:22)

Brothers and sisters, time is the most honest of sieves.

But the confirmation of time calls for two attitudes.

The first is waiting. God’s promises often have a “gestation period.” Joseph had his two dreams at seventeen and stood before Pharaoh only at thirty — with thirteen years of pit, slavery and prison in between (Genesis 37:2; 41:46). The books of Samuel tell us that after David was anointed, years of life as a fugitive passed before he took the throne. God’s word had not failed; it was simply still on its way. So don’t hurry to dismiss something just because you haven’t seen it yet; and don’t take matters into your own hands to make it happen just because the wait has been long.

The second is humility. If what you received doesn’t come to pass, you need to adjust humbly. This is the hurdle many people find hardest to get over. Once someone has publicly announced “God told me,” it is very hard to admit they heard wrong. So some begin to revise what they said, to explain it away, to blame others for not having enough faith.

sections.heading: What the 321 Vision Says Here, and It Cuts to the Heart: The Humble Will Correct Themselves; the Proud Will Dig In.
sections.html:
Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights — wanting to take God’s place. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. When I say, “I definitely didn’t hear wrong,” I put myself in God’s place; when I say, “Lord, perhaps I heard wrong — please teach me again,” I return to man’s originally intended position.

Scripture says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) Someone willing to admit they heard wrong will hear more accurately next time; someone who refuses ever to admit a mistake will drift further off the more they listen. For pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Brothers and sisters, hearing wrong is not the frightening thing; refusing to correct it is. These three confirmations — the confirmation of Scripture, the confirmation of the body, the confirmation of time — are like a tripod: take away one leg and it falls. With all three legs in place, our hearts can stand firm, neither closed nor confused.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Only Selfless Ears Can Hear God’s Voice
sections.html:
When we set this lesson back into the whole picture of 321, we see it more clearly still.

First, the Three Foundations are precisely the three coordinates of discernment. Jesus is my role model — so every voice must point to Jesus, and anything that does not lift up Jesus calls for us to stop. The Bible is my standard — so every prompting must pass the test of truth. The Holy Spirit is my guide — so we don’t rely on our own cleverness to guess, but on the Holy Spirit to receive. When the Three Foundations are steady, the ears are steady.

Second, the Two Core Values are precisely the direction we take after we have heard. Let Jesus be King — God speaks to me not to satisfy my curiosity but so that he may take the throne in every corner of my life. Let Jesus receive all the glory — so when God speaks a word through me that builds someone up, the glory goes to him, not to me. Someone who pockets the glory for himself will soon stop hearing.

Third, the Goal is to establish God’s system. God has never spoken in order to create stars, but in order to build up the body. He entrusts his heart to people so that people will be connected to one another, confirm one another and walk together in his will, fulfilling what the Lord’s Prayer says: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)

Fourth, the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Self-centred ears mostly hear themselves; only selfless ears can hear God. Selflessness is not wiping yourself out, not becoming someone with no thoughts of your own; selflessness is “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). When “I” stop hogging the microphone, God’s voice naturally becomes clear.

Fifth, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. What this lesson must change first is our mindset — so God really does speak; so God speaks in all kinds of ways; so after hearing, we must discern. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. Many people want to change their ministry directly but refuse to change their mindset first, and so however large their ministry grows, inside they are still the old self.

Sixth, a change of perspective. From man’s perspective to God’s: I no longer ask, “What’s in this for me?” I ask, “Lord, what do you want to say?” From the earthly to the heavenly: I no longer see only the difficulty in front of me; I see the One on the throne. From the temporary to the eternal: I am no longer swept away by passing emotions; I care about the will that lasts for ever. From the worldly to the godly: I no longer measure God’s guidance by the world’s idea of success.

Seventh, the 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. When I live out the selfless “0”, the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow between me and that person: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, this is in fact the best discernment tool of all. Something truly received from God will make me more loving, more patient and gentler towards my “2”; if a “word I’ve received” makes me harsher, more judgemental or more impatient with people, then I need to be careful.

Eighth, the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. First let the Holy Spirit guide (Spirit), then come to understanding through the Bible (Understanding), then live out the life of Jesus (Life), then let Jesus be King in our service (Service), and at last give all the glory to God (God). Hearing God’s voice is only the starting point of this road; walking the whole road is the purpose of God’s speaking.

Brothers and sisters, rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the heart, and you rejoice; rely on the brain, and you worry. God has never wanted us to become spiritual detectives who take everything apart to analyse it; he wants us to be his children, lying quietly at his feet and saying, like Samuel, “Speak; for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:10)

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson has prepared three practices for us. Let’s use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to put them into effect one by one.

Practice 1: Build the habit of discernment; don’t rush to conclusions

When you have a prompting, a dream or something you believe you’ve received, don’t rush to decide that it’s God. First bring it before God in prayer and test it against the Bible, and slowly cultivate spiritual sensitivity.

Information: today you have already received the information — God speaks in all kinds of ways, but everything must be brought back to the Bible to be tested.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to turn this information into light within you, so that you really see: “I often take my own voice for God’s voice.”

Conviction: acknowledge from your heart that the Bible’s authority is higher than my feelings. This step is a surrender of the will, not an agreement of the brain.

Implementation: from today, keep a “listening notebook.” Record promptings, dreams, verses and confirmations in separate columns, with dates. Don’t reach a conclusion straight away; leave it for seven days. During those seven days do only two things: pray, and study the Bible.

Evaluation: after seven days, look back. Does this word lift up Jesus? Does it agree with Scripture? Does it bring peace or panic? Does it bear the fruit of the Spirit?

Correction: if you find it was your own idea, write honestly in your notebook, “This one was mine.” That single line will help you hear more accurately next time.

Repetition: set a regular time each week to review your notebook. Discernment is not a gift; it is a habit formed by training. Hebrews says that mature people are those “who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil” (Hebrews 5:14). In the original, “exercised” carries the sense of an athlete’s long training.

Multiplication: teach your method to a brother or sister and do the seven days alongside them. Only what you have taught becomes truly yours.

Practice 2: Learn to confirm God’s leading in community

Bring the important things you believe you’ve received to your spiritual companions or to the church for fellowship, and let the body discern together, so that you don’t slip into mere personal subjectivity but walk on the road of unity.

Information: God has established the witness of two or three as the standard of confirmation (2 Corinthians 13:1).

Revelation: let the Holy Spirit shine his light on you — have you been fighting on your own all along? Do you only go to people who will agree with you?

Conviction: admit that I need the body. Admit that on my own I have blind spots. This is the first step of humility.

Implementation: find your “2” — a selfless spiritual companion who loves the Lord and is willing to tell the truth. This week, bring to them one matter you are hesitating over — not to get their agreement, but to pray and test it together.

Evaluation: after you have talked it through, notice your own reaction. When they offered a different view, were you grateful or defensive? A defensive reaction is very often a sign that “self” is still there.

Correction: if you find you were only looking for approval, confess it to God and put the decision back into God’s hands.

Repetition: make this kind of fellowship a regular rhythm, at least once a month. Let the 235 relationships be truly established in your life.

Multiplication: once you have experienced the blessing of the body’s confirmation, go and be a confirmer for someone else. Be a spiritual companion who is willing to listen, willing to pray and willing to tell the truth.

Practice 3: Turn what you receive into obedient action

Don’t stop at “discerning”; go on into “doing.” Once you are sure it comes from God, step out boldly and let God’s word be fulfilled in your life.

Information: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)

Revelation: ask the Lord to show you what is actually holding you back from obeying — is it fear? Face? Something you can’t bear to let go?

Conviction: say to the Lord from your heart: whatever you say, I am willing to obey.

Implementation: this week choose just one act of obedience — the smallest, most concrete one, one you can complete within seven days. Make that phone call, say that sorry, give that gift, begin those fifteen minutes a day of drawing near to God. Obedience never starts with the big things.

Evaluation: once you have done it, write down what God did and what changed in your heart.

Correction: if you find yourself putting it off, face honestly the fear behind the delay and hand it to the Lord.

Repetition: let “hear it, then do it” become your reflex. Every act of obedience deepens your familiarity with God’s voice.

Multiplication: tell the story of your obedience to someone who needs courage. Your testimony will become their strength.

Brothers and sisters, please remember: hearing is grace, discerning is responsibility, obeying is fruit. God will not entrust more of his words to someone who refuses to act on them.

A Gentle Reminder

God speaks in many ways, but there is only one truth.

God’s voice is neither confused nor contradictory.

God’s voice brings life, peace and unity.

So don’t limit God — don’t say, “God wouldn’t do that today”; and don’t jump to conclusions either — don’t say, “This is definitely God.” Between the two runs a narrow road, and the name of that road is humility.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Jesus Is Always the Focal Point
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters,

God speaks in endlessly varied ways, but his heart has only one aim — to bring you back into his will.

Elijah waited for God at the mouth of the cave on Mount Horeb. Scripture records that a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke the rocks in pieces before him, but Yahweh was not in the wind; after the wind an earthquake, but Yahweh was not in the earthquake; after the earthquake a fire, but Yahweh was not in the fire; and after the fire, a still small voice (1 Kings 19:11–12). Brothers and sisters, of course God has the power to use wind, earthquake and fire, but that day he chose to use a still small voice. Because what he wanted was not to overwhelm, but for you to draw near.

So don’t chase special methods, and don’t exalt spiritual experiences. Jesus is always the focal point.

When you are selfless and humble and rely on the heart, you will discover something wonderful: God is speaking to you everywhere. He speaks in the Bible you open, in your early-morning prayers, in something your child says, at the door you thought was a dead end. Your life will be full of guidance and light.

Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27) The sheep can hear because they know the shepherd; the sheep can keep up because they trust the shepherd.

This morning, let’s learn one thing, and only this one thing:

Lord, whatever way you choose, I am willing to listen, and willing to obey.

Let Jesus be King over our ears, let Jesus be King over our decisions, let Jesus be King over our obedience. May all the glory be his.

keyVerses: “knowing this first, that no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation. For no prophecy ever came by the will of man: but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.” (2 Peter 1:20–21)

“God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds.” (Hebrews 1:1–2)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, let us stand together and declare to the Lord:

Lord Jesus, I believe you are a God who speaks. You are still speaking to me today. I will listen with my heart rather than analyse with my brain. Holy Spirit, guide me to discern, so that I neither stray nor fall into confusion. I will be someone who hears clearly, discerns rightly and walks accurately. Whatever you say, I am willing to obey. In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare it. Amen!

prayer: Lord Jesus, I believe you are a God who speaks.
In the past you spoke to the fathers at many times and in various ways; in these last days you have spoken to us by your Son; and today you are still speaking to me.

Forgive me for so often analysing with my brain instead of listening with my heart; forgive me for chasing special experiences while overlooking your ordinary voice; forgive me for taking my own ideas for your will.

Holy Spirit, guide me to discern, so that I neither stray nor fall into confusion. Lord, place the Bible in my heart as my standard, place spiritual companions beside me as confirmation, and keep time in your hands as proof.
I want to be someone who hears clearly, discerns rightly and walks accurately.
Lord, I give you my ears, my heart and my plans. Whatever you say, I am willing to obey.
Reign as King in my life, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Think back over the past year. In what ways has God spoken to you (the Bible, a sermon, a prompting in prayer, a dream, circumstances, or something a brother or sister said)? How did you discern it at the time? Reflect on “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27), and share whether you “heard” — or whether you “followed.”

Of the three tests — the confirmation of Scripture, the confirmation of the body and the confirmation of time — which do you most often neglect? Reflect on “Don’t quench the Spirit. Don’t despise prophecies. Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.” (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21), discuss together how to keep the balance between “not quenching” and “testing all things,” and pray for one another.

blog.title: God Has Always Been Speaking — You’re Just Tuned to the Wrong Channel

blocks.x: The Ways God Speaks to People (Part 2)

In 1953 Colin Cherry of Imperial College London discovered an intriguing phenomenon, later called “the cocktail party effect”: in a banquet hall full of voices, a person can somehow pick out, from dozens of sounds, the one voice he is concentrating on; and even when you’re busy talking, if someone in the distance calls your name, your ears turn towards it instantly.
Hearing, it turns out, has never been passive reception; it is an active choice.

So often it isn’t that we can’t hear God; it’s that we aren’t listening. Like a radio that isn’t tuned properly, the whole room fills with static. The problem isn’t the station — the station has been transmitting all along. The problem is the reception.
God Speaks in All Kinds of Ways
From its very first page the Bible tells us that God is a God who speaks. And Hebrews goes further, showing us how richly he speaks:
“God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son.” (Hebrews 1:1–2)
In the original, “at many times and in various ways” means: speaking portion by portion, and through many different channels.

He speaks through prophecy — and prophecy is not predicting the future but conveying God’s heart. On the day of Pentecost Peter proclaimed, “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy.” (Acts 2:17) From a small group of prophets in the Old Testament to every child of God in the New, God is willing to use your mouth and mine to build people up, console them and encourage them.

He speaks through visions and dreams — Paul saw the vision of the man of Macedonia, and the gospel crossed from Asia into Europe; the wise men were warned in a dream, and the life of the holy Child was saved. A vision is like a video from God; a dream is like a message from God.

He also speaks through angels and circumstances — an angel brought the news to Mary, made the announcement to the shepherds and led Peter out of prison; a ram took Isaac’s place, and a pair of hands took hold of Lot as he lingered. Sometimes the things that happen to you are God speaking.
But Not Every Voice Is God’s Voice
Here’s the question: if God speaks in so many ways, how do I know which one is him?

Many people go to one of two extremes: either not believing at all that God still speaks today, or treating every voice as God’s voice, until the more they listen, the more confused they become. God’s heart is neither of these extremes. It is this — truly to hear, and rightly to discern.
The Bible gives us three confirmations.

The first is the confirmation of Scripture. God’s word “is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12). Our greatest difficulty is not telling God’s voice apart from the devil’s; it is telling God’s voice apart from our own. Psychology has identified “confirmation bias”: once people have a hypothesis, they look only for evidence that supports it. So when I already want something in my heart, it is very easy for me to “hear” God agreeing with me. That isn’t God speaking. That’s me speaking — just using God’s voice. Anything that conflicts with the Bible is certainly not God.

The second is the confirmation of the body. It was as the church at Antioch served the Lord and fasted together that the Holy Spirit spoke; the conclusion of the Council of Jerusalem was, “it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us.” If God is speaking to the church, he won’t let only one person know. What truly comes from God brings unity, not division.

The third is the confirmation of time. What God says will surely come to pass. Joseph had his dreams at seventeen and stood before Pharaoh only at thirty — thirteen years in between. God’s word had not failed; it was simply still on its way. And if what you received doesn’t come to pass, you need to adjust humbly — the humble will correct themselves; the proud will dig in.
The Focus Is Not the Method — the Focus Is Jesus

Elijah waited for God at Mount Horeb. A great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke the rocks in pieces, but Yahweh was not in the wind; after the wind an earthquake, but Yahweh was not in the earthquake; after the earthquake a fire, but Yahweh was not in the fire; and after the fire, a still small voice.
Of course God has the power to use wind, earthquake and fire, but that day he chose to use a still small voice. Because what he wanted was not to overwhelm, but for you to draw near.

So don’t chase special methods, and don’t exalt spiritual experiences. Jesus is always the focal point. When we are selfless and humble and rely on the heart, we discover that God is speaking to us everywhere: in the Bible we open, in our early-morning prayers, at the door that seemed to have closed.
Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and things are clear; rely on the brain and ourselves, and things are confused.

May we all become people who hear clearly, discern truly and walk surely, and say to the Lord the simplest yet most powerful words: Lord, whatever way you choose, I am willing to listen, and willing to obey.
Reflection Question
Over the past year, in what ways has God spoken to you? Did you put it in a “listening notebook”, or did you let it slip past your ears?
