Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 127
“Holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit”
(2 Peter 1:21)
Key points:
• The title comes from the lesson’s declaration of faith: hear clearly, discern truly, walk surely.
• Key verses: 2 Peter 1:20–21, together with Hebrews 1:1–2.
• Open with one line: God speaks; the question is whether we are listening.
• Warm tone; invite the brothers and sisters to grow still.
Are You Listening?
God doesn’t just speak
he speaks in all kinds of ways
The key isn’t the method — it’s listening
The focus isn’t the method — it’s Jesus
Key points:
• Example: Colin Cherry’s “cocktail party effect” (1953) — amid the noise we can focus on one voice.
• It isn’t that we can’t hear; it’s that we aren’t listening.
• Illustration: a badly tuned radio fills the room with static; the problem isn’t the station but the reception.
• 321 Insight: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and things are clear; rely on the brain and ourselves, and things are confused.
• Proverbs 4:23 “out of it is the wellspring of life”.
At Many Times and in Various Ways
“Spoken to the fathers … at many times and in various ways”
“Has … spoken to us by his Son”
(Hebrews 1:1–2)
Many ways, one centre: Jesus
Key points:
• Greek polymerōs (many times, portion by portion), polytropōs (various ways, many channels).
• Peter saw the Transfiguration, yet said, “We have the more sure word of prophecy” (2 Peter 1:19).
• “Moved” — Greek pherō, carried along by the wind; the prophet is the ship, the Holy Spirit the wind.
• Revelation 19:10 “the testimony of Jesus is the Spirit of Prophecy”.
God Speaks Through Prophecy
Prophecy is not predicting the future
it is conveying God’s heart
“Your sons and your daughters will prophesy”
(Acts 2:17)
Key points:
• “Prophet” — Hebrew nabi, Greek prophētēs: one who speaks on God’s behalf.
• Amos 3:7: the Lord does nothing without revealing his secret to the prophets.
• Old Testament: a small group of prophets; New Testament: “all flesh” — God is willing to use everyone who belongs to him.
• 1 Corinthians 14:3: edification, exhortation, consolation.
• 321: the self-centred speak their own minds; the selfless become God’s outlet.
God Speaks Through Visions and Dreams
A vision is like God’s video
A dream is like God’s message
The point isn’t how overwhelming the picture is
but what God wants you to understand
Key points:
• Paul’s vision of Macedonia (Acts 16:9), Jacob’s stairway (Genesis 28:12), the wise men warned in a dream (Matthew 2:12).
• Peter in a trance (Acts 10:10–11); Ezekiel lifted up by the Spirit (Ezekiel 8:3).
• Science: Aserinsky and Kleitman discovered REM sleep in 1953; adults go through about four to six sleep cycles a night, each about ninety minutes.
• Jeremiah 23:28: the dream is straw, God’s word is wheat.
• 321: don’t pursue experiences — pursue God’s heart.
God Speaks Through Angels and Circumstances
Angels are messengers who are sent
Circumstances are God’s megaphone
But circumstances are not the standard
Let the Holy Spirit help you read them
Key points:
• Angels bring news (Luke 1:30–31), announce to the shepherds (Luke 2:10–11), rescue Peter from prison (Acts 12:7).
• Hebrews 1:14: angels are serving spirits, sent out to do service.
• Circumstances: the ram of “Yahweh Will Provide” (Genesis 22:13–14); the hands that took hold of Lot (Genesis 19:16).
• C. S. Lewis is generally credited with saying in The Problem of Pain that pain is God’s megaphone to rouse a deaf world.
• Caution: Jonah boarded a ship with ease, yet it was the road of running from God; smoothness isn’t God’s permission.
4a. The Confirmation of Scripture
God’s voice never contradicts the Bible
“Able to discern the thoughts
and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12)
If it conflicts with the Bible, it is not God
Key points:
• Hebrews 4:12: God’s word divides soul from spirit — divides “what I want” from “what God wants”.
• Isaiah 8:20: if they don’t speak according to this word, surely there is no morning for them.
• Checklist: lifts up Jesus; brings edification, exhortation and consolation; bears the fruit of the Spirit; makes us more humble.
• The second of the 321 Three Foundations: the Bible is my standard; the measuring rod doesn’t bend to feelings.
4b. The Confirmation of the Body
“At the mouth of two or three witnesses”
“shall every word be established”
(2 Corinthians 13:1)
What truly comes from God brings unity
Key points:
• The Holy Spirit spoke as the church at Antioch served and fasted together (Acts 13:2).
• The Council of Jerusalem: “it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us” (Acts 15:28).
• Psychology: Solomon Asch’s conformity experiment (1951) — about a third of answers in the critical rounds followed the majority into error; a group needs the standard of truth.
• The 321 235 relationships: spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, fivefold-ministry comrades.
4c. The Confirmation of Time
“So is my word that goes out of my mouth”
“it will not return to me void”
(Isaiah 55:11)
The humble will correct themselves
Key points:

• The humble will correct themselves; the proud will dig in — James 4:6.

Don’t rush to conclusions
Confirm it in community
Turn it into obedient action
Hear, discern, obey

• Practice 2: find a selfless “2” who will tell the truth, and test it together.
• Practice 3: this week choose the smallest act of obedience and complete it within seven days.

• James 1:22: be doers of the word, and not only hearers.

Don’t chase special methods
Don’t exalt spiritual experiences
Selfless, humble, relying on the heart
God is speaking to you everywhere
Key points:
• Elijah at Mount Horeb: after the wind, the earthquake and the fire, a still small voice (1 Kings 19:11–12).
• What God wants is not to overwhelm, but for you to draw near.
• John 10:27: My sheep hear my voice.
• Call: let Jesus be King over our ears, our decisions and our obedience.
Prayer of Response and Blessing
Lord, whatever you say
I am willing to listen and to obey
May Jesus be King in my heart
May all the glory be his

script: Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re looking together at Lesson 127 of Morning Devotion 321, on the theme “The Ways God Speaks to People (Part 2)”. I’ve boiled this lesson down to six words: hear clearly, discern truly, walk surely. Our key verse is 2 Peter 1:21: “For no prophecy ever came by the will of man: but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.” Brothers and sisters, God has always been speaking. This morning, let’s quieten our hearts and learn together how to listen and how to discern.

Let me start with a question: are you listening? In 1953 the British scientist Colin Cherry identified something called “the cocktail party effect”. In a deafeningly noisy banquet hall, you can somehow hear the one voice you want to hear. Hearing, it turns out, isn’t passive; hearing is a choice. Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that we can’t hear; it’s that we aren’t listening. Like a radio that isn’t tuned properly, the whole room fills with static. The problem isn’t the station — the station has been transmitting all along. The problem is the reception.

Hebrews 1 says, “God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son.” In Greek, “at many times and in various ways” means speaking portion by portion, and in many ways. God has many channels for speaking, but the centre of his speaking is One alone — Jesus. Peter saw the Transfiguration with his own eyes, yet he said, “We have the more sure word of prophecy.” Brothers and sisters, if even an apostle put Scripture above his own experience, how can we put a dream above the Bible?

First, God speaks through prophecy — he entrusts his heart to people. Prophecy is not predicting the future; prophecy is conveying God’s heart. In Old Testament times God spoke through a small group of prophets; but in the New Testament, Acts 2:17 says, “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy.” From a small group of people to everyone who belongs to God. God doesn’t use only special people; God is willing to use you. But, brothers and sisters, the wider the door opens, the more important discernment becomes. The self-centred speak their own minds; only the selfless become God’s outlet.

Second, God speaks through visions and dreams — he opens our spiritual eyes. Paul saw the vision of the man of Macedonia, and the gospel crossed from Asia into Europe. Jacob dreamed of a stairway and woke up saying, “Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn’t know it!” The wise men were warned in a dream, and the life of the holy Child was saved. A vision is like a video from God; a dream is like a message from God. But remember: the point isn’t how overwhelming the picture is, but what God wants you to understand. Don’t pursue experiences; pursue God’s heart.

Third, God speaks through angels and circumstances — he rules over all things. An angel brought the news to Mary, made the announcement to the shepherds and led Peter out of prison. Hebrews says angels are all serving spirits, sent out to do service. God also speaks through circumstances: a ram took Isaac’s place, and a pair of hands took hold of Lot. Brothers and sisters, sometimes the things that happen to you are God speaking. But be careful: things going smoothly doesn’t necessarily mean God has given permission, and obstacles don’t necessarily mean God has forbidden something. Circumstances are God’s megaphone; the Bible is the standard.

So how do we discern? The first confirmation is the confirmation of Scripture. Hebrews 4:12 says that the word of God is living, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Brothers and sisters, our hardest task is not telling God’s voice apart from the devil’s; it’s telling God’s voice apart from our own. God’s word is like a supremely sharp blade that divides “what I want” from “what God wants”. So please remember: every prompting must be brought back to the truth to be tested; if it conflicts with the Bible, it is certainly not God.

The second confirmation is the confirmation of the body. 2 Corinthians 13:1 says, “At the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.” It was as the church at Antioch served and fasted together that the Holy Spirit spoke; the Council of Jerusalem said, “it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us.” Brothers and sisters, if God is speaking to the church, he won’t let only one person know. What truly comes from God brings unity, not division. If something you’ve received makes you start drifting away from the body, that voice is already wrong in itself.

The third confirmation is the confirmation of time. Isaiah 55:11 says, “So is my word that goes out of my mouth: it will not return to me void.” What God says will surely come to pass. Time will prove everything. But time calls for two attitudes. The first is waiting: Joseph had his dream at seventeen and stood before Pharaoh only at thirty. The second is humility: if it doesn’t come to pass, we must adjust. Brothers and sisters, the humble will correct themselves; the proud will dig in. Hearing wrong is not the frightening thing; refusing to correct it is.

Next come our practices for daily living — three of them. First, build the habit of discernment; don’t rush to conclusions. When you have a prompting or a dream, first bring it before God in prayer, test it against the Bible, and leave it for seven days. Second, learn to confirm God’s leading in community: bring the important things you receive to your spiritual companions and let the body discern together. Third, turn what you receive into obedient action. This week, choose just one, very small act of obedience and do it. Hearing is grace, discerning is responsibility, obeying is fruit.

Brothers and sisters, God speaks in endlessly varied ways, but his heart has only one aim: to bring you back into his will. At Mount Horeb Elijah saw the wind pass, the earthquake pass and the fire pass, and at last there came a still small voice. What God wants is not to overwhelm you; what God wants is for you to draw near. So don’t chase special methods, and don’t exalt spiritual experiences. Jesus is always the focal point. When you are selfless and humble and rely on the heart, you will discover that God is speaking to you everywhere.

Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, I believe you are a God who speaks, and you are still speaking to me today. I will listen with my heart rather than analyse with my brain. Holy Spirit, guide me to discern, so that I neither stray nor fall into confusion. I want to be someone who hears clearly, discerns truly and walks surely. Whatever you say, I am willing to obey. Reign as King in my life, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, may the Lord himself speak to you today. Have a blessed day.

Our key verse is 2 Peter 1:21: “For no prophecy ever came by the will of man: but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.” Brothers and sisters, God has always been speaking. This morning, let’s lay aside our restlessness and learn together how to listen, how to discern and how to obey. For when we hear clearly, life has direction; when we discern truly, our steps don’t go astray; when we walk surely, life bears fruit.

Let me start with a question: are you listening? In 1953 Colin Cherry of Imperial College London identified a phenomenon later called “the cocktail party effect”. In a banquet hall full of voices, you can somehow pick out the one voice you are concentrating on; and even while you’re talking to someone, if a person in the distance calls your name, your ears turn towards it instantly. Hearing, it turns out, isn’t passive reception; hearing is an active choice. Brothers and sisters, so often it isn’t that we can’t hear; it’s that we aren’t listening.

It’s like a radio that isn’t tuned properly: the whole room fills with hissing static. The problem isn’t the station — the station has been transmitting all along. The problem is the reception. In the last lesson we saw that God is a God who speaks. Today we go a step further: he doesn’t speak in only one way. He speaks through prophecy, through visions and dreams, through angels, through circumstances. But the key isn’t the method; it’s two questions: Are you listening? Are you discerning? 321 says: the focus is not the method; the focus is Jesus. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and things are clear; rely on the brain and ourselves, and things are confused.

Let’s look at the background. Peter wrote 2 Peter before his martyrdom, at a time when false teachers in the church were interpreting God’s word to suit themselves. Peter speaks of the Transfiguration, which he saw with his own eyes, and then says, “We have the more sure word of prophecy.” Brothers and sisters, if even an apostle handed the highest authority to Scripture, how can we put a dream above the Bible? Hebrews 1 says, “God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son.” The channels are many; the centre is One alone — Jesus.

Our first point: God speaks through prophecy — he entrusts his heart to people. As soon as many people hear the word “prophecy”, they think of fortune-telling. But prophecy in the Bible is not predicting the future; it is conveying God’s heart. The Greek word “prophet” means “one who speaks on behalf of another”. Amos 3:7 says, “Surely the Lord Yahweh will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.” The God who created the universe is willing to tell what is on his heart to weak people — like a father crouching down to tell his child the family’s plans; not because the child is able to carry them, but because the father wants the child to have a share in them. Brothers and sisters, God entrusting his heart to you is grace, not qualification.

In the Old Testament God spoke chiefly through a small group of prophets. But on the day of Pentecost Peter proclaimed, “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy.” Brothers and sisters, hear the shift: from a small group of people to all flesh. God doesn’t use only special people; God is willing to use everyone who belongs to him. Paul says that he who prophesies speaks to people for their edification, exhortation and consolation. God wants to use one word from you to lift up someone who has lost heart.

But the wider the door opens, the more important discernment becomes. Not every voice is God’s voice. Paul says, “Don’t quench the Spirit. Don’t despise prophecies. Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.” Don’t quench — but don’t believe blindly either. Psychology reminds us that in 1960 Peter Wason’s experiment uncovered “confirmation bias”: once people have a hypothesis, they look only for evidence that supports it. When I already want something, it is very easy for me to “hear” God agreeing with me. 321 says: the self-centred speak their own minds; the selfless become God’s outlet.

Our second point: God speaks through visions and dreams. Paul saw the vision of the man of Macedonia in the night, and the gospel crossed from Asia into Europe. Jacob fell asleep with a stone for a pillow and dreamed of a stairway set upon the earth, its top reaching to heaven; he woke and said, “Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn’t know it!” The wise men from the east were warned in a dream, and one dream saved the life of the holy Child. Peter, praying on the roof, fell into a trance; Ezekiel was lifted up by the Spirit and brought in the visions of God to Jerusalem. God really does speak in pictures — sometimes in prayer, sometimes in sleep, sometimes at the moments when we are least on guard. The purpose of these experiences was never mystery for its own sake, but to lead people into God’s heart.

We could put it this way: a vision is like a video from God; a dream is like a message from God. A video lets you see the whole situation; a message arrives at the critical moment. But in both cases the point isn’t how overwhelming the picture is; it’s what God wants you to understand. Science gives us a reminder too: in 1953 researchers at the University of Chicago discovered rapid eye movement sleep. Adults go through roughly four to six sleep cycles a night, each lasting about ninety minutes, and most dreams happen in REM sleep. So not every dream has spiritual significance; most dreams are just the afterimages of the day.

So what do we do? The Bible gives us the standard. Jeremiah 23:28 says, “The prophet who has a dream, let him tell a dream; and he who has my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the straw to the wheat?” God doesn’t reject dreams; he simply ranks them: the dream is straw, the word is wheat. Straw is not evil; you just can’t make a meal of it. 321 says: don’t pursue experiences; pursue God’s heart. This is exactly the change of perspective — from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal.

Our third point: God speaks through angels and circumstances — he rules over all things. The angel said to Mary, “Don’t be afraid, Mary!” The angel said to the shepherds, “Don’t be afraid, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy.” The angel struck Peter on the side to wake him, and the chains fell off his hands. In the original, the word “angel” simply means “messenger, one who is sent”. Hebrews 1:14 says that angels are all serving spirits, sent out to do service for the sake of those who will inherit salvation. So please remember: the one we worship is always God, never angels. Angels are sent; they faithfully deliver the word of the One who sent them and never act on their own initiative.

God also speaks through circumstances. Abraham’s knife was already raised when he lifted up his eyes and saw a ram caught in the thicket by its horns. That ram was God speaking, and so he called the place “Yahweh Will Provide”. Lot couldn’t bear to leave, and the men, Yahweh being merciful to him, took him by the hand and led him out. Those hands were God speaking. Brothers and sisters, sometimes the things that happen to you are God speaking. C. S. Lewis is generally credited with saying that pain is God’s megaphone to rouse a deaf world. It isn’t that God’s volume is too low; it’s that our ears are too hard.

But be careful. Things going smoothly doesn’t necessarily mean God has given permission, and obstacles don’t necessarily mean God has forbidden something. When Jonah fled towards Tarshish, there happened to be a ship in the harbour, and he happened to be able to afford the fare — everything went smoothly. Yet that was the road he had chosen for himself. When Paul was thrown into prison in Philippi, nothing went smoothly — yet it was God’s plan to bring the jailer and his household to salvation. Psychology calls it illusory correlation: people link two unrelated events into cause and effect. So when we already want to do something, every green light along the way becomes “God’s permission”. 321 says: circumstances are a megaphone; the Bible is the standard.

Our fourth point: how do we discern? The Bible gives us three confirmations. First, the confirmation of Scripture. Hebrews 4:12 says that the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Brothers and sisters, our hardest task is not telling God’s voice apart from the devil’s; it’s telling God’s voice apart from our own. Isaiah 8:20 says that if they don’t speak according to this word, surely there is no morning for them. Anything that conflicts with the Bible is certainly not God — no need to pray about it for three more days, no need to ask three more people. Someone may say, “But my feeling is so strong.” Yet fear can be strong, and desire can be strong; a strong feeling does not mean it comes from God.

Second, the confirmation of the body. 2 Corinthians 13:1 says, “At the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.” It was as the church at Antioch served the Lord and fasted that the Holy Spirit spoke; the conclusion of the Council of Jerusalem was, “it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us.” If God is speaking to the church, he won’t let only one person know. But beware of group pressure too. In 1951 Solomon Asch’s conformity experiment found that when everyone else in the room gave the wrong answer, about a third of participants’ answers in the critical rounds went along with them. What truly comes from God brings unity.

Third, the confirmation of time. Isaiah 55:11 says, “So is my word that goes out of my mouth: it will not return to me void.” What God says will surely come to pass; time is the most honest of sieves. But time calls for two attitudes. The first is waiting: Joseph had his dream at seventeen and stood before Pharaoh only at thirty — thirteen years in between. God’s word had not failed; it was simply still on its way. The second is humility: if it doesn’t come to pass, we must adjust. 321 says: the humble will correct themselves; the proud will dig in. Hearing wrong is not the frightening thing; refusing to correct it is.

Next come our practices for daily living. The first: build the habit of discernment; don’t rush to conclusions. When you have a prompting, a dream or something you believe you’ve received, first bring it before God in prayer and test it against the Bible. Here’s a concrete suggestion: keep a “listening notebook”. Record promptings, verses and confirmations in separate columns, with dates, and leave each one for seven days; during those seven days do only two things — pray, and study the Bible. The second: learn to confirm in community. Find a selfless “2” who will tell you the truth, and bring them the matter you’re hesitating over — not to get their agreement, but to test it together. Notice your own reaction: when they offer a different view, are you grateful or defensive? A defensive reaction is very often a sign that “self” is still there.

The third: turn what you receive into obedient action. James 1:22 says, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” This week, choose just one act of obedience — the smallest one, which you can complete within seven days: make that phone call, say that sorry. Obedience never starts with the big things. Walk these three practices through the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Hearing is grace, discerning is responsibility, obeying is fruit.

Let’s set this lesson back into the picture of 321. The Three Foundations are the three coordinates of discernment: Jesus is my role model, so every voice must point to Jesus; the Bible is my standard, so every prompting must pass the test of truth; the Holy Spirit is my guide, so we don’t rely on our own cleverness. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. Then there is the fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Today we change our mindset first; change the mindset, and life changes, daily living changes, relationships change, ministry changes. And there is the 920 practice: towards every “2” I relate to, live out the selfless life and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.

Brothers and sisters, God speaks in endlessly varied ways, but his heart has only one aim: to bring you back into his will. At Mount Horeb a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke the rocks in pieces, but Yahweh was not in the wind; after the wind an earthquake, but Yahweh was not in the earthquake; after the earthquake a fire, but Yahweh was not in the fire; and after the fire, a still small voice. What God wants is not to overwhelm you, but for you to draw near. So don’t chase special methods, and don’t exalt spiritual experiences. Jesus is always the focal point. When you are selfless and humble and rely on the heart, God is speaking to you everywhere.

Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, I believe you are a God who speaks, and you are still speaking to me today. Forgive me for so often analysing with my brain instead of listening with my heart; forgive me for chasing special experiences while overlooking your ordinary voice. Holy Spirit, guide me to discern, so that I neither stray nor fall into confusion. Place the Bible in my heart as my standard, and place spiritual companions beside me as confirmation. I want to be someone who hears clearly, discerns truly and walks surely. Whatever you say, I am willing to obey. May all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Signal Kept Coming, but the Receiver Was Switched Off
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let’s begin with something that really happened in history.

Late on the night of 14 April 1912, the surface of the North Atlantic was uncannily calm. Less than twenty nautical miles from the Titanic lay a cargo ship, the Californian. That evening the Californian’s wireless operator, Cyril Evans, sent out ice warnings to the ships around him again and again. When he broke in on the Titanic’s channel one last time to tell them, “We are stopped and surrounded by ice,” the Titanic’s operator, busy sending private telegrams for first-class passengers, snapped back: “Shut up, I am busy.”

Not long afterwards, Evans switched off his set and went to bed.

At 11:40 p.m. the Titanic struck the iceberg. For the next two hours and more, the Titanic’s wireless sent out distress calls frantically — CQD, SOS — over and over again. The signals crossed the dark night and reached the Californian’s aerial. But on that ship, no one was wearing the headphones. The British inquiry into the disaster later left behind a heartbreaking conclusion: that ship was close enough — close enough that, had anyone been listening, many lives could have been saved.

Brothers and sisters, the real tragedy of that night was not that the signal was never sent. It was that the receiver had been switched off.

And that is exactly the spiritual lesson we are going to face together today.

This world is full of voices. The voices of people, the voices of our circumstances, the voices of our emotions, the voices of our own thoughts — and the voices online that never stop, day or night, an endless feed you can scroll forever and never reach the end of. But among all these voices, the one that matters most is the voice of God.

The question is this: when God speaks, are we sure to hear him?

The Bible gives us a very sobering answer. Isaiah 6:9 records what Yahweh said to the prophet: “He said, ‘Go, and tell this people, “You hear indeed, but don’t understand. You see indeed, but don’t perceive.”’”

This is a spiritual crisis: some people have ears and yet cannot hear; some have eyes and yet cannot see.

Why?

Because hearing God’s voice has never been an outward ability. It is a condition of the inner life.

Proverbs 20:12 says, “The hearing ear, and the seeing eye, Yahweh has made even both of them.”

To be able to hear is grace; to be able to understand is blessing. God made our ears, and he made our hearts too. But the key is this: are you ready to listen by relying on the heart?

Today the Lord Jesus himself is going to lead us into one of the parables he told. In this parable there is the same sower, the same handful of seed, the same morning — and yet four completely different outcomes. The difference is not in the seed, and not in the sower. It is in the soil.

Brothers and sisters, that soil is your heart.

This morning, may we not simply listen to one more message, but let the Lord’s plough turn over the ground in our hearts that needs turning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Teacher Seated in a Boat, a Field by the Sea
sections.html: To truly understand this parable, we first need to stand where Jesus stood that day and look at the scene in front of him.

sections.heading: 1. Author and Audience
sections.html:
Church history consistently identifies the author of Matthew’s Gospel as the apostle Matthew — Levi, the tax collector whom the Lord called (Matthew 9:9). It is generally dated between AD 50 and 70, before Jerusalem was destroyed in AD 70. Matthew wrote first and foremost for Christians of Jewish background. That is why the whole book quotes the Old Testament so heavily and keeps repeating, “This was to fulfil what was spoken by the prophet.” His aim was to prove that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the King of the Kingdom of Heaven.

Matthew’s Gospel has a very clear structure: the whole book is built around five great discourses of Jesus. The first is the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7); the second is the teaching on sending out the Twelve (chapter 10); the third is the one we are reading today, the parables of the Kingdom (chapter 13); the fourth is the teaching on life in the church (chapter 18); and the fifth is the discourse on the end times (chapters 24–25).

sections.heading: 2. Historical Setting: The Turning Point of the Parables
sections.html:
Matthew 13 does not appear out of nowhere. It follows straight on from chapter 12. Chapter 12 records the Pharisees accusing Jesus of casting out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons — a public, formal and hostile rejection. From that moment on, Jesus’ way of teaching changed: he began to speak in parables.

The disciples found this strange and came to ask him why. Jesus answered, “To you it is given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven, but it is not given to them” (Matthew 13:11). Then he quoted Isaiah 6:9–10, saying, “for this people’s heart has grown callous, their ears are dull of hearing, they have closed their eyes; or else perhaps they might perceive with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and would turn again; and I would heal them” (Matthew 13:15).

Brothers and sisters, please notice: a parable is a double-edged sword. To those willing to listen, a parable is revelation — it lays the mysteries of the Kingdom open before them, vivid and alive. To those unwilling to listen, a parable is a veil — they hear it and move on, as if it were just a story about a farmer.

The same words: some hear the Kingdom of Heaven in them, others hear only a story. Where is the difference? In the heart.

sections.heading: 3. Geographical Setting: A Pulpit in a Boat
sections.html:
Matthew 13:1–2 says, “On that day Jesus went out of the house, and sat by the seaside. Great multitudes gathered to him, so that he entered into a boat, and sat, and all the multitude stood on the beach.”

This is the north-western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Along that stretch there is a natural, half-moon-shaped little bay, which later came to be called the “Cove of the Sower”. Researchers in acoustics have taken measurements there and found that when someone speaks from the surface of the water, the sound reflects off the water and the slope of the hillside, so that several thousand people on the shore can hear clearly. The Lord Jesus chose the best amplifier there was — he wanted people to hear.

And as he looked up at the hillside above the shore, he may well have seen a farmer out in the field sowing seed. Pointing to the scene before him, he said, “Behold, a farmer went out to sow” (Matthew 13:3).

sections.heading: 4. Farming Background: Sow First, Plough Afterwards
sections.html:
This point is vital, or else we’ll think this farmer rather foolish — how could he throw seed onto the path, onto the rocks, into the thorns?

In first-century Palestine, the farmer’s method was “sow first, plough afterwards”. With a bag of seed on his back, he scattered it evenly across the whole field, and only then brought the ox to draw the plough and turn the seed into the soil. So as he sowed, seed naturally fell on the little path that cut across the field, on the places where the thin soil lay over a bed of limestone, and in the corners where last year’s thorn roots were still buried in the ground.

The farmer showed no favouritism. The sower sowed fairly and generously.

Brothers and sisters, this is a perfect picture of the gospel. God is never stingy with his word. His word comes to the rich and to the poor, to the old and to the young, to those who have believed in the Lord for thirty years and to those opening the Bible for the very first time today.

Luke 8:11 says it plainly: “Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.”

The seed is equally good; the sower is equally generous; and yet there are four outcomes. There is only one reason: the soil is different.

So on the surface this parable is “the parable of the sower”, but at its core it is “the parable of the hearer”. What it asks us is not “Did you listen?” but what Jesus said in Mark 4:24: “He said to them, ‘Take heed what you hear.’” In Luke 8:18 the Lord puts it even more directly: “Be careful therefore how you hear.”

Not “what you hear”, but “how you hear”.

Now let’s walk through it, one patch of soil at a time.

sections.heading: 1. The Roadside Heart: Unwilling to Listen, Unable to Hear
sections.html:
1. The Text: The Seed That Was Snatched Away

Jesus said, “When anyone hears the word of the Kingdom, and doesn’t understand it, the evil one comes, and snatches away that which has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown by the roadside” (Matthew 13:19).

Notice the three actions in this verse: hearing, not understanding, being snatched away.

2. Light from the Original: What “Understand” Means

The word “understand” is the Greek syniēmi, which literally means “to put together”, “to bring scattered pieces together into one”. It describes not the receiving of information but the connecting of insight — God’s word lining up with my life, being joined to it, the current switched on.

In other words, a person can take in every word of a message through his ears and write it all down in neat notes, yet never once syniēmi — because those words have never been wired into his life.

And the word for “roadside”, hodos, simply means “road” or “way”: the footpath along the edge of the field, worn down by people walking.

3. Why Is the Roadside Hard?

No path is born hard. A path is trodden into being.

That strip of earth at the edge of the field was originally the very same soil as the field itself. But because countless feet walked over it time after time, year after year, it was packed down and trampled hard, until it became a path that not even a seed could get into.

Brothers and sisters, our hearts are trampled hard in just the same way. Trampled hard by what?

By habit — we’ve heard the same verses so many times that we no longer feel anything. By prejudice — “I already know that,” and so God can’t get a new word in. By hurt — someone once wounded us, so we laid a coat of tarmac over our hearts, and from then on no one could get in, not even God. By busyness — too many footsteps, too fast, too crowded, and the soil never gets a chance to loosen.

The Bible uses a very weighty expression to describe a heart like this: “stiff-necked”.

Exodus 32:9: “Yahweh said to Moses, ‘I have seen these people, and behold, they are a stiff-necked people.’”

The Hebrew is qāshēh ’ōrep, literally “hard of neck”. It is a farmer’s expression. A farmer yokes his ox to plough the field; a light pull on the reins, and the ox should turn. But there is a kind of ox whose neck is rigid: however you pull, it simply will not turn. What a farmer dreads most is not a lazy ox but a stiff-necked one — because it will not be led.

To be stiff-necked is to insist on our own ideas and refuse to submit to God.

4. Pride: The Greatest Obstacle to Hearing God

The prophet Jeremiah could not have put it more clearly: “Hear, and give ear. Don’t be proud, for Yahweh has spoken” (Jeremiah 13:15).

Look at the order of this verse: first “hear”, then “give ear”, and then, straight away — “don’t be proud”.

Why, while speaking about hearing the word, does he suddenly turn to pride? Because in God’s eyes they are really one and the same thing. The proud cannot hear.

The Hebrew root for “pride”, gā’āh, originally means “to rise up, to swell” — like floodwaters rising, like a person propping himself up higher. Someone who has raised himself up cannot hear the voice that comes from above, because he feels he is already up there.

James 4:6 says, “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’”

Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that God doesn’t speak to the proud; it’s that God himself resists them. How serious that is.

5. A Picture: Seed on Concrete

God’s word is like seed; a proud heart is like a concrete floor.

However good the seed, however plump, however full of life, if it’s scattered on concrete it can only lie on the surface, baking in the sun. Nothing is wrong with the seed; there’s simply no crack in the ground.

And what happens to seed lying on concrete? The sparrows come and peck it up in one bite.

Jesus said, “The evil one comes, and snatches away that which has been sown in his heart.” The easiest work Satan ever does is his work in a hardened heart. He doesn’t need to argue, doesn’t need to attack, doesn’t need to tempt — he only needs to wait. Wait until the meeting ends, until the person is driving home, scrolling on the phone — and within thirty minutes that seed is gone.

6. Psychology Bears Witness: Our Brains Are Built to “Not Hear” Selectively

In 1953 the British cognitive scientist Colin Cherry published his famous study of the “cocktail party effect” in the Journal of the Acoustical Society of America. He had subjects hear different messages in each ear at the same time while attending to only one of them. He found that, of the ignored ear, subjects could not even say what language the message had been in. The sound had plainly entered their ears, but it had never entered their awareness.

In 1999 Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris of Harvard published the even more famous “invisible gorilla” experiment in the journal Perception. Subjects were asked to count the number of passes in a basketball game, and about half of them completely failed to see a person in a gorilla suit walk right through the middle of the scene, beat their chest and leave. This is called “inattentional blindness”.

Then there is the theory of “cognitive dissonance”, put forward by Leon Festinger in 1957: when new information clashes with a position we already hold, people often don’t revise the position — they reject the information, because changing position hurts too much.

Brothers and sisters, science tells us something entirely in keeping with the Bible: when people “can’t hear”, it is often not because their ears are broken, but because their hearts are already occupied with another focus, another position, another insistence.

That isn’t an excuse. It’s a warning.

7. A 321 Insight: Pride Holds On to Self; Humility Opens Up the Self

Pride is holding on to “self”; humility is opening up the self.

This is precisely the very heart of the 321 vision: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem.

What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. When I say to God’s word, “I don’t agree,” I have in fact taken the judge’s seat and put God in the dock. That is leaving our originally intended position.

What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Brothers and sisters, only selflessness can hear God. For the heart of a self-centred person is already filled with self; there’s no room left for God’s word.

The Lord Jesus himself is our role model. Philippians 2:8 says, “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” The One with the most authority in the universe chose the lowest place. This is what “Jesus is my role model” means.

8. One Thing You Can Do Today

If you find that your heart has been trodden into a path, what should you do?

Hosea 10:12 gives the answer: “Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.”

“Break up your fallow ground” — the sense of the original is “break open hard ground that has long lain unworked”. The plough hurts. But if you won’t let the plough go in, the seed will never go in either.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, are you willing to say to the Lord: “Lord, I won’t insist on my own ideas. Please break open the hard ground in my heart”?

sections.heading: 2. The Shallow Heart: Unwilling to Act, Unable to Understand
sections.html:
1. The Text: The Fastest to Grow, the Fastest to Wither

Jesus said, “What was sown on the rocky places, this is he who hears the word, and immediately with joy receives it; yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while. When oppression or persecution arises because of the word, immediately he stumbles” (Matthew 13:20–21).

Notice the two contrasts: “immediately with joy receives it” set against “immediately he stumbles”.

The same person, the same heart. As fast as it sprouts, so fast it withers.

2. Original Language and Geography: Rocky Ground Isn’t Ground Full of Rocks

The “rocky places” here, Greek petrōdē, does not mean a field strewn with loose stones. It means a whole shelf of limestone bedrock with only a thin layer of soil over it. Ground like this is everywhere in the hills of Galilee.

This kind of ground has one peculiarity: the thin soil is quickly warmed by the sun, quickly heated, so seed sprouts there faster and more vigorously than anywhere else. From the outside, this is the most beautiful patch in the whole field.

But when the roots push downwards, they hit bedrock and can go no further. So the roots can only spread sideways, tangling shallowly.

Once the sun comes up and the moisture evaporates, it is the first thing in the whole field to wither.

Brothers and sisters, the most dangerous thing in the spiritual life is often not coldness, but “warming up fast with no root”.

3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Roots Go Down as We Do the Word

“Root” is the Greek rhiza. The Bible uses it again and again to describe the depth of a life.

Colossians 2:6–7 says, “As therefore you received Christ Jesus, the Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him, and established in the faith, even as you were taught, abounding in it in thanksgiving.”

Notice the order: “walk in him” comes first, “rooted and built up” comes after. Roots aren’t grown by sitting and listening; they’re grown by walking.

Jeremiah 17:8 describes the one who trusts in Yahweh: “For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit.”

The same heat, the same drought. Where there are roots, the leaves stay green; where there are none, it withers at once. The difference isn’t the weather. It’s the roots.

The Lord Jesus himself used the picture of a house: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock” (Matthew 7:24–25).

Hearing and doing is a foundation; hearing and not doing is empty talk.

James puts it even more bluntly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22). He goes on to describe such a person: “For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was” (James 1:23–24).

He studies himself in the mirror very carefully, then turns round and forgets what he looks like. Brothers and sisters, does that picture feel a little familiar?

4. A Picture: Rain and Roots

Hearing the word is like rain; obeying it is like putting down roots.

When a good rain falls on ground with no roots, the water just runs off, carrying away the topsoil and leaving the ground thinner than before. When a good rain falls beside a tree with roots, every drop goes downwards — into the roots, into the growth rings, and becomes next year’s fruit.

Without roots, no amount of water helps; in fact, the more water there is, the thinner the soil becomes.

This also explains something: why do some brothers and sisters hear sermons for thirty years, and yet their lives seem to stay exactly where they were? It isn’t that they haven’t heard enough. It’s that they haven’t done enough.

5. Evidence from Science and Psychology: Knowing Is a Long Way from Doing

First, the forgetting curve. In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus experimented on memory with himself as the subject. He found that if what we learn is not reviewed, forgetting is sharpest in the earliest stretch of time, and after one day often only about a third remains. Hearing the word is just the same: moved to tears on Sunday morning, and by Monday lunchtime you can’t remember what the sermon was about. Unless — you put it into practice.

Second, the gap between intention and action. In a meta-analytic review published in 2002, the psychologist Paschal Sheeran showed that people’s “behavioural intentions” account, on average, for only about 28 per cent of the variation in their actual behaviour. In other words, between someone sincerely “intending” to do something and actually doing it, there is still a long distance. Being moved is not the same as being changed.

Third, neuroplasticity. In 1949 the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb proposed the famous Hebb’s rule, which later generations often summarise in one line: “Neurons that fire together, wire together.” Repeated behaviour strengthens neural pathways, so that they run more and more smoothly. It’s the same in the spiritual life: obey once, and it is easier to obey a second time; hear once, and it is easier to hear a second time.

Brothers and sisters, this confirms an old saying: we don’t become clear first and then obey; we obey first and then become clear.

6. A Word of Warning

In “The Cost of Discipleship” the twentieth-century German pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a well-known warning: cheap grace is the deadly enemy of the church. What he called “cheap grace” is wanting grace without following, wanting forgiveness without repentance, wanting to hear the word without doing it.

And 1 Samuel 15:22 said the same thing three thousand years ago: “Samuel said, ‘Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.’”

7. A 321 Insight: Those Who Rely on the Heart Obey; Those Who Rely on the Brain Only Analyse

The 321 vision puts it well: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and find joy, rely on the brain and find worry.

When people who rely on the brain hear God’s word, their first reaction is: “Is this reasonable?” “Can it be done?” “What will others think?” By the time the analysis is over, the moment has passed and the stirring has faded.

When people who rely on the heart hear God’s word, their first reaction is: “Lord, I’m willing.”

Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” The fruit of a whole life flows out of the heart, not out of the brain.

The 321 vision speaks of a “fivefold change”: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. And for a mindset to become life, the bridge in between is called “Implementation”.

If we hear but do not put it into practice, the fivefold change stalls at the first stage and never gets any further.

Obey once, and you see a little more clearly. Brothers and sisters, that is a law of the spiritual world.

sections.heading: 3. The Thorny Heart: Crowded Out, Unable to Hear Clearly
sections.html:
1. The Text: It Grew Up, but Bore Nothing

Jesus said, “What was sown among the thorns, this is he who hears the word, but the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and he becomes unfruitful” (Matthew 13:22).

This kind of soil is actually good soil. It has depth, it has nutrients; the seed really did sprout, really did grow up.

The problem is this: it doesn’t grow only God’s word. At the same time, it grows thorns.

2. Light from the Original: “Choke” Means Strangle

The word “choke” is the Greek sympnigō, made up of “together with” plus “to squeeze tight, to suffocate”. The same root (pnigō) with a different prefix gives apopnigō, the word Luke 8:33 uses to describe the herd of pigs rushing down the steep bank and being “drowned”.

This is a violent word. The thorns don’t defeat God’s word; they strangle it. They don’t need to cut it down or pull it up. They only need to wind themselves around it day after day, stealing its sunlight, stealing its water, stealing its nourishment — and the wheat withers all by itself.

Mark’s Gospel lists the thorns more fully: “and the cares of this age, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful” (Mark 4:19).

Cares, riches, desires — three thorns.

3. Where Thorns Come From: Nobody Plants Them; They Grow on Their Own

In Genesis 3:18 God said to Adam, “It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field.”

Brothers and sisters, please notice something: thorns are a product of the fall — and nobody needs to plant thorns.

Wheat has to be sown, watered and tended; thorns only need you to leave them alone, and they grow fast and strong.

This is why the spiritual life needs to be intentional. You don’t have to try to become worldly. Just do nothing at all, and the world will grow over your whole heart by itself.

The Lord Jesus said, “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24).

The thorny heart is not a heart that doesn’t love God. It’s a heart in which too many things matter as much as God — or even more than God.

4. The Classic Example: The Rich Young Ruler

In Matthew 19 a young man ran up to Jesus and asked a good question: “What good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?”

He had zeal, he had morals, he had wealth, he had a future. Mark’s Gospel even records that Jesus, “looking at him loved him”.

Then the Lord spoke: “Jesus said to him, ‘If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me’” (Matthew 19:21).

He heard it. He heard the voice of God clearly and unmistakably.

And the result?

“But when the young man heard the saying, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions” (Matthew 19:22).

Brothers and sisters, this is one of the most heartbreaking verses in all the Gospels. It wasn’t that he couldn’t hear. It was that he couldn’t let go.

Hearing God’s voice comes at a cost. It isn’t entertainment; it isn’t a spiritual tonic to make us feel good. It is meant to change the direction of our lives.

So sometimes, when we “can’t hear clearly”, it’s really because deep down we already sense what he is going to say — and we aren’t yet ready to pay that price.

5. Psychology and Data: The Truth about Worry, the Limits of Money

First, worry. In 2020 Lucas LaFreniere and Michelle Newman of Penn State University published a study in the journal Behavior Therapy. They asked people with generalised anxiety disorder to write down each worry they had every day, and then tracked what actually happened. They found that about 91.4 per cent of the things the participants worried about never came to pass.

We give a great deal of our life’s soil, sunlight and nourishment to feeding a patch of thorns, 91 per cent of which never bear anything at all.

The Lord Jesus said it long ago: “Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient” (Matthew 6:34).

Second, money. In 2010 the Nobel laureate in economics Daniel Kahneman and the economist Angus Deaton published a study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Analysing some 450,000 survey responses in the United States, they found that higher income does improve day-to-day emotional well-being, but that beyond a certain level the improvement levels off. Later studies have differed over this “turning point” and revised it, but on one thing they agree: the happiness money can buy has a ceiling.

The peace God gives has no ceiling.

Third, distraction. In 2017 Adrian Ward and three colleagues published an intriguing experiment in the Journal of the Association for Consumer Research: simply having your own phone on the desk — even face down, even switched off — lowered subjects’ performance on cognitive tests. The researchers called it “brain drain”.

Brothers and sisters, that phone didn’t even ring. It was just “there”. Thorns are like that too. They don’t need to say a word; they only need to occupy a seat in your heart, and they can choke God’s word.

6. A Picture: The Pruning Hand

In John 15:2 the Lord says, “Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away. Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.”

Vineyard workers know one thing better than anyone: an unpruned vine grows a beautiful canopy of leaves but produces only a few bunches of grapes, because all its strength has gone into “growing leaves”.

Pruning hurts, because what gets cut away is often not a bad thing but a “good thing” — it simply stands in the way of the “better thing”.

God prunes us not because he doesn’t care what we lose, but because he cares too much to lose us — he cannot bear to see us busy all our lives and then come before the Lord empty-handed.

7. A 321 Insight: It Isn’t That God Isn’t Speaking; It’s That We Won’t Let Go

The 321 vision says that the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than possessions.

The thorny heart turns that order upside down: tasks first, then possessions, and only then does God get his turn.

The 321 vision also says our perspective must shift — from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly.

The rich young ruler used an earthly abacus and a short-term view. The conclusion he reached was “too expensive”. Had he done the sums once with an eternal view, he would have discovered that this was the one deal in his whole life that could never lose.

Only selflessness can keep us from being choked by the world. For selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

Only when we put down what fills our two hands can we catch the fullness God wants to give.

sections.heading: 4. The Good-Soil Heart: Those Who Truly Hear
sections.html:
1. The Text: Thirty, Sixty, a Hundredfold

Jesus said, “What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit, and produces, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty” (Matthew 13:23).

Luke’s account adds two very important words: “Those in the good ground, these are those who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance” (Luke 8:15).

“Hold it tightly” and “perseverance”. Good soil doesn’t appear overnight.

2. True “Hearing” Has Three Levels

What does it mean to truly hear?

It isn’t hearing with the ears, and it isn’t being emotionally moved. It has three levels:

First, hearing (akouō) — the message comes in.

Second, understanding (syniēmi) — the message is wired into life.

Third, obeying and bearing fruit (karpophoreō) — life produces fruit.

Many people reach the first level; fewer reach the second; only the third is what the Lord is after.

The Lord Jesus said to his disciples, “But blessed are your eyes, for they see; and your ears, for they hear” (Matthew 13:16).

Brothers and sisters, being able to hear is a blessing. But that blessing is only truly cashed in at the third level.

3. What a Hundredfold Really Means

Under the farming conditions of first-century Palestine, an ordinary harvest was about seven to ten times what was sown. Thirtyfold was already a good year; sixtyfold, a bumper crop; a hundredfold was a figure farmers of that age wouldn’t have dared dream of.

It appears once in the Bible: “Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him” (Genesis 26:12) — and that year was a year of famine.

Here the Lord Jesus is telling us that a heart of good soil will bear fruit beyond human common sense. Because that isn’t agriculture; that’s a miracle.

Notice too that the Lord didn’t demand that every patch of good soil yield a hundredfold. Thirtyfold is good soil too; sixtyfold is good soil too. God doesn’t measure you by someone else’s multiple; he measures you by your own soil. As long as you are good soil, you will surely bear fruit.

4. Good Soil Isn’t Born; It’s Cultivated

This is the most hope-filled line in the whole parable.

Brothers and sisters, if the four soils were fixed from birth, this parable would be a verdict, not good news. But thank God — the roadside can be ploughed open, the stones can be prised out, the thorns can be burned away.

That is why the prophet cries out: “For Yahweh says to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, ‘Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns’” (Jeremiah 4:3).

Good soil is soil that has been turned over, soil cleared of stones, soil rid of thorns. Behind every patch of good soil is the sweat of a farmer.

And that farmer is the Lord himself.

5. A Role Model: The Boy Samuel

In 1 Samuel 3, in an age when “Yahweh’s word was rare in those days. There were not many visions,” God called a child. Once, twice, three times he ran the wrong way, until the old priest Eli taught him how to answer.

So that night Scripture recorded a timeless sentence: “Then Samuel said, ‘Speak; for your servant hears’” (1 Samuel 3:10).

Notice the structure of that sentence. It isn’t “Lord, you listen, for your servant is speaking”; it is “Speak; for your servant hears.”

How often our prayers are the former — we talk and talk, and when we’ve finished, we leave, without leaving a single minute for God.

Brothers and sisters, a good-soil heart is a heart that knows how to be still. When Elijah met God at Horeb, Scripture says, “After the earthquake a fire passed; but Yahweh was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice” (1 Kings 19:12).

God’s voice is often small. Not because God is speaking quietly, but because he wants us to draw near.

6. Science Bears Witness: What Can’t Be Seen Is What Matters

The Natural Resources Conservation Service of the US Department of Agriculture points out that one small teaspoon of healthy soil may contain more microorganisms than there are people on earth. The fertility of soil doesn’t lie in how lovely its surface looks, but in the ecosystem underneath that you can’t see at all.

Brothers and sisters, the spiritual life is the same. God doesn’t look at our surface; he looks at the world beneath that no one else sees — your prayers when you are alone, the obedience nobody knows about, your faithfulness in small things.

That is “good soil”.

In “The Problem of Pain” C. S. Lewis wrote a much-quoted passage: God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains; pain is his megaphone to rouse a deaf world.

God is always speaking. It’s just that sometimes he has to turn the volume up to the level at which we’re willing to listen.

7. A 321 Insight: Hearing God Is Not an Ability but a Condition of Life

The Lord Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27).

Notice that the Lord didn’t say, “My sheep are very good listeners.” He said, “My sheep hear my voice.” Sheep can hear the shepherd not because their ears are especially good, but because they are sheep — they belong to this shepherd, and they follow this shepherd every day.

This is the core of the 321 vision: hearing God is not a technique. It is an identity, a condition of life.

The Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Jesus is my role model: he said, “I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge” (see John 5:30). Even the Son of God, while on earth, was one who “heard first, then acted”.

The Bible is my standard: every voice must be brought before Scripture and checked against it. Hebrews 4:12 says, “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.”

The Holy Spirit is my guide: Isaiah 30:21 promises, “and when you turn to the right hand, and when you turn to the left, your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it.’”

When the heart is right, the voice becomes clear.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Four Soils, One Way Forward
sections.html: Brothers and sisters, let’s look at these four soils once more, in the light of 321.

sections.heading: 1. The Four Soils Are Really Four Spiritual Conditions
sections.html:
The roadside heart is a self-centred heart — holding on to its own ideas, with pride blocking out God’s voice.

The shallow heart is a heart that “relies on the brain and not the heart” — moved but not obedient, the fivefold change stuck at the level of mindset.

The thorny heart is a “worldly, temporary” heart — its priorities upside down, tasks bigger than relationships, possessions bigger than God.

The good-soil heart is a selfless heart — laying down self and letting Jesus be King.

sections.heading: 2. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal
sections.html:
The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. When these three are firmly in place, our ears have a reference pitch to tune by.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. Anyone who truly hears God will end up here in the end — not “God, please listen to my plan,” but “Lord, you be King.”

The Goal: establish God’s system. When God speaks, it is never merely to comfort one person’s feelings; it is to build his Kingdom on earth.

sections.heading: 3. Humility Overcomes Pride; Selflessness Overcomes Satan
sections.html:
In this parable the evil one appears only once — on the hard ground by the roadside.

What does that tell us? The place where Satan most easily gets his way is a proud heart. He hardly has to lift a finger: as long as that person keeps holding on to “self”, he can carry the seed off in his beak.

Conversely, humility is the most powerful weapon in spiritual warfare. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. The moment we say to God, “I’m willing to be adjusted by you,” Satan loses his foothold.

sections.heading: 4. The Fivefold Change: From Mindset to Ministry
sections.html:
A change of mindset: I no longer ask, “Why doesn’t God speak to me?” I begin to ask, “What kind of soil is my heart?”

A change of life: the hard ground is ploughed open, the stones are prised out, the thorns are cleared away.

A change of daily living: I begin to put what I hear into practice straight away, even if it’s only one small step.

A change of relationships: a soft, selfless heart will change my relationships with my spouse, my children and my co-workers.

A change of ministry: thirty, sixty, a hundredfold — the fruit isn’t borne for ourselves; it’s borne for others.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The order cannot be reversed. Many people skip life and go straight to ministry, and end up as that shallow ground — quick to grow on the surface, quick to wither the moment trouble comes.

sections.heading: 5. The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships
sections.html:
The 920 practice: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”. As we practise living out the selfless “0”, the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit will grow in these relationships — “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, this is the most practical way to test whether we have “truly heard”: when you get home, do you have a little more patience with your spouse? At the office, do you have a little more gentleness towards the colleague who’s hardest to get along with?

Good soil bears fruit, and the fruit grows in relationships.

235 relationships: find a brother or sister who also longs for selflessness and become each other’s “2” — spiritual companions who remind each other, “What did God say to you this week, and have you done it?” Then build a “3”, upwards and downwards — spiritual parents and spiritual children. And finally, with co-workers from a fivefold-ministry team, become a “5” — a team of spiritual comrades.

One person listening to God alone can easily go astray; when a group of selfless people listen together, the voice becomes clear.

sections.heading: 6. The Path of Serving
sections.html:
Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory).

Notice that the first stop on this path is “Spirit”, not “Service”. We are all too quick to start with serving and forget to start with listening.

First listen, then understand; first understand, then live it out; first live it out, then serve; and finally, all the glory goes to him.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s take them deeper, one by one, using the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Cultivate a Humble Heart and Open Your Ears

Pray to God every day: “Lord, I won’t insist on my own ideas; I’m willing to be adjusted by you.” Deliberately lay down self-centredness and let your heart become soft — good soil that can receive God’s word.

Information: first take the truth in — pride is the greatest obstacle to hearing God (Jeremiah 13:15); God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6).

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light and show you exactly which trodden-hard path runs through your heart — which prejudice, which hurt, which “I already know that”.

Conviction: admit that it really is pride, and stop giving it other names, such as “principle”, “personality” or “I just have strong opinions”.

Implementation: make your first prayer every morning: “Lord, I won’t insist on my own ideas; I’m willing to be adjusted by you.” Say it out loud — don’t just think it.

Evaluation: every evening, spend three minutes looking back — was there a moment today when I knew I should give way, and yet I stiffened my neck?

Correction: apologise to that person, or at least confess it before God.

Repetition: forty days in a row, without a break. Hard ground isn’t loosened by a single pass of the plough.

Multiplication: invite your “2” to do these forty days of practice with you, and ask each other: “This week, what did God adjust in you?”

Practice 2: Put What You Hear into Practice at Once

When you’re stirred in prayer or in reading Scripture, don’t stay at the level of feelings; take one concrete action straight away. Even a very small step — obedience will make you more and more sensitive.

Information: whoever hears and does, his house will not fall (Matthew 7:24–25); be doers of the word, and not only hearers (James 1:22).

Revelation: ask God one very specific question: “Lord, what is the one thing this passage wants me to do today?”

Conviction: believe that “obey once, and you see a little more clearly”. We don’t become clear first and then obey; we obey first and then become clear.

Implementation: set yourself a “twenty-four-hour rule” — whatever you’re stirred to do, take at least one step within twenty-four hours. Make that phone call, write that message, pay back that money, say that “I’m sorry”.

Evaluation: keep two columns in a notebook — “What God said” and “What I did”. Open it a week later: how many lines match up?

Correction: for the lines that don’t match, don’t just feel regret; put them back into next week’s diary.

Repetition: make “hear it, do it” a habit. Hebb’s rule reminds us that a path, once walked, runs more smoothly each time.

Multiplication: take your “What God said, what I did” notebook and share it with a spiritual child, and teach them to keep one too.

Practice 3: Clear the Thorns out of Your Life

Face honestly the worries, cravings and things you can’t let go of; bring them before God and entrust them to him; let God prune them, and recover your sensitivity to his voice.

Information: the cares of this age, the deceitfulness of riches and the lusts of other things choke the word (Mark 4:19).

Revelation: take a sheet of paper, be still for ten minutes, and ask the Holy Spirit to let you write down your three thickest thorns — the one thing you worry about most often, the one possession you can least bear to part with, and the one habit that eats up the most time.

Conviction: admit that they really are competing with God for sunlight. Only by admitting it can you let go.

Implementation: for each thorn, set a concrete “cut” — for example, regular giving, to turn “I can’t bear to part with it” into “I’m glad to give it”; switching off your phone for an hour each day and giving that time back to God; turning that worry into a one-sentence prayer and praying it every time it comes to mind.

Evaluation: a week later, check — did the thing you were worried about happen? Remember that study: about 91 per cent of worries never come true.

Correction: thorns grow back. When you spot a new shoot, cut it at once.

Repetition: set aside a “spiritual pruning day” once every quarter — just half a day, to be still, examine, and entrust.

Multiplication: lead your family or small group through a time of clearing thorns together, and let “glad to give” become your culture.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Lord, I Am Willing to Be Good Soil
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters,

let’s go back to those three gentle reminders:

God is always speaking; the question lies with your heart.

The key to hearing God is not technique; it is life.

Without obedience, the voice grows fainter and fainter.

That is why the Lord Jesus said, “Take heed what you hear” (Mark 4:24). And again: “Be careful therefore how you hear” (Luke 8:18).

God has never stopped speaking, yet people so often fail to hear.

The problem isn’t with God; it is with the heart.

The roadside heart is closed; the rocky heart has no root; the thorny heart is choked.

But God is looking for a certain kind of person — someone willing to open up, willing to obey, willing to pay the price.

People like that will surely hear God.

Brothers and sisters, the four soils are really not four kinds of people; they are often four corners of the same person. Perhaps one patch of your heart is already good soil, while another corner is still concrete; one patch has been cleared, yet in the corner by the wall the thorns are putting out new shoots again.

So this parable isn’t meant for us to sort other people into categories. It’s meant for us, this morning, to grow still and say one thing to the Lord:

“Lord, please come and turn over this soil of mine.”

Let Jesus be King — not only King in church, but King over my ideas, King over my diary, King over my wallet.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when the fruit comes, thirty, sixty, a hundredfold, we all know it isn’t my ability; it is the generosity of the Sower and the kindness of the One who prunes.

From today, let’s learn one thing and say one sentence:

Lord, I am willing to be good soil; let your voice bear fruit in me.

keyVerses: “What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit, and produces, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.” (Matthew 13:23)
“The hearing ear, and the seeing eye, Yahweh has made even both of them.” (Proverbs 20:12)
practices: Cultivate a humble heart and open your ears
Put what you hear into practice at once
Clear the thorns out of your life
prayer: Lord Jesus, we thank you.
You have never stopped speaking. It is our hearts that are so often too hard, too shallow, too full.
Lord Jesus, I believe you are speaking to me.
Please give me a soft, humble, selfless heart.
With your plough, break open the trodden-hard path within me; with your hand, prise up the bedrock in me that stops the roots; with your fire, burn away the thorns in me that choke your word.
Take away the pride, the laziness and the crush of the world within me.
Let me not only hear, but understand and obey.
Lord, like Samuel, today I say: Speak; for your servant hears.
I want to be good soil and bear the fruit of life — thirty, sixty, a hundredfold — all of it given back to you.
Reign as King in my life, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “When anyone hears the word of the Kingdom, and doesn’t understand it, the evil one comes, and snatches away that which has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown by the roadside.” (Matthew 13:19) Think back to the last time you “heard but felt nothing”.
