blog.title: The Signal Keeps Coming — Is Your Receiver Switched On?

blocks.x: What the Parable of the Sower Tells Us about Why We Can’t Hear God’s Voice
Late on that April night in 1912, the Titanic sent out distress calls for more than two hours. Less than twenty nautical miles away lay another ship, and the signals reached her aerial without fail.
But on that ship no one was wearing the headphones — the wireless operator had long since switched off his set and gone to bed.
The real tragedy of that night was not that the signal was never sent. It was that the receiver had been switched off.
Isn’t that a picture of many Christians too? We read the Bible, we pray, we go to meetings — and yet a voice inside us asks: God, are you still speaking?
The Bible’s answer is clear: he has been speaking all along. The problem has never been at the transmitting end, but at the receiving end.
The Same Handful of Seed, Four Outcomes

The Lord Jesus told a parable: a farmer went out to sow, and the seed fell on four kinds of ground — the roadside, the rocky places, among the thorns, and the good ground. The same sower, the same handful of seed, sown fairly and generously — and yet completely different outcomes.
The difference is not in the seed but in the soil. And that soil is our heart.

The first is the roadside heart. The Lord said, “When anyone hears the word of the Kingdom, and doesn’t understand it, the evil one comes, and snatches away that which has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown by the roadside.” (Matthew 13:19)

No path is born hard. A path is trodden into being, one footstep at a time. Our hearts are the same — trampled hard by habit, until we’ve heard something so often that we feel nothing; trampled hard by prejudice, until “I already know that” shuts the door; trampled hard by hurt, until we lay a coat of tarmac over our hearts; trampled hard by busyness, until the soil never gets a chance to loosen.
God’s word is like seed; a proud heart is like a concrete floor. However good the seed, it cannot get in.

The second is the shallow heart. A thin layer of soil lies over a whole shelf of bedrock; the seed sprouts fastest and withers fastest, because the roots cannot go down. People like this are deeply moved when they hear the word, but never put it into practice.

The third is the thorny heart. This is actually good soil, and the seed really did grow up; the problem is that thorns grow there at the same time — the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word.

Nobody needs to plant thorns; they grow on their own. That is why the spiritual life must be “intentional”: you don’t have to try to become worldly — just do nothing at all, and the world will grow over your whole heart by itself.
Good Soil Isn’t Born; It’s Cultivated

The fourth is the good-soil heart. True “hearing” has three levels: hearing, understanding, and then obeying and bearing fruit. Many people reach the first level; fewer reach the second; only the third is what the Lord is after.
And here is the best news of all: good soil isn’t born.

If the four soils were fixed from birth, this parable would be a verdict, not good news. But thank God — the roadside can be ploughed open, the stones can be prised out, the thorns can be burned away. That is why the prophet cries out: “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.” (Jeremiah 4:3)
Behind every patch of good soil is the sweat of a farmer. And that farmer is the Lord himself.
Three Practices You Can Start Today
First, practise humility and open your ears. Make your first prayer every morning, said out loud: “Lord, I won’t insist on my own ideas; I’m willing to be adjusted by you.”

Second, put what you hear into practice at once. Set yourself a “twenty-four-hour rule”: whatever you’re stirred to do, take at least one step within a day. Remember: we don’t become clear first and then obey; we obey first and then become clear.

Third, clear the thorns out of your life. Write down your three thickest thorns — the one thing you worry about most often, the one possession you can least bear to part with, and the one habit that eats up the most time — and bring them to the Lord for him to prune.

In 2020 Lucas LaFreniere and Michelle Newman of Penn State University published a study in the journal Behavior Therapy that tracked the worries recorded by anxious people, and found that about 91.4 per cent of them never came to pass. We give so much of our life’s sunlight and nourishment to feeding a patch of thorns, 91 per cent of which never bear anything at all.
When the Heart Is Right, the Voice Becomes Clear
The 3-2-1 vision reminds us: pride holds on to self; humility opens up the self. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.
Have you noticed? In this parable the evil one appears only once — on the hard ground by the roadside. Because the place where Satan most easily gets his way is a proud heart.

The Lord Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27) Sheep can hear the shepherd not because their ears are especially good, but because they belong to this shepherd and follow him every day.
Hearing God has never been a technique; it is a condition of life.

The four soils are really not four kinds of people; they are often four corners of the same person. So this parable isn’t meant for us to sort other people into categories. It’s meant for us to grow still today and say one thing to the Lord:
Lord, please come and turn over this soil of mine. I am willing to be good soil; let your voice bear fruit in me.
Reflection Question
If the Lord Jesus asked you today, by name, to lay down one thing, what would spring to mind first? This week, what concrete action will be your first “cut”?

brief12.title: How to Hear God’s Voice
notes: Slide text:
Four Kinds of Soil, Four Outcomes
“What was sown on the good ground, this is he who
hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit”
(Matthew 13:23)
Key points:
• Open with a greeting; explain that this lesson comes from the Lord Jesus’ parable of the sower.
• Read the full key verse, Matthew 13:23, and also Proverbs 20:12: “The hearing ear, and the seeing eye, Yahweh has made even both of them.”
• State the thread of the whole lesson: the seed is equally good, the sower equally generous; the difference is the soil.
• That soil is your heart.

brief12.title: Introduction: The Signal Kept Coming
notes: Slide text:
The Titanic’s distress calls kept coming
but the nearby ship had switched off its set
God has never stopped speaking
The problem lies with the receiving heart
Key points:
• Example: when the Titanic sank in 1912, the wireless operator of the nearby Californian had switched off and gone to bed.
• The British inquiry concluded the ship was close enough that, had anyone been listening, lives could have been saved.
• Move to Isaiah 6:9: “You hear indeed, but don’t understand.”
• Proverbs 20:12: to be able to hear is grace; to be able to understand is blessing.
• Ask: are you ready to listen by relying on the heart?

brief12.title: Key Verse and Background
notes: Slide text:
“You hear indeed, but don’t understand”
(Isaiah 6:9)
Matthew 13: the parables of the Kingdom
Sow first, plough afterwards; the seed is God’s word
Key points:
• Author: Matthew, c. AD 50–70, writing for believers of Jewish background.
• Chapter 13 is the third of Matthew’s five great discourses, following straight on from the Pharisees’ public rejection in chapter 12.
• Setting: the shore of the Sea of Galilee; Jesus sat in a boat to teach (Matthew 13:1–2).
• Farming background: in the first century they sowed first and ploughed afterwards, so seed fell on the path, the rocks and among thorns.
• Luke 8:11 “The seed is the word of God”; the point is not what you hear but how you hear (Mark 4:24).

brief12.title: 1. The Roadside Heart: Unwilling to Listen, Unable to Hear
notes: Slide text:
“The evil one comes, and snatches away
that which has been sown in his heart” (Matthew 13:19)
Paths are trodden hard: habit, prejudice,
hurt, busyness; the stiff-necked cannot hear
Key points:
• Original: “understand” — syniēmi, to put the pieces together; wiring into life, not receiving information.
• “Stiff-necked” (Exodus 32:9) is a farmer’s expression: an ox with a rigid neck won’t turn however you pull.
• Jeremiah 13:15 “Hear, and give ear. Don’t be proud, for Yahweh has spoken.”
• Picture: God’s word is like seed, a proud heart like a concrete floor; however good the seed, it can’t get in.
• Psychology: Cherry’s cocktail party effect (1953); Simons and Chabris’ invisible gorilla (1999).

brief12.title: 2. The Shallow Heart: Unwilling to Act, Unable to Understand
notes: Slide text:
“He has no root in himself … immediately he stumbles”
(Matthew 13:21)
Hearing is like rain; obeying is like putting down roots
Without roots, no amount of water helps
Key points:
• Rocky places — petrōdē: thin soil over a whole shelf of bedrock; fastest to sprout, fastest to wither.
• Matthew 7:24–25: whoever hears and does, his house doesn’t fall, for it is founded on the rock.
• James 1:22 “Be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”
• Data: Ebbinghaus’ forgetting curve (1885); Sheeran’s 2002 meta-analysis: intentions explain only about 28% of behaviour.
• 321: those who rely on the heart obey; those who rely on the brain only analyse. Obey once, and you see a little more clearly.

brief12.title: 3. The Thorny Heart: Crowded Out, Unable to Hear Clearly
notes: Slide text:
“The cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches
choke the word” (Matthew 13:22)
Nobody plants thorns; they grow on their own
The rich young ruler went away sad
Key points:
• Original: “choke” — sympnigō, to squeeze tight together, to suffocate; a violent word.
• Genesis 3:18: thorns are a product of the fall and grow without being planted — so the spiritual life needs to be intentional.
• Matthew 19:22 “When the young man heard the saying, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions.”
• Data: LaFreniere and Newman (2020): about 91.4% of what anxious people worried about never happened.
• 321: it isn’t that God isn’t speaking; we won’t let go. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than possessions.

brief12.title: 4. The Good-Soil Heart: Those Who Truly Hear
notes: Slide text:
“He who hears the word, and understands it, who bears fruit,
some one hundred times as much” (Matthew 13:23)
Good soil isn’t born; it’s cultivated
When the heart is right, the voice becomes clear
Key points:
• An ordinary harvest then was about seven to ten times; a hundredfold is miracle territory (see Isaac, Genesis 26:12).
• Luke 8:15 adds “hold it tightly” and “perseverance”: good soil doesn’t appear overnight.
• Jeremiah 4:3 “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns” — good soil can be cultivated.
• Role models: 1 Samuel 3:10 “Speak; for your servant hears”; 1 Kings 19:12 “After the fire, there was a still small voice.”
• John 10:27 “My sheep hear my voice” — hearing is an identity, not a technique.

brief12.title: Three Levels of Truly Hearing
notes: Slide text:
Hearing: the message comes in
Understanding: it’s wired into life
Obeying and bearing fruit: fruit appears
“Blessed are … your ears” (Matthew 13:16)
Key points:
• Three Greek words: akouō, hear; syniēmi, understand; karpophoreō, bear fruit.
• Many reach the first level, fewer the second; only the third is what the Lord is after.
• Matthew 13:16 in full: “But blessed are your eyes, for they see; and your ears, for they hear.”

• Science: the US Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service notes that a teaspoon of healthy soil may hold more microorganisms than there are people on earth — what matters is the unseen layer beneath.
• God looks at the prayers, obedience and faithfulness in small things that no one sees.

brief12.title: 321 Insight: Only the Selfless Can Hear
notes: Slide text:
The old self is self-centred; the new self selfless
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
Let Jesus be King; all the glory to him
Key points:
• The evil one appears only once in the parable, on the hard roadside ground — pride is where Satan most easily gets his way.
• Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.
• The fivefold change: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry; change your mindset and your life changes.
• The 920 practice: everyone I relate to is my “2”; live out the selfless “0” and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23).
• The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

brief12.title: Putting It into Practice
notes: Slide text:
Practise humility and open your ears
Put what you hear into practice at once
Clear the thorns out of your life
Eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation
Key points:
• Practice 1: pray every day, “Lord, I won’t insist on my own ideas; I’m willing to be adjusted by you” — forty days in a row.
• Practice 2: set a twenty-four-hour rule — take one step within a day on any prompting; keep two columns, “What God said” and “What I did”.
• Practice 3: write down your three thickest thorns — the worry most often on your mind, the possession you can least part with, the habit that eats the most time.
• The full eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
• Multiplication: invite your “2” to practise with you, and ask each other, “This week, what did God adjust in you?”

brief12.title: Closing and Call
notes: Slide text:
God is always speaking; the question lies with your heart
The key is not technique but life
Willing to open up, to obey, to pay the price
“Take heed what you hear” (Mark 4:24)
Key points:
• Three gentle reminders: God is always speaking; the key is life, not technique; without obedience, the voice grows fainter and fainter.
• The four soils are often four corners of the same person, not categories for sorting others.
• Call: “Lord, please come and turn over this soil of mine.”
• Let Jesus be King over my ideas, my diary and my wallet.
• Closing line: Lord, I am willing to be good soil; let your voice bear fruit in me.

brief12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, I believe you are speaking to me
Give me a soft, humble, selfless heart
Let me not only hear but obey
Speak; for your servant hears (1 Samuel 3:10)
Key points:
• Lead the congregation in praying aloud together, in a quiet, warm tone.
• Elements of the prayer: ask the Lord to break up the hard ground, prise up the bedrock and burn away the thorns.
• Close with Samuel’s response: “Speak; for your servant hears!”
• Blessing: may the Lord’s word bear fruit in the brothers and sisters — thirty, sixty, a hundredfold.
• In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
