root in himself … immediately he stumbles”
(Matthew 13:20–21)
The fastest to sprout is the fastest to wither
Key points:
• Contrast: “immediately with joy receives it” against “immediately he stumbles”.
• Rocky places — petrōdē: not ground full of stones, but thin soil over a whole shelf of limestone bedrock.
• The thin soil warms quickly, so the seed sprouts most vigorously — from outside, the loveliest patch in the field.
• The roots hit bedrock and can’t go down; when the sun comes up, it is the first to wither.
• The most dangerous thing spiritually is not coldness but warming up fast with no root.

brief21.title: 2.2 Hearing Plus Doing Equals a Foundation
notes: Slide text:
“Everyone who hears these words of mine, and does them …
it didn’t fall” (Matthew 7:24–25)
“Be doers of the word, and not only hearers”
(James 1:22)
Key points:
• Colossians 2:6–7: first “walk in him”, then “rooted and built up in him” — roots are grown by walking.
• Jeremiah 17:8: a tree planted by the waters, roots by the river, unconcerned in the year of drought, never ceasing to yield fruit.
• James 1:23–24: a hearer who is not a doer is like a man who looks in a mirror and immediately forgets what he looks like.
• 1 Samuel 15:22 “To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.”
• Without roots, no amount of water helps; the more water, the thinner the topsoil is washed.

brief21.title: 2.3 The Data and a 321 Insight
notes: Slide text:
Forgetting curve: without review, a third remains after a day
Intentions explain only about 28% of behaviour
The heart obeys; the brain only analyses
Obey once, and you see a little more clearly
Key points:
• Ebbinghaus’ forgetting curve (1885); Sheeran’s 2002 meta-analysis: behavioural intentions explain on average only about 28% of the variation in behaviour.
• Hebb’s rule (1949): neurons that fire together, wire together — obedience forms spiritual pathways.
• Bonhoeffer, The Cost of Discipleship: cheap grace is the deadly enemy of the church.
• 321: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and find joy, rely on the brain and find worry.
• The fivefold change: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry; the bridge in between is called “Implementation”.

brief21.title: 3.1 The Thorny Heart: The Text
notes: Slide text:
“The cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches
choke the word, and he becomes unfruitful”
(Matthew 13:22)
“Choke”: to squeeze tight together, to suffocate
Key points:
• This is actually good soil: it has depth and nutrients, and the seed really did sprout and grow.
• The problem is that thorns grow there at the same time.
• Original: sympnigō, to squeeze tight together, to suffocate — a violent word.
• Mark 4:19 lists more fully: the cares of this age, the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things.
• Thorns needn’t cut or uproot; they only wind round day after day, stealing sunlight and nourishment.

brief21.title: 3.2 Nobody Plants Thorns
notes: Slide text:
“It will yield thorns and thistles to you”
(Genesis 3:18)
Wheat must be sown; thorns grow if left alone
So the spiritual life must be intentional
Key points:
• Thorns are a product of the fall; nobody needs to plant thorns.
• You don’t have to try to become worldly; just do nothing, and the world will grow over your whole heart by itself.
• Matthew 6:24 “You can’t serve both God and Mammon.”
• Example: the rich young ruler in Matthew 19 — he had zeal, morals, wealth and a future.
• Matthew 19:22 “When the young man heard the saying, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions.”

brief21.title: 3.3 Pruning and a 321 Insight
notes: Slide text:
John 15:2: pruned to bear more fruit
91% of worries never come to pass
It isn’t that God isn’t speaking; we won’t let go
People matter more than tasks; relationships more than things
Key points:
• John 15:2 “Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.”
• Pruning hurts because what is cut is often not bad but a good thing that stands in the way of a better thing.
• LaFreniere and Newman (2020, Behavior Therapy): about 91.4% of the worries anxious people recorded never came true.
• Ward et al. (2017): simply having a phone on the desk lowers cognitive performance (“brain drain”).
• 321: the order of relationships is first with God, then ourselves, then others, last with things; from the temporary to the eternal.

brief21.title: 4.1 The Good-Soil Heart: Three Levels
notes: Slide text:
Hearing: the message comes in
Understanding: it’s wired into life
Bearing fruit: the fruit of life appears
“Blessed are … your ears” (Matthew 13:16)
Key points:
• Greek: akouō, hear; syniēmi, understand; karpophoreō, bear fruit.
• Luke 8:15 adds two key words: “hold it tightly” and “perseverance”.
• Matthew 13:16 “But blessed are your eyes, for they see; and your ears, for they hear.”
• Many reach the first level, fewer the second; only the third is what the Lord is after.

brief21.title: 4.2 Good Soil Is Cultivated
notes: Slide text:
A hundredfold: ordinary harvests were seven to ten times
“Break up your fallow ground” (Jeremiah 4:3)
The roadside can be ploughed, the stones prised out
the thorns burned away — good soil isn’t born
Key points:
• Genesis 26:12: Isaac reaped a hundredfold in a year of famine, and Yahweh blessed him.
• Thirtyfold is good soil too, and sixtyfold; God measures you by your own soil.
• If the four soils were fixed from birth, the parable would be a verdict, not good news — thank God, soil can be turned.
• Role model: 1 Samuel 3:10 “Speak; for your servant hears!” — not “Lord, you listen, your servant is speaking.”
• 1 Kings 19:12 “After the fire, there was a still small voice” — God speaks softly so that we draw near.

brief21.title: 4.3 When the Heart Is Right, the Voice Is Clear
notes: Slide text:
“My sheep hear my voice” (John 10:27)
Hearing is not technique but identity and life
Jesus my role model, the Bible my standard
the Holy Spirit my guide
Key points:
• Sheep hear the shepherd not because their ears are especially good, but because they belong to him and follow him every day.
• Science: the US Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service notes a teaspoon of healthy soil may hold more microorganisms than there are people on earth.
• Fertility lies not on the surface but in the unseen layer below — God looks at the prayers and obedience no one knows about.
• Hebrews 4:12: the word of God is living and active, able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
• Isaiah 30:21 “Your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it.’”

brief21.title: Practices 1 and 2
notes: Slide text:
Practise humility and open your ears
“Lord, I’m willing to be adjusted by you” — forty days
Put what you hear into practice at once
Take one step within twenty-four hours
Key points:
• Practice 1, Information: Jeremiah 13:15 — pride is the greatest obstacle; James 4:6 — God gives grace to the humble.
• Practice 1, Implementation: say your first prayer each morning out loud, not just in your head; three minutes of review each evening.
• Practice 2: we don’t become clear first and then obey; we obey first and then become clear.
• Practice 2, Implementation: keep two columns in a notebook — “What God said” and “What I did” — and compare after a week.
• Practice 2, Multiplication: show the notebook to a spiritual child and teach them to keep one too.

brief21.title: Practice 3 and the Eight Stages
notes: Slide text:
Clear the thorns out of your life
Write down your three thickest thorns; let God prune
Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation
Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
Key points:
• Three thorns: the one worry most often on your mind, the one possession you can least part with, the one habit that eats the most time.
• Set a concrete “cut” for each: regular giving, switching off your phone for an hour a day, turning the worry into a one-sentence prayer.
• Evaluation: a week later, did the thing you worried about happen? Remember the 91% figure.
• Repetition: once a quarter, set aside half a day as a “spiritual pruning day” — be still, examine, entrust.
• Multiplication: lead your family or small group in clearing thorns together, and let “glad to give” become your culture.

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
notes: Slide text:
The old self is self-centred; the new self selfless
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
Let Jesus be King; all the glory to him
Key points:
• The four soils match four spiritual conditions: self-centred, relying on the brain not the heart, worldly and temporary, selfless.
• The evil one appears only once in the parable, on the hard roadside ground — pride is where Satan most easily gets his way.
• Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.
• The 920 practice: everyone I relate to is my “2”; live selflessly and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23).
• The 235 relationships: become a “2” with someone selfless, build the “3” of spiritual parents and children, and form a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: Slide text:
God is always speaking; the question lies with your heart
The key is not technique but life
Willing to open up, to obey, to pay the price
“Take heed what you hear” (Mark 4:24)
Key points:
• Three gentle reminders: God is always speaking; the key is life; without obedience, the voice grows fainter and fainter.
• The four soils are often four corners of the same person, not categories for sorting others.
• Call: “Lord, please come and turn over this soil of mine.”
• Let Jesus be King over my ideas, my diary and my wallet; let him receive all the glory.
• Closing line: Lord, I am willing to be good soil; let your voice bear fruit in me.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, I believe you are speaking to me
Give me a soft, humble, selfless heart
Let me not only hear but understand and obey
Speak; for your servant hears (1 Samuel 3:10)
Key points:
• Lead the brothers and sisters in praying aloud together, in a quiet, warm tone.
• Elements of the prayer: ask the Lord to break up the hard ground with his plough, prise up the bedrock, and burn away the thorns with his fire.
• Ask the Lord to remove the pride, the laziness and the crush of the world within.
• Blessing: may the Lord’s word bear fruit in the brothers and sisters — thirty, sixty, a hundredfold.
• In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning.
Today we’re going to ask a question: why is it that we read the Bible and pray, and yet it seems we can’t hear God’s voice?

Our key verse is Matthew 13:23: “What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit, and produces, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.”
Four kinds of soil, four outcomes. The seed is equally good; the sower is equally generous. So where is the difference? In the soil. And that soil is your heart.

Let me begin with a true story. In 1912 the Titanic struck an iceberg and sent out distress calls for more than two hours. Less than twenty nautical miles away lay another ship — but her wireless operator had long since switched off his set and gone to sleep.
The signal arrived, but no one was wearing the headphones.
Brothers and sisters, the real tragedy of that night was not that the signal was never sent. It was that the receiver had been switched off.
God has never stopped speaking. The problem lies with the receiving heart.
This world is full of voices. But the Bible says, “You hear indeed, but don’t understand. You see indeed, but don’t perceive.” (Isaiah 6:9)

Today’s passage comes from the parables of the Kingdom in Matthew 13. Jesus was sitting in a boat by the Sea of Galilee, and on the shore a farmer was sowing. In those days they sowed first and ploughed afterwards, so the seed naturally fell on the path, on the rocky places and among the thorns.
Luke says, “The seed is the word of God.” (Luke 8:11) The sower showed no favouritism; the only difference was the soil.
The first soil is the roadside heart. Unwilling to listen, and so unable to hear.
The Lord said, “The evil one comes, and snatches away that which has been sown in his heart.” (Matthew 13:19)
Brothers and sisters, no path is born hard; a path is trodden into being, one footstep at a time.
Trodden hard by what? By habit, by prejudice, by hurt, by busyness — the footsteps come so thick and fast that the soil never gets a chance to loosen.
The Bible calls this being “stiff-necked”. Jeremiah says, “Hear, and give ear. Don’t be proud, for Yahweh has spoken.” (Jeremiah 13:15)
God’s word is like seed; a proud heart is like a concrete floor. However good the seed, it cannot get in.
The 321 Insight says: pride holds on to self; humility opens up the self. Only selflessness can hear God.
The second soil is the shallow heart. Unwilling to act, and so unable to understand.
The Lord said, “He has no root in himself … immediately he stumbles.” (Matthew 13:21)

This is a thin layer of soil over a whole shelf of bedrock. It sprouts fastest and withers fastest, because the roots cannot go down. The most dangerous thing is not coldness; it is warming up fast with no root.
The Lord said, “Everyone who hears these words of mine, and does them … it didn’t fall.” (Matthew 7:24–25) Hearing and doing is a foundation; hearing and not doing is empty talk.
Psychological research has found that people’s behavioural intentions account, on average, for only about 28 per cent of their actual behaviour. Being moved is not the same as being changed.
Hearing the word is like rain; obeying it is like putting down roots. Without roots, no amount of water helps.
The 321 Insight says: those who rely on the heart obey; those who rely on the brain only analyse. Obey once, and you see a little more clearly.
The third soil is the thorny heart. Crowded out, and so unable to hear clearly.
The Lord said, “The cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word.” (Matthew 13:22)
In the original, “choke” means “to squeeze tight, to suffocate”. The thorns only need to wind themselves around it, stealing its sunlight and nourishment, and the wheat withers all by itself.
Brothers and sisters, nobody needs to plant thorns; they grow on their own. Wheat has to be sown, watered and tended; thorns grow best when you leave them alone.

The classic example is the rich young ruler in Matthew 19. He heard clearly and unmistakably. And the result? “When the young man heard the saying, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions.”
It wasn’t that he couldn’t hear. It was that he couldn’t let go.
One study tracked the things anxious people worried about and found that about 91 per cent of them never came to pass. We give so much nourishment to feeding a patch of thorns that bear nothing.
The 321 Insight says: it isn’t that God isn’t speaking; it’s that we won’t let go. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than possessions.
The fourth soil is the good-soil heart. The Lord said, “What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit.” (Matthew 13:23)
In that age an ordinary harvest was seven to ten times what was sown; a hundredfold was a figure farmers wouldn’t have dared dream of.

Brothers and sisters, here is wonderful news: good soil isn’t born; it’s cultivated. The roadside can be ploughed open, the stones can be prised out, the thorns can be burned away. The prophet says, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.” (Jeremiah 4:3)
When the heart is right, the voice becomes clear.
So what does it mean to “truly hear”? It isn’t hearing with the ears, and it isn’t being emotionally moved. It has three levels.
First, hearing — the message comes in.
Second, understanding — it is wired into my life.
Third, obeying and bearing fruit — fruit appears.
Many people reach the first level; fewer reach the second; only the third is what the Lord is after.
The Lord said, “Blessed are … your ears, for they hear.” (Matthew 13:16)

Brothers and sisters, the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Have you noticed? In this parable the evil one appears only once — on the hard ground by the roadside. The place where Satan most easily gets his way is a proud heart.
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.
Life first, then relationships, then ministry. And in the end, let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.
Today we have three practices.
First, practise humility and open your ears. Make your first prayer every morning, said out loud: “Lord, I won’t insist on my own ideas; I’m willing to be adjusted by you.”
Second, put what you hear into practice at once. Set yourself a twenty-four-hour rule: whatever you’re stirred to do, take at least one step within a day.

Third, clear the thorns out of your life. Write down your three thickest thorns — the worry most often on your mind, the possession you can least part with, the habit that eats up the most time — and bring them to the Lord for him to prune.
Changing our mindset has eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Brothers and sisters, don’t stop at the first one.
Dear brothers and sisters,
God is always speaking; the question lies with your heart.
The key to hearing God is not technique; it is life.
Without obedience, the voice grows fainter and fainter.
The Lord said, “Take heed what you hear.” (Mark 4:24)
The roadside heart is closed; the rocky heart has no root; the thorny heart is choked.
But God is looking for a certain kind of person — someone willing to open up, willing to obey, willing to pay the price.
People like that will surely hear God.
Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, I believe you are speaking to me.

Please give me a soft, humble, selfless heart. With your plough, break open the trodden-hard path within me; with your fire, burn away the thorns that choke your word. Take away the pride, the laziness and the crush of the world within me, and let me not only hear, but understand and obey.
Lord, like Samuel, today I say: Speak; for your servant hears.
I want to be good soil and bear the fruit of life, with all the glory given to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord’s word bear fruit in you today — thirty, sixty, a hundredfold.
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.
This morning I want to ask a very honest question: how long has it been since you clearly heard God speak to you?
Today we are reading the parable of the sower, told by the Lord Jesus himself.

Our key verse is Matthew 13:23: “What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit, and produces, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.”
Four kinds of soil, four outcomes.
Please remember today’s main thread: the seed is equally good, the sower is equally generous; the only difference is the soil. And that soil is your heart.
Let’s begin with something that really happened in history.

Late on the night of 14 April 1912, less than twenty nautical miles from the Titanic, a cargo ship lay stopped. That evening her wireless operator sent out ice warnings again and again; when he broke in on the Titanic’s channel one last time, the operator there, busy sending private telegrams, snapped back: “Shut up, I am busy.” Not long afterwards he switched off his set and went to bed.
At 11:40 p.m. the Titanic struck the iceberg. For the next two hours and more, distress calls reached that ship’s aerial over and over again.
But on that ship, no one was wearing the headphones.
Brothers and sisters, the real tragedy of that night was not that the signal was never sent. It was that the receiver had been switched off.
This world is full of voices, but the one that matters most is the voice of God. The question is this: when God speaks, are we sure to hear him?
The Bible says, “You hear indeed, but don’t understand. You see indeed, but don’t perceive.” (Isaiah 6:9)
Some people have ears and yet cannot hear. Why? Because hearing God has never been an outward ability; it is a condition of the inner life.
Proverbs 20:12 says, “The hearing ear, and the seeing eye, Yahweh has made even both of them.”
Brothers and sisters, the key comes down to one question: are you ready to listen by relying on the heart?

First, the background. Matthew’s Gospel was written by Matthew the tax collector, sometime between AD 50 and 70, for believers of Jewish background. Chapter 13 is the third of the book’s five great discourses — the parables of the Kingdom.

The timing matters. In chapter 12 the Pharisees had only just publicly accused Jesus of casting out demons by the prince of demons. From that moment on, the Lord began to speak in parables. A parable is a double-edged sword: to those willing to listen it is revelation; to those unwilling to listen it is just a story.

That day the Lord sat in a boat by the Sea of Galilee, and on the hillside a farmer was sowing. In the first century they sowed first and ploughed afterwards, so the seed naturally fell on the little path, on the thin soil and among the thorns.
Luke says, “The seed is the word of God.” (Luke 8:11)
So at its core this is a parable about hearing. What it asks is not “Did you listen?” but “How do you listen?”
The first soil is the roadside heart.
The Lord said, “When anyone hears the word of the Kingdom, and doesn’t understand it, the evil one comes, and snatches away that which has been sown in his heart.” (Matthew 13:19)
Notice the three actions: hearing, not understanding, being snatched away.
The word “understand” here is the Greek syniēmi, meaning “to bring scattered pieces together into one”. It is not the receiving of information; it is life being connected through.
Brothers and sisters, a person can take in every word of a message through his ears and never once truly understand — because those words have never been wired into his life.
So why is the roadside hard?

Brothers and sisters, no path is born hard. That strip of earth at the edge of the field was originally the very same soil as the field itself; it is only because countless feet walked over it time after time that it became so hard not even a seed could get in. Our hearts are trampled hard in just the same way.
Trampled hard by habit — we’ve heard it so many times that we no longer feel anything.
Trampled hard by prejudice — “I already know that.”
Trampled hard by hurt — someone wounded us, so we laid a coat of tarmac over our hearts.
Trampled hard by busyness — too many footsteps, and the soil never gets a chance to loosen.

The Bible calls a heart like this “stiff-necked”. A farmer gives the reins a light pull, and the ox should turn; but there is a kind of ox that won’t turn however you pull. Jeremiah says, “Hear, and give ear. Don’t be proud, for Yahweh has spoken.” (Jeremiah 13:15)

God’s word is like seed; a proud heart is like a concrete floor. However good the seed, scattered on concrete it can only lie on the surface, baking in the sun. And then the sparrows come and peck it up in one bite. The easiest work Satan ever does is his work in a hardened heart — he doesn’t need to argue; he only needs to wait.

Psychology bears this out too. In Simons and Chabris’ 1999 “invisible gorilla” experiment, about half the people never saw the gorilla walk right through the middle of the scene. When people can’t hear, it is often not because their ears are broken, but because their hearts are already full of themselves.

So the 321 Insight says: pride holds on to self; humility opens up the self. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place; humility is returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.
James 4:6 says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” Only selflessness can hear God.
The second soil is the shallow heart.

The Lord said, “He who hears the word, and immediately with joy receives it; yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while … immediately he stumbles.” (Matthew 13:20–21) Listen to the contrast: as fast as it sprouts, so fast it withers.

The “rocky places” are not ground strewn with loose stones, but a whole shelf of bedrock with a thin layer of soil over it. The thin soil warms quickly, so the seed sprouts most vigorously, and it looks like the loveliest patch in the field; but the roots hit the bedrock and can go no further, and when the sun comes up it is the first to wither.
Brothers and sisters, the most dangerous thing in the spiritual life is not coldness; it is warming up very fast with no root.
So how do the roots go down?

Colossians 2:6–7 says, “As therefore you received Christ Jesus, the Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him.” Notice the order: walking comes first, rooting comes after. Roots aren’t grown by sitting and listening; they’re grown by walking.
The Lord himself said, “Everyone who hears these words of mine, and does them … it didn’t fall.” (Matthew 7:24–25) Hearing plus doing equals a foundation; hearing without doing equals empty talk.

James puts it even more bluntly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) He says a person like that is like someone who looks in a mirror, walks away and immediately forgets what he looks like. Brothers and sisters, does that picture feel a little familiar?

Let’s look at some data. In a 2002 meta-analysis the psychologist Paschal Sheeran showed that people’s behavioural intentions account, on average, for only about 28 per cent of their actual behaviour. In other words, between sincerely “intending” to do something and actually doing it, there is still a long distance. Being moved is not the same as being changed.
Bonhoeffer gave us a warning: cheap grace is the deadly enemy of the church.

So 321 says: those who rely on the heart obey; those who rely on the brain only analyse. The fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry; and for a mindset to become life, the bridge in between is called “Implementation”.
Hearing the word is like rain; obeying it is like putting down roots. Without roots, no amount of water helps.
The third soil is the thorny heart.
The Lord said, “What was sown among the thorns, this is he who hears the word, but the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and he becomes unfruitful.” (Matthew 13:22)
Brothers and sisters, please notice: this patch is actually good soil. It has depth, it has nutrients, and the seed really did grow up. The problem is that thorns grow there at the same time.

“Choke” is the Greek sympnigō: “to squeeze tight together, to suffocate”. The thorns don’t need to cut it down or pull it up; they only need to wind themselves around it day after day, stealing its sunlight and nourishment, and the wheat withers all by itself.
Mark’s Gospel lists them more fully: the cares of this age, the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things — three thorns.

Genesis 3:18 says, “It will yield thorns and thistles to you.” Nobody needs to plant thorns. Wheat has to be sown, watered and tended; thorns only need you to leave them alone, and they grow fast and strong.
That is why the spiritual life needs to be “intentional”: you don’t have to try to become worldly — just do nothing at all, and the world will grow over your whole heart by itself.
The classic example is the rich young ruler in Matthew 19. The Lord said to him: go, sell what you have, and give to the poor; and come, follow me.
He heard it clearly and unmistakably. And the result? “But when the young man heard the saying, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions.” (Matthew 19:22)
It wasn’t that he couldn’t hear; it was that he couldn’t let go. Hearing God’s voice comes at a cost.
The Lord said, “Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.” (John 15:2)

An unpruned vine grows a beautiful canopy of leaves but produces only a few bunches of grapes. Pruning hurts, because what gets cut away is often not a bad thing but a good thing — it simply stands in the way of something better.

In 2020 LaFreniere and Newman of Penn State University published a study in the journal Behavior Therapy which found that about 91.4 per cent of the worries recorded by anxious people never came to pass.
Brothers and sisters, we give so much sunlight and nourishment to feeding a patch of thorns, 91 per cent of which never bear anything at all.
Another study, from 2017, found that simply having your phone on the desk — even switched off — lowered people’s performance on cognitive tests. That phone didn’t even ring. It was just “there”.
So 321 says: it isn’t that God isn’t speaking; it’s that we won’t let go. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than possessions.
The fourth soil is the good-soil heart. The Lord said, “What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit.” (Matthew 13:23)
What does it mean to truly hear? It isn’t hearing with the ears, and it isn’t being emotionally moved. It has three levels.
First, hearing — the message comes in.
Second, understanding — it is wired into my life.
Third, obeying and bearing fruit — fruit appears.
Many people reach the first level; fewer reach the second; only the third is what the Lord is after.
Luke adds two more words: “Those … who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance.” (Luke 8:15) Good soil doesn’t appear overnight.
The Lord said, “Blessed are … your ears, for they hear.” (Matthew 13:16)
Brothers and sisters, here is the best news of the day.
In the first century an ordinary harvest was about seven to ten times what was sown. Thirtyfold was a good year; sixtyfold a bumper crop; a hundredfold a figure farmers wouldn’t have dared dream of.

But the even better news is this: good soil isn’t born; it’s cultivated. If the four soils were fixed from birth, this parable would be a verdict, not good news. But thank God — the roadside can be ploughed open, the stones can be prised out, the thorns can be burned away. The prophet says, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.” (Jeremiah 4:3)
And the Lord didn’t demand that every patch of good soil yield a hundredfold. God measures you by your own soil.

Look at a role model. In an age when “Yahweh’s word was rare”, God called a child. That night Scripture recorded a timeless sentence: “Then Samuel said, ‘Speak; for your servant hears.’” (1 Samuel 3:10) Brothers and sisters, how often we talk and talk, and when we’ve finished, we leave, without leaving a single minute for God.
The Lord said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27)

Notice that the Lord didn’t say, “My sheep are very good listeners.” Sheep can hear the shepherd not because their ears are especially good, but because they belong to this shepherd and follow him every day. So hearing God is not a technique; it is an identity, a condition of life.

This is exactly the 321 Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Every voice must be brought before Scripture and checked against it; and the Holy Spirit promises, “Your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it.’” (Isaiah 30:21)

The Natural Resources Conservation Service of the US Department of Agriculture points out that one small teaspoon of healthy soil may contain more microorganisms than there are people on earth. Fertility doesn’t lie on the surface but in the unseen world underneath.
Brothers and sisters, that is where God looks too — at your prayers when you are alone, at the obedience nobody knows about. That is good soil. When the heart is right, the voice becomes clear.
Now let’s turn this into practice.
The first practice: cultivate a humble heart and open your ears. Pray to God every day: “Lord, I won’t insist on my own ideas; I’m willing to be adjusted by you.”

Take it deeper with the eight stages of changing our mindset. Information: know that pride is the greatest obstacle. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to show you the trodden-hard path in your heart. Conviction: admit that it really is pride, and stop calling it “principle”. Implementation: make that your first prayer every morning, said out loud. Evaluation: spend three minutes each evening looking back — was there a moment today when I knew I should give way, and yet I stiffened my neck? Keep it up for forty days in a row, because hard ground isn’t loosened by a single pass of the plough.

The second practice: put what you hear into practice at once. Set yourself a “twenty-four-hour rule”: whatever you’re stirred to do, take at least one step within a day. Then keep two columns in a notebook — “What God said” and “What I did”. Open it a week later: how many lines match up?
Brothers and sisters, remember: we don’t become clear first and then obey; we obey first and then become clear.

The third practice: clear the thorns out of your life. Be still for ten minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to let you write down your three thickest thorns: the one thing you worry about most often, the one possession you can least bear to part with, and the one habit that eats up the most time.

Set a concrete “cut” for each thorn: regular giving, to turn “I can’t bear to part with it” into “I’m glad to give it”; switching off your phone for an hour each day and giving that time back to God; turning that worry into a one-sentence prayer.
A week later, check: did the thing you were worried about happen? Don’t forget the figure — about 91 per cent never come to pass.

Thorns grow back. When you spot a new shoot, cut it at once. The last of the eight stages is “Multiplication”, so lead your family or small group in clearing thorns together, and let “glad to give” become your culture.
Brothers and sisters, let’s look at these four soils once more in the light of 321.
The roadside heart is a self-centred heart.
The shallow heart is a heart that relies on the brain and not the heart.
The thorny heart is a worldly, temporary heart.
The good-soil heart is a selfless heart.

Have you noticed? In this parable the evil one appears only once — on the hard ground by the roadside. The place where Satan most easily gets his way is a proud heart. So humility is the most powerful weapon in spiritual warfare: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.
321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people skip life and go straight to ministry, and end up as that shallow ground.

The 920 practice reminds us that everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. As we live out the selfless “0”, the ninefold fruit of the Spirit grows in these relationships. This is the most practical test of all: when you get home, do you have a little more patience with your spouse?

The 235 relationships remind us too: find a brother or sister who also longs for selflessness and become each other’s “2”; build a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.
Dear brothers and sisters, let’s remember three sentences:
God is always speaking; the question lies with your heart.
The key to hearing God is not technique; it is life.
Without obedience, the voice grows fainter and fainter.
The Lord said, “Take heed what you hear.” (Mark 4:24) And again: “Be careful therefore how you hear.” (Luke 8:18)
But God is looking for a certain kind of person — someone willing to open up, willing to obey, willing to pay the price. People like that will surely hear God.

Brothers and sisters, the four soils are really not four kinds of people; they are often four corners of the same person. So this parable isn’t meant for us to sort other people into categories. It’s meant for us, this morning, to grow still and say one thing to the Lord: Lord, please come and turn over this soil of mine.
Let Jesus be King — not only King in church, but King over my ideas, King over my diary, King over my wallet; and let Jesus receive all the glory.
Let’s pray together.
Lord Jesus, we thank you. You have never stopped speaking. It is our hearts that are so often too hard, too shallow, too full.
Lord Jesus, I believe you are speaking to me. Please give me a soft, humble, selfless heart.

With your plough, break open the trodden-hard path within me; with your fire, burn away the thorns that choke your word. Take away the pride, the laziness and the crush of the world within me, and let me not only hear, but understand and obey.
Lord, like Samuel, today I say: Speak; for your servant hears.
I want to be good soil and bear the fruit of life — thirty, sixty, a hundredfold — all of it given back to you.
Reign as King in my life, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, may the Lord’s word fall today on the good soil of your heart, and take root, and sprout, and bear abundant fruit.

l129.intro:
I. Introduction: The Problem Isn’t God’s Mouth but Our Hearts

Brothers and sisters, good morning. For today’s Morning Devotion, I’d like to begin by asking you to try a little experiment.

Please stop, be quiet for ten seconds, and then count: in those ten seconds, how many different sounds did you hear?

Perhaps the low hum of the air conditioning; perhaps cars or birds outside the window; perhaps the footsteps of the neighbours next door; perhaps the sound of your own breathing. The remarkable thing is that before you “started paying attention”, these sounds were there all along. They didn’t suddenly appear. Your attention just hadn’t been given to them.

The spiritual world is like that too.

In my years of pastoring, the sigh I hear most often is this: “Pastor, I’ve been praying for so long, but God just doesn’t speak.” Those who say it often have weariness in their eyes, a sense of grievance, even a little of the pain of feeling abandoned by God. I completely understand that feeling. But I often ask a question in return: “In these days, what has been filling your heart the most?”

Nine times out of ten, the answer isn’t “God”. The answer is the mortgage, the children’s exam results, the redundancy list at work, the results of a medical check-up, the family member you still haven’t made peace with.

So the real question is often not: has God spoken?

The real question is: are we ready to listen?

In the last lesson we said that God still speaks today — through the Bible, through the Holy Spirit, through circumstances, through people. In this lesson we want to go a step further and ask: if God is always speaking, why can’t I hear him?

The Lord Jesus gave the answer long ago in the parable of the sower. He said that the seed sown is all the same, and the sower is the same one. Where is the difference? The difference is the soil. The same word falls by the roadside, on the rock, among the thorns, on good soil — and the outcomes are completely different. There’s nothing wrong with the seed and nothing wrong with the sower; the problem is the condition of the heart.

That is the core of this lesson: hearing God’s voice is not a matter of technique; it is a matter of the condition of the heart.

The Lord Jesus points out three things that stop up our ears: worry, the world and our values. These three are not outside noise; they’re inside noise. Outside noise you can shut out by closing the window. Inside noise follows you wherever you go.

In 321 terms, this is a question of the self-centred life versus selflessness. When my heart is filled with “my needs, my future, my face, my losses”, that’s the self-centred life. Self-centred people only ever hear the echo of themselves. When I’m willing to lay myself down and let Jesus be King, my heart is cleared, and God’s voice can get in. That is selflessness.

Today we’ll learn three things together: first, worry and the world make people unable to hear God’s voice; second, only by becoming good soil can we truly hear and obey God’s word; and third, suffering is an important way of restoring our spiritual hearing.

May the Lord himself touch our ears this morning.

II. Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Settings

The main passages in this lesson come from three different eras and three different settings, yet they all point to the same thing: a person’s heart determines a person’s ears.

sections.heading: 1. Matthew 6: The Kingdom’s Values in the Sermon on the Mount
sections.html:
Matthew is the most Jewish in flavour of the four Gospels. It is generally held to have been written by the apostle Matthew, a former tax collector, sometime between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish Christians. Matthew quotes the Old Testament constantly, wanting to prove to his own people that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah foretold in the Old Testament, the Son of David, the true King.

Matthew 5–7 is the famous “Sermon on the Mount” — the constitution of the people of the Kingdom of Heaven. Chapter 6 deals with three “secret disciplines”: giving, prayer and fasting. Then it turns to treasure, the eye and two masters, and finally devotes a whole passage to “do not worry”.

This arrangement matters a great deal. The Lord Jesus didn’t speak first about worry and then about serving. He first said, “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21), then, “No one can serve two masters,” and only last of all spoke about worry. In other words, worry isn’t a stand-alone emotional problem. Worry is the fruit that inevitably grows once our values are out of place.

Galilee at that time was an agricultural society under the rule of the Roman Empire. Heavy taxes, natural disasters and disease meant that ordinary people lived in real want. Those to whom the Lord Jesus said “do not worry” were not well-fed aristocrats; they were the poor, who genuinely had to wonder each day whether there would be food tomorrow. That gives his words all the more weight: he isn’t telling people to be irresponsible; he’s telling them to shift their focus from the “provision” to the “Provider”.

sections.heading: 2. Luke 8: The Parable of the Sower
sections.html:
Luke was a Gentile physician and Paul’s co-worker, and his Gospel is generally dated to the AD 60s. Luke wrote for Theophilus, a Gentile of some standing. Luke cares especially about people’s hearts and the transformation of lives, so when he records the parable of the sower he uses a very particular expression: “with an honest and good heart … hold it tightly”.

In Palestine, farmers sowed differently from today. They sowed first and ploughed afterwards, scattering seed over ground not yet prepared, so the seed would fall on the hard paths running through the field, on places where thin soil covered limestone, and on places where thorn roots were still buried in the earth. When the Lord Jesus told this parable, what came to his hearers’ minds was a real scene they saw every day.

Having told the parable, the Lord Jesus left a solemn reminder: “Be careful therefore how you hear” (Luke 8:18). Notice that he didn’t say, “Be careful what you hear.” He said, “Be careful how you hear.” The same sermon, the same passage, the same Morning Devotion — one person’s life is turned upside down, another feels nothing at all. The difference is in “how you hear”.

sections.heading: 3. Isaiah: The Ear of the Taught and the Bread of Adversity
sections.html:
Isaiah was a prophet of the eighth century BC, whose ministry spanned four kings of Judah: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. Isaiah 30 is set in the days of King Hezekiah, when Judah faced the threat of Assyria. Instead of seeking God, the leaders secretly sent envoys down to Egypt for help. The prophet rebuked them for seeking “to strengthen themselves in the strength of Pharaoh”, and pointed out that God’s way was: “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence” (Isaiah 30:15). But the people — “You refused.”

And so God spoke words both stern and full of love: though the Lord gives you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your teachers will no longer be hidden. Hardship became the food on the table — but it was at that very table that the teacher appeared.

Isaiah 50 is the third of the “Servant Songs”, foreshadowing the perfectly obedient Messiah, the Servant. What is this Servant’s secret? Not eloquence, but ears. “He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear” — notice the words “morning by morning”. Hearing God’s voice isn’t a one-off mystical experience; it’s a habit of every morning. This is exactly the spiritual basis of 321 Morning Devotion.

III. Key Point 1: Worry and the World Make Us Unable to Hear God’s Voice

sections.heading: 1. At Its Core, Worry Is a Heart Torn Apart
sections.html:
The Lord Jesus said, “Therefore I tell you, don’t be anxious for your life: what you will eat, or what you will drink; nor yet for your body, what you will wear. Isn’t life more than food, and the body more than clothing?” (Matthew 6:25). And again, “For the Gentiles seek after all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things” (Matthew 6:32).

The Greek word for “be anxious” here is merimnaō (μεριμνάω), generally thought to be related to the idea of “dividing, splitting apart”. The true face of worry is a heart torn into several pieces — one piece on tomorrow’s bills, one piece in yesterday’s regrets, one piece in other people’s opinions — with only a very small piece left over for God.

How can a heart that has been torn apart possibly listen with all its attention?

The Bible’s diagnosis of worry is very precise. The Lord Jesus goes on to ask, “Which of you, by being anxious, can add one moment to his lifespan?” (Matthew 6:27). That question exposes the most absurd truth about worry: worry has never solved a single problem. It merely carries tomorrow’s burden onto today’s shoulders ahead of time. So the Lord says, “Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient” (Matthew 6:34).

So what is the root of worry? Spiritually speaking, there are two: first, not trusting God; second, putting the focus on ourselves.

We don’t trust God because deep down we secretly think: if I don’t worry about it, no one will worry about it for me. We put the focus on ourselves because we make ourselves the centre of the universe, and everything has to revolve around our needs. Put those two together and you have what 321 calls the self-centred life. A self-centred person, even sitting in the quietest room, has a heart as noisy as a market.

sections.heading: 2. Confirmation from Psychology: Scarcity Eats Up Mental Bandwidth
sections.html:
In their 2013 book “Scarcity”, the Harvard economist Sendhil Mullainathan and the Princeton psychologist Eldar Shafir put forward an important finding: when people are under the pressure of scarcity — short of money, short of time, short of security — the brain is “hijacked” by that scarcity. They call it a “bandwidth tax”. Their research showed that the same group of people performed noticeably worse on cognitive tasks when they were under heavy financial pressure.

Notice: they didn’t become less intelligent. Their mental bandwidth was taken up.

That is exactly the spiritual reality the Lord Jesus describes. Worry won’t turn you into a bad person, but it will turn you into someone with “no bandwidth left to hear God speak”. Your heart is full to bursting.

Another interesting study comes from Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris of Harvard. In 1999 they published the famous “invisible gorilla” experiment: subjects were asked to count the number of passes, and about half of them completely failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walk into the scene, beat their chest and walk out again. The researchers called this “inattentional blindness”.

When our attention is wholly occupied by one thing, we fail to see even the most obvious thing in front of us. It’s the same spiritually — we can be earnestly counting up our troubles and be utterly unaware that the Lord is already standing beside us, speaking to us.

sections.heading: 3. One Level Deeper: Whom Do You Choose to Listen To?
sections.html:
Next, the Lord Jesus raises the issue from “emotion” to “allegiance”: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24).

“Mammon” is originally an Aramaic word for wealth or assets, and its root is generally thought to be connected with “that in which one trusts”. That is very telling: what makes Mammon dangerous is not that it is money, but that it has become the one the heart relies on. Money itself can’t talk, but when money becomes my master, it gives me orders every day.

The apostle John also warns, “Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love isn’t in him” (1 John 2:15). John goes on to explain that what fills the world is “the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16).

So the question has never been “Did you hear?” The question is “Whom do you choose to listen to?”

There’s a very apt scientific confirmation here. In 1953 the British cognitive scientist Colin Cherry published his famous study of the “cocktail party effect”: at a noisy party, a person can lock on to and follow one particular person’s conversation out of countless voices. This shows that human hearing isn’t passive reception but active selection. Our ears are directed by our attention.

Brothers and sisters, this is the point: you can hear God in the midst of noise, and you can fail to hear God in perfect quiet. What decides it is not the volume but which way your heart is turned.

sections.heading: 4. A 321 Insight and Application
sections.html:
It isn’t that God doesn’t speak; it’s that the heart is filled with the world. It isn’t that we can’t hear; it’s that we choose not to listen.

The fivefold change of 321 is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Everything starts with mindset. And the change of mindset runs in four directions: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly.

Paul says it clearly: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2).

Worry is, at heart, “earthly, temporary” values taking control. So the remedy isn’t “telling yourself not to think about it”; it’s exchanging it for a greater focus. The prescription the Lord Jesus gives is: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well” (Matthew 6:33).

321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. It also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and find worry, rely on the heart and find joy. Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.”

Brothers and sisters, remember: if you want to hear God today, the first step isn’t to find a quieter place; it’s to let Jesus truly be King in your heart.

IV. Key Point 2: Only by Becoming Good Soil Can We Truly Hear and Obey God’s Word

sections.heading: 1. Four Soils, Four Hearts
sections.html:
The Lord Jesus said, “Those in the good ground, these are those who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance” (Luke 8:15). Matthew records it like this: “What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit, and produces, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty” (Matthew 13:23).

The four soils are really four hearts:

The roadside heart is a heart trodden hard. It hears, but the word stays on the surface, and the enemy snatches it away at once.

The rocky heart is a shallow heart. It receives the word with joy but has no root, and falls back at the first trial.

The thorny heart is a crowded heart. The Lord Jesus himself explains: “That which fell among the thorns, these are those who have heard, and as they go on their way they are choked with cares, riches, and pleasures of life, and bring no fruit to maturity” (Luke 8:14).

The good-soil heart is a heart that is soft, deep and clean.

Notice that the problem with the thorny ground isn’t “not hearing”, but “being choked after hearing”. That follows straight on from the first key point: worry and the world are those thorns.

sections.heading: 2. Three Marks of Good Soil
sections.html:
From Luke 8:15 we can see three marks of good soil.

First, it takes God’s word seriously — “having heard the word”.

Second, it is willing to pay the price of obeying — “with an honest and good heart … hold it tightly”. The Greek for “hold tightly” is katechō (κατέχω), meaning to grip firmly, to hold fast and not let go.

Third, it doesn’t only hear; it does, and it holds out — “produce fruit with perseverance”. The Greek for “perseverance” is hypomonē (ὑπομονή), literally “remaining in place under a heavy load”. This isn’t passive putting-up-with; it is the strength to keep standing under pressure.

James puts it bluntly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22).

There’s a wonderful light from the original languages here. The Greek word for “obey” is hypakouō (ὑπακούω), made up of “under” (hypo) and “hear” (akouō) — obeying, literally, is “standing under the word and listening”. Likewise the Hebrew word for “hear” is shama (שָׁמַע), and that one word means both “to hear” and “to obey”. The Old Testament Shema — “Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4) — was never just a call to prick up one’s ears; it was a call to hand over one’s whole life.

In other words, in the language of the Bible there’s simply no such thing as “hearing but not doing”. If it hasn’t been lived out, it hasn’t been heard.

sections.heading: 3. Noah: One Man’s Obedience, One Family’s Salvation
sections.html:
Noah is the finest example of good soil.

God said to him: build an ark. In those days it was an all-but-absurd assignment. The project was enormous — the ark was three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide and thirty cubits high (Genesis 6:15), which works out at a length of over 130 metres. No one supported him; the people of his day mocked him. And, according to the biblical record, the earth had never yet seen rain like that.

But the Bible’s verdict on Noah is so simple it’s stunning:

“Thus Noah did. He did all that God commanded him” (Genesis 6:22).

“Noah did everything that Yahweh commanded him” (Genesis 7:5).

He didn’t merely “hear”; he obeyed completely.

Hebrews explains him like this: “By faith, Noah, being warned about things not yet seen, moved with godly fear, prepared a ship for the saving of his house, through which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is according to faith” (Hebrews 11:7).

Notice the result: he and his whole household were saved, and he became a witness to his generation. That is “bearing fruit”.

The German theologian and martyr Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in his book “The Cost of Discipleship”, left a line that rings out: “Only those who believe obey, and only those who obey believe.” Faith and obedience are not two things; they are two sides of one and the same thing.

sections.heading: 4. A Piercing Fact of Nature: Good Soil Is Soil That Has Been Turned
sections.html:
I love to look at this parable through the eyes of farming.

It is commonly estimated that nature takes several hundred years to form one centimetre of topsoil. Topsoil is the most precious resource, yet also the most easily lost. And for a field to become good soil, the farmer must do three things: turn the soil, so that the hard becomes soft; remove the stones, picking out whatever blocks the roots; and pull the thorns, rooting out the brambles that steal the nutrients.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? Not one of these three things is comfortable.

Good soil isn’t born; good soil is worked. When God allows certain things to turn your pride over, to pick out what you’ve been clinging to, to pull up by the roots the thorns you’ve been quietly keeping — that isn’t punishment. That’s the farmer preparing the ground.

sections.heading: 5. The More We Obey, the More We Hear
sections.html:
Isaiah 50:4 says, “He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” The next verse goes on: “The Lord Yahweh has opened my ear. I was not rebellious. I have not turned back” (Isaiah 50:5).

The order is very clear: God opens the ear, and the servant doesn’t rebel; the servant doesn’t rebel, and God goes on awakening him morning by morning.

“Those who are taught” here is the Hebrew limmudim (לִמּוּדִים), meaning “those who are instructed, disciples”. The mark of a disciple isn’t beautiful notes; it’s doing what was taught.

The Lord Jesus also said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27). “Hear” and “follow” are joined together in the same verse.

After telling the parable of the sower, the Lord Jesus said, “Take heed what you hear. With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you, and more will be given to you who hear” (Mark 4:24). The size of the measure you listen with is the size of the measure God speaks to you with.

sections.heading: 6. A 321 Insight and Application
sections.html:
Hearing is not the goal; obeying is the key. The more we obey, the more we hear; the more we hold back, the less we hear.

321 says the Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

The Lord Jesus himself is our role model of “hearing and obeying”: “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:8). Hebrews goes further: “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8).

The Bible is the standard, so we don’t judge by feelings whether something is God’s voice; we test every stirring in the light of Scripture. Any “voice” that contradicts the Bible is, without exception, not the voice of God.

The Holy Spirit is the guide, so the Lord Jesus promises, “But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you” (John 14:26).

321 also reminds us: rely on the heart, and you will hear; rely on the brain, and you will doubt. People who rely on the brain take God’s word and analyse it, assess it, count the cost; people who rely on the heart take God’s word and obey it. Had Noah relied on his brain, he would never have built the ark, because every single figure was urging him to give up.

This is the 920 practice: before every person I’m in a relationship with, practising a selfless life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Real “good soil” isn’t being moved during Morning Devotion; it’s actually bearing love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control when you’re with your colleagues at lunchtime today.

V. Key Point 3: Suffering Is an Important Way of Restoring Spiritual Hearing

sections.heading: 1. It Isn’t That God Doesn’t Speak; It’s That We’re Too Noisy
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, sometimes it isn’t that God doesn’t speak; it’s that we’re too noisy.

What’s making the noise? Busyness, desires, “self” and the voices of the world are all making noise.

A modern person’s day may begin with the phone’s alarm and end with the phone’s screen. In our lives there’s hardly a single stretch of true silence. Elijah’s experience at Horeb is worth meditating on: “but Yahweh was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake; but Yahweh was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake a fire passed; but Yahweh was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice” (1 Kings 19:11–12). What God uses most often isn’t the great wind or the great fire, but the still small voice. And a still small voice can only be heard in stillness.

Hearing needs protecting. The World Health Organization’s “World Report on Hearing”, published in 2021, states that more than 1.5 billion people worldwide are living with some degree of hearing loss. The cochlea of the human inner ear has about 15,000 hair cells, which turn sound waves into nerve signals; once damaged by prolonged noise, they do not grow back.

That is a very sobering spiritual parable: spiritual hearing, too, can be dulled by long exposure to noise. The Lord Jesus quoted Isaiah: “for this people’s heart has grown callous, their ears are dull of hearing, they have closed their eyes; or else perhaps they might perceive with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and would turn again; and I would heal them” (Matthew 13:15). “Their ears are dull of hearing” — what a frightening diagnosis.

sections.heading: 2. God’s Way: Taking the Interference Away
sections.html:
So God sometimes allows suffering to come.

“Though the Lord may give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your teachers won’t be hidden any more, but your eyes will see your teachers; and when you turn to the right hand, and when you turn to the left, your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it’” (Isaiah 30:20–21).

Notice the structure of this passage: first adversity and affliction, then “your teachers won’t be hidden any more”, and finally “your ears will hear a voice behind you”.

The order is: suffering comes, the teacher appears, the voice is heard.

Suffering has three functions.

First, it takes away the interference. When someone is lying in a hospital bed, many things they once thought they couldn’t live without suddenly don’t matter at all. God isn’t trying to rob you of your joy; he’s switching off the channels that were so loud you couldn’t hear him.

Second, it tears down pride. When things are going well, it’s very hard to admit we need help. After everything he went through, Job said, “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you” (Job 42:5). What lay between hearing of him and seeing him with his own eyes was precisely that suffering.

Third, it turns our focus back. Only when a person reaches the bottom of the valley do they start asking the most important question: “God, what is your will?”

The psalmist bears witness from his own experience: “Before I was afflicted, I went astray; but now I observe your word” (Psalm 119:67). And again: “It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn your statutes” (Psalm 119:71).

sections.heading: 3. Suffering Is Not Punishment but Grace
sections.html:
We must be clear about this: the Bible never glamourises suffering, nor does it say that all suffering is directly arranged by God. Some of this world’s suffering comes from human sin, some from Satan’s attacks, some from the corruption of creation. But the Bible firmly declares that, for those in Christ, God can make all things work together for good for those who love him.

Hebrews says, “All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11).

In “The Problem of Pain” the English writer and apologist C. S. Lewis penned those famous words: God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains; pain is his megaphone to rouse a deaf world.

Psychology offers supporting evidence too. In the 1990s Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun of the University of North Carolina at Charlotte put forward the concept of “post-traumatic growth”. Their research found that many people who go through major trauma, once they have come through it, show significant growth in the depth of their relationships, their appreciation of life, their personal strength, new possibilities, and the spiritual dimension.

Note that the researchers never claim that “suffering is a good thing”. What they point out is that the “rebuilding” after suffering is the key to growth. This matches the Bible’s teaching exactly — suffering in itself doesn’t make anyone holy; “turning to God” in suffering does.

There’s also a phenomenon often cited in medicine: as a fracture heals, a callus forms, so that for a time the broken place is harder than before. The place of breaking can become the strongest place. That is exactly the work God does in our lives.

sections.heading: 4. Hosea’s Wilderness
sections.html:
The prophet Hosea records an exceedingly tender word from God: “Therefore behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her” (Hosea 2:14).

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: God led her into the wilderness not to punish her but in order to “speak tenderly to her”. What kind of place is the wilderness? A place with no audience, no entertainment, no way back. The wilderness is a room God prepares in order to speak.

If you’re in the wilderness today, please don’t only ask, “God, when will you bring me out?” Please also ask, “Lord, you brought me in here — what do you want to say to me?”

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight and Application
sections.html:
It isn’t that the circumstances change; it’s that the heart is adjusted. Suffering isn’t an obstacle; it’s an opportunity to turn to God. When you are willing to be humble, you will hear again.

The core message of 321 is: pride is the root of the problem; humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

The greatest use of suffering is to invite us down from the seat where we have been “standing in for God”. When we’re healthy, we’re often the chief executive of our own lives; only in a hospital bed do we remember that there has always been a true Lord.

Peter says, “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time, casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:6–7).

Notice how these two verses connect: first “humble yourselves”, then “cast your worries”. Humility is the door through which we unload our worries. For proud people don’t dare hand their burdens over — they’re afraid others won’t do it well enough, and God is no exception.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When you choose humility in suffering, you not only hear God again; the people around you will be drawn by your softness.

VI. Integrating the 321 Vision: From Self-Centred Listening to Selfless Listening

sections.heading: 1. The Three Foundations: Three Rulers for Discerning Voices
sections.html:
Jesus is my role model: he rose each morning and went out to a solitary place to pray; he said, “The Son can do nothing of himself.” He is the perfect pattern of “hearing and obeying”.

The Bible is my standard: every stirring, every dream, every confirmation must pass the test of Scripture. The Bible will not say one thing while the Holy Spirit does another.

The Holy Spirit is my guide: the Holy Spirit is the Counselor who “teaches and reminds” us of the words of Scripture in our concrete situations.

Not one of the Three Foundations can be missing. A role model without a standard turns into imitation by feeling; a standard without the Holy Spirit turns into the dead letter; the Holy Spirit without the Bible turns into dangerous subjectivism.

sections.heading: 2. The Two Core Values: The Key to Hearing
sections.html:
Let Jesus be King. Very often we can’t hear God’s voice not because our ears are broken but because the throne is occupied. When “I” sit on the throne, God’s word, when it comes into me, can only be treated as a “suggestion” to consider. A suggestion can be ignored; only a command must be obeyed. When Jesus is truly King, the moment he speaks, I obey.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. Some people want to hear God’s voice in order to get directions so that their own plans will succeed, or in order to look spiritual in front of their brothers and sisters. If that’s the case, God’s silence is actually a grace. For God will never give his glory to another.

sections.heading: 3. The Goal: Establish God’s System
sections.html:
God never speaks merely to soothe an individual’s feelings. God speaks in order to build. He spoke to Noah to preserve the human race; he spoke to Abraham so that all nations would be blessed; he spoke to Moses to establish a people belonging to God.

So when you hear God’s voice, please don’t only ask, “What’s in this for me?” Ask, “What does God want to establish through me?”

sections.heading: 4. Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
sections.html:
321 says: people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than possessions. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

Many people can’t hear God because the order has been turned upside down. We get busy with ministry first, deal with people next, and only at the very end squeeze out a little time for God. The result is that we do a great deal for God, yet haven’t heard him speak for a very long time.

The parable of the good soil reminds us: first there must be soil, then there can be fruit. The depth of our life determines the length of our service.

sections.heading: 5. 235 Relationships: Becoming Good Soil Together
sections.html:
Practising alone, it’s easy to slacken off; with companions, you go much further.

235 means: becoming a “2” with a selfless person, building a spiritual companionship; then building a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally becoming a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

The practice of listening to God’s voice is best done with a spiritual companion. Every day you share with them one sentence God has said to you, and they share with you one sentence God has said to them; you remind each other, review with each other, hold each other up. You’ll find that when you have to tell someone whether you “actually did it”, your obedience gets a lot quicker.

sections.heading: 6. A Shift of Perspective
sections.html:
From man’s perspective to God’s: what you see is redundancy; what God sees is the new door he has prepared for you.

From an earthly perspective to a heavenly one: what you see is loss; what God sees is a reward in heaven.

From a temporary perspective to an eternal one: what you see is these three months; what God sees is your whole life and eternity.

From a worldly perspective to a godly one: what you see is “what I want”; what God sees is “what kind of person I am to become”.

Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2). Notice that the prerequisite for “proving God’s will” is “being transformed by the renewing of your mind”. If the mindset doesn’t change, you won’t hear.

VII. Putting It into Practice: Living a Life That Can Hear God’s Voice

The lesson gives us three concrete practices. We’ll use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to carry them through solidly.

Practice 1: Practise Letting Go of Worry and Turning to Trust

When you begin to worry, pray at once: “Lord, you know what I need; I choose to trust you.” Let your heart turn from “the problem” to “God”.

Information: first remember God’s promise. “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:6–7).

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you — behind the thing you worry about most often, which form of the self-centred life is hiding? Fear of losing control? Fear of losing face? Fear that no one will love you?

Conviction: admit from the heart that worry solves nothing, and that the heavenly Father really does know.

Implementation: this week, whenever a worrying thought arises, stop at once for thirty seconds and say that prayer: “Lord, you know what I need; I choose to trust you.” Then add a word of thanks.

Evaluation: every evening, write down: how many times did I worry today? How many times did I really hand it over?

Correction: if one particular thing keeps occupying your heart, write it down on paper, entrust it specifically, and find your spiritual companion to pray about it with you.

Repetition: practise for twenty-one days in a row. God’s peace isn’t a one-off experience; it’s a habit that is built up.

Multiplication: share your experience with a brother or sister who is worried right now.

Practice 2: Do One Act of “Obedience” Every Day

Don’t stop at hearing. Ask yourself: what does God want me to do today? Then go and do it straight away — even in small things, obey.

Information: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22).

Revelation: after Morning Devotion each day, be still for one minute and ask the Holy Spirit to put “today’s one thing” on your heart.

Conviction: believe that obedience in small things is the threshold to being entrusted with great things.

Implementation: choose just one thing each day, write it down, and do it within twenty-four hours. For example: phone someone you haven’t been in touch with for a long time, apologise to a family member, give a certain sum away, stop joining in the criticism in that group chat.

Evaluation: check every evening — did I do it? If not, did I forget, or was I unwilling?

Correction: take the item you were “unwilling” to do before God and deal with it specifically. Usually that one is exactly what God most wants to deal with.

Repetition: keep it up for a month, and you’ll find God speaking to you noticeably more often.

Multiplication: invite your “2” — your spiritual companion — to do this practice with you, and report one sentence to each other every day.

Practice 3: Seek God’s Voice in Difficulty

When you hit hard times, don’t complain; ask instead, “Lord, what do you want to say to me?” Turn suffering into an opportunity to hear God.

Information: “Though the Lord may give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your teachers won’t be hidden any more, but your eyes will see your teachers” (Isaiah 30:20).

Revelation: ask God to show you which piece of interference inside you this difficulty is meant to take away.

Conviction: believe that suffering is not punishment but grace; not an obstacle but an opportunity to turn to God.

Implementation: this week, whenever anything goes wrong, don’t complain first; first say, “Lord, what do you want to say to me?” and then be still for three minutes.

Evaluation: write down every sentence you hear in the midst of difficulty.

Correction: if you find you still complain first, try another way — give thanks first, then ask.

Repetition: train this response until it becomes a natural reflex of your life.

Multiplication: let the words God spoke to you in your wilderness become comfort for others.

A Gentle Reminder

It isn’t that you can’t hear God; it’s that you haven’t got ready to listen.

It isn’t that God is silent; it’s that the heart is too noisy.

When you are still, humble and obedient, you’ll discover that God has been speaking all along.

The psalmist says, “My soul, wait in silence for God alone, for my expectation is from him” (Psalm 62:5).

And God himself says, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10).

VIII. Closing and Call

Brothers and sisters, hearing God’s voice is not the privilege of a few.

It isn’t for spiritual geniuses, it isn’t for full-time ministers, it isn’t for certain people with special gifts. It is for everyone who is willing to be selfless.

The Lord Jesus says, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him, and will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20). The Lord who knocks has been outside the door all along; the question has never been whether he is knocking, but whether we will open.

When you let go of the world, when you align yourself with God, when you are willing to obey, you’ll enter a new condition of life:

God speaks, you listen; God leads, you follow.

From then on, no more losing your way; only walking on the right path.

Augustine says in his “Confessions”: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” The reason our hearts are so noisy is that they keep searching for a place only God can fill.

So this morning I want to extend an invitation to you:

Give the throne back to Jesus. Let him be King, not merely a consultant.

Give your ears to the Holy Spirit. Awakened morning by morning, taught morning by morning.

Give the glory to Jesus. What you hear, what you obey, the fruit you bear — none of it is your achievement; it is his grace.

May we together become that good soil — soil turned and loosened, cleared of stones, rid of thorns; soft, deep, clean good soil. May God’s word be sown in our hearts, take root, sprout, persevere and bear fruit, thirty, sixty, a hundredfold.

Glory to Jesus.

Matthew 6:24: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.”

Isaiah 50:4: “The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.”
