prayer: Lord Jesus, I want to be someone who can hear your voice.
I confess that my heart is often too noisy. I have piled too many worries, too many plans, too much of the world onto the place where you want to speak. Please forgive me.
I declare:
I will no longer be filled with worry; I choose to trust God;
I will no longer love the world; I will love you alone;
I will not only hear the word; I will obey your word.
Lord, please loosen my hard heart, pick out the stones that block me, pull up the thorns that choke me, and make me good soil.
Please open my ears, so that every day I hear your voice and walk in your ways.
In my worry, be my peace; in my wilderness, be my teacher; in my weakness, be my strength.
Reign as King in my heart, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

How specifically do you plan to pull it out?

blog.title: God Has Never Been Silent — Your Heart Is Just Too Noisy

blocks.x: Choose God, Become Good Soil
Have you ever said this: “I’ve prayed for so long, and God says nothing”?

In all my years of pastoring, that is the sigh I have heard most often. The people who say it usually have weariness and hurt in their eyes. I understand completely. But I often ask a question back: in these days, what fills your heart the most?
Nine times out of ten, the answer isn’t God. The answer is the mortgage, the children’s school results, that medical report you haven’t opened yet.
So perhaps the real question has never been “Is God speaking?” but “Am I ready to listen?”
1. Whatever Fills Your Heart Is What You Hear

The Lord Jesus gave us the answer long ago in the parable of the sower. The seed scattered is all the same, and the sower is the same person. So where is the difference? The difference is in the soil.

The most dangerous of them is not the roadside, nor the rocky ground, but the thorns. For the problem with the thorny ground isn’t “not hearing”, but “being choked after hearing”. The Lord Jesus put it very plainly:
“That which fell among the thorns, these are those who have heard, and as they go on their way they are choked with cares, riches, and pleasures of life, and bring no fruit to maturity” (Luke 8:14).
The cares of life are worry; riches and pleasures are the world.

The Greek word for worry is generally thought to be related to the idea of “dividing, splitting apart”. Worry tears the heart into several pieces: one piece on tomorrow’s bills, one piece in yesterday’s regrets, with only a very small piece left for God. How can a heart that has been torn apart possibly listen with all its attention?

Science offers supporting evidence too. In 1953 Colin Cherry published his famous study of the “cocktail party effect”: at a noisy party, a person can lock on to one particular person’s conversation out of countless voices. It turns out that our ears are directed by our attention.
In other words, you can hear God in the midst of noise, and you can fail to hear God in perfect quiet. What decides it is not the volume but which way your heart is turned.
2. Good Soil Isn’t Born; It’s Worked
So what kind of heart can hear? The Lord Jesus said:
“Those in the good ground, these are those who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance” (Luke 8:15).
Good soil has three marks: it takes God’s word seriously; it is willing to pay the price of obeying; it doesn’t only hear, it does.

There’s a light hidden in the original languages. The Greek word for “obey” is made up of “under” and “hear” — obeying is standing under God’s word and listening. The Hebrew word for “hear” means both “to hear” and “to obey”. So in the language of the Bible there’s simply no such thing as “hearing but not doing”. If it hasn’t been lived out, it hasn’t been heard.

Noah is the finest example. God told him to build an ark: an enormous project, no one supporting him, the people of his day mocking him. Yet the Bible’s verdict on him is a single sentence: “Noah did everything that Yahweh commanded him” (Genesis 7:5). The result? He and his whole household were saved, and he became a witness to his generation.

And good soil is never born that way. For a field to become good soil, the farmer has to turn the soil, remove the stones and pull the thorns — and not one of these is comfortable. So when God allows certain things to turn your pride over and to pick out what you’ve been clinging to, that isn’t punishment. That’s the farmer preparing the ground.
3. The Wilderness Is a Room God Prepares in Order to Speak

Sometimes we can’t hear, not because God is silent, but because we’re too noisy. Busyness makes noise, desires make noise, the self makes noise, the voices of the world make noise. At Horeb Elijah went through a great wind, an earthquake and a fire, and God was in none of them; after the fire there was a still small voice. And a still small voice can only be heard in stillness.

So God sometimes allows suffering to come. Isaiah says that though the Lord gives you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your teachers won’t be hidden any more (Isaiah 30:20). Notice the order: suffering comes, the teacher appears, the voice is heard.

Suffering does three things: it takes away the interference, it tears down pride, it turns our focus back. After everything he went through, Job said, “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.” What lay between hearing of him and seeing him was precisely that suffering. In “The Problem of Pain” C. S. Lewis says that pain is God’s megaphone to rouse a deaf world.
So if you’re in the wilderness today, don’t only ask, “Lord, when will you bring me out?” Please also ask, “Lord, you brought me in here — what do you want to say to me?”
Three Practices You Can Start Today
1. When worry rises, pray at once: “Lord, you know what I need; I choose to trust you.”
2. Ask every day: what does God want me to do today? Then do it within twenty-four hours, even if it’s something small.
3. When difficulty comes, don’t complain first; ask first, “Lord, what do you want to say to me?” and then be still for three minutes.

Hearing God’s voice is not the privilege of a few; it is something everyone who is willing to be selfless can experience. When you let go of the world, align yourself with God and are willing to obey, you’ll enter a new condition: God speaks, you listen; God leads, you follow. From then on, no more losing your way; only walking on the right path.
Reflection question: if God wanted to say one sentence to you this morning, is there room in your heart right now to hold it?

“Having heard the word, hold it tightly with an honest and good heart”
Luke 8:15
Key points:
Open with a small experiment: “Be still for ten seconds and count how many sounds you can hear.”
The sounds were there all along; the difference is whether our attention was on them.
State the theme: hearing God isn’t a matter of technique but of the state of the heart.
Read the key verse, Luke 8:15.
Introduction: The Problem Isn’t God’s Mouth
God is always speaking
The question is: are we ready to listen?
Worry, the world, our values
can all leave us unable to hear
Key points:
Pastoral example: “Pastor, I’ve prayed for so long and God says nothing.” Ask back: what has filled your heart most lately?
Noise outside stops when you shut the window; noise inside follows you wherever you go.
In 321 terms: the self-centred person only ever hears their own echo.
Preview the three key points: worry and the world, becoming good soil, suffering.
Key Verses and Background
Sermon on the Mount: no one can serve two masters
Parable of the sower: four soils, four hearts
Servant Song: he awakens me morning by morning
Isaiah: the teacher in adversity
Key points:
Matthew was written around AD 50–70 for Jewish Christians; chapter 6 speaks first of treasure, then of two masters, and only last of worry.
Worry isn’t a stand-alone emotional problem; it’s the fruit of values that are out of place.
Luke 8:18: “Be careful therefore how you hear” — not what you hear, but how you hear.
Background to Isaiah 30: instead of seeking God, Judah secretly went down to Egypt for help.
Isaiah 50 is the third Servant Song; “morning by morning he awakens” is the very basis of Morning Devotion.
Key Point 1: Worry Makes Us Deaf
“Don’t be anxious for your life: what you will eat”
Matthew 6:25
At heart, worry is not trusting God
Focused on self, the heart is full
Key points:
Light from the original: “be anxious”, merimnaō, generally thought to be related to “dividing, splitting apart”; the heart is torn into pieces.
Matthew 6:27: “Which of you, by being anxious, can add one moment to his lifespan?”
Data: Mullainathan and Shafir’s 2013 book “Scarcity” describes a “bandwidth tax” — scarcity eats up mental bandwidth.
Simons and Chabris’s 1999 “invisible gorilla” experiment at Harvard: about half the subjects saw nothing at all.
Application: worry won’t make you a bad person, but it will leave you no bandwidth to hear God speak.
Key Point 1: Whom Do You Choose to Hear?
“You can’t serve both God and Mammon”
Matthew 6:24
Not unable to hear, but choosing not to listen
From earthly values to heavenly ones
Key points:
Mammon is originally Aramaic for wealth; its root is generally thought to be connected with “that in which one trusts”.
1 John 2:15: “Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world.”
Scientific confirmation: Colin Cherry’s 1953 “cocktail party effect” — hearing is active selection, not passive reception.
321: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.
Colossians 3:2: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.”
Key Point 2: Three Marks of Good Soil
Taking God’s word seriously
Willing to pay the price to obey
Not only hearing, but doing
Luke 8:15
Key points:
Four soils are four hearts; the problem with the thorny ground isn’t not hearing but being choked after hearing (Luke 8:14).
Original languages: “hold tightly”, katechō, is to grip firmly; “perseverance”, hypomonē, is remaining in place under a heavy load.
“Obey”, hypakouō = “under” + “hear”; the Hebrew shama means both to hear and to obey.
James 1:22: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers.”
Farming illustration: good soil isn’t born; it’s worked — by turning the soil, removing stones and pulling thorns.
Key Point 2: Noah’s Complete Obedience
“Noah did everything that Yahweh commanded him”
Genesis 7:5
A huge task, no support, mocked
He and his household saved — a witness
Key points:
The ark was three hundred cubits long, fifty wide and thirty high (Genesis 6:15) — a length of over 130 metres.
Genesis 6:22: “He did all that God commanded him.”
Hebrews 11:7: by faith, moved with godly fear, he saved his household.
Quotation: Bonhoeffer, “The Cost of Discipleship” — “Only those who believe obey, and only those who obey believe.”
321: rely on the heart and you hear; rely on the brain and you doubt. Had Noah relied on his brain, the ark would never have been built.
Key Point 3: It Isn’t That God Doesn’t Speak
We’re too noisy: busyness, desire, self
The world’s voices drown out God’s
“After the fire, there was a still small voice”
1 Kings 19:12
Key points:
Elijah at Horeb: God was not in the wind, not in the earthquake, not in the fire, but in the still small voice.
Data: the WHO’s 2021 “World Report on Hearing” states that more than 1.5 billion people worldwide have hearing loss.
The human cochlea has about 15,000 hair cells, which do not grow back once damaged.
Matthew 13:15: “their ears are dull of hearing” — spiritual hearing, too, can be dulled by noise.
Application: a modern person’s day begins and ends with the phone; there is hardly any true silence.
Key Point 3: Suffering Restores Hearing
“Though the Lord may give you the bread of adversity”
Isaiah 30:20
Removes interference, tears down pride, refocuses
Suffering is not punishment but grace
Key points:
The order in the text: adversity comes, the teacher appears, the voice is heard (Isaiah 30:20–21).
Job 42:5: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.”
Psalm 119:71: “It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn your statutes.”
Quotation: C. S. Lewis, “The Problem of Pain” — pain is God’s megaphone to rouse a deaf world.
Psychology: Tedeschi and Calhoun’s concept of “post-traumatic growth” from the 1990s; the key is rebuilding after suffering — spiritually, turning to God.
Practices for Daily Life
Let go of worry, turn to trust
One act of obedience every day
Seek God’s voice in difficulty
God isn’t silent; the heart is too noisy
Key points:
Practice 1: when worry rises, pray at once, “Lord, you know what I need; I choose to trust you,” and add a word of thanks.
Practice 2: after Morning Devotion, be still for one minute, write down one small act of obedience for today and do it within twenty-four hours.
Practice 3: when things go wrong, don’t complain first; ask first, “Lord, what do you want to say to me?” and then be still for three minutes.
Deepen them with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Invite a spiritual companion to practise together — this is the starting point of 235 relationships.
Closing and Call
Hearing God isn’t the privilege of a few
It’s for all who are willing to be selfless
God speaks, you listen; God leads, you follow
No more lost; only on the right path
Key points:
Revelation 3:20: the Lord has been knocking outside the door all along; the question is whether we will open.
Augustine, “Confessions”: our heart is restless until it rests in you.
Three invitations: give the throne back to Jesus, give your ears to the Holy Spirit, give the glory to Jesus.
Call everyone to become good soil — turned, cleared of stones, rid of thorns — bearing thirty, sixty, a hundredfold.
Prayer of Response and Blessing
Lord, please open my ears
so that every day I hear your voice
Reign as King in my heart
May all the glory be yours
Key points:
Lead everyone in declaring together: no longer filled with worry, no longer loving the world, not only hearing the word but doing it.
Pray especially for members who are in the wilderness, that God would let them hear, “This is the way.”
Close with a blessing: may God be your peace in your worry and your teacher in your wilderness.
Remind them to continue tomorrow morning: he awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to be still for ten seconds and count how many sounds you can hear. The air conditioning, the traffic, the birds, your own breathing. The wonderful thing is that all these sounds were there all along, before you noticed them. The spiritual world is the same. Today’s theme is: Choose God, Become Good Soil. Our key verse is Luke 8:15: “Those in the good ground, these are those who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance.”

Brothers and sisters, the sigh I hear most often is this: “Pastor, I’ve prayed for so long, and God says nothing.” And I often ask back: in these days, what fills your heart the most? Nine times out of ten, the answer isn’t God; it’s the mortgage, the children, a medical report. So the real question isn’t whether God is speaking, but whether we’re ready to listen. Worry, the world and our values can leave us unable to hear. Noise outside stops when you shut the window; noise inside follows you wherever you go.

In the Sermon on the Mount the Lord Jesus said: no one can serve two masters. In the parable of the sower he said: the same seed falls on four kinds of soil, with completely different outcomes. Isaiah 50 says: morning by morning the Lord awakens my ear. Isaiah 30 says: in adversity, the teacher is no longer hidden. Brothers and sisters, notice: there’s nothing wrong with the seed, nothing wrong with the sower; the problem is the soil. Hearing God isn’t a matter of technique; it’s a matter of the state of the heart.

First, worry makes us unable to hear. The Lord Jesus said, “Don’t be anxious for your life: what you will eat, or what you will drink.” The original word for worry is generally thought to be related to “dividing, splitting apart”. Worry tears the heart into several pieces. One piece on tomorrow’s bills, one piece in yesterday’s regrets, and only a small piece left for God. What is worry at its core? It is not trusting God; it is putting the focus on ourselves. Researchers at Harvard carried out a famous experiment: the subjects concentrated on counting passes, and half of them completely failed to see a gorilla walk across the scene. Brothers and sisters, we too can be counting up our troubles and fail to notice that the Lord is standing right beside us.

Then the Lord Jesus raises the issue a level higher: “You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” Mammon is Aramaic; it means wealth, and also that in which a person trusts. John says, “Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world.” So the question has never been whether you heard; the question is whom you choose to listen to. In 1953 there was a famous study called the “cocktail party effect”: at a very noisy party, a person can lock on to one person’s voice and listen to it. It turns out the ear is directed by attention. Brothers and sisters, you can hear God in the midst of noise, and you can fail to hear God in perfect quiet.

Second, become good soil. Good soil has three marks: it takes God’s word seriously, it is willing to pay the price of obeying, and it doesn’t only hear but does. The original languages are fascinating here: the Greek word for “obey” is “under” plus “hear” — obeying is standing under God’s word and listening. The Hebrew word for “hear” itself means “obey”. So in the language of the Bible there’s no such thing as “hearing but not doing”. If it hasn’t been lived out, it hasn’t been heard. And good soil isn’t born; good soil is worked — turned and loosened, cleared of stones, rid of thorns.

Noah is the finest example. God said: build an ark. An enormous project, no one supporting him, the people of his day mocking him. But the Bible sums him up in one sentence: “Noah did everything that Yahweh commanded him.” He didn’t merely hear; he obeyed completely. And the result? He and his whole household were saved, and he became a witness to his generation. Bonhoeffer put it well: only those who believe obey, and only those who obey believe. Brothers and sisters, the more we obey, the more we hear; the more we hold back, the less we hear. Rely on the heart, and you will hear; rely on the brain, and you will doubt.

Third, suffering restores our spiritual hearing. Sometimes it isn’t that God doesn’t speak; it’s that we’re too noisy. Busyness makes noise, desires make noise, the self makes noise, the voices of the world make noise. At Horeb Elijah went through wind, earthquake and fire, but God was not in them; after the fire there was a still small voice. A still small voice can only be heard in stillness. The World Health Organization tells us that more than 1.5 billion people worldwide have hearing loss; the hair cells in our cochlea do not grow back once damaged. Brothers and sisters, spiritual hearing is just the same: soak in noise for long enough, and it grows dull.

So God sometimes allows suffering to come. Isaiah says, “Though the Lord may give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your teachers won’t be hidden any more.” Look at the order: suffering comes, the teacher appears, the voice is heard. Suffering does three things: it takes away the interference, it tears down pride, it turns our focus back. Job said, “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.” What lay between hearing of him and seeing him was precisely that suffering. Brothers and sisters, suffering is not punishment but grace; not an obstacle but an opportunity to turn to God.

There are three practices for today. First, let go of worry and turn to trust. When worry rises, pray at once: “Lord, you know what I need; I choose to trust you.” Second, do one act of obedience every day. Ask yourself: what does God want me to do today? Then go and do it straight away, even if it’s something small. Third, seek God’s voice in difficulty. Don’t complain; ask first, “Lord, what do you want to say to me?” Brothers and sisters, remember: it isn’t that you can’t hear God; it’s that you haven’t got ready to listen. It isn’t that God is silent; it’s that the heart is too noisy.

Brothers and sisters, hearing God’s voice is not the privilege of a few. It is for everyone who is willing to be selfless. The Lord says, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him.” He has been knocking all along; the question is whether we will open. When you let go of the world, when you align yourself with God, when you are willing to obey, you’ll enter a new condition of life: God speaks, you listen; God leads, you follow. From then on, no more losing your way; only walking on the right path.

Let us pray together. Lord Jesus, I want to be someone who can hear your voice. I declare: I will no longer be filled with worry; I choose to trust God. I will no longer love the world; I will love you alone. I will not only hear the word; I will obey your word. Please open my ears, so that every day I hear your voice and walk in your ways. Reign as King in my heart, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen. May God bless you, and may you become that good soil today.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come to the second talk in our series “How to Hear God’s Voice”, and the title is: Choose God, Become Good Soil. Our key verse is Luke 8:15: “Those in the good ground, these are those who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance.” Today we’re going to ask three questions: Why can’t I hear? What kind of heart can hear? And what means does God use to restore my hearing?

Let’s begin with a small experiment. Please be still for ten seconds and count how many sounds you can hear. Perhaps the low hum of the air conditioning, perhaps birdsong outside the window, perhaps your own breathing. Brothers and sisters, the wonderful thing is that these sounds were there all along, before you noticed them. They didn’t suddenly appear; your attention just wasn’t directed to them. God’s voice is like that too. The Lord says, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock.” He has been knocking all along.

In these years of pastoring, the sigh I’ve heard most often is: “Pastor, I’ve prayed for so long, and God says nothing.” And I often ask back: in these days, what fills your heart the most? Nine times out of ten, the answer isn’t God; it’s the mortgage, the children’s school results, that medical report you haven’t opened yet. So the real question isn’t whether God is speaking, but whether we’re ready to listen. Worry can leave us unable to hear; the world can leave us unable to hear; values that are out of place can leave us unable to hear. Noise outside stops when you shut the window; noise inside follows you wherever you go. In the language of 321, this is a question of the self-centred life versus selflessness: the self-centred person only ever hears their own echo.

Today’s passages come from three different eras. Matthew 6 is the Sermon on the Mount. Notice the order: the Lord first speaks of “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also”, then of “no one can serve two masters”, and only last of all of “don’t be anxious”. So worry isn’t a stand-alone emotional problem; it’s the fruit that grows from values out of place. Luke 8 is the parable of the sower, and when he finishes it the Lord says, “Be careful therefore how you hear.” Not what you hear, but how you hear. Isaiah 50 is a Servant Song, and the Servant’s secret isn’t eloquence; it’s ears.

Key point one: worry makes us unable to hear God’s voice. The Lord Jesus said, “Don’t be anxious for your life: what you will eat, or what you will drink; nor yet for your body, what you will wear.” Brothers and sisters, the Greek word for “be anxious” is generally thought to be related to “dividing, splitting apart”. The true face of worry is a heart torn into several pieces: one piece on tomorrow’s bills, one piece in yesterday’s regrets, and only a very small piece left for God. How can a heart that has been torn apart possibly listen with all its attention?

The Lord goes on to ask, “Which of you, by being anxious, can add one moment to his lifespan?” Worry has never solved a single problem; it merely carries tomorrow’s burden onto today’s shoulders ahead of time. Mullainathan of Harvard and Shafir of Princeton, in their 2013 book “Scarcity”, put forward the idea of a “bandwidth tax”: under the pressure of scarcity, the brain is hijacked by that scarcity, and cognitive performance drops noticeably. People haven’t become less intelligent; their mental bandwidth has been taken up. There’s an even more famous experiment: in 1999 Simons and Chabris at Harvard asked people to concentrate on counting passes, and about half of them completely failed to see a gorilla walk across the scene. Brothers and sisters, we too can be earnestly counting up our troubles and be utterly unaware that the Lord is standing right beside us, speaking. Worry won’t turn you into a bad person, but it will leave you no bandwidth to hear God speak.

Then the Lord raises the issue a level higher: “You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” Mammon is originally an Aramaic word for wealth, and its root is generally thought to be connected with “that in which one trusts”. Money itself can’t talk, but when money becomes my master, it gives me orders every day. John says, “Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world.” In 1953 Colin Cherry’s study of the “cocktail party effect” found that people can lock on to one voice in the midst of noise and listen to it. It turns out the ear is directed by attention. You can hear God in the midst of noise, and you can fail to hear God in perfect quiet.

Here is a 321 insight: it isn’t that God doesn’t speak; it’s that the heart is filled with the world. It isn’t that we can’t hear; it’s that we choose not to listen. 321 says the fivefold change begins with mindset. How does a mindset turn? From man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. The Lord Jesus’ prescription isn’t to tell you not to think about it, but to exchange it for a greater focus: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness.” Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit and find joy; rely on the brain and ourselves and find worry.

Key point two: become good soil. The four soils are really four hearts. The roadside heart is a heart trodden hard. The rocky heart is a heart with no root, which falls back at the first trial. The thorny heart is a crowded heart. The Lord himself explains: “they are choked with cares, riches, and pleasures of life, and bring no fruit to maturity.” Notice that the problem with the thorny ground isn’t not hearing; it’s being choked after hearing. Worry and the world are those thorns. And the good-soil heart is a heart that is soft, deep and clean.

Good soil has three marks: it takes God’s word seriously, it is willing to pay the price of obeying, and it doesn’t only hear but does. The original languages are fascinating here. The Greek for “hold tightly” means to grip firmly and not let go; “perseverance” literally means remaining in place under a heavy load. Even more wonderful, the Greek word for “obey” is “under” plus “hear” — obeying is standing under God’s word and listening. The Hebrew word for “hear” itself means to obey. So in the Bible there’s no such thing as “hearing but not doing”. If it hasn’t been lived out, it hasn’t been heard.

Noah is the finest example. God said: build an ark. The ark was three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide and thirty cubits high — over 130 metres long; no one supported him, and the people of his day mocked him. But the Bible’s verdict on him is so simple it’s stunning: “Noah did everything that Yahweh commanded him.” He didn’t merely hear; he obeyed completely. Hebrews says that by faith, moved with godly fear, he prepared an ark for the saving of his house. And the result? He and his whole household were saved, and he became a witness to his generation. That is bearing fruit. In “The Cost of Discipleship” Bonhoeffer says: only those who believe obey, and only those who obey believe. Faith and obedience are two sides of the same thing.

A second 321 insight: hearing is not the goal; obeying is the key. The more we obey, the more we hear; the more we hold back, the less we hear. Isaiah 50 says, “The Lord Yahweh has opened my ear. I was not rebellious. I have not turned back.” The Lord Jesus also said, “My sheep hear my voice … and they follow me.” Hearing and following are joined together. Had Noah relied on his brain to count the cost, the ark would certainly never have been built. This is the 920 practice: before every person I’m in a relationship with, living a selfless life and bearing the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.

Key point three: suffering is an important way of restoring spiritual hearing. Sometimes it isn’t that God doesn’t speak; it’s that we’re too noisy. Busyness makes noise, desires make noise, the self makes noise, the voices of the world make noise. At Horeb Elijah went through a great wind, an earthquake and a fire, and Yahweh was in none of them; after the fire there was a still small voice. The World Health Organization’s 2021 “World Report on Hearing” states that more than 1.5 billion people worldwide live with some degree of hearing loss; the roughly 15,000 hair cells in our inner ear, once damaged by prolonged noise, do not grow back. Spiritual hearing can grow dull in just the same way. The Lord Jesus quoted Isaiah, saying that this people’s “ears are dull of hearing”. Brothers and sisters, what a frightening diagnosis. What God uses most often isn’t the great wind or the great fire, but the still small voice; and a still small voice can only be heard in stillness.

And so God allows suffering to come. Isaiah says, “Though the Lord may give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your teachers won’t be hidden any more … your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it.’” Look at the order: suffering comes, the teacher appears, the voice is heard. In Hosea God says, “Therefore behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her.” Brothers and sisters, the wilderness isn’t punishment; the wilderness is a room God prepares in order to speak.

Suffering has three functions. First, it takes away the interference. When someone is lying in a hospital bed, many things they once couldn’t live without suddenly don’t matter at all. Second, it tears down pride. Job said, “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.” What lay between hearing of him and seeing him was precisely that suffering. Third, it turns our focus back. Only when we reach the bottom of the valley do we start asking: God, what is your will? The psalmist says, “It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn your statutes.” C. S. Lewis says: pain is God’s megaphone to rouse a deaf world.

A third 321 insight: it isn’t that the circumstances change; it’s that the heart is adjusted. Suffering isn’t an obstacle; it’s an opportunity to turn to God. 321 says pride is the root of the problem; humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place; humility is returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Peter says, “Humble yourselves … casting all your worries on him.” First humble yourselves, then cast your worries. Humility is the door through which we unload our worries. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Now let’s talk about practice. First, let go of worry and turn to trust. When worry rises, stop at once for thirty seconds and pray: “Lord, you know what I need; I choose to trust you.” Then add a word of thanks. Second, do one act of obedience every day. After Morning Devotion, be still for one minute and ask yourself: what does God want me to do today? Write it down and do it within twenty-four hours. It might be phoning someone you haven’t been in touch with for a long time; it might be apologising to a family member. Even if it’s something small, obey.

Third, seek God’s voice in difficulty. When you hit hard times, don’t complain; ask instead, “Lord, what do you want to say to me?” Then be still for three minutes and write down the one sentence God says. We deepen these three practices with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Remember: it isn’t that you can’t hear God; it’s that you haven’t got ready to listen. It isn’t that God is silent; it’s that the heart is too noisy.

Let’s draw the 3-2-1 vision together. The Three Foundations are three rulers for discerning voices: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values are the key to hearing: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. Very often we can’t hear God not because our ears are broken but because the throne is occupied. When “I” sit on the throne, God’s word is treated as a mere suggestion; a suggestion can be ignored, only a command must be obeyed. The Goal is to establish God’s system. Please find a spiritual companion to be your “2”, and share with each other every day one sentence God has said.

Brothers and sisters, hearing God’s voice is not the privilege of a few; it is for everyone who is willing to be selfless. The Lord says, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him.” He has been knocking all along; the question is whether we will open. Augustine said: our heart is restless until it rests in you. So this morning I want to extend three invitations: give the throne back to Jesus, give your ears to the Holy Spirit, give the glory to Jesus. May we become that good soil, bearing thirty, sixty, a hundredfold.

Let us pray together. Lord Jesus, I want to be someone who can hear your voice. I confess that my heart is often too noisy; please forgive me. I declare: I will no longer be filled with worry; I choose to trust God. I will no longer love the world; I will love you alone. I will not only hear the word; I will obey your word. Please loosen my hard heart, pull up the thorns that choke me, and make me good soil; please open my ears, so that every day I hear your voice. Reign as King in my heart, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen. May God be your peace in your worry and your teacher in your wilderness.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: God Has Always Been Speaking — Who Turned the Volume Down?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to recall, honestly, something very small.

This morning, after you opened your eyes, what was the first thing you saw? What was the first thing you heard?

A sister once told me her answer: her phone. The alarm went off, she reached over to silence it, and then, without thinking, she swiped the screen open. News alerts, group messages, short videos, shopping ads — one after another. By the time she came to herself, twenty-five minutes had gone. She scrambled out of bed, washed her face and dashed out of the door, and only when her car was up on the flyover did she remember: she hadn’t read the Bible today, and she hadn’t prayed. So at a red light she closed her eyes and hurriedly said, “Lord, please lead me today.” Then the light turned green, and off she went.

She asked me, “Pastor, why is it that after all these years of praying, I have almost never clearly heard God speak to me? Does God play favourites? Does he only speak to certain spiritual people?”

Brothers and sisters, I want to hand that same question back to each one of you. Have you ever asked it too? Have you ever sat alone in the dark late at night, crying out in your heart: God, where are you? Why don’t you speak?

Today’s lesson will help us see a truth that cuts to the heart — and yet sets us free.

God has never stopped speaking. The problem is not God’s volume; the problem is our reception.

We often treat “hearing God’s voice” as a technique. We imagine that if we can just learn a certain method of prayer, a certain posture of stillness, a certain formula for discernment, we’ll be able to tune in to heaven’s frequency. So we sign up for courses, we buy books, and we ask other people, “How did you hear him?”

But the answer Scripture gives us is both deeper and simpler than any technique:

Whether a person can hear God’s voice depends not on method but on life.

And the core of life is not outside us; it is in the heart.

That is why Scripture says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

What your life becomes begins with your heart; and whether you can hear God begins with your heart as well.

Many people are in a hurry to ask, “How do I hear God?” But today God wants us first to ask a deeper question: what state is your heart in right now?

Because when the heart is right, we hear; when the heart is wrong, we don’t.

This is exactly the 321 insight: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living. And the starting point of it all is the heart.

Brothers and sisters, this morning let’s not rush to ask for a method. Let’s first let God examine our hearts.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: A Father Places Three Generations of Wisdom in His Son’s Hands
sections.html:
To truly understand Proverbs 4, we first need to know the setting in which these words were spoken.

The main author of Proverbs is Solomon, king of Israel. Scripture opens by stating plainly, “The proverbs of Solomon, the son of David, king of Israel.” (Proverbs 1:1) Solomon reigned around the tenth century BC. The book of Proverbs was not composed all at once: chapter 10 to 22:16 and chapters 25 to 29 are proverbs of Solomon, and chapters 25 to 29 were copied out later by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah (see Proverbs 25:1) — by which time we have reached the eighth century BC. That tells us something: God’s wisdom was treasured and handed down from one generation to the next.

Proverbs 1 to 9 forms the prologue to the whole book, and its form is quite distinctive. It is not a string of stand-alone sayings, but a series of long exhortations from a father to his son. The address “my son” recurs throughout. In the wisdom literature of the ancient Near East, “my son” meant not only a son by blood; it was also how a master addressed a disciple, or an elder someone younger. In other words, here is someone who has walked the road, solemnly placing the lessons he learned through a lifetime of stumbling into the hands of the next generation.

More moving still, Proverbs 4 contains a rare piece of autobiography. Solomon says, “For I was a son to my father, tender and an only child in the sight of my mother. He taught me, and said to me: ‘Let your heart retain my words. Keep my commandments, and live.’” (Proverbs 4:3–4)

Brothers and sisters, notice who this “father” is. It is David. So Proverbs 4 is really a conversation across three generations: David passes the words to Solomon, Solomon passes them to his son, and the Holy Spirit carries them all the way down into our hands today. David’s greatest failure in life was that he did not guard his eyes; David’s greatest restoration was that his heart was remade by God. The first thing he said to his son was not “You must know how to govern,” but “Let your heart retain my words.”

Then we come to the last section of chapter 4, which is our theme passage today. This section (Proverbs 4:20–27) is the summit of the whole chapter, and its structure is very clear: from the ears and the eyes, to the heart, and then to the mouth, the eyes and the feet. The father inspects every gateway of his son’s body in turn. He says, “Put away from yourself a perverse mouth. Put corrupt lips far from you. Let your eyes look straight ahead. Fix your gaze directly before you. Make the path of your feet level. Let all of your ways be established. Don’t turn to the right hand nor to the left. Remove your foot from evil.” (Proverbs 4:24–27)

And this whole chain of guarding revolves around one centre — the heart of verse 23. The ears and eyes are the inputs, the mouth and feet are the outputs, and the heart is the central processor. The father is saying: every gateway must be guarded, but the one that matters most is the heart.

Isaiah 57:15 paints a different picture against a different background. The prophet Isaiah ministered around the eighth century BC; he was called in the year King Uzziah died (Isaiah 6:1) and served right through to the later years of King Hezekiah. Isaiah 40 onwards is often called the “Book of Comfort”; its message looks towards the exiled people and their future return. The first half of chapter 57 is a stern rebuke: the people worshipped idols under every green tree, built high places on the mountains, and their hearts were far from God. And right in the middle of that darkness, verse 15 suddenly blazes with light.

God introduces himself as “the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy.” It is one of the most exalted self-descriptions in the whole Bible. Yet the next line is astonishing: this Most High dwells in the high and holy place — and also “with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see the contrast? The highest God dwells within the lowest person. The holy of holies in heaven and a broken heart on earth turn out to share the same address.

So the four key points we’ll look at today are really a road home: from adjusting what we see and hear, to guarding the heart, to learning humility, and finally into a life cycle of continual renewal.

sections.heading: 3. Key Point 1: Seeing and Hearing Shape Our Life — What You Feed On Is What You Live Out
sections.html:
Scripture says, “My son, attend to my words. Turn your ear to my sayings. Let them not depart from your eyes. Keep them in the center of your heart.” (Proverbs 4:20–21)

In just two short verses we find four key actions in a row: attend, turn your ear, let them not depart from your eyes, keep them in your heart.

Let’s look at the original first. “Attend” is the Hebrew qashav, meaning to focus one’s attention, to listen intently — not listening as if to background music, but listening with every faculty. “Turn your ear” is literally “incline your ear” (natah ozen). Picture an elderly man who can’t hear well. What does he do? He turns his ear towards the speaker, leans forward, draws his whole body closer. That movement is itself an attitude: what you have to say matters to me.

And “keep” in “keep them in your heart” carries the sense of watching over and guarding — not leaving something lying around, but guarding it the way a sentry guards a treasury.

Brothers and sisters, these four actions tell us one thing: spiritual life is shaped by what we “see” and what we “hear”.

The Lord Jesus put it even more directly. He said, “Be careful therefore how you hear. For whoever has, to him will be given; and whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he thinks he has.” (Luke 8:18) Notice that the Lord did not say “be careful what you hear”; he said “how you hear”. The attitude with which we listen determines the measure we receive. When Mark records the same teaching, the Lord says, “Take heed what you hear. With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you, and more will be given to you who hear.” (Mark 4:24) However large the vessel you bring to listen with, that is the size of vessel God will fill for you.

It’s the same with the eyes. The Lord Jesus said, “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23) The psalmist also cried out, “Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things. Revive me in your ways.” (Psalm 119:37)

Now let’s ask ourselves honestly: what are we seeing and hearing every day?

Short videos on social media, news scrolling twenty-four hours a day, endless arguments in group chats, desire and comparison pushed at us with pinpoint precision by algorithms. In a single day we may spend three hours looking at screens and three minutes reading the Bible.

And the result? Our thinking is shaped by the world, our hearts are filled by the world, and so we cannot hear God’s voice.

It isn’t that God isn’t speaking. It’s that — it’s too noisy inside you.

Let me give you a picture. God’s voice is often like what we read in 1 Kings: Elijah at Horeb, first a wind, then an earthquake, then a fire — “but Yahweh was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake; but Yahweh was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake a fire passed; but Yahweh was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice.” (1 Kings 19:11–12) God’s voice is very often that still small voice. And the voice of the world is like a sound system turned all the way up. If you leave the speakers blaring and then complain that you can’t hear a whisper — is that fair?

Unless we first switch off the world, we cannot hear God.

This is not only a spiritual metaphor; science bears it out as well. The World Health Organization’s World Report on Hearing, published in 2021, states that more than 1.5 billion people worldwide already live with some degree of hearing loss, and projects that the figure will approach 2.5 billion by 2050; among people aged twelve to thirty-five, over a billion young people are at risk of hearing damage from prolonged exposure to recreational noise — including headphones played too loud and noisy entertainment venues. More sobering still, the hair cells in the cochlea of the inner ear that receive sound are limited in number, and once they are damaged by noise they do not grow back.

Brothers and sisters, what an exact spiritual picture this is. Long-term noise gradually robs a person of hearing, and the damage cannot be undone. It’s the same spiritually: if you keep feeding yourself on worldly, chaotic, negative input over the long term, your spiritual hearing grows duller day by day, until one day God speaks and you feel nothing at all.

Psychological research points in the same direction. In a 2009 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), three Stanford scholars, Ophir, Nass and Wagner, found that “heavy media multitaskers” — people who habitually use several media at once — actually performed worse than light users at filtering out irrelevant information, resisting distraction and switching between tasks. In other words, you think you are training yourself to do many things at once; in fact you are training yourself to be unable to concentrate.

And God’s voice is precisely the kind that can only be heard with concentration.

On the other hand, there is a hopeful side to this too. The Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb, in his 1949 book The Organization of Behavior, set out a famous principle often summarised as: neurons that fire together wire together. That is, the neural pathways you use repeatedly grow stronger and stronger. This is exactly why morning devotion works: when you set your eyes, ears and mind on God’s word every day, the path that leads to God gets walked into a broad highway.

Brothers and sisters, the 321 insight here is very clear: what you see and what you hear is what you become.

Paul says, “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” (2 Corinthians 3:18) Note the order: first “seeing”, and only then “transformed”. As you look at Jesus and listen to the truth day by day, your life gradually becomes like Jesus.

This is the first step of the fivefold change that 321 speaks of: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes. And where does our mindset come from? From what we see and hear every day.

So what you feed on is what you live out. This morning, what will you decide to feed yourself on?

sections.heading: 4. Key Point 2: The Heart Is the Key — The Wellspring of Life Flows from the Heart
sections.html:
Scripture says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

Many commentators call this verse the heart of the whole book of Proverbs. Let’s take it apart.

The Hebrew for “heart” is lev. In biblical usage the heart is not merely the seat of emotion; it is the sum of a person’s thinking, will, choices and values, the control centre of the whole inner life. When Scripture says “heart”, it means “the real you”.

The word for “keep” is natsar: to watch over, to guard, to keep watch — a military term, the kind of guarding a soldier does at a city gate.

And “with all diligence” is, literally, something close to “above everything that must be guarded”. In other words, there are many things you must guard in this life — your reputation, your health, your marriage, your work, your possessions — but there is one thing that matters more than all of these, and that is your heart.

As for “wellspring”, the root of the original word totsa’ot carries the sense of an “outlet”; in Joshua’s descriptions of territorial borders, the same word is used where a boundary “runs out” to a certain point. It describes the outlet from which a spring flows. So the picture in this verse is this: your heart is the source, and your whole life is the river that flows out of it.

Brothers and sisters, what does this mean?

It isn’t your circumstances that determine you, and it isn’t other people who determine you; it is your heart that determines you.

By the same logic: it isn’t that God doesn’t speak; it’s whether your heart is receiving.

The Lord Jesus could not have put it more clearly: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34) And again: “But the things which proceed out of the mouth come out of the heart, and they defile the man. For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual sins, thefts, false testimony, and blasphemies.” (Matthew 15:18–19)

The heart is a receiver. Think of it this way: a radio doesn’t fall silent because the station has gone off air; the station is broadcasting all the time, and the problem is usually the tuning. When the dial is on the frequency, the sound is clear; when it drifts, all you get is static.

So what keeps our hearts from picking up the signal? The lesson gives us four answers: emotions, hurts, anxieties and self.

The first is emotions. When we are swamped by anger, fear or anxiety, that noise grows loud enough to drown out everything else.

The second is hurts. A heart carrying unhealed wounds becomes defensive towards every voice. God says “I love you”, and the wounded heart hears “He’s lying to me”.

The third is anxieties. In the parable of the sower the Lord Jesus put it precisely: “What was sown among the thorns, this is he who hears the word, but the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and he becomes unfruitful.” (Matthew 13:22) Notice that word — “choke”. Anxieties don’t take the word away; they choke it. Your heart is crammed so full that God’s word can’t get in.

The fourth is self. We’ll leave this one to look at in detail in the third key point.

A well-known finding in psychology helps us understand this. In 1953 the British cognitive scientist Colin Cherry described the “cocktail party effect”: at a noisy party, with voices coming from every direction, you can still hear what the person beside you is saying to you; and if someone across the room says your name, even quietly, you notice at once.

What does that show? That human hearing is not just a function of the ears but a function of attention. What you hear depends on what you care about.

Brothers and sisters, this is a tremendous spiritual reminder. At the party of your life, if God’s name matters most to you, then however faint his voice, you will hear it; if God’s name is just one voice among many, then however loud the proclamation, you’ll miss it.

So God does not first change your circumstances. He first does one thing: he renews your heart.

He promised it long ago: “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” (Ezekiel 36:26) After David fell, this is what he prayed for too: “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10)

And the Lord Jesus gave his greatest promise to those whose hearts are clean: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” (Matthew 5:8)

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: the condition for seeing God is not cleverness, not gifting, not seniority — it is a pure heart.

This is what 321 means when it says: rely on the heart, and you find joy; rely on the brain, and you find worry.

Because the Holy Spirit lives in our hearts, not in our heads. Paul says, “And because you are children, God sent out the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father!’” (Galatians 4:6) God’s Spirit is crying out in your heart; if you keep using your brain to analyse, to calculate, to worry, you will miss that cry.

Those who rely on the brain turn God’s word into knowledge; those who rely on the heart let God’s word become life.

So 321 reminds us: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. If the wellspring of life flows from the heart, then the thing most worth investing in for a lifetime is this heart.

sections.heading: 5. Key Point 3: Humility Is the Key — Only Selflessness Can Hear God
sections.html:
Scripture says, “For the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy, says: ‘I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.’” (Isaiah 57:15)

This verse answers two vitally important questions: with whom does God dwell? And to whom does God speak?

The answer is: the humble.

The original is well worth noticing. The Hebrew for “contrite” is dakka, from a root meaning “crushed”, like grain ground between millstones. “Humble” is shephal-ruach, literally “low in spirit”. God says he dwells in the highest place, and also in the lowest heart. Between high and low there is no middle ground — God does not dwell in those who think they’re just about right as they are.

Why the humble?

Because the proud already have their own voice inside; only the humble are willing to listen to someone else’s voice — to listen to God’s voice.

What is pride? In 321 terms, pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. In practice it shows up as clinging to our own ideas and insisting on our own way.

What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. In practice it shows up as setting ourselves aside and letting Jesus be King.

The lesson uses a fine illustration: a cup full of water can’t take in any new water; only an emptied cup can be filled. Only selflessness can be filled by God.

Scripture also gives us two contrasting pictures.

The first is Samuel. The spiritual climate of his day was bleak: “The child Samuel ministered to Yahweh before Eli. Yahweh’s word was rare in those days. There were not many visions, then.” (1 Samuel 3:1) Yet God called a child. Samuel learned one sentence: “Speak; for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:10) Notice how that sentence is built — not “Lord, your servant is speaking; please listen”, but “Speak; for your servant hears.” Who is the subject? God. Who is on the receiving end? Me. If our prayers are so often the other way round, no wonder we can’t hear. Later Scripture says, “Samuel grew, and Yahweh was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground.” (1 Samuel 3:19)

The second picture is Jesus himself. The Lord Jesus said, “I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me.” (John 5:30)

Brothers and sisters, what an astonishing statement. The Son of God says that of himself he can do nothing. That isn’t incapacity; that is selflessness. Paul describes this life more fully: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)

Jesus is my role model. He of all people had the right to insist on himself, and yet he chose to empty himself.

Psychology also describes clearly how pride blocks the ears. In 1999 the psychologists Justin Kruger and David Dunning published research in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology showing that the people least competent in a given area are often the most likely to overestimate their performance, because they lack the very competence needed to recognise their own shortcomings. This later became known as the “Dunning–Kruger effect”.

Add to that an earlier finding: in experiments in 1960, the British psychologist Peter Wason demonstrated “confirmation bias” — our tendency to look for evidence that supports what we already think, while ignoring or even rejecting evidence to the contrary.

Brothers and sisters, put those two together and you have a spiritual X-ray: a proud person both overrates himself and will only listen to what he likes to hear. A heart like that won’t take in anything God says, however he says it.

The theologian Andrew Murray reminds us in his book Humility that humility is not some especially lofty virtue; it is simply the creature content to be in the creature’s place, letting God be God. And at the opening of his Confessions, Augustine voiced the other side of the same truth: you made us for yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you.

Scripture’s declaration is absolutely unequivocal: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) The psalmist also says, “He will guide the humble in justice. He will teach the humble his way.” (Psalm 25:9) And again: “The friendship of Yahweh is with those who fear him. He will show them his covenant.” (Psalm 25:14)

Guiding, teaching, friendship, showing — all four are given to the humble.

Brothers and sisters, this is the core message of 321: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

And remember: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. At home, at work, at church, every time you insist “I’m right”, what you usually get in return is not being heard but a relationship that goes dead.

Remember too: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

So it isn’t that God doesn’t speak; it’s that there is too much “self” inside us.

This morning, if you are willing to lay down that “self” which never stops talking, you will be amazed to discover that God’s voice has been there all along.

sections.heading: 6. Key Point 4: The Right Cycle — Seeing and Hearing, Life, Then Seeing and Hearing Again
sections.html:
At this point we need to see a vitally important spiritual cycle.

What you see and hear shapes your life; and your life, in turn, determines what you will go on to see and hear.

It’s a cyclical system. It spins faster and faster, and it only goes in two directions.

The wrong cycle goes like this: look at the world, and you think about the world; think about the world, and you live out the world; live out the world, and you want to look at the world all the more. And so each turn carries you further from God.

The right cycle goes like this: look at Jesus, and you think on the truth; think on the truth, and you live out Christ; live out Christ, and you long all the more to look at Jesus. And so each turn makes you more like Jesus.

Paul turned this cycle into a command: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) Notice the order: first we are transformed by the renewing of our mind, and only then can we prove God’s will. To prove it means to discern what God is saying. If you are not renewed, you won’t be able to discern it.

He also says, “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:1–2) And he gives a list: “Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8)

Brothers and sisters, this list is really a “spiritual viewing guide”. What will you watch and listen to this morning? Run it through these eight descriptions, and it will become clear.

Brain science also confirms how real this cycle is. Ann Graybiel, a neuroscientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, has spent many years studying the basal ganglia and has shown that habits are stored by the brain as “loops”: a cue triggers a chain of behaviour, the behaviour brings a reward, and the reward strengthens the loop. Once formed, it runs with almost no willpower. That’s why your finger opens that app without your ever deciding to; and it’s also why, once morning devotion becomes a habit, you don’t have to struggle — when the time comes, your heart simply turns towards God.

The management writer Jim Collins, in Good to Great, uses the image of a “flywheel” for the same thing: a huge flywheel takes enormous effort to push through its first turn, and the second turn is still hard work, but once you push past a certain point, its own momentum carries it round.

The spiritual life is a flywheel like that. For the first few days of getting up early to read the Bible, it will feel like pushing a boulder; keep pushing long enough, and the wheel will start pushing you.

So 321 gives us a clear standard so that we know how to choose:

Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. These are the Three Foundations.

Let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. These are the Two Core Values.

Establish God’s system. This is the Goal.

When you use this standard to choose what you’ll look at, listen to and think about each day, you will begin to “see rightly” and “hear rightly”, and your life will be changed.

And 321 calls this road the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. First let the Holy Spirit guide, then let Scripture open our understanding, then live out the life of Jesus, then in service let Jesus reign as King, and finally let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask you: which way is your flywheel turning today?

sections.heading: 7. Integrating the 321 Vision: The Fivefold Change from Mindset to Ministry
sections.html:
Let’s place today’s message within the overall framework of 321.

First, the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal. We don’t hear God’s voice to satisfy our curiosity; we hear it so that Jesus may reign as King. The Three Foundations answer the question “Whom do I listen to?”: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values answer “Why do I listen?”: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal answers “Having heard, what do I do?”: establish God’s system.

Second, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The four key points of today’s lesson are exactly the first two links of this chain. What you see and hear every day forms your mindset; when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships are healed; and when relationships are healed, ministry at last has a foundation.

Third, life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people are desperate to hear God’s voice because they want to know which ministry to take up, whether to change jobs, whether to get married. But what God cares about more is you as a person. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is clear too: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. If your relationship with God is clear, everything else will gradually become clear as well.

Fourth, a shift of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. A change in what we see and hear is, at bottom, a change of perspective. If you keep looking at earthly things, your heart will only respond to earthly voices.

Fifth, the 920 practice. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; as we practise living out the selfless “0” in every relationship, we bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, notice this: the most honest test of whether you have truly heard God lies not in your feelings, but in whether one more fruit is growing in your relationship with the “2” beside you.

Sixth, 235 relationships. We become a “2” with a selfless person, each being the other’s spiritual companion; we build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and from there we become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Those who hear God don’t walk alone; God’s voice is very often confirmed through a spiritual companion.

sections.heading: 8. Putting It into Practice: Turning Light into Life
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s deepen them using the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Deliberately adjust what you see and hear each day.

Review the information you take in every day. Cut back on excessive worldly, negative or chaotic content, and add more Bible reading, worship and spiritual teaching, so that God’s voice becomes the main current of your life.

Information: today you have heard Proverbs 4:20–23. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to show you what your heart is being fed on. Conviction: admit that “what I see and hear really is shaping me”. Implementation: starting tomorrow morning, give the first ten minutes after you open your eyes to God, and don’t touch your phone. Evaluation: every Sunday evening, honestly note how many days this week you managed it. Correction: if you can’t manage it, move your phone charger out of the bedroom. Repetition: keep it up for forty days and let it become a flywheel. Multiplication: share this practice with your “2” and invite them to do it with you.

Practice 2: Practise guarding your heart every day.

Through prayer, hand your emotions, anxieties and burdens over to God, and ask the Lord to cleanse your heart, so that it stays soft and simple — a place that can receive God’s voice.

Information and Revelation: meditate on Proverbs 4:23, and let the Holy Spirit point out the thorns that are choking you. Conviction: believe that the heart matters more than circumstances. Implementation: every evening, spend three minutes in a “clean-heart prayer”, handing over the day’s emotions, hurts and anxieties one by one; then be still for a minute and say only, “Lord, what do you want to say to me?” Evaluation and Correction: notice which anxiety keeps coming back most often — that is the breach that needs special entrusting to God. Repetition: do it every day, until it becomes like breathing. Multiplication: lead the brothers and sisters in your small group in praying this prayer together.

Practice 3: Choose humility and lay down your own ideas.

When God’s word clashes with your own ideas, learn to say, “Lord, I am willing to lay myself down and choose to obey you.” Every time you lay yourself down, you will hear God more clearly.

Information and Revelation: see what it is that your heart clings to most stubbornly. Conviction: admit that insisting is not the same as being right. Implementation: at least once this week, in an argument where you are sure you’re in the right, choose to stop talking first, listen first, apologise first. Evaluation: after that, did the relationship grow closer or more distant? Correction: change “I want to win” into “I want to love”. Repetition: let humility become your first reaction, not your last resort. Multiplication: when your family see that you no longer insist on your own way, you are already passing humility on.

sections.heading: 9. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Hearing God is not a technique; it is a life.

If the heart is chaotic, the voice is chaotic; if the heart is simple, the voice is clear.

To guard your heart is to guard your spiritual hearing.

sections.heading: 10. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, do you want to hear God?

The answer is not to go looking for a method, but to return to one place — your heart.

When your heart is guarded, when your eyes are adjusted, when your ears are cleansed, when you are willing to be humble, you will discover one thing: God has been speaking all along, and you have finally heard him.

The Lord Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27) Notice that this is the instinct of sheep, not the privilege of super-saints. If you belong to him, you can hear him.

The servant in Isaiah also left us words perfectly suited to morning devotion: “He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” (Isaiah 50:4) Every morning God is awakening us. The only question is to whom we lend our ears once we’re awake.

So from today, make a choice: adjust what you see and hear, and align your heart with God.

Turn off some of the noise — not because all those voices are bad, but because there is a more beautiful voice that deserves your full attention.

May we not only hear God’s voice but also let Jesus reign as King in our hearts; may the wellspring of our whole life flow from a heart that God guards, giving all the glory to Jesus.

For they are life to those who find them, and health to their whole body. Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life. (Proverbs 4:20–23)

For the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy, says: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.” (Isaiah 57:15)
declarations: Lord Jesus, I am willing to give my heart to you.
Cleanse my heart, and adjust everything I see and hear.
Let me no longer be filled with the world, but filled with your word.
I choose to be humble and selfless, and to let you reign as King within me.
I will be someone who sees you, hears you and lives you out.
In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare it. Amen!

Practise guarding your heart every day
Choose humility and lay down your own ideas
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you. You have never stopped speaking; it is our hearts that are too noisy, too full, too hard.

Lord, this morning we come before you; search our hearts, we pray. Where they are swamped by emotion, calm them; where they are blocked by hurt, heal them; where they are choked by anxiety, clear it away; where they are occupied by self, tear it down.

Give us a new heart; take away the heart of stone and give us a heart of flesh. Cleanse our eyes, so that we turn them away from worthless things; cleanse our ears, so that morning by morning we may hear as those who are taught.
Lord Jesus, we are willing to lay down our own ideas and let you be King. May the Holy Spirit guide us, so that all we see, hear, think and do today is pleasing to you.
May we become people who hear you and who live you out. May all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

blog.title: God Is Always Speaking — It’s Just Too Noisy Inside You

blocks.x: Why Have I Prayed for Years and Hardly Ever Heard God Speak?

A sister once told me that every morning, the first thing she does when she opens her eyes is silence the alarm, and the second is swipe her phone open. News, group chats, short videos, one after another, and twenty-five minutes are gone. Only when she is out on the road does she remember she hasn’t read the Bible today, so at a red light she hurriedly says, “Lord, please lead me today.”
She asked me: why is it that after all these years of praying, I have almost never clearly heard God speak?
Have you, too, cried out in your heart late one night: God, why don’t you speak?
But the truth may be the opposite of what we think. God has never stopped speaking. The problem is not God’s volume; the problem is our reception.
Spiritual Life Is Shaped by What We “See” and “Hear”
Scripture says, “My son, attend to my words. Turn your ear to my sayings. Let them not depart from your eyes. Keep them in the center of your heart” (Proverbs 4:20–21).

Two short verses, four actions: attend, turn your ear, let them not depart from your eyes, keep them in your heart. The first two are about the ears, the third about the eyes, the fourth about the heart. The entrances lead to the centre.
In other words, whatever you feed yourself on every day is what you will live out.

Today we spend three hours a day looking at screens and three minutes reading the Bible. The result is that our thinking is shaped by the world, our hearts are filled by the world, and so we cannot hear God.

God’s voice is like the still small voice Elijah heard at Horeb after the fire; the voice of the world is like a sound system turned all the way up. If you don’t switch off the speakers, how can you hear a whisper?

The World Health Organization’s 2021 World Report on Hearing states that more than 1.5 billion people worldwide already live with hearing loss; and the hair cells in the inner ear that receive sound, once damaged by noise, do not grow back. Long-term noise gradually robs a person of hearing. What an exact spiritual picture this is.
When the Heart Is Right, We Hear; When It’s Wrong, We Don’t
The heart of the whole book of Proverbs is this verse: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).
The Hebrew word for “keep” is a military term — guarding the way a soldier guards a city gate; and the “heart” is not just the emotions but the sum of our thinking, will and choices.
The heart is like a receiver. Tuned to God, the sound is clear; drifting from God, all you get inside is static.

What stops us picking up the signal? Emotions, hurts, anxieties — and self. The Lord Jesus put it most precisely: the cares of this age “choke” the word, and it becomes unfruitful. Not taken away, but choked. The heart is crammed so full that God’s word can’t get in.

In 1953 the cognitive scientist Colin Cherry described the “cocktail party effect”: at a noisy party, if someone across the room says your name, you notice at once. What you hear depends on what you care about.
So at the party of your life, where does God’s name rank?
Only Selflessness Can Hear God
God says, “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit” (Isaiah 57:15).
The highest God dwells in the lowest heart. The holy of holies in heaven and a broken heart on earth turn out to share the same address.

Why the humble? Because the proud already have their own voice inside; only the humble are willing to listen to God’s voice. A cup full of water can’t take in any new water; only an emptied cup can be filled.

The sentence Samuel learned is worth practising for a lifetime: “Speak; for your servant hears.” Not “Lord, your servant is speaking; please listen.” If our prayers are so often the other way round, no wonder we can’t hear.
This is the very core of 321: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.
Three Choices to Start This Morning
First, adjust what you see and hear each day. From tomorrow, give the first ten minutes after you open your eyes to God, and don’t touch your phone.

Second, guard your heart every day. In the evening, take three minutes to hand your emotions, hurts and anxieties over to God one by one; then be still for a minute and ask just one thing: Lord, what do you want to say to me?
Third, humbly lay down your own ideas. When God’s word clashes with your ideas, learn to say: Lord, I am willing to lay myself down and choose to obey you.
Hearing God is not a technique; it is a life. If the heart is chaotic, the voice is chaotic; if the heart is simple, the voice is clear. To guard your heart is to guard your spiritual hearing.
When your heart is guarded, when your ears are cleansed, when you are willing to be humble, you will discover this: God has been speaking all along, and you have finally heard him.
Reflection Question
This week, what has most often filled your heart — emotions, hurts, anxieties, or self? Are you willing to hand it over to God today?
