script: Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we’re looking together at Lesson 131 of Morning Devotion 321, and the theme is “Thinking Rightly”. Our key verse is 2 Corinthians 10:5: “bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.” Notice those words, “bringing into captivity”. To take something back means the territory had been seized by someone else. What God wants to take back today is our thoughts.

Brothers and sisters, I want to ask a question: where is the real battlefield of a human life? We often say it’s the workplace, the family, our health, our finances. But in the same workplace, one person withers and another rejoices; in the same hospital ward, one person despairs and another praises. The circumstances are the same, yet the outcomes are different. Why? Because the real battlefield isn’t in our circumstances or in other people, but in our thoughts. That’s why 321 tells us: change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your living changes.

Paul wrote 2 Corinthians around AD 55 to 57. At that time some people were attacking him, saying his bodily presence was weak and his speech despised. How did Paul respond? He said, “For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds.” The Greek word for “stronghold” means a hilltop fortress. Brothers and sisters, in our minds, too, stand fortress after fortress. Proverbs 23:7 also says, “For as he thinks about the cost, so he is.” As you think, so you are. Today we’re going to learn four things together.

First, the mind is a battlefield — not neutral, but a war zone. What are the strongholds? Wrong mindsets, self-centred thinking, logic not after God’s heart, and the world’s value system. Paul calls them “every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God”. Notice that phrase: “high thing”. The mind is like a castle that is never left empty. If it isn’t filled with truth, it will be occupied by error. The light of 321 is this: self-centred thinking has self at the centre; selfless thinking has Christ at the centre.

Second, thoughts determine outcomes: one thought brings blessing, one thought brings ruin. Scripture shows us this through one and the same man: David. In 2 Samuel 11, when it was time to go to war he stayed in the city, got up only in the evening and strolled on the roof. One wrong thought brought adultery, brought murder, brought a breach in his household that never closed. But in 2 Samuel 7, again in days of peace, what was in his heart was God’s ark, and the result was God’s pleasure and the promise of an everlasting kingdom. Brothers and sisters, the turning points of life lie not in our actions but in where our thinking begins. Thoughts are seeds; behaviour is fruit. Right seed, right result.

Third, what you think about in idle moments sets your direction. Let me ask a question: when you have nothing to do, what do you think about? When you’re busy, you are occupied by tasks; only when you’re idle does your true nature show. A 2010 Harvard study of 2,250 people found that for about 47 per cent of their waking hours, people’s minds are not on the present. Nearly half, brothers and sisters! Today many people scroll their phones the moment they have a spare minute, look at the world the moment they have a spare minute, and so their thoughts are filled with the world and their hearts gradually drift away from God. Brothers and sisters, God isn’t against rest; the problem isn’t having free time, it’s whom we hand our thoughts to when we have it.

Fourth, thinking rightly means letting our thoughts be filled with God’s word. Psalm 1:2 says, “But his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.” The Hebrew word for “meditates” describes something said aloud over and over, like a lion’s growl or a dove’s moaning. Meditation isn’t zoning out; it’s chewing over and over. Many brothers and sisters read the Bible and pray, but the problem is that they don’t meditate. They read and forget; they pray and that’s the end of it. But God wants his word to remain in you. A person like that is like a tree planted by the streams of water, and whatever he does shall prosper.

Paul says, “Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable … think about these things.” Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: this is an imperative. That means our thoughts can be chosen. You don’t have to be dragged along by every passing thought. Brain science also tells us that neural connections grow stronger with repeated use. Every time you choose to meditate on God’s word, you widen a road in your heart. The road you travel most becomes, in the end, your motorway. What you think on is what you become; think on Christ, and you live out Christ.

Let’s set this lesson back within 321. Jesus is my role model: when he was tempted in the wilderness, all three times he answered, “It is written” — that was a battle of the mind. The Bible is my standard — not feelings, not public opinion. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he guides us into all truth. And the core is this: let Jesus be King in my thoughts, let Jesus receive all the glory. From man’s perspective to God’s, from the temporary to the eternal. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Next come the practices — there are three. First, notice what you are thinking. Be still for a few minutes each day and ask yourself: what have I been thinking about most lately? Write down the thoughts that are untrue. Second, replace wrong thinking with God’s word. Don’t suppress, don’t indulge — replace. Third, build a habit of meditating on God’s word. One verse a day: copy it out in the morning, recite it as you leave home, think on it at midday, pray it before bed. Brothers and sisters, all together it takes less than five minutes, yet it can change a whole life.

Dear brothers and sisters, our lives aren’t lost on ability; they’re lost in our thinking. Wrong thinking, wrong life; right thinking, right life. Paul and Silas, in the prison at Philippi, prayed and sang hymns to God at midnight. The prison didn’t change; their thinking had changed, and so the chains came loose. When your thoughts are ruled by Christ, your choices will change, your life will change, and the course of your life will change too. Starting today, let’s make a decision together: my thoughts no longer belong to me; they fully obey Christ.

Let us pray together. Lord Jesus, I am willing to give my thoughts to you. Tear down every false stronghold within me, and remove every thought that is not of you. Today I will take back my thoughts and bring every thought into obedience to Christ. I will think on the truth and live out the truth, so that my life becomes more and more like yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, may God help you keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life. May the Lord bless you, and may you have a good day today.

Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. May the Lord’s peace fill you this morning. Today we’re looking together at Lesson 131 of Morning Devotion 321, and the theme is “Thinking Rightly”. Our key verse is 2 Corinthians 10:5: “bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.” Brothers and sisters, notice those words, “bringing into captivity”. Taking something back means that the territory was ours but was seized by someone else. What God wants to take back today isn’t your house or your money, but your thoughts.

Let me begin with a question: where is the real battlefield of a human life? Some say it’s the workplace, because the competition is fierce; some say it’s the family, because that’s where the friction is worst; some say it’s the body, because illness has them in its grip. These are all real hardships. But brothers and sisters, have you noticed? In the same workplace, one person withers and another rejoices; in the same hospital ward, one person despairs and another praises; the very same remark leaves one person wounded for three years and makes another laugh it off. The circumstances are the same, yet the outcomes are completely different. Why?

Because the real battlefield isn’t in our circumstances or in other people, but in a place where we spend every day and yet seldom put in order — our thoughts. The Frenchman Pascal said: man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed. Human dignity lies in the capacity to think, and human fall also begins in our thoughts. Proverbs 23:7 says, “For as he thinks about the cost, so he is.” So if we want our lives to change, we don’t change our behaviour first; we change our thinking first. This is the first light of 321: change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your living changes.

Let’s look at the background first. 2 Corinthians was written by the apostle Paul around AD 55 to 57, while he was in Macedonia. Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia, a trading port — populous, full of competing ideas and morally corrupt. At that time a group calling themselves super-apostles were attacking Paul, saying his bodily presence was weak and his speech despised. Paul didn’t strike back with their weapons. He said, “For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds.” The Greek word for “stronghold” means a hilltop fortress that could hold out against a great army for years. Today we’re going to learn four things.

The first thing: the mind is a battlefield — not neutral, but a war zone. Paul says there are “strongholds” in the mind. Strongholds don’t appear out of nowhere; a fortress is built brick by brick. The lesson tells us these strongholds are four things: first, wrong mindsets, such as “That’s just the way I am; I can’t change”; second, self-centred thinking, which asks first in everything, “Am I losing out?”; third, logic that is not after God’s heart — the strongest of all, because it sounds perfectly reasonable; and fourth, the world’s value system, which measures achievement by money and meaning by applause.

What do these strongholds keep us from? They keep us from knowing God, from obeying God, from hearing God. Paul’s original puts it even more precisely: “every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God”. Brothers and sisters, listen to that phrase — high thing. Strongholds block God not because they are low but because they are high. They are the “I” that lifts itself up and wants to take God’s place. The Lord Jesus told a parable: an unclean spirit leaves a man, comes back, finds the house swept and put in order, and brings along seven other spirits more evil than itself to live there. A house left empty isn’t safe; it’s dangerous. An empty mind isn’t neutral; it’s up for rent.

Psychology bears this out too. Dr Aaron Beck of the University of Pennsylvania founded cognitive therapy in the 1960s. He found that people’s emotional distress often comes not directly from events but from spontaneous, unexamined “automatic thoughts”, and that beneath them lie deeper “core beliefs”. Core beliefs are like the foundation, and thoughts are like walls built on that foundation; knock down the walls without touching the foundation, and the walls soon go back up. Brothers and sisters, Beck’s “core beliefs” and Paul’s “strongholds” describe the same thing. The difference is this: psychology can help you see the fortress, but it has no weapon to tear it down; the gospel does. The light of 321 is this: self-centred thinking has self at the centre; selfless thinking has Christ at the centre.

The second thing: thoughts determine outcomes — one thought brings blessing, one thought brings ruin. Scripture shows us this through one and the same man: David. The same man, two ways of thinking, two endings. 2 Samuel 11 records: “At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel … But David stayed at Jerusalem. At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to look at.” Notice: when it was time to go to war, he didn’t go; he got up only in the evening. This is not a man so busy he lost control; this is a man so idle he let down his guard.

Seeing was not yet sin, but next a wrong thought took shape in his heart. James 1 describes it with pinpoint accuracy: “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” One thought led to adultery; when the adultery couldn’t be covered up, it led to murder; and after the murder came a breach in his household that never closed. The prophet Nathan said, “Now therefore the sword will never depart from your house.” The later affair of Amnon and the rebellion of Absalom all fulfilled those words. Brothers and sisters, one thought, and the damage ran on for three generations.

But 2 Samuel 7 is a different scene. “When the king lived in his house, and Yahweh had given him rest from all his enemies all around, the king said to Nathan the prophet, ‘See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but God’s ark dwells within curtains.’” Again these were days of peace, again there was no war to fight. But this time what he was thinking about was not his own comfort but God’s dwelling place. And God said, “Your house and your kingdom will be made sure forever before you.” Brothers and sisters, the turning points of life lie not in our actions but in where our thinking begins. Thoughts are seeds; behaviour is fruit. Right seed, right result; wrong seed, wrong result. The rational emotive therapy of the American psychologist Albert Ellis says the same: events don’t directly determine outcomes; there is always a belief in between. 321 says it more simply: it isn’t events that make you fail; it’s how you think that makes you fail.

The third thing: what you think about in idle moments sets your direction. Brothers and sisters, I want to ask a question that few people ask, yet one that cuts to the heart: when you have nothing to do, what do you think about? When you’re busy, you are occupied by tasks; only when you’re idle does your true nature show. When you’re busy, your thoughts run on rails; when you’re idle, your thoughts automatically slide down the road they know best. And that road is the real direction of your life. David sinned in a time of idleness; David was also blessed in a time of peace. The same idleness, different thoughts, different lives.

There are two scientific findings worth noting here. In 2001 Marcus Raichle and his colleagues at Washington University described the brain’s “default mode network”. They found something counter-intuitive: when people stop and do nothing, the brain doesn’t go quiet; instead, a particular set of brain regions becomes more active. You think you’re daydreaming, but inside, you’re running at full speed. In 2010 Killingsworth and Gilbert of Harvard University tracked 2,250 participants and found that for about 47 per cent of their waking hours, people’s minds were not on the present, and that when their minds wandered, they were less happy than when focused. Nearly half our waking hours, brothers and sisters! Where has that time gone?

The truest picture of today is this: the moment we have a spare minute, we scroll our phones; the moment we have a spare minute, we look at the world. And so our thoughts are filled with the world, and our hearts slowly drift away from God. It’s not because we’ve committed some great evil, but because we have handed over the softest, most malleable part of our time for others to shape. But hear this clearly: God isn’t against rest. The Lord Jesus said to his disciples, “You come apart into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” The problem isn’t having free time; it’s whom we hand our thoughts to when we have it. Rest is handing that space over to God; emptiness is handing it over to the world. 321 reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and find worry, rely on the heart and find joy.

The fourth thing: thinking rightly means letting our thoughts be filled with God’s word. Psalm 1:2 says, “But his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.” Psalm 1 is the prologue to the whole Psalter, like a doorway. It divides people into two paths, and the dividing point, at first, isn’t behaviour but “counsel” and “meditation”. The Hebrew for “meditates” here is wonderfully vivid: it is used of a lion’s growl and of a dove’s moaning. So biblical meditation isn’t zoning out; it is like a lion that has seized its prey and won’t let go — holding a word in your mouth and chewing on it again and again.

This exposes the bottleneck in many people’s devotional lives. The lesson is very honest: many people read the Bible and pray, but they don’t meditate. They read and forget; they pray and that’s the end of it. The verse goes in through the eyes and out through the eyes, without staying in the heart for even a minute. But God’s desire is that his word should remain in you and guide your thoughts. God said to Joshua, “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it.” The psalmist said, “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.” Such a person “will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither”. Notice: not watered, but planted by the streams. When a drought year comes, other trees wither but it stays green, because its water source is not the clouds in the sky but the stream beneath the ground.

Paul also says, “Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report … think about these things.” Brothers and sisters, this is an imperative, which means our thoughts can be chosen. There’s a beautiful insight from the original here: “think about” and the “imaginations” that must be thrown down in our key passage share the same Greek root. The same capacity for thinking, turned downwards, builds a stronghold; turned upwards, it builds an altar. Brain science confirms it too: neural connections grow stronger with repeated use and weaker with long disuse. Every time you choose to meditate on God’s word, you widen a road in your brain. The one you travel most becomes, in the end, your motorway. Romans 12:2 says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” What you think on is what you become; think on Christ, and you live out Christ.

Next come the practices; the lesson gives us three. First, notice what you are thinking. Be still for a few minutes each day and ask yourself: what have I been thinking about most lately? Write down the thoughts that are negative, self-centred or anxious. You can use David’s prayer: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.” Second, replace wrong thinking with God’s word. Notice these two phrases in the lesson: don’t suppress, don’t indulge. Suppressed thoughts pop up somewhere else; indulged thoughts build themselves into fortresses. Scripture’s third way is replacement. In the wilderness the Lord Jesus didn’t debate with Satan; he simply said, “It is written …”

Third, build a habit of meditating on God’s word. Choose one verse a day: copy it out in the morning, recite it as you leave home, think on it at midday, pray it before bed. All together it takes less than five minutes, yet it can change a whole life. 321 has the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Brothers and sisters, many people stop at the first stage, “Information” — deeply moved by what they hear, but never moving into “Implementation”. Real change means walking all eight stages, and finally “Multiplication” — taking it to the people around you.

Let’s set this lesson back within the whole panorama of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — when he was tempted in the wilderness, all three times he answered, “It is written”; that was a battle fought purely in the realm of thought, and the Lord won it with Scripture. The Bible is my standard — not feelings, not public opinion. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he will guide us into all truth. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. We often let Jesus be King of Sunday, yet don’t let him be King of that thought inside us. The Goal: establish God’s system — and a system begins with thoughts renewed one by one. Then there is the 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”, and of the nine fruits of the Spirit, which one doesn’t happen first in our thoughts?

Dear brothers and sisters, let’s return to the question we began with. Your life isn’t lost on ability; it’s lost in your thinking. Wrong thinking, wrong life; right thinking, right life. We often ask God to change our circumstances, change our husband, change our children, change our boss. God hears all of it; but today God wants first to do something more fundamental: to renew your thinking and rebuild what is inside you. Because if your circumstances change but your thinking doesn’t, you’ll repeat the old pain in the new circumstances. Paul and Silas, in the prison at Philippi, with their feet in the stocks, were at midnight “praying and singing hymns to God”. The prison didn’t change; their thinking had changed, and so the ground shook violently and the chains came loose. When your thoughts are ruled by Christ, your choices will change, your life will change, and the course of your life will change too.

So from today, let’s make a decision together: my thoughts no longer belong to me; they fully obey Christ. Let us pray together. Lord Jesus, I am willing to give my thoughts to you. Tear down every false stronghold within me, and remove every thought that is not of you. I confess that I often rely on the brain and on myself; I confess that I have often given my free time to the world. Today I will take back my thoughts and bring every thought into obedience to Christ. I will think on the truth and live out the truth, so that my life becomes more and more like yours. Let your Kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, may God help you keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life. May the Lord bless you.

sections.heading: Introduction: Your First Reaction Betrays Your Thinking
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning, let us grow quiet together and first ask ourselves a very simple, yet very honest, question —

When circumstances turn against you and things don’t go the way you hoped, what is your first reaction?

Is it worry? Is it fear? Does your mind immediately start playing the worst possible outcome on a loop?

The test results aren’t even back, and in your heart you’ve already passed a death sentence on yourself; your child is half an hour late home, and your mind has already run an entire disaster film; your manager glances at you one second too long, and you spend the whole afternoon wondering whether he’s about to let you go; you haven’t finished reading the text from the bank, and your heart has already sunk to the bottom. Brothers and sisters, we often say, “People are knocked down by their circumstances.” In fact, they aren’t. Very often, before circumstances have lifted a finger, our thoughts have already knocked us down.

This is the most honest picture of the human condition — our thinking is led around by our circumstances. Whatever the circumstances say, we think; when the circumstances turn dark, our thinking turns dark with them; when the circumstances fall into chaos, our thinking falls into chaos too. We are like a little boat without an anchor: wherever the wind blows, there the boat drifts.

But God’s intention is nothing like that. God’s intention is this: not that your circumstances should decide your thinking, but that truth should lead your thinking.

Scripture says, “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). The Chinese Union Version, with many ancient manuscripts, reads “the word of Christ”. This verse is a chain of life: the word of Christ enters our ears and becomes “hearing”; that hearing enters our thinking, is digested and believed, and becomes “faith”. In other words, faith is not a feeling that appears out of nowhere; faith is the fruit that grows out of “right thinking”. How you think determines how much faith you have; how much faith you have determines how much of God’s work you experience.

So the 321 insight is very clear: it is not events that change you; it is how you think that decides whether you overcome.

In the last lesson we saw that our thinking is contested territory, that the real battlefield of life lies in the mind. In this lesson we go a step further and look at four keys: what right thinking is, how to cut off the wrong voices, how to step beyond past experience, and how the thinking of faith brings forth a victorious life.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Chain from “Hearing” to “Faith”
sections.html:
To understand “right thinking”, we first need to understand the background of today’s two key passages.

Romans was written by the apostle Paul, probably between AD 56 and 57, very likely in Corinth. At that time he was preparing to take the offering from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem, and then to go on west to Spain (Romans 15:24–26). The church in Rome that received the letter was not one Paul had planted himself; its members included Jewish believers and a great many Gentile believers, and the tension between the two groups was considerable. So in this letter Paul sets out the gospel of “justification by faith” from chapter 1 to chapter 8, and from chapter 9 to chapter 11 he deals specifically with one heavy question: why is it that Israel, God’s chosen people, stumbled before the gospel?

Paul’s answer is not that they lacked zeal, but that their thinking was pointed in the wrong direction. He says, “For I testify about them that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Romans 10:2). The zeal was there, but it was built on a wrong mindset — “seeking to establish their own righteousness” (Romans 10:3) instead of submitting to God’s righteousness. Brothers and sisters, please notice: what was lost here was not, at heart, behaviour. It was mindset.

So in chapter 10, verses 13–17, Paul draws out a complete chain: “For, ‘Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.’ How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher? And how will they preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10:13–15a). Then he draws his conclusion: “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17).

Read backwards, the chain is clearer still: the word of Christ → hearing → faith → calling on him → salvation. The link in the middle is precisely our subject today — what you take in through hearing, and what you think about, determines the weight of your faith.

The word “faith” in the original is pistis, that is, “faith”; the word “hearing” is akoē, meaning “the message heard”. So the sentence could also be rendered literally: faith comes from the message heard, and the message heard comes through the word of Christ. Whatever your thinking feeds on, that is the shape your faith will grow into.

The other key passage comes from 1 John. In his old age the apostle John lived in Ephesus, and he wrote this letter somewhere between AD 85 and 95 to the churches around Asia Minor. False teachers had already appeared, denying that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh (1 John 4:2–3), and shaking the foundations of believers. In that setting John wrote, “For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith” (1 John 5:4).

Notice the tense of the verb in this verse. In the original, “has overcome the world” is in a completed tense — not “will overcome”, but “has already overcome”. Victory is not a battle still waiting to be fought; victory is an accomplished fact, waiting for us to draw on it by faith. And faith, as Romans says, comes from right hearing and right thinking.

Put the two passages together, and you have today’s main line: rightly hearing God’s word → thinking rightly → faith arising → living out victory.

sections.heading: 1. Right Thinking: Return to 321 — Let Truth Overcome the Facts
sections.html:
Many people assume that “right thinking” simply means positive thinking. Today slogans like these are everywhere: be optimistic, motivate yourself, believe in yourself, attract good things. Brothers and sisters, these words sound warm, but they are not the “right thinking” the Bible speaks of.

Right thinking is not “optimism”; right thinking is “God-centredness”.

Where is the difference? Optimism focuses on myself — I believe I can. Right thinking focuses on God — I believe God can. Optimism is cheering yourself on in the dark; right thinking is lifting your head in the dark and seeing that God is still seated as King. Optimism is held up by emotion, and when the emotion collapses, everything collapses; right thinking stands on the word of God, and however bad the circumstances become, the word does not move.

So where does right thinking begin? It begins by returning to 321:

Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide; let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; in order to establish God’s system.

When your thinking is anchored by these Three Foundations, Two Core Values and one Goal, your whole inner set of coordinates changes. When something happens, the first question you ask is no longer “What am I going to do?” but “What would Jesus do?”; no longer “What will other people say?” but “What does the Bible say?”; no longer “How do I feel?” but “Where is the Holy Spirit leading me?”

When you think this way, you will discover a vitally important principle: truth is always greater than the facts.

What are the facts? The facts are the situation your eyes can see right now. What is truth? Truth is what God has said, the word that never changes. Facts pass away; truth does not pass away. Facts are temporary; truth is eternal.

Circumstances often say three things to us: impossible, too late, no hope. But God’s word answers with three things: possible, not too late, God can do a new thing.

There are two people in the Bible who lived out this principle beautifully.

The first is the centurion of Capernaum. His servant was paralysed and suffering terribly. Jesus said he would go to his house, but the centurion replied, “Lord, I’m not worthy for you to come under my roof. Just say the word, and my servant will be healed” (Matthew 8:8). This centurion was a Roman officer who lived every day within a “chain of command”. His reasoning went like this: if I, a minor officer, give an order and the soldiers go and do it, then when the Lord of all things speaks a word, how could the sickness not leave? He was looking not at his servant’s condition but at the authority of Jesus’ word. When Jesus heard it, he marvelled and said, “Most certainly I tell you, I haven’t found so great a faith, not even in Israel” (Matthew 8:10b).

The second is the woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years. She pushed her way through the crowd and touched the fringe of Jesus’ garment. Scripture records what was in her mind: “for she said within herself, ‘If I just touch his garment, I will be made well’” (Matthew 9:21). Notice this phrase — Scripture deliberately points out that she “said within herself”. Her healing did not begin with her hand; it began with her thinking. She settled the matter in her mind first, and only then reached out to touch.

Brothers and sisters, their thinking determined their experience.

Notice that both of them were in very unfavourable situations. The centurion was a Gentile and an officer of the occupying army; by Jewish custom, a rabbi who entered his house would become unclean. The woman with the bleeding was unclean under the regulations of Leviticus 15; in everyone’s eyes, reaching out to touch someone was breaking the rules. Their “facts” were not pretty. But they did not look at the facts; they looked at whether the Lord’s word had power. Truth is greater than the facts — not by denying the facts, but by refusing to let the facts have the final word.

Psychology bears this out as well. In the 1960s Aaron T. Beck, a psychiatrist at the University of Pennsylvania, developed “cognitive therapy”. He found that what drags people into depression is often not the event itself, but the “automatic thoughts” that flash by between the event and the emotion, so fast that people do not even notice them. At almost the same time, the psychologist Albert Ellis put forward his well-known ABC model: A is the Activating event, C is the Consequence; but what determines C is not A, but B in the middle — the Belief.

Psychology has seen that “B” exists; the Bible tells us what that “B” ought to contain. God’s children do not simply swap negative thoughts for positive ones; they exchange human thoughts for the word of God. “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2).

A 321 insight: think on God’s word and faith is born; think on your circumstances and fear is born. This is exactly the change of perspective — from man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one, from a worldly perspective to a godly one. Four shifts, one direction: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

sections.heading: 2. Don’t Dwell on the Enemy’s Words: Cut Off the Wrong Source
sections.html:
How did humanity’s first fall happen?

In the Garden of Eden, Eve’s sin did not begin with an action. It began with — a thought.

Scripture records it in remarkable detail. The serpent spoke first: “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1b). Then it went on: “You won’t really die, for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:4–5). And then Scripture says, “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate” (Genesis 3:6a).

Look closely at the route: first she “listened” to the serpent’s words, then she “looked” at the fruit, then she began to “think” — thinking that this fruit was good for food, a delight to the eyes, able to make one wise — and only then did she reach out and “do”.

Listen wrongly and you look wrongly; look wrongly and you think wrongly; think wrongly and you act wrongly. Change the thinking and the action changes; change the action and the ending changes.

Brothers and sisters, notice one thing: the serpent did not force the fruit into Eve’s mouth. Satan has no power to compel anyone to sin. His only skill is to “speak” — to drop a sentence into your thinking. The Lord Jesus said, “He was a murderer from the beginning, and doesn’t stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks on his own; for he is a liar, and the father of lies” (John 8:44b). Satan’s weapon is the lie; his battlefield is the mind.

So what is the safest way? Don’t let the wrong voices in.

Many people think, “It won’t hurt to listen for a moment,” “It makes no difference if I take a look,” “I’m only finding out about it.” But the truth is this: once something enters your thinking, it begins to affect your life. You cannot drop a drop of ink into clear water and then say, “It was only one drop.” The water is already different.

In a study in 1960, the psychologist Peter Wason identified what is now called “confirmation bias”: once people have accepted a certain hypothesis, they unconsciously gather evidence that supports it and ignore the evidence against it. This reveals something frightening — once a lie has moved into your thinking, your mind will start finding reasons for it, building it a house and paying its rent. That is why “debating with Satan” is always a losing battle: the moment you open your mouth to argue, you are already standing on his question.

A series of studies from 1991 onwards by the psychologist Susan Nolen-Hoeksema (then at Stanford, later at Yale) showed that “rumination” — chewing over negative events again and again — markedly deepens and prolongs depressed moods. People often think that if they go over something a few more times, they will think it through; in reality, going over it a few more times only digs the rut deeper. Brothers and sisters, some thoughts cannot be “thought through”; they can only be “cut off”.

The Lord Jesus gives us the best role model. When he was tempted in the wilderness, he did not discuss things with Satan, did not analyse, did not explain. He said only, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth’” (Matthew 4:4b). Three temptations, three times “It is written”. This is what “the Bible is my standard” means — not debating, only declaring.

The apostle James says, “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). The order matters: first submit to God, then resist the devil. A person who will not submit to God has no power to resist the devil; when a person who submits to God stands up, the devil runs.

The Reformer Martin Luther is commonly said to have put it like this: you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest in your hair. A thought flying past is not your sin; letting it stay, feeding it and living alongside it is what becomes your snare.

A 321 insight: do not debate with Satan, and do not let the lie in. For our thinking is not a toy; it is a battlefield. And that is why “selflessness overcomes Satan” — every attack of Satan is designed to stir up our “self”: my face, my rights, my grievances, my fears. When the “self” is exalted, the lie has a foothold; when we return to selflessness and let Jesus be King, the enemy’s words can no longer stick to us.

sections.heading: 3. Don’t Be Limited by the Past: God Is Doing a New Thing
sections.html:
The third key is to walk out of the “past”.

Scripture says, “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert” (Isaiah 43:18–19).

The background of these words matters. Isaiah 40–66 is God’s word of comfort to a people who would go into exile and would also return. Just before this, God has reminded them of his mighty power at the Exodus — how he made a way through the Red Sea (Isaiah 43:16–17); and immediately afterwards he says: don’t remember the former things. God is not asking them to forget his works; he is asking them not to lock him into the way he acted “that one time before”. Last time it was a way through the sea; this time it is a way through the wilderness. Last time he parted the Red Sea; this time he brings rivers to the desert. The method is different; God is the same.

Yet many people’s thinking is tied up by the “past”.

They failed once, so they conclude they will certainly fail this time too; they were hurt once, so they conclude that no one can be trusted; they prayed once and were not healed, so they conclude that God probably won’t do anything more for them. And so two sentences quietly move into the heart: this time nothing will change; God probably won’t act.

Brothers and sisters, those two sentences do not come from God; they come from experience. And experience is always smaller than God.

This is exactly where Martha and Mary landed. Lazarus fell ill, and the sisters sent word to Jesus, yet Jesus stayed where he was for two more days. By the time Jesus reached Bethany, Lazarus had already been in the tomb for four days. Martha came out to meet him and said, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died” (John 11:21). Later, when Mary saw Jesus, she fell at his feet, and what she said was exactly the same: “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died” (John 11:32b).

Where did the two sisters’ faith stop? It stopped at “if you would have been here”. They believed Jesus could heal the sick — because they had seen it; but they did not believe Jesus could raise the dead — because they had never seen it. Their thinking had a line drawn across it by experience.

But Jesus rubbed that line out. He said, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” (John 11:25–26). And at the tomb he said to Martha again, “Didn’t I tell you that if you believed, you would see God’s glory?” (John 11:40).

Listen carefully to the order here: not “see, then believe”, but “believe, and then you will see”. Man’s order is that seeing is believing; God’s order is that believing is the evidence. “For we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7).

God is never limited by his own past methods either. Take the healing of leprosy. In the Old Testament, Elisha sent a messenger to Naaman, saying, “Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall come again to you, and you shall be clean” (2 Kings 5:10). In the New Testament, the Lord Jesus stretched out his hand and touched a man with leprosy, saying, “I want to. Be made clean” (Matthew 8:3b). Another time he said to ten men with leprosy, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And as they went, they were cleansed (Luke 17:14). Washing seven times, a touch of the hand, cleansed along the road — the methods were all different, yet the God who healed was one and the same.

God himself could not say it more clearly: “‘For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,’ says Yahweh. ‘For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts’” (Isaiah 55:8–9).

Psychology offers a painful piece of corroborating evidence for this truth. In 1967 Martin Seligman and Steven Maier conducted their well-known experiments on “learned helplessness” at the University of Pennsylvania: when animals repeatedly experienced pain they could not control, later, even when the door of escape was open, they no longer tried; they simply lay down and endured it. People are the same. If experiences of failure are not renewed by truth, they become an invisible door — the door is actually open, yet the person no longer walks out.

The good news is that the brain God made is not set in concrete either. Neuroscience today widely recognises “neuroplasticity”: the brain’s neural connections change with repeated thoughts and experiences, and they keep changing throughout life. The principle the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed in 1949 was later often summed up in one sentence: neurons that fire together wire together. Whatever you think about repeatedly, that road grows wider and wider. The old pathways of thought were worn in over decades; a new pathway can begin to be walked from today.

Abraham is a role model of exactly this. “Without being weakened in faith, he didn’t consider his own body, already having been worn out, (he being about a hundred years old), and the deadness of Sarah’s womb. Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God” (Romans 4:19–20). Here the Chinese Union Version, following other ancient manuscripts, reads that he did “consider” his own body as good as dead. Notice, then: he did not deny the facts — he truly took account of a body as good as dead; but above the facts, he looked to the greater promise.

So a person limited by the past has in fact shrunk God down to the size of his own memory. That is not humility; it is actually a hidden pride — I have used my limited experience to draw a boundary around the infinite God. Return to your originally intended position, brothers and sisters: let man be man and let God be God. Man’s position is to believe; God’s position is to act.

A 321 insight: don’t define God by the past, and don’t limit God by experience. God is the God who is forever doing new things. “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23). He who sits on the throne is still saying today, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5b).

sections.heading: 4. The Thinking of Faith: Bringing Forth a Victorious Life
sections.html:
The fourth key is to carry right thinking all the way into a victorious daily life.

Scripture says, “For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith” (1 John 5:4).

The key to victory is faith. So where does faith come from? It comes from our thinking. “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17).

Put these two verses together and you have one complete lifeline: God’s word → hearing → thinking → faith → victory.

When you think on God’s word, three things happen: your faith is built up, your life is lifted, your circumstances are turned around. When you think on negative words, three things also happen: your faith is weakened, your emotions are crushed, your life is trapped. The same twenty-four hours, the same head on your shoulders — whatever you feed it is what grows.

Here is a picture: your thinking is like a steering wheel, and your life is like a car. Set the direction right and the road is right; set the direction wrong and, however hard you press the accelerator, you only go wrong faster. Many people are not lacking in effort; they are working hard with the steering wheel turned the wrong way. That is also why God’s order is to change the mindset first and then the behaviour — if the steering wheel hasn’t turned, no amount of acceleration will help.

But brothers and sisters, please be sure to remember this: faith is not a feeling; faith is choosing to believe God’s word.

Feelings change; the word does not. Feelings rise and fall with sleep, blood sugar, the weather and the look on other people’s faces; but God’s word is “settled in heaven forever” (see Psalm 119:89). If we build our faith on feelings, it is like building a house on the waves. The Bible defines faith like this: “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). Neither “assurance” nor “proof” is the language of emotion; they are the language of law and property — a title deed for something not yet seen, yet already held in your hand.

This is exactly where the Israelites lost at Kadesh Barnea. Twelve spies saw the same land of Canaan and the same sons of Anak, but they brought back two kinds of thinking. Ten of the spies said, “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Numbers 13:33b). But Caleb said, “Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!” (Numbers 13:30b). The difference was not in the intelligence they gathered but in their thinking; not in how tall the giants were but in what they saw themselves as in their own hearts. In the end, the generation that said “grasshoppers” fell dead in the wilderness, while Caleb, who said “well able to overcome”, was still going up to take the hill country at eighty-five.

In 1998 the psychologist Barbara Fredrickson put forward her “broaden-and-build theory”, showing that positive emotions broaden the range of a person’s thinking and action in the moment, while negative emotions narrow attention. This is a glimmer of light within common grace; but the thinking of faith goes deeper than positive emotion — positive emotion looks inward for resources, while the thinking of faith draws upward on God’s resources. “Above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the fiery darts of the evil one” (Ephesians 6:16).

The concentration-camp survivor and psychologist Viktor Frankl wrote a stunning sentence in Man’s Search for Meaning: everything can be taken from a man but one thing, the last of the human freedoms — the freedom to choose one’s attitude in any given set of circumstances. Even in the darkest place, a person still has one authority that cannot be taken away: the choice of how to think. Brothers and sisters, how much more is this true for God’s children: not only can we choose how to think, we also have God’s word to think on, and the Holy Spirit within us guiding our thinking.

So how, concretely, do we practise the thinking of faith? Paul gives us a list: “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things” (Philippians 4:8). Eight qualities, like eight thresholds. Before any thought comes in, ask it first: Are you true? Are you honourable? Are you pure? Whatever cannot get over the threshold, show it the door. This is something every brother and sister can begin doing today.

A 321 insight: faith is not a feeling; it is choosing to believe God’s word. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you find joy, rely on the brain and you find worry. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: It Begins with a Change of Mindset
sections.html:
Let us set today’s four key points back into the full picture of 321.

First, the Three Foundations are the three pillars of “right thinking”. Jesus is my role model — however he thought in the wilderness, that is how I think. The Bible is my standard — it isn’t right because I feel it is right; it counts only because God has said it. The Holy Spirit is my guide — the Counsellor who lives within me reminds me whenever my thinking drifts.

Second, the Two Core Values are the direction of “right thinking”. Let Jesus be King: only one can sit on the throne of my thinking — not my circumstances, not other people’s verdicts, not my emotions, but Jesus. Let Jesus receive all the glory: when I choose to believe God’s word and experience God’s work, the glory goes not to my optimism, not to my willpower, but entirely to him.

Third, the Goal is where “right thinking” belongs. Only a person whose thinking has been renewed by truth can be of one heart with others and establish God’s system together.

Fourth, the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Think about it: almost all our negative thoughts revolve around a “self” — my face, my losses, my grievances, my sense of security, my future. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; when I insist on thinking my own way, I am really trying to make God’s decisions for him. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. So only the selfless can truly rest: I hand the facts over to God, and I am responsible only for believing the truth. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Fifth, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. This lesson moves the very first link. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. Life first, then relationships, then ministry — the order cannot be reversed.

Sixth, the change of perspective. From man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. The facts are earthly and temporary; truth is heavenly and eternal.

Seventh, the 920 practice. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”. When we think on God’s word and live out a selfless (0) life, the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23a) — flow naturally in our relationships. You will find that once your thinking changes, the words that come out of your mouth are different; once your words are different, the atmosphere at home is different.

Eighth, the 235 relationships. Fighting your own thoughts alone is very hard. Find a selfless spiritual companion to be your “2”, reminding each other and praying for each other; be shepherded, and shepherd others, within the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally, in the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, fight this battle of the mind together. One person thinking alone easily goes round in circles; when two or three think God’s word through together, they become an alliance for victory.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let us use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to carry them through thoroughly.

Practice 1: When problems come, go back to God’s word first

When you face difficulty, don’t start by analysing the circumstances; start by asking: “What does God’s word say?” Let truth be the starting point of your thinking.

Information: today, copy three verses onto a card — Romans 10:17, 1 John 5:4 and Isaiah 43:19. Information is the entrance; words you have not stored up cannot be drawn on in an emergency.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine on them, so that one of the verses suddenly “lights up” and becomes his word to you personally.

Conviction: settle it in your heart — not “let’s try and see”, but “this is how it is”.

Implementation: from tomorrow morning, whenever anything goes wrong, pause for three seconds and ask, “What does God’s word say?” Only then speak, only then act.

Practice 2: Deliberately reject negative and lying thoughts

When a negative thought appears, immediately replace it with a declaration of God’s word, such as “God reigns” or “God can make a way”, and stop the wrong thought from developing any further.

Evaluation: every evening, take three minutes to look back — which thought did I let settle in today? Did it come from God, or from the enemy?

Correction: not suppression, but replacement. An empty house will be occupied again; only when God’s word moves in does the lie have nowhere to live. “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11).

Practice 3: Practise thinking with faith every day

Choose one of God’s promises, think on it and declare it again and again, so that your system of thinking is renewed by faith and transformation begins from within.

Repetition: one verse, one week — morning, noon and night, read it once, think on it once, declare it once. Neural pathways are worn in by repetition, and so are spiritual pathways.

Multiplication: share what you have experienced with your “2”. When you speak the truth out, it takes root more deeply in you; when you help someone begin to think rightly, you have taken part in establishing God’s system.

A Gentle Reminder

If our thinking is not led by truth, it will be carried off by circumstances.

If you don’t deal with your thoughts, your thoughts will bind you.

God’s word is the one standard for your thinking.

So pay attention to “what you are thinking”.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Change Your Thinking, Change Your Life
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, the key to life lies not in circumstances but in thinking.

Think wrongly and you fall into trouble; think rightly and you enter into victory.

Today God is inviting you: change your thinking, change your way of seeing, change your life.

When you begin to think God’s way, you will discover — there is a way in the wilderness, there are rivers in the desert, there is resurrection in the midst of death. The wilderness is still the wilderness, but now there is a road through it; the desert is still the desert, but now there are rivers in it; the tomb is still the tomb, but in front of it stands the Lord who said, “I am the resurrection and the life.”

All this change is not merely so that life will go a little more smoothly for us; it is so that Jesus may reign as King in our thinking, and so that Jesus may receive all the glory in our lives.

So from today, let us make a decision: I will no longer think by feelings; I will think by the truth.

keyVerses: “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” (Romans 10:17)
“For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith.” (1 John 5:4)
declarations: Lord Jesus, I choose to believe your word.
Whatever my circumstances, I will not dwell on the negative, and I will not accept the enemy’s lies.
I will think on the truth, on your promises and on your power.
Let my thinking be filled with faith.
By faith I will overcome the world.
In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare it. Amen!
practices: When problems come, go back to God’s word first
Deliberately reject negative and lying thoughts
Practise thinking with faith every day
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.
You know how easily our thinking is led around by our circumstances. Forgive us, Lord: so often we worry before we have prayed, and draw conclusions before we have searched your word.

Lord, renew our hearts and minds with your truth. Help us no longer to think by our feelings but by your word; no longer to be limited by the past, but to believe that you are still doing new things today. Give us strength, so that when the enemy’s lies come, we do not argue and do not accept them, but simply declare your word.
Holy Spirit, guide our thinking every day; let Jesus reign as King on the throne of our minds, and let all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: What recent situation has led your thinking around by the circumstances? Set beside “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17), which verse of God’s word could you put in its place as a new starting point for your thinking?

Recall a disappointment of the “if you would have been here” kind. As you read, “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing” (Isaiah 43:18–19a), in what matter are you willing to believe afresh that God can work in an entirely new way?

l132.subtitle: Thinking Rightly (Part 2): Circumstances Don’t Decide Whether You Overcome — How You Think Does

blog.title: It Isn’t Your Circumstances That Knock You Down

blocks.x: It’s your own thoughts that knock you down

The test results aren’t even back, and in your heart you’ve already passed a death sentence on yourself; your child is half an hour late home, and your mind has already run an entire disaster film; your manager glances at you one second too long, and you spend the whole afternoon wondering whether he’s about to let you go.
We often say people are knocked down by their circumstances. In fact, they aren’t. Very often, before circumstances have lifted a finger, our thoughts have already knocked us down.

God’s intention is not that your circumstances should decide your thinking, but that truth should lead your thinking. Scripture says, “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). Faith is not a feeling that appears out of nowhere; faith is the fruit that grows out of right thinking.
1. Right thinking isn’t optimism — it’s God-centredness

Many people assume that “right thinking” simply means positive thinking. It doesn’t. Optimism says, “I believe I can”; faith says, “I believe God can.” Optimism is cheering yourself on in the dark; right thinking is lifting your head in the dark and seeing that God is still seated as King.
Right thinking means returning to 321: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide; let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

Whoever thinks this way discovers a principle: truth is always greater than the facts. Facts pass away; truth does not pass away. Circumstances often say, “Impossible, too late, no hope”; but God’s word says, “Possible, not too late, God can do a new thing.”

Of the woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years, Scripture deliberately records one sentence: “for she said within herself, ‘If I just touch his garment, I will be made well’” (Matthew 9:21). Her healing did not begin with her hand; it began with her thinking.
2. Two things to cut off: the enemy’s words and past experience

Eve’s fall did not begin with an action; it began with a thought. First she “listened” to the serpent’s words, then she “looked” at the fruit, then she began to “think”, and only then did she “do”. Listen wrongly and you look wrongly; look wrongly and you think wrongly; think wrongly and you act wrongly.

Notice this: the serpent did not force the fruit into her mouth. Satan has no power to compel anyone to sin; his only skill is to “speak”. So the safest way is not to let the wrong voices in. When the Lord Jesus was tempted, he did not debate and did not explain; three times he said just one thing: “It is written.”

The other thing to cut off is the past. Martha and Mary said exactly the same sentence: “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.” They believed Jesus could heal the sick, because they had seen it; but they did not believe Jesus could raise the dead, because they had never seen it. Their thinking had a line drawn across it by experience.

But God says, “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing” (Isaiah 43:18–19a). Don’t define God by the past, and don’t limit God by experience.
3. Your thinking is the steering wheel

Your thinking is like a steering wheel, and your life is like a car. Set the direction right and the road is right; set the direction wrong and, however hard you press the accelerator, you only go wrong faster.

Twelve spies saw the same land of Canaan. Ten of them said they were “as grasshoppers”, but Caleb said, “We are well able to overcome it!” The difference was not in how tall the giants were but in what they saw themselves as in their own hearts.
Faith is not a feeling; it is choosing to believe God’s word. And that choice can be made afresh every morning.

Start today with three small things: when problems come, first ask, “What does God’s word say?”; the moment a negative thought appears, replace it with a declaration of God’s word; every day, choose a promise, think on it again and again, and declare it again and again.
When you begin to think God’s way, you will discover — there is a way in the wilderness, there are rivers in the desert, there is resurrection in the midst of death.
Reflection question
This week, which thought have you “let settle in”? Which verse of God’s word are you willing to put in its place, as the new starting point for your thinking?

brief12.title: Let Truth Lead Our Thinking
notes: Slide text:
Thinking Rightly (Part 2)
“So faith comes by hearing,
and hearing by the word of God.”
(Romans 10:17)
Key points:
1. Greet the congregation; announce the lesson title, “Let Truth Lead Our Thinking”, and the key verse, Romans 10:17.
2. Point out that this is Part 2 of “Thinking Rightly”, following on from the last lesson, “The Mind Is a Battlefield”.
3. Set the tone in one sentence: faith is not a feeling that appears out of nowhere; it is the fruit that grows out of right thinking.
4. Preview the four points: God-centredness, cutting off the enemy’s words, stepping beyond the past, the thinking of faith.

brief12.title: Introduction: Your First Reaction
notes: Slide text:
When things go wrong, what do you think first?
Worry? Fear? The worst outcome?
Not circumstances deciding your thinking,
but truth leading your thinking.
Key points:
1. Ask: when things go wrong, what is your first reaction? Let the listeners answer for themselves.
2. Everyday examples: test results not yet back, a child half an hour late home, a manager’s second glance.
3. Key line: very often, before circumstances have lifted a finger, our thoughts have already knocked us down.
4. Bring out the 321 insight: it is not events that change you; it is how you think that decides whether you overcome.

brief12.title: Key Verses and Background
notes: Slide text:
God’s word → hearing → thinking → faith → victory
Romans written around AD 56
“This is the victory that has overcome
the world: your faith.” 1 John 5:4
Key points:
1. Background: Romans, written around AD 56–57 by Paul in Corinth to the church in Rome.
2. Context: chapters 9–11 deal with Israel’s stumbling — not a lack of zeal, but a wrong mindset (Romans 10:2–3).
3. The chain: the word of Christ → hearing → faith → calling on him → salvation (Romans 10:13–17).
4. 1 John, written around AD 85–95 by John in Ephesus; “has overcome the world” is a completed tense in the original — the victory is already accomplished.

brief12.title: 1. Right Thinking Is God-Centred
notes: Slide text:
Not optimism, but God-centredness.
Optimism says: I believe I can.
Faith says: I believe God can.
Return to 321 — let Jesus be King.
Key points:
1. Clear up the misunderstanding: right thinking is not the same as positive thinking or optimism.
2. Contrast: optimism focuses on myself; right thinking focuses on God.
3. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide; the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.
4. Change the question: no longer “What am I going to do?” but “What would Jesus do? What does the Bible say?”

brief12.title: Truth Is Always Greater Than the Facts
notes: Slide text:
Circumstances say: impossible, too late.
God says: possible, not too late.
“Just say the word,
and my servant will be healed.” Matthew 8:8
Key points:
1. Definitions: the facts are the situation your eyes can see; truth is God’s never-changing word.
2. The centurion: an officer’s chain-of-command reasoning — he looked at the authority of the word (Matthew 8:8–10).
3. The woman with the bleeding: Scripture deliberately says “she said within herself” — healing began with her thinking (Matthew 9:21).
4. Supporting evidence from psychology: Aaron T. Beck’s automatic thoughts in the 1960s; Albert Ellis’s ABC model.
5. The change of perspective: from man’s to God’s, earthly to heavenly, temporary to eternal, worldly to godly.

brief12.title: 2. Don’t Dwell on the Enemy’s Words
notes: Slide text:
Listen wrongly → look wrongly → think wrongly → act wrongly
Eve’s fall began with a thought.
Don’t debate with Satan;
don’t let the lie in.
Key points:
1. Genesis 3: the serpent spoke first; Eve then looked, then thought, and only then acted.
2. The key: Satan has no power to compel anyone to sin; his only weapon is to “speak” (John 8:44).
3. Illustration: drop a drop of ink into clear water, and the water is already different.
4. The Lord Jesus’ example: three times “It is written” — not debating, only declaring (Matthew 4:4).
5. Martin Luther is commonly said to have put it: you cannot stop the birds flying over, but you can stop them building a nest.

brief12.title: 3. Don’t Be Limited by the Past
notes: Slide text:
“Don’t remember the former things…
I will do a new thing.” Isaiah 43:18–19
Martha: “If you would have been here.”
Different methods, the same God.
Key points:
1. Background: just before this, Isaiah 43 recalls the way through the Red Sea, then says, “Don’t remember the former things.”
2. Martha and Mary said the same sentence, “If you would have been here” — their faith stopped at the boundary of experience (John 11:21, 32).
3. Jesus’ order: not “see, then believe”, but “believe, and you will see” (John 11:40).
4. Three ways of healing leprosy: Naaman washing seven times, the Lord’s touch, ten men cleansed on the road.
5. Supporting evidence from psychology: Seligman and Maier’s learned helplessness (1967); neuroplasticity shows a new road can be worn in.

brief12.title: 4. The Thinking of Faith Brings Victory
notes: Slide text:
Thinking is the wheel, life is the car.
Right direction, right road.
Faith is not a feeling;
it is choosing to believe God’s word.
Key points:
1. Key verse: 1 John 5:4 — the key to victory is faith.
2. The lifeline: God’s word → hearing → thinking → faith → victory.
3. Illustration: thinking is the steering wheel; set the direction wrong and the harder you try, the further off you go.
4. Defining faith: the “assurance” and “proof” of Hebrews 11:1 are the language of property, not of emotion.
5. The contrast among the twelve spies: grasshopper thinking versus Caleb’s “well able to overcome” (Numbers 13:30, 33).

brief12.title: The 321 Insight
notes: Slide text:
Think on God’s word and faith is born;
think on circumstances and fear is born.
Change your mindset and your life changes;
humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan.
Key points:
1. Sum up how the Three Foundations, Two Core Values and the Goal take shape in our thinking.
2. The old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless: almost all negative thoughts revolve around a “self”.
3. The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry; life first, then relationships, then ministry.
4. The 920 practice and 235 relationships: thinking alone easily goes round in circles; when two or three think the truth through together, they overcome.

brief12.title: Practice for Daily Living
notes: Slide text:
First ask: what does God’s word say?
Replace negative thoughts with God’s word
Think on a promise every day
Eight stages: Information to Multiplication
Key points:
1. Read through the lesson’s three practices one by one, stressing “first ask what God’s word says”.
2. Replace rather than suppress: Psalm 119:11, “I have hidden your word in my heart.”
3. The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
4. Concrete action: copy three verses onto a card; when something happens, pause for three seconds first.

brief12.title: Closing and Call
notes: Slide text:
Think wrongly and you fall into trouble;
think rightly and you enter into victory.
A way in the wilderness, rivers in the desert,
resurrection in the midst of death.
Key points:
1. Return to the lesson’s conclusion: the key to life lies not in circumstances but in thinking.
2. Three “changes”: change your thinking, change your way of seeing, change your life.
3. Imagery: the wilderness is still the wilderness, but now there is a road through it; before the tomb stands the Lord who said, “I am the resurrection.”
4. Point to the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King in our thinking, let Jesus receive all the glory.

brief12.title: Response Prayer and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
I will no longer think by feelings;
I will think by the truth.
May the Lord’s peace guard your hearts
and minds — let Jesus be King.
Key points:
1. Lead the congregation in declaring together: I will no longer think by feelings; I will think by the truth.
2. A short response prayer: ask the Holy Spirit to renew our hearts and minds every day.
3. Blessing: may the Lord’s peace guard your hearts and minds (see Philippians 4:7).
4. Invitation: this week, find a spiritual companion to remind and pray for each other.
