1. The author is James, the Lord’s brother (Galatians 1:19; Acts 15:13), writing around AD 45–49.
2. The recipients were Jewish Christians scattered by persecution (James 1:1; Acts 8:1).
3. From the original: “drawn away” (exelkō) is luring prey out of its hole; “enticed” (deleazō) has “bait” at its root — Satan shows you only the bait, never the hook.
4. “Conceived” (syllambanō) and “produces” (apokyeō) are words of childbirth; James 1:18 uses the same word for God giving birth to us by the word of truth.
5. Summary: the theme of this passage is “two kinds of birth” — lust gives birth to sin and death; the word of truth gives birth to us as first fruits.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 133, entitled “Thinking Is a Process of Conceiving”. The subtitle is: managing your thoughts is managing the source of life.

Our key verses are James 1:14–15: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.”
Please hold one sentence in your heart to begin with: whatever is born today was conceived yesterday.

Brothers and sisters, picture a scene. In a delivery room, the nurse says to the mother, “Congratulations — your baby was born today.” That is quite true. But we all know this child did not begin today. He has been forming in his mother’s womb for two hundred and eighty days.

Life is like that too. We often hear people say, “How could he suddenly turn into this?” Brothers and sisters, I must tell you honestly: nothing happens suddenly. Whatever can be seen on the outside has long been growing to maturity on the inside.
Many people think the problem is what they did wrong. But God wants us to see a deeper layer: we don’t do wrong first; we think wrong first.

The author of this book is James, the brother of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh. He wrote it around AD 45 to 49, to Jewish believers scattered everywhere by persecution. They were suffering, and the easiest thing for them to do was to complain in their hearts.

James makes it very clear: the source of temptation is not God but our own lust. God uses the very same circumstances to test us, while lust uses them to tempt us; the difference is not in the circumstances but in the “thinking” inside.
The original is very vivid. “Drawn away” means luring prey out of its hole, and the root of “enticed” is “bait”. Brothers and sisters, Satan never shows you the hook; he only shows you the bait.
James uses a very striking metaphor — conception.
Our thinking is like a womb; a thought is like a seed. Whatever is planted in it is what will grow.
Brothers and sisters, there is no such thing as being “a little bit pregnant”. When a thought comes in and you take it in, the gestation has already begun.
Many people say, “I’m only thinking about it; I haven’t actually done anything.” But God says: you are already pregnant.
So please remember: thinking is not “no big deal”; thinking is “something happening right now”.
The Lord Jesus puts it even more directly: “everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart” (Matthew 5:28).
Notice the word “already”. Nothing has yet been done on the outside, but on the inside it is already complete.
Look at Eve again. The order in Genesis 3:6 is: saw, a delight to the eyes, to be desired — and only then took, ate, gave. Before her hand ever reached out, her heart had already reached out.

The psychiatrist Aaron Beck found that people do not first feel low and then have negative thoughts; first comes a chain of thoughts they are not aware of, and then the emotions catch up. That is the clinical version of the book of James.
There is a story in the Bible that plays out this process to the full.
John the Baptist said to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6:18). One sentence, and it fell into Herodias’ heart.
Scripture goes on: “Herodias set herself against him, and desired to kill him, but she couldn’t” (Mark 6:19).

Brothers and sisters, listen to these words — “but she couldn’t”. It was not that she did not want to; it was that she could not yet. Her actions were held back, but her thinking was not. So she kept thinking, and thinking.
Then the opportunity came. On his birthday Herod swore, “Whatever you shall ask of me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom” (Mark 6:23).
Half a kingdom lay before her. Herodias wanted none of it; she wanted only one head.
Why so extreme? Because once something carried for too long reaches its due date, reason has nothing more to say. She was not acting on impulse in that moment; in that moment she was giving birth.

So, brothers and sisters, behaviour is not sudden; it accumulates. Sin is not accidental; it is conceived. Don’t deal only with the wrong thing done; go back to the source and deal with the wrong thought thought.
So where do thoughts come from?
Thoughts don’t appear out of nowhere. Their source is what you see and what you hear.

The Lord Jesus said, “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light” (Matthew 6:22). And Proverbs says, “My son, attend to my words. Turn your ear to my sayings” (Proverbs 4:20).
What are you looking at every day? What are you listening to every day? That is deciding what kind of life you are carrying within.
Wrong seeing and hearing nurture the old self; right seeing and hearing nurture the new self.
Brothers and sisters, the Three Foundations of 321 line up exactly with our three entrances.

Jesus is my role model — this is the direction of the eyes; the focus is Jesus. The Bible is my standard — this is the content of the ears. The Holy Spirit is my guide — this is the renewal of the heart.

Paul says, “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Fix your eyes on the Lord, and you will become like the Lord.

So the key to victory is not struggling not to sin, but, at the source, not letting sin conceive. Those who try to stop it at the exit grow more and more weary; those who stand guard at the entrance find the going lighter and lighter.
Today there are five practices.
First, awareness: catch the first thought and ask, “Did this thought come from God?”

Second, exchange: don’t suppress it, and don’t let it run free either; replace lies with truth. The psychologist Daniel Wegner did the white bear experiment — the harder you try not to think of it, the more you think of it. That is why Paul speaks of bringing every thought “into captivity”; taking captive is not emptying, it is a change of master.
Third, cleansing: change your input. Fourth, let the Holy Spirit govern your thinking. Fifth, don’t make yourself king; ask instead, “If Jesus were me, how would Jesus think?”
Brothers and sisters, life is not lost in our behaviour; it is lost in our thinking.
The humble let God shine his light on their thinking; the proud protect their own ideas. Only humility can stop the wrong gestation; only selflessness can let Christ be formed within.
Paul says, “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19).
At this moment, either sin is taking shape in you, or Christ is. Today, admit one thought, hand it over, put a verse in its place, and find a spiritual companion to walk with you.
Let us pray together.

Lord, please govern my thinking. I will not let lust conceive within me; I will let Christ be formed in me. I reject every wrong thought; I choose to think on God’s word; I choose to look to Jesus, listen to Jesus and follow Jesus. I will surely be an overcomer.
May the Lord bless you, may Christ be formed in you; let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 133, entitled “Thinking Is a Process of Conceiving”, with the subtitle: managing your thoughts is managing the source of life.

Our key verses are James 1:14–15: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.”
Please hold one sentence in your heart to begin with: whatever is born today was conceived yesterday.

Brothers and sisters, picture a scene in your mind. In a delivery room, the nurse says to the mother, “Congratulations — your baby was born today.” That is quite true. But we all know this child’s life did not begin today; he has been forming in his mother’s womb for two hundred and eighty days. What we see today is simply the unseen process at last coming into view.

Life is like that too. We often see it in the news: someone who has always been gentle suddenly does something unbelievable; a co-worker who has served for years suddenly falls. People shake their heads and say, “How could he suddenly turn into this?”
Brothers and sisters, nothing happens suddenly. Whatever can be seen on the outside has long been growing to maturity on the inside.
Many people think the problem in life is “what I did wrong”. But God wants us to see a deeper layer: we don’t do wrong first; we think wrong first.
Life begins with “thinking”; and thinking is a process of gestation. Whatever you are thinking inside is what you will one day live out.

That is why changing a life does not start with changing behaviour; it starts with changing how we “think”. Behaviour is the fruit; thinking is the root. If you only prune the fruit, next year the same fruit will grow again.
321 puts it clearly: the old self is self-centred — it thinks about itself, conceives sin and brings death; the new self is selfless — it thinks about Jesus, conceives life and brings victory.

Let’s first get to know this book. Its author is James, the brother of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh. It was written around AD 45 to 49, and may well be one of the earliest books of the New Testament. Its recipients were Jewish Christians scattered everywhere by persecution. They had lost their property and were living as strangers in foreign places. Brothers and sisters, in a situation like that, the easiest thing for anyone to do is to complain in their heart.
So James is absolutely categorical: the source of temptation is not God but our own lust.
The original is very vivid. “Drawn away” means luring prey out of its hole, and the root of “enticed” is “bait”. Satan never shows you the hook; he only shows you the bait.
And a few verses later James says, “Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth.” The theme of this whole passage is two kinds of birth.
James uses a very striking metaphor — conception.
Our thinking is like a womb; a thought is like a seed. Whatever is planted in it is what will grow.

Brothers and sisters, there is no such thing as being “a little bit pregnant”. When a thought enters you, you either hand it back or you take it in; and once you have taken it in, the gestation has already begun.
What you constantly think about inside will not disappear by itself. It will only grow, accumulate, mature, and finally be born.
Many people say, “I’m only thinking about it; I haven’t actually done anything.” But God says: you are already pregnant.
The Lord Jesus puts it even more directly: “everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart” (Matthew 5:28).
Notice the word “already”. Nothing has yet been done on the outside, but on the inside it is already complete. Human courts begin their judgement with behaviour; God’s court begins with the thought.
The Lord also said, “For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries” (Matthew 15:19). Evil thoughts come first. Evil thoughts are the firstborn, and all the rest are their brothers.
Let us trace it back further, to humanity’s first fall.
“When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired… she took some of its fruit, and ate” (Genesis 3:6).

Count the verbs here: saw, delighted, desired, took, ate. The first three are all on the inside; only the last two are on the outside. Before Eve’s hand ever reached out, her heart had already reached out.

The generation before the Flood, Scripture sums up in a single sentence: “every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil” (Genesis 6:5). What God saw first was not their violence but their thinking. For the thinking is the factory; the behaviour is only the product.

Brothers and sisters, 321 says the fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The first stop is mindset, not ministry. Many people have the order reversed: rush into ministry first, while the mindset never moves at all. The result is a lot of activity on the outside, but no change on the inside.

Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2). This word “transformed” in the original is the same change as a caterpillar becoming a butterfly.

Brain science bears this out too. In 1949 the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed that neurons repeatedly active at the same time become connected. Think it once and you have walked across a lawn; think it a thousand times and it has become a tarmac road.
There is a story in the Bible that plays out the process of thoughts in gestation to the full.
John the Baptist said to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6:18). John said what ought to be said, and that one sentence fell into someone’s heart.
What Scripture records next is very important: “Herodias set herself against him, and desired to kill him, but she couldn’t” (Mark 6:19).
The original word behind “set herself against him” literally means holding something tightly inside, gripping it and never letting go. Brothers and sisters, that is precisely a picture of conception.
Listen to these words — “but she couldn’t”.

It was not that she did not want to; it was that she could not yet. Her actions were held back, but her thinking was not. So through those days of “couldn’t”, she kept thinking, and thinking, and thinking.
And what was the result? The thought began to gestate, the hatred began to build.

In 1991 the psychologist Susan Nolen-Hoeksema, who later taught at Yale, put forward her “response styles theory”, studying a habit called “rumination”: going over negative emotions again and again without taking any action. Her research showed that people in the habit of rumination have a markedly higher risk of later becoming depressed, and that rumination amplifies hostility.
Then the due date arrived.
On Herod’s birthday a banquet was held; the daughter came in and danced, and the king swore, “Whatever you shall ask of me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom” (Mark 6:23).

There is a detail here we must read carefully: it was Herod, not Herodias, who offered “half of my kingdom”. The daughter went out and asked her mother, and her mother’s answer was only a few words: the head of John the Baptist.

Brothers and sisters, do you see the terrible arithmetic? Half a kingdom lay before her, and she wanted none of it — only one head. For once something carried for too long reaches its due date, reason is gone. She was not acting on impulse in that moment; in that moment she was giving birth.
This is not an isolated case.

God said to Cain, “Sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it” (Genesis 4:7). The picture in the original is of a wild beast crouching at the doorway. God said you must rule over it, but Cain fed it instead, and in the very next verse there is blood in the field.

Absalom hated Amnon, and spoke to him neither good nor bad; and then Scripture says, “After two full years” (2 Samuel 13:23). Brothers and sisters, two years. Those were not two years of forgetting; they were two years of gestation.
321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. Herodias protected her marriage, Herod protected his face; they both won that banquet, and both lost themselves.
Brothers and sisters, we have already seen that thoughts conceive and thoughts give birth. So now we must ask an even more crucial question: where do thoughts come from?
Thoughts don’t appear out of nowhere. Thoughts have a source, and that source is what you “see” and what you “hear”.
Wrong seeing brings wrong thinking; right hearing brings life-giving intentions.
What are you looking at every day? What are you listening to every day? That is deciding what kind of life you are carrying within.
“The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness” (Matthew 6:22–23).

Notice that a lamp is not the thing you look at; a lamp is the thing that decides what you are able to see. And the context of these words: just before, “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also”; just after, “No one can serve two masters.” In other words, the eye is the door of the heart.
Job said, “I made a covenant with my eyes” (Job 31:1). He does not say, “I try hard not to think about it”; he deals with the entrance.
David said, “I will set no vile thing before my eyes” (Psalm 101:3).
Proverbs says, “My son, attend to my words. Turn your ear to my sayings… Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:20–23).
Look at the order: attend, turn your ear, keep them before your eyes, keep them in your heart, keep your heart. From the entrance outside to the source within.
The Hebrew word for “keep” means to guard or watch over, used of keeping watch over a city. Your heart is a city, and sentries must be posted at the city gate.
Paul says, “So faith comes by hearing” (Romans 10:17). Faith comes by hearing; and bitterness and fear come by hearing too.
In Numbers 13, twelve spies explored the land of Canaan. Forty days later they returned, bringing back the same grapes and the same city walls — yet two completely different reports.
Ten of the spies said, “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers” (Numbers 13:33). Who said they were grasshoppers? Not God — they came to see themselves that way by looking at themselves.
But Caleb said, “Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!” (Numbers 13:30).

Where was the difference? The ten spies looked at the giants and then looked back at God; Caleb looked at God and then looked back at the giants. And forty days of spying out the land bought them forty years in the wilderness.

Paul says, “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Fix your eyes on the Lord, and you will become like the Lord.
Brothers and sisters, today there are five practices.

First, awareness: catch the first thought. When negative thoughts, lustful thoughts or judgemental thoughts appear, ask yourself at once, “Did this thought come from God?” Awareness is not condemnation; awareness is standing guard.

Second, exchange: don’t suppress it, and don’t let it run free either; replace lies with truth. In 1987 the psychologist Daniel Wegner did the white bear experiment: he asked people not to think of a white bear for five minutes, and the harder they tried not to, the more often the white bear appeared.
So Paul speaks of “bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). Taking captive is not emptying; taking captive is a change of master.

Third, cleansing: change your input. Cut down on negative information, sexual stimulation and content that breeds comparison; increase Bible reading, worship and spiritual teaching. Here is a simple check: open your phone’s screen time for the past seven days and take a look. This is not law; it is a health check.

Fourth, walking with the Holy Spirit: pray every day, “Lord, govern my thinking.” Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Holding down a thought with willpower is like holding a ball under water with your hand — the moment you let go, it bounces back up.
Fifth, choosing selflessness: when “what I want” rises to the surface, stop, and ask instead, “If Jesus were me, how would Jesus think?”
Then go deeper with 321’s eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Brothers and sisters, let us set today’s message within the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations line up exactly with three entrances: Jesus is my role model, so the direction of my thinking is corrected; the Bible is my standard, so the content of my thinking is renewed; the Holy Spirit is my guide, so the power behind my thinking is exchanged.
The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — including in my thinking; let Jesus receive all the glory — including in my most hidden thoughts. The Goal: establish God’s system.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, wanting to take God’s place; humility is returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.
The person who most easily takes over your thoughts is exactly the “2” God has given you. Don’t fight your own thoughts alone: a thought kept hidden will grow; a thought spoken aloud will shrink.
Dear brothers and sisters, life is not lost in our behaviour; it is lost in our thinking.
Thinking is where everything begins; thinking is the gestation of life.
Today God is not asking you to try harder. God is inviting you: begin with your thinking, and return to him.
The humble let God shine his light on their thinking; the proud protect their own ideas. Only humility can stop the wrong gestation; only selflessness can let Christ be formed within.
Paul says, “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). At this moment, either sin is taking shape in you, or Christ is.
So this morning, please do four things: admit a thought you have been feeding for a long time, hand it over right now, put a verse in its place, and find a spiritual companion to walk with you.
Let us pray together.
Dear Heavenly Father, you search us and you know us. You see not only our actions but our thoughts.

Lord, we confess that there are thoughts within us that we have been feeding for a long time: bitterness, comparison, fear, judgement. We once thought it was only thinking and did no harm; today you have shown us that it is a pregnancy under way. Forgive us, and wash our hearts and minds clean with your precious blood.
Holy Spirit, take control of our thinking yourself. When we are weak and lose our ground, lift us up, and do not let us lie down in self-reproach.
Lord Jesus, be formed in us; it is no longer we who live, but you who live in us.
May the Lord bless you; let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Thought That Sits on the Edge of Your Bed at 3 a.m.
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Before we come to today’s lesson, let me first walk with you into a night that many of us know all too well.

It is three o’clock in the morning. You didn’t want to wake up, but you’re awake. The house is still, the family is asleep, and there’s no hint of daylight at the window. You lie there. Nothing has happened yet, and yet a thought is already sitting on the edge of the bed, waiting for you.

Maybe it’s something a colleague said during the day. You smiled it off at the time, but now it replays, line by line. Maybe it’s someone you have already forgiven three times. You thought that page was long turned, but now that hot, sour feeling rises in your chest again. Maybe it’s an image you shouldn’t have looked at twice. At the time you just scrolled past it, but now it floats back up on its own, sharp and clear.

You tell yourself: stop thinking about it, stop thinking about it, go to sleep. But the harder you tell yourself not to think about it, the clearer the thought becomes. You roll over, and it rolls over with you; you shut your eyes, and there it is, behind your closed eyelids.

Brothers and sisters, if you have ever had a night like that, then today’s lesson is something God has prepared especially for you.

In our last lesson we saw together a very deep truth: thinking is a process of conception. Whatever you are thinking inside will give birth to something. A thought doesn’t stay a thought; a thought grows. Desire doesn’t stay desire; desire conceives. Scripture puts it very plainly: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:14–15)

Once they grasped this truth, many brothers and sisters immediately asked a second question: “Pastor, I know that thoughts conceive. But I didn’t invite the thought — it came by itself. So what am I supposed to do?”

What a good question. If faith stops at “knowing”, people only end up blaming themselves more. Faith has to move on to “knowing what to do” before people can be set free.

So today God wants to take us a step further: the point is not only that “thoughts conceive”; the point is “how we manage the process of conception”.

The question has never been “Will we think?” As long as we’re alive, we will think. The question is this — how do we deal with the thoughts that have already appeared in our hearts?

Brothers and sisters, please remember this sentence; it is the key to the whole lesson today: some thoughts are not ones we actively choose, but we can choose — whether to let them stay, and whether to let them grow.

Whether a thought comes is not entirely up to you; whether it moves in is entirely up to you.

There is a saying, usually attributed to the Reformer Martin Luther, that puts it beautifully: “You cannot keep the birds from flying over your head, but you can keep them from building a nest in your hair.” A bird flying over takes a second; a bird building a nest takes a whole season. The flying over is called temptation; the nesting is called sin. God hasn’t asked you to chase every bird out of the sky. He asks you not to build them a nest on your head.

So how do we do it? Today Scripture gives us three very clear directions, the three teachings of this lesson. First, “I made a covenant with my eyes” (Job 31:1) — manage the entrance at the source. Second, all bitterness and wrath — “let [them] be put away from you” (Ephesians 4:31) — end the conception early. Third, “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2) — overcome by replacing, not merely by refusing.

Put these three passages side by side and a beautiful order appears: one at the entrance, one in the process, one at the root. Job deals with “what hasn’t come in yet”; Ephesians deals with “what has already come in”; Romans deals with “the whole system”.

So, brothers and sisters, today we need to see one thing: God doesn’t merely want you not to sin; God wants to renew the whole system of your thinking.

Not sinning is defence; renewing the system is rebuilding. God doesn’t just want to give you stronger willpower; he wants to give you a new mind. This is exactly the starting point of the fivefold change 321 speaks of — change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. Everything begins with the mindset; everything begins with our thoughts.

This morning, may the Holy Spirit himself come — not merely to prune the branches and leaves of our thinking, but to renew its roots.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Battlefields
sections.html:
To truly understand today’s message, let’s first stand at the historical scene of these three passages and hear the situations in which they were first spoken.

The first is Job 31:1.

The author of Job is unknown. It is generally thought to be one of the oldest books in the Bible, and its story is most likely set in the patriarchal period, around the time of Abraham. Job was a man of “the land of Uz”, and “this man was the greatest of all the children of the east” (Job 1:3).

Job 31 is the close of Job’s final defence. From chapter 29 to chapter 31, before God and before his three friends, he sets out his conduct item by item, like a “checklist of conscience”: how he treated his servants, how he cared for orphans and widows, his heart towards money, his heart towards his enemies.

What deserves our attention is the very first item on that list. It isn’t conduct, it isn’t money, it isn’t speech — it’s the eyes. “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1)

“Covenant” in Hebrew is berit, one of the most solemn words in the Old Testament: God made a covenant with Noah, with Abraham, and with Israel at Mount Sinai. A covenant is not a passing thought or a momentary feeling. It is a formal commitment, with witnesses, with terms, with a cost, one you can be held to account for.

Brothers and sisters, Job didn’t say, “I’ll try not to look.” He said, “I made a covenant with my eyes.” This isn’t a resolution; it’s a covenant.

The second is Ephesians 4:31.

Ephesians was written by the apostle Paul, generally dated between AD 60 and 62. It is one of the “prison letters” Paul wrote during his first imprisonment in Rome, addressed to the churches of Ephesus and the surrounding province of Asia.

Ephesus was a great city of the Roman province of Asia, home to the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. The city was not only idolatrous; it was steeped in sorcery. Acts records that when Paul preached in Ephesus, “Many of those who practiced magical arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. They counted their price, and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver.” (Acts 19:19)

In other words, the believers in the Ephesian church had been rescued out of an extremely polluted world of thought. That is why Paul says, “you no longer walk as the rest of the Gentiles also walk, in the futility of their mind” (Ephesians 4:17).

Then Paul gives a vitally important structure: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:22–24)

Look closely at these three verbs: put away, be renewed, put on. The middle one, “be renewed in the spirit of your mind”, is precisely the renewal of our thinking. And from 4:25 onwards Paul works this principle out point by point: don’t lie, speak the truth; don’t steal any more, but work honestly with your own hands; let no corrupt speech come out of your mouth, only what builds others up. Only then does he arrive at today’s verse (Ephesians 4:31).

So remember: Ephesians 4:31 is not an isolated moral command. It is one link in the whole “put off — put on” structure. And it is followed immediately by verse 32: “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” (Ephesians 4:32)

Where there is “putting away”, there must also be “putting on”. That is exactly what sets up today’s third teaching.

The third is Romans 12:2.

Romans is the most complete of Paul’s letters, generally dated around AD 56–57, very likely written from Corinth in Greece. Chapters 1 to 11 set out the truth of the gospel; from chapter 12 on he sets out the life of the gospel. Romans 12:1–2 is the hinge of that door:

“Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service. Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:1–2)

Here two Greek verbs form a beautiful contrast.

“Be conformed” is syschēmatizō, from the root schēma, meaning outward form, appearance, fashion. Think of a biscuit pressed out of a mould: its shape follows the mould.

“Be transformed” is metamorphoō, from the root morphē, meaning the essential form within. We know this word already — the biological term “metamorphosis” comes from it. When a caterpillar becomes a butterfly, nobody paints the caterpillar a new colour; it is remade entirely from the inside.

What’s more, both verbs are present-tense imperatives in the original. They aren’t one-off actions but continual ones: keep refusing to be pressed into the world’s mould; keep letting yourself be renewed and transformed.

“Mind” in the original is nous, the faculty of thought, understanding and judgement — in other words, the inner system by which a person “sees things”.

Brothers and sisters, put these three passages together and you see a complete picture:

Job guards the entrance — he doesn’t let the wrong seed in.

Paul in Ephesians deals with the process — what has already come in must be removed, not merely held down.

Paul in Romans renews the system — the whole mind remade by God, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly.

These three steps are today’s three teachings.

sections.heading: 3. Teaching One: What We See and Hear Sets the Odds of a Thought Being Conceived
sections.html:
The lesson says something very precise: the conception of a thought is not random; it has “odds”.

The more you see, the more likely conception becomes; the more you hear, the more easily it enters your thinking.

Brothers and sisters, read that slowly, twice. It turns something we always assumed was “beyond our control” into something we “can manage”. We often think thoughts are random, like the weather — something we can only endure. They aren’t. What springs up in your heart is closely tied to what you have been feeding it over the past few months.

The lesson uses the simplest picture of all: it’s like a field. Whatever seed you sow most of, that’s what grows most.

This is the very principle Scripture repeats again and again: “Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.” (Galatians 6:7–8)

Notice what Paul says first: “Don’t be deceived.” Why? Because sowing time is when we most easily deceive ourselves. A tiny seed drops into the ground, nothing on the surface changes, and we tell ourselves: “It’s only a quick look. Listening for a bit won’t hurt.” But harvest season will surely come. The soil doesn’t debate fairness with you; it simply, faithfully grows whatever you planted.

So the lesson puts it bluntly: if someone constantly takes in what is negative, complaining, comparing or lustful, wrong thoughts will naturally be conceived within them. If someone constantly takes in God’s word, his grace and Jesus, thoughts of life will naturally be conceived within them.

The Lord Jesus himself taught the same. He said: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23)

The Lord Jesus also said: “Take heed what you hear.” (Mark 4:24) Luke records it another way: “Be careful therefore how you hear.” (Luke 8:18)

Brothers and sisters, notice that the Lord Jesus didn’t say, “Be careful what you say.” He said, “Be careful how you hear.” Because hearing is the entrance; speaking is only the exit. Problems at the exit are always caused at the entrance.

Science makes this even clearer. The human optic nerve is made up of more than a million nerve fibres — the widest information channel into the brain. Your eye is not a window; it’s a conveyor belt, every second carrying things into your heart. And neuroscience has a famous principle, from the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb’s 1949 book “The Organization of Behavior”: neurons that fire together wire together. The more often you think two things together, the thicker, faster and more automatic that pathway in the brain becomes. So a person who constantly watches angry content finds anger rising without any reason at all — because he himself has worn that road into a motorway.

Brothers and sisters, which road are you paving in your heart every day?

That is why Job said: “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1)

Look at two details.

First, Job didn’t wait until he had sinned to deal with it; he set a boundary at the source. The Lord Jesus said: “but I tell you that everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart.” (Matthew 5:28) Job had already grasped the same spiritual principle: the battlefield isn’t the behaviour; the battlefield is the eyes.

Second, the word Job uses is “covenant”. Not “I’ll be careful”, not “I’ll do my best”, but a commitment with witnesses, a cost and accountability. Brothers and sisters, between us and our eyes there is usually only a “suggestion”, never a “covenant”. That’s why we keep losing ground, time after time.

David made the same covenant: “I will set no vile thing before my eyes” (Psalm 101:3). And he prayed: “Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things. Revive me in your ways.” (Psalm 119:37)

Psychology bears witness in the same direction. The process model of emotion regulation proposed in 1998 by the Stanford psychologist James Gross divides strategies for regulating emotion into two broad types: “antecedent-focused” and “response-focused”. Antecedent-focused strategies — choosing not to enter a situation, for example, or turning your attention elsewhere — happen before the emotion is fully formed; they work well and cost little. Response-focused strategies — forcing an emotion down once it has already surged — work poorly, cost a great deal, and drain a large amount of mental resources.

In other words, what scientific research has discovered is exactly what the Bible said three thousand years ago: dealing with things at the entrance is far, far easier than dealing with them at the exit.

Let me give you a picture. A waterworks doesn’t put most of its effort into your kitchen tap; it puts it into the intake. Brothers and sisters, your eyes and ears are the water intake of your life.

I have to be very honest: the challenge of this generation is far greater than in Job’s day. For Job to “look lustfully” he still had to lift his head and walk to the door. We lie in bed, flick a finger, and the filth of the whole world plays automatically — and it learns your preferences, getting more accurate the more you feed it.

So, brothers and sisters, the most urgent question today is not “Why do I have thoughts like this?” but —

What am I letting into my heart today?

This brings us to the 321 insight.

The selfless manage the entrance; the self-centred leave the entrance wide open, and in the end are ruled by sin.

Why? Because at the heart of the self-centred life is this: “I have the right to decide what I watch and what I listen to.” That sounds like freedom, but it is actually the greatest bondage. When you insist on that “right”, you hand yourself over to the hand that feeds you; and in the end, it isn’t you who decides what you think — it’s a system you don’t even know.

Selflessness doesn’t mean gouging out your eyes; selflessness means handing the sovereignty over your eyes back to God. The selfless person says: my eyes are not my own, my ears are not my own; they are the Lord’s. This is what it means to let Jesus be King — and his reign begins with reigning over my eyes.

321 says: the Bible is my standard. A standard isn’t a feeling; it’s a measuring rule. When I’m unsure whether I should watch something, the question isn’t “Does this count as sin?” but “Will this make God’s word clearer in my heart?”

321 also says: the Holy Spirit is my guide. Brothers and sisters, very often, before we tap, the Holy Spirit has already gently held us back once. That moment isn’t a struggle; it’s guidance. The first step to victory is often not a hard-fought battle but obeying that gentle nudge.

So the first step to victory is not struggle but choice.

sections.heading: 4. Teaching Two: When a Wrong Thought Appears, End the Conception Early
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, if we’re honest we all know one thing: even when we guard the entrance, things still get in.

Some come from what other people say, some float up from memory, and some are flaming arrows fired straight in by Satan. So when a wrong thought has already got in, what do we do?

The lesson points out that many people handle it in one of two wrong ways.

The first wrong way: letting it run. We think, “What harm can a bit of thinking do? Let it be.”

The second wrong way: suppressing it. We frantically tell ourselves not to think about it, grit our teeth, and push back with willpower.

Brothers and sisters, one of these is too loose and the other too tight, but the outcome is the same — failure.

First, the danger of letting it run. Scripture says: “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:15) This verse uses the language of childbirth: conceiving, bearing, growing to full size. A thought that lingers in your heart doesn’t stay the way it is. It grows.

Before the first murder in human history, God warned Cain: “If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.” (Genesis 4:7) Picture it: sin crouching at the door like a wild beast. It hasn’t come in yet; it’s waiting for you to open the door. God didn’t say, “You must put up with it.” He said, “You are to rule over it.”

Now, the futility of suppression. This is one of the lesson’s most precious reminders: dealing with a thought is not a matter of fighting it non-stop. Because the more you fight it, the more you are actually thinking about it.

Psychology has a famous experiment on this. In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner and his colleagues published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They asked participants to do something that sounds simple: for the next five minutes, don’t think of a white bear. The result? Those told “don’t think of a white bear” thought of white bears more often than those who weren’t told; and once the restriction was lifted, their white-bear thoughts even rebounded. Wegner called this the “rebound effect” of thought suppression.

Brothers and sisters, this research isn’t teaching us a new truth; it simply bears witness to Scripture: fighting with willpower is itself a form of constant attention. You can’t shine a searchlight on something and then order yourself not to look at the beam.

So God gives us a deeper, more precise principle: “deal with it”, don’t just “put up with it”.

What does Scripture say? “Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.” (Ephesians 4:31)

The word for “put away” in Greek is airō, meaning “to lift up, take away, remove, carry off”; it is used of carrying things away and lifting off a burden. When John the Baptist saw Jesus he said: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29) The “takes away” there is the same word.

So God doesn’t say “hold it down”; God says “put it away”.

When you hold it down, the thing is still in the house — it’s just been stuffed into a cupboard. When you put it away, you carry it out of the door. Holding it down takes constant effort; putting it away deals with it once and for all.

So in practice, how do we “put it away”? Scripture’s answer isn’t gritting our teeth; it’s three actions: confess it in the light, lay it at the foot of the cross, and put on what God gives. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9) And Ephesians 4:32 follows straight on: “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” (Ephesians 4:32)

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? The way to put away bitterness isn’t to stop thinking about the person who hurt you; it’s to forgive them. Forgiveness isn’t suppression; forgiveness is dealing with it. Forgiveness formally transfers that debt from your hands into God’s.

Next, the lesson gives us a vital principle of timing: if a wrong thought isn’t dealt with, it will grow, take shape and give birth to action. So the sooner you deal with it, the better.

The lesson uses a wonderful picture: it’s like a flame. At first it’s easy to put out; once it’s blazing, there’s a price to pay.

Firefighters often say the first few minutes of a fire are critical. In the first minute a small extinguisher can save a whole building; the same extinguisher at the tenth minute can only help you get out faster. The fire hasn’t got worse; it has just got bigger.

It’s like tooth decay. At first it’s a small dark spot, and the dentist can fill it in five minutes. If you put it off — “It doesn’t even hurt” — by the time it does hurt, you need a root canal and a crown, and if you keep putting it off, the tooth has to come out.

So here is a spiritual principle; hold on to it firmly:

The earlier you deal with a thought, the smaller the cost; the later you deal with it, the greater the cost.

Scripture says: “lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us” (Hebrews 12:1). Notice the words “so easily entangles”. Sin doesn’t bind you with one iron chain all at once; it wraps you thread by thread. The first thread you can snap with a tug; by the hundredth thread, you can’t move.

Brothers and sisters, that very second, the moment a thought first pops up, is the moment you have the most power. If you turn to the Lord then, the cost is almost nothing.

Here again we come to the 321 insight.

First, humility overcomes pride. What is pride in dealing with our thoughts? It’s “I can hold this down myself.” The proud won’t admit there is anything inside them that needs to be put away; they want to tough it out alone, because admitting it means losing face. The humble, the moment they notice something wrong, go straight to God and say: Lord, there is bitterness in me; please take it away. Scripture says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (1 Peter 5:5) So you see, those who deal with things early are always the humble.

Second, rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Relying on the brain and ourselves is a one-man tug of war with Satan on the other end of the rope: the harder you pull, the harder he pulls. Relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit is turning around, taking refuge, putting your hand in the Lord’s. Scripture says: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:7) Look carefully at the order: first submit to God, then resist the devil. Get the order backwards, and you’re fighting a battle without the Lord.

Third, the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, and finally with others. When a wrong thought appears, the first thing isn’t to phone someone and have it out, nor to give yourself a good scolding, but to come back before God. Once your relationship with God is set right, your relationship with yourself becomes settled; once you’re settled with yourself, there’s a way forward with others. Reverse the order and usually pride provokes pride, and both sides lose.

Brothers and sisters, when the flame first catches, don’t look anywhere else. Turning to the Lord is that bucket of water.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Three: True Victory Comes by “Replacing”, Not by “Refusing”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, now we come to the most crucial part of today’s lesson, and the most important strategy in spiritual warfare.

The lesson says: don’t just refuse wrong thoughts; “replace” them with right ones.

Why? The lesson gives a very precise reason: a person can only focus on one thought at a time. When you are thinking about what is “right”, you naturally won’t be thinking about what is “wrong”.

Psychology has been studying this for more than half a century. In 1958 the British psychologist Donald Broadbent proposed his famous filter theory of attention: at every moment our senses receive a flood of information, but the channel through which it enters awareness and is processed in depth is very narrow. Later research kept revising the details, but one conclusion has never been overturned — attention is a limited resource; you cannot give two things your full focus at the same time.

More interesting still, after the white-bear experiment Wegner also found that instead of telling people “don’t think about it”, giving them something specific and different to think about works markedly better. He called this method “focused distraction”.

Brothers and sisters, do you see? Psychology went the long way round and finally arrived where Scripture had been standing all along.

What does Scripture say? “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

The lesson has a beautiful line, and I’d like you to write it down: renewal is not emptying; renewal is replacing.

Brothers and sisters, this matters enormously. Because emptying alone is dangerous.

The Lord Jesus told a parable that should make us tremble: “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and doesn’t find it. Then he says, ‘I will return into my house from which I came out,’ and when he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order. Then he goes, and takes with himself seven other spirits more evil than he is, and they enter in and dwell there. The last state of that man becomes worse than the first.” (Matthew 12:43–45)

Notice those three descriptions: empty, swept, put in order. The house wasn’t dirty; it had even been done up. It had just one problem — it was empty. It had no master.

Brothers and sisters, so many people’s repentance stops at “swept clean”. They give up a habit, delete a few apps, cut off a few relationships — and then what? The inside sits empty. And three months later, what comes back is more, and worse, than what left.

So renewal isn’t emptying the heart; renewal is having a new Master move in.

The lesson gives an example close to all of us: when there is “resentment” inside you, don’t keep thinking, “I mustn’t hate.” Because you’re still thinking about “hate”. The right way is to turn to thinking about “God’s love”, to meditate on “how God has accepted me”. As love grows more and more, hate naturally loses its place.

This is just what Paul writes at the end of the same chapter: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” (Romans 12:21)

Notice: it isn’t “overcome evil with nothing”; it’s “overcome evil with good”. Evil isn’t driven out by a vacuum; evil is crowded out by good.

Paul gives us a very concrete replacement list: “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8)

“Think about” in the original is logizomai, meaning “to reckon, to weigh up, to keep turning something over in your mind”. Paul didn’t say, “Don’t think about bad things.” He said, “Think about these things.” He gives us a list of what to think about, not a list of what we mustn’t.

Colossians puts it even more directly: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2) First set your mind on things above, and only then not on things on the earth. The order is the strategy.

Let me give you a few pictures.

The first is darkness. There’s something fascinating in physics: darkness is not a thing. There are photons, but there are no “dark-ons”. Darkness has no mass, no speed, no particles; darkness is simply the absence of light. So you can never sweep darkness out of a room. You can’t sweep it with a broom or carry it out in a bucket. You can do only one thing — switch on the light.

This is exactly what the lesson says: when the light comes, darkness leaves of its own accord.

Scripture says: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.” (John 1:5) And again: “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.” (1 John 1:5) Brothers and sisters, you don’t need to negotiate with the darkness; you only need to let the light in.

The second picture is a glass of muddy water. How do you make muddy water clear? Do you pick out the mud grain by grain, or do you put the glass under the tap and let clean water keep flowing in and spilling over? God’s word is that living water.

At the opening of Book One of his Confessions, Augustine wrote a line that has been repeated for sixteen hundred years: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” There is a place in the human heart that only God can fill. If you don’t let God move in, something else will.

This is spiritual victory: not by willpower, but by the replacement of one life with another.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to this distinction. Willpower is me trying to out-muscle sin; the replacement of life is Christ living in me.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Paul used the same strategy against the desires of the flesh: “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16) He didn’t say, “Hold down your lusts with all your might, and then you’ll be able to walk by the Spirit.” He said the reverse — walk by the Spirit, and the lusts naturally fall behind. No one can walk in two directions at once.

Here the 321 insight comes into view.

The lesson says: rely on the heart and the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and life is renewed naturally; rely on the brain and fight in your own strength, and you are far more likely to get stuck in a loop.

Those who rely on the brain and themselves have their focus on “that sin”; those who rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit have their focus on Jesus. 321 says it very clearly: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. And now we add one more: not that sin either.

Because if you stare at sin, sin grows bigger; if you fix your eyes on Jesus, Jesus fills you.

321 also says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. We empty ourselves not in order to stay empty, but in order to be filled by God. This is the spiritual principle behind renewal and replacement. The old self is self-centred, so it keeps clinging to its own ideas, its own rights, its own wounds; the new self is selfless, so it is willing to let the thoughts of Christ replace its own.

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5)

This is why 321 puts “Jesus is my role model” first among the Three Foundations. Victorious thinking isn’t a set of techniques; it’s a Person — the mind of Christ, living in you.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: God’s System Begins with Our Thoughts
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, put today’s three teachings back into the framework of 321 and you’ll see a complete picture.

The Three Foundations correspond exactly to today’s three teachings.

Jesus is my role model. When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, he didn’t debate with Satan, nor did he grit his teeth and suppress it. Three times he said, “It is written…” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10) He replaced the enemy’s words with God’s words. That is the role model for “replacing”.

The Bible is my standard. The standard isn’t whether I feel something is all right; the standard is what God’s word says. The psalmist says: “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.” (Psalm 119:11) Notice that hiding it in the heart is done before sinning, not after.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. “Walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16) The renewal of our thinking isn’t a self-improvement project; it’s the work the Holy Spirit does within.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, the truest battlefield for letting Jesus be King isn’t the pulpit; it’s that thought no one else sees. A person can let Jesus reign as King at church, and at three in the morning let bitterness reign. True kingship sits on the throne of our thoughts. And when others see the change in us, we get the chance to say: it isn’t that I’ve become better; it’s Jesus living in me. That is letting Jesus receive all the glory.

The Goal: establish God’s system.

Where does a system begin? A system begins with mindset. A family’s system is how the whole family thinks; a church’s system is how everyone in it thinks. So when God sets out to establish his system, he will surely begin by renewing our minds. Today’s lesson isn’t a psychology class; it is God preparing, for the last days, a people whose thinking has been renewed.

The fivefold change is in today’s message too.

Change of mindset — I understand now: whether a thought comes is not up to me; whether it moves in is up to me.

Change of life — I no longer rely on suppressing things myself; I let Christ live in me.

Change of daily living — my phone, my eyes and my ears begin to have a new order.

Change of relationships — bitterness is put away, forgiveness comes in, and relationships come alive.

Change of ministry — only someone whose thinking is clean can become a blessing to others.

The shift in perspective is in today’s message too.

From man’s perspective to God’s: man says, “What harm can a bit of thinking do?” God says, “the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin.”

From the earthly to the heavenly: man says, “Everyone’s watching it.” God says, “Set your mind on the things that are above.”

From the temporary to the eternal: the pleasure of that one look lasts a few seconds; its consequences may last for years.

From the worldly to the godly: the world feeds you “You deserve it”; God says, “whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are pure… think about these things.”

Next, the 920 practice.

920 says: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; with them we practise living out the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, see how perfectly today’s message fits 920. What is to be put away? Bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry and slander. What is to be put on? Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Exchange them one for one: bitterness for love, wrath for kindness, anger for patience, outcry for peace, slander for goodness. That is replacing, not refusing.

And best of all — you cannot “strive” to bear fruit. Fruit grows out of life; it isn’t squeezed out by willpower. “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Finally, 235 relationships.

Renewing our thinking is a road that’s hard to walk alone. 235 says: become a “2” with a selfless person — a spiritual companion; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Brothers and sisters, if you have a spiritual companion you can honestly tell, “This week I failed twice in this area,” then the moment those words are spoken, the darkness has already lost half its power. Scripture says: “But all things, when they are reproved, are revealed by the light, for everything that reveals is light.” (Ephesians 5:13) The battle of the mind is fought in secret, and the light very often shines in through a spiritual companion.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Renewing and Replacing Our Thoughts
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five practices. Let’s take them one at a time and deepen each with the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice one: managing the entrance — choosing what I see and hear today.

Every day, choose deliberately: less contact with negative, lustful and comparing content; more contact with God’s word, worship and testimonies. Begin by lowering the odds of wrong thoughts at the source.

What does that look like in practice? Set yourself three boundaries, and write them down. For example: when you wake in the morning, read one verse of God’s word before you turn on your phone; after a certain time at night, the phone doesn’t come into the bedroom; unfollow the two or three accounts that always leave your heart feeling sour and dark.

Practising the eight stages: Information is hearing today that “what we see and hear sets the odds of conception”; Revelation is the Holy Spirit showing you what you are actually being fed; Conviction is admitting before God that this is true, without defending yourself; Implementation is unfollowing those two accounts today.

Practice two: noticing in the moment — recognising wrong thoughts.

When bitterness, irritation, lust or judgement appears, notice it at once and don’t let it develop any further. Ask yourself: “Is this from God?”

Brothers and sisters, form a habit: the moment you notice your heart “heating up” or “going dark”, immediately call out in your heart, “Lord!” No long prayer — just that one word. That is the bucket of water when the flame first catches.

Practising the eight stages: Evaluation means spending three minutes each evening looking back — at what moment today was I too slow to notice? Where was I? Who was I with? What had I just been looking at? Evaluation isn’t condemning yourself; it’s tracing the enemy’s line of attack. David’s prayer is the best evaluation of all: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Practice three: replacing thoughts — exchanging error for truth.

Don’t fight the wrong thought; turn directly to the right one. For example: with resentment, turn to meditating on God’s love; with anxiety, turn to declaring that God reigns. Fill your thoughts with truth.

I suggest you prepare a “replacement list” and put it somewhere you’ll see it: when bitter, read Ephesians 4:32; when anxious, read Philippians 4:6–7; when tempted by lust, read Philippians 4:8; when you feel worthless, read Romans 8:31–39.

Practising the eight stages: Correction. The first time, you may find you can’t even get to your replacement list in time, because the thought comes too fast. That’s all right — correct it. Shorten the verse to a single line, short enough to say in three seconds. Correction isn’t failure; correction is the road to maturity.

Practice four: meditating on Scripture — letting God’s word take the lead.

Each day choose one verse to ponder and declare again and again, letting God’s word be “conceived” in your thoughts so that life grows out of it naturally.

Brothers and sisters, this is the most beautiful contrast of the day. In our last lesson we saw: desire conceives and gives birth to sin. Today we see: God’s word conceives too, and gives birth to life. Your heart will always conceive something; the only question is — whom do you let move in?

Scripture says: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.” (Joshua 1:8)

The word “meditate” in Hebrew is hagah, which originally means to murmur, to mutter under your breath, like the cooing of a dove. It isn’t reading something quickly; it’s turning it over and over in your mouth and keeping it in your heart.

Practising the eight stages: Repetition. One verse read for seven days has more power than seven verses read for one day each. Repetition is the only road by which truth sinks from the head down into the heart.

Practice five: selfless surrender — letting Jesus hold sovereignty over my thoughts.

When “what I want” rises up, stop and ask: “If Jesus were me, how would he think?” Then choose to obey, rather than let things run.

Brothers and sisters, this practice is the root of the other four. Who is managing the entrance? Who does the replacing? In the end it all comes back to one question — who is sitting on the throne of my thoughts?

Practising the eight stages: Multiplication. Once you have walked this road for a while, go and find someone and pass on what you’ve learned. Find a spiritual companion too, and ask each other: “This week, what has been conceiving in your heart?” Multiplication is the most solid step of all — because whatever you teach others, you will live out first yourself.

“for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:4–5)

“Bringing into captivity” is the language of war. Brothers and sisters, your mind is territory God has bought back. Rise up and take it back.

sections.heading: 8. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, at the very end the lesson gives us four short but powerful reminders. Let me read them to you one at a time.

First, thoughts are not the surface of the problem; thoughts are the root of the problem.

We often spend a lifetime pruning branches and leaves: I said the wrong thing, so I apologise; I did something badly, so I put it right. But if the root isn’t touched, the same branches will grow back next year. The Lord Jesus said: “For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual sins, thefts, false testimony, and blasphemies.” (Matthew 15:19) Evil thoughts come first; everything else follows.

Second, don’t wait until the behaviour shows before you repent; turn the moment the thought appears.

The Greek word for repentance is metanoia, which literally means “a change of mind”. True repentance has never started with behaviour; it starts with thought. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

Third, don’t strain to drive out the darkness; let the light in. When the light comes in, darkness leaves of its own accord.

Fourth, the humble are willing to let God adjust their thinking; the proud insist on their own ideas.

Brothers and sisters, this is the line that cuts deepest today. Why won’t a person change their thinking? Not because they don’t understand, but because that idea is “mine”. What the self-centred life clings to is often not money or power, but “my opinion”; letting go of an opinion is harder than letting go of money. That is why the lesson says: humility brings renewal; selflessness brings freedom.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. This law holds just as true inside our own heads: the prouder you are of your own ideas, the more tightly they bind you; the humbler you are before God, the freer you become.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, today we have seen together that your thoughts are not beyond your control; your thoughts are something you can choose.

You can’t decide whether a thought will come, but you can decide whether it stays.

What God has given us today is a road to victory. It isn’t the road of suppressing or fighting; it is the road of renewing and replacing.

When you let God’s word in, when you let Jesus fill your thoughts, you’ll find two wonderful things happening at once: sin no longer has room, and life grows naturally.

Brothers and sisters, notice that word “naturally”. Holiness isn’t squeezed out; it grows. An apple tree doesn’t have to grit its teeth to produce apples; it only needs to be joined to its roots and to have sunlight and water. “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit.” (John 15:5)

So this morning I want to give you three calls.

First, the call at the entrance. Today, like Job, make a covenant with your eyes. Don’t just make a resolution; make a covenant before God.

Second, the call to act early. That bitterness you’ve been holding on to for three years, that thought you assumed would one day disappear by itself — bring it to the Lord today and say: Lord, please take it away.

Third, the call to replace. Today, choose one verse of God’s word and let it live in your heart for a whole week. Stop shouting at the darkness — go and switch on the light.

May we walk this road all our lives: conceiving no sin, conceiving only Christ.

Let us live out the selfless life and let Jesus live in us; let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: Job 31:1
“I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1)
Ephesians 4:31–32

“Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice. And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” (Ephesians 4:31–32)
Romans 12:2
“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)
declarations: In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare:
My thoughts will be renewed by God; my mind will be transformed by the truth.
I reject every wrong thought; I will not let sin conceive within me.
I will fill my thoughts with God’s word; I will let God’s love replace all bitterness.
Jesus reigns as King within me; the Holy Spirit guides my thoughts.
I live in the new self; I live in victory.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
practices: Manage the entrance: choose what I see and hear today
Notice in the moment: recognise wrong thoughts
Replace my thoughts: exchange error for truth
Meditate on Scripture: let God’s word take the lead
Surrender selflessly: let Jesus hold sovereignty over my thoughts
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you that this morning you have not only reminded us to be careful with our thoughts, but have clearly shown us the road to victory.

Lord, we confess that we often leave the entrance wide open, and then often try to suppress things in our own strength; struggling and failing, struggling and failing, until we are worn out. Today we are willing to take a different road.
Help me to make a covenant with my eyes, and a covenant with my ears. Shine your light on me, and let me see what I am actually being fed.
Lord, the bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry and slander already inside me, and all malice — I will no longer hold them down. I lay them one by one at the foot of your cross; please take them away.
Replace my hatred with your love, my anxiety with your peace, the enemy’s voice with your word. Lord, please come in, for when the light comes, darkness leaves of its own accord.
Jesus, reign as King on the throne of my thoughts. All my life, may I conceive no sin, but conceive only Christ.
May all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
discussion: Job said: “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1) In your life right now, which entrance most needs a “covenant”? Your phone, your eyes, your ears, or a particular conversation? What specific boundary are you willing to set today?

Paul said: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) Share one wrong thought that keeps coming back to you most often, and together find a verse that can “replace” it, to meditate on every day this week.

blog.title: Thoughts Will Come

blocks.x: But you can decide whether they stay
Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 134 · Blog post
It is three o’clock in the morning. You didn’t want to wake up, but you’re awake.

Nothing has happened yet, and yet a thought is already sitting on the edge of the bed, waiting for you. Maybe it’s something said during the day; maybe it’s someone you thought you had long since forgiven.
You tell yourself: stop thinking about it, go to sleep. But the harder you tell yourself not to think about it, the clearer it becomes.
If you have ever had a night like that, this article is for you.
Whether a thought comes isn’t up to you; whether it moves in is
Thinking is a process of conceiving. Scripture says, “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death” (James 1:15).
The problem is that very often we didn’t invite the thought in.
There is a saying, usually attributed to Martin Luther, that puts it beautifully: you cannot keep the birds from flying over your head, but you can keep them from building a nest in your hair.
A bird flying over takes a second; a bird building a nest takes a whole season. The flying over is called temptation; the nesting is called sin.

So the first step to victory is not struggle but choice. Job said, “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1). Notice that he didn’t say, “I’ll try not to look”; he made a “covenant”. He didn’t wait until he had sinned to deal with it; he set a boundary at the source.
The more you see, the more likely conception becomes; the more you hear, the more easily it enters your thinking. It’s like a field: whatever seed you sow most of, that’s what grows most.
Suppression doesn’t work — the more you fight it, the more you think about it
Many people have only two ways of handling wrong thoughts: letting them run, or holding them down. One is too loose and the other too tight, but the outcome is the same.

In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner published his famous “white bear experiment” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology: he asked people not to think of a white bear for five minutes. The result was that those told not to think of it thought of white bears more often; and once the restriction was lifted, the thoughts even rebounded.
This is exactly what Scripture told us long ago: fighting with willpower is itself a form of constant attention.
So God doesn’t say “hold it down”; he says “put it away”: “Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice” (Ephesians 4:31).
What’s more, the earlier you deal with it, the smaller the cost. When the flame first catches, a cup of water is enough; once it’s blazing, there’s a price to pay.
True victory comes by replacing, not by refusing
Here is the most crucial line of all: renewal is not emptying; renewal is replacing.

The Lord Jesus told a parable that should make us tremble: an unclean spirit returns to the house it left, finds it empty, swept and put in order, and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself (Matthew 12:44–45). The house wasn’t dirty. It had just one problem — it was empty.

So when there is resentment inside you, don’t keep thinking, “I mustn’t hate”, because you are still thinking about hate. Turn instead to meditating on God’s love. As love grows more and more, hate naturally loses its place.
Darkness is not a thing; darkness is simply the absence of light. You can’t sweep darkness out of a room with a broom; you can only switch on the light.
When the light comes, darkness leaves of its own accord.
This is spiritual victory: not by willpower, but by the replacement of one life with another. It isn’t that I’ve become better; it’s Jesus living in me.
May we walk this road all our lives: conceiving no sin, conceiving only Christ.
Reflection question: Today, which “entrance” do you most need to make a covenant over? Which verse of God’s word will you choose to replace the thought that keeps coming back?

“Be transformed by the renewing of your mind”

Key points:

brief12.title: The Thought on the Edge of the Bed
