brief12.title: A Great Promise Written in Prison
notes: Slide text:
Paul in chains, yet thinking without limits
“Exceedingly abundantly …
according to the power that works in us”
(Ephesians 3:20)
Key points:
1. Ephesians was written by Paul during his first imprisonment in Rome, c. AD 60–62.
2. In Ephesians 3:1 and 4:1 he calls himself “the prisoner”; his body was chained, his thinking was not.
3. Ephesus had the temple of Artemis; believers were surrounded by an idol-worshipping system of thought.
4. “Works” is the Greek energeō, root of “energy”, also used in Philippians 2:13.

brief12.title: Receiving Is Not Fulfilment
notes: Slide text:
“Ask, and it will be given you”
(Matthew 7:7) is receiving
“Exceedingly abundantly above all”
(Ephesians 3:20) is fulfilment
Key points:
1. Matthew 7:7 speaks of “receiving”; Ephesians 3:20 speaks of “fulfilment”.
2. Receiving is not fulfilment; in between lies a process of carrying the promise.
3. “Exceedingly abundantly” is hyperekperissou in the original: beyond the very limit.
4. Ask: has God’s promise to you stopped at receiving, or is it moving towards fulfilment?

brief12.title: The Picture of Pregnancy
notes: Slide text:
Receiving a promise is like conceiving
Doubting and giving up is like miscarriage
Keep thinking with faith
and the promise grows to fulfilment
Key points:
1. The lesson’s pregnancy picture: conceiving is receiving; giving birth is fulfilment.
2. Doubting, giving up and looking only at circumstances amount to a spiritual miscarriage.
3. James 1:14–15: lust conceives and bears sin; thoughts of faith conceive too.
4. Whichever thought you feed is the one that grows.

brief12.title: Abraham Thought with Faith

“Fully assured that what he had promised,

he chose to think with faith
Key points:
1. Romans 4:19–21: he considered his body as good as dead, yet was fully assured.
2. “Fully assured” is plērophoreō in the original: filled to overflowing.
3. Genesis 15:5: God told him to count the stars; the night sky became daily promise meditation.
4. Hebb’s 1949 principle and Maguire’s 2000 study of London taxi drivers.

brief12.title: One Thought Brings a Miracle

First think, then act, then receive

1. John 13:2: “put into the heart” is ballō in the original — to throw, to cast in.

2. Give two pairs of contrasting thoughts and let the brothers and sisters find themselves in them.
3. What decides a life is not big events but the thoughts no one sees.
4. Big events don’t happen every day, but thoughts happen every minute.

brief21.title: Thinking Is No Small Thing
notes: Slide text:
Thinking is a spiritual tool
of tremendous power
How you think decides how you live
and whether God can work in you
Key points:
1. Many people value prayer but neglect their thinking.
2. Ephesians 3:20 sets “ask” and “think” side by side; God also works through what you think.
3. Illustration: thinking is the soil, prayer the seed; if the soil is wrong, the seed struggles to bear fruit.
4. Pascal’s “Pensées”: man is a thinking reed.

brief21.title: A Great Promise Written in Prison
notes: Slide text:
Paul imprisoned in Rome, c. AD 60
“Exceedingly abundantly …
according to the power that works in us”
(Ephesians 3:20)
Key points:
1. Paul’s first imprisonment in Rome, c. AD 60–62; one of the prison letters.
2. Ephesians 3:1 and 4:1: he calls himself a prisoner; his body was chained, his thinking was not.
3. Ephesus had the temple of Artemis (one of the Seven Wonders); Acts 19:19, books burned worth fifty thousand pieces of silver.
4. “Works” is energeō in the original; Ephesians 3:20 and Philippians 2:13 use the same word.

brief21.title: Receiving Is Not Fulfilment
notes: Slide text:
“Ask, and it will be given you”
(Matthew 7:7) is receiving
“Exceedingly abundantly above all”
(Ephesians 3:20) is fulfilment
Key points:
1. Matthew 7:7 is “receiving”; Ephesians 3:20 is “fulfilment”.
2. “Exceedingly abundantly” is hyperekperissou in the original: beyond the very limit.
3. “Think” is noeō; its noun nous is the “mind” of Romans 12:2.
4. Ask: has God’s promise stopped at receiving, or is it moving towards fulfilment?

brief21.title: Pregnancy and Miscarriage
notes: Slide text:
An answered prayer is like conceiving
Doubting, giving up, eyeing circumstances
is like a miscarriage along the way
The key is how you think
Key points:
1. The lesson’s picture: conceiving is receiving; giving birth is fulfilment.
2. In between, the life must be carried; doubting, giving up and eyeing circumstances amount to a miscarriage.
3. James 1:14–15: lust conceives and bears sin; thoughts of faith conceive too.
4. Whichever thought you feed day by day is the one that grows.

brief21.title: Abraham Thought with Faith
notes: Slide text:
“Fully assured that what he had promised,
he was also able to perform” (Romans 4:21)
God told him to count the stars (Genesis 15:5)
The night sky became daily meditation
Key points:
1. Romans 4:19–21: he considered his body as good as dead, yet was fully assured.
2. “Fully assured” is plērophoreō in the original: filled to overflowing.
3. Genesis 15:5, counting the stars: through twenty-five years of waiting he meditated on the promise daily.
4. It isn’t that he had no pressure; under pressure he chose to think with faith.

brief21.title: Heart or Brain?
notes: Slide text:
Heart, thinking in faith → promise carried
Brain, analysing circumstances → doubt
Rely on the heart and be glad; the brain, and be troubled
Out of the heart is the wellspring of life
Key points:
1. 321 Insight: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves.
2. Hebb, 1949, “The Organization of Behavior”: neurons that fire together wire together.
3. Maguire’s 2000 study: London taxi drivers had a larger rear hippocampus.
4. Proverbs 4:23: out of the heart is the wellspring of life.

brief21.title: One Sentence from the Woman with the Bleeding
notes: Slide text:
Twelve years, all spent, only worse
“She said within herself, ‘If I just
touch his garment, I will be made well’ ”
(Matthew 9:21)
Key points:
1. Matthew 9:20–21; Mark 5:26: she had spent all she had and only grew worse.
2. Leviticus 15: a woman with a discharge was unclean; she lost her health and her relationships.
3. By her circumstances she should have despaired, yet she spoke a sentence of faith in her heart.
4. “Said within herself” is imperfect tense in the original: she kept saying it all the way.

brief21.title: First Think, Then Act, Then Receive
notes: Slide text:
“Your faith has made you well”
(Matthew 9:22)
The crowd pressed on him; only one
touched him with a thought of faith
Key points:
1. Matthew 9:22: “Daughter, cheer up! Your faith has made you well.”
2. The order: first think, then act, finally receive; the miracle began in her thinking.
3. Mark 5:31: the crowd pressed against him; only one touched his power.
4. Application: many hear the word; those who receive are the ones who first say in their hearts, “It will surely be fulfilled.”

brief21.title: A Thought Thrown into Judas’s Heart
notes: Slide text:
“The devil having already put
into the heart of Judas … to betray him”
(John 13:2)
A thought arriving is not sin
Key points:
1. John 13:2: “put into the heart” is ballō in the original — to throw, to cast in.
2. A thought being thrown in is not sin; the Lord had thoughts thrown at him in the wilderness too (Matthew 4:3).
3. The Lord’s response was “It is written”; he did not hold a conversation with the thought.
4. The question is not whether a thought comes, but how you respond to it.

brief21.title: Accept It, and Head for Destruction
notes: Slide text:
He didn’t refuse it; he fed it
“Then Satan entered into him”
Betrayal, remorse, self-destruction
Key points:
1. John 12:6: Judas was a thief; the thought had long been living in him.
2. John 13:27: Satan entered into him; first a guest, later the master.
3. Matthew 27:3–5: remorse, throwing down the silver, going out and hanging himself.
4. Contrast Peter (weeping bitterly, Matthew 26:75) and the two kinds of sorrow in 2 Corinthians 7:10.

brief21.title: Take Your Thoughts Captive
notes: Slide text:
“Bringing every thought into captivity
to the obedience of Christ”
(2 Corinthians 10:5)
Don’t talk with the thought — swap it out
Key points:
1. 2 Corinthians 10:4–5: take every thought captive and make it obey Christ.
2. “Bringing into captivity” is aichmalōtizō in the original — to take prisoner; military language.
3. Aaron Beck, University of Pennsylvania, 1960s: “automatic thoughts” and cognitive therapy.
4. Proverbs 4:23: “keep” is natsar, used of watchmen on a city wall; Luther’s picture of the birds.

brief21.title: God Is at Work in Your Heart
notes: Slide text:
“It is God who works in you
both to will and to work”
(Philippians 2:13)
He doesn’t force you; he invites you
Key points:
1. Philippians 2:12–13: work it out, for it is God who works in you.
2. “To will” belongs to the realm of thought; God starts his work with your “wanting to”.
3. When promptings come: to reach out to someone, to forgive someone, to take a step of faith.
4. God doesn’t force you; he invites you to respond with the way you think.

brief21.title: The Grasshopper View
notes: Slide text:
“We were in our own sight
as grasshoppers” (Numbers 13:33)
They weren’t defeated by giants
but by their own thinking
Key points:
1. Numbers 13:33: we were in our own sight as grasshoppers.
2. Nobody had measured their height; they had shrunk themselves first.
3. Moses in Exodus 3:11 and 4:10; Gideon’s excuses in Judges 6:15.
4. As a result that generation fell in the wilderness and could not enter Canaan for forty years.

brief21.title: Mary’s Response
notes: Slide text:
“Behold, the servant of the Lord; let it be
done to me according to your word”
(Luke 1:38)
Thinking shapes receiving and fulfilment
Key points:
1. Luke 1:34–38: Mary asked an honest question, then submitted.
2. James 1:6–8: “double-minded” literally means “two-souled”, like a wave of the sea.
3. Crum and Langer, 2007, “Psychological Science”: the hotel room attendants study.
4. Philippians 4:13: not “I am very capable”, but “he gives the strength”.

brief21.title: The Five Practices (1)
notes: Slide text:
Promise meditation: let the word work
Faith visualisation: see it fulfilled first
Refusing doubt: don’t talk with it
Prepare a verse as your “answering line”
Key points:
1. Practice 1: one promise a day, turned over and over (Psalm 119:11).
2. Practice 2: faith visualisation isn’t creating reality; it is seeing ahead what God has already said (Hebrews 11:1).
3. Practice 3: don’t hold a conversation with doubt; swap it out, one verse for one thought (Philippians 4:13).
4. Eve lost once she started discussing with the serpent; the Lord only said, “It is written.”

brief21.title: The Five Practices (2)
notes: Slide text:
Walking with the Spirit: alert to promptings
Selfless obedience: how would Jesus think?
Eight stages: Information, Revelation,
Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction …
Key points:
1. Practice 4: discern promptings with the Three Foundations; keep a promptings notebook (Isaiah 26:3).
2. Practice 5: ask, “If Jesus were me, how would he think?”; the role model of Gethsemane.
3. The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
4. Pick one practice and do it for seven days, then evaluate and correct.

brief21.title: Summing Up the 3-2-1 Vision
notes: Slide text:
Mindset → life → living → relationships → ministry
The self-centred cling; the selfless hand over
Humility overcomes pride
Selflessness overcomes Satan
Key points:
1. The fivefold change starts with mindset, not with serving twice as hard.
2. Self-centred: “I feel”, “I don’t want to”, “Why should I?”; selfless: let Jesus be King.
3. 920: change your thinking first, and then you can bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23).
4. C. S. Lewis: pride is the complete anti-God state of mind, and it breaks out first in our thinking.

brief21.title: Working with God Through Our Thinking
notes: Slide text:
As you think, so you live
The humble let God govern their thinking
The proud insist on their own ideas
Let Jesus be King in your thinking
Key points:
1. Return to the lesson’s conclusion: as you think, so you head towards your end.
2. Illustration: water needs a channel to irrigate; God’s word is the channel for our thinking.
3. Philippians 4:8 and Romans 12:2: think about these things; be transformed by the renewing of your mind.
4. Call: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

brief21.title: Response Prayer and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, renew our minds
Set our minds on the things above
To the Lord Jesus be the glory
to all generations. Amen
Key points:
1. Lead the brothers and sisters to pray aloud together, in a warm, unhurried tone.
2. Confess that we have valued our actions and neglected to guard our thoughts; ask the Lord’s forgiveness.
3. Ask the Holy Spirit to renew our minds, so we set our minds on things above (Colossians 3:2).
4. Close with Ephesians 3:21: to him be the glory to all generations.

script12.title: The Power of Thinking
script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are reading Lesson 135 together, and the theme is “The Power of Thinking”. Our key verse is Ephesians chapter 3 verse 20: “Now to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us.” Notice those last few words — ask, or think. Today we are going to see together that thinking is no small thing; thinking is a spiritual tool of tremendous power. How you think decides how you live; and how you think also decides whether God can work in you.

script12.title: What Was Your First Thought Today?
script: Brothers and sisters, this morning, before you had even opened your eyes, before you had got out of bed, a first thought had already surfaced in your heart. What was that thought? Was it “Here we go again,” or “Lord, walk with me today”? We often assume that what decides a life is the big events. Not really. What decides a life are the thoughts that no one sees and no one hears. Big events don’t happen every day, but thoughts happen every minute. Brothers and sisters, many of us set great store by prayer, yet we neglect our thinking. But Paul says that God works not only through what you ask; God also works through what you think.

script12.title: A Great Promise Written in Prison
script: Who wrote these words? Paul. He says: “I, Paul, am the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles” (Ephesians 3:1). When he wrote this letter he was a prisoner in Rome, around AD 60. Brothers and sisters, a man in chains wrote one of the most expansive sentences in the whole Bible. His body was chained; his thinking was not. His surroundings were a prison; his thinking was in heaven. The word “works” is the Greek energeō, the root of the word “energy”. God’s mighty power is not waiting far away up in heaven; it has already been set in motion inside you.

script12.title: Receiving Is Not Fulfilment
script: The Lord Jesus said: “Ask, and it will be given you” (Matthew 7:7). That is receiving. Paul says God is able “to do exceedingly abundantly” (Ephesians 3:20). That is fulfilment. Brothers and sisters, remember this distinction: receiving is not the same as fulfilment. Many people think that once a prayer is answered, that’s the end of it; in fact it is only the beginning. God has already placed the seed inside you, and there is still a stretch of road ahead.

script12.title: The Picture of Pregnancy
script: The lesson uses a beautiful illustration. A woman prays for a child, and she conceives. Has she received? Yes, she has. Has the child been brought to fulfilment? Not yet. In between lie ten months of carrying that life. Spiritual things work the same way. God gives you a promise, and you have already received; what matters from there on is how you think. If you doubt, give up, look only at your circumstances, it is like a miscarriage. If you keep meditating on God’s promise, the promise will grow and move towards fulfilment.

script12.title: Abraham Thought with Faith
script: The Bible says Abraham was “fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform” (Romans 4:21). It isn’t that he had no pressure — a hundred-year-old body was right there in front of him. Under that pressure he chose to think with faith. God once took him outside to count the stars and said: “So your offspring will be” (Genesis 15:5). From then on, every night sky was another meditation. Brothers and sisters, whatever you think about day after day, that is the kind of person you become, day by day.

script12.title: One Thought Brings a Miracle
script: The woman with the bleeding had been ill for twelve years; she had spent all she had and only grew worse. Yet the Bible records the one sentence in her heart: “If I just touch his garment, I will be made well” (Matthew 9:21). First she thought, then she acted, and finally she received. The Lord said: “Your faith has made you well” (Matthew 9:22). Brothers and sisters, that day so many people were crowding around Jesus, yet only one touched his power. Where was the difference? The difference was a single thought of faith.

script12.title: One Thought Brings Destruction
script: Now look at the other side. “The devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him” (John 13:2). Brothers and sisters, a thought being thrown in is not sin. The Lord had thoughts thrown at him in the wilderness too, and the Lord said: “It is written” (Matthew 4:4). The question is not whether a thought comes, but how you respond. Judas did not refuse it; he fed it instead, and the result was thought, action, destruction.

script12.title: God Is at Work in You
script: Paul says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). Brothers and sisters, when the thought suddenly rises in your heart to reach out to someone, to forgive someone, very often that is not something you came up with; it is God at work within you. God does not force you; he invites you. You can say “I can’t”, or you can say “Lord, I am willing.” James says: “For that man shouldn’t think that he will receive anything from the Lord” (James 1:7). It isn’t that God is stingy; it’s that while one of our hands reaches out, the other pulls back, and so we can’t catch hold of what is given. Brothers and sisters, thinking affects receiving; thinking also affects fulfilment.

script12.title: Five Practices of Faith-Filled Thinking
script: The lesson gives us five practices. First, promise meditation: one verse a day, turned over and over in your mind. Second, faith visualisation: see in your heart, ahead of time, what God has said fulfilled. Third, refusing doubt: don’t hold a conversation with it; swap it out, one verse for one thought. Fourth, walking with the Spirit: when you feel a prompting, stop and ask whether it is from God. Fifth, selfless obedience: ask yourself, “If Jesus were me, how would he think?” Brothers and sisters, don’t try all five at once — you won’t keep it up. Pick one first, do it for seven days, then evaluate and correct.

script12.title: Working with God Through Our Thinking
script: Brothers and sisters, as you think, so you live; as you think, so you head towards your end. Water without a channel floods everywhere; water with a channel can irrigate the fields. Today God wants to cut a channel for your thinking, and that channel is called the word of God. The humble let God govern their thinking; the proud insist on their own ideas. Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2). Brothers and sisters, change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your living changes. May we let Jesus be King in our thinking, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

script12.title: Response Prayer and Blessing
script: Let us pray together. Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for reminding us that thinking is no small thing. Lord, forgive us for paying so much attention to our actions and keeping so little watch over our thoughts. Place a sentence of faith in our hearts, so that all along the way we keep saying: the Lord will surely accomplish it for me. Holy Spirit, renew our minds, so that we set our minds on the things that are above. To you be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus, to all generations. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus. Amen.

script21.title: The Power of Thinking
script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are reading Lesson 135 of Morning Devotion 321 together. The theme is “The Power of Thinking”, and the subtitle is “Think in Faith and Work Together with God”. Our key verse is Ephesians chapter 3 verse 20: “Now to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us.” Notice those last few words — ask, or think. Today we are going to see together that “thinking” is a spiritual tool of tremendous power that God has placed in our hands.

script21.title: What Was Your First Thought Today?
script: Brothers and sisters, please take three quiet seconds to recall something. This morning, before you had even opened your eyes, before you had got out of bed, a first thought had already surfaced in your heart. What was that thought? Was it “Here we go again,” or “This is the day that Yahweh has made”? Was it “I can’t keep going,” or “Lord, walk with me today”? We often assume that what decides a life is the big events — changing jobs, moving house, falling ill, retiring. Not really. What decides a life are the thoughts that no one sees. Big events don’t happen every day, but thoughts happen every minute.

script21.title: Thinking Is No Small Thing
script: Brothers and sisters, many of us set great store by prayer, and rightly so; but we tend to neglect our thinking. We imagine that as long as the ten minutes on our knees are spiritual, it doesn’t matter what we think about for the other fourteen hours. But Paul says that God works not only through “what you ask” but also through “what you think”. Thinking is the soil and prayer is the seed; if our thinking is wasteland, even good seed will struggle to bear fruit. Pascal wrote in his “Pensées” that man is only a reed, but he is a thinking reed. Brothers and sisters, the spiritual battle is not fought with physical strength, but in our thoughts.

script21.title: A Great Promise Written in Prison
script: Who wrote these words? The apostle Paul. At the very opening of chapter 3 he says: “I, Paul, am the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles” (Ephesians 3:1). In the view of most scholars, he wrote this letter as a prisoner in Rome, around AD 60 to 62. A man in chains wrote one of the most expansive sentences in the whole Bible: his body was chained, his thinking was not. The church in Ephesus that received it lived in the city of the temple of Artemis, surrounded day after day by a system of thought given over to idol worship. The word “works” is the Greek energeō, the root of the word “energy”, and the same word appears in Philippians chapter 2 verse 13. God’s mighty power is not waiting far away up in heaven; it has already been set in motion inside you.

script21.title: Receiving Is Not Fulfilment
script: The Lord Jesus said: “Ask, and it will be given you” (Matthew 7:7). That is receiving. Paul says God is able “to do exceedingly abundantly” (Ephesians 3:20). That is fulfilment. Brothers and sisters, remember this distinction: receiving is not the same as fulfilment. “Exceedingly abundantly” in the original is hyperekperissou, meaning beyond the very limit. “Think” in the original is noeō, and its noun is the very “mind” in Romans chapter 12 verse 2, “the renewing of your mind”. What God means to accomplish is always bigger than your imagination, but he accomplishes it through your mind.

script21.title: Pregnancy and Miscarriage
script: The lesson uses a beautiful illustration. A woman prays for a child; God answers, and she conceives. Has she received? Yes, she has. Has the child been brought to fulfilment? Not yet. In between lie ten months of carrying that life. Spiritual things work the same way. God gives you a promise, and at that moment you have already received; what matters from there on is how you think. If you doubt, give up, look only at your circumstances, it is like a miscarriage. James says: “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin” (James 1:15). Brothers and sisters, negative thoughts conceive; and by the same token, thoughts of faith conceive too. Whichever one you feed day by day is the one that grows.

script21.title: Abraham Thought with Faith
script: How does the Bible describe Abraham? “Without being weakened in faith, he didn’t consider his own body, already having been worn out, (he being about a hundred years old) … Yet, looking to the promise of God … being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform” (Romans 4:19–21). Notice that he was well aware his body was as good as dead — he did not run away from reality; and yet at the same time he was “fully assured”, in the original plērophoreō, filled to overflowing. How did he manage it? God brought him outside and said: “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars … So your offspring will be” (Genesis 15:5). From then on, every night sky was another promise meditation, and he went on meditating for twenty-five years.

script21.title: Heart or Brain?
script: Brothers and sisters, this is what 321 means when it says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Thinking with the heart means thinking on the promise with faith, and the promise is carried to term; thinking with the brain means only calculating the odds and looking at circumstances, and the promise is cut short. Rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Brain science gives us supporting evidence: in 1949 Hebb proposed that neurons that fire together wire together; in 2000 Maguire’s team at University College London found that taxi drivers who had spent years memorising complex routes had a larger rear hippocampus than a control group. Whatever you think about over and over paves a road in your brain. That is why Proverbs says: “Out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

script21.title: One Sentence from the Woman with the Bleeding
script: Now let us look at two extremely sharp contrasts. The first is the woman with the bleeding. She had been ill for twelve years; Mark says she “had spent all that she had, and was no better, but rather grew worse” (Mark 5:26). Under the regulations of Leviticus she was unclean and could not go into the temple; she lost not only her health but her relationships. Thinking according to her circumstances, she should have said, “It’s no use.” Yet the Bible makes a point of recording the one sentence in her heart: “If I just touch his garment, I will be made well” (Matthew 9:21). In the original, “she said within herself” is in the imperfect tense, showing that she said it to herself again and again, all the way.

script21.title: First Think, Then Act, Then Receive
script: Brothers and sisters, look carefully at the order: first she thought, then she acted, and finally she received. The Lord turned and said to her: “Daughter, cheer up! Your faith has made you well” (Matthew 9:22). The Lord did not say, “Your hand has made you well”; he said, “Your faith has made you well.” And her faith began with a single thought. That day the disciples said: “You see the multitude pressing against you” (Mark 5:31). How many people bumped against Jesus’ body, yet only one touched his power! The difference was that only one person came carrying a thought of faith. It is the same today: many hear the word, but those who truly receive are the ones who first say in their hearts, “God’s word will surely be fulfilled in me.”

script21.title: A Thought Thrown into Judas’s Heart
script: Now look at the other side. “During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him” (John 13:2). “Put into the heart” in the original is ballō, meaning to throw, to cast in. Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: a thought being thrown in is not, in itself, sin. The Lord Jesus himself had thoughts thrown at him. During the forty days in the wilderness Satan said: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread” (Matthew 4:3). How did the Lord answer? “It is written” (Matthew 4:4). The Lord did not debate with the thought. The question is not whether a thought comes, but how you respond to it.

script21.title: Accept It, and Head for Destruction
script: Judas did not deal with it. Far from refusing it, he fed it. John chapter 12 verse 6 tells us he was a thief who used to steal from the money box — that thought had been living inside him for a long time. At first it was “put into the heart”; later it was “then Satan entered into him” (John 13:27). At first a guest was knocking at the door; later the master was sitting in the living room. And the end? He felt remorse, threw the silver down in the sanctuary, went away and hanged himself (Matthew 27:3–5). Judas was not the only one who fell that night; Peter also denied the Lord three times. Where was the difference? Peter went out and wept bitterly, and brought himself back to the Lord; Judas threw down the silver, but did not give himself back to the Lord. Paul says: “For godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation … But the sorrow of the world produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

script21.title: Take Your Thoughts Captive
script: So what are we to do? Paul gives us orders for battle: “Bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). “Bringing into captivity” in the original is aichmalōtizō, a military word meaning to take prisoner. Don’t let your thoughts take you prisoner — you take your thoughts prisoner. In the 1960s Beck at the University of Pennsylvania described “automatic thoughts”; the heart of his therapy is to catch the thought, write it down and check whether it is true. Testing our thoughts against the facts already helps a great deal, but God tells us to test our thoughts against the truth. Proverbs says, “Keep your heart”, and the word “keep” is the word used for the watchmen on a city wall. A saying commonly attributed to Martin Luther puts it this way: you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest in your hair.

script21.title: God Is at Work in Your Heart
script: The third teaching. Paul says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). Brothers and sisters, notice that even the “will” is God at work in you. God’s work does not begin with your hands; it begins with your “wanting to”. So when a thought suddenly rises in your heart — to reach out to someone, to forgive someone who has wronged you — very often that is not something you came up with yourself. It is God already at work within you. God does not force you; he invites you to take part. How do you take part? By responding to him with the way you think.

script21.title: The Grasshopper View
script: All too often we take the first path: doubt and retreat. Moses said: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh?” (Exodus 3:11). Gideon said: “I am the least in my father’s house” (Judges 6:15). The classic case is the ten spies: “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Numbers 13:33). Brothers and sisters, nobody had measured their height; they had shrunk themselves first. They were not defeated by giants; they were defeated by their own thinking. It wasn’t that the giants were too big; it was that God was too small in their thinking. As a result that whole generation fell in the wilderness.

script21.title: Mary’s Response
script: The other path is meditation and response. Mary heard something utterly beyond reason, and she asked an honest question: “How can this be, seeing I am a virgin?” (Luke 1:34). But after the angel answered, she said: “Behold, the servant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). James reminds us: “For that man shouldn’t think that he will receive anything from the Lord” (James 1:7). It isn’t that God is stingy; it’s that while one of our hands reaches out, the other pulls back. In 2007 Crum and Langer at Harvard studied hotel room attendants; they simply let one group know that their work already met the recommended level of exercise, and four weeks later that group showed measurable improvements in weight and blood pressure. If a single idea can affect the body like that, how much more when God’s word enters our thinking!

script21.title: The Five Practices (1)
script: The lesson gives us five practices. First, promise meditation: choose one promise each day and turn it over and over — not just reading it, but thinking it. The psalmist says: “I have hidden your word in my heart” (Psalm 119:11). Second, faith visualisation: see in your heart, ahead of time, what God has said fulfilled. We need to be clear: this is not using the power of imagination to create reality; it is because God has already spoken that I see it ahead of time. Hebrews says: “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for” (Hebrews 11:1). Third, refusing doubt: don’t hold a conversation with it. Eve lost the moment she started discussing things with the serpent; the Lord only said, “It is written.” The method is one sentence for another: prepare a verse in advance as the “answering line” for your negative thoughts.

script21.title: The Five Practices (2)
script: Fourth, walking with the Spirit: when you feel a prompting, stop and ask, is this from God? Use the Three Foundations as a filter — is it in line with Scripture? Is it like Jesus? Is there peace inside? Fifth, selfless obedience: when “I don’t want to” shows up, ask yourself, “If Jesus were me, how would he think?” In Gethsemane the Lord said: “Not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39). That is selflessness. Then use the eight stages of changing our mindset to drive it deeper: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Don’t try all five at once — you won’t keep it up. Pick one, do it for seven days, then evaluate and correct, and finally pass it on to the next person.

script21.title: Summing Up the 3-2-1 Vision
script: Brothers and sisters, the fivefold change of 321 is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Notice that the first step is not behaviour; it is mindset. Change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your living changes. How many people try to start straight with ministry, being twice as busy, without ever dealing with their thinking, and after years of service, inside they are just the same as before! The self-centred most often say “I feel” and “I don’t want to”; the selfless say “let Jesus be King”. C. S. Lewis said pride is the complete anti-God state of mind — and the first place pride breaks out is not the mouth but the mind. It is the same with 920: if you dwell on that person’s faults every day, however gentle you try to look, you won’t last three days. To bear the ninefold fruit, first change the way you think.

script21.title: Working with God Through Our Thinking
script: Brothers and sisters, “thinking” is an invisible power, yet it produces visible results. As you think, so you live; as you think, so you head towards your end. Water without a channel floods everywhere and ends up as mud; water with a channel can irrigate good fields. Today God wants to cut a channel for your thinking, and that channel is called “the word of God”. Paul says: “Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report … think about these things” (Philippians 4:8). The humble let God govern their thinking; the proud insist on their own ideas. May we live out a selfless life, let Jesus be King in our thinking, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

script21.title: Response Prayer and Blessing
script: Let us pray together. Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you. Thank you for reminding us this morning that thinking is no small thing. Lord, forgive us for paying so much attention to our outward actions and keeping so little watch over our inner thoughts; we let doubt and bitterness settle in, without noticing that they were robbing us of the good purpose you want to accomplish. As you did for the woman with the bleeding, place a sentence of faith in our hearts, so that all along the way we keep saying: the Lord will surely accomplish it for me. When a wrong thought is thrown in, enable us to refuse it at once and turn at once to your word. Holy Spirit, renew our minds every day, so that we set our minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth. Reign as King in our thinking. To you be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus, to all generations, forever and ever. We pray in the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Bible Covered in Highlights
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Before we come to today’s lesson, let me describe a scene that many of us will recognise.

There is a sister who has believed in the Lord for twenty years. Her Bible is beautiful — not beautiful in the way a new one is, but beautiful in the way a well-read one is. The edges of the pages curl, the leather of the cover is a little cracked, and inside it is full of highlighter: yellow, green, pink, the key points neatly marked; and in the margins there are little handwritten notes recording a sentence some pastor said on such-and-such a date.

One day she sat across from me, her eyes red, and said something. She said: “Pastor, I’ve been reading the Bible for twenty years. I know everything I’m supposed to know. But last night my husband said one thing, and I just exploded. Twenty years of teaching, gone in a second.”

Brothers and sisters, I believe that isn’t her story alone.

We read the Bible, we listen to sermons, we pray; we can even recite dozens of verses. But when the crucial moment comes — the moment we are misunderstood, the moment we are rejected, the moment our child answers back, the moment the test results come out — our reactions seem hardly any different from before we believed.

Why?

The lesson asks this question very honestly right at the start: we already know that thinking matters, but today God wants to take us deeper into a crucial question — how far does your thinking go? How deep does it reach?

Many people’s lives don’t change, not because they don’t think.

But because they don’t think deeply enough, they don’t think long enough, and their thinking never reaches the heart.

Let me use a very small example. When you make tea, if you dip the teabag into hot water for one second and pull it out, the water is still water, with a little colour at most; leave the teabag in for three minutes, and the colour, the aroma and the flavour of the whole cup are completely changed. Same teabag, same cup of water; there is only one difference — time, that is, how long it steeps.

Brothers and sisters, God’s word is just the same. The same verse steeped in you for one second, or steeped for three years, gives completely different results.

The Bible says: “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11).

Notice that the psalmist doesn’t say, “I have copied your word into a notebook,” nor “I have memorised your word in my head.” What he says is — hidden in my heart.

God’s word is not meant only to get into the brain; God’s word is meant to get into the heart.

In the 321 vision we put it even more clearly: relying on the brain is relying on ourselves; relying on the heart is relying on the Holy Spirit. Those who rely on the brain know a great deal but can’t live it out; those who rely on the heart let the truth enter their life and live out Christ. Rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad.

In today’s lesson we will learn one key thing together: how God’s word moves from “knowing” to “becoming”.

Not reading one more verse, but reading more deeply; not hearing one more sermon, but letting it get into your heart.

Brothers and sisters, are you ready? Let us ask ourselves this question together: how deep has my thinking gone?

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: A Long Poem Written for the Word of God
sections.html:
Today’s theme verse comes from Psalm 119. To grasp the weight of this verse, we first need to get to know this psalm.

First, it is the longest chapter in the whole Bible, with 176 verses.

Second, it is a carefully crafted acrostic poem. The whole psalm is divided into twenty-two stanzas of eight verses each; the twenty-two stanzas correspond to the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and all eight verses in a stanza begin with the same letter. Today’s verse 11 belongs to the second stanza — the Beth stanza, verses 9 to 16.

In the ancient world this form was a tool for memory, and also a declaration of devotion: from the first letter to the last, from A to Z, I will use all my language and all my life to speak of God’s word. In other words, the very form of this psalm is telling us something — meditating on God’s word is meant to be done “from beginning to end, leaving nothing out”.

Third, the author of this psalm is not named. Traditionally some have held that it was David; others, Ezra or some devout scribe from the period of the return from exile. From the repeated lines such as “Though princes sit and slander me” (Psalm 119:23) and “The arrogant mock me excessively, but I don’t swerve from your law” (Psalm 119:51), the author was clearly someone who, under pressure and hostility, still chose to hold tight to God’s word. He did not write this psalm in a quiet study; he wrote it in the midst of the storm.

Fourth, almost every verse of this psalm contains a synonym for God’s word: law, testimonies, precepts, statutes, commandments, ordinances, word, promise, ways. Scholars often call it “a symphony on the word of God”. The psalmist uses nine different terms, from nine angles, circling the same subject for 176 verses — all to make one point: God’s word is the standard for my whole life.

Fifth, let’s look at the context of verse 11. The second stanza (Psalm 119:9–16) begins like this: “How can a young man keep his way pure? By living according to your word” (Psalm 119:9). Next comes: “With my whole heart, I have sought you. Don’t let me wander from your commandments” (Psalm 119:10). Only then comes verse 11: “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.”

Brothers and sisters, notice the order: first the question, “How can I keep my way pure?”, then “with my whole heart I have sought you”, and finally “hidden in my heart”.

This is exactly the order 321 speaks of — not changing behaviour first, but changing what is inside first. Behaviour is the fruit; the heart is the root. If you don’t deal with the root and only prune the fruit, next year the same thing will grow again.

Sixth, the word “hidden” is the Hebrew tsaphan (צָפַן), whose basic meaning is “to treasure, to store away, to hide”. In Exodus this word describes Moses’ mother hiding the baby for three months (Exodus 2:2), and it is also used of storing treasure in the most secret place. Job says: “I have treasured up the words of his mouth more than my necessary food” (Job 23:12). That kind of treasuring is the flavour of tsaphan.

So verse 11 does not say, “I have written down your word”; it says: I have taken your word as my most precious treasure and stored it in the deepest, innermost, safest place of my life.

Seventh, the word “heart” is the Hebrew lev (לֵב). This is very important. In Chinese we often take “heart” to mean the emotions; but in the Hebrew mindset the heart is the centre of a person’s thinking, will and decisions. So “hidden in my heart” does not mean “being moved for a moment”; it means letting God’s word become the way I think, the basis of my choices and the instinct behind my reactions.

Brothers and sisters, this is today’s theme. God’s word in the brain is information; God’s word in the heart is life.

With the same verse, you can merely “know” it, or you can let it “become you”.

The difference lies in how deep your thinking goes.

sections.heading: 3. Teaching One: From “Words in the Head” to “Words in the Heart”
sections.html:
1. Two Kinds of Words, Two Outcomes

The lesson puts it very directly:

When God’s word gets into the “brain”, you will know it; when God’s word gets into the “heart”, you will live it out.

Words in the head are easily forgotten; words in the heart become life.

This is a very solid observation. In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus carried out a series of memory experiments on himself and plotted the famous “forgetting curve”. He found that newly learned material, if not reviewed, is lost fastest in the very first stretch of time, and only afterwards does the loss slowly level off. In other words, simply “remembering” something will never hold on its own.

Brothers and sisters, that is a picture of many people’s spiritual lives. On Sunday we hear a very moving sermon; on Monday we still remember half of it; by Wednesday all we remember is a joke the pastor told; by Friday we’ve forgotten even the joke.

It isn’t that the sermon was poor; it’s that the sermon only got as far as the head and never reached the heart.

2. Why, after so many sermons, are we still the same at the crucial moment?

The lesson asks a question that cuts to the heart: why is it that many people have heard many sermons and memorised many verses, yet at the crucial moment still react in their own way?

The answer is a single sentence: the word is in the head and has not got into the heart.

The psychologist Daniel Kahneman, winner of the 2002 Nobel Prize in Economics, in “Thinking, Fast and Slow” (2011), divides human thinking into two systems: System 1 is fast, automatic and almost effortless — that is intuition; System 2 is slow, effortful and requires concentration — that is analysis. He points out that the vast majority of our everyday reactions are run by System 1; System 2 often comes on stage only afterwards, to find reasons for what System 1 has already done.

Brothers and sisters, this gives us a very important reminder: the verses you have memorised usually live in System 2; but the remark that wounds you strikes System 1.

So in that half-second when conflict erupts, before you have time to look up a verse or recall your notes, whatever reaction comes out of you — that is what truly lives inside you.

The Bible said it earlier and more deeply than psychology: “The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45).

The Lord Jesus speaks of “the treasure of his heart” and “the abundance of the heart”. He doesn’t ask what is in your head; he asks what is stored in your heart.

3. What does “getting into the heart” mean?

The lesson gives three very concrete definitions: it becomes your instinct, it becomes your reaction, it becomes your choice.

I love these three phrases, because they make “spiritual” something very down to earth.

When you are offended: if your first reaction is “anger”, the word is still in your head; if your first reaction is “forgiveness”, the word is already in your heart.

This is not condemnation; it is a health check.

It’s like taking your blood pressure. The blood pressure monitor isn’t there to shame you; it’s there to tell you the truth. Your first reaction is the blood pressure monitor of your spiritual life.

So the key to spiritual growth is not “how much I know” but “how much is in me”.

Paul said something very weighty to the church in Corinth: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1). He goes on: “But if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he doesn’t yet know as he ought to know” (1 Corinthians 8:2).

Brothers and sisters, we must be very careful: knowledge can become a breeding ground for pride. A person can be familiar with the map of the whole Bible and yet never have walked the road.

4. From “knowing” to “becoming”

The Bible has a beautiful picture of exactly this.

Jeremiah says: “Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words were to me a joy and the rejoicing of my heart, for I am called by your name, Yahweh, God of Armies” (Jeremiah 15:16).

Notice the verb — ate.

A recipe stuck on the fridge won’t put a single kilo on you. Food has to be eaten, digested and absorbed by the body, until it finally becomes your blood, your bones, your flesh — that is nourishment. God’s word is the same. On a bookshelf, on a wall, saved in your phone — none of that counts; it has to be eaten, digested, and become you.

Charles Spurgeon is commonly said to have described John Bunyan, the author of “The Pilgrim’s Progress”, like this: prick him anywhere, and what flows out is Scripture.

That is “becoming”. Not that he could quote the Bible, but that the Bible was already flowing in his blood.

5. A 321 Insight: Selflessness Lets God’s Word Rule in the Heart

Here the lesson gives us a ray of light: selflessness lets God’s word dwell in the heart; the self-centred life lets our own ideas rule.

Brothers and sisters, this is the very core message of 321.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life doesn’t necessarily mean doing something wicked; the self-centred life means that inside me, the one who has the final say is me. I hear the sermon, I nod, I agree, and then I go on living my own way as before.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

Notice: not “I try hard to live like Christ”, but “Christ lives in me”.

So in the language of 321, “getting into the heart” means letting Jesus be King in my thinking.

The second of the Three Foundations is: the Bible is my standard. Brothers and sisters, a standard isn’t a slogan hanging on the wall; a standard is the steering wheel you turn by at the crossroads. If the Bible is only in your head, it is a reference book; only when it gets into your heart is it your standard.

sections.heading: 4. Teaching Two: Let Your Thinking Become a Picture, Until Faith Is Built
sections.html:
1. Not “Thinking for a Moment”, but Thinking Again and Again, Thinking Deeply

The lesson says: for God’s word to get into the heart, it is not a matter of “thinking about it for a moment”; it means meditating on it again and again, meditating on it deeply, until it forms a “picture”.

The depth of your thinking determines the strength of your faith.

The Bible’s word for “meditate” is the Hebrew hagah (הָגָה). It is a fascinating word: its original meaning is “to murmur, to mutter to oneself”, and the prophet Isaiah uses the same word for a lion “growling” over its prey (Isaiah 31:4). So biblical meditation is not quietly emptying the mind; it is like a cow chewing the cud — bringing up a mouthful of grass and chewing it again, bringing it up and chewing it again; and like a lion standing over its prey, refusing to let go.

God said to Joshua: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success” (Joshua 1:8).

The psalmist says: “but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2).

“Day and night” — that is depth. Not thinking about it for a moment, but thinking by day and thinking by night.

In the New Testament Luke uses a beautiful word to describe Mary: “But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19). The Greek for “pondering” is symballō (συμβάλλω), which literally means “to put things together, to compare and piece together”. Mary took the angel’s words, the shepherds’ words and her present circumstances and put them together piece by piece, slowly assembling a complete picture.

Brothers and sisters, this is what it looks like when thinking goes deep.

2. The Woman with the Bleeding: She First Saw the Picture in Her Heart

The example the lesson gives is very clear — the woman with the bleeding.

Mark records it like this: “A certain woman, who had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and had suffered many things by many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better, but rather grew worse, having heard the things concerning Jesus, came up behind him in the crowd, and touched his clothes. For she said, ‘If I just touch his clothes, I will be made well’ ” (Mark 5:25–28).

Notice: she was not merely “hoping to be healed”.

The lesson puts it well: she “saw” a picture in her heart.

She imagined it: the crowd is huge; she pushes her way in; she reaches out her hand; she touches him.

This was not idle thinking, but very specific, very clear, very real thinking.

The original is richer still. “Made well” is the Greek sōzō (σῴζω), a word that can equally be translated “saved”. And Mark uses the future tense — what she kept saying in her heart was: “I will be saved.” Not “I wonder whether …”, but “I will.”

And the result? “Immediately the flow of her blood was dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her affliction” (Mark 5:29).

Jesus turned and said to her: “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be cured of your disease” (Mark 5:34).

Brothers and sisters, the Lord did not say, “My power has healed you”; what the Lord said was, “Your faith has made you well.”

Where did that faith come from? From the picture in her heart, the one she thought over again and again until it grew clearer and clearer.

The more concrete your thinking, the more real your faith; the deeper your thinking, the more thoroughly your life is persuaded.

3. Two More Pictures in the Bible

The Bible gives two more examples, one positive and one negative, that make this even plainer.

The positive one is Abraham. God brought him outside and said: “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” And he said to him, “So your offspring will be” (Genesis 15:5).

Brothers and sisters, God could simply have said, “You will have many descendants.” But he didn’t. He brought him out of the tent, had him lift up his head, let him see the whole sky full of stars, and let that picture be engraved on his eyes.

Paul later describes Abraham like this: “Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God, and being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform” (Romans 4:20–21).

The negative one is the twelve spies. Ten of them came back and said: “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Numbers 13:33).

Do you see it? They had a picture in their hearts too — only in that picture the main character was a grasshopper, not God.

Brothers and sisters, there is certainly a picture in your heart. The question has never been “Should I have a picture?” The question is — who is the main character in your picture?

4. The Essence of Faith Is Seeing the Unseen

The lesson says: many people can’t believe because they haven’t “seen”; but the very essence of faith is seeing what cannot be seen.

That statement is entirely biblical.

Hebrews says: “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1).

And of Moses it says: “By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible” (Hebrews 11:27).

Paul also says: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

Brothers and sisters, this is the shift of perspective 321 speaks of: from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal.

Not hypnotising ourselves with our eyes shut, but opening the eyes of the heart to see the reality God has revealed.

Incidentally, psychology has observed a related phenomenon. In 1994 John Driskell and colleagues published a meta-analysis in the “Journal of Applied Psychology” showing that “mental practice” — rehearsing an action over and over in the mind — really does improve actual performance; the effect is not as great as real practice, but clearly better than no practice at all.

I want to say this very carefully: this does not mean that “imagination can create reality”. Our faith is not built on the power of imagination but on the promises of God. God’s word is true first, and then we meditate on it; it doesn’t become true once we have thought it through. Mental rehearsal simply reminds us, from one angle, that concrete, repeated thinking really does change what a person does.

5. A 321 Insight: Relying on the Heart, We See Spiritual Reality

The insight the lesson gives here is: meditating with the heart, we see spiritual reality; analysing with the brain, we are hemmed in by circumstances.

Brothers and sisters, the one who relies on the brain stands outside the crowd doing sums: with a crowd like this pressing in, how could I ever squeeze through? I’ve been bleeding for twelve years, the doctors can do nothing — what good will touching his clothes do?

The one who relies on the heart sees a different picture: Jesus is right there, and I only need to touch him.

Rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. Focus on your circumstances and the more you calculate, the more hopeless you become; focus on Jesus and the more you meditate, the stronger you grow.

This is exactly what 321 means by “the Holy Spirit is my guide”. Only by the Holy Spirit do we have spiritual eyesight; relying on our own brain, all we can do is keep calculating our own impossibilities.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Three: Let God’s Word Reach “Saturation Point”, and Life Changes Naturally
sections.html:
1. Thinking Can Become “Saturated”

The lesson says: thinking can become “saturated”. As God’s word keeps entering you — thought over once, ten times, a hundred times — little by little it fills your heart.

“Saturation” is a very precise metaphor.

In chemistry saturation has a clear definition. At 20 degrees Celsius, 100 grams of water can dissolve about 36 grams of table salt; beyond that amount, however much you stir, the salt won’t dissolve and simply sinks to the bottom of the glass. That critical point is called the saturation point.

Brothers and sisters, our hearts have a saturation point too. The difference is what you let fill them.

The lesson uses an even simpler image: when a cup is full of clean water, dirty water can’t be poured in.

In the same way, when the heart is filled with God’s word, wrong thoughts cannot grow.

2. Repetition Is the Only Road to Saturation

Between “thinking it once” and “saturation” stands one word: repetition.

Psychology offers strong support on this point. In 2006 Nicholas Cepeda, Harold Pashler and colleagues published a meta-analysis covering more than a hundred studies in the “Psychological Bulletin”. The conclusion was clear: for the same total time, spreading review across several days and several sessions is far more effective than cramming it all into one. This is the so-called “spacing effect”.

In addition, a 1992 study by John Driskell and colleagues showed that “overlearning” — continuing to practise after you have already learned something — markedly extends how long the memory is retained.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: continuing after you have already learned it.

Isn’t that exactly what the psalmist means by “meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2)? Isn’t it exactly what the lesson means by “thought over once, ten times, a hundred times”?

We often stop at the point of “I already know that.” But God’s word often only begins truly to change us in the stretch after “I already know that”, when we keep on meditating anyway.

Brain science also offers a remarkable piece of supporting evidence. In 2000 Eleanor Maguire and colleagues at University College London published a study in the “Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences” (PNAS) showing that the rear part of the hippocampus in London taxi drivers’ brains was markedly larger than in ordinary people, and the longer they had been driving, the more marked the difference. The learning principle put forward in 1949 by the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb in his book “The Organization of Behavior” is also commonly summed up as “neurons that fire together wire together”.

Brothers and sisters, when God made us, he wrote into our very bodies the fact that “repetition shapes you”.

Only one question remains: what are you going to repeat?

3. Not Avoiding Sin by Gritting Your Teeth, but Having No Room Inside

Here the lesson has a sentence that I think is the most precious in the whole lesson:

“We don’t avoid sin by gritting our teeth; we avoid it because there is no room inside for sin.”

Brothers and sisters, the difference between these two is the difference between heaven and earth.

The person who relies on gritting their teeth shuts sin outside the door and then holds the door shut with their body. The strength outside the door doesn’t get any weaker, but your strength grows weaker and weaker. So many people are not ungodly; they are simply exhausted.

The person who has been filled is different. They aren’t holding the door shut; they have filled the house.

The Lord Jesus told a very solemn parable: “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and doesn’t find it. Then he says, ‘I will return into my house from which I came out,’ and when he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order. Then he goes, and takes with himself seven other spirits more evil than he is, and they enter in and dwell there. The last state of that man becomes worse than the first” (Matthew 12:43–45).

Notice those three words: empty, swept, put in order.

That house was very clean; the problem was — it was empty.

Brothers and sisters, the most dangerous state for the spiritual life is not dirty; it is empty.

So Paul’s command is not “don’t be filled with the world”, but: “Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18). In the original, “be filled” is a present passive imperative, meaning — be filled continually, on and on.

And he says to the church in Colossae: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom …” (Colossians 3:16). The Greek for “dwell” is enoikeō (ἐνοικέω), meaning “to take up residence, to settle”. Not coming as a guest, but moving in to stay.

4. The question is not “Why do I still sin?” but “What am I filled with?”

The lesson turns the question completely on its head — a very important change of mindset.

We are used to asking: why do I still lose my temper? Why am I still jealous? Why am I still weak?

Asked that way, the focus is on ourselves; the more we ask, the more we condemn ourselves, and the more we condemn ourselves, the more powerless we become.

The lesson teaches us to ask instead: what am I filled with?

Asked that way, the focus shifts to “what have I been feeding?”

How much time do I spend each day watching short videos? How much listening to the news? How much reading God’s word? I’m not saying watching the news is a sin; I’m saying — whatever you pour in is what will spill out.

The Lord Jesus said: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34).

When someone bumps into a cup, what splashes out? Whatever was already in it.

Brothers and sisters, the people and events in daily life that “bump into you” don’t create your reactions; they only splash out what was already inside you.

So don’t blame the person who bumped into you. Thank them — they’ve given you a free health check.

5. From Saturation to Second Nature

The lesson says: when you let God’s word reach saturation point, your thinking will change, your reactions will change, your life will change.

Notice the order of those three: thinking, reactions, life.

This is exactly 321’s fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that we often want to start in the middle? We want to change our behaviour directly, fix our relationships directly, charge straight into ministry. But if the root isn’t changed, the fruit can’t be changed.

Here’s another picture. A small cucumber that falls into vinegar for three seconds comes out still a cucumber; soak it for three days and it becomes a pickle — and it can never turn back.

That is what saturation means: not straining, but steeping; not forcing, but coming naturally.

6. A 321 Insight: Filled with God, or Filled with Self

The lesson’s insight is: selflessness lets God’s word fill the heart; the self-centred life lets the world and self fill the heart.

Brothers and sisters, the most frightening thing about the self-centred life is not that it is vicious, but that it is so reasonable. It says: “There’s nothing wrong with thinking this way.” “Anyone would be angry.” “I’m just stating the facts.”

Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

When my heart is filled with my own reasoning, there is no place left for God’s word. It’s not that God’s word isn’t good enough; it’s that the cup is already full.

So “emptying” and “filling” are two sides of the same thing. Selflessness is not merely reducing ourselves to zero; selflessness is letting the infinite Lord fill every room within me.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s message back within the whole picture of 321 and look at it once more.

1. The Three Foundations: Only When the Word Gets into the Heart Is the Standard Truly a Standard

Jesus is my role model. When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, he didn’t open a book; he simply said: “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth’ ” (Matthew 4:4). At the moment when he was hungriest, most exhausted and most pressed, what came out was the word of God — because the word of God had long been in him.

The Bible is my standard. If the standard is only in the head, it is knowledge; when the standard gets into the heart, it becomes the steering wheel.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. It is the Holy Spirit who turns the letter into life. Paul says: “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). If we read the Bible relying only on the brain, what we read is the letter; relying on the Holy Spirit, we meet the Lord who is speaking.

2. The Two Core Values: Let Jesus Be King in Our Thinking

Let Jesus be King — brothers and sisters, the first place the King must reign is your thinking.

Paul says: “throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5).

“Bringing into captivity” is a vivid picture: every single thought must be marched back before Jesus.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when someone is offended and their first reaction is forgiveness, the people around them will ask, “How did you do that?” At that moment the glory doesn’t go to your good character; it goes to the One who lives in you.

3. The Goal: Establish God’s System

God’s system is not an organisation; it is a group of people filled within by God’s word, joined to one another, living out the kingdom of God.

One person’s heart being filled is grace; a whole group’s hearts being filled — that is God’s system.

4. Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry

Today’s lesson is entirely about life.

People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. And the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

If God’s word has not got into my heart, my relationship with God stays at the level of information; my relationship with myself will be full of condemnation; and my relationships with others can only be propped up by gritted teeth.

5. The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

920: every person connected with us is our “2”. When God’s word reaches saturation in me, then facing my “2” — the family member who most easily makes me lose patience, the colleague who is hardest to get along with — I can live out selflessness (0) and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

Brothers and sisters, remember: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Fruit is borne, not squeezed out. When the roots have drunk enough water, the fruit will be sweet of its own accord.

235: on the journey of renewing our thinking, it’s hard to go far alone. Find a selfless “2” as your spiritual companion, and remind each other how deep your thinking has gone today; build the “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing on what you have received; and go on to become the “5”, a team of spiritual comrades.

6. The Shift of Perspective

From man’s to God’s: no longer asking “How do I feel?” but “What does God say?”

From the earthly to the heavenly: no longer blocked by the crowd in front of us, but seeing Jesus in the middle of the crowd.

From the temporary to the eternal: twelve years of illness were temporary; the Lord’s one word, “Daughter”, is eternal.

From the worldly to the godly: no longer calculating our own chances by the world’s arithmetic.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Five Practices for Getting God’s Word into the Heart
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five very practical exercises. Let’s look at them one by one, and use 321’s “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to deepen them.

Practice 1: Repeated Meditation — Moving Scripture from the Head into the Heart

Each day choose one verse and meditate on it again and again: in the morning, at midday, in the evening, until the verse surfaces of its own accord.

Brothers and sisters, please don’t be greedy for more. One verse a day is better than ten chapters.

The method is simple: read it aloud in the morning, think it through once on your commute, once before lunch, and once more before bed. The next day, the same verse again.

George Müller, the nineteenth-century father of orphanages in England, mentions in his own account that from 1841 onwards he changed the order of his mornings: instead of beginning to pray as soon as he got up, he first meditated on God’s word until his heart was fed, comforted and guided, and then prayer flowed naturally out of the meditation. He said this change made all the difference to his spiritual life and his ministry.

Practice 2: Picturing Scripture — Turning God’s Word into Images

Turn the scripture into a concrete scene: imagine yourself in that situation, and let the truth become real and visible.

For example, when you read “Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing” (Psalm 23:1), don’t just repeat it — see it: the green pastures, the still waters, the rod, the staff, the table prepared for you in the presence of your enemies.

When you read about the woman with the bleeding, see that outstretched hand; when you read about Abraham, look up and see the sky full of stars.

Brothers and sisters, this is not fantasy; it is letting what God has already said develop in your heart. It’s like old-fashioned photographic film: it has to soak long enough in the developer before the image slowly emerges, bit by bit.

Practice 3: Declaring to Internalise — Using the Mouth to Help the Heart Receive

Declare God’s word again and again: let your ears hear it, let your heart be persuaded.

Paul says: “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17).

Interestingly, in 2010 Colin MacLeod and colleagues at the University of Waterloo in Canada described the “production effect”: the same material is remembered better when it is read aloud than when it is read silently.

Brothers and sisters, God knew this long ago. That is why he said to Joshua: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth” (Joshua 1:8).

Shall not depart from your mouth — read God’s word out loud.

Practice 4: Checking Your Reactions — Testing the Depth of Your Thinking in Daily Life

In conflict, under pressure, in temptation, observe your first reaction and check whether God’s word is in your head or in your heart.

I suggest a very concrete method: every evening, spend three minutes recalling the moment today that stirred your emotions most. Don’t pass judgement on yourself; just honestly write down: what was my first thought at that moment?

After a week you will see a pattern. That pattern is your real lesson.

James says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22). He goes on to use the image of a mirror: someone who hears the word but doesn’t do it is like a man who looks at himself in a mirror, goes away, and forgets what he looks like (James 1:23–24).

Checking your reactions is refusing to walk away and forget.

Practice 5: Humble Longing — Admitting I Haven’t Thought Deeply Enough

When you find you can’t live it out, don’t condemn yourself; humbly ask God: Lord, let me understand your word more deeply.

Brothers and sisters, this one is very important, because after doing the first four for a while, they can easily turn into another kind of law.

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

Dallas Willard put it well: grace is not opposed to effort; it is opposed to earning.

We practise not to earn anything, but so that we are able to receive.

Using the Eight Stages to Deepen These Five Practices

Stage one, Information: today’s lesson and this verse first get into the head — a necessary first step, but only the first step.

Stage two, Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to open up the words. When you are reading for the fifth or tenth time and suddenly a sentence leaps out and speaks to you, that is revelation.

Stage three, Conviction: not just nodding, but being truly persuaded in your heart. The woman with the bleeding reached out her hand only after she had been persuaded.

Stage four, Implementation: in the very next situation you face, respond once according to that verse.

Stage five, Evaluation: in the evening, look back honestly — did I do it? Where did I get stuck?

Stage six, Correction: not blaming yourself, but adjusting. Perhaps the timing was wrong; perhaps you chose too many verses.

Stage seven, Repetition: go back to stage four and do it again. Brothers and sisters, saturation happens at this stage.

Stage eight, Multiplication: pass on what you have experienced to your “2”. As soon as you teach someone else, it goes deeper in you; what you can put into words is what has truly got into your heart.

sections.heading: 8. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Every word of the lesson’s gentle reminder is a needle.

Don’t be content with “knowing”; pursue “entering in”. Don’t stop at “having heard”; go on to “living it out”.

If your thinking doesn’t go deep enough, your life won’t change; if your thinking goes deep enough, your life will change naturally.

The lesson goes on: the humble keep letting God’s word into their hearts; the proud think they already know.

Brothers and sisters, that sentence is worth stopping on for another thirty seconds.

The greatest obstacle on the spiritual road is often not ignorance but “I already know.”

Those three words shut the door of the heart. Because once someone feels they already know, they stop longing, stop meditating, stop waiting. They clutch a Bible covered in highlights, yet inside they are empty.

Humility brings deeper sight; selflessness lets the truth become life.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

It is the same with reading the Bible. When I humbly say, “Lord, I still don’t understand,” God shows me more; when I proudly say, “I’ve heard this one before,” I stay right where I am.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson closes beautifully:

A changed life is no accident; it is the accumulation of thinking.

As deeply as you think, so truly you live.

Today God invites us not just to read his word, but to enter into his word.

When you keep meditating until you see, until you are persuaded, until you are filled, you will find that change is no longer hard and victory comes naturally.

Let me say this once more, and please keep it in your heart — victory is not something you squeeze out by gritting your teeth; victory is something that overflows.

When a cup is filled, you don’t need to order it to overflow; it simply overflows.

So this morning I’m not asking you to try harder; I’m asking you to steep yourself more deeply.

Let’s go back to that sister’s story. Later on she did something very small: instead of reading through the Bible once a month, she began to steep herself in it verse by verse. She chose one verse — “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32) — and thought on it morning, noon and night. For a whole month she meditated on that one verse alone.

Three months later she told me: “Pastor, my husband said the very same thing, and what rose up in my heart first wasn’t fire — it was that verse.”

Brothers and sisters, it wasn’t that she had become impressive; it was that God’s word had reached a certain depth in her.

May we all become people like this: God’s word saturating our hearts, the life of Christ shining out from within.

Living out a selfless life, letting Jesus live in us, letting Jesus be King, letting Jesus receive all the glory.
