l136.subtitle: Let God’s Word Move from the Head to the Heart
l136.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

blog.title: Twenty Years of Bible Reading — Undone by One Remark?

blocks.x: Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 136 · How Deep Must Our Thinking Go?

There is a sister who has believed in the Lord for twenty years. Her Bible is beautiful — not beautiful in the way a new one is, but beautiful in the way a well-read one is: the pages curl, and inside it is full of highlighter and little handwritten notes.
One day, her eyes red, she said: “Pastor, I know everything I’m supposed to know. But last night my husband said one thing, and I just exploded. Twenty years of teaching, gone in a second.”

Have you had moments like that too? You read the Bible, listen to sermons and pray — nothing is missing. Yet at the moment you are misunderstood, the moment your child answers back, the moment the test results come out, your reactions seem hardly any different from before you believed.
The question is not whether you “think”, but how far your thinking goes.
1. Words in the Head, or Words in the Heart?
When God’s word gets into the brain, you will know it; when God’s word gets into the heart, you will live it out.
Words in the head are easily forgotten; words in the heart become life.

In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus plotted the famous “forgetting curve”: newly learned material, if not reviewed, is lost fastest in the very first stretch of time. On Sunday we are deeply moved; by Friday we’ve forgotten even the pastor’s joke — not because the sermon was poor, but because it only got as far as the head and never reached the heart.
How can you tell? Look at your first reaction when you are offended.
If your first reaction is anger, the word is still in your head; if your first reaction is forgiveness, the word is already in your heart.

The Lord Jesus said: “The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45).
This is not condemnation; it is a health check. Your first reaction is the blood pressure monitor of your spiritual life.
2. Think Until You See, and Faith Is Built

The woman with the bleeding had been ill for twelve years; she had spent all she had and only grew worse. She pushed into the crowd, saying in her heart: “If I just touch his clothes, I will be made well” (Mark 5:28).

Notice: she was not merely “hoping to be healed”. She saw a picture in her heart — the crowd is huge; she pushes her way in; she reaches out her hand; she touches him. In the original, “made well” can equally be translated “saved”, and it is in the future tense: I will be saved. Not “I wonder whether …”, but “I will.”
And the result? Jesus turned and said to her: “Daughter, your faith has made you well.”
The more concrete your thinking, the more real your faith; the deeper your thinking, the more thoroughly your life is persuaded.

The Bible’s word for “meditate” is the Hebrew hagah, which originally means to murmur — like a cow chewing the cud, like a lion standing over its prey and refusing to let go. That is why God said to Joshua: “You shall meditate on it day and night” (Joshua 1:8). Day and night — that is depth.
3. Let God’s Word Reach Saturation Point
At 20 degrees Celsius, 100 grams of water can dissolve only about 36 grams of table salt; any more simply won’t dissolve. That critical point is called the saturation point.
Our hearts have a saturation point too. When a cup is full of clean water, dirty water simply can’t be poured in.
So “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11) doesn’t mean avoiding sin by gritting our teeth; it means there is no room inside for sin.

The person who relies on gritting their teeth shuts sin outside the door and holds the door shut with their body — the strength outside the door doesn’t get any weaker, but your strength grows weaker and weaker. The person who has been filled is different: they aren’t holding the door shut; they have filled the house.
So the question is not “Why do I still sin?” but “What am I filled with?”

A small cucumber that falls into vinegar for three seconds comes out still a cucumber; soak it for three days and it becomes a pickle — and it can never turn back. Saturation is not straining; it is steeping.
Five Small Things You Can Start Today
1. Repeated meditation: choose just one verse a day, and think on it morning, noon and night.
2. Picturing Scripture: turn the verse into a concrete scene, and let the truth become visible.
3. Declaring to internalise: read it out loud. “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth” (Joshua 1:8).
4. Checking your reactions: three minutes each evening, honestly writing down what your first thought was today.
5. Humble longing: when you can’t live it out, don’t condemn yourself; just ask the Lord to help you understand his word more deeply.
The humble keep letting God’s word into their hearts; the proud think they already know.
The greatest obstacle on the spiritual road is often not ignorance but those three words: “I already know.”
Brothers and sisters, victory is not something you squeeze out by gritting your teeth; victory is something that overflows. When a cup is full, you don’t need to order it to overflow.

May we all become people like this: God’s word saturating our hearts, the life of Christ shining out from within — living out a selfless life, letting Jesus be King, letting Jesus receive all the glory.
Reflection
This month, which verse will you choose to think over again and again, every day, until it forms a picture in your heart?

script12.title: How Deep Must Our Thinking Go?
script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are looking together at Lesson 136 of Morning Devotion 321: How Deep Must Our Thinking Go? — Let God’s Word Move from the Head to the Heart.
Our key verse is Psalm 119 verse 11: “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.”

script12.title: How Far Does Your Thinking Go?
script: There is a sister who has believed in the Lord for twenty years, and her Bible is covered in highlighter. One day, her eyes red, she said: “Pastor, I know everything I’m supposed to know. But yesterday my husband said one thing, and I just exploded.”
Brothers and sisters, isn’t this our story too?
Today God wants to ask us a deeper question: how far does your thinking go?
Many people’s lives don’t change, not because they don’t think, but because they don’t think deeply enough, they don’t think long enough, and their thinking never reaches the heart.

It’s like making tea. Dip the teabag in for one second, and it’s still a cup of water; leave it for three minutes, and the colour, the aroma and the flavour are completely changed. There is only one difference — how long it steeps.

script12.title: Key Verse and Background
script: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the whole Bible, with 176 verses. It is an acrostic poem of twenty-two stanzas of eight verses each, matching the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet.

“Hidden” is the Hebrew tsaphan, meaning to store treasure away in the most secret place. “Heart” is the Hebrew lev, which means not just the emotions but the centre of our thinking, will and decisions.
So “hidden in my heart” doesn’t mean being moved for a moment; it means letting God’s word become the way I think.

script12.title: Words in the Head, Words in the Heart
script: The lesson says: when God’s word gets into the brain, you will know it; when it gets into the heart, you will live it out.
In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus plotted the forgetting curve. He found that newly learned material, if not reviewed, is lost fastest in the very first stretch of time.
Brothers and sisters, that is a picture of us. On Sunday we are deeply moved; by Friday we have forgotten it all.
It isn’t that the sermon was poor; it’s that the sermon only got as far as the head and never reached the heart.

script12.title: Your First Reaction Is the Test
script: How can you tell whether God’s word is in your head or in your heart? Look at what your first reaction is when you are offended.
If your first reaction is anger, the word is still in your head; if your first reaction is forgiveness, the word is already in your heart.

The psychologist Daniel Kahneman says in “Thinking, Fast and Slow” that we have two systems of thinking: System 1 is fast and automatic, System 2 slow and effortful. The verses you have memorised live in System 2, but the remark that wounds you strikes System 1.
The Lord Jesus said: “For out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45).
This is not condemnation; it is a health check.

script12.title: Think Until You See
script: The second teaching: let your thinking become a picture, until faith is built.
The Bible’s word for “meditate” is the Hebrew hagah, which originally means to murmur — like a cow chewing the cud, like a lion standing over its prey and refusing to let go.
That is why God said to Joshua: “You shall meditate on it day and night” (Joshua 1:8).
Day and night — that is depth. The depth of your thinking determines the strength of your faith.

script12.title: The Picture in the Bleeding Woman’s Heart
script: The woman with the bleeding had been ill for twelve years and had spent all she had. She pushed into the crowd, saying in her heart: “If I just touch his clothes, I will be made well” (Mark 5:28).
Brothers and sisters, she wasn’t merely “hoping”. She saw a picture in her heart: the crowd is huge; she pushes her way in; she reaches out her hand; she touches him.
In the original, “made well” can also be translated “saved”, and it is in the future tense — I will be saved.
Jesus turned and said to her: “Daughter, your faith has made you well” (Mark 5:34).
The more concrete your thinking, the more real your faith.

script12.title: Let God’s Word Reach Saturation
script: The third teaching: let God’s word reach saturation point.
At 20 degrees Celsius, 100 grams of water can dissolve only about 36 grams of salt; any more simply won’t dissolve. That is called the saturation point.
The lesson’s picture is even simpler: when a cup is full of clean water, dirty water can’t be poured in.
Thought over once, ten times, a hundred times, God’s word slowly fills your heart.
A cucumber in vinegar for three seconds is still a cucumber; soak it for three days and it becomes a pickle, and it can never turn back.

script12.title: Not Holding Back, but No Room
script: So the meaning of this verse is not that we avoid sin by gritting our teeth, but that there is no room inside for sin.
The person who relies on gritting their teeth is holding the door shut with their body. The strength outside the door doesn’t get any weaker, but your strength grows weaker and weaker.

The Lord Jesus said that when the unclean spirit comes back and finds the house “empty, swept, and put in order” (Matthew 12:44), it brings in seven other spirits more evil than itself to live there. That house was very clean; the problem was that it was empty.
That is why Paul says: “Be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18).
The question is not “Why do I still sin?” but — “What am I filled with?”

script12.title: Five Practices
script: The lesson gives us five practices.
First, repeated meditation: one verse a day, thought on morning, noon and night.
Second, picturing Scripture: turn the verse into a picture.
Third, declaring to internalise: read it out loud, because “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth” (Joshua 1:8).
Fourth, checking your reactions: three minutes each evening, honestly writing down your first thought of the day.
Fifth, humble longing: when you can’t live it out, don’t condemn yourself; just ask the Lord to help you understand his word more deeply.
Then deepen them with 321’s eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Saturation happens at the stage of Repetition.

script12.title: As Deeply as You Think, So Truly You Live
script: The lesson reminds us: the humble keep letting God’s word into their hearts; the proud think they already know.
Brothers and sisters, the greatest obstacle on the spiritual road is often not ignorance but “I already know.”
Later that sister spent a whole month thinking on just one verse. Three months on she said: “My husband said the very same thing, and what rose up in my heart first wasn’t fire — it was that verse.”
Victory is not something you squeeze out by gritting your teeth; victory is something that overflows.

script12.title: Response Prayer and Blessing
script: Let us declare together: I will let God’s word enter my heart; my heart is filled with the truth, and sin has no room in me; I will surely live out Christ, and I will be a Victor.
Dear Lord Jesus, carry your word from our heads into our hearts, until it reaches saturation. Whenever we want to say, “I already know this,” remind us to think it through once more, a little deeper.
Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you and give you peace.

script21.title: How Deep Must Our Thinking Go?
script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are looking at Lesson 136 of Morning Devotion 321: How Deep Must Our Thinking Go? — Let God’s Word Move from the Head to the Heart.
Our key verse is Psalm 119 verse 11: “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.”
Please read it softly to yourself once first. Don’t rush; let it rest in your heart for a moment.

script21.title: The Bible Covered in Highlights
script: There is a sister who has believed in the Lord for twenty years. Her Bible is beautiful — not beautiful in the way a new one is, but beautiful in the way a well-read one is, full of highlighter and notes.
One day, her eyes red, she said: “Pastor, I know everything I’m supposed to know. But last night my husband said one thing, and I just exploded. Twenty years of teaching, gone in a second.”
Brothers and sisters, that isn’t her story alone. At the moment we are misunderstood, the moment our child answers back, our reactions seem hardly any different from before we believed. Why?

script21.title: How Far Does Your Thinking Go?
script: The lesson asks very honestly: we already know that thinking matters — but how far does your thinking go?
Many people’s lives don’t change, not because they don’t think, but because they don’t think deeply enough, they don’t think long enough, and their thinking never reaches the heart.

When you make tea, if you dip the teabag in for one second and pull it out, it’s still a cup of water; leave it for three minutes, and the colour, the aroma and the flavour are completely changed. There is only one difference — how long it steeps.
The same verse steeped in you for one second, or steeped for three years, gives completely different results.

In the 321 vision: relying on the brain is relying on ourselves; relying on the heart is relying on the Holy Spirit. Today we are going to learn one thing: how to move God’s word from “knowing” to “becoming”.

script21.title: Key Verse and Background
script: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the whole Bible, with 176 verses. It is an acrostic poem: twenty-two stanzas of eight verses each, matching the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet. The form itself is saying something — meditating on God’s word is meant to be done from beginning to end, leaving nothing out.

The author is not named, but from lines like “The arrogant mock me excessively, but I don’t swerve from your law” (Psalm 119:51), we can tell he didn’t write it in a quiet study; he wrote it in the midst of the storm.
Just before it comes: “How can a young man keep his way pure? By living according to your word” (Psalm 119:9). Notice the order — not changing behaviour first, but changing what is inside first.
“Hidden” is the Hebrew tsaphan, meaning to store treasure away in the most secret place.

script21.title: Words in the Head, Words in the Heart
script: The first teaching. The lesson says: when God’s word gets into the brain, you will know it; when it gets into the heart, you will live it out. Words in the head are easily forgotten; words in the heart become life.
In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus plotted the famous forgetting curve. He found that newly learned material, if not reviewed, is lost fastest in the very first stretch of time.
Brothers and sisters, that is a picture of us. On Sunday we are deeply moved; on Monday we still remember half of it; by Friday we’ve forgotten even the joke.
It isn’t that the sermon was poor; it’s that the sermon only got as far as the head and never reached the heart.

script21.title: The “Heart” in the Bible
script: What does the Bible mean by the “heart”? The Hebrew is lev. In Chinese we tend to take the heart to mean the emotions, but the Hebrew heart is the centre of a person’s thinking, will and decisions.
That is why Proverbs says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).
So “hidden in my heart” doesn’t mean being moved for a moment; it means letting God’s word become the way I think and the instinct behind my reactions.

Jeremiah says: “Your words were found, and I ate them” (Jeremiah 15:16). Notice the verb — ate. A recipe stuck on the fridge won’t put a single kilo on you; food has to be eaten before it becomes your flesh and blood.

script21.title: Your First Reaction Is the Test
script: How can you tell whether God’s word is in your head or in your heart? Look at what your first reaction is when you are offended.
If your first reaction is anger, the word is still in your head; if your first reaction is forgiveness, the word is already in your heart.

The psychologist Daniel Kahneman says in “Thinking, Fast and Slow” that we have two systems of thinking: System 1 is fast and automatic, System 2 slow and effortful; most of our everyday reactions are run by System 1.
Brothers and sisters, the verses you have memorised live in System 2, but the remark that wounds you strikes System 1.
The Lord Jesus said it long before: “For out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45).
This is not condemnation; it is a health check. Your first reaction is the blood pressure monitor of your spiritual life.

script21.title: Selflessness Lets God’s Word Rule
script: The lesson’s insight is this: selflessness lets God’s word dwell in the heart; the self-centred life lets our own ideas rule.
The self-centred life doesn’t necessarily mean doing something wicked. The self-centred life means that inside me, the one who has the final say is still me.
Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is entering into the infinite. Paul says: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).
The second of the Three Foundations is: the Bible is my standard. A standard isn’t a slogan hanging on the wall; it is the steering wheel you turn by at the crossroads.
Charles Spurgeon is commonly said to have described John Bunyan like this: prick him anywhere, and what flows out is Scripture. That is “becoming”.

script21.title: Think Again and Again, Think Deeply
script: The second teaching: let your thinking become a picture, until faith is built.
“Meditate” is the Hebrew hagah, which originally means to murmur; Isaiah uses the same word for a lion growling over its prey (Isaiah 31:4).
So biblical meditation is not emptying the mind; it is like a cow chewing the cud, bringing up a mouthful of grass and chewing it again; like a lion standing over its prey and refusing to let go.
God said to Joshua: “You shall meditate on it day and night” (Joshua 1:8). The psalmist says: “But his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2).
Day and night — brothers and sisters, that is depth.
Luke says: “But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19). In the original, it means putting things together piece by piece, slowly assembling a complete picture.

script21.title: The Picture in the Bleeding Woman’s Heart
script: The example the lesson gives is very clear — the woman with the bleeding. She had been ill for twelve years; she “had spent all that she had, and was no better, but rather grew worse” (Mark 5:26).
She pushed into the crowd, saying in her heart: “If I just touch his clothes, I will be made well” (Mark 5:28).
Brothers and sisters, she wasn’t merely “hoping”. She saw a picture in her heart: the crowd is huge; she pushes her way in; she reaches out her hand; she touches him.
In the original, “made well” is sōzō, which can equally be translated “saved”, and it is in the future tense — I will be saved. Not “I wonder whether …”, but “I will.”
And immediately the flow of her blood was dried up. Jesus turned and said: “Daughter, your faith has made you well” (Mark 5:34).
The Lord did not say, “My power has healed you”; what the Lord said was, “Your faith has made you well.”

script21.title: Counting Stars, Seeing Grasshoppers
script: The Bible gives two more examples, one positive and one negative.

The positive one is Abraham. God brought him outside and said: “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them … So your offspring will be” (Genesis 15:5). God could simply have said, “You will have many descendants,” but he let that picture be engraved on his eyes.
The negative one is the ten spies: “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers” (Numbers 13:33).
They had a picture in their hearts too — only in that picture the main character was a grasshopper, not God.
Brothers and sisters, the question has never been whether to have a picture, but — who is the main character in your picture?

script21.title: Seeing the Unseen
script: The lesson says: the very essence of faith is seeing what cannot be seen.
Hebrews says: “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). Moses too “endured, as seeing him who is invisible” (Hebrews 11:27).

Paul says: “For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18). This is 321’s shift of perspective: from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal.

A 1994 meta-analysis by John Driskell and colleagues showed that rehearsing an action over and over in the mind really does improve performance. But I want to say this very carefully: faith is built not on the power of imagination but on the promises of God.
The one who relies on the brain stands outside the crowd doing sums: how could I ever squeeze through? The one who relies on the heart sees this: Jesus is right there, and I only need to touch him.

script21.title: Thinking Can Become Saturated
script: The third teaching: let God’s word reach saturation point, and life changes naturally.

In chemistry, at 20 degrees Celsius, 100 grams of water can dissolve about 36 grams of table salt; beyond that amount, however much you stir, it won’t dissolve. That critical point is called the saturation point.
Brothers and sisters, our hearts have a saturation point too. The difference is what you let fill them.
The lesson’s picture is even simpler: when a cup is full of clean water, dirty water can’t be poured in.
A small cucumber that falls into vinegar for three seconds is still a cucumber; soak it for three days and it becomes a pickle — and it can never turn back.
That is what saturation means: not straining, but steeping; not forcing, but coming naturally.

script21.title: Repetition Is the Only Road
script: Between “thinking it once” and “saturation” stands one word: repetition.

In 2006 Nicholas Cepeda, Harold Pashler and colleagues published a meta-analysis covering more than a hundred studies in the “Psychological Bulletin”: for the same total time, spreading review across several days is far more effective than cramming it all into one. Other research shows that continuing to practise after you have already learned something markedly extends how long the memory is retained.
Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: continuing after you have already learned it. Isn’t that exactly “meditating day and night”?

In 2000 Eleanor Maguire and colleagues at University College London found that the rear part of the hippocampus in London taxi drivers was markedly larger than in ordinary people, and the longer they had been driving, the more marked the difference. When God made us, he wrote into our very bodies the fact that repetition shapes you. Only one question remains: what are you going to repeat?

script21.title: Not Holding Back, but No Room
script: Here the lesson has its most precious sentence: we don’t avoid sin by gritting our teeth; we avoid it because there is no room inside for sin.

The person who relies on gritting their teeth shuts sin outside the door and holds the door shut with their body. The strength outside the door doesn’t get any weaker, but your strength grows weaker and weaker. So many people are not ungodly; they are simply exhausted.
The person who has been filled is different. They aren’t holding the door shut; they have filled the house.

The Lord Jesus said that when the unclean spirit comes back and finds the house “empty, swept, and put in order” (Matthew 12:44), it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself to live there.
That house was very clean; the problem was — it was empty. The most dangerous state for the spiritual life is not dirty; it is empty.
That is why Paul says: “Be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18). In the original it is in the present tense: be filled continually, on and on.

script21.title: What Am I Filled With?
script: The lesson turns the question completely on its head.

We are used to asking: why do I still lose my temper? Asked that way, the focus is on ourselves; the more we ask, the more we condemn ourselves, and the more we condemn ourselves, the more powerless we become.
The lesson teaches us to ask instead: what am I filled with?
The Lord Jesus said: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34).
When someone bumps into a cup, what splashes out? Whatever was already in it.
Brothers and sisters, the people and events that bump into you don’t create your reactions; they only splash out what was already inside you.
So don’t blame the person who bumped into you. Thank them — they’ve given you a free health check.

script21.title: Practices 1 to 3
script: The lesson gives us five practical exercises.

First, repeated meditation: each day choose one verse and think on it morning, noon and night, until it surfaces of its own accord. Please don’t be greedy for more; one verse a day is better than ten chapters. George Müller mentions in his own account that from 1841 onwards he changed his order: instead of beginning to pray as soon as he got up, he first meditated on God’s word until his heart was fed.

Second, picturing Scripture: when you read “Yahweh is my shepherd” (Psalm 23:1), see the green pastures and the still waters. This is not fantasy; it is letting God’s word develop in your heart, like old-fashioned film that has to soak long enough.

Third, declaring to internalise: read it out loud. In 2010 Colin MacLeod and colleagues at the University of Waterloo described the “production effect”: what we read aloud is remembered better than what we read silently. That is why God said: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth” (Joshua 1:8).

script21.title: Practices 4 and 5, and the Eight Stages
script: Fourth, checking your reactions: every evening, spend three minutes recalling the moment today that stirred your emotions most. Don’t pass judgement on yourself; just honestly write down your first thought. After a week you will see a pattern, and that pattern is your real lesson. James says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22).

Fifth, humble longing: when you can’t live it out, don’t condemn yourself; just ask the Lord to help you understand his word more deeply. “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). Dallas Willard said: grace is not opposed to effort; it is opposed to earning.

Then deepen them with 321’s eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Saturation happens at Repetition; and what has truly got into your heart is what you can explain to someone else — that is Multiplication.

script21.title: Summing Up the 3-2-1 Vision
script: Let’s set today’s message back within the whole picture of 321.

Jesus is my role model: when the Lord was tempted in the wilderness, at the moment he was hungriest, what came out was “It is written” (Matthew 4:4) — because the word of God had long been in him. The Bible is my standard, and the Holy Spirit is my guide: it is the Holy Spirit who turns the letter into life.
Let Jesus be King — the first place the King must reign is your thinking. Paul speaks of “bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5).
The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change your mindset and your life changes.
920: live out selflessness before every “2”, and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. Fruit is borne, not squeezed out.
235: find a spiritual companion and ask each other — how deep has your thinking gone today?

script21.title: As Deeply as You Think, So Truly You Live
script: Every word of the lesson’s gentle reminder is a needle: don’t be content with “knowing”; pursue “entering in”. Don’t stop at “having heard”; go on to “living it out”. The humble keep letting God’s word into their hearts; the proud think they already know.

Brothers and sisters, the greatest obstacle on the spiritual road is often not ignorance but those three words, “I already know.” Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Later that sister chose one verse and for a whole month thought on that verse alone. Three months on she said: “My husband said the very same thing, and what rose up in my heart first wasn’t fire — it was that verse.”
Brothers and sisters, victory is not something you squeeze out by gritting your teeth; victory is something that overflows. When a cup is full, you don’t need to order it to overflow.

script21.title: Response Prayer and Blessing
script: Let us declare together: I will meditate on God’s word; I will let God’s word enter my heart. My heart is filled with the truth; sin has no room in me. I will surely live out Christ; I will surely be an overcomer. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!

Dear Lord Jesus, thank you that this morning you have spoken to us once again. We know a great deal and live out very little; have mercy on us. Carry your word from our heads into our hearts; let the letter become life, let knowledge become faith. Let your word reach saturation in us — so saturated that sin has no room.
Guard our humility. Whenever we want to say, “I already know this,” remind us to think it through once more, a little deeper.
Living out a selfless life, letting Jesus be King, letting Jesus receive all the glory. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; may the Lord lift up his face toward you and give you peace.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Every Day You Use a Power You Think Is Ordinary
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

In 321 Morning Devotion we have already walked together through “seeing”, “listening” and “thinking”. We have learned what our eyes should look at, what our ears should listen to, and what our minds should dwell on. Today God wants to lead us into a dimension that is absolutely crucial and deeply practical: “speaking”.

Please be still for three seconds and think back: from yesterday morning until now, how much have you said? What did you say to your family? What did you type in your group chats? What did you say to yourself in your own heart?

In 2007 the psychologist Matthias Mehl of the University of Arizona and his colleagues published a study in the journal Science. Using recording devices that sampled at random, they captured the everyday conversation of nearly four hundred university students, and they found that men and women alike speak, on average, about sixteen thousand words a day. Sixteen thousand words is six times the length of a long sermon. Brothers and sisters, every day we sow sixteen thousand “seeds”, and yet very few of us have ever seriously asked: what exactly am I scattering?

Many people assume that speaking is just expression, just habit, just a matter of pouring out whatever is in our heads. But the Bible shows us something entirely different:

Speech is a power.

Speech is an influence.

Speech is the outlet of life.

James puts it plainly: “So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!” (James 3:5)

The flame of a single match is so small you can pinch it out between two fingers; yet drop that same match onto a dry forest floor and it can burn down a whole mountainside. The tongue is like that. It is one of the smallest organs in the human body, weighing only sixty-odd grams, yet it can kindle the fury of an entire household, and it can also kindle the hope of a whole lifetime.

One sentence can set a person alight.

One sentence can also destroy a person.

I often think of a scene that really happened. A sister in her forties, successful in her career, was weeping in her small group so hard she could not speak. She said, “When I was in the third grade, my teacher said in front of the whole class, ‘Someone like you will never amount to anything.’ More than thirty years have passed, and those words are still ringing in my ears.” Brothers and sisters, that teacher has probably long forgotten what she said. But those words were like a red-hot iron, branding a little girl’s heart for thirty years.

That is the power of “speaking”.

In the 321 vision we see this very clearly:

The selfless person lets God govern his mouth, and his words build up life.

The self-centred person lets himself govern his mouth, and his words release destruction.

So what we are learning today is not “speaking skills” and not a “communication course”. It is something deeper: letting our mouths become vessels for God’s work, and letting our “speaking” bring forth life and revival.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: Why James Spends a Whole Chapter on the Tongue
sections.html:
Before we come to the three teachings, let us first get our footing on the scriptural foundation.

Our theme passage comes from James chapter 3. The author of the letter of James is generally held to be James, the brother of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh (Galatians 1:19 calls him “James, the Lord’s brother”). This James did not at first believe in Jesus (John 7:5 records, “For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.”), until the risen Lord appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7). Then he became a pillar of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:9), and he presided over the Jerusalem Council around AD 50 (Acts 15).

The letter of James is generally dated quite early, somewhere around AD 45 to 50, and it may well be one of the earliest books of the New Testament to be written. He wrote to “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1) — Jewish believers scattered across the Roman Empire by persecution. They lived under pressure, in poverty, oppressed and tested.

Brothers and sisters, please notice something: when people are under pressure, the first thing to give way is usually the mouth. James knew this all too well. So right at the start of his letter he says, “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Then at the end of the first chapter he adds a very weighty sentence: “If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn’t bridle his tongue, but deceives his heart, this man’s religion is worthless.” (James 1:26)

In other words, as James sees it, whether a person’s faith is genuine is shown not by how many meetings he attends, but by his mouth.

By chapter 3 he simply devotes an entire chapter to the matter. He begins with three images: the horse’s bit (verse 3), the ship’s rudder (verse 4) and fire (verses 5–6). What the three images share is this — something small with a great effect.

“Indeed, we put bits into the horses’ mouths so that they may obey us, and we guide their whole body.” (James 3:3)

“Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds, are yet guided by a very small rudder, wherever the pilot desires.” (James 3:4)

“So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!” (James 3:5)

“And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.” (James 3:6)

See the order here: the bit and the rudder are about “direction”; the fire is about “destruction”. The tongue sets the direction of a person’s life, and it can also burn up everything in a person’s life. On a three-hundred-thousand-tonne oil tanker, the rudder is less than one per cent of the size of the hull, yet it decides where the ship goes. Brothers and sisters, your tongue is the rudder of your life.

Our other theme passage, Matthew 12:34, has a different background. The Pharisees had seen Jesus cast out demons, and they went so far as to say that he cast them out by Beelzebul, the prince of demons (Matthew 12:24). Jesus answered them: “You offspring of vipers, how can you, being evil, speak good things? For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34) Then he went on: “The good man out of his good treasure brings out good things, and the evil man out of his evil treasure brings out evil things.” (Matthew 12:35)

The Lord Jesus ties the “mouth” directly to the “heart”. The mouth is not an organ that operates on its own; the mouth is the outlet of the heart.

With this background in place, we can enter today’s three teachings.

sections.heading: 3. Teaching 1: Speaking Is the Fruit of Life and the Outlet of Life
sections.html:
1. The Lord Jesus’ diagnosis: the mouth is the heart’s dashboard

The Lord Jesus said:

“For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34b)

Luke records it more fully: “The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.” (Luke 6:45)

The word “abundance” is the Greek perisseuma, meaning “what overflows”, “the surplus that spills over”. The same family of words is used in Matthew 14:20 of what was left after the five loaves and two fish: “They took up twelve baskets full of that which remained left over from the broken pieces.” In other words, what comes out of your mouth is not the part of your heart you “carefully select”; it is the part your heart is “too full to hold, so that it spills out on its own”.

Brothers and sisters, this is why someone can be perfectly well-mannered most of the time, yet the moment you touch a sore spot, the words come bursting out. That is not “abnormal”; that is what is “normal” — it is what is overflowing from inside.

So “speaking” is not only a problem; “speaking” is an indicator. It is like a car’s dashboard. When a red light comes on, you don’t cover it with tape; you check the engine. Yet the way we deal with our own mouths is often just “applying tape”: holding it in, putting on good behaviour, rephrasing things more nicely. God wants us to open the bonnet.

2. Two lists: what is your mouth revealing?

When a person is always complaining, always judging, always negative, that is not a problem of the mouth; it is that the heart is full of these things.

When a person is always encouraging, always building up, always full of faith, it is not that he is eloquent; it is because there is life within him.

Solomon put this truth beautifully: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

The wellspring of life flows from the heart — not from the mouth. The mouth is only the pipe that carries it.

So “speaking” has two functions:

First, it reveals what is inside you.

Second, it releases what is inside you.

Whatever is inside will flow out. If the water drawn up from a well is salty, you don’t blame the bucket. That is exactly what James says: “Does a spring send out from the same opening fresh and bitter water?” (James 3:11)

3. Confirmation from psychology: the ratio of five to one

From the 1970s onwards, the psychologist John Gottman, of the University of Washington, studied the interaction of married couples over many years using video recordings and physiological measurements. He and Robert Levenson found a remarkably stable pattern: in couples whose relationships stayed stable, the ratio of positive to negative behaviour in their interactions was about five to one, while in couples heading towards breakdown that ratio was markedly lower. Gottman described long-term contempt, criticism, defensiveness and stonewalling as destructive patterns of interaction in a relationship.

Please note, this is not a technique of “say more nice things and all will be well”. On the contrary, Gottman’s research confirms the Bible’s order: those five-to-one positive interactions are not performed; they flow from a heart that still treasures the other person. If the heart has dried up, nice words won’t hold out for long.

Science can only measure the “ratio”; the Bible tells us the “source”. The source is the heart.

4. An everyday example: the spilled glass of milk

A brother once told me that when he was little he knocked over a glass of milk at the dinner table. His father didn’t scold him. He just picked up a cloth and, as he wiped, said, “Never mind — your hands are still learning.” He said that one sentence, “your hands are still learning”, gave him the courage all his life to try, to fail and to have another go.

The same glass of milk, and a father in another family might say, “How can you be so stupid!” — the same incident, two sentences, two different lives.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? That father was able to say “your hands are still learning” not because he had studied communication skills, but because there was grace in his heart towards his child. Only a person with grace in his heart can have grace flow from his mouth.

5. A 321 insight: thinking determines speaking; speaking reveals the heart

In the 321 sequence we see a clear chain:

See → Listen → Think → Speak.

Thinking determines speaking; speaking reveals the heart.

So don’t change only your “speaking”. To change only the speaking is to work on the fruit; God wants us to go back to the root.

Change your “seeing” — where are your eyes fixed? On your circumstances, or on Jesus?

Change your “listening” — what voices do you let into you every day? The voices of the world, or the word of God?

Change your “thinking” — what fills your mind? The human, the earthly, the temporary, the worldly; or the divine, the heavenly, the eternal, the godly?

This is exactly the fivefold change that 321 speaks of: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes.

When the inside is right, the outside will naturally be right. You no longer need to “control” your mouth, because a heart filled with the Holy Spirit will naturally pour out words that build up.

sections.heading: 4. Teaching 2: Speaking Is Sowing, and It Determines the Fruit to Come
sections.html:
1. Words are seeds

When the Lord Jesus explained the parable of the sower, he said:

“Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.” (Luke 8:11)

Brothers and sisters, see this spiritual principle: words are seeds.

God himself created the world by his word. “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” (Genesis 1:3) The writer to the Hebrews says, “By faith, we understand that the universe has been framed by the word of God, so that what is seen has not been made out of things which are visible.” (Hebrews 11:3)

We are created in the image of God (Genesis 1:27). Our words certainly do not have the power to create a universe, but God has placed a real “authority to sow” in our mouths. Solomon says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” (Proverbs 18:21)

Notice the second half — “will eat its fruit”. The words you send out today will one day become food, served back up at your own table.

2. You are sowing every day

You speak to yourself: “I can’t do it”, “That’s just the way I am”, “I’m bound to mess it up again”.

You speak to others: “Why are you always like this?”, “You’re hopeless”, “Suit yourself”.

You speak to your circumstances: “It’s impossible”, “It’s too late”, “This family is finished”.

The question is not “Are you sowing?” but “What are you sowing?”

If you keep saying “I can’t”, “It’s impossible”, “It’s bound to fail”, you are sowing negative seeds, and one day you will reap negative fruit.

If you keep saying “God can”, “God reigns”, “God will surely accomplish it”, you are sowing seeds of faith, and one day you will reap the fruit of life.

Paul states this principle with absolute firmness: “Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.” (Galatians 6:7) In the next verse he divides the seed into two kinds: “For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.” (Galatians 6:8)

3. A warning from the wilderness: Israel buried itself with its own mouth

There is a deeply sobering account in the Bible. Twelve spies came back from Canaan, and ten of them said, “The land, through which we have gone to spy it out, is a land that eats up its inhabitants; and all the people who we saw in it are men of great stature.” (Numbers 13:32) “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.” (Numbers 13:33)

When the whole congregation heard it, they wept aloud and grumbled: “We wish that we had died in the land of Egypt, or that we had died in this wilderness!” (Numbers 14:2)

And then God’s answer is one of the most fearful sentences in the whole Bible:

“Tell them, ‘As I live, says Yahweh, surely as you have spoken in my ears, so I will do to you.’” (Numbers 14:28)

Brothers and sisters, God was saying: as you have spoken, so I will bring it about. They said, “We wish we had died in this wilderness,” and they really did die in the wilderness. With their own mouths they dug their own graves.

By contrast, Caleb and Joshua said, “Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!” (Numbers 13:30) Forty years later, only those two men entered Canaan.

The same wilderness, the same God; different words, different endings.

4. Supporting evidence from psychology and science

Barbara Fredrickson, a psychologist at the University of North Carolina, proposed the “broaden-and-build theory” (1998, 2001). Her research shows that positive emotions broaden the range of thoughts and actions open to a person in the moment, and over time build up personal psychological, social and physical resources, whereas negative emotions narrow our thinking.

This explains exactly why negative words have a compounding effect: they make a person’s world smaller with every word, their options fewer and fewer, until at last they truly come to a dead end.

Another classic study is the experiment published in 1998 by the Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck and Claudia Mueller. After children completed a task, they were praised in different ways: one group was told, “You’re very clever,” the other, “You worked very hard.” In later tests, the children praised for being “clever” tended to choose easier problems and their performance dropped after a setback, while the children praised for “effort” were more willing to take on difficult problems.

Brothers and sisters, both were “kind words”, but the seeds sown were different. What one sentence plants may be the posture with which a person faces difficulty for the rest of his life.

5. A 321 insight: the selfless speak God’s words; the self-centred speak their own

In the 321 vision this is very clear:

The selfless person speaks God’s words and sows the seed of life.

The self-centred person speaks his own words and sows the seed of corruption.

The self-centred mouth has three typical voices: complaining (I am not satisfied with God’s arrangements), judging (I want to sit in the judgement seat) and boasting (I want others to notice me). All three share the same root — pride. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. When I judge someone, I have in fact climbed onto the seat only God may sit on.

Selflessness does not mean saying nothing; it does not mean becoming a silent person. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20a). When Christ lives in me, he also speaks in me.

So every day we need to ask ourselves one question:

Are the words I have spoken today building the future, or tearing it down?

sections.heading: 5. Teaching 3: Right Speaking Brings Change and Revival
sections.html:
1. If no one speaks, no one hears

Right speaking affects not only ourselves but others too.

In Romans, Paul pushes this sequence all the way with a string of questions:

“How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher? And how will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things!’” (Romans 10:14–15)

Then Paul sums it up: “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” (Romans 10:17)

Brothers and sisters, see this chain:

Because someone speaks, someone hears; because someone hears, someone believes; because someone believes, someone is changed.

There is a word here well worth noticing. “Preach the Good News … bring glad tidings” in Romans 10:15 is quoted from Isaiah 52:7, and the Greek uses euangelizō, the verb “to announce good news”; the noun “gospel” (euangelion) comes from the same root. The gospel is not, in itself, an idea; the gospel is “good news that must be spoken”. Good news that is never spoken might as well not exist for the one who never hears it.

2. The Lord Jesus’ ministry began with “speaking”

The very first thing the Lord Jesus did when he began his ministry was to speak:

“From that time, Jesus began to preach, and to say, ‘Repent! For the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.’” (Matthew 4:17)

He didn’t first build a synagogue or first organise a team; first he opened his mouth. The disciples heard, left their nets and followed him (Matthew 4:20).

On the day of Pentecost, Peter stood up and preached. What kind of Peter was this? The same Peter who, a few weeks earlier, had three times denied the Lord before a servant girl. But once he was filled with the Holy Spirit, he opened his mouth. And the Bible records: “Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls.” (Acts 2:41)

Three thousand people, one sermon. Not because Peter was eloquent, but because the Holy Spirit was in him, and a risen Lord with him.

Later, Peter and John were arrested by the council, and the rulers strictly forbade them to teach any more in the name of Jesus. Their reply was:

“For we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.” (Acts 4:20)

“We can’t help telling” — how powerful those words are! When it is in you, you will surely speak. When it isn’t in you, even what you say is empty.

3. The pathway of revival: seeing, hearing, understanding, speaking out

Brothers and sisters, this is the pathway of revival:

Seeing → Hearing → Understanding → Speaking out.

If it stays only “inside”, revival will not happen. The light God gives you, if it stays only in your notebook, is merely your own property; when you speak it out, it becomes food for others.

It must be spoken out before it can flow out.

Church history bears witness to this. In the Welsh Revival of 1904, a young miner named Evan Roberts led meeting after meeting in which people prayed, confessed their sins out loud and praised God out loud. Within just a few months, by some estimates, more than a hundred thousand people came to faith in Christ, and the pubs and the courts of the coalfields became noticeably quiet. The change began with a group of people who were willing to open their mouths.

Look further back: the Reformation of the sixteenth century began when Luther nailed his “Ninety-five Theses” to the church door in Wittenberg — that too was “speaking”, only with a pen. The Great Awakening of the eighteenth century began with George Whitefield and John Wesley preaching in the open fields — again, “speaking”.

Our own era is no different. On 28 August 1963, in front of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, Dr Martin Luther King Jr delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech, and it changed the conscience of a nation. Words have that kind of power.

4. But be careful: speaking can also hinder God’s work

But, brothers and sisters, we must be honest. Speaking can bring revival, and speaking can also quench it.

In a small group, it takes only one person who keeps complaining, judging and taking potshots for the fire of the whole group to slowly go out. This is what James means: “And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.” (James 3:6)

James goes on with words that should make us blush: “With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God. Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.” (James 3:9–10)

The same mouth sings praise to God on Sunday and curses people at the office on Monday. James says: these things ought not to be so.

So Paul gives us a very practical standard:

“Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.” (Ephesians 4:29)

“What is good for building others up as the need may be” — not saying pretty things, but saying words that build people up “according to the need of the moment”. The original word for “building up” (oikodomē) is a builder’s term; it means “putting up a house”. Every word you speak either adds a brick to someone’s life or pulls one out.

Paul also says, “Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.” (Colossians 4:6) Salt does two things: it gives flavour and it preserves. Gracious words make people willing to listen; words seasoned with salt keep people from going bad.

5. Supporting evidence from psychology: expectations come true

In 1968 the American psychologists Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson carried out a famous study at a primary school in San Francisco. They tested the pupils, then chose some of them at random and told the teachers that these children were “about to blossom”. A school year later, the children who had been picked at random really did show greater gains on intelligence tests than the others. The researchers called this the “Pygmalion effect” — other people’s expectations, conveyed through language and interaction, actually shape a person’s performance.

Brothers and sisters, psychology calls it “expectation”; the Bible calls it “blessing”. Jacob blessed his twelve sons (Genesis 49), Isaac blessed Jacob (Genesis 27), and the Lord Jesus laid his hands on the children and blessed them (Mark 10:16). God’s children have authority to bless.

Did you know? In a child’s life, the first person who tells him “You can do it” often decides whether he will dare to try.

6. A 321 insight: speaking for the Lord brings forth God’s work

The selfless person speaks for the Lord, and so brings forth God’s work.

The self-centred person either says nothing or speaks recklessly, and so hinders God’s work.

“Saying nothing” usually comes from fear — fear of rejection, fear of being laughed at, fear of losing face. The root of that fear is still the self-centred life: I care too much about myself.

“Speaking recklessly” usually comes from wanting — wanting to prove I’m right, wanting to beat the other person, wanting people to notice me. That too is the self-centred life.

A selfless mouth has one distinguishing mark: it doesn’t fight for itself, but it speaks for God. Moses said, “I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” (Exodus 4:10b) But God answered him: “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.” (Exodus 4:11–12)

So right speaking is the key to bringing revival.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: Letting Jesus Be King Begins with Governing My Mouth
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let us set what we have learned today back into the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations: three sights for my mouth

Jesus is my role model — how did he speak? To tax collectors and sinners he spoke words of grace; to hypocritical religious leaders he spoke words of rebuke; to those who suffered he spoke words of healing. Peter says, “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” (1 Peter 2:23) At the very moment when the Lord Jesus was most able to defend himself, he chose not to, because there was no “self” in him to protect.

The Bible is my standard — the words I speak must be tested by the word of God. Whatever God’s word says, I say; where God’s word is silent, I don’t speak carelessly.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — before speaking, first ask the Holy Spirit. Isaiah says, “The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” (Isaiah 50:4) Notice: first comes the “taught ear”, and only then the “tongue of those who are taught”. Only an ear awakened morning by morning produces a mouth that can sustain the weary.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive the glory

Let Jesus be King — the most practical testing ground of his kingship is your mouth. A person can say, “Lord, I give you everything,” and yet refuse to swallow the cutting remark already on the tip of his tongue. Brothers and sisters, if Jesus cannot be King of my tongue, he is not yet King of my life.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — Paul says every knee will bow, “and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:11) The highest use of the mouth is to give glory to God. If our words only pull the focus back onto ourselves, we are stealing God’s glory.

The Goal: establish God’s system

God’s system is made up of a community of people who have life in their mouths. In this system, what passes between people is not gossip, not complaint, not comparison, but truth, grace and building up.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

The self-centred mouth: complaining, judging, boasting, arguing, self-pity.

The selfless mouth: thanksgiving, blessing, confession, encouragement, declaring God’s faithfulness.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. In speech, pride says, “I will pass judgement on God’s behalf”; humility says, “I hand the right of judgement back to God.”

And remember: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Nowhere is this clearer than in speech. One defiant word draws an even harsher one back, and both people are hurt; but one gentle word can soften the whole room. Solomon said it long ago: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Proverbs 15:1)

A shift in perspective

Before our mouths speak, let us make four shifts:

From the human perspective to God’s perspective — don’t ask, “What do I want to say?” Ask, “What does God want me to say?”

From the earthly perspective to the heavenly perspective — don’t ask, “How can I say this so I don’t lose out?” Ask, “How can I say this so heaven’s will is done?”

From the temporary perspective to the eternal perspective — a remark that feels good for a moment may wound someone for a lifetime.

From the worldly perspective to the godly perspective — we don’t win people with clever talk; we gain them with truth.

The Lord Jesus said, “I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” (Matthew 12:36–37) This passage reminds us that words carry eternal weight.

The 920 practice and 235 relationships

The 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”. Living the selfless (0) life, we will bear in these relationships the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, notice this: at least eight of these nine graces are seen in the way we speak. Love is spoken; joy is spoken; peace is brought by the mouth; patience and gentleness show most plainly in “speaking when we should and keeping silent when we shouldn’t”; and self-control is hardest, and most real, on the tongue. So the first battlefield of the 920 practice is our mouth.

235 relationships: becoming a “2” with a selfless person — spiritual companions must be able both to speak the truth and to hear it; establishing a “3” — the words of spiritual parents to their spiritual children are seeds of life; becoming a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades is a company of people who open their mouths for the Lord.

You can tell the spiritual temperature of a small group by listening to thirty minutes of its conversation.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves

When we speak relying on the brain and ourselves, we calculate, we defend, we want to win; when we speak relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit, we are simple, we are at peace, we bless.

Rely on the brain and you worry; rely on the heart and you rejoice. The wellspring of life flows from the heart (Proverbs 4:23).

So this is also how we walk the Path of Serving: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide) → Understanding (the Bible is my standard) → Life (Jesus is my role model) → Service (let Jesus be King) → God (let Jesus receive all the glory). Our mouths must walk this whole road.

sections.heading: 7. Practice for Daily Living: Building a Life of Right Speaking
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, hearing the word isn’t hard; doing it is. The five practices below are the road this lesson asks us to walk together. Please don’t treat them as five rules; treat them as five doors, and walk through them one by one.

Practice 1: Awareness of speech — notice what you say each day

Every day, observe what you say: is it complaint, or faith? Is it judgement, or building up?

How to do it: set two reminders on your phone, one at midday and one before bed. Ask yourself three questions: What was the most powerful thing I said today? What was the thing I most regret saying today? If Jesus were sitting beside me, which sentence would I want to take back?

Why does awareness matter? Because most hurtful words are forgotten by us the moment we say them, while the one who was hurt remembers them for a long time. The psalmist prays, “Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” (Psalm 141:3) In the original, “keep” carries the sense of “guarding a city gate”. If no one guards the city gate, anything can come and go.

Brothers and sisters, from today on, post a guard at your mouth.

Practice 2: Transforming your words — turn the negative into the positive

When you want to say something negative, deliberately turn it into words of faith.

For example: “It’s hard” → “With the Lord I can.”

A few more examples:

“I can’t do it” → “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13).

“There’s nothing more we can do” → “With God all things are possible” (Matthew 19:26b).

“He’ll never change” → “God can change him, and I am praying for him.”

“This family is hopeless” → “As for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh” (Joshua 24:15b).

Please note, this is not self-hypnosis or the power of suggestion. Suggestion repeats to yourself a sentence you don’t even believe; a declaration of faith repeats to yourself what God has already said. The first relies on yourself; the second relies on God’s faithfulness.

A pastor once reminded his congregation: don’t tell God how big your problem is; tell your problem how big your God is. That is the essence of transforming your words.

Practice 3: Declaring Scripture — fill your mouth with God’s word

Every day, open your mouth and declare God’s promises, so that your mouth comes into line with God and your faith is built up.

How to do it: choose one verse for this week, and read it aloud three times when you get up in the morning. Reading aloud matters — Paul says, “So faith comes by hearing” (Romans 10:17a). Your own ears need to hear your own mouth speaking God’s word.

Suggested verses to declare this week:

“Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” (Proverbs 18:21)

“Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, Yahweh, my rock, and my redeemer.” (Psalm 19:14)

When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, three times he struck back at the enemy with “It is written” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). Brothers and sisters, God’s word spoken aloud is the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17).

Practice 4: Building others up — speak more encouragement and blessing

Every day, speak words that build up to at least one person: encouragement, affirmation, blessing.

How to do it: pick someone today and be specific. Don’t say, “You’re great.” Say, “Yesterday you kept on being patient over that matter — I saw it, and it wasn’t easy.” Vague praise is like sweets; specific affirmation is like bread.

“A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.” (Proverbs 25:11)

“Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.” (Proverbs 16:24)

Brothers and sisters, “health to the bones” — Solomon knew that words can reach right into our bones. Modern medicine also tells us that when people live for long periods surrounded by belittling language, their stress hormones stay elevated, affecting sleep and immunity. God said it long ago: a gentle tongue is a tree of life (Proverbs 15:4a).

Practice 5: Selfless surrender — let Jesus govern my mouth

Pause for one second before you speak and ask yourself, “If Jesus were me, how would he say it?” Then choose to say what pleases God.

That one second is the cross. In that one second, the “self” has to die once more.

James’ reminder is the most practical of all: “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19b). Swift to hear, slow to speak — people today do exactly the opposite: swift to speak, slow to hear, and very swift to anger.

Brothers and sisters, in that one second, if you let Jesus be King, your words will be different.

Deepening these five practices with the eight stages of changing our mindset

321 practice is not about gritting your teeth by willpower; it is about having your mindset changed. There are eight stages of changing our mindset; let us take today’s lesson through all of them:

Stage 1, Information: I now know — the tongue is a fire, and also a rudder; out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks; words are seeds.

Stage 2, Revelation: the Holy Spirit lets me see myself. Ask the Lord to shine his light: What is the negative thing I say most often? What is the “self” behind it? Is it fear? Is it wanting? Is it resentment?

Stage 3, Conviction: I don’t just agree; I truly believe. I believe my words carry weight; I believe what I say today will become tomorrow’s fruit.

Stage 4, Implementation: start today. Of the five practices, pick one and do it for seven days. Don’t do all five at once — that usually means none of them gets done.

Stage 5, Evaluation: spend three minutes before bed each night facing things honestly. Where did I hold the line today? Where did I give way? At the moment I gave way, what was going on in my heart?

Stage 6, Correction: confess to God, and where necessary apologise to people. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9) One sincere apology often carries more power than a hundred fine speeches.

Stage 7, Repetition: once doesn’t count, twice doesn’t count. Neuroscience tells us that changing behaviour takes repeated practice before stable pathways are formed. Spiritual practice is the same — only repetition takes us from “I am holding back” to “this is simply who I am”.

Stage 8, Multiplication: pass on what you have received. Find someone, share with them how your “speaking” has changed this week, and invite them to practise with you. This is the “3” — spiritual parents bringing forth spiritual children.

sections.heading: 8. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Never underestimate a single sentence, because one sentence can change a whole life.

Words are seeds — sown today, reaped tomorrow.

Words are fire — they can cook a meal, and they can burn down a house.

Words are power — you use this power every day, and you are either building up or tearing down.

Brothers and sisters, please remember:

The humble let God govern their mouths; the proud say whatever they please.

Humility brings forth words of life.

Selflessness lets Jesus speak through you.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters,

“Speaking” is no small thing; “speaking” is the outlet of your life.

Whatever is inside you is what will come out.

What God invites us to today is not merely a change of behaviour, but letting him govern our mouths.

Do you remember Isaiah in the temple? He saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and he cried out, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips: for my eyes have seen the King, Yahweh of Armies!” (Isaiah 6:5)

Brothers and sisters, notice: his first reaction on seeing God was not “my hands are unclean” or “my feet are unclean”, but “I am a man of unclean lips”.

And then what did God do? “Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar. He touched my mouth with it, and said, ‘Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven.’” (Isaiah 6:6–7)

God cleansed his lips. Only then, in the very next verse, did Isaiah hear the Lord say, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” And he said, “Here I am. Send me!” (Isaiah 6:8)

First the mouth is cleansed, then the person is sent. Brothers and sisters, this morning, are you willing to bring your mouth to the altar?

When you begin to speak God’s words, words of faith, words that build up, you will see lives changed, relationships established and revival set in motion.

May we all become people like this: mouths full of life, words that bring forth revival.

Living the selfless life, letting Jesus live in us, letting Jesus be King, letting Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!” (James 3:5)
“For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34b)
declarations: In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare:
My mouth will be governed by God, and my words will bring forth life.
I reject all negativity and judgement; I choose to speak faith and truth.
God’s word fills my heart, and God’s word fills my mouth.
I will build people up with my words; I will glorify God with my words.
What I speak will bring forth the fruit of life; what I speak will become a blessing.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
practices: Awareness of speech — notice what you say each day
Transforming your words — turn the negative into the positive
Declaring Scripture — fill your mouth with God’s word
Building others up — speak more encouragement and blessing
Selfless surrender — let Jesus govern my mouth
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

Thank you that this morning you have shone your light on us through your word. You have shown us that our mouths are not just organs of speech; they are the outlet of our lives, the place where what is within us is revealed.

Lord, we confess that we have often hurt people with our mouths, grumbled against you with our mouths, argued for ourselves with our mouths, and sown seeds of unbelief with our mouths. Please forgive us. As you cleansed Isaiah’s lips, cleanse our lips with the fire of the altar.

Lord, we give our mouths to you. Be King of our tongues. When we want to complain, remind us of your faithfulness; when we want to judge, remind us of your mercy; when we want to stay silent rather than bear witness to you, put within us the fire that says, “We can’t help telling.”
Fill our hearts with your word, so that our mouths naturally pour out your word. Make us people who, at home, at work and in our small groups, speak what is good for building others up.
May the words of our mouths and the meditation of our hearts be acceptable in your sight. May every word we speak in our whole lives become a seed of life, bearing fruit that glorifies you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
discussion: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34b) Looking back over this week, what have you said most often? What does that reveal your heart is currently full of? Which part of your “inside” are you willing to ask God to change first?

“Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” (Proverbs 18:21) Share specifically one practice you plan to take up this week (awareness, transforming, declaring, building up, selfless surrender), and say to whom you will speak a word that builds up. Group members can pray for one another and check in with each other next week.

l137.subtitle: Let Jesus Rule My Mouth; Let My Words Bring Life
