script12.title: Right Speaking and Wrong Speaking
script: Brothers and sisters, good morning.
Today we are going to look together at “right speaking and wrong speaking”.
In the last lesson we saw how important “speaking” is. Since it matters so much, today we’ll go a step further and ask: what is right speaking? And what is wrong speaking?
Our key verse is John 12:49: “For I spoke not from myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.”
Please notice: Jesus did not speak whenever he felt like it; Jesus spoke only when the Father wanted him to speak.

script12.title: Four Hundred Million Words in a Lifetime
script: Brothers and sisters, first let me ask you to do some arithmetic.

In 2007 the journal Science published a study by Mehl and his colleagues. They recorded the everyday conversations of three hundred and ninety-six university students and found that, men and women alike, a person speaks on average about sixteen thousand words a day.
Live to seventy, and that is more than four hundred million words. What will those four hundred million words leave behind?
A sister told me that twenty years ago her husband said to her, “If I’d known, I’d never have married you” — and she still remembers it today.
A brother also told me that on the day he failed his entrance exam his mother said to him, “Son, God still has a better plan.” That sentence has walked with him for thirty years.
Solomon says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.” (Proverbs 18:21)

script12.title: Key Passage and Background
script: John’s Gospel was written around AD 85 to 95, and its author is the apostle John.
Chapter 12 is a turning point. Verses 44 to 50 are the last proclamation of his public ministry. A person’s parting words are often the words he values most.
And the testimony Jesus left last was this: everything I speak is what the Father wants me to speak.
John 1:1 says, “the Word was God.” If even the Word does not speak from himself, what right do we have to speak from ourselves?

script12.title: Not from Himself, Only from the Father
script: Teaching one: right speaking is not from ourselves, but from God.
Jesus said, “The things therefore which I speak, even as the Father has said to me, so I speak.” (John 12:50)
In the original, “what I should say” focuses on content, and “what I should speak” focuses on manner. The Father sets not only the content but the manner too.
Yet we so often do the opposite. We speak by emotion, by feeling, by habit. And once the words are out, they bring hurt.
I once saw a minor car accident. The two drivers got out, and the first thing they said was not “Are you hurt?” but “Can’t you drive?” By the second sentence they were trading insults.
321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

script12.title: Swift to Hear, Slow to Speak
script: Why do we say the wrong thing? Brothers and sisters, because we are too quick.
James says, “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” (James 1:19)
The psychologist Daniel Goleman coined a term, the “amygdala hijack” — when we are provoked, the brain’s emotional alarm seizes control in a split second, and the words burst out.
So the spiritual discipline comes down to just three actions: pause first, listen first, then speak.
What did Samuel say? “Speak; for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:10) He did not say, “Servant, speak; Lord, listen.” So often we say it the wrong way round.
Before you open your mouth, ask one question: if Jesus were me, how would he say it?

script12.title: Speak More of What God Says to You
script: Teaching two: right speaking means speaking more of God’s words and less of our own.
When the council forbade Peter and John to speak, they said, “For we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.” (Acts 4:20)
The original is a double negative — we are not able not to speak. That wasn’t bravado; it was pressure from within.
Brothers and sisters, when God moves you and shines his light on you, don’t just keep it in your heart — speak it out. Not to show off how spiritual you are, but to help yourself live in the truth.

script12.title: Three Fruits of Speaking It Out
script: Why speak it out? There are three results.
Speaking it out deepens it. Psychology has something called the “production effect”: the same material, read aloud, is remembered more firmly than when read silently.
Speaking it out makes it certain. Paul says, “For with the heart, one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation.” (Romans 10:10)
Speaking it out leads to living it out. Moses said we are to talk of these words when we sit in our house, when we walk by the way, when we lie down and when we rise up.

Brothers and sisters, the Jordan flows into the Sea of Galilee and out again, so it is a lake of living water. The same river flows into the Dead Sea and never flows out again; its salt is ten times that of seawater, so it is called the Dead Sea.
When God’s word comes in and flows out again, you are a lake of living water; if it only comes in and never goes out, in time it turns salty and bitter.

script12.title: Always Thankful, Always Praising
script: Teaching three: right speaking means always giving thanks and praise, and never grumbling.
Paul says, “In everything give thanks” (1 Thessalonians 5:18), and Hebrews tells us to “offer up a sacrifice of praise to God continually”, which is “the fruit of lips” (Hebrews 13:15).
The Greek word for “give thanks” literally means “speaking well because of grace”. And notice the word “sacrifice” — a sacrifice has a cost.
Giving thanks when things go well is easy; giving thanks when things go badly is faith.
Brothers and sisters, this is not a mood; it is a choice.

script12.title: Grumbling in the Wilderness, Praise in Prison
script: The Bible gives us two contrasting pictures.

In the wilderness the Israelites grumbled again and again. They said, “We wish that we had died in this wilderness!” And God answered, “Surely as you have spoken in my ears, so I will do to you.” (Numbers 14:28)
Their own mouths pronounced their sentence; with their mouths they shut off the Promised Land.

But Paul and Silas, with wounds on their backs and their feet in the stocks, were locked in the inner prison. The Bible says, “But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God… Suddenly there was a great earthquake… and immediately all the doors were opened.” (Acts 16:25–26)
The same kind of hardship, different “speaking”, and completely different outcomes.
The key is not what happens, but how you speak about it.

script12.title: Five Disciplines of Speaking
script: Next come five practices. This week, please pick one and start.
One: pause for one second. Before you speak, pause and ask, “Is this what God wants me to say?”
Two: share God’s word every day. One verse, one prompting, one testimony — two or three sentences are enough.
Three: every day, speak out three things you are thankful for and three sentences of praise to God. Notice — “speak out”, not just think it.
Four: when you feel like grumbling, turn it at once into a prayer or a thanksgiving. Five: in conflict, ask, “If Jesus were me, how would he say it?” and then choose to submit.
The eight stages of 321 are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Once you’re steady in it, bring someone along with you.

script12.title: A Gentle Reminder and Closing
script: Brothers and sisters, a gentle reminder.
Don’t be in a hurry to speak; first learn to listen to God. Don’t speak out of habit; learn to discern before you speak. Saying the right thing matters more than saying a lot.
The humble let God govern their mouths; the proud are used to speaking for themselves.
Jesus said, “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34)
How you speak determines how you live.

Today God invites us: no longer to speak from ourselves, but to let him speak. When you begin to speak God’s words, words of thanksgiving, words of faith, you will see lives changed and circumstances turned around.

script12.title: Declaration of Faith and Prayer of Response
script: Finally, let us declare together:
My mouth will no longer speak from itself; my mouth will be governed by God. I will always give thanks; I will always praise. My words will bring forth life; my words will bring forth blessing.
Let us pray together.

Dear Lord Jesus, you had the authority to say anything at all, yet you willingly said, “I spoke not from myself.” Please forgive the words we have spoken out of our emotions, and forgive our grumbling.
Cleanse our lips; give us the ear of those who are taught, and give us the tongue of those who are taught.
Lord, we hand you this small rudder, our tongue. Please take the helm.
May the words of our mouths and the meditation of our hearts be acceptable in your sight. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
May the Lord bless you. Let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

script21.title: Right Speaking and Wrong Speaking
script: Brothers and sisters, good morning.
Today we are going to look together at “right speaking and wrong speaking”.
In the last lesson we saw how important “speaking” is. Since it matters so much, today we’ll go a step further and ask: what is right speaking? And what is wrong speaking?
Our key verse is John 12:49: “For I spoke not from myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.”
Notice the difference here. Jesus did not “speak whenever he felt like it”; Jesus spoke “only when the Father wanted him to speak”.

script21.title: Four Hundred Million Words in a Lifetime
script: Let’s start by doing some arithmetic.

In 2007 the journal Science published a study by Mehl, Pennebaker and their colleagues. They recorded the everyday conversations of three hundred and ninety-six university students and found that, men and women alike, a person speaks on average about sixteen thousand words a day.
Live to seventy, and you will speak more than four hundred million words in a lifetime. Brothers and sisters, what will those four hundred million words leave behind?
A sister told me that twenty years ago her husband said to her, “If I’d known, I’d never have married you” — and she still remembers it today. A handful of words; twenty years.
A brother also told me that on the day he failed his entrance exam his mother said to him, “Son, God still has a better plan for you.” That one sentence has walked with him for thirty years.
Solomon says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.” (Proverbs 18:21)

script21.title: We Want to Speak Rightly, but Don’t Know How
script: Brothers and sisters, the truth is we all want to say the right thing. The problem lies in two things.
First, we don’t know what actually counts as right. Second, we don’t know when we ought to speak.
So we speak by feeling, by habit, by emotion — and only afterwards do we regret it.

In the 321 vision, this is precisely the watershed between the self-centred life and selflessness. The self-centred life means I decide for myself what I am going to say; selflessness means letting God decide what I am going to say.
Today has only one aim: that our mouths would no longer belong to ourselves, but would become God’s outlet.

script21.title: Key Passage and Background
script: Let’s look first at the background.
The author of John’s Gospel is the apostle John. The book is generally thought to have been written between AD 85 and 95, and tradition places its writing in Ephesus.
Chapter 12 is a turning point. The second half of verse 36 says that Jesus said these things and departed and hid himself from them; verses 44 to 50 are the last proclamation of his public ministry.
A person’s parting words are often the words he values most. And what Jesus left last was a testimony about “speaking”.

The Graeco-Roman world of the time idolised eloquence; whoever could speak held the power. In just such an age, John 1:1 says “the Word was God”, and yet this Lord, the Word made flesh, says: I spoke not from myself.
If even the Word does not speak from himself, what right do we have to speak from ourselves?

script21.title: Not from Himself, Only from the Father
script: Teaching one: right speaking is not from ourselves, but from God.
Jesus said, “The things therefore which I speak, even as the Father has said to me, so I speak.” (John 12:50)
In the original, “what I should say” focuses on content, and “what I should speak” focuses on manner. The Father set not only what he said, but also how he spoke and when he spoke.
And the word “commandment”, in the original, means a specific instruction issued by a king or a father.
Jesus did not speak out of some vague feeling; he spoke according to a clear commission. Brothers and sisters, before we open our mouths, have we first received the commandment?

script21.title: Three Times “Not of Myself”
script: Letting Scripture interpret Scripture, we find a whole string of the same confession in John’s Gospel.
“The Son can do nothing of himself.” (John 5:19)
“I do nothing of myself.” (John 8:28)
“The words that I tell you, I speak not from myself.” (John 14:10)
Three times, “not of myself”. Brothers and sisters, it was not that Jesus lacked the power to act of himself; he was willing not to act of himself.
That is what 321 calls “selflessness”. Paul says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

script21.title: Why Do We Speak Wrongly? We Are Too Quick
script: But we so often do the opposite. We speak by emotion, by feeling, by habit — and once the words are out, they bring hurt.

I once saw a minor car accident. The two drivers got out, and the first thing they said was not “Are you hurt?” but “Can’t you drive?” By the second sentence they were trading insults. The damage was two bumpers; the cost was a whole day’s peace.
321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.
Why do we say the wrong thing? Because we are too quick. James says, “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” (James 1:19)

In Emotional Intelligence, the psychologist Daniel Goleman describes the “amygdala hijack”: when we are provoked, the brain’s emotional alarm seizes control in a split second, and before we have time to think, the words are already out.

In 2007 Lieberman’s team published a study in Psychological Science showing that when people are willing to stop and name their emotions, activity in the amygdala goes down. That is what “slow to speak” looks like in scientific terms.

script21.title: Pause First, Listen First, Then Speak
script: So right speaking involves just three actions: pause first, listen first, then speak.

Pause first. The psalmist says, “Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” (Psalm 141:3) “Keep” is a military term — like a guard at a city gate, checking each one before letting them through.

Listen first. Samuel said, “Speak; for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:10) Brothers and sisters, he did not say, “Servant, speak; Lord, listen.” Our problem is very often that we say it the wrong way round.
Then speak. Isaiah says the Lord gave him the tongue of those who are taught, and awakened his ear morning by morning. First comes the taught ear, then the taught tongue.
So every time before you open your mouth, ask one question: if Jesus were me, would he speak now? And how would he say it?

script21.title: When It Is Inside, We Can’t Help Speaking
script: Teaching two: right speaking means speaking more of God’s words and less of our own.
The council strictly forbade Peter and John to speak any more in the name of Jesus. They replied, “For we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.” (Acts 4:20)
The original is a double negative; literally, “we are not able not to speak”. That wasn’t bravado; it was a pressure from within. When it is inside, nothing can hold it back.
Jeremiah said the same: if he would not mention Yahweh, it was as if a burning fire were shut up in his bones, and he could not hold it in.
Brothers and sisters, is that fire burning in you?

script21.title: Three Fruits of Speaking It Out
script: So we have a very practical discipline: speak more of “what God has said to you”.
Why speak it out? There are three results.

First, speaking it out deepens it. Cognitive psychology has the “production effect”: a 2010 study by MacLeod at the University of Waterloo showed that words read aloud are remembered more firmly than words read silently.
Second, speaking it out makes it certain. Paul says, “For with the heart, one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation.” (Romans 10:10)
Third, speaking it out leads to living it out. Moses said, “Talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.” (Deuteronomy 6:7)
Sitting, walking, lying down, rising up — that is the whole of a day. If God’s word is to become our daily living, it must first become our conversation.

script21.title: The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea
script: Brothers and sisters, I often use an example from geography.

The Jordan flows first into the Sea of Galilee, then out again from its southern end. It has an inflow and an outflow, so it is a lake of living water, full of fish — and there Jesus called his disciples.

The same river flows into the Dead Sea and never flows out again. The Dead Sea has no outlet; it loses water only by evaporation, and its salt reaches around thirty per cent, roughly ten times that of seawater. No fish live there, so it is called the Dead Sea.
The same water — with an outlet it lives; without an outlet it dies.
When God’s word comes in and flows out again, we become a lake of living water. Jesus said, “From within him will flow rivers of living water.” (John 7:38)

script21.title: Not a Spiritual Show, but Living in the Truth
script: Some people worry: if I often talk about God’s word, will it look like I’m putting on a show?
Jesus did warn us: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them.” (Matthew 6:1) So the key is motive, not volume.

In Life Together, Dietrich Bonhoeffer placed “the ministry of holding one’s tongue” first among the ways believers serve one another — only when we have learned to keep our mouths shut rather than judge a brother are we fit to open them to build him up.
Speaking more doesn’t make you spiritual; speaking rightly does.
The fivefold change of 321 is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Brothers and sisters, “speaking” is the bridge from mindset to life.
The Bible is my standard. On the bookshelf, the standard can’t govern the tongue; only in the mouth can it hold the tongue in check.

script21.title: Always Thankful, Always Praising
script: Teaching three: right speaking means always giving thanks and praise, and never grumbling.

The Bible says, “giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to God, even the Father” (Ephesians 5:20). And again, “In everything give thanks.” (1 Thessalonians 5:18)
And also: “Through him, then, let’s offer up a sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of lips which proclaim allegiance to his name.” (Hebrews 13:15)
The Greek for “give thanks” is made up of “good” and “grace”; literally, speaking well because of grace. And the Hebrew for “praise” is the root of Hallelujah.
Notice two words: a sacrifice has a cost; fruit needs a seed first.
Giving thanks when things go well is easy; giving thanks when things go badly is faith. This is not a mood; it is a choice.

script21.title: Grumbling in the Wilderness
script: The Bible gives us a grievous negative example.
Twelve spies came back, and ten brought an evil report: “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.” (Numbers 13:33)
Brothers and sisters, notice the second half. The enemy had not said a word, and they had already said it all on the enemy’s behalf.

The whole congregation joined in grumbling: we wish we had died in this wilderness. The Hebrew for “murmur” originally means to lodge overnight, to stay; what makes grumbling so dreadful is that it moves in.
And how did God answer? “Surely as you have spoken in my ears, so I will do to you.” (Numbers 14:28) Their own mouths pronounced their sentence.
But Caleb said, “Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!” (Numbers 13:30) The same land, two ways of speaking, two endings.

script21.title: Praise in Prison
script: Now look at the other side.
Philippi was a Roman colony. There Paul and Silas had their clothes torn off, were beaten with many rods, thrown into the inner prison, and had their feet fastened in the stocks.
Wounds on their backs, stocks on their feet, and the time was midnight. What would a person say in such a situation?

The Bible says, “But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God… Suddenly there was a great earthquake… and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened.” (Acts 16:25–26)
Notice the order: first prayer and praise, then the great earthquake; first the fruit of lips, then the prison doors flung open.

That night the jailer’s whole household was saved, and the church in Philippi was born. The Israelites grumbled in the wilderness and talked themselves out of the Promised Land; Paul praised God in prison and talked that prison into a delivery room for the church.

script21.title: The Focus Is Jesus, Not Our Circumstances
script: Someone asks: giving thanks can’t change the facts, so why give thanks?
True, thanksgiving often doesn’t change the facts — but it changes the person looking at the facts.
In 2003, a study by Emmons and McCullough found that the group who wrote down five things they were grateful for each week rated their lives more positively and were more willing to help others.
A 2001 paper by Baumeister and others also pointed out that negative words generally have a stronger impact than positive words of equal weight.
But brothers and sisters, these studies are not our reason for believing in thanksgiving — the Bible is. Science merely catches up from behind and takes a photograph of what God’s word has said.
The Bible says, “Whoever offers the sacrifice of thanksgiving glorifies me.” (Psalm 50:23) Giving thanks glorifies God.
321 says: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. From the human perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal.

script21.title: Practices 1–2
script: Next come five practices.
One: the one-second pause. Every time you are about to speak, pause for one second and ask yourself, “Is this what God wants me to say?”
One second is very short, but that second decides whether the next sentence will be a blessing or a curse. You can put a mark on your steering wheel or your desk to remind yourself.
Two: sharing God’s word. Each day find one opportunity to share a verse, a prompting or a testimony.
No need for a long speech; two or three sentences are enough. Remember the “production effect” — only what is spoken out is remembered; only what is spoken out is lived out.

script21.title: Practices 3–5
script: Three: thanksgiving and praise. Every day, deliberately speak out three things you are thankful for and three sentences of praise to God. Please note — “speak out”, not just think it in your heart.
Four: turning the negative around. When you feel like grumbling, immediately turn that complaint into a prayer or a thanksgiving.
Change “How could this happen?” into “Lord, what do you want to teach me in this?”; change “How could he do that?” into “Lord, please bless him, and change me too.”
Five: selfless surrender. In conflict or when emotions run high, ask, “If Jesus were me, how would he say it?” Then choose to submit to God.
This question is not asking us to pretend; it is asking us to change places — from my throne to his throne.

script21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
script: Brothers and sisters, let’s bring it together through 321.

The Three Foundations are three gatekeepers standing in front of our lips. Jesus is my role model — he did not speak from himself; the Bible is my standard — I speak more of God’s words; the Holy Spirit is my guide — speak when it’s time to speak, stop when it’s time to stop.

The Two Core Values are the two purposes of speaking. James says the tongue is like the small rudder of a ship; whoever holds the helm decides the course. To hand over the helm is to let Jesus be King. And I open my mouth not to win, but so that Jesus may receive all the glory.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. Paul says, speak “only what is good for building others up” (Ephesians 4:29). “Building up” is a builder’s term in the original. Every day we are either building a house with our mouths or pulling one down.
The 920 practice says everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”. Count the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23 — every one of them grows on the lips.

And the eight stages of changing our mindset are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Once you’re steady in it, bring someone along with you.

script21.title: A Gentle Reminder and Closing Call
script: Brothers and sisters, a gentle reminder.
Don’t be in a hurry to speak; first learn to listen to God. Don’t speak out of habit; learn to discern before you speak. Saying the right thing matters more than saying a lot.
Solomon says, “In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.” (Proverbs 10:19)
The humble let God govern their mouths; the proud are used to speaking for themselves. Humility brings right speaking; selflessness lets Jesus speak through you.
Jesus said, “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34) How you speak determines how you live.

Today God invites us: no longer to speak from ourselves, but to let him speak. When you begin to speak God’s words, words of thanksgiving, words of faith, you will see lives changed, circumstances turned around, and miracles begin to happen.

script21.title: Declaration of Faith and Prayer of Response
script: Finally, let us declare together:

In the name of the Lord Jesus I declare — my mouth will no longer speak from itself; my mouth will be governed by God. I will say what God wants me to say, and I reject all wrong words. I will always give thanks; I will always praise. My words will bring forth life; my words will bring forth blessing. Amen!
Let us pray together.

Dear Lord Jesus, you had the authority to say anything at all, yet you willingly said, “I spoke not from myself.” Please forgive the words we have spoken out of our emotions, forgive our grumbling, and cleanse our lips.
Give us the ear of those who are taught, and give us the tongue of those who are taught. Holy Spirit, in the very second we are about to open our mouths, remind us: pause, and listen to you first.

Lord, we hand you this small rudder, our tongue. Please take the helm. May the words of our mouths and the meditation of our hearts be acceptable in your sight. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
May the Lord bless you. Live the selfless life, let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: Introduction: Once Words Are Spoken, They Are Not Over
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

In our last lesson we learned together to “speak the right words.” This morning God wants to help us in a more specific, more personal way, by asking two very practical questions —

What words “should not be spoken”? What words “should be spoken”?

Brothers and sisters, we need to be honest about something: much of the time, it isn’t that we don’t know we should “speak good words.” We’ve heard that since we were children. The real difficulty lies in two other things — first, we don’t know which words are actually “wrong”; second, we don’t know how to tell.

A sister once said through her tears, “I thought I was simply concerned for that brother. That’s why I told two other people about what was going on in his family. I didn’t mean any harm.” Yet three weeks later that brother left the small group and never came back. She hadn’t lied. Every sentence she said was true. Her motive was even kind. But those words still killed a relationship.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the difficulty we face today: it isn’t only “false words” that wound — many “true words” wound too; it isn’t only “malice” that is sin — much that is “thoughtless” must also be accounted for.

Jesus spoke of this with great seriousness:

“I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” (Matthew 12:36–37)

Notice one word: “every.” Not “more or less,” not “the important parts” — every word.

So the mindset the Bible gives us is this: once words are spoken, they are not over. Words must be accounted for.

In our generation, speech has never been so cheap. In the past, passing on a message meant walking for miles; today, one press of a finger, and within a second a sentence can reach the other side of the earth — and stay in the cloud for ever. The cost of broadcasting has fallen almost to nothing, but the weight of our words before God has not lessened one bit.

In the 321 vision we see a clear dividing line:

Self-centred people speak carelessly — because their centre is themselves. They speak to express themselves, to prove themselves, to protect themselves, and the result is loss.

Selfless people speak before God — because their centre is Jesus. Before they speak, they first look up; as they speak, they speak in reverence; and the result is life.

Brothers and sisters, in this lesson today we are going to do one thing: examine our words by God’s standard.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Words Jesus Spoke in a Dispute, a Letter Paul Wrote amid Chaos
sections.html:
To receive today’s message accurately, we first need to understand where our two key passages come from.

The first is Matthew 12:36–37.

The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, the tax collector sitting at the tax booth when the Lord called him (Matthew 9:9). This Gospel is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, mainly for Jewish readers. Throughout, it quotes the Old Testament again and again to prove that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the son of David, the King of kings.

The context of these two verses matters a great deal. Jesus had just healed a man who was demon-possessed, blind and mute, and all the crowds were amazed and said, “Can this be the son of David?” (Matthew 12:23) But when the Pharisees heard it, they said that Jesus drove out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons. What a grave thing to say — they called the work of the Holy Spirit the work of a demon. It was in this setting that Jesus gave a teaching about “words”:

“You offspring of vipers, how can you, being evil, speak good things? For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks. The good man out of his good treasure brings out good things, and the evil man out of his evil treasure brings out evil things.” (Matthew 12:34–35)

Brothers and sisters, see the order here: the heart comes first, the mouth comes after. The mouth is the outlet of the heart; words are the water pipe of our life. What flows out of a pipe isn’t decided by the pipe — it’s decided by the source. That is why Jesus goes on to say that every idle word must be accounted for. He isn’t talking about rhetoric. He is talking about life.

The Greek word for “idle” is ἀργός (argos), formed from the negative prefix a plus ergon, “work.” Literally it means “not working,” “idle,” “bearing no fruit.” The same word is used in Matthew 20:3 for the labourers “standing idle in the marketplace.” So the idle words Jesus speaks of are not necessarily foul words, not necessarily lies, but “words that are not at work” — words that spin in neutral, words that produce nothing, words that contribute nothing at all to the kingdom of God.

And that is precisely why idle words are so dangerous: they look the most innocent.

The second passage is 1 Corinthians 14:3.

First Corinthians was written by the apostle Paul around AD 55, during his third missionary journey, while he was in Ephesus, to the church in Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:8). Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia and one of the most prosperous ports in Greece — a city of constant comings and goings, a jumble of ideas, morally corrupt. The Corinthian church was rich in gifts yet riddled with problems: factions, quarrels, lawsuits, incest, food offered to idols, disorderly meetings.

In chapters 12 to 14, Paul deals specifically with spiritual gifts. At the centre of these three chapters stands the great love chapter, chapter 13. Paul’s logic is clear: the value of a gift lies not in how conspicuous it is, but in whether it has love and whether it builds people up. So when he reaches chapter 14, he sets speaking in tongues beside prophesying, and says:

“But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” (1 Corinthians 14:3)

Brothers and sisters, notice Paul’s standard. He doesn’t ask: Was that beautifully said? Was it profound? Did it win applause? He asks only three things: Did it build up? Did it comfort? Did it encourage?

One is a warning Jesus gave in the middle of a dispute; the other is a standard Paul wrote in the middle of chaos. One tells us what we should not say; the other tells us what we should say. Put together, these two passages become the two doors of today’s lesson.

Teaching 1. Wrong Speech: Words We Should Not Say

Brothers and sisters, the Bible is deeply loving and also deeply honest. It doesn’t only show us the direction; it plainly points out where the landmines are. Today we will look at three kinds of words we should not say.

First, Idle Words: Seemingly Harmless, Actually the Most Costly

Idle words are words without meaning, without upbuilding, without value.

They aren’t lies, they aren’t curses, they aren’t slander. They are simply … useless. They are like an engine revving in neutral: the fuel still burns, the noise still roars, the temperature still climbs — and the car does not move forward a single inch.

First, a number. In 2007 Matthias Mehl of the University of Arizona and his colleagues published a study in the journal Science. Using recording devices, they actually captured university students’ everyday conversations, and found that, men and women alike, people speak on average around sixteen thousand words a day.

Brothers and sisters, what does sixteen thousand words look like? Roughly one chapter of a master’s thesis. Every day, we “publish” a chapter with our mouths. Over a year, that is nearly six million words. The question is: of those six million words, how many are “words at work”? How many are words God can use to build people up?

Now another study. In 2019 Megan Robbins and Alexander Karan of the University of California, Riverside, published research in the journal Social Psychological and Personality Science. Analysing near round-the-clock recordings of more than four hundred participants, they found that adults spend on average about fifty-two minutes a day talking about people who are not present. The researchers noted that most of this was in fact neutral exchange of information, while clearly negative content made up a little over a tenth.

This study is revealing because it shows two things at once: first, talking about others is an extremely common human behaviour — we do it more often than we think; second, precisely because it is so common and so natural, we hardly notice we are doing it.

Fifty-two minutes a day. That is more than three hundred hours a year. Brothers and sisters, if someone told us, “This year you are going to spend three hundred hours on something that neither builds anyone up nor glorifies God,” we would be shocked. Yet that is exactly how we live.

Idle words bring three losses.

The first: they waste life. Moses prayed, “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” (Psalm 90:12) Time is the fairest resource God has given us, and the one we can least recover. Money spent can be earned again; time once gone cannot be recalled by a single second. The most frightening thing about idle words is not how bad they are, but that what they steal can never be given back.

The second: they create problems. Once words leave our lips, they no longer belong to us. They are repeated, edited, embellished. What you said at six out of ten has become ten out of ten by the time it reaches the third person, and by the fifth it is unrecognisable. There is a vivid picture for this: idle talk is like flinging a pillowful of feathers into the wind — by the time you regret it, you can never gather them back.

The third: they damage relationships. James puts it even more strongly: “See how a small fire can spread to a large forest! And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.” (James 3:5b–6)

That image rings even truer today. According to the U.S. National Park Service, about 85 per cent of wildland fires in the United States are caused by people. Most are not arson, but campfires left smouldering, cigarette ends tossed aside, sparks no one noticed. One cigarette end burns down a forest. Brothers and sisters, our idle words are often that cigarette end — we drop it without any malice, but the wind blows, and the whole mountainside goes up in flames.

A 321 Insight: idle talk is the self-centred life’s most comfortable resting posture. We are at our most relaxed in idle talk, because in that moment we don’t have to take responsibility, we don’t have to be examined, we don’t have to pay a price. But precisely because we are relaxed, the old self’s tone of voice quietly slips out. Selfless people are not those who keep their mouths shut, but those who have handed their mouths to Jesus, so that every word is at work.

Second, Judgemental Words: Judging Others by Our Own Standard

“Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged. For with whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you.” (Matthew 7:1–2)

The Greek word for “judge” is κρίνω (krinō). Its root meaning is “to separate, to distinguish,” and by extension “to pass judgement, to condemn.” Jesus does not forbid us to discern right from wrong — in the same chapter he says, “Therefore by their fruits you will know them.” (Matthew 7:20) What he forbids is our taking the judge’s seat.

Brothers and sisters, what is the essence of judging? Its essence is this: judging others by our own standard.

And inside it hides a problem we find very hard to admit — judging is in fact a form of pride. When I judge someone, I do three things: I assume my standard is right; I assume what I see is the whole picture; I assume I am qualified to sit in that seat.

But what is the truth?

Truth one: we cannot see completely. We see behaviour, not motive; we see this moment, not the thirty years he has walked through; we see the outcome, not how many times he has already resisted, how many nights he has struggled. God says, “For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7b)

Truth two: we have problems of our own. Jesus used an image almost tinged with humour:

“Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye? Or how will you tell your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye;’ and behold, the beam is in your own eye? You hypocrite! First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.” (Matthew 7:3–5)

The “speck” is a splinter of wood; the “beam” is the main timber of a house. A man with a roof beam sticking out of his eye wants to pick a splinter out of someone else’s. The picture is so absurd it’s funny — and yet, brothers and sisters, that man is so often us.

Psychology confirms this. Social psychology has a repeatedly verified phenomenon called the “fundamental attribution error,” a concept formally put forward by the American psychologist Lee Ross in 1977: when we explain other people’s failures, we tend to attribute them to their “character”; when we explain our own, we tend to attribute them to the “situation.” Someone else is late because he’s irresponsible; I’m late because of the traffic today. Someone else loses his temper because he lacks self-discipline; I lose mine because I’m under so much pressure.

Brothers and sisters, this is why judging is always strict with others and lenient with ourselves. Not because we are especially wicked, but because our “self” sits in the middle and blocks our view.

The Bible reminds us of something even more fundamental: that office simply isn’t ours.

“Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand.” (Romans 14:4)

“Don’t speak against one another, brothers. He who speaks against a brother and judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law. … Only one is the lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge another?” (James 4:11–12)

At bottom, judging is “leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, and wanting to take God’s place” — and that is the very definition of pride. One saint in church history understood this deeply. According to his biographer Possidius in his Life of Augustine, Augustine of Hippo (AD 354–430) had two lines inscribed on his own dining table, to this effect: whoever loves to wound the good name of the absent is not welcome at this table. Once, when some of his own fellow bishops began to talk about others at the meal, he rebuked them sternly on the spot. A giant of theology used a dining table to guard the purity of fellowship.

The Reformer Martin Luther (1483–1546), explaining the eighth commandment, “You shall not give false testimony,” in his Small Catechism (1529), said that we must not only refrain from slandering our neighbour with lies, but rather defend him, speak well of him, and put the best construction on everything. Brothers and sisters, that one phrase — “put the best construction on everything” — is the antidote to judging.

A 321 Insight: judging is the self-centred life’s most hidden throne. Sitting on it, I feel a little higher, a little more right, a little cleaner. Selfless people step down from that seat, hand judgement back to God, and keep mercy for their brothers and sisters. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Third, Words Unlike Christ: Lies, Slander, Malice, Bitterness, Empty Chatter

The Bible lists this third kind of forbidden speech very specifically. Paul says:

“but now you also put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and shameful speaking out of your mouth. Don’t lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old man with his doings,” (Colossians 3:8–9)

“Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.” (Ephesians 4:31)

Let’s look at them one by one.

Lies. What makes lies so terrible is not only that they twist the facts, but that they twist our relationship with God. Jesus said the devil “is a liar, and the father of lies” (John 8:44b). When we lie, we are speaking the enemy’s mother tongue.

Slander. The original word is βλασφημία (blasphēmia). Used of God, it is translated “blasphemy”; used of people, it is translated “slander.” The very same word! Brothers and sisters, hear this warning: to slander a person made in the image of God is, in God’s eyes, of a piece with blasphemy.

Malice and bitterness. The original word for “bitterness” is πικρία (pikria), meaning “a bitter taste.” The most frightening thing about bitterness is that it embitters us first. We mix a cup of poison meaning to throw it at someone else, and most often we are the ones who end up drinking it. Hebrews warns: “looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and many be defiled by it,” (Hebrews 12:15) Bitterness has a root, and once the root goes down, our words carry poison.

Empty chatter. The original word is κενοφωνία (kenophōnia), formed from kenos, “empty,” plus phōnē, “sound” — literally, “empty noise.” Paul warned Timothy twice: “Timothy, guard that which is committed to you, turning away from the empty chatter and oppositions of what is falsely called knowledge,” (1 Timothy 6:20) “But shun empty chatter, for it will go further in ungodliness,” (2 Timothy 2:16)

Notice Paul’s wording: “it will go further in ungodliness.” Empty chatter doesn’t stay where it is; it moves downhill. A little empty talk today, a little colder tomorrow, a little further away the day after.

These five kinds of words share three features: they don’t build people up, they don’t glorify God, and they are not like Jesus.

So the principle is perfectly clear — any word that is not like Jesus should not be spoken.

Brothers and sisters, how did our Lord speak? “All testified about him, and wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth” (Luke 4:22a). The officers sent to arrest him came back empty-handed and reported, “No man ever spoke like this man!” (John 7:46b) And when he was falsely accused, insulted and crucified, Peter says: “who didn’t sin, ‘neither was deceit found in his mouth.’ When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” (1 Peter 2:22–23)

When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. Brothers and sisters, this is the hardest test of all. We may manage not to lie and not to slander, but in the moment we are wronged, the words practically burst out by themselves.

A 321 Insight: self-centred people let the old self do the talking — that’s just my personality, he started it, I’m only telling the truth. Selfless people refuse the old self’s tone of voice — because it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20).

So from today on, there is one question we need to ask ourselves often. Just one is enough:

Does this sound like Jesus?

Teaching 2. Right Speech: Words We Should Say

Brothers and sisters, God never simply tells us “don’t.” When he closes one door, he always opens another for us. He tells us not to speak idle words because he wants us to speak living words; he tells us not to judge because he wants us to bless.

So what should we say? Paul gives a very clear direction:

“But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” (1 Corinthians 14:3)

Three standards — and each of them is something we do.

Standard 1: Building Up — Helping People Be Established

The Greek word for “edification” is οἰκοδομή (oikodomē), compounded from oikos, “house,” and the root for “build” — literally, “house-building.”

That’s a telling picture. Building a house is slow; it goes up one brick at a time. Demolishing a house is fast; one machine can do it in half a day. Brothers and sisters, our words are the same: words that build people up must be spoken a hundred times before you see the result; words that tear people down need only be spoken once.

Psychology has solid research on this imbalance. In 2001 the American psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues published a well-known paper in the Review of General Psychology, titled simply “Bad Is Stronger Than Good.” Reviewing a large body of research, they showed that in human psychological experience, negative events generally have a stronger impact than positive events of equal intensity.

In other words, one wounding word takes several upbuilding words to repair.

The marriage research that John Gottman and Robert Levenson of the University of Washington began publishing in 1992 likewise showed that what predicts whether a marriage will be stable is not whether there is conflict, but the ratio of positive to negative interactions; among couples in stable relationships, that ratio leans clearly towards the positive.

Brothers and sisters, this isn’t asking us to go and calculate ratios. It’s asking us to understand one thing: relationships are built by words, brick by brick, and they are also torn down by words, blow by blow.

That is why Paul says, “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.” (Ephesians 4:29)

Those words “as the need may be” are precious. Words that build people up are not rehearsed lines; they are spoken on the spot, according to the situation and the need of the moment. And to be able to speak “as the need may be,” there has to be something stored up inside us all along — only what fills the heart can come out of the mouth.

Standard 2: Comforting — Bringing Encouragement and Healing

The two words rendered “exhortation” and “consolation” here are, in the original, παράκλησις (paraklēsis) and παραμυθία (paramythia).

παράκλησις is formed from para, “beside,” and kaleō, “to call” — meaning “to call alongside”: going over, standing beside someone, giving them a hand up. The name of the Holy Spirit, the “Counsellor,” παράκλητος (paraklētos), comes from exactly the same root. Brothers and sisters, what a high standard this is: when we comfort people, we are doing what the Holy Spirit does.

παραμυθία carries the sense of “speaking softly at someone’s side,” used especially when a person is grieving. It isn’t reasoning with them; it’s keeping them company. It isn’t solving the problem; it’s not leaving them alone.

The Bible defines comfort very practically: “who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.” (2 Corinthians 1:4)

Notice this “chain of comfort”: God comforts us, and we comfort others. So the wounds we have received, if placed in God’s hands, become someone else’s medicine.

Here is a saying worth keeping in our hearts: “Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.” (Proverbs 16:24) The bones are the deepest part of the body. Words can reach that deep.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: is there such a sentence in our own lives? Perhaps twenty years ago, at our most desperate moment, someone said, “It’s all right. I’m here with you.” That sentence is still holding us up today. God wants us to be the ones who say that sentence to others.

Standard 3: Encouraging — Helping People Walk the Right Path

Exhortation is bringing someone who has strayed back onto the right path.

Exhortation is not rebuke, and it is not flattery. Rebuke cares only about truth and not about the person; flattery cares only about the person and not about truth. Exhortation wants both: it won’t give up the truth, and it won’t give up this person.

“Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” (Galatians 6:1)

The original word for “restore,” καταρτίζω (katartizō), is used in Matthew 4:21 of James and John “mending their nets,” and in medical usage it also meant “setting a dislocated bone.” Brothers and sisters, this is the heart of exhortation: bone-setting. Setting a bone hurts, but the aim is restoration, not punishment. And the one setting the bone needs hands that are steady, gentle and skilled.

That is why Paul says “in a spirit of gentleness,” and also “looking to yourself.” Whoever exhorts others must first be standing firm themselves.

These three standards can become the “filter” for our mouths. Before a word goes out, let it pass three checkpoints:

Does what I’m about to say build anyone up?

Does it comfort anyone?

Does it point in the right direction?

But Take Note: Right Words Are Not the Same as Pleasant Words

Brothers and sisters, there is a pit here that is very easy to fall into.

Some people hear “build up, comfort, encourage” and think that Christian speech means: from now on, say only nice things, only what makes people happy, and never anything hard to hear.

No. Right words must be true.

Jesus said, “But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.” (Matthew 5:37)

In Jesus’ day the Jews had developed an elaborate set of rules for oaths: swearing by the temple didn’t count, but swearing by the gold of the temple did; swearing by the altar didn’t count, but swearing by the gift on the altar did (Matthew 23:16–18). On the surface it was piety; in reality it was a way of keeping a back door open in what one said — leaving room to go back on one’s word.

Jesus cut through all of it at a stroke. He said: you don’t need to swear at all, because if a person’s word is true, “Yes” is enough.

Brothers and sisters, there is a deep spiritual principle here: when a person has to work hard to guarantee what he says, it is often precisely because his words carry no weight of their own.

So the Bible binds truth and love together: “but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,” (Ephesians 4:15)

The original, ἀληθεύοντες ἐν ἀγάπῃ (alētheuontes en agapē), literally means “being truthful in love.” Truth and love have never been two options; they are two sides of the same thing.

We can remember it like this: truth is the foundation; love is the manner.

Truth without love is a stone — throw it, and it will injure someone. Love without truth is sugar water — drink it, and it will only leave people weaker. And our Lord Jesus Christ, “The Word became flesh, and lived among us … full of grace and truth” (John 1:14) — in him grace and truth are both full, and both at once.

A 321 Insight: self-centred people can only ever choose one, truth or love — either they say false nice things to protect the relationship, or they hurt people to stand their own ground. Selfless people don’t have to choose, because their centre is not themselves: they don’t need false niceness to buy others’ acceptance, and they don’t need to be right to prove their own worth. They can speak the truth, and speak it with love.

Teaching 3. The Highest Purpose of Speech: Building Relationships, Drawing People to God

Brothers and sisters, let’s take one more step forward.

When we speak, it isn’t only that the content must be right; more importantly — the purpose must be right.

A person can speak truth that is one hundred per cent correct and still push people further from God. Job’s three friends are the best example. Much of what they said sounds very pious and very theological, yet in the end God said to one of them, “My wrath is kindled against you, and against your two friends; for you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.” (Job 42:7b)

Right doctrine, wrongly used, is still wrong.

So what is the right purpose? Jesus gave us the greatest standard of all:

“Jesus said to him, ‘ “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.” This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” ’” (Matthew 22:37–39)

Love God, love people. All our speaking should head in these two directions.

So before we speak each time, we can ask two questions:

Will this help someone come closer to God?

Will this help a relationship be built up?

Not Only What We Say, but How We Say It

Brothers and sisters, we must admit something: some words, though “true,” still knock people down. Why? Because besides content, three other things determine the effect of what we say.

First, the wrong timing. “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.” (Proverbs 25:11) The Hebrew behind “fitly” carries the sense of “in its season, as its wheel turns” — the same sentence spoken too early is pressure, spoken too late is hindsight, and only spoken at the right moment is it a golden apple. As Ecclesiastes says so well, “a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;” (Ecclesiastes 3:7b)

Second, the wrong tone. “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Proverbs 15:1) The same words — “How could you forget again?” — said in different tones, can be a reminder or a humiliation. God cares about our tone, because our tone gives away our heart.

Third, the wrong motive. This is the deepest layer. Sometimes we say something that on the surface is for the other person’s good, but underneath we want him to know we were right; on the surface it is concern, underneath it is curiosity; on the surface it is a reminder, underneath it is revenge. People may not hear it, but God does — and in fact, the listener can usually sense it too.

So the conclusion is clear: it’s not only “what we say,” but also “how we say it.”

And sometimes the best choice is not to speak at all.

“In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.” (Proverbs 10:19)

“Even a fool, when he keeps silent, is counted wise. When he shuts his lips, he is thought to be discerning.” (Proverbs 17:28)

Brothers and sisters, better not to speak than to speak wrongly. A word left unspoken, we remain its master for ever; once it is spoken, we become its servant.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906–1945), in Life Together (1939), devotes an entire section to the discipline of the tongue. His point, in essence, is this: in Christian fellowship, what most protects one another is often the discipline of not speaking about a brother behind his back; when a person stops talking about his brother, he truly begins to learn to pray for him.

Brothers and sisters, this is worth remembering for a lifetime: only when we stop talking about others do we start interceding for them.

Speech That Truly Belongs to God

So what is speech that truly belongs to God? It’s simple — look at the fruit:

It makes people love Jesus more.

It makes people love one another more.

If, at the end of a conversation, the other person wants to draw nearer to God, wants to be reconciled with their brothers and sisters — that was speech that belongs to God. If, at the end of a conversation, the other person is colder towards God and more guarded towards people — then however correct our content was, we need to re-examine it before God.

A 321 Insight: self-centred people speak for themselves — to prove they are right, to be seen, to make themselves comfortable — and the result is that pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. Selfless people speak for love — to build people up, to glorify God — and the result is that humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

This is exactly the 321 order of “life first, then relationships, then ministry.” When our life is right, our words are right; when our words are right, relationships are built; when relationships are built, ministry has a foundation. We often do it backwards — rushing to get the task done, and wrecking people along the way. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From a Self-Centred Mouth to a Selfless Mouth
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s message back on the foundation of the 321 vision.

The Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

When it comes to speaking, these Three Foundations become three lines of defence.

Jesus is my role model: so the question I ask is not “What do other people say?” but “What would Jesus say?” When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back; he spoke gracious words to sinners; he spoke hard words to hypocritical religious leaders; and when it was time to be silent, he answered not a single word (Matthew 27:14). His mouth is my pattern.

The Bible is my standard: so my standard for speaking is not my feelings, not my personality, not my culture, but the word of God. Building up, comforting, encouraging — the Bible set this, not I.

The Holy Spirit is my guide: so before I open my mouth, I must first be still and let the Holy Spirit tell me what to say, when to say it and in what tone. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll find joy, rely on the brain and you’ll find worry.

The Two Core Values — let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

To let Jesus reign as King, the first place we must surrender is often our mouth. For the mouth is the last fortress of the “self.” A person can offer up money, time and talent, and still cling tightly to the sovereignty of his speech: I’ll say what I like, I have a right to say it, I’m only telling the truth. Brothers and sisters, if Jesus is King, then he has the authority to decide what I say today and what I don’t.

To let Jesus receive all the glory means this: my words are not so that people will see how eloquent I am, how insightful, how spiritual, but so that people will see Jesus.

The Goal — establish God’s system.

God’s system is built with words. In the beginning, when God created the heavens and the earth, he did it by speaking: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” (Genesis 1:3) And the system of Babylon is also built with words — with lies, with slander, with judgement, with empty chatter. Brothers and sisters, every day we are building a house with our mouths; the only question is: whose house are we building?

Now look at the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Today’s lesson starts precisely at the first link. Our mindset changes from “speaking is my right” to “speaking is a stewardship God has entrusted to me”; once the mindset changes, our life gains reverence; once our life changes, our everyday conversations are different; once our daily living changes, our family and colleagues can feel it; once our relationships change, our witness has power.

A shift of perspective is in this too. From man’s perspective, a word is over once it is said; from God’s perspective, every word must be accounted for. From an earthly perspective, speaking is socialising; from heaven’s perspective, speaking is service. From a temporary perspective, this is just a chat; from an eternal perspective, it echoes in eternity.

Finally, let’s bring it down to the 920 practice.

The 920 practice is this: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life; and what is produced is the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions.

Brothers and sisters, notice something beautiful: almost every one of the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit are borne in our mouths.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23a)

Love gives our words warmth; joy makes our words carry hope; peace keeps us from saying words that stir up strife; patience keeps our mouths shut when we are misunderstood; kindness softens our tone; goodness keeps our motives pure; faithfulness makes us do what we say; gentleness keeps us from wounding people when we exhort them; and self-control — this one is the most direct of all: it bridles the tongue.

That is exactly what James says: “Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.” (James 3:2b) The original word for “bridle,” χαλιναγωγέω (chalinagōgeō), means “to guide with a bit.” A horse weighing a ton can be steered with one small bit; a person’s whole life is likewise carried along by one small tongue.

Brothers and sisters, every “2” we face each day — husband or wife, children, parents, colleagues, neighbours, the brothers and sisters in our small group — is a lesson God gives us for practising selflessness. And the front line of that practice is on our lips.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Building the Ability to Discern and to Speak
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five practices. Let’s combine them with the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that these five practices really take hold.

Practice 1. The Three-Question Filter: Check Before You Speak

Every time before you speak, ask three questions: Does this build people up? Is this true? Does this carry love?

Information: Copy 1 Corinthians 14:3, together with Ephesians 4:15 and 4:29, onto a card and stick it on the back of your phone or in front of your desk.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to let us see with our own eyes the harm one of our sentences once caused. Not condemnation — revelation. When revelation comes, the principle becomes true knowing.

Conviction: Admit before God: my mouth needs to be governed by God.

Implementation: Starting today, for thirty days, stop at least one sentence a day that fails the three questions.

Evaluation: Every evening, be still for three minutes and recall which sentence today should not have been said.

Correction: Apologise to the person we hurt — no explaining, no defending, just owning it.

Repetition: If you can’t manage it one day, try again the next, until it becomes a reflex.

Multiplication: Teach these three questions to our children, our small group, our co-workers.

Practice 2. Stopping the Mouth: Learning Not to Say the Wrong Thing

When the urge to gossip or to judge rises in your heart, choose “not to say it,” and let your mouth be still.

This is the simplest practice, and also the hardest. The prefrontal cortex is the region of the brain responsible for restraining impulses, and long-term brain-imaging research from the U.S. National Institute of Mental Health shows that this region does not fully mature until around the age of twenty-five. In other words, “holding back from speaking” is physiologically hard work in the first place — no wonder it takes practice, and no wonder it takes the Holy Spirit.

David’s prayer can become our prayer every morning: “Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” (Psalm 141:3) The Hebrew paints a vivid picture here: “the door of my lips.” David is asking God to post a guard at the door of his lips. Brothers and sisters, our mouths need a doorkeeper.

In practice: when the urge comes, count to three silently in your heart, and at the same time say, “Lord, I hand this sentence to you.”

Practice 3. Blessing Instead: Replacing Bad Words with Good Ones

When you want to criticise, speak a blessing instead; when you want to blame, speak encouragement instead.

The principle behind this practice is that old habits can’t be removed by “deleting” them; they can only be crowded out by “replacing” them. An empty seat will always be taken back by the old thing.

“not rendering evil for evil, or insult for insult; but instead blessing, knowing that you were called to this, that you may inherit a blessing.” (1 Peter 3:9)

In practice: every day, for the one person who makes us most uncomfortable, say one sincere good word — whether to their face or before God. Keep it up for thirty days. Brothers and sisters, we will discover something wonderful: the one who changes most is not the other person, but ourselves.

Practice 4. Relationships First: Let Love Be the Starting Point of Our Words

In a conflict, don’t rush to prove you’re right; choose first to protect the relationship.

This is the most practical exercise of the 321 conviction that “people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.” When we argue, there is actually a pair of scales in our hearts: on one side, “I am right”; on the other, “this person.” Self-centred people choose the former; selfless people choose the latter.

In practice: in your next conflict, begin with this sentence: “I’d like to hear you out first.” Then genuinely close your mouth and listen to the end.

“So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;” (James 1:19)

God gave us two ears and one mouth — a ratio of two to one.

Practice 5. Selfless Obedience: Let Jesus Decide What I Say

Before speaking, ask: if Jesus were in my place, would he say it? How would he say it? Then obey the Holy Spirit’s guidance.

This is the highest of the five practices, because it is no longer a technique but a surrender of sovereignty.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20a)

Brothers and sisters, if it is no longer I who live, then it is no longer I who speak.

In practice: early every morning, place the people you will meet today, the meetings you will attend, the messages you will reply to, one by one into the Lord’s hands, and pray: “Lord, today my mouth is yours. Give me the tongue of those who are taught.”

For Isaiah gives us a beautiful promise, one prepared especially for the early morning:

“The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” (Isaiah 50:4)

He awakens morning by morning. Brothers and sisters, this is what our morning devotion is about: first let the ear be taught, and then the mouth will be taught.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, before we finish, there are a few words I want to lay gently on our hearts.

Not everything that “can be said” should be said; not everything that is “true” is fitting to say.

Speaking is not only a right; speaking is a responsibility.

One sentence can heal a person; one sentence can also harm a person. “There is one who speaks rashly like the piercing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals.” (Proverbs 12:18) The same tongue — one is a sword, the other is medicine.

Humble people restrain their mouths; proud people say whatever they please.

Why? Because proud people think their opinions are so important that they simply must say them; humble people know their limits, so they listen first, think next and speak last.

Humility brings wise words; selflessness lets love flow out.

On the day the prophet Isaiah saw God, the first thing he discovered was not other people’s problems, but his own mouth: “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips: for my eyes have seen the King, Yahweh of Armies!” (Isaiah 6:5) Then God did something: “Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar. He touched my mouth with it, and said, ‘Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven.’” (Isaiah 6:6–7)

Brothers and sisters, only lips that have been cleansed can say, “Here I am. Send me!”

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters,

“Speaking” is a spiritual discipline to be learned.

What we should say and what we should not say — all of it needs learning, all of it needs practice, all of it needs the Holy Spirit.

Today God has given us a very clear direction: refuse wrong words, speak right words.

Brothers and sisters, when we begin to practise like this, what will happen?

Our life will change — because the mouth is the outlet of the heart, and the process of governing our mouth is really God repairing our heart.

Our relationships will change — because relationships are built with words, and once our words change, relationships begin to be rebuilt.

Our surroundings will change — because “Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” (Proverbs 18:21) The Hebrew puts it even more directly: death and life are “in the hand of the tongue.”

For words are an authority God has given us.

God created the world with words, and God has also placed words in our hands. This is no small thing; it is a very weighty trust.

So may we all become people like this:

Truth in our mouths, love in our hearts, and lives that bring blessing.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, let us hand over our mouths.

Not to self-discipline, not to technique, but to the Lord who sits on the throne.

Live out the selfless life, let Jesus live in us, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” (Matthew 12:36–37)
“But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” (1 Corinthians 14:3)
declarations: Let us declare together — in the name of the Lord Jesus we declare:
My mouth will be cleansed by God; my words will bring forth life.
I reject all idle words and judgement; I reject every word that does not please God.
I will speak words that build up; I will speak words that comfort; I will speak words that encourage.
My words will be true; my words will carry love.
I will build relationships with my words; I will glorify God with my words.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
practices: The three-question filter: check before you speak
Stopping the mouth: learn not to say the wrong thing
Blessing instead: replace bad words with good ones
Relationships first: let love be where your words begin
Selfless obedience: let Jesus decide what I say
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

This morning you have shone your word on the state of our mouths. Lord, we confess: we have said many things we should not have said. We have spoken idle words and wasted the time you gave us; we have judged our brothers and sisters and sat in a seat that does not belong to us; we have spoken words unlike Jesus and brought loss to your name. Lord, please forgive us.
As you once cleansed Isaiah, touch our mouths with the live coal from the altar; cleanse our lips, and cleanse our hearts too, for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.

Lord Jesus, today we hand the sovereignty of our speech to you. From today on, may we look up to you before every time we open our mouths; may all that comes out of our mouths be words that build up, comfort and encourage; may we speak the truth with love, and love people without losing the truth.
Holy Spirit, please be our guide. When we are about to speak idle words, remind us; when we are about to judge, stop us; when someone needs a word, put that word in our mouths.
May the words of our mouths and the thoughts of our hearts be acceptable in your sight. May our mouths become instruments for establishing God’s system.
In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
discussion: Matthew 12:34b says, “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” Looking back over the past week, which thing you said do you regret most? What does that sentence reveal was filling your heart at the time? Are you willing to ask the Lord to work in that place?

1 Corinthians 14:3 says, “But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” Who around you most needs a word of building up, comfort or encouragement right now? When and how do you plan to say that word to them this week?
