l139.subtitle: What Should Not Be Said, and What Should
l139.partTitle: Unit 8 · The Foundation of Revival — Life

blog.title: The Sixteen Thousand Words You Spoke Today

blocks.x: How many of them were words at work?
Brothers and sisters, there is a piece of research that may give you a jolt.

In 2007 Matthias Mehl of the University of Arizona and his colleagues published a study in the journal Science, using recording devices to capture people’s everyday conversations. They found that, men and women alike, we speak on average about sixteen thousand words a day. Over a year, that is nearly six million words.
In other words, every day we “publish” a chapter of a book with our mouths.
The question is: of those six million words, how many are actually at work?
1. Not every true word should be spoken
Jesus said something that makes the heart tremble:

“I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” (Matthew 12:36–37)
Notice the word “every”. Not “more or less”, not “the important parts” — every word.

The Greek word for “idle” is argos, formed from a negative prefix plus the word for “work”; literally, “not working”. So the idle words Jesus speaks of are not necessarily foul words, not necessarily lies, but — words that are not at work.
They are like an engine revving in neutral: the fuel still burns, the noise still roars, and the car does not move forward a single inch.

I know a sister who, out of kindness, told two other people about what was going on in a brother’s family. She didn’t lie; every sentence she said was true. Yet three weeks later that brother left the small group and never came back.
It turns out that it isn’t only false words that wound. True words can kill a relationship too.
The Bible points out three kinds of words we should not say: idle words, judgemental words, and every word unlike Christ — lies, slander, malice, bitterness, empty chatter.
The principle for telling them apart really comes down to one sentence: any word that is not like Jesus should not be spoken.
2. So what should we say?
God never simply tells us “don’t”. When he closes one door, he always opens another for us.
Paul gives three standards:
“But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” (1 Corinthians 14:3)

Edification — in the Greek, literally “house-building”. Building a house is slow, one brick at a time; demolishing one is fast — half a day is enough. In 2001 the psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues published a paper titled simply “Bad Is Stronger Than Good”, showing that negative experiences generally hit harder than positive experiences of equal intensity. No wonder one wounding word takes several good words to repair.
Comfort — the original means “to call alongside”, from the same root as the Holy Spirit’s name, the “Counsellor”. When we comfort people, we are doing what the Holy Spirit does.
Exhortation — the original carries the sense of “mending nets, setting bones”. Setting a bone hurts, but the aim is restoration, not punishment.

But take care: right words are not the same as pleasant words. Truth is the foundation; love is the manner. Truth without love is a stone — throw it, and it will injure someone. Love without truth is sugar water — it will only leave people weaker.
3. Better not to speak than to speak wrongly
Some words, though true, still wound — because the timing is wrong, the tone is wrong, the motive is wrong.
So it’s not only “what we say”, but also “how we say it”. And sometimes the best choice is not to speak at all.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer writes in Life Together about the discipline of the tongue. His point, in essence, is this: in fellowship, what most protects one another is often the discipline of not speaking about a brother behind his back; when a person stops talking about his brother, he truly begins to learn to pray for him.
Only when we stop talking about others do we start interceding for them.

This is exactly the light of 321: self-centred people speak for themselves — to prove they are right, to make themselves comfortable — and the result is that pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. Selfless people speak for love — to build people up, to glorify God — and the result is that humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

This week, why not try three small things: before you speak, ask, “Does this build people up? Is it true? Does it carry love?”; when you want to judge, choose to keep your mouth shut; when you want to criticise, speak a blessing instead.
May we all become people like this: truth in our mouths, love in our hearts, and lives that bring blessing. Let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.
A reflection
Think back over the past week: of all the things you said, which do you most regret? What does that sentence reveal about what was filling your heart at the time?

1. Data: Mehl et al., Science (2007) — people speak about 16,000 words a day on average.
2. Data: Robbins and Karan (2019) — adults spend about 52 minutes a day talking about people who are not present.
3. Image: idle words are an engine revving in neutral — the fuel burns, the noise roars, and the car does not move an inch.
4. Quote James 3:5–6: how a small fire can spread to a large forest.
5. Science: according to the U.S. National Park Service, about 85 per cent of wildland fires are caused by people.

brief12.title: Wrong Speech 2: Judgemental Words
notes: Slide text:
“Don’t judge,
so that you won’t be judged.”
(Matthew 7:1)
Seeing their speck, forgetting our beam
Key points:
1. “Judge” is the Greek krinō, originally “to separate, to distinguish”, by extension “to pass judgement, to condemn”; what the Lord forbids is taking the judge’s seat.
2. The essence of judging: judging others by our own standard; behind it is pride — leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place.
3. Quote Matthew 7:3–5: a speck is a splinter of wood; a beam is the main timber of a house.
4. Psychology: Lee Ross’s “fundamental attribution error” (1977) — we blame others’ character, and excuse ourselves by the situation.
5. Quote Romans 14:4 and James 4:12: who are you to judge another?

brief12.title: Wrong Speech 3: Words Unlike Christ
notes: Slide text:
Lies, slander, malice, bitterness
Empty chatter
They don’t build up, glorify God or sound like Jesus
Does this sound like Jesus?
Key points:
1. Quote Colossians 3:8–9 and Ephesians 4:31, listing these words one by one.
2. “Slander” is blasphēmia, translated “blasphemy” when used of God; “bitterness”, pikria, means a bitter taste — it embitters us first.
3. “Empty chatter” is kenophōnia, literally “empty noise”; 2 Timothy 2:16 says it will go further in ungodliness.
4. Jesus’ mouth: Luke 4:22, “the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth”; 1 Peter 2:23, “when he was cursed, he didn’t curse back”.
5. The conclusion in one sentence: any word that is not like Jesus should not be spoken.

brief12.title: Right Speech: Build Up, Comfort, Encourage
notes: Slide text:
“Speaks to men for their edification,
exhortation, and consolation.”
(1 Corinthians 14:3)
Building up is house-building; comfort is company
Key points:
1. “Edification” is the Greek oikodomē, literally house-building; building goes brick by brick, demolishing takes one sentence.
2. Psychology: Baumeister et al., “Bad Is Stronger Than Good” (2001) — negative impact outweighs equal positive impact.
3. Research: Gottman and Levenson’s marriage studies — in stable relationships positive interactions clearly outnumber negative ones.
4. Original language: the two words for “exhortation” and “consolation” are paraklēsis and paramythia; the first shares its root with the Spirit, the Counsellor.
5. Quote Ephesians 4:29 and Galatians 6:1: “restore” in the original carries the sense of “setting bones, mending nets”.

brief12.title: Right Words Must Be True
notes: Slide text:
“Let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’
and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’”
(Matthew 5:37)
Truth is the foundation; love is the manner
Key points:
1. Background: the Jews of the day used elaborate rules for oaths to keep a back door open in what they said; the Lord cut through it at a stroke.
2. Spiritual principle: those who must work hard to guarantee their words often do so because their words carry no weight of their own.
3. Quote Ephesians 4:15: speaking truth in love; the original literally means “being truthful in love”.
4. Image: truth without love is a stone; love without truth is sugar water.
5. A 321 insight: the self-centred either say false nice things or hurt people; the selfless can speak the truth, and speak it with love.

brief12.title: The Highest Purpose: Love God, Love People
notes: Slide text:
“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,
with all your soul, and with all your mind…
You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
(Matthew 22:37–39)
Key points:
1. Not only must the content be right; the purpose must be right even more. Job’s three friends sounded pious, yet God was displeased.
2. Two questions: will this help someone come closer to God? Will it help a relationship be built up?
3. Three factors that determine the effect: timing, tone, motive; quote Proverbs 25:11 and 15:1.
4. Better not to speak than to speak wrongly: Proverbs 10:19 and 17:28.
5. Bonhoeffer’s reminder in Life Together: only when we stop talking about a brother do we truly begin to pray for him.

brief12.title: Putting It into Practice: Five Practices
notes: Slide text:
Three-question filter  2. Stopping the mouth
Blessing instead  4. Relationships first
Selfless obedience: how would Jesus say it?
Builds up? True? Carries love?
Key points:
1. The three-question filter: does it build people up? Is it true? Does it carry love? Write it on a card and put it where you’ll see it.
2. Stopping the mouth: quote Psalm 141:3; the Hebrew paints the picture of “the door of my lips”.
3. Blessing instead: old habits can’t be deleted, only replaced; quote 1 Peter 3:9.
4. Relationships first: quote James 1:19 — swift to hear, slow to speak.
5. Deepen with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

brief12.title: Closing and Call
notes: Slide text:
Refuse wrong words; speak right words
Life, relationships and surroundings will change
Truth on our lips, love in our hearts
Let Jesus be King and receive all the glory
Key points:
1. Quote Proverbs 18:21: death and life are in the power of the tongue; the Hebrew says “in the hand of the tongue”.
2. Words are an authority God has given us: God created the world with words, and has placed words in our hands too.
3. The call: this morning, hand over our mouths — not to self-discipline or technique, but to the Lord on the throne.
4. Isaiah 6:6–7: the coal touched his mouth; only cleansed lips can say, “Here I am. Send me!”
5. Close with the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

brief12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, cleanse my mouth with the coal from the altar
May the words of my mouth be acceptable to you
(Psalm 19:14)
May our words become a blessing
Key points:
1. Lead in confession: idle words, judging, words unlike Jesus — confess them one by one before the Lord.
2. Ask the Holy Spirit to guide: to remind us when we are about to speak idly, to stop us when we are about to judge, and to put the right word in our mouths when it is needed.
3. Declare: I will speak words that build up, comfort and encourage; my words will be true and carry love.
4. Bless the congregation: may brothers and sisters have truth on their lips, love in their hearts, and lives that bring blessing.

brief21.title: Truth on the Lips, Love in the Heart
notes: Slide text:
What should not be said, and what should
“Every idle word that men speak,
they will give account of it.”
(Matthew 12:36)
Key points:
1. Open with a greeting; read out the lesson title and the key passage, Matthew 12:36–37.
2. Explain that this is the second session on “right speaking”; today we specifically discern what should and should not be said.
3. Stress the word “every”: words are not over once spoken; words must be accounted for.
4. Preview the three points and the five practices.

brief21.title: Introduction 1: Our Real Difficulty
notes: Slide text:
We know we should speak good words,
but not which words are wrong,
nor how to tell.
True words can wound too.
Key points:
1. Example: a sister, meaning well, passed on a brother’s family matters; three weeks later he left the small group.
2. Every sentence she said was true and her motive was kind, yet a relationship was still killed.
3. Name the two blind spots: we don’t know which words are actually wrong, and we don’t know how to tell.
4. Reminder: it isn’t only false words that wound, and it isn’t only malice that must be accounted for.

brief21.title: Introduction 2: Words Must Be Accounted For
notes: Slide text:
Words are not over once spoken;
words must be accounted for.
Self-centred: careless words bring loss
Selfless: speaking before God, in reverence
Key points:
1. Today the cost of passing on a word is almost nothing, but its weight before God has not lessened.
2. A sentence reaches the other side of the earth in a second — and stays in the cloud for ever.
3. A 321 insight: the self-centred have themselves at the centre, speaking to express, prove and protect themselves.
4. The selfless have Jesus at the centre: they look up before they open their mouths, and speak in reverence.
5. The aim of this lesson: to examine our words by God’s standard.

brief21.title: Key Passages and Background
notes: Slide text:
“For their edification, exhortation, and consolation.”
(1 Corinthians 14:3)
Matthew: c. AD 50–70, for Jewish readers
1 Corinthians: c. AD 55
Key points:
1. Matthew’s Gospel was written by Matthew the tax collector, around AD 50–70, for Jewish readers.
2. Background to chapter 12: the Pharisees said Jesus drove out demons by Beelzebul, and the Lord spoke about words and the heart.
3. Quote Matthew 12:34–35: out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.
4. 1 Corinthians was written around AD 55 in Ephesus; chapters 12–14 deal with gifts, with the love chapter, 13, at the centre.
5. Paul’s standard is not whether it sounds good, but: did it build up? Did it comfort? Did it encourage?

brief21.title: Wrong Speech 1: What Are Idle Words?
notes: Slide text:
No meaning, no upbuilding, no value
“Idle” in the original: words not at work
Like an engine revving in neutral
Fuel burns, but the car goes nowhere
Key points:
1. “Idle” is the Greek argos, a negative prefix plus ergon, “work” — literally “not working”.
2. The same word is used in Matthew 20:3 of the labourers standing idle in the marketplace.
3. Idle words are not necessarily foul words or lies, but words not at work, words that bear no fruit.
4. Image: an engine revving in neutral — the fuel burns, the noise roars, the temperature climbs, and the car does not move an inch.
5. What makes them most dangerous: they look the most innocent.

brief21.title: The Cost of Idle Words: The Numbers Speak
notes: Slide text:
About 16,000 words a day on average
52 minutes a day talking about others
Over 300 hours a year
Are these words at work?
Key points:
1. Mehl et al., Science (2007): men and women alike speak about 16,000 words a day on average.
2. Sixteen thousand words a day is nearly six million a year — every day we publish a chapter with our mouths.
3. Robbins and Karan (2019): adults spend on average about 52 minutes a day talking about people who are not present.
4. The study also noted most of this was neutral exchange of information, with clearly negative content a little over a tenth.
5. That adds up to over 300 hours a year; ask: what is this time building?

brief21.title: Three Losses from Idle Words
notes: Slide text:
They waste life: time never comes back
They create problems: words get embellished
They damage relationships: a small fire, a large forest
(James 3:5)
Key points:
1. Wasting life: quote Psalm 90:12, “teach us to count our days”.
2. Creating problems: image — idle talk is like flinging a pillowful of feathers into the wind; you can never gather them back.
3. Damaging relationships: quote James 3:5–6, the tongue is a fire.
4. Science: according to the U.S. National Park Service, about 85 per cent of U.S. wildland fires are caused by people.
5. A 321 insight: idle talk is the self-centred life’s most comfortable resting posture; once we relax, the old self’s tone slips out.

brief21.title: Wrong Speech 2: Judgemental Words
notes: Slide text:
“Don’t judge,
so that you won’t be judged.”
(Matthew 7:1)
Judging others by our own standard
Key points:
1. “Judge” is the Greek krinō, originally “to separate, to distinguish”, by extension “to pass judgement, to condemn”.
2. The Lord does not forbid discernment: in the same chapter, verse 20, he says by their fruits you will know them.
3. What he forbids is taking the judge’s seat; the essence of judging is judging others by our own standard.
4. Judging is a form of pride: assuming my standard is right, what I see is the whole picture, and I am qualified to sit there.
5. Quote 1 Samuel 16:7: man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.

brief21.title: Speck and Beam: We Cannot See Completely
notes: Slide text:
You see the speck in your brother’s eye,
but don’t consider the beam in your own.
(Matthew 7:3)
A speck is a splinter; a beam is a main timber
Key points:
1. Read Matthew 7:3–5 in full; the picture is so absurd it’s funny — and that man is so often us.
2. Psychology: Lee Ross’s “fundamental attribution error” (1977).
3. We attribute others’ failures to their character, and our own to the situation.
4. Someone else is late because he’s irresponsible; I’m late because of the traffic. Someone else loses his temper for lack of self-discipline; I lose mine because I’m under pressure.
5. Not because we are especially wicked, but because the “self” sits in the middle and blocks our view.

brief21.title: Judging: Sitting in a Seat Not Ours
notes: Slide text:
“Who are you who judge
another’s servant?”
(Romans 14:4)
Let man be man; let God be God
Key points:
1. Quote Romans 14:4 and James 4:11–12: only one is the lawgiver and judge.
2. At bottom, judging is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take God’s place — the very definition of pride.
3. Church history: according to Possidius’ Life of Augustine, Augustine had words inscribed on his dining table forbidding backbiting.
4. Martin Luther’s Small Catechism (1529) on the eighth commandment: defend your neighbour and put the best construction on everything.
5. A 321 insight: humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man, and let God be God.

brief21.title: Wrong Speech 3: Words Unlike Christ
notes: Slide text:
Lies, slander, malice
Bitterness, empty chatter
(Colossians 3:8–9)
They don’t build up; they don’t glorify God
Key points:
1. Quote Colossians 3:8–9 and Ephesians 4:31, listing them one by one.
2. Lies: quote John 8:44 — when we lie, we speak the enemy’s mother tongue.
3. Slander is blasphēmia, translated “blasphemy” when used of God; slandering a person made in God’s image is of a piece with it.
4. Bitterness, pikria, is a bitter taste that embitters us first; quote the root of bitterness in Hebrews 12:15.
5. Empty chatter, kenophōnia, is literally “empty noise”; 2 Timothy 2:16 says it will go further in ungodliness.

brief21.title: The Principle: Does It Sound Like Jesus?
notes: Slide text:
“When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back.
When he suffered, he didn’t threaten.”
(1 Peter 2:23)
No word unlike Jesus should be spoken
Key points:
1. Jesus’ mouth: Luke 4:22 — all wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth.
2. John 7:46 — the officers said, “No man ever spoke like this man!”
3. 1 Peter 2:22–23: he didn’t sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth.
4. Not cursing back is the hardest test; when we are wronged, the words practically burst out by themselves.
5. A 321 insight: the selfless refuse the old self’s tone of voice, because it is no longer I who live (Galatians 2:20).

brief21.title: Right Speech 1: Building Up
notes: Slide text:
“For their edification, exhortation, and consolation.”
(1 Corinthians 14:3)
“Edification” in the original: house-building
Building is slow; demolishing is fast
Key points:
1. “Edification” is the Greek oikodomē, from oikos, “house”, and “build” — literally house-building.
2. A house goes up brick by brick and comes down in half a day; words that build up must be said a hundred times, words that tear down only once.
3. Psychology: Baumeister et al., “Bad Is Stronger Than Good”, Review of General Psychology (2001).
4. Gottman and Levenson’s marriage research: stability depends on the ratio of positive to negative interactions.
5. Quote Ephesians 4:29: only what is good for building others up.

brief21.title: Right Speech 2: Comforting
notes: Slide text:
“Comfort” in the original: to call alongside
Same root as the Spirit, the Counsellor
“Pleasant words are a honeycomb…
and health to the bones.” (Proverbs 16:24)
Key points:
1. The two words for “exhortation” and “consolation” in the original are paraklēsis and paramythia.
2. Paraklēsis combines “beside” and “call”; the Holy Spirit’s title, the Counsellor, comes from the very same root.
3. Paramythia carries the sense of speaking softly beside someone who grieves: not reasoning, but keeping them company.
4. Quote 2 Corinthians 1:4: comfort others with the comfort God gives us — our wounds become someone else’s medicine.
5. Ask: is there a sentence spoken twenty years ago that is still holding you up today?

brief21.title: Right Speech 3: Encouraging
notes: Slide text:
“Restore such a one
in a spirit of gentleness.”
(Galatians 6:1)
“Restore” in the original: mending nets, setting bones
Key points:
1. Exhortation brings someone who has strayed back onto the right path; it is neither rebuke nor flattery.
2. Rebuke cares only about truth, not the person; flattery only about the person, not truth; exhortation wants both.
3. “Restore” is katartizō, used of mending nets in Matthew 4:21, and in medicine of setting bones.
4. Setting a bone hurts, but the aim is restoration, not punishment; the one setting it needs steady, gentle hands.
5. The three standards become a filter: does it build up? Does it comfort? Does it point the right way?

brief21.title: Right Words Must Be True
notes: Slide text:
“Let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’
and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’”
(Matthew 5:37)
Truth is the foundation; love is the manner
Key points:
1. Background: the Jews of the day used elaborate rules for oaths to keep a back door open in what they said (Matthew 23:16–18).
2. Spiritual principle: those who must work hard to guarantee their words often do so because their words carry no weight of their own.
3. Quote Ephesians 4:15: speaking truth in love; the original literally means “being truthful in love”.
4. Image: truth without love is a stone; love without truth is sugar water.
5. Quote John 1:14: the Lord is full of grace and truth.

brief21.title: The Highest Purpose: Love God, Love People
notes: Slide text:
“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,
with all your soul, and with all your mind…
You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
(Matthew 22:37–39)
Key points:
1. Not only must the content be right; the purpose must be right even more.
2. Job’s three friends sounded pious, yet God said they had not spoken of him what was right, as Job had (Job 42:7).
3. Two questions: will this help someone come closer to God? Will it help a relationship be built up?
4. Three factors that determine the effect: timing, tone, motive; quote Proverbs 25:11 and 15:1.
5. A 321 insight: the self-centred speak for themselves and both sides lose; the selfless speak for love and both sides win.

brief21.title: Better Not to Speak than to Speak Wrongly
notes: Slide text:
“In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience,
but he who restrains his lips does wisely.”
(Proverbs 10:19)
Stop talking about others, start interceding
Key points:
1. Quote Proverbs 10:19 and 17:28: even a fool, when he keeps silent, is counted wise.
2. A word left unspoken, we are its master; once spoken, we become its servant.
3. Bonhoeffer, Life Together (1939), on the discipline of the tongue: not talking about a brother protects the fellowship.
4. His point, in essence: when a person stops talking about his brother, he truly begins to pray for him.
5. Speech that truly belongs to God is known by its fruit: people love Jesus more, and love one another more.

brief21.title: Practices 1–3
notes: Slide text:
Three-question filter: check before you speak
Stopping the mouth: let it be still
Blessing instead: speak encouragement
“Set a watch before my mouth; keep the door of my lips!”
Key points:
1. The three-question filter: does it build people up? Is it true? Does it carry love? Write it on a card and put it where you’ll see it.
2. Stopping the mouth: brain-imaging research from the U.S. National Institute of Mental Health shows the prefrontal cortex matures only around age twenty-five.
3. Holding back from speaking is physiologically hard work, so it needs practice — and it needs the Holy Spirit.
4. The Hebrew of Psalm 141:3 paints “the door of my lips”: asking God to post a guard at the door.
5. Blessing instead: old habits can only be crowded out by replacement; quote 1 Peter 3:9, “but instead blessing”.

brief21.title: Practices 4–5 and the Eight Stages
notes: Slide text:
Relationships first: protect the relationship
Selfless obedience: how would Jesus say it?
Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation
Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
Key points:
1. Relationships first: quote James 1:19 — swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger.
2. In conflict, begin with “I’d like to hear you out first”, then genuinely close your mouth and listen to the end.
3. Selfless obedience: quote Galatians 2:20 — if it is no longer I who live, then it is no longer I who speak.
4. Early each morning, place the people you will meet, the meetings and the messages one by one into the Lord’s hands.
5. Quote Isaiah 50:4: he awakens morning by morning — first the ear is taught, then the mouth.

brief21.title: Closing, Prayer and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Refuse wrong words; speak right words
Truth on our lips, love in our hearts
“Death and life are in the power of the tongue”
Let Jesus be King and receive all the glory
Key points:
1. Quote Proverbs 18:21: the Hebrew says “in the hand of the tongue”.
2. Isaiah 6:5–7: the coal touched his mouth; only cleansed lips can say, “Here I am. Send me!”
3. Lead the declaration of faith: my mouth will be cleansed by God; my words will bring forth life.
4. Prayer of response: confession, asking for cleansing, handing over the sovereignty of our speech, asking for the Holy Spirit’s guidance.
5. Bless the congregation: may brothers and sisters have truth on their lips, love in their hearts and lives that bring blessing, and may Jesus receive all the glory.

script: Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 139, titled “Truth on the Lips, Love in the Heart”, with the subtitle: what should not be said, and what should. Our key verse is Matthew 12:36: “I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment.” Brothers and sisters, please notice one word — “every”. Not more or less, not the main points — every word.

In the last lesson we learned to “speak the right words”. But brothers and sisters, where does our real difficulty lie? It isn’t that we don’t know we should speak good words. The real difficulty is this: we don’t know which words are actually wrong, and we don’t know how to tell.

A sister once said that she was simply concerned for a brother, and that was why she told two other people about what was going on in his family. She meant no harm, and every sentence she said was true. Yet three weeks later that brother left the small group and never came back.
Brothers and sisters, it isn’t only false words that wound; true words wound too. Words are not over once they are spoken; words must be accounted for.

When the Lord said this, the Pharisees were accusing him of driving out demons by the prince of demons. He said, “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” The heart comes first, the mouth after. The mouth is the outlet of the heart.
The Greek word for “idle” means “not working”. So idle words are not necessarily foul words, not necessarily lies, but words that are not at work.
And in 1 Corinthians 14:3 Paul gives us the positive standard: “But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.”

The first kind of words we should not say is idle words. Without meaning, without upbuilding, without value. They are like an engine revving in neutral: the fuel still burns, the noise still roars, and the car does not move forward a single inch.

In 2007 Mehl and his colleagues published in the journal Science that people speak on average about sixteen thousand words a day. In 2019 another study found that adults spend about fifty-two minutes a day talking about people who are not present — more than three hundred hours a year.

Idle words bring three losses: they waste life, they create problems, they damage relationships. James says, “See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!” According to the U.S. National Park Service, about 85 per cent of wildland fires in the United States are caused by people. Our idle words are so often that cigarette end that was never put out.
The second kind is judgemental words. Jesus said, “Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged.”

What is the essence of judging? It is judging others by our own standard. The problem is: we cannot see completely, and we have problems of our own. That is why the Lord said we see the speck in our brother’s eye but don’t consider the beam in our own.

In 1977 the psychologist Lee Ross put forward the “fundamental attribution error”: when others fail, we blame their character; when we fail, we blame the circumstances. Why? Because the “self” sits in the middle and blocks our view. Humility is stepping down from the judge’s seat — let man be man, and let God be God.
The third kind is words unlike Christ: lies, slander, malice, bitterness, empty chatter.
In the original, “slander”, when used of God, is translated “blasphemy”; “bitterness” means a bitter taste, and the first one it embitters is ourselves; “empty chatter” literally means “empty noise”.

These words share three features: they don’t build people up, they don’t glorify God, and they are not like Jesus. So the principle is simple — any word that is not like Jesus should not be spoken. When our Lord was cursed, he didn’t curse back; when he suffered, he didn’t threaten. From today on, let us often ask: does this sound like Jesus?
So what should we say? Paul gives us three words: build up, comfort, encourage.

“Edification” in the original is house-building. Building is slow, brick by brick; demolishing is fast — one sentence is enough. In 2001 a study by Baumeister and others showed that bad is stronger than good. One wounding word takes several upbuilding words to repair.
“Comfort” in the original means “to call alongside”, from the same root as the Holy Spirit, the Counsellor. Comfort is not reasoning with someone; it is going over and standing beside them.
“Exhortation” in the original carries the sense of mending nets and setting bones. Setting a bone hurts, but the aim is restoration, not punishment.
But brothers and sisters, there is a pit here: right words are not the same as pleasant words.
Jesus said, “Let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’” People in his day used complicated rules for oaths to keep a back door open for themselves, and the Lord cut through it at a stroke.

So remember: truth is the foundation; love is the manner. Truth without love is a stone — throw it, and it will injure someone; love without truth is sugar water — it will only leave people weaker. Paul says, “speaking truth in love.” The original literally means — being truthful in love.

Let’s take one more step. When we speak, it isn’t only the content that must be right; the purpose must be right even more. Jesus gave us the greatest standard of all: love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your mind, and love your neighbour as yourself.
So before you speak, you can ask two questions: will this help someone come closer to God? Will this help a relationship be built up?

Some words, though true, still wound because the timing is wrong, the tone is wrong, the motive is wrong. So it’s not only what we say, but how we say it. Proverbs says, “In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.” Better not to speak than to speak wrongly.
Next come our practices for this week — five in all.

One, the three-question filter: before you speak, ask, does this build people up? Is it true? Does it carry love? Two, stopping the mouth: when you want to gossip or judge, choose not to say it. Three, blessing instead: when you want to criticise, speak a blessing instead. Four, relationships first: in conflict, don’t rush to prove you’re right; protect the relationship first. Five, selfless obedience: before you speak, ask, if Jesus were me, how would he say it?

Brothers and sisters, walk these five practices all the way through the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Brothers and sisters, “speaking” is a spiritual discipline to be learned. What we should say and what we should not say — all of it needs learning.

Today God has given us a clear direction: refuse wrong words, speak right words. When we practise like this, our lives will change, our relationships will change, and our surroundings will change too. For Proverbs says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.”

Words are an authority God has given us. May we all become people like this: truth in our mouths, love in our hearts, and lives that bring blessing. Live out the selfless life, let Jesus live in us, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.
Let us pray together.

Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you. This morning you have shone your light on the state of our mouths. We confess that we have spoken idle words, judged our brothers and sisters, and said things unlike Jesus. Please forgive us. As you once cleansed Isaiah, cleanse our lips with the live coal from the altar, and cleanse our hearts too.
Lord Jesus, today we hand the sovereignty of our speech to you. May the words of our mouths and the thoughts of our hearts be acceptable in your sight. Holy Spirit, please be our guide.
In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
May you, brothers and sisters, have truth on your lips today, love in your hearts, and lives that bring blessing.
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come to Lesson 139, titled “Truth on the Lips, Love in the Heart”, with the subtitle: what should not be said, and what should.
Our key verse is Matthew 12:36: “I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment.”
Please notice one word — “every”. Not “more or less”, not “the important parts” — every word.
In the last lesson we learned to “speak the right words”. Today God wants to help us in a more specific way.
Where does our real difficulty lie? It isn’t that we don’t know we should speak good words. The real difficulty is this: we don’t know which words are actually “wrong”, and we don’t know how to tell.

A sister once said, “I was simply concerned for that brother. That’s why I told two other people about what was going on in his family.” Three weeks later that brother left the small group. She hadn’t lied; every sentence she said was true; her motive was even kind. But those words still killed a relationship.
Brothers and sisters, it isn’t only false words that wound — true words wound too; it isn’t only malice that must be accounted for — thoughtlessness must be accounted for too.
Words are not over once they are spoken. Words must be accounted for.

In our generation, speech has never been so cheap. One press of a finger, and within a second a sentence reaches the other side of the earth. But the weight of our words before God has not lessened one bit.

The dividing line in 321 is clear: self-centred people speak carelessly, because their centre is themselves; selfless people speak before God, because their centre is Jesus — before they open their mouths, they first look up.
Let’s look first at the background.

The author of Matthew’s Gospel is Matthew the tax collector; it was written around AD 50 to 70, for Jewish readers. The scene in chapter 12: Jesus healed a man who was demon-possessed, but the Pharisees said he drove out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons. In the middle of this dispute the Lord said, “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” The heart comes first, the mouth after.

First Corinthians was written by Paul in Ephesus around AD 55. Chapters 12 to 14 deal with spiritual gifts, with the love chapter, chapter 13, at the centre. Paul’s standard is not how beautifully something is said, but three things: did it build up? Did it comfort? Did it encourage?
Our first point: wrong speech. The first kind is idle words.
Idle words are words without meaning, without upbuilding, without value. They aren’t lies, they aren’t curses; they are simply … useless.
The Greek word for “idle” is argos, literally “not working”; the same word describes the labourers standing idle in the marketplace.

So the idle words the Lord speaks of are not necessarily foul words or lies, but words that are not at work. They are like an engine revving in neutral: the fuel still burns, the noise still roars, and the car does not move forward a single inch. What makes idle words most dangerous is that they look the most innocent.
Let’s look at a few numbers.

In 2007 Matthias Mehl of the University of Arizona and his colleagues published a study in the journal Science: men and women alike, people speak on average about sixteen thousand words a day — nearly six million words a year.

In 2019 Robbins and Karan of the University of California, Riverside, published research finding that adults spend on average about fifty-two minutes a day talking about people who are not present; the study also noted that most of this was neutral exchange of information, with clearly negative content a little over a tenth.
Fifty-two minutes a day — more than three hundred hours a year. Brothers and sisters, what exactly is this time building?
Idle words bring three losses.
First, they waste life. Moses prayed, “So teach us to count our days.” Once time has gone, not a single second can be recalled.

Second, they create problems. What you said at six out of ten has become ten out of ten by the time it reaches the third person. Idle talk is like flinging a pillowful of feathers into the wind — by the time you regret it, you can never gather them back.

Third, they damage relationships. James says, “See how a small fire can spread to a large forest! And the tongue is a fire.” According to the U.S. National Park Service, about 85 per cent of wildland fires in the United States are caused by people — mostly campfires left smouldering and cigarette ends tossed aside. One cigarette end burns down a forest.
A 321 insight: idle talk is the self-centred life’s most comfortable resting posture. The moment we relax, the old self’s tone of voice slips out.
The second kind of words we should not say is judgemental words.
Jesus said, “Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged.”

The Greek word for “judge”, krinō, originally means to separate, to distinguish, and by extension to pass judgement, to condemn. The Lord does not forbid discernment, because in the same chapter he says, “Therefore by their fruits you will know them.” What he forbids is our taking the judge’s seat.

The essence of judging is judging others by our own standard. And inside it hides a problem we find very hard to admit: judging is in fact a form of pride. When I judge someone, I assume three things at once — my standard is right, what I see is the whole picture, and I am qualified to sit in that seat.

But the truth is: we cannot see completely. We see behaviour, not motive; we see this moment, not the thirty years he has walked through. God says, “For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”

And we have problems of our own. The Lord said: why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye but don’t consider the beam in your own? A “speck” is a splinter of wood; a “beam” is the main timber of a house. A man with a roof beam sticking out of his eye wants to pick a splinter out of someone else’s.

In 1977 the American psychologist Lee Ross put forward the “fundamental attribution error”: when others fail, we attribute it to their character; when we fail, we attribute it to the situation. Someone else is late because he’s irresponsible; I’m late because of the traffic. It isn’t that we are especially wicked, but that the “self” sits in the middle and blocks our view.
The Bible reminds us of something even more fundamental: that office simply isn’t ours.
Paul says, “Who are you who judge another’s servant?” James says, “But who are you to judge another?”
At bottom, judging is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take God’s place — and that is the very definition of pride.

According to his biographer Possidius, Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, had two lines inscribed on his own dining table, to this effect: whoever loves to wound the good name of the absent is not welcome at this table.

Martin Luther, explaining the eighth commandment in his Small Catechism, said that we must not only refrain from slandering our neighbour, but rather defend him, speak well of him, and put the best construction on everything.
“Put the best construction on everything” — that is the antidote to judging. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man, and let God be God.
The third kind of words we should not say is words unlike Christ. Paul lists them very specifically: lies, slander, malice, bitterness, empty chatter.
Lies: Jesus said the devil “is a liar, and the father of lies”. When we lie, we are speaking the enemy’s mother tongue.
Slander: the original is blasphēmia. Used of God, it is translated “blasphemy”; used of people, it is translated “slander”. The very same word.
Bitterness: the original is pikria, meaning “a bitter taste”. We mix a cup of poison meaning to throw it at someone else, and most often we are the ones who end up drinking it.

Empty chatter: the original is kenophōnia, literally “empty noise”. Paul says, “But shun empty chatter, for it will go further in ungodliness.” Empty chatter doesn’t stay where it is; it moves downhill.

These words share three features: they don’t build people up, they don’t glorify God, and they are not like Jesus. So the principle is perfectly clear — any word that is not like Jesus should not be spoken.
How did our Lord speak? All “wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth”. The officers sent to arrest him came back empty-handed and said, “No man ever spoke like this man!”
And when he was wronged, Peter says, “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten.”

When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. Brothers and sisters, this is the hardest test of all. We may manage not to lie and not to slander, but in the moment we are wronged, the words practically burst out by themselves.

A 321 insight: the self-centred let the old self do the talking; the selfless refuse the old self’s tone of voice, because it is no longer I who live. So from today on, let us often ask: does this sound like Jesus?
God never simply tells us “don’t”. When he closes one door, he always opens another.
Paul says, “But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” Three standards, three verbs.

First, building up. The Greek is oikodomē, literally house-building. Building is slow, brick by brick; demolishing is fast — half a day is enough. Words that build people up must be spoken a hundred times before you see the result; words that tear people down need only be spoken once.

In 2001 the American psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues published a paper titled “Bad Is Stronger Than Good”, showing that negative events generally have a stronger impact than positive events of equal intensity. Gottman and Levenson’s marriage research also found that what decides whether a marriage is stable is not whether there is conflict, but the ratio of positive to negative interactions.
Second, comforting.
The two words rendered “exhortation” and “consolation” are, in the original, paraklēsis and paramythia.

Paraklēsis is formed from “beside” and “call” — to call alongside: going over and giving someone a hand up. The Holy Spirit’s title, the “Counsellor”, comes from exactly the same root. When we comfort people, we are doing what the Holy Spirit does.
Paramythia carries the sense of “speaking softly at someone’s side”: not reasoning with them, but keeping them company; not solving the problem, but not leaving them alone.
Proverbs says, “Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.” The bones are the deepest part of the body. Words can reach that deep.
Third, encouraging. Exhortation is bringing someone who has strayed back onto the right path.
Exhortation is not rebuke, and it is not flattery. Rebuke cares only about truth and not about the person; flattery cares only about the person and not about truth. Exhortation wants both.

Paul says, “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.” The original word for “restore” is used of mending nets, and in medicine it also meant setting a dislocated bone. This is the heart of exhortation: bone-setting. Setting a bone hurts, but the aim is restoration, not punishment.
So building up, comforting and encouraging become the filter for our mouths: does this build anyone up? Does it comfort anyone? Does it point in the right direction?
But there is a pit here that is very easy to fall into: right words are not the same as pleasant words.

Jesus said, “Let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’” In his day the Jews had developed an elaborate set of rules for oaths to keep a back door open in what they said, and the Lord cut through all of it at a stroke.
There is a deep principle here: when a person has to work hard to guarantee what he says, it is often precisely because his words carry no weight of their own.
So the Bible binds truth and love together: “speaking truth in love.” The original literally means “being truthful in love”.

Truth is the foundation; love is the manner. Truth without love is a stone — throw it, and it will injure someone; love without truth is sugar water — it will only leave people weaker. And our Lord is “full of grace and truth”.
Our third point: the highest purpose of speech.

When we speak, it isn’t only the content that must be right; the purpose must be right even more. Job’s three friends sounded very pious, yet God said, “You have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.” Right doctrine, wrongly used, is still wrong.
Jesus gave us the greatest standard of all: love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul and with all our mind, and love our neighbour as ourselves.
So before every time we speak, we can ask two questions: will this help someone come closer to God? Will this help a relationship be built up?

Some words, though true, still knock people down, because three other things determine the effect — timing, tone and motive. Proverbs says, “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.”
A 321 insight: the self-centred speak for themselves, and both sides lose; the selfless speak for love, and both sides win.
And sometimes the best choice is not to speak at all.
Proverbs says, “In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.” And again, “Even a fool, when he keeps silent, is counted wise.”
Better not to speak than to speak wrongly. A word left unspoken, we remain its master; once it is spoken, we become its servant.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer writes in Life Together about the discipline of the tongue. His point, in essence, is this: in fellowship, what most protects one another is often the discipline of not speaking about a brother behind his back; when a person stops talking about his brother, he truly begins to pray for him.
Only when we stop talking about others do we start interceding for them.

What is speech that truly belongs to God? Look at the fruit: it makes people love Jesus more, and love one another more. This is exactly the order of “life first, then relationships, then ministry” — people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.
Next come this week’s practices.
One, the three-question filter: before you speak, ask, does this build people up? Is it true? Does it carry love? Copy the verses onto a card and put it where you can see it.

Two, stopping the mouth: when you want to gossip or judge, choose not to say it. Brain-imaging research from the U.S. National Institute of Mental Health shows that the prefrontal cortex, which restrains impulses, does not fully mature until around the age of twenty-five — “holding back from speaking” is hard work in the first place; no wonder it takes practice, and no wonder it takes the Holy Spirit. David prayed, “Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” The Hebrew paints a vivid picture: “the door of my lips”. Our mouths need a doorkeeper.
Three, blessing instead: when you want to criticise, speak a blessing instead. Old habits can’t be removed by deleting them; they can only be crowded out by replacing them.

Four, relationships first: in conflict, don’t rush to prove you’re right; protect the relationship first. In your next conflict, begin with this sentence: “I’d like to hear you out first,” and then genuinely close your mouth and listen to the end. James says, “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.”

Five, selfless obedience: before you speak, ask — if Jesus were me, would he say it? How would he say it? Paul says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” If it is no longer I who live, then it is no longer I who speak.
Walk these five practices all the way through the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Isaiah gives us a promise prepared especially for the early morning: “He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear.” First let the ear be taught, and then the mouth will be taught.
Dear brothers and sisters, “speaking” is a spiritual discipline to be learned. What we should say and what we should not say — all of it needs learning.

Today God has given us a clear direction: refuse wrong words, speak right words. When we practise like this, our lives will change, our relationships will change, and our surroundings will change too. For Proverbs says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.”
Words are an authority God has given us. May we all become people like this: truth in our mouths, love in our hearts, and lives that bring blessing.

Let us pray together. Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you. This morning you have shone your light on the state of our mouths. We confess that we have spoken idle words, judged our brothers and sisters, and said things unlike Jesus. Please forgive us. As you once cleansed Isaiah, cleanse our lips with the live coal from the altar, and cleanse our hearts too. Lord Jesus, today we hand the sovereignty of our speech to you. Holy Spirit, please be our guide. In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
May you, brothers and sisters, have truth on your lips, love in your hearts, and lives that bring blessing. Live out the selfless life, let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: Introduction: One Mouth, Two Outcomes
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to be still for thirty seconds and call two sentences to mind.

The first is a kind word someone once spoke to you — one you still remember to this day. Perhaps it was a primary-school teacher who crouched down beside you and said, “You’re actually very bright — you just haven’t found the way yet.” Perhaps it was your mother, on the day you failed, who simply warmed up the food and said, “You’re home. That’s all that matters.” Perhaps it was an older believer who, when you were at your lowest, laid a hand on your shoulder and said, “I’m praying for you. God hasn’t given up on you.” That sentence may have been only a handful of words, yet it was like a nail driven into the wall of your life, and for decades afterwards you have been able to hang your hope on it.

The second is a wounding word someone once spoke to you — one you still haven’t entirely forgotten. Perhaps it was “How can you be so stupid?” Perhaps it was “This family would be no different with you or without you.” Perhaps it was in church, when a brother said to you in a very “spiritual” tone, “That’s not what I’d call submission.” That sentence may have been only a few words, yet it lodged in you like a thorn, and every time the weather turns grey it still aches.

Brothers and sisters, both of those sentences came out of a human mouth. The same organ, the same vibration of air, the same language — and yet two utterly different outcomes. Proverbs 18:21 says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” This verse uses a very weighty word — “power.” The tongue carries authority. It is not the strongest muscle in the body, but it is the most influential organ. James 3:5 says, “So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!”

In a study published in 2007 in the journal Science, the psychologist Matthias Mehl of the University of Texas and his colleagues used recording devices to capture the everyday conversations of nearly four hundred university students. They found that men and women alike speak on average about sixteen thousand words a day. Brothers and sisters, sixteen thousand words a day comes to nearly six million words a year. Printed as books, that would fill dozens of volumes every year. The question is: of those dozens of volumes, how much is a tree of life, and how much is the deceit that crushes the spirit? How much brings health to people’s bones, and how much breaks their hearts?

We often think of the spiritual disciplines as prayer, Bible reading, gathering together and giving. But there is one discipline we practise every day — sixteen thousand times a day — and yet very few of us practise it seriously: speaking. James 3:2 says, “For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.” So by the Bible’s standard, our words are the most honest thermometer of our spiritual maturity.

Today’s lesson is called “The Art of Speaking.” Please notice: the Bible never teaches us how to “speak beautifully.” What the Bible teaches us is how to let our mouths become an outlet for life. And there is a crucial dividing line here — not a line of technique, but the line of “self.” When the old self is self-centred, words become a tool for protecting ourselves, proving ourselves and venting ourselves. When the new self is selfless, words become a channel for the Holy Spirit, a vessel of grace and a seed of life.

So today we will look at five things together: the motive of our speaking, the relationship behind our speaking, the authority and timing of our speaking, the outcome of our speaking, and learning to bridle the tongue and wait for God’s time. May the Holy Spirit shine his light on each of our mouths this morning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Seven Passages, One Thread
sections.html: Today’s key passages span the Old and New Testaments. They may look scattered, but they are tied together by a very clear thread. Let’s first get the background of each one straight, so that our interpretation doesn’t go astray.

sections.heading: 1. Proverbs: A “Theology of Speech” in the Wisdom Literature
sections.html:
The principal author of Proverbs is King Solomon. Proverbs 1:1 says, “The proverbs of Solomon, the son of David, king of Israel:” Solomon reigned from roughly 970 to 930 BC. 1 Kings 4:32 records, “He spoke three thousand proverbs; and his songs numbered one thousand five.” The later part of Proverbs also gathers the words of Agur and of King Lemuel, and Proverbs 25:1 notes, “These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out.” Clearly this book is a treasury of wisdom, preserved by the Holy Spirit and compiled over a long span of years.

Proverbs belongs to the genre of Hebrew wisdom literature. It is not a code of law; it is a set of standards for daily living that grow out of “the fear of Yahweh.” Here is something worth noticing: in the mere thirty-one chapters of Proverbs, there are more than a hundred verses about lips, the tongue and speech. That is an exceptionally high proportion for any book of the Bible. Why? Because in the societies of the ancient Near East there were no recordings, and written contracts were far from common; the most important asset between one person and another was their “word.” Once a word was spoken, a covenant was made; once a word was spoken, a judgement was passed. Solomon was the most eloquent man in all Israel — when the Queen of Sheba heard his words of wisdom, 1 Kings 10:5 says, “there was no more spirit in her” — and yet it is this most eloquent of kings who devoted the most space to warning us: speaking is dangerous.

Proverbs 15:4 says, “A gentle tongue is a tree of life.” That image of the “tree of life” carries us all the way back to the Garden of Eden in Genesis 2:9. Humanity left the tree of life because of one sentence spoken by a serpent; now a tongue renewed by God’s grace can once again hand the fruit of the tree of life to someone else. What a restoration that is!

sections.heading: 2. Matthew 7:6: A Sense of Proportion in the Sermon on the Mount
sections.html:
The author of Matthew’s Gospel is Matthew the tax collector. He wrote chiefly for Jewish readers, and the Gospel is generally dated between AD 50 and 70. Matthew 7:6 sits in the final chapter of the Sermon on the Mount, and its context is crucial. Just before, in 7:1–5, the Lord Jesus says, “Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged.” Then, right after, in verse 6, he says, “Don’t give that which is holy to the dogs, neither throw your pearls before the pigs.”

Is that a contradiction? No. The Lord Jesus first blocks our pride — do not judge; then he blocks our sentimentality — do not fail to discern. Not judging deals with “self”; discerning deals with indiscriminateness. Put together, it means this: you have no right to pass judgement on others, but you do have a responsibility to discern the right moment. In Leviticus, “that which is holy” refers to the sacrificial meat offered to God, which only the priests could eat; and in those days pearls were things of very great value. The Lord Jesus is not saying that certain people are dogs and pigs — that is the most common misunderstanding. He is saying that if the most precious truth is thrown into a heart that isn’t yet ready, the result is not that the other person receives it, but that the truth is trampled and the speaker is torn to pieces. Brothers and sisters, this is the skeleton of today’s lesson: truth is a pearl, but pearls are to be handed over, not thrown.

sections.heading: 3. Ephesians 4:15: The Secret of the Body’s Growth
sections.html:
Ephesians is a letter the apostle Paul wrote during his first imprisonment in Rome, generally dated to AD 60–62, addressed to the churches in Ephesus and across the province of Asia Minor. The theme of Ephesians 4 is “unity and growth.” Verses 11–12 say that God gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” Verse 14 says that we should no longer be children, “tossed back and forth and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the trickery of men, in craftiness, after the wiles of error.”

Only then comes verse 15: “but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ.” Here “speaking truth in love” is in Greek alētheuontes en agapē, literally “being truthful in love.” Please notice that the emphasis of the original is not only on “speaking” but on “living out the truth in love.” Truth is not a stone hurled at someone; it is life handed over in the warmth of love. Verse 16 goes on: “from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love.” So this is how the church grows: by speaking the truth in love. Words are the body’s circulation.

sections.heading: 4. James 4:6: The Battle Behind Our Words
sections.html:
The author of James is generally held to be James, the Lord Jesus’ brother according to the flesh and the leader of the Jerusalem church. It may have been written as early as AD 45–50, making it one of the earliest books of the New Testament, and it is addressed to “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1). The whole of James 3 is about the tongue, and chapter 4 opens by asking, “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?”

In other words, James connects “the problem of the tongue” directly to “the problem of self.” In 4:6 he quotes the Septuagint of Proverbs 3:34: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” The Greek for “resists” is antitassomai, a military term for an army drawing up in battle formation against an enemy. Brothers and sisters, how sobering this is: when we speak with a proud mouth, God doesn’t merely disapprove — God draws up his battle lines against us. Verse 7 follows straight on: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” Submission and humility come first; resisting Satan comes after. This is exactly what 321 says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

sections.heading: 5. 1 Corinthians 10:23–24: The Boundary of Freedom Is Love
sections.html:
1 Corinthians is the letter Paul wrote from Ephesus to the church in Corinth, generally dated to around AD 55. Corinth was a prosperous port city, and its church was full of spiritual gifts — and full of strife: factions, lawsuits, food offered to idols, disorder at the Lord’s Supper, confusion over tongues. Chapters 8 to 10 deal with the question of whether food offered to idols may be eaten. Paul’s conclusion is superb: “‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are profitable. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.”

The Greek for “lawful” is exestin, meaning “to have the right”; “build up” is oikodomei, whose root means “to build a house.” Paul is saying: having a right doesn’t mean you ought to exercise it; the measure is not whether I am free, but whether the other person has been built up. Brothers and sisters, apply that principle to today’s theme and it becomes: having the right to say something doesn’t mean you ought to say it. Being right doesn’t mean the other person has been built up.

sections.heading: 6. One Thread
sections.html: Set the seven passages side by side and the thread emerges: words are pearls (Matthew 7:6), a honeycomb (Proverbs 16:24), a tree of life (Proverbs 15:4); but they must be handed over in love (Ephesians 4:15), handed over at the right time (Proverbs 15:23), handed over by a humble person (James 4:6), and handed over for the good of others (1 Corinthians 10:23–24). This is “the art of speaking” — not the art of eloquence, but the art of life.

sections.heading: 1. The Motive of Our Speaking: Without Love, Don’t Speak
sections.html:
Ephesians 4:15: “but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,”

1 Corinthians 13:1: “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal.”

Brothers and sisters, speaking in itself is never the problem; the motive is what matters. The same words — “What you’re doing is wrong” — spoken out of love are healing; spoken out of emotion, they wound. The same verse of Scripture spoken from a heart of grace is living water; spoken from a heart of grievance, it is a stone.

Here is the self-deception we fall into most easily: we think we are “speaking the truth,” when in fact we are “venting our emotions.” Truth becomes the respectable justification for our feelings, and Scripture becomes the ammunition for our attacks. The Lord Jesus put it with piercing clarity in Matthew 12:34: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” The idea in the original is overflow — what the mouth says is simply what the heart holds, spilling over. When a cup gets knocked, what splashes out doesn’t depend on who knocked you; it depends on what was in the cup to begin with.

So the question is never “How could he say that about me?” The question is “What is inside me?” Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” The wellspring of life flows not from the mouth but from the heart; the mouth is only the heart’s estuary.

The self-centred life and selflessness: two sources of speech

The core insight of 321 applies perfectly here: when there is “self” inside a person, the purpose of their speaking is to prove themselves right; only when a person enters into selflessness does the purpose of their speaking become a longing for the other person to be built up. The self-centred person wants to win the conversation; the selfless person wants to love in the conversation. When the self-centred person hears a different opinion, their first reaction is to defend; when the selfless person hears a different opinion, their first reaction is to listen.

Paul says in 1 Corinthians 8:1, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” Knowledge inflates people; love builds people. Inflating is blowing yourself up; building is putting the other person up. Brothers and sisters, do we want to be balloons blown up big, or labourers building houses?

Psychology bears witness: contempt is the fatal wound to a relationship

The American psychologist John Gottman of the University of Washington has studied marital interaction for more than forty years. In research he published with Robert Levenson in 1992, he found that in stable, happy marriages the ratio of positive to negative interactions is roughly five to one. He also identified the “Four Horsemen” of relationships: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. Of these, the most destructive — and the strongest predictor of divorce — is contempt.

What is contempt? Contempt says, “I am above you.” It can hide in a roll of the eyes, in a cold laugh, in a remark like “I told you so.” Brothers and sisters, notice this: the essence of contempt is pride, and the essence of pride is the self-centred life. What psychology has measured, the Bible said long ago: “God resists the proud.”

In addition, the social psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues published a well-known paper in 2001 in the Review of General Psychology whose very title was “Bad Is Stronger Than Good.” Drawing together a large body of research, they showed that negative events have a far greater psychological impact on people than positive events of equal strength. That explains Gottman’s five to one exactly — because it takes five kind words to make up for the damage of one harsh one. Brothers and sisters, what we often tear down in a minute takes a year to build back up.

Relying on the heart, or relying on the brain?

The lesson leaves us with two sentences to remember: the person who relies on the heart speaks for the other person’s good; the person who relies on the brain speaks for their own comfort. The 321 teaching puts it well: rely on the heart and you will have joy; rely on the brain and you will have worry. Relying on the brain means calculating for ourselves, scheming for ourselves, finding our own justifications; relying on the heart means depending on the Holy Spirit, following the Holy Spirit and being guided by the Holy Spirit.

So if you are still angry inside, still feeling wronged, still nursing a grievance — don’t speak yet. First come before God and deal with that “self.” A saying generally attributed to the American writer Ambrose Bierce goes, “Speak when you are angry and you will make the best speech you will ever regret.” Brothers and sisters, that one deserves a place on the fridge door.

James 1:19 says, “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;” Look at the order: swift to hear comes first, slow to speak in the middle, slow to anger last. God gave us two ears and one mouth — a ratio of two to one; the discipline of Scripture is to live out that ratio.

Applying the 321 Vision: deal with “self” first, then open your mouth

On the 321 Path of Serving, the order is Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the Holy Spirit is my guide, the Bible is my standard, Jesus is my role model, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. Our speaking should follow that same order. First let the Holy Spirit guide my heart, then let the Bible be my standard, then learn the way of Jesus, and finally let Jesus be King in this conversation and let the glory go to him.

Brothers and sisters, before you open your mouth, ask one question: is this sentence going out to make me feel better, or for his good? Is it to prove that I’m right, or to let Jesus be King? If the answer is the former, close your mouth and go and pray first. Without love, don’t speak.

sections.heading: 2. The Relationship Behind Our Speaking: Without Relationship, Don’t Speak
sections.html:
John 15:15: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.”

Proverbs 27:6: “The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.”

Brothers and sisters, the depth of our words depends on the depth of our relationship. This is a law of spiritual physics; break it, and no matter how much force you put behind your words, they won’t get through.

Jesus is the best role model

The Lord Jesus did not begin by speaking his deepest words. He first called his disciples and walked with them for three years — walking the roads together, eating together, sailing together, sleeping out in the wilderness together. He washed their feet; he turned water into wine at the wedding they attended; he calmed the wind and the waves when they were frightened half to death. The relationship was built, and only then did he gradually open the Father’s heart to them.

Only at the Last Supper did he say, “I have called you friends.” And even then, in John 16:12, he still said, “I still have many things to tell you, but you can’t bear them now.” Brothers and sisters, look at that: even the Son of God held words back for the sake of the relationship and of what the hearers could carry! Who are we, then, to think we can pour out everything we see onto someone all at once?

Mark 4:33 also says, “With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it.” “As they were able to hear it” — that is the art of speaking. Not according to what I want to say, but according to what he is able to hear.

Why do words that are correct still wound?

This is why some things that are “correct in content” still sound harsh, cause offence, and can even break a relationship. Truth without relationship becomes pressure; only truth with relationship becomes provision. The same sentence, from an older believer who walked with you through the valley, is support; from someone who has met you three times online, it is commentary.

This is precisely the wisdom of Matthew 7:6: don’t throw your pearls before the pigs. There is nothing wrong with the pearl itself; the problem lies in the act of “throwing,” and in a receiving heart that isn’t yet prepared. Pearls are to be handed over, not thrown. Handing over requires being close enough; handing over requires reaching out your hand; handing over requires the other person being willing to take it.

Psychological safety: confirmation from modern research

In 1999 Amy Edmondson, a professor at Harvard Business School, introduced the concept of “psychological safety” — the belief among team members that they can take interpersonal risks without being humiliated or punished. Beginning in 2012, Google carried out “Project Aristotle,” analysing more than a hundred and eighty teams within the company, and in 2015–2016 it published its conclusion: the most important factor in predicting a high-performing team was not how clever its members were or how senior, but “psychological safety.”

Brothers and sisters, how closely that finding agrees with the Bible. People don’t change when they are corrected; people change when they are loved. Galatians 6:1 says, “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” The Greek word for “restore” is katartizō; ancient medicine used it for setting a dislocated bone, and fishermen used it for mending nets. How close must a bonesetter come to the patient? How gentle must the net-mender be? That is the attitude we ought to have when we speak to others.

Paul’s example: give life first, then words

In 1 Thessalonians 2:7–8 Paul says, “But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children. Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.” Brothers and sisters, this was the apostle’s secret: what he gave was not only teaching, but his very life. That is why his words carried weight.

Applying the 321 Vision: life first, then relationships, then ministry

321 has a very clear order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Notice that ministry always comes last. Pointing out someone’s fault, teaching them, correcting them — that is all ministry; and ministry must stand on relationship, and relationship must stand on life.

The lesson puts it beautifully: it isn’t first about “getting the words right” but about “getting the love right.” As deep as the relationship goes, that is how deep you may speak; without relationship, however right your words are, they find no way in. 321 also reminds us of the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. People matter more than things; relationships matter more than possessions. The “thing” you want to correct will never matter more than the person.

This is exactly the training ground of the 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2.” Within those “2” relationships we practise living out a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. Galatians 5:22–23 says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” Brothers and sisters, notice that the last one is self-control — the fruit of the Spirit includes the power not to speak.

So when you badly want to say something harsh to someone, first ask yourself: have I made enough deposits in his life? Have I walked alongside him? Have I wept for him? How many times have I prayed for him? If the balance in the relationship account is zero, don’t make a withdrawal yet. Without relationship, don’t speak.

sections.heading: 3. The Authority and Timing of Our Speaking: Without Authority, Without Prayer, Don’t Speak
sections.html:
James 4:6: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’”

Proverbs 15:23: “Joy comes to a man with the reply of his mouth. How good is a word at the right time!”

Brothers and sisters, not every problem you see requires you to open your mouth. Please hear that once more: not every problem you see requires you to open your mouth. Seeing is a burden God gives you; opening your mouth requires God’s sending.

The rush to correct is often pride doing the talking

Sometimes when we rush to correct others, it is actually “pride doing the talking,” not “the Holy Spirit leading.” 321 defines pride very clearly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When I am in a hurry to change someone, I have actually stepped into the Holy Spirit’s place and am trying to do the Holy Spirit’s work with my tongue.

James says, “God resists the proud.” Even God himself does not force anyone to listen. In Genesis 3:9, when the man had sinned and was hiding, God did not shout a rebuke; he asked only one question: “Where are you?” In Luke 15 the father did not chase his younger son to the far country to lecture him; he waited at the door of his house. Brothers and sisters, if even God is willing to wait, why can’t we?

321 says: pride stirs up pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. A correction delivered from on high only ignites the same pride in the other person, and then both people lose.

True authority is the other person’s willingness to let you speak

True authority is not only a matter of position; it is whether the other person is willing to let you speak. This must be said plainly: an office gives you a position; a life gives you weight. Position without weight, and your words only provoke defensiveness; only words that carry weight can get into the heart.

In 2 Samuel 12 the prophet Nathan went to see King David, who had committed adultery and murder. He didn’t walk in and jab a finger in the king’s face; first he told a story about a poor man and his little ewe lamb.
