Only when David’s heart had been opened and his righteous anger aroused did Nathan speak those four words: “You are the man” (2 Samuel 12:7). Brothers and sisters, Nathan had a prophet’s authority, yet he still took the path of wisdom. And the result? David didn’t kill him; David repented and wrote Psalm 51. That is a word spoken with authority and at the right time.

Before you speak, always pray first

What’s more, our speaking must always pass through prayer first. Not saying what we want to say, but saying what the Holy Spirit wants said. The Lord Jesus says in John 12:49, “For I spoke not from myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.” Brothers and sisters, even the Lord Jesus did not speak from himself! On what grounds do we speak from ourselves?

In Nehemiah 2:4 the Persian king asked Nehemiah, “What is your request?” And Scripture records, “So I prayed to the God of heaven.” Standing before the king, in those few brief seconds, Nehemiah prayed first and then spoke. That one opening of his mouth rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. Brothers and sisters, isn’t your most important conversation worth three seconds of silent prayer first?

Timing: the chemistry of a single sentence

Proverbs 25:11 says, “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.” Notice the word “fitly” — fitting the moment. With the wrong timing, even truth turns into hurt; with the right timing, a single sentence can turn a life around. Ecclesiastes 3:7 says, “a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.” Silence comes before speech.

Sometimes God is already at work in the other person’s heart, and all we need to do is say the right word at the right moment. It’s like a midwife at a birth: the child is made by God, the due date is set by God, and the midwife simply reaches out her hands at the right moment. Job 2:13 records of Job’s three friends: “So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.” Those seven days were the best thing they did in the whole book; from chapter 3 onwards, the moment they opened their mouths, the more they said, the more wrong they got.

Neuroscience, too, reminds us how much timing matters. A study by Matthew Lieberman’s team at the University of California, Los Angeles, published in 2007 in the journal Psychological Science, found that when people put their emotions into words, activity in the amygdala goes down and the regulating function of the prefrontal cortex goes up. This shows that at the peak of emotion, the reasoning brain is temporarily “offline.” Brothers and sisters, reasoning with someone whose reason is offline is like typing commands into a computer that’s switched off.

Applying the 321 Vision: the focus is on Jesus

So before you open your mouth, ask yourself: have I prayed? Is this God’s time? 321 reminds us: the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. When my focus is on myself, I’m in a hurry to prove myself; when my focus is on others, I’m in a hurry to correct them; when my focus is on my circumstances, I’m in a hurry to fix them. Only when my focus is on Jesus can I wait quietly for him to say, “Now — speak.” Without authority, without prayer, don’t speak.

sections.heading: 4. The Outcome of Our Speaking: Without a Way Forward, Don’t Speak
sections.html:
1 Corinthians 10:23–24: “‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are profitable. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.”

Ephesians 4:29: “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.”

Brothers and sisters, the purpose of truth is not to make people “see the problem” but to help them “find the way forward.” If a sentence only leaves someone more self-reproachful, more ashamed and more helpless, yet brings no hope and no direction, then that sentence is not building up — it is tearing down.

God’s pattern: naming the sin and offering salvation at the same time

Look at how God himself speaks. In Genesis 3, as God names the sin of Adam and Eve, in that very passage — verse 15 — he promises the offspring who will crush the serpent’s head. This is the first gospel in the Bible. God shines his light into the darkness and at the same time brings a way out.

In John 8, the woman caught in adultery is thrown down in front of the Lord Jesus. The Lord Jesus doesn’t say, “You have no sin.” What he says is: “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more” (John 8:11). The first half is grace; the second half is truth and direction. Grace is given first, direction afterwards — that is the order of speaking in the kingdom of heaven.

John 1:14 says, “The Word became flesh, and lived among us… full of grace and truth.” Notice the order: grace first, truth after; and both are there in fullness. The lesson puts it superbly: truth plus grace equals life; truth minus grace equals accusation. And accusation is never the work of the Holy Spirit — Revelation 12:10 tells us that the one who accuses our brothers before our God day and night is Satan.

A scientific picture: why honey heals

Proverbs 16:24 says, “Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.” Scientifically, this picture is remarkably precise. Honey has a very low water content and a very high sugar content, creating a high-osmotic environment in which bacteria struggle to survive; honey is acidic, with a pH of roughly 3.2 to 4.5; and the glucose oxidase that bees secrete slowly releases tiny amounts of hydrogen peroxide. Precisely because of these properties, medical-grade manuka honey dressings have been cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration for wound care.

Brothers and sisters, three thousand years ago the Holy Spirit used a picture that laboratories only confirmed in the twenty-first century: kind words are not merely sweet — kind words disinfect, heal and help new flesh to grow. And the verse says “health to the bones” — the bones are the deepest, hardest, innermost part of the body, and the place where blood is made. A good word can reach a person’s deepest place and make new blood for them.

Hope is the name of the way forward

So before you open your mouth each time, ask: will what I’m about to say help this person move forward, or leave them stuck? Words that truly come from God always carry “an outlet of hope.” Romans 8:1 says, “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.” That is the gospel; that is the way forward.

In psychology, the American psychologist Barbara Fredrickson proposed the “broaden-and-build theory” in 1998. She showed that positive emotions broaden a person’s immediate range of thought and action and, over time, build up lasting personal psychological resources; negative emotions, by contrast, narrow a person’s attention and responses. This explains why shame leaves people stuck while hope moves them forward: the person who has been shamed has a narrowed field of vision and thinks only of escape or counter-attack; only the person upheld by hope can see their options.

Applying the 321 Vision: a shift of perspective

321 speaks of a shift of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Man’s perspective sees “he’s wrong”; God’s perspective sees “he’s still on the way.” The earthly perspective wants the problem solved immediately; the heavenly perspective is willing to wait for the work God is completing in him. The temporary perspective just wants to get everything said today; the eternal perspective cares whether this person will still be in God’s house thirty years from now.

Brothers and sisters, do you want to be the one who freezes a person on their worst day, or the one who points them towards the best ending God has for them? Without a way forward, don’t speak.

sections.heading: 5. Learning to Bridle the Tongue: Waiting for God’s Time
sections.html:
Proverbs 15:23: “Joy comes to a man with the reply of his mouth. How good is a word at the right time!”

James 3:2: “For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.”

Brothers and sisters, very often the problem isn’t that we can’t speak, but that we speak too soon. The lesson reminds us of three sentences — please hold them in your heart: speaking when you shouldn’t is hurtful; not speaking when you should is a debt left unpaid; only speaking in God’s time is a blessing.

Knowing how to speak, and how not to

One important mark of spiritual maturity is “knowing how to speak, and knowing how not to.” James 3:2 says something very weighty: the one who does not stumble in word is a perfect person. The original word for “bridle” is chalinagōgeō, formed from the words for “bit” and “lead” — literally, “to steer with a bit.” This word tells us two things. First, the tongue is like a powerful, untamed horse. Second, the untamed horse is not to be killed but to be steered. God doesn’t want us to become mute; God wants our tongues to be steered by the Holy Spirit.

In Psalm 39:1 David says, “I will watch my ways, so that I don’t sin with my tongue. I will keep my mouth with a bridle while the wicked is before me.” And in Psalm 141:3 he prays, “Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” The original carries the sense of “keeping the door” — asking God to post a doorkeeper on my lips. Brothers and sisters, does your mouth have a doorkeeper?

Proverbs 10:19 says, “In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.” This is a law of probability: the more you talk, the greater the odds of getting something wrong. The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer says in Life Together that the first service a Christian owes his brother is to listen; and he warns that the one who will not listen to his brother will soon no longer be listening to God either.

Bridling the tongue is denying of self

This is the discipline of denying of self — not saying whatever we feel like saying, but letting Jesus reign as King within us. Matthew 16:24 says, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” One of the most concrete battlegrounds of denying ourselves is the sentence that has already reached the tip of your tongue and that you swallow back down.

321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Galatians 2:20 says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” When we are selfless, our mouths no longer speak for ourselves; they become an outlet for the Holy Spirit.

Isaiah 50:4 describes the suffering Servant: “The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” Brothers and sisters, look at the order: first an ear that is taught, then a tongue that is taught; first listening morning by morning, then knowing how to sustain the weary. This is exactly what morning devotion is for — we come every morning to listen, so that every sentence we speak today can hold up someone who is weary.

Applying the 321 Vision: let Jesus be King

The Two Core Values of 321 are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Letting Jesus be King in our speech means handing the decision “Should I say this or not?” entirely back to him. The focus is not on whether I want to speak; the focus is on whether Jesus wants me to speak.

Brothers and sisters, silence sometimes takes more faith than speaking. Because when I am silent, I have to trust that God does not need a sentence from me to accomplish his work. This is the deepest humility — laying down our rights, returning to our originally intended position, letting man be man and letting God be God.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Words Are an Outlet for Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, set today’s five points within the 321 framework and you will see a complete picture.

The Three Foundations determine the groundwork of our speaking. Jesus is my role model — he spoke as people were able to hear; he waited three years for the sake of relationship; he gave grace first and direction afterwards. The Bible is my standard — what I say is not my opinion; it is God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — I don’t speak from my emotions, but by the Holy Spirit’s guidance.

The Two Core Values determine the aim of our speaking. Let Jesus be King: who has the final say in this conversation? Not my face, not my position — him. Let Jesus receive all the glory: when this sentence goes out, is it my insight that gets exalted, or his grace?

The Goal determines the direction of our speaking: establish God’s system. A system is made up of relationships, and relationships are nourished by words. Every sentence you speak today is either building God’s house or tearing it down.

The fivefold change is the very path of this lesson: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. When my mindset shifts from “I must get the words right” to “I must get the love right,” my life changes; when my life changes, the language of my daily living changes; when my language changes, relationships are healed; and when relationships are healed, ministry finally has a foundation. So the order is always: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

The 920 practice is the best training ground for our words. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”: spouse, children, parents, colleagues, small-group members. In every “2” relationship we practise living out a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. Today’s assignment is very concrete: in front of the “2” you most easily speak harshly to, bear these two fruits first — gentleness and self-control.

235 relationships are the safest setting for our words. Becoming a “2” with a selfless person — a spiritual companion — means having someone with whom we can speak the truth to each other; building a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children — means relationships that can bear the weight of the truth; becoming a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades — means a unit that can fight the battle together with the truth. Brothers and sisters, truth needs a vessel that can carry it; 235 is that vessel.

Finally, there is the shift of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. When I look at the person in front of me with eternal eyes, I’m willing to wait; when I look at this conflict with heavenly eyes, I don’t need to win. Because humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan; pride stirs up pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Let Your Words Become an Outlet for Life
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five practices. Let’s use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to put them into practice one by one.

Practice 1: Pause for three seconds — let your heart grow quiet before you speak

Every time you’re about to speak, pause for three seconds and ask yourself: am I relying on my heart right now, or on my emotions? Am I doing this for the other person, or for myself? Practise letting the Holy Spirit speak first, and then open your mouth.

Information and Revelation: know that “out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34), and ask the Holy Spirit to show you what your heart really holds. Conviction and Implementation: from today on, every time you’re about to respond, count silently to three and say, “Lord, you speak.” Evaluation and Correction: each evening, look back — how many times did I pause today, and how many times didn’t I? On the occasions I didn’t, what was the “self” in me?

Practice 2: Build the habit of “five questions before speaking”

Before every important conversation, ask yourself five questions: One, is this coming from love? Two, is my relationship with him deep enough? Three, do I have the authority to say it? Four, have I prayed? Five, am I offering a way forward? Let these five questions become the spiritual filter for your words.

Repetition and Multiplication: write the five questions on your phone’s wallpaper or on the first page of your notebook, and practise them for forty days straight; then teach your family and your small-group members to ask them too. The final stage of the eight is Multiplication — a mouth that has been healed should multiply into many more healed mouths.

Practice 3: Move from “explaining what’s right” to “offering a way forward”

When you need to point out a problem, prepare three things at the same time: one concrete suggestion, one act of companionship and one prayer of blessing. Let your words not only point out the problem but lead the person towards change.

An example of Implementation: don’t just say, “Your devotions have been really slack lately.” Say instead, “I’ve been finding it hard to be still lately too. Why don’t we send each other a verse every morning at seven? And I’ll pray for you today.” — suggestion, companionship and blessing, three in one.

Practice 4: Practise a life of “speaking less and loving more”

Deliberately cut down on meaningless, emotional, critical and judgemental words, and replace them with more encouragement, affirmation and blessing. Let your mouth become a tree of life.

Evaluation and Correction: remember Gottman’s five to one. Of the things you said to your family today, what was the ratio of positive to negative? If you spoke a harsh word yesterday, then today you need to add five sincere kind words — not flattery, but repair.

Practice 5: Bless someone with one sentence every day

Every day, speak at least one word that builds someone up: encouragement, thanks, affirmation, blessing. Let your words begin to become instruments of healing and building.

Multiplication: three hundred and sixty-five sentences of blessing a year are three hundred and sixty-five seeds of life. Ephesians 4:29 says, “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.”

A Gentle Reminder

The ability to speak is not the same as spiritual maturity; speaking a lot doesn’t mean speaking rightly; and speaking rightly doesn’t mean speaking at the right time. Truly godly people are not those who are “good with words,” but those who “let God decide when to speak, what to say and how to say it.” The focus is not on whether I want to speak; the focus is on whether Jesus wants me to speak. When you let Jesus be King, your mouth will become an outlet for life.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: One Mouth — What Will You Let It Become?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, words are an outlet for life.

The same mouth can build people up or tear them down; it can bring revival or bring ruin. James 3:9–10 says, “With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God. Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.”

The key is not “whether you can speak” but “who is speaking inside you.” When you choose selflessness and let Jesus live in you, your words are no longer merely a human voice but a voice that carries the power of the kingdom of heaven.

This morning I want to issue you a call: place your tongue back into the hands of Jesus. Let him be King of your mouth. Let every time you open it first pass through his permission; let every silence become an act of trust in him.

Let us spend our whole lives learning this heavenly art — letting every sentence become a seed of life. May the fruit of our mouths not be praise for our cleverness, but that Jesus Christ receives all the glory.

keyVerses: Matthew 7:6
“Don’t give that which is holy to the dogs, neither throw your pearls before the pigs, lest perhaps they trample them under their feet, and turn and tear you to pieces.”

prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.
You are the Word; you are the God who spoke, and it was done, who commanded, and it stood firm. This morning we bring our mouths before you.

Lord, forgive us for wrapping our emotions in the packaging of truth; forgive us for rushing to speak when we had no love, no relationship, no authority, no prayer and no way forward to offer. Forgive us for using our tongues to tear down the people you love.

Cleanse our hearts, for out of them is the wellspring of life. Post a doorkeeper on our lips, so that we may be swift to hear and slow to speak. Give us the tongue of those who are taught, so that we may know how to sustain with words those who are weary.
Lord, let our mouths no longer speak for ourselves, but for you. Let our tongues become a tree of life, and our pleasant words a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and health to the bones.
Be King in our words, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

blog.title: Let the Mouth Be an Outlet of Life

blocks.x: Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 140 · Blog Post
One sentence can make a person live — or make a person die
Please call two sentences to mind.

The first is a kind word someone once spoke to you, one you have remembered all your life. Perhaps it was only “You’re home. That’s all that matters,” yet it was like a nail driven into the wall of your life, and for decades afterwards you have been able to hang your hope on it.

The second is a wounding word someone once spoke to you, one that still aches today. Perhaps it was only a few words, yet it lodged in you like a thorn, and every time the weather turns grey it flares up again.
Both of those sentences came out of a human mouth. The same organ, the same vibration of air — and yet two utterly different outcomes.
Proverbs 15:4 says, “A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.”

According to a study by the psychologist Matthias Mehl and his colleagues, published in the journal Science in 2007, a person speaks on average about sixteen thousand words a day. That is nearly six million words a year — enough to print dozens of books. The question is: of those dozens of books, how much is a tree of life?
Five questions before you speak

When the Bible talks about speaking, it never talks about technique, only about the source. The Lord Jesus said, “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34) When a cup gets knocked, what splashes out doesn’t depend on who knocked you; it depends on what was in the cup to begin with.
So before you open your mouth, ask yourself five questions:

1. Is this coming from love? Without love, don’t speak. We often think we are speaking the truth when in fact we are venting our emotions. Truth becomes the respectable justification for our feelings, and Scripture becomes the ammunition for our attacks.

2. Is my relationship with him deep enough? Without relationship, don’t speak. The depth of our words depends on the depth of our relationship. The Lord Jesus walked with his disciples for three years, and only at the Last Supper did he say, “I have called you friends”; and he still said, “You can’t bear them now.” If even the Son of God held words back, who are we to think we can pour out everything we see onto someone all at once?

3. Do I have the authority to say it? True authority is not only a matter of position; it is whether the other person is willing to let you speak. An office gives you a position; a life gives you weight.

4. Have I prayed? When the prophet Nathan went to see David, he didn’t walk in and start rebuking; first he told the story of a little ewe lamb, and only when David’s heart had opened did he speak those four words: “You are the man!” The result? David didn’t kill him; David repented.
5. Am I offering a way forward? The purpose of truth is not to make people see the problem, but to help them find the way forward. Truth plus grace equals life; truth minus grace equals accusation.
Knowing how to speak, and how not to
One important mark of spiritual maturity is not being good with words, but “knowing how to speak, and knowing how not to”.

James 3:2 says that the one who does not stumble in word is “able to bridle the whole body also”. The original word for “bridle” means “to steer with a bit”. God doesn’t want us to become mute; God wants our tongues to be steered by the Holy Spirit. The untamed horse is not to be killed, but to be steered.

Proverbs 16:24 says, “Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.” Scientifically, this picture is remarkably precise: honey’s very high sugar content creates a high-osmotic environment, and it is acidic and contains glucose oxidase, so it fights bacteria; today medical-grade honey dressings have been cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration for wound care. Kind words are not merely sweet — kind words disinfect, heal and help new flesh to grow.

The key is not “whether you can speak” but “who is speaking inside you”. While there is still “self” inside us, words become a tool for protecting ourselves, proving ourselves and venting ourselves; when we are selfless and let Jesus live within, our mouths become an outlet for the Holy Spirit.

Today you can do one very small thing: speak one word that builds someone up — encouragement, thanks, affirmation or blessing. Three hundred and sixty-five sentences of blessing a year are three hundred and sixty-five seeds of life.
Reflection question
This week, was there something you said that you regretted as soon as it was out? If you could say it again, which question would you ask yourself first?
