prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you that your word has come to us this morning and shone its light on what is within us.

Lord, we confess that we have spent too much strength on the outside and too seldom come back to the inside. We have covered dryness with busyness and replaced reliance with effort. We have done many right things, yet inside we have grown ever more tired and ever more joyless.
Lord, have mercy on us.

Renew our minds; turn us from man’s eyes to your eyes, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from temporary sight to eternal sight. Help us to put off the old self of our former way of life and put on the new self, created in the likeness of God in righteousness and holiness of truth.
Lord, today we no longer ask for more strength; we ask for you yourself. We no longer say, “I must try harder”; we say, “Lord, I can’t, but you can. Please live it out in me.”
Holy Spirit, shine your light on us so that we see our true condition; guide us so that we have strength to walk in the truth.
May Jesus reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Ephesians 4:22–24: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” Please share: what “way of seeing things” has God been renewing in you lately? How has that renewal affected your words or actions?

Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” Please share honestly: what is one thing in your life right now that is “acted out” rather than “lived out”? How will you hand it over to the Lord this week and learn to let him live it?

blog.title: Are You a Real Flower or a Silk One?

blocks.x: Why does trying harder only make us more tired?
Two pots of flowers sit on a table. The one on the left is evenly coloured and never wilts, all year round; the one on the right has insect bites on its leaves, and in a few days it will fade.
If we looked only at the outside, most of us would choose the one on the left. But the pot on the left is silk flowers. The pot on the right is real.
Silk flowers need no sunlight, no water, no roots. They are always that beautiful, because they have never been alive.

That is where so many Christians’ weariness lies. We try hard to read the Bible, try hard to come to meetings, try hard to love people, try hard not to lose our temper. Yet late at night, when all is still, there is an emptiness in our hearts we can’t put into words. The more we do, the drier we feel inside; the better we perform, the more false we feel within.
The problem isn’t that we haven’t done well enough. It’s that we are always “doing” and never “living”.
The Bible’s Order: Seeing and Listening First, Behaviour After
In Ephesians Paul sets out a very clear order:

“But you didn’t learn Christ that way, if indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:20–24)
First hearing, then receiving, then learning — and only at the very end, putting off the old self and putting on the new self.
Notice: the change in behaviour comes last, not first. It is not the starting point; it is the result.

If a person has not first changed his “seeing” and “listening”, his “doing” is only imitation, suppression or forcing. See wrongly, and you will hear wrongly; hear wrongly, and you will think wrongly; think wrongly, and you will do wrongly. Turn it around: only by seeing rightly will you hear rightly; only by hearing rightly will you think rightly; only by thinking rightly will you do rightly.

In 1999 the psychologists Simons and Chabris published a famous experiment in the journal Perception. Participants concentrated on counting the passes in a short film, while a person in a gorilla suit walked slowly through the middle of the scene — and about half of them never saw it at all.
What we see depends on what we are paying attention to. It isn’t the eyes that decide what we see; it’s the heart.
Two Kinds of Doing: A Tree and a Christmas Tree
“Doing” has two different sources.

The first kind of doing is “lived out”, like a tree. When the root is healthy, it bears fruit naturally; when the life is right, the behaviour is right. This kind of doing takes time, but it is stable, lasting and full of life.

The second kind of doing is “acted out”, like a Christmas tree. A Christmas tree is a tree that has been cut down. Severed from its roots, it is hung with baubles and strung with lights, and for the first few days it looks better than any tree on the mountainside. But day by day its needles drop, and all you can do is hang on more decorations to cover the bare patches.
Under pressure, you do it; without pressure, you stop. The more you do, the more tired you get; the more you do, the more false you become; the more you do, the less joy you have.
What God wants is not “doing right” but “living right”.
Real Change Is the Work of Grace
So where does change come from?
Paul says: “I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)
On one side, working harder than all of them; on the other, “yet not I”. This is no contradiction. It is working very hard at relying, not working very hard at holding it together yourself.
Change is not “I try harder”; change is “I let God do it”.

Relying on the brain and on ourselves, acting it out — exhausting. Relying on the heart and on the Holy Spirit, living it out — natural. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is letting Jesus live within.
The true Victor is not the one who tries hardest, but the one most willing to let the Lord be King.
Three Practices to Begin Today
1. Start from the source every day. First ask yourself: am I seeing things today with God’s eyes?
2. Discern your doing. Are you doing this because of pressure, or because life is flowing out? If it is reluctance, go back to God; don’t grit your teeth and push through.
3. Exchange “I must try harder” for a prayer: “Lord, I can’t, but you can. Please live it out in me.”

Don’t look only at outward behaviour; God looks at the life within. Don’t rush to get things right; first let the inside be set right. Don’t strain to change yourself; learn to let Christ live in you.
When the inside is right, the outside will naturally be right.
Question for reflection: This week, which “right thing” have you actually been acting out rather than living out? Are you willing to hand it to the Lord and let him live in you?

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning let’s read Ephesians 4:20–24 together. Paul says: “But you didn’t learn Christ that way, if indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” The theme of this lesson is: right doing is not done from without; it is lived out from within.

Brothers and sisters, picture a scene. There are two pots of flowers on a table. The one on the left is evenly coloured and never wilts, all year round. The one on the right has insect bites on its leaves, and in a few days it will fade. The left is silk flowers; the right is real. Silk flowers are always beautiful, because they have never been alive. Let me ask you: which pot is your life like? Many of us try very hard — try hard to read the Bible, try hard to come to meetings, try hard not to lose our temper. Yet late at night, when all is still, our hearts are weary. Why? Because we are always “doing”, and never “living”.

Brothers and sisters, Paul wrote Ephesians in prison in Rome. A man with chains on his hands wrote the most expansive book in the whole Bible. Ephesus was a city of idol worship, of show and of outward appearance. In a city like that, someone who only looked like a Christian on the outside wouldn’t last long. So Paul first gives three chapters of doctrine, and then three chapters on daily living; first who you are, then what you do. Grace first, then conduct; identity first, then responsibility. And that is exactly what 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Brothers and sisters, look at the order Paul sets out. First, you heard his word. Second, you received his teaching. Third, you learned his truth. Fourth — only then — you put off the old self and put on the new. See it clearly: behaviour comes fourth, not first. The change in behaviour is not the starting point; it is the result. If we haven’t first changed our “seeing” and “listening”, our “doing” is only imitation, suppression, forcing. In “be renewed in the spirit of your mind”, the word “mind” in the original means the way we think, the angle from which we see things. And “renewed” is passive — you don’t renew yourself; you are renewed by God.

Brothers and sisters, the lesson puts it well: see wrongly, and you hear wrongly; hear wrongly, and you think wrongly; think wrongly, and you do wrongly. Turn it around: only by seeing rightly do you hear rightly; only by hearing rightly do you think rightly; only by thinking rightly do you do rightly. Proverbs 4:23 says: “for out of it is the wellspring of life.” In 1999 two psychologists ran a famous experiment, asking people to count the passes in a short film. A person in a gorilla suit walked through the middle of the scene, and about half of them never saw it at all. Brothers and sisters, what we see depends on what we are paying attention to. 321 says: change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your living changes.

Brothers and sisters, there are two kinds of “doing”. The first is doing that is lived out, like a tree. When the root is healthy, it bears fruit naturally; when the life is right, the behaviour is right. The Lord Jesus said: “A good tree can’t produce evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree produce good fruit.” And he said: “apart from me you can do nothing.” The branch’s work is not bearing fruit; the branch’s work is staying connected. A tree’s roots often spread wider than its crown. What we see is the branches and leaves; what we don’t see is the roots. The stronger the wind, the more the roots matter. Ask yourself: how much of my time goes into the branches and leaves, and how much into the roots?

Brothers and sisters, the second kind is doing that is acted out, like a Christmas tree. What is a Christmas tree? It is a tree that has been cut down. Severed from its roots, it is hung with baubles and strung with lights, and for the first few days it looks better than any tree on the mountainside. But day by day its needles drop, and all you can do is hang on more decorations to cover the bare patches. The lesson says: under pressure, you do it; without pressure, you stop; the more you do, the more tired you get, the more false you become, the less joy you have. The Lord Jesus said the Pharisees were like whitened tombs — beautiful outside, but unclean within. What God wants is not doing right, but living right.

Brothers and sisters, so where does real change come from? In 1 Corinthians 15:10 Paul says that by the grace of God he is what he is; and he says, “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” A man who once persecuted the church went on to write nearly half the books of the New Testament. He knew better than anyone: this was not self-cultivation; it was grace. Philippians 2:13 says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work.” So change is not “I try harder”; change is “I let God do it”. Only when the Holy Spirit shines his light on us do we see our own problems; only when the Holy Spirit guides us do we have the strength to live out the truth.

Brothers and sisters, think about this: did you remind yourself this morning, “Heart, remember to beat”? No. Your heart beats about a hundred thousand times a day without any help from your will. But raising your hand or walking takes willpower — and it tires you. Whatever is held up by willpower will surely tire; only what flows out from life within can last. 321 says: relying on the brain and on ourselves, acting it out — exhausting; relying on the heart and on the Holy Spirit, living it out — natural. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is letting Jesus live within. The true Victor is not the one who tries hardest, but the one most willing to let the Lord be King.

Brothers and sisters, we have five practices. First, start from the source every day, and first ask: am I seeing things today with God’s eyes? Second, discern your doing — is it lived out, or acted out? If it is reluctance, go back to God; don’t grit your teeth and push through. Third, stop relying on yourself; exchange “I must try harder” for “Lord, I can’t, but you can.” Fourth, in everything ask: if Jesus were me, how would he live? Fifth, give yourself time. A seed in the soil is unseen, but something is happening.

Brothers and sisters, let’s return to those two pots of flowers. Silk flowers never wilt, because they have never been alive. What God wants is not a showpiece that never goes wrong, but a life that is truly growing. The lesson says: while you are still “doing”, you will be weary; when you begin to “live”, you will have joy. God has not called us to be people who perform well; he has called us to become people through whom Christ is lived out. So today, put down the decorations in your hands, go back to your roots, and let Jesus be King. When the inside is right, the outside will naturally be right.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we confess that we have covered dryness with busyness and replaced reliance with effort. Please renew our minds, and help us to put off the old self and put on the new. Lord, we no longer ask for more strength; we ask for you yourself. We say: Lord, I can’t, but you can. Please live it out in me. May Jesus reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you and enable you to live out the righteousness and holiness of truth.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we read Ephesians 4:20–24. Paul says: “But you didn’t learn Christ that way, if indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” The theme of this lesson is very clear: right doing is not something done from without; it is something lived out from within. We will look at three key points: beginning with seeing and listening, the two kinds of doing, and the work of the Holy Spirit.

Brothers and sisters, picture a scene. There are two pots of flowers on a table. The one on the left never wilts, all year round, and is spotless; the one on the right has insect bites on its leaves, and in a few days it will fade. Which one would you choose? The left is silk flowers; the right is real. Silk flowers need no sunlight, no water, no roots. They are always beautiful, because they have never been alive. Inside the real flowers runs an unseen channel of water, from the root all the way to the tip of every petal. Let me ask you: which pot is your life like?

Brothers and sisters, many of us try very hard. We try hard to read the Bible, try hard to come to meetings, try hard to love people, try hard not to lose our temper. Yet late at night, when all is still, there is a weariness in our hearts we can’t put into words. The more you do, the emptier you feel; the better you perform, the more false you feel within. Why? Not because we haven’t done well enough, but because we are always “doing”, and never “living”. In Book One of his Confessions, Augustine says: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

Brothers and sisters, Ephesians is one of Paul’s prison letters, generally thought to have been written during his first imprisonment in Rome, around AD 60 to 62. A man in chains wrote the most expansive book in the whole Bible. Ephesus was the capital of the province of Asia, and its Temple of Artemis was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Acts 19 records that Paul reasoned daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus; many who practised magic repented and burned their books, and when they counted their price, it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. It was a city of idol worship, of show and of outward appearance. In a city like that, merely looking like a Christian on the outside wouldn’t last long. So Paul uses three chapters to tell you who you are, and then three chapters to tell you how to live. Grace first, then conduct — and that is exactly what 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Brothers and sisters, look at the order Paul sets out. First, you heard his word. Second, you received his teaching. Third, you learned his truth. Fourth — only then — you put off the old self and put on the new. Do you see it? Behaviour comes fourth, not first. The change in behaviour is not the starting point; it is the result. Many people rush to change their behaviour, but if they haven’t first gone through the three steps before it, their resolutions won’t survive three months. Because you are only managing the fruit; you haven’t dealt with the root. The lesson puts it precisely: if “seeing” and “listening” haven’t changed first, “doing” is only imitation, suppression or forcing.

Brothers and sisters, “be renewed in the spirit of your mind” — the word “mind” in the original is the Greek nous, meaning the way we think, the angle from which we see things. In Romans 12:2, “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” uses the same word. Notice especially that “renewed” in the original is passive. You don’t renew yourself; you are renewed by God. The one doing the renewing is God. So what we must do is not grit our teeth and hold on, but place ourselves where God’s word and the Holy Spirit can renew us. The Bible doesn’t tell us to grit our teeth; the Bible tells us to change the way we see.

Brothers and sisters, the lesson says: see wrongly, and you hear wrongly; hear wrongly, and you think wrongly; think wrongly, and you do wrongly. Turn it around: only by seeing rightly do you hear rightly; only by hearing rightly do you think rightly; only by thinking rightly do you do rightly. Proverbs 4:23 says: “for out of it is the wellspring of life.” In 1999 the psychologists Simons and Chabris published an experiment in the journal Perception: participants concentrated on counting the passes in a short film, a person in a gorilla suit walked through the middle of the scene, and about half of them never saw it at all. Brothers and sisters, it isn’t the eyes that decide what we see; it’s the heart.

Brothers and sisters, 321 says the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. This order can’t be reversed. Many people start with ministry; they are very zealous, but the roots never go down, and after a while they dry up. How is our perspective to change? From man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal. There was a man who wore glasses with yellowed lenses. He complained that the sky wasn’t blue enough, so he changed the curtains and changed the light bulbs. Until one day he wiped his glasses clean, and suddenly the world was bright. How many years have we spent changing the curtains, without ever thinking of cleaning our glasses?

Brothers and sisters, the second key point. When Paul says “put on the new self”, he doesn’t mean adding a new coat over the old self. First “put away”, then “put on”, and between them stands “be renewed in the spirit of your mind”. The new self is not an upgraded version of the old self; the new self is another person altogether. The lesson divides “doing” into two kinds. The first is doing that is lived out: it flows naturally from the life within; it takes time, but it is stable and lasting. The second is doing that is acted out: it is forced, imitated and demanded from the outside; it looks good, but over time it becomes wearying and painful.

Brothers and sisters, the first kind of doing is like a tree. When the root is healthy, it bears fruit naturally; when the life is right, the behaviour is right. The Lord Jesus said: “A good tree can’t produce evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree produce good fruit.” Notice: “can’t”, not “shouldn’t”. Fruit is the expression of life, not the product of outside force. In John 15:5 the Lord says: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” The branch’s work is not bearing fruit; it is staying connected. A tree’s roots often spread wider than its crown. The stronger the wind, the more the roots matter.

Brothers and sisters, the second kind of doing is like a Christmas tree. What is a Christmas tree? It is a tree that has been cut down. Severed from its roots, it is hung with baubles and strung with lights, and for the first few days it looks better than any tree on the mountainside. But day by day its needles drop, and all you can do is hang on more decorations to cover the bare patches. Doesn’t that look like our condition? More and more hung on the outside, drier and drier on the inside. The lesson says: under pressure, you do it; without pressure, you stop; the more you do, the more tired you get, the more false you become. The Lord Jesus said the Pharisees were like whitened tombs — beautiful outside, but inwardly full of all uncleanness.

Brothers and sisters, Colossians 2:23 says that rules and severity to the body “aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh”. Not of little value — of no value at all. In 1985 Deci and Ryan put forward self-determination theory, showing that behaviour driven by outside control is hard to sustain. In 1981 Maslach and Jackson identified three dimensions of burnout: emotional exhaustion, coldness towards people, and a reduced sense of accomplishment. But the deepest root of burnout isn’t too much work; it is the self-centred life. 321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Galatians 2:20: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

Brothers and sisters, the third key point. Real change doesn’t depend on human effort; it depends on God’s grace. 1 Corinthians 15:10 says: “I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” On one side, working harder than all of them; on the other, yet not I. So is it effort, or not effort? The answer is: working very hard at relying, not working hard at holding it together yourself. Philippians 2:13 says: “it is God who works in you both to will and to work.” So change is not “I try harder”; change is “I let God do it”.

Brothers and sisters, this is not a teaching found only in the New Testament. In Ezekiel 36:26 God promises: “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” Only in the next verse does he say, “and cause you to walk in my statutes.” Look at the order: first a new heart, and obedience follows. God never required his people to obey first and get a new heart afterwards. Zechariah 4:6 says: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,” says Yahweh of Armies.

Brothers and sisters, the Holy Spirit does two things. The first is illumination — letting us see our own problems. John 16:8 says that when he comes, he will convict the world about sin. The second is guidance — giving us strength to live out the truth. Romans 8:13 says: “if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.” By the Spirit — not by gritted teeth. Here is a simple fact: an adult’s heart beats about seventy times a minute, about a hundred thousand times a day. Did you remind yourself this morning, “Heart, remember to beat”? No. Whatever is sustained by willpower will surely tire; only what flows from life within can last.

Brothers and sisters, 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll have joy, rely on the brain and you’ll have worry. The lesson says: relying on the brain and on ourselves, acting it out — exhausting; relying on the heart and on the Holy Spirit, living it out — natural. This isn’t telling us not to use our minds. The mind is a vessel for receiving, not an engine for generating power; the engine is the Holy Spirit. The Lord Jesus said: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me … and you will find rest for your souls.” The Lord didn’t take the yoke away. Whether you’re weary depends on who is pulling beside you. The lesson says: the true Victor is not the one who tries hardest, but the one most willing to let the Lord be King.

Brothers and sisters, let’s look at the practices. First, start from the source every day. First ask yourself: am I seeing things today with God’s eyes? I suggest you write Ephesians 4:20–24 on a card and put it somewhere you will see it every day, for forty days in a row. Second, discern your doing — is it lived out, or acted out? Ask yourself: am I doing this because of pressure, or because life is flowing out? If it is reluctance, go back to God; don’t grit your teeth and push through. Third, stop relying on yourself. When you come to something you can’t do, don’t blame yourself; pray instead: “Lord, I can’t, but you can.”

Brothers and sisters, fourth, practise letting Jesus live. In everything ask: if Jesus were me, how would he live? Choose the situation where you most easily lose control, be still for three seconds first, and say, “Lord, you come.” Fifth, give yourself time. Mark 4:28 says: “For the earth bears fruit: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.” A farmer doesn’t dig up his seeds every day to check on them. The 321 eight stages can help us go deeper: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Brothers and sisters, let’s look over the 321 map. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. The 920 practice says: everyone we relate to is our “2”; before them we live out the selfless “0”, and let the Holy Spirit bear his ninefold fruit. Galatians 5:22–23 says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” Notice that the passage speaks of the fruit of the Spirit, not the performance I produce by effort. The 235 relationships also tell us: first the “2” of spiritual companions, then the “3” of spiritual parents and children, and finally becoming the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Brothers and sisters, let’s return to those two pots of flowers. Silk flowers never wilt, because they have never been alive. What God wants is not a showpiece that never goes wrong, but a life that is truly growing. The lesson says: while you are still “doing”, you will be weary; when you begin to “live”, you will have joy. God has not called us to be people who perform well; he has called us to become people through whom Christ is lived out. So today I extend three invitations. First, put down the decorations in your hands; stop using more service to cover the dryness within. Second, go back to your roots, and begin again with seeing and listening. Colossians 3:2 says: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” Third, let Jesus be King. Not your consultant — your King. When you place your life in the King’s hands, you will discover that you no longer need to strain so hard, because the one really doing the work is him. When the inside is right, the outside will naturally be right.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we confess that we have spent too much strength on the outside and too seldom come back to the inside; we have covered dryness with busyness and replaced reliance with effort. Please renew our minds; turn us from man’s eyes to your eyes, from the temporary to the eternal. Help us to put off the old self and put on the new, in righteousness and holiness of truth. Lord, we no longer ask for more strength; we ask for you yourself. May Jesus reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you, so that from today you live it out from within.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Seed in Your Hand That Was Never Sown
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to ask you first to be still for thirty seconds and answer one question: over this past year, of the things God has shone his light on in your heart, how many have you actually gone and done?

Not “how many have you agreed with”, not “how many have moved you”, but “how many have you lived out”.

An old farmer once said something that has stayed with me ever since: “A farmer’s greatest failure in life isn’t a poor harvest; it’s keeping his seed in his pocket until it goes mouldy.” Seed in the pocket can be touched, can be counted, can even be taken out and shown to people. But a seed’s destiny isn’t to be looked at; it’s to be buried in the ground. Only when it falls into the earth does it die; only when it dies does it grow; only when it grows does it bear thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. A seed left in the pocket is only ever a seed.

The greatest trap in the spiritual life is “stopping at knowing”.

Christians of our generation are the least short of “information” of any generation in history. One swipe of the phone and there are countless sermons; open the computer and there are pages of exposition. We know far more than believers did a hundred years ago. But we must honestly ask: are our lives stronger than theirs? Are our families more united than theirs?

That is the question this lesson has to face. In the last lesson we talked about “right doing”, and saw the importance and the direction of doing the word; this lesson takes one step further — from knowing to doing, and from doing to receiving.

Between these three words stand two checkpoints. The first lies between “knowing” and “doing”, where a chasm called “procrastination and self-deception” stretches across the way; the second lies between “doing” and “receiving”, and what it requires is the perseverance of “continuing”. Most people get stuck at the first.

Brothers and sisters, remember the heart of today: knowing is not having; only doing leads to receiving.

God’s word is living and powerful, but his power isn’t released in our notebooks; it’s released in our obedience. That seed you’re holding in your hand — will you sow it this morning?

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Scenes
sections.html: Today’s theme passages are three, from three different writers and three different scenes. When we see the backgrounds clearly, we can see the consistent intention of the Holy Spirit throughout the whole Bible.

sections.heading: 1. James 1:22–25: A Family Letter to People Scattered Abroad
sections.html:
Evangelical scholars generally hold that the author of James was James, the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh (Matthew 13:55 names James among Jesus’ brothers), who later became the leader of the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; Galatians 2:9). James may well be one of the earliest books of the New Testament to be written, dating from around the AD 40s, and it was addressed “to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1) — that is, to Jewish Christians scattered abroad by persecution.

Notice who James was. He grew up alongside Jesus. John 7:5 says, “For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.” James at first did not believe; then the risen Lord appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7), and only then did he become God’s servant. A man who went from “knowing a great deal about Jesus” to “truly knowing Jesus” is the one best qualified to say, “not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” For he himself had once known the most and yet been furthest away.

The style of James is like the wisdom literature of the Old Testament — every sentence practical, every line piercing. The flow of chapter 1 runs: trials (verses 2–12), temptation (verses 13–18), and then hearing and doing the word (verses 19–27). James doesn’t trade works for salvation; he says works prove salvation.

The “mirror” of verse 23 was, in the first century, a mirror of polished metal, usually bronze or silver — not as clear as today’s glass mirrors. To see clearly you had to lean in, catch the light and stay there. So James draws a weighty contrast: one kind of person takes just a “look” and walks away; the other kind “looks into” it. The Greek for “looks into” is parakuptō, which means to bend down, to stoop and lean close to look carefully; the same word is used in John 20:5, when John ran to the empty tomb and, “stooping and looking in”, saw the linen cloths. James is saying: that is the posture we should take towards the word of God.

sections.heading: 2. John 13:17: A Word Spoken Beside the Washbasin
sections.html:
The scene of this verse is the Last Supper. The Lord Jesus got up from the table, took off his outer garment, tied a towel around his waist, poured water into a basin, and washed his disciples’ feet one by one. When he had finished, he put his clothes back on, sat down and spoke to them, and then came verse 17: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.”

Pay attention to the Lord’s wording: “If you know … if you do them … blessed are you.” Knowing is a premise already established; doing is a condition not yet fulfilled; blessing is the result once the condition is met. The Lord did not say, “Blessed are you if you know”; he said, “blessed are you if you do them.” Nowhere in the whole Bible is there a promise that “those who know are blessed”, yet again and again it promises that “those who obey are blessed” (Psalm 1:1–2; Luke 11:28; Revelation 22:14).

What’s more, the context of this sentence is foot-washing. What the Lord wanted his disciples to go and do was not some lofty set of doctrines; it was the posture of bending down to serve others. We often think of “doing the word” as some great, hard undertaking, yet the Lord placed it in a basin of water and a towel.

sections.heading: 3. Matthew 7:24–25: The Seal on the Sermon on the Mount
sections.html:
Matthew chapters 5 to 7 are the Sermon on the Mount. The Lord Jesus spoke of the blessings, of the true meaning of the law, of prayer, of not worrying, of not judging. When he had finished, he closed with a parable: two men, two houses, two outcomes.

Notice that this is the very last part of the whole sermon. The Lord Jesus didn’t close with a prayer, nor with a blessing; he closed with “doing or not doing”. It’s as if he were saying: I’ve spoken for three chapters, and you’ve listened for three chapters; now everything depends on what you do after you come down the mountain.

Verses 26–27 are the other half: “Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it fell — and great was its fall.” Both men heard; the only difference was one word — “do”.

The terrain of Palestine makes this parable especially real. There are many dry riverbeds there, known by the Arabic word wadi (in Hebrew, nachal). In the dry season the riverbed is a flat stretch of soft sand, the easiest place of all to build; but when the rainy season comes, water pours down from the hills, and within a few hours that stretch of sand becomes a torrent. A house built on it is swept away, foundations, walls and all. The Lord’s hearers had all seen such things.

Brothers and sisters, three passages, three scenes, one message: God’s word counts only when it is lived out.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Only by Moving from Knowing to Doing Do We Receive
sections.html:
“If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17)

The greatest trap in the spiritual life is stopping at “knowing”.

There are so many people around us like this — perhaps we ourselves are such people: we know a great many truths, have heard a great many messages, can even preach a great deal, yet our lives haven’t changed. Why? Because the most crucial step is missing — “doing”.

sections.heading: 1. See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do, Receive: A Six-Stage Spiritual Cycle
sections.html:
For a truth to enter our lives, it usually passes through six stages: seeing, listening, thinking, speaking, doing and receiving.

“Seeing” is contact, “listening” is reception, “thinking” is digestion, “speaking” is putting it in order, “doing” is transformation, “receiving” is possession.

The trouble is that the first four stages all give us the illusion that “I’ve already made progress”. We see a moving testimony and our hearts burn; we hear a piercing message and our eyes fill with tears; we meditate on a verse again and again and feel full of light; we tell others about that light and are even praised for it. We can go through all four stages and our lives may not have moved an inch.

Because it is in the fifth stage, “doing”, that truth turns from knowledge into life. Without “doing”, we never reach “receiving”.

It’s like a seed. You may have seen the seed, heard all about the seed, thought about what the seed will grow into, even shown the seed to others — and the seed is still a seed. The Lord Jesus said: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) Falling into the ground — that is “doing”.

sections.heading: 2. Knowing Can Deceive: Two Real Studies
sections.html:
Psychology has some well-known findings that can help us see clearly how unreliable “knowing” is.

The first is the forgetting curve. In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus carried out a series of memory experiments with himself as the subject, and found that newly learned material, if not reviewed or used, is lost in large amounts within a very short time; after one day, often only about a third is retained. Brothers and sisters, what does that mean? It means that if the message you hear this morning is only “heard”, by this time tomorrow two thirds of it will be gone. The only way to keep hold of the truth isn’t to hear it again; it’s to do it once. Because what we have done stays in our muscles, stays in our relationships, stays in our lives.

The second is “the curse of knowledge”. In 1990 Elizabeth Newton, a psychology researcher at Stanford University, carried out an experiment: one group was asked to tap out with their fingers the rhythm of a song everyone knows well, and another group had to guess which song it was. The tappers predicted that the listeners would guess right about half the time; in fact, out of a hundred and twenty songs only three were guessed correctly — a hit rate of about two and a half per cent. The reason is simple: the tappers had the melody in their heads; the listeners had only the tapping in their ears.

This experiment is a wake-up call for us. When we “know” a truth, we have the whole melody in our heads, and so we think we already possess it. But what others see isn’t the melody in our heads; it’s the sound our hands tap out — that is, what we actually live. And that is how God sees us too.

sections.heading: 3. The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea: Only What Flows In and Out Is Alive
sections.html:
Israel has two famous bodies of water, both fed by the Jordan River, yet with completely opposite fates. In the north, the Sea of Galilee: water flows in from the north and out to the south; it teems with fish, the towns on its shores have flourished, and most of the Lord Jesus’ ministry took place there. In the south, the Dead Sea: water only flows in and never out, its one exit being evaporation, so the salt keeps building up; fish can’t live there and plants can’t grow, and so it is called the “Dead Sea”.

The same living water — one becomes a sea of life, the other a sea of death, and the difference lies in one thing only: whether there is an outlet.

Brothers and sisters, our spiritual lives are the same. God’s word keeps flowing in, but if there is no outlet of “doing”, the truth that comes in settles inside, crystallises and turns salty — until it becomes knowledge for judging others, a standard for criticising sermons, a heart that understands everything and yet moves for nothing.

sections.heading: 4. A 321 Insight: Changing the Mindset Is the Beginning; Living Out the Life Is the Result
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry.

Notice that “mindset” is only the first of the five, not the last. Many people treat a “change of mindset” as the finish line — they celebrate having worked it out, having understood it, and then they stop there. But the fivefold change is a chain, and if any link in the middle breaks, nothing after it will happen. And the link that joins mindset to life is precisely “doing”.

The 321 vision also reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll have joy, rely on the brain and you’ll have worry. Proverbs 4:23 says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” Relying on the brain, you can know a great deal, yet produce no fruit; what flows out of a whole life comes from the heart, and the heart’s outlet is action.

Brothers and sisters, here is this morning’s first decision: no longer be satisfied with “I understand”. From today, when you finish hearing a message, don’t ask, “What did I learn?” Ask instead, “What am I going to do today?”

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Not Doing the Word Is Spiritual Self-Deception
sections.html:
“But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)

These are very weighty words. It turns out that a person may think he is growing, yet if there is no “doing”, he is actually “deceiving himself”.

sections.heading: 1. How Weighty the Original Is: “Deluding Your Own Selves”
sections.html:
The Greek for “deluding” is paralogizomai, made up of two parts, “beside” and “to reckon, to reason”; literally it means “to miscalculate the accounts”, “to mislead with plausible but false reasoning”. The same word appears in Colossians 2:4: “Now I say this that no one may delude you with persuasiveness of speech.”

In other words, people who only hear the word and don’t do it aren’t stupid; they know how to keep accounts — they’ve just got the sums wrong. They have entered “heard it” as “received it”, “moved” as “obeyed”, “agreed” as “changed”. In their spiritual passbook the figures look very fine, but in reality it’s a set of falsified books.

And the most dangerous thing is this: no one else is deceiving them; they are deceiving themselves. When others deceive you, someone can still warn you; when you deceive yourself, you have switched off the alarm yourself.

sections.heading: 2. Three Actions in Front of the Mirror
sections.html:
James uses the mirror as a picture, describing three actions of such a person: “for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.” (James 1:24)

He sees — the truth shows up the problem.

He goes away — his body leaves the mirror.

He forgets — his heart leaves the light as well.

Brothers and sisters, aren’t those three actions a portrait of our every Sunday? The meeting is moving, the sermon pierces us, and by the time we reach the car park after church we’re back to how we were; we get home to the same temper, the same coldness, the same hurtful remark.

There’s nothing wrong with the mirror, nothing wrong with the light; the problem is that we’ll only “take a glance” and won’t “bend down”. As we said earlier, “looks into” in verse 25 is parakuptō — to stoop, to bend low and lean in close to look carefully. Truly doing the word means being willing to stay in front of that mirror thirty seconds longer, letting the truth shine on the places in ourselves we’d rather it didn’t.

sections.heading: 3. Knowing Without Doing Ends in Becoming a Pharisee
sections.html:
This is James’s deepest warning, and the Lord Jesus’ sternest rebuke.

Matthew 23:2–3 records the Lord’s words: “The scribes and the Pharisees sat on Moses’ seat. All things therefore whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do, but don’t do their works; for they say, and don’t do.”

“They say, and don’t do” — those few words are the most dreadful end that spiritual knowledge can come to. The Pharisees didn’t know too little; they knew too much and did too little. If knowledge isn’t used to deal with ourselves, it automatically turns to deal with others.

The Lord goes on: “For they bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not lift a finger to help them.” (Matthew 23:4) This is the inevitable end of not doing the word: a life that stalls, a spirit that dries up, even a turning to judge others — demanding of others what we don’t demand of ourselves.

Psychology has observed something similar. In 1957 the American psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”: when a person’s beliefs and behaviour don’t match, an inner tension arises, and there are two ways to resolve it — one is to change the behaviour so that it fits the belief; the other is to reinterpret things so that the conscience goes quiet. The second way is much cheaper, so most people take it. “I haven’t managed it, but at least I agree with it.” “That truth was meant for so-and-so.” “I’ll deal with it when things are a bit better.” Brothers and sisters, we’ve all said such things. This is exactly how “deluding your own selves” works at the psychological level.

sections.heading: 4. A 321 Insight: Pride Is Leaving Our Originally Intended Position — Using Truth to Make Demands of Others Is Pride
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Using the truth to press down on others is the classic case of leaving our originally intended position. The truth belongs to God, and shining light on people is the Holy Spirit’s work; when I take the truth into my hand as a measuring rod to measure others, judge others and condemn others, I’ve sat down in a seat that isn’t mine. And God’s response is very clear: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

So the 321 vision says: selflessness means dealing with ourselves first, not using the truth to press down on others. The Lord Jesus asks: “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3) Notice the Lord’s words — the other person’s is a “speck”, our own is a “beam”. Our eyes come fitted by nature with a magnifying glass for looking at others and a reducing glass for looking at ourselves. Doing the word means swapping those two lenses back.

A truly spiritual person isn’t the one who says the most, but the one who can live it out.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Doing Is Food for the Spiritual Life
sections.html:
“Jesus said to them, ‘My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.’” (John 4:34)

So “doing” isn’t a burden; it is nourishment for life.

sections.heading: 1. What the Lord Jesus Said by the Well
sections.html:
The background to this saying is John chapter 4. The Lord Jesus had walked all day and sat down by Jacob’s well, tired and thirsty. The disciples came back from buying food in the town and urged him, “Rabbi, eat.” But the Lord answered, “I have food to eat that you don’t know about.” The disciples said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?” And the Lord spoke the words of verse 34.

See how wonderful this scene is: because the Lord Jesus had talked with the Samaritan woman and brought a broken life to God, his weariness was gone. Obeying the Father’s will didn’t drain him; on the contrary, it fed him.

Many people think: doing the word is hard work, and obedience is a strain. But the truth is exactly the opposite — it’s not doing that makes us wither; it’s not obeying that brings us pain.

sections.heading: 2. A Picture from the Body: Unused Muscles Waste Away
sections.html:
The human body God made bears witness to spiritual principles at every turn. Modern medical research on long-term bed rest and on weightlessness in space shows the same thing: muscles left unused for a long time waste away rapidly, strength drops markedly within a few weeks, and bone is lost too for lack of load. That’s why astronauts on the space station have to spend hours exercising every day; otherwise, when they return to earth, they can hardly stand. This is “use it or lose it”.

Our spiritual lives follow the same law. Hebrews 5:14 says: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.”

The Greek for “exercised” is gymnazō, the root of our word “gymnasium”; it refers to an athlete’s repeated training. Spiritual discernment isn’t something you hear; it’s something you train.

So, just as going without food leaves us hungry, a spirit that doesn’t do the word will die. Doing the word isn’t an extra burden; doing the word is the meal we need to eat every day.

sections.heading: 3. Only by Doing Do We Know: Obedience Is the Door to Knowing God
sections.html:
The Lord Jesus said something very important: “If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I am speaking from myself.” (John 7:17)

Notice the order: first the desire to do it, then the knowing. The world’s order is “understand it first, then do it”; God’s order is “do it, and then you’ll understand”.

It’s like learning to swim. You can know the principles of buoyancy inside out, you can memorise every step of the breathing technique, but if you don’t get into the water you’ll never swim; and once you’re in the water, what your body learns in three minutes surpasses three months of reading on the bank.

The German martyr-pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote in The Cost of Discipleship: “Only he who believes is obedient, and only he who is obedient believes.” Faith and obedience aren’t two things, one after the other; they are two sides of one thing. If we stop at believing without obeying, that faith will wither sooner or later; James 2:17 says: “Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.”

Samuel, too, said to Saul: “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” (1 Samuel 15:22) What God wants has never been our religious performance; it is our obedience.

sections.heading: 4. Doing Doesn’t Depend on Effort — It’s Letting the Lord Live Himself Out in You
sections.html:
By now, some hearts are bound to be sinking: “Pastor, I know I should do it, but I just can’t.”

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly the key. If “doing” depended on our gritting our teeth and trying hard, this message would only lay a heavier burden on you. But the good news of the gospel is this: doing isn’t something we hold together by ourselves; it is letting Christ live himself out in us.

Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

The Lord Jesus also says: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) A branch bears fruit not by straining, but by staying joined to the vine.

Philippians 2:13 gives us enormous comfort: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” Even the “willing” is God at work in our hearts!

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll have joy, rely on the brain and you’ll have worry. Thinking with the brain, we rely on ourselves, and the result is powerlessness; doing from the heart, we rely on the Holy Spirit, and the result is life.

The 321 vision also says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. So the true definition of “doing the word” isn’t that I do things for God; it’s that I step aside and let God do things through me. The more selfless I am, the more room the Lord has within me; the more room the Lord has, the more naturally it is lived out.

The 321 Path of Serving follows the same order: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). “Service” comes after “Life” — first there is life, then there is service; what is lived out is the overflow of life, not the struggle of the flesh.

Brothers and sisters, this morning please change one mindset: doing the word doesn’t drain you; doing the word feeds you. When we begin to do it, God’s word turns from “knowledge” into “life” — do it, and you experience God; do it, and you gain God; do it, and your life is fed.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: Doing Lays the Foundation of Life
sections.html:
“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.” (Matthew 7:24–25)

The Lord Jesus closes the Sermon on the Mount with a very vivid picture: those who do the word build their house on the rock; those who don’t build their house on the sand.

sections.heading: 1. What the Two Men Had in Common, and What They Didn’t
sections.html:
Look carefully at what is the same and what is different in this parable.

Four things are the same: both men heard the Lord’s words; both men built a house; from the outside both houses looked like houses; both houses met the same rain, floods and wind.

Only two things are different: one did it, the other didn’t; one house never fell, the other fell, and great was its fall.

Brothers and sisters, what cuts deepest in this parable is this: the difference wasn’t in the hearing, wasn’t in appearances, wasn’t in what befell them — it was only in the “doing”. And that difference can’t be seen at all before the storm comes. On a sunny day both houses look equally fine; the one on the sand may even have gone up faster, more easily, and been finished sooner.

The Lord calls the one who doesn’t do the word a “foolish man”; the Greek is mōros, the root of the English word “moron”. It refers not to low intelligence but to foolish judgement — saving trouble now at the cost of everything later.

sections.heading: 2. The Foundation Is Unseen, Yet It Decides Everything
sections.html:
The world’s most famous case of foundation failure is the Leaning Tower of Pisa in Italy. Construction began in 1173, and before the tower had reached its third storey it began to lean. The cause wasn’t in the design of the tower but underground — the foundation was too shallow, and beneath it lay soft alluvial soil without enough bearing capacity. For more than eight hundred years people have used every engineering method they could think of to save it, yet they can never make it stand straight again. However beautiful what’s built above, if the foundation is wrong, it’s wrong.

The opposite example is Taipei 101. Everyone can see the part of this 508-metre building that stands above the ground, but the real work lies unseen beneath it: the engineering team sank 380 foundation piles, anchored deep into the hard bedrock below, and added a massive foundation structure, so that it can withstand typhoons and earthquakes.

Brothers and sisters, nobody takes photos of foundations; nobody applauds a foundation. Foundations are laid when no one is watching. The spiritual life is the same — the foundation isn’t built in the storm; the foundation is “done” in ordinary days.

Many people don’t do the word in ordinary times, and only think of relying on God when trouble comes — by then it’s too late. Trying to reinforce the foundation once the earthquake has hit is too late.

sections.heading: 3. Every Act of Obedience Is Another Foundation Pile
sections.html:
Someone asks: then how long do I have to keep doing it before the foundation is firm?

A study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology by Phillippa Lally and colleagues, psychologists at University College London, found that it takes on average sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit, with wide individual variation — anywhere from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. This study gives us two reminders: first, don’t expect to change in three days — forming a habit takes time; second, don’t give up because you occasionally miss a day — the study found that an occasional lapse doesn’t ruin the whole process.

One act of obedience looks very small, just as one foundation pile looks very thin. But 380 piles can hold up a tower more than five hundred metres tall. Every time you hold back that retort, every time you take the initiative to say sorry, every time you choose honesty where no one can see, you have sunk another pile.

A pastor once put it well: character is who you are when no one is looking. And character is precisely the foundation that lets you stand when the storm comes.

sections.heading: 4. A 321 Insight: Overcoming Isn’t a One-Off Performance; It’s the Accumulation of Everyday Selflessness
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Life is the foundation, relationships are the structure, ministry is the façade. People always want to start building from the façade; God always builds from the foundation.

The 321 vision also says: turn from man’s perspective to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. The house on the sand is “man’s, earthly, temporary, worldly” — quick to build, easy to see, praised by people; the house on the rock is “God’s, heavenly, eternal, godly” — slow to build, unseen, yet never shaken. Paul says: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

Brothers and sisters, overcoming isn’t a one-off performance; it’s the accumulation of everyday selflessness. Every act of obedience is laying the foundation. In the end, your life will stand on the rock.

And who is that rock? Paul says: “and the rock was Christ.” (1 Corinthians 10:4) The final purpose of doing the word isn’t to make us people who are very good at doing the word; it’s to have our whole life standing on Christ.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: The Road from Knowing to Receiving
1. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal All Come Down to “Doing”
sections.html:
The Three Foundations of 321 are: Jesus is my role model; the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Notice that not one of these three sentences is the language of “knowing”; every one of them is the language of “doing”. A role model is there to be followed, not admired; a standard is there to measure ourselves, not others; a guide is there to be obeyed, not debated.

The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. What does it mean to let Jesus be King? When a king speaks, his word must be carried out; otherwise he isn’t king. When I know the Lord’s will and don’t do it, I call him Lord with my lips, but in reality I am still the one sitting on the throne. The Lord Jesus asks very directly: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46)

The Goal is: establish God’s system. That system isn’t something spoken into being; it is lived into being — people who do the word, joined together one by one, becoming God’s dwelling place on earth.

sections.heading: 2. The Self-Centred Life and Selflessness: The Real Reason We Can’t Live It Out
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem.

When we can’t live it out, the surface reasons are weakness, busyness, circumstances; the real reason is often the self-centred life. Because to do the word, I have to lay down my face, my rights, my comfort, my timetable. The reason that “sorry” won’t come out isn’t that I don’t know I should say it; it’s that the “I” is too big.

So the 321 vision says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. What Satan fears most isn’t a Christian who knows a great deal; it’s a Christian willing to lay himself down and obey. Because knowledge won’t pull down his strongholds — obedience will.

The 321 vision also says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When we use the truth to make demands of others, their pride is stirred at once, and both sides lose; when we live it out first, others are moved by our humility, humility draws out humility, and both sides win. People who do the word don’t need to argue; their lives are the argument.

sections.heading: 3. The Fivefold Change: Letting Mindset Travel All the Way to Ministry
sections.html:
Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — this fivefold change is the very skeleton of today’s lesson. “Knowing” stops at the first; “doing” joins the first to the second and third; “receiving” is the fruit God brings about in us once all five have been travelled.

The order the 321 vision stresses is: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

So when we practise doing the word, we follow the same order. First, do it in our relationship with God — whatever God has said to me today, I go and do. Then in our relationship with ourselves — facing ourselves honestly, not deceiving ourselves. Then in our relationships with others — that person I’ve never forgiven, that word I’ve never said. And only last in our tasks.

sections.heading: 4. The 920 Practice: Bringing Doing the Word Down to Every Person
sections.html:
The 321 920 practice says: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; with them we are to practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

Galatians 5:22–23 says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.”

Brothers and sisters, notice: not one of these nine graces can be borne alone in your room. Patience needs someone to provoke you before you can show patience; kindness needs someone who needs you before you can give it; gentleness needs someone to answer you back before it can be seen. God puts people beside us to give us a place to do the word. So stop waiting for “an environment better suited to growth”. Your family, colleagues and neighbours right now are the training ground God has prepared for you. Today, with which “2” will you live out which fruit?

sections.heading: 5. The 235 Relationships: People Who Do the Word Need People to Walk With
sections.html:
The 321 235 relationships say: become a “2”, spiritual companions, with someone selfless; build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Why does doing the word need companions? Because self-deception can’t see itself. Someone looking in a mirror forgets what he looks like, but if there’s a spiritual companion beside you, he’ll remind you: “That reconciliation you said you’d go and make last month — have you done it?” Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 said it long ago: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.”

Brothers and sisters, if after hearing this message today you simply nod quietly, in three days you’ll have forgotten it; but if today you find a spiritual companion, tell him the one thing you are going to do, and ask him to check with you in a week, the outcome will be completely different.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Living the Truth Out
sections.html:
The lesson has prepared five practices for us. We don’t only want to remember them; we want to use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to walk each practice through to the end.

Practice 1: Each day, choose one verse and actually do it

Don’t be greedy. Each morning, after reading the Bible, ask just one question: what does God want me to do today? Forgive, for example, or give thanks, be patient, bless. Shift the focus from “how much I read” to “how much I live”.

Deepen it with the eight stages. Information — what does the verse I read today mean? Revelation — which phrase in this verse is the Holy Spirit shining on for me in particular? Conviction — I acknowledge that this word is right, and that it is spoken to me. Implementation — with whom, when and how will I live it out today? Evaluation — before bed, look back: did I do it, and where was it hard? Correction — tomorrow, adjust the method or the person. Repetition — keep practising until it becomes natural. Multiplication — teach this practice to someone else.

A reminder: the Implementation step must be concrete down to “who, when, where and what”. In 1999 the psychologist Peter Gollwitzer published research on “implementation intentions”: when a vague “I’m going to do it” is rewritten as a clear “when such-and-such happens, I will do such-and-such”, the rate at which people actually follow through rises markedly. God’s word is the same — the more concrete it is, the more it gets lived out.

Practice 2: Build the habit of doing it the same day

When God shines his light on something for you: don’t delay, don’t over-analyse, do it that same day. The key to obedience is “immediately”.

Deepen it with the eight stages. Information and Revelation often arrive together — you suddenly remember a certain person, some unfinished business, and that is most likely the Holy Spirit’s prompting. Conviction — admit that delay is unbelief. Implementation — take the smallest step at once; a phone call or a single message counts. Evaluation — what’s my pattern of delay: fear of losing face, or fear of the hassle? Correction — shorten the distance between “light” and “action”. Repetition — let immediate obedience become a reflex. Multiplication — bring this habit into your small group.

Remember the forgetting curve we mentioned earlier: if the light isn’t turned into action that same day, by tomorrow only a third remains, and by the day after almost nothing. Satan doesn’t need to make you oppose the truth; he only needs to get you to say, “I’ll deal with it later.”

Practice 3: Practise small actions, great obedience

Don’t wait for big things before you obey; start with small things: a gentle word, a moment of holding back your anger, a gesture of care you take the initiative to offer. Small acts of doing are a great foundation.

Deepen it with the eight stages. Information — the Lord says: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” (Luke 16:10) Revelation — see that you’ve been waiting for “a grand occasion worthy of obedience”. Conviction — admit that what God values is faithfulness, not scale. Implementation — do one very small act of obedience today. Evaluation — have I been looking down on small things? Correction — change the standard from “big” to “real”. Repetition — one each day. Multiplication — do it together with your family.

Think of those 380 foundation piles: not one of them is impressive, yet together they hold up a skyscraper. Your gentle word today is one foundation pile.

Practice 4: Stop judging, start doing

When you want to point out someone else’s problem, first ask two questions: have I lived this out myself? What does God want me to do right now? Shift the focus from “others” back to “myself”.

Deepen it with the eight stages. Information — “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3) Revelation — the Holy Spirit shows me that my displeasure with a certain person hides my own pride. Conviction — admit that judging is leaving our originally intended position. Implementation — every time I want to judge, first pray for that person for one minute. Evaluation — how many times have I judged this week? Correction — turn words of criticism into words of intercession. Repetition — until, when I see a person, I first see God’s grace. Multiplication — in the small group, don’t talk about people who aren’t present.

The 321 vision says it very clearly: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. Judging happens because the focus has drifted onto other people; move the focus back to Jesus, and judging naturally falls away.

Practice 5: Use prayer to turn knowing into doing

Pray every day: “Lord, I don’t just want to know; I want you to help me live it out.” Hand your powerlessness to God, and hand your obedience to the Holy Spirit.

Deepen it with the eight stages. Information — “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:13) Revelation — see that you’ve been “doing the word” in your own strength, and that’s why you’re tired and frustrated. Conviction — admit that apart from the Lord I can do nothing. Implementation — each morning, first entrust to the Holy Spirit the one thing you are to do that day. Evaluation — today, did I rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, or on the brain and myself? Correction — come back to the Lord and draw on him afresh. Repetition — make “pray first, then act” your settled order. Multiplication — teach others to pray this way.

Brothers and sisters, if you can choose only one of these five practices today, choose the second — do it the same day. Because that is the switch that connects all the other practices to the power.

A Gentle Reminder

Knowing a lot doesn’t mean a mature life; speaking well doesn’t mean living it out.

Don’t stop at being moved; move into action. Don’t stop at receiving; move into obedience.

The focus isn’t “how much I know”; the focus is “how much I live out”.

Only when you begin to do do you truly begin to live.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let Jesus Truly Be King
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the question we began with: over this past year, of the things God has shone his light on in your heart, how many have you actually gone and done?

The key to the spiritual life isn’t how much you know, but how much you live out. When you begin to do it, God’s word is no longer only teaching; it becomes your life.

This morning the Lord isn’t asking you to make some grand resolution; he only asks you to sow one seed. That seed might be a phone call you’ve never made, an apology you’ve never spoken, a person you’ve never forgiven.

To let Jesus be King is to let his word be carried out in you. If a king speaks and no one acts on it, his kingdom is a kingdom in name only. The Lord’s Prayer says: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10) How does God’s kingdom come into your home? In the very moment you do his will.

And when we live it out, the glory goes to Jesus. What people see isn’t how well we can speak, but that our lives have really changed; they’ll ask, “How did you become so different?” And we’ll be able to say: it isn’t I, it’s Christ living in me. The Lord Jesus said: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16)

From today, don’t stop at “knowing” any more; let every word you receive become action. Because — the truth you live out is the truth you truly possess.

Brothers and sisters, decide right now: today, what one thing will you do?

keyVerses: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was. But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets, but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does.” (James 1:22–25)
“If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17)

“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.” (Matthew 7:24–25)
declarations: In the name of the Lord Jesus, I declare:
I am no longer only a hearer of the word; I will be a doer of the word.
I will not deceive myself; I will live out the truth.
God’s word within me will become my life.
I obey every day, and every day I live it out.
My life is built on the rock; whatever the wind and rain, it cannot be shaken.
I am an overcomer, living out the life of Christ.
Amen.
practices: Each day, choose one verse and actually do it
Build the habit of doing it the same day
Practise small actions, great obedience
Stop judging, start doing
Use prayer to turn knowing into doing
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We confess before you that what we know far outweighs what we live out. We have heard much and been moved much, yet so often we turn away and forget. Forgive our self-deception; forgive us for using the truth to make demands of others while letting ourselves off.
Lord, we don’t want to be people who glance in the mirror and walk away any more. Give us hearts that bend down and look carefully into your word, and give us the courage to obey that same day.

We confess that apart from you we can do nothing. Holy Spirit, work within us, giving us both the will and the doing, to accomplish your good pleasure. Let us not rely on our own effort, but let Christ live himself out in us.

Lord, help us from today on, so that every word we receive becomes an act of obedience, and every act of obedience becomes another foundation pile, until our lives are built on you, the Rock, and do not fall when the wind and rain come.
May our families, our fellowship and our church all see your glory because we truly do your word. Reign as King in us, and receive all the glory.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: James 1:23–24 says: “For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.” Please share: when was the last time God’s word shone its light on you and you “turned away and forgot”? What kept you from living it out?

Matthew 7:24–25 says: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.” Let each person name concretely “one small thing I will do this week”, and agree together to ask one another at the next meeting whether it has been done.
