blog.title: The Seed in Your Pocket

blocks.x: Why We Know So Much, Yet Our Lives Haven’t Changed
An old farmer once said something that has stayed with me ever since: “A farmer’s greatest failure in life isn’t a poor harvest; it’s keeping his seed in his pocket until it goes mouldy.”

Seed in the pocket can be touched, can be counted, can even be taken out and shown to people. But a seed’s destiny isn’t to be looked at; it’s to be buried in the ground. The Lord Jesus said: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

Our generation is the least short of “information” of any generation in history. We know far more than believers did a hundred years ago. But we must honestly ask: are our lives really stronger than theirs?
Knowing Can Deceive
In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus discovered the famous “forgetting curve”: newly learned material, if not reviewed or used, is often only about a third retained after one day.
In other words, if the message that moved you this morning is only “heard”, by this time tomorrow two thirds of it will be gone.
The only way to keep hold of the truth isn’t to hear it again; it’s to do it once. What we have done stays in our relationships and stays in our lives.

James puts it even more strongly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) The Greek for “deluding” literally means “to miscalculate the accounts”. We enter “heard it” as “received it”, and “moved” as “obeyed”. The books look very fine, but in reality they’re falsified.

And the most dangerous thing is this: no one else is deceiving us; we are deceiving ourselves. When others deceive you, someone can still warn you; when you deceive yourself, you have switched off the alarm yourself.
Foundations Are Laid on Sunny Days

The Lord Jesus closes the Sermon on the Mount with a parable: those who hear and do are like someone who builds a house on the rock; those who hear and don’t do are like someone who builds a house on the sand.

“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.” (Matthew 7:24–25)

Notice: both men heard, and both houses met the same storm; the only difference was one word — “do”. And that difference can’t be seen at all before the storm comes. On a sunny day both houses look equally fine, and the one on the sand may even have been finished sooner.

The world’s most famous case of foundation failure is the Leaning Tower of Pisa in Italy. Construction began in 1173, and before the tower had reached its third storey it began to lean. The cause wasn’t in the tower but underground: the foundation was too shallow and the soil too soft. For more than eight hundred years people have tried every engineering method, yet they can never make it stand straight again.
By contrast, the real work of Taipei 101, a building 508 metres tall, lies unseen beneath the ground — 380 foundation piles, anchored deep into the bedrock.

Nobody takes photos of foundations; nobody applauds a foundation. Foundations are laid when no one is watching. The spiritual life is the same: the foundation isn’t built in the storm; the foundation is “done” in ordinary days.
Today, Live Out One Thing

How long do we have to keep doing it? A 2010 study by Phillippa Lally and colleagues, psychologists at University College London, found that it takes on average sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit, with individual variation from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. So don’t expect to change in three days, and don’t give up because you miss a day.

Don’t be greedy. Choose just one verse each day and ask one question: what does God want me to do today? Forgive, give thanks, be patient, bless — choose one, and do it that same day. The key to obedience is “immediately”. Satan doesn’t need to make you oppose the truth; he only needs to get you to say, “I’ll deal with it later.”

And don’t wait for big things before you obey. A gentle word, a moment of holding back your anger, a gesture of care you take the initiative to offer — small acts of doing are a great foundation. Every act of obedience sinks another foundation pile.

And when you find you can’t live it out, remember: doing doesn’t depend on gritting your teeth and trying hard; it is letting Christ live himself out in you. “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:13)
The key to the spiritual life isn’t how much you know, but how much you live out.
Because the truth you live out is the truth you truly possess.
Question for Reflection
Over this past month, what is the one thing God has shone his light on most clearly in your heart? Today, what is the smallest, most concrete step you are willing to take towards it?

The 235 relationships: find a spiritual companion, tell them the one thing you are going to do, and ask them to check with you in a week.
What You Live Out Is Yours
Not how much you know
but how much you live out
Let Jesus be King in you
Let Jesus receive all the glory
Key points:
Return to the opening question, and invite everyone to name one thing they will do today.
Matthew 6:10: let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Matthew 5:16: that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.
Closing line: the truth you live out is the truth you truly possess.
Prayer of Response and Blessing
Lord, I don’t just want to know
I want you to help me live it out
Let your will be done on earth
as it is in heaven (Matt 6:10)
Key points:
Lead the brothers and sisters in praying together, confessing that we know more than we live out.
Ask the Holy Spirit to work within us, giving us both the will and the doing (Philippians 2:13).
Invite each person to pray specifically about the one thing they will do today, and to pray for one another.
Close with the heart of the Lord’s Prayer and bless the congregation: today, live out one thing.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to the second message on “doing rightly” — from knowing to doing, and from doing to receiving.
The Lord Jesus said: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17)
Brothers and sisters, notice the Lord’s words. He didn’t say, “Blessed are you if you know”; he said, “blessed are you if you do them.”
I’d like to ask you all a question first: over this past year, of the things God has shone his light on in your heart, how many have you actually gone and done?
Not how many you’ve agreed with, not how many have moved you, but how many you’ve lived out.
An old farmer once said: a farmer’s greatest failure in life isn’t a poor harvest; it’s keeping his seed in his pocket until it goes mouldy.
Seed in the pocket can be touched and counted, but it is only ever a seed.
The greatest trap in the spiritual life is stopping at “knowing”.
Today we have three passages. James 1:22 says: be doers of the word, and not only hearers.

The man who wrote this letter was James, the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh. He had once been closest to Jesus, yet for a time he didn’t believe; then the risen Lord appeared to him, and only then did he truly know the Lord. So he is the one best qualified to say: don’t delude your own selves.
John 13:17 was spoken by the Lord after he had washed his disciples’ feet. Matthew 7:24 is the close of the Sermon on the Mount.
Three passages, one message: God’s word counts only when it is lived out.
The first key point: only by moving from knowing to doing do we receive.
For a truth to enter our lives, it passes through six stages: seeing, listening, thinking, speaking, doing and receiving.

Where’s the trouble? The first four stages all fool us into thinking we’ve made progress. We’re moved, we’re pierced, we receive light, we even tell others about it. Yet our lives haven’t moved an inch.
Why? Because it is in the fifth step, “doing”, that truth turns from knowledge into life.
Brothers and sisters, knowing is not having; only doing leads to receiving.
“Knowing” can deceive.
In 1885 the German psychologist Ebbinghaus discovered that what we newly learn, if we don’t use it, is only about a third retained after one day.
So if today’s message is only “heard”, by this time tomorrow two thirds of it will be gone.
The only way to keep hold of the truth isn’t to hear it again; it’s to do it once.
Look at Israel’s two bodies of water: the Sea of Galilee flows in and out and teems with fish; the Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out, and nothing can live there.
Brothers and sisters, “doing” is the outlet for living water. Without an outlet, even the best truth that comes in will in the end turn salty.
The second key point: not doing the word is spiritual self-deception.
James says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”
The Greek for “deluding” means miscalculating the accounts. We enter “heard it” as “received it”, and “moved” as “obeyed”. The books look very fine, but they’re falsified.
James says that such a person does three things in front of the mirror: he sees, goes away, and immediately forgets.
Brothers and sisters, isn’t that a portrait of our every Sunday? The meeting is moving, and by the car park we’re back to how we were.
If we only know and never do, what do we end up becoming? We become Pharisees.
The Lord Jesus said: “for they say, and don’t do.” (Matthew 23:3)
If knowledge isn’t used to deal with ourselves, it automatically turns to deal with others.
321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place. When I take the truth in my hand to measure others, I’ve sat down in a seat that isn’t mine.
Selflessness means dealing with ourselves first, not using the truth to press down on others.
A truly spiritual person isn’t the one who says the most, but the one who can live it out.
The third key point: doing is food for the spiritual life.
The Lord Jesus, tired and thirsty, sat by the well, and after reaching a Samaritan woman he said: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me.”
Brothers and sisters, obedience didn’t drain the Lord; obedience fed him.
We often think doing the word is hard work. In fact it’s exactly the opposite: it’s not doing that makes us wither; it’s not obeying that brings us pain.
It’s like muscles that waste away when they’re not used. Go without food and you get hungry; a spirit that doesn’t do the word will die.

Someone says: but I just can’t live it out. Don’t be afraid. Paul says: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. Doing doesn’t depend on effort; it is letting the Lord live himself out in you.
The fourth key point: doing lays the foundation of life.
The Lord says: those who hear and do are like someone who builds a house on the rock; those who hear and don’t do build their house on the sand.
Both men heard; both houses met the same storm; the only difference was one word — “do”.
And on a sunny day you can’t tell the difference at all; the house on the sand may even go up faster.
Why can’t the Leaning Tower of Pisa be straightened? Because its foundation is too shallow. Why does Taipei 101 stand firm? Because 380 foundation piles were sunk beneath it.
Brothers and sisters, the foundation isn’t built in the storm; the foundation is “done” in ordinary days. Every act of obedience sinks another foundation pile.
So how do we do it? The lesson gives us five practices.
First, choose just one verse each day and actually do it. What does God want me to do today? Forgive, give thanks, be patient, bless.
Second, do it the same day. Don’t delay, don’t over-analyse. The key to obedience is “immediately”.
Third, small actions, great obedience. A gentle word, a moment of holding back your anger, a gesture of care you take the initiative to offer.
Fourth, stop judging. When you want to point out someone else’s problem, first ask: have I lived this out myself?
Fifth, use prayer to turn knowing into doing. Hand your powerlessness to God, and hand your obedience to the Holy Spirit.
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the question we began with: of the things God has shone his light on for you, how many have you lived out?
The key to the spiritual life isn’t how much you know, but how much you live out.
To let Jesus be King is to let his word be carried out in you. If a king speaks and no one acts on it, his kingdom is a kingdom in name only.
When you live it out, what people see isn’t how well you can speak, but that your life has really changed. And the glory goes to Jesus.
Because the truth you live out is the truth you truly possess.
Let’s pray together.
Dear Lord Jesus, we confess that what we know far outweighs what we live out. Please forgive our self-deception.
Lord, give us the courage to obey that same day, and may the Holy Spirit work within us, giving us both the will and the doing.
Let our lives be built on you, the Rock, so that when the wind and rain come, they do not fall.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you. Today, live out one thing.
Brothers and sisters, good morning. May the Lord’s peace fill you this morning.
Today we come to the second message on “doing rightly” — from knowing to doing, and from doing to receiving.
The Lord Jesus said: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17)
Listen carefully: the Lord didn’t say, “Blessed are you if you know”; he said, “blessed are you if you do them.”
Nowhere in the whole Bible is there a promise that “those who know are blessed”, yet again and again it promises that “those who obey are blessed”.
I’d like to ask you a question first.
Over this past year, of the things God has shone his light on in your heart, how many have you actually gone and done?
Not how many you’ve agreed with, not how many have moved you, but how many you’ve lived out.
An old farmer once said: a farmer’s greatest failure in life isn’t a poor harvest; it’s keeping his seed in his pocket until it goes mouldy.

Seed in the pocket can be touched and counted, but it is only ever a seed. The Lord said: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone.” (John 12:24) Falling into the ground — that is “doing”.
Our generation is the least short of information of any in history. But we must honestly ask: are our lives stronger than those of believers a hundred years ago?
Between knowing and receiving stand two checkpoints.
The first lies between knowing and doing, where the chasm of “procrastination and self-deception” stretches across the way.
The second lies between doing and receiving, and what it requires is what James calls “and continues”.
Brothers and sisters, most people get stuck at the first. So the heart of today is this: knowing is not having; only doing leads to receiving.
Today we have three passages.

James 1:22: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” The writer was James, the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh, writing around the AD 40s to Jewish believers scattered abroad. He had once been closest to Jesus, yet for a time he didn’t believe, so he is the one best qualified to say: don’t delude your own selves.
John 13:17 was spoken by the Lord after he had washed his disciples’ feet. What the Lord wanted his disciples to do wasn’t some lofty doctrine; it was to bend down and serve others.
Matthew 7:24 is the close of the Sermon on the Mount. When the Lord had spoken for three chapters, he sealed the whole sermon with “doing or not doing”.
Three passages, one message: God’s word counts only when it is lived out.
The first key point: only by moving from knowing to doing do we receive.
For a truth to enter our lives, it passes through six stages: seeing, listening, thinking, speaking, doing and receiving.
Where’s the trouble? The first four steps all give the illusion that “I’ve made progress”. We’re moved, we’re pierced, we receive light, we tell others and are even praised for it.
We can go through all four steps and our lives may not have moved an inch. Because it is in the fifth step, “doing”, that truth turns from knowledge into life.

Brothers and sisters, seeing is contact, listening is reception, thinking is digestion, speaking is putting it in order; but “doing” is transformation, and “receiving” is possession. Without the fifth step, we never reach the sixth.
Brothers and sisters, “knowing” can deceive.
In 1885 the German psychologist Ebbinghaus discovered that what we newly learn, if we don’t use it, is only about a third retained after one day.
So if today’s message is only “heard”, by this time tomorrow two thirds of it will be gone. The way to keep hold of the truth isn’t to hear it again; it’s to do it once.

In 1990 Elizabeth Newton at Stanford University asked people to tap out with their fingers a song everyone knows well, for others to guess. The tappers expected half to be guessed; in fact only three out of a hundred and twenty were right — about 2.5 per cent.
Because the tappers had the melody in their heads, while the listeners heard only the tapping. It’s the same with us: what others see is only how we actually live.
Israel has two bodies of water, both fed by the Jordan River.

The Sea of Galilee flows in and out and teems with fish, and most of the Lord’s ministry took place there; the Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out, its salt keeps building up, and nothing grows.
The same living water — one becomes a sea of life, the other a sea of death, and the only difference is whether there is an outlet.
God’s word keeps flowing in, but if there is no outlet of “doing”, the truth settles inside and turns salty, until it becomes knowledge for judging others.
321 says: the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Mindset is only the first; the link that joins mindset to life is precisely “doing”.
The second key point: not doing the word is spiritual self-deception.
The Greek for “deluding” literally means “miscalculating the accounts”.

People who only hear the word and don’t do it aren’t stupid; they’ve just got the sums wrong: they enter “heard it” as “received it”, “moved” as “obeyed”, “agreed” as “changed”. The books look fine, but they’re falsified.

And the most dangerous thing is this: no one else is deceiving them; they are deceiving themselves. When others deceive you, someone can still warn you; when you deceive yourself, you have switched off the alarm yourself.
Brothers and sisters, James speaks very weightily here, because he knows: a person may think he is growing, yet if there is no doing, he is actually marking time.
James uses the mirror as a picture, saying that such a person does three things: he sees, goes away, and immediately forgets.
He sees — the truth shows up the problem; he goes away — his body leaves the mirror; he forgets — his heart leaves the light as well.
Brothers and sisters, isn’t that a portrait of our every Sunday? The meeting is moving, and by the time we reach the car park we’re back to how we were.

There’s nothing wrong with the mirror, nothing wrong with the light; the problem is that we’ll only take a glance and won’t bend down. James says “looks into”, and that Greek word means to stoop, to bend low and lean in close to look carefully — the same word used of John stooping to look into the empty tomb.
If we only know and never do, we end up becoming Pharisees.
The Lord said: “for they say, and don’t do.” (Matthew 23:3) They lay heavy burdens on people’s shoulders, but won’t lift a finger themselves.
If knowledge isn’t used to deal with ourselves, it automatically turns to deal with others.

In 1957 the psychologist Festinger put forward “cognitive dissonance”: when beliefs and behaviour don’t match, a person can change the behaviour, or change the explanation; the second way is cheaper, so most people take it.

321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place; humility is returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Selflessness means dealing with ourselves first.
The third key point: doing is food for the spiritual life.

The Lord Jesus had walked all day and sat down by Jacob’s well, tired and thirsty. The disciples urged him to eat, and he said: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.” (John 4:34)
Brothers and sisters, the Lord had brought a broken life to God, and his weariness was gone. Obedience didn’t drain the Lord; obedience fed him.
We often think doing the word is hard work. The truth is exactly the opposite: it’s not doing that makes us wither; it’s not obeying that brings us pain.
The body God made bears witness to spiritual principles at every turn.
Muscles left unused for a long time waste away rapidly, which is why astronauts have to exercise for hours every day; otherwise, when they return to earth, they can hardly stand.

Hebrews 5:14 speaks of those “who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” The Greek for “exercised” is the root of our word “gymnasium”. Spiritual discernment isn’t something you hear; it’s something you train.

The Lord also said: “If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God.” (John 7:17) The world’s order is to understand first and then do; God’s order is to do it and then understand — like learning to swim: three minutes in the water beats three months of reading on the bank.
Some hearts are bound to be sinking: I know I should do it, but I just can’t.
Brothers and sisters, doing doesn’t depend on gritting our teeth and trying hard; it is letting Christ live himself out in us.

Paul says: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) The Lord says: “apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) A branch bears fruit not by straining, but by staying joined to the vine.
Philippians 2:13 says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work.” Even the willing is God’s work.
So 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves.
The fourth key point: doing lays the foundation of life.
The Lord closes the Sermon on the Mount with a vivid parable: those who hear and do build their house on the rock; those who hear and don’t do build their house on the sand.

Four things are the same: both heard, both built a house, both houses looked like houses, both met the same storm. Only two things differ: one did it and the other didn’t; one house never fell, and the other fell, and great was its fall.
What cuts deepest is this: the difference can’t be seen at all before the storm comes. On a sunny day both houses look equally fine; the one on the sand may even go up faster.

The world’s most famous case of foundation failure is the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Construction began in 1173, and before it had reached its third storey it began to lean, because the foundation was too shallow and the soil too soft. For more than eight hundred years people have tried every engineering method, and they can never make it stand straight again.
However beautiful what’s built above, if the foundation is wrong, it’s wrong.
The opposite is Taipei 101. The real work of this 508-metre building lies unseen beneath the ground: 380 foundation piles, anchored deep into the bedrock.
Brothers and sisters, nobody photographs or applauds a foundation. Foundations are laid when no one is watching. The foundation isn’t built in the storm; it is “done” in ordinary days.
Someone asks: how long do I have to keep doing it before the foundation is firm?

A 2010 study by Lally and colleagues at University College London found that it takes on average about sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit, with individual variation from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days.
Two reminders: don’t expect to change in three days, and don’t give up because you miss a day.
One act of obedience is very small, just as one foundation pile is very thin; but 380 of them can hold up a tower more than five hundred metres tall.
321 says: overcoming isn’t a one-off performance; it’s the accumulation of everyday selflessness. And Paul says that the rock was Christ.
So how do we do it? The lesson gives us five practices.
First, choose one verse each day and actually do it. Don’t be greedy; ask just one question: what does God want me to do today? Shift the focus from “how much I read” to “how much I live”.
In 1999 the psychologist Gollwitzer put forward “implementation intentions”: when “I’m going to do it” is rewritten as “when, with whom, and what”, the rate of follow-through rises markedly.
Second, do it the same day. Don’t delay, don’t over-analyse. Satan doesn’t need to make you oppose the truth; he only needs to get you to say, “I’ll deal with it later.”
Third, small actions, great obedience. A gentle word, a moment of holding back your anger, a gesture of care you take the initiative to offer.
Fourth, stop judging. When you want to point out someone else’s problem, first ask: have I lived this out myself? What does God want me to do right now?

The Lord asks: “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3) Doing the word means swapping the magnifying glass and the reducing glass back.
Fifth, use prayer to turn knowing into doing. Hand your powerlessness to God, and hand your obedience to the Holy Spirit.

These five practices can be walked through to the end with the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
If you can choose only one today, choose the second — do it the same day. That is the switch that connects to the power.
Let’s bring 321 together.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, and a role model is there to be followed; the Bible is my standard, and a standard is there to measure ourselves; the Holy Spirit is my guide, and a guide is there to be obeyed. Not one of these is the language of “knowing”.
The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Lord asks: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46)
The 920 practice says: everyone we relate to is our “2”; with them we live out selflessness and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. You can only show patience when someone provokes you.

The 235 relationships say: doing the word needs companions. Find a spiritual companion, tell them the one thing you are going to do, and ask them to check with you in a week — the outcome will be completely different.
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the question we began with: of the things God has shone his light on for you, how many have you lived out?
The key to the spiritual life isn’t how much you know, but how much you live out.
The Lord isn’t asking you to make some grand resolution; he only asks you to sow one seed — a phone call you’ve never made, an apology you’ve never spoken, a person you’ve never forgiven.
To let Jesus be King is to let his word be carried out in you. The Lord’s Prayer says: “Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)
When we live it out, what people see isn’t how well we can speak, but that our lives have really changed, and the glory goes to Jesus. Because the truth you live out is the truth you truly possess.
Let’s pray together.
Dear Lord Jesus, we confess that what we know far outweighs what we live out. Forgive our self-deception; forgive us for using the truth to make demands of others while letting ourselves off.

Lord, give us hearts that bend down and look carefully into your word, and give us the courage to obey that same day. We confess that apart from you we can do nothing. Holy Spirit, work within us, giving us both the will and the doing.

Let every word we receive become an act of obedience, and every act of obedience become another foundation pile, so that our lives are built on you, the Rock, and do not fall when the wind and rain come.
Reign as King, and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you. Today, live out one thing.

sections.heading: Introduction: Children Don’t Listen to What We Say — They Watch How We Live
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

I’d like to begin with a question — one that may make us a little uncomfortable, but one well worth facing honestly.

Suppose a brand-new believer followed you around for a whole week. Not to hear you preach, but simply to tag along quietly: stuck in the same traffic, standing in the same queues, there when that infuriating phone call comes in, there when you face the colleague with the sharp tongue, there when you walk back through your own front door and they hear how you speak to your family. After seven days, what kind of Jesus would that person have learned?

Brothers and sisters, we often assume that spiritual influence flows from the pulpit. It doesn’t. It flows from daily living.

Our series has now reached the third message on “doing what is right.” Today we look further ahead — doing what is right lives out an example, brings victory, and leaves a legacy.

A mother once said something to me that I haven’t been able to forget. She said, “What I fear most isn’t that my children won’t listen to me. What I fear most is that they’ll live exactly the way I do.”

Those words put a spiritual truth into plain speech: our lives are more honest than our mouths. People forget what we say; they remember how we live — and without noticing, they start living it too.

In 1961 the Stanford psychologist Albert Bandura conducted his famous “Bobo doll experiment.” One group of nursery-school children watched an adult hit and kick an inflatable doll; another group watched an adult play quietly beside it. Then each child was left alone in a room with the very same doll. The result was unmistakable: the children who had seen the adult attack the doll attacked it themselves, copying right down to the stance and the words the adult had shouted. From this Bandura developed his “social learning theory” — that people learn chiefly not by being taught but by watching and imitating.

Brothers and sisters, there is nothing new in that discovery. Two thousand years ago the Lord Jesus had already demonstrated this principle with his whole life. He founded no seminary; he left no book. He did one thing: he chose twelve men “that they might be with him” (Mark 3:14), so they could watch every day how he lived.

Three years later, those twelve men changed the whole world.

So this morning, may the Lord plant one mindset deep within us: God doesn’t only want you to “know what’s right”; he wants you to “live what’s right.” God doesn’t only want you to be someone who hears about an example; he wants you to become an example.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Last Supper, the Sermon on the Mount, Letters from Prison
sections.html: Today’s six theme passages come from four different authors writing in four different situations. Once the background is clear, the message comes alive in three dimensions.

sections.heading: 1. John 13: The Basin and the Towel on the Eve of Passover
sections.html:
The Gospel of John was written by the apostle John, the disciple whom the Lord loved. He is generally thought to have shepherded the church in Ephesus, in Asia Minor, in his later years, writing this Gospel around AD 85 to 90. Rather than repeating the narratives of the first three Gospels, he focuses on this: “that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (John 20:31).

John 13 is the turning point of the whole book. In the first twelve chapters Jesus reveals himself to the world; from chapter 13 on he opens his heart to his disciples.

The place is a prepared upper room in the city of Jerusalem. The time is the night before Passover. The text says, “Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” (John 13:1)

Consider the setting. In first-century Palestine the roads were dirt and gravel, people wore sandals, and after any walk your feet were bound to be caked in dust. So when guests entered a home, the host would provide water, and the lowliest servant would wash their feet. It was the most menial job in the household — Jewish custom even held that a Jewish servant shouldn’t be asked to do it; it usually fell to a Gentile slave.

And that night the upper room had water, a basin and a towel — but not one person was willing to pick them up. For at that very table, “A dispute also arose among them, which of them was considered to be greatest.” (Luke 22:24)

Twelve men sat there, each feeling far too great to be washing feet. And so the greatest One in all the world stood up.

sections.heading: 2. Matthew 20 and 5: A Kingdom of Servants and a Blessing for Enemies
sections.html:
The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, a former tax collector. It is generally dated between AD 50 and 70 and was addressed chiefly to Jewish Christian communities, which is why it quotes the Old Testament so heavily to prove that Jesus is the promised Messiah.

The background to Matthew 20 is the mother of James and John asking for the seats at Jesus’ right and left for her sons, which made the other ten disciples indignant. In the middle of that quarrel Jesus turned the values of the kingdom completely upside down: whoever would be great must be a servant; whoever would be first must be a slave.

Matthew 5 is part of the Sermon on the Mount. “Love your enemies” was an earth-shaking thing to say at the time. The Jews knew the law’s command to “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18), but the tradition of the day had tacked on a phrase the law never contained. The Lord Jesus said, “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’” (Matthew 5:43) Jesus tore down that added boundary line.

sections.heading: 3. Luke 23: The First Word from the Cross
sections.html:
Luke was a Gentile, a physician and a co-worker of Paul. Luke 23:34 records the first words the Lord Jesus spoke as he was being crucified. He did not cry out at the injustice; he did not curse. His first words were an intercession for the men nailing him there.

Brothers and sisters, set these words beside Matthew 5:44: “love your enemies … pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you.” This is Scripture interpreting Scripture at its most solid: what Jesus taught on the mountain, Jesus carried out on the cross. Between his teaching and his life there isn’t the slightest gap.

sections.heading: 4. James 4 and Philippians 4: The Charge of Two Shepherds
sections.html:
The letter of James is generally attributed to James, the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh and leader of the Jerusalem church. It was quite possibly written in the late AD 40s to Jewish Christians scattered abroad and facing trials. The whole letter is packed with imperative verbs, and it has a single theme: faith without works is dead.

Philippians was written by Paul around AD 61, while he was imprisoned in Rome. The church at Philippi was the first church he planted in Europe. The letter has been called “the epistle of joy” — a man bound in chains who keeps returning to joy, again and again.

And at the end of the letter Paul says something only a man living an open, upright life would dare to say: “The things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me: do these things, and the God of peace will be with you.” (Philippians 4:9)

Notice the four verbs Paul uses: learned, received, heard, saw. The first two concern the passing on of doctrine; the last two concern watching a life up close. Paul didn’t only let people hear his message; he let them see the man.

With the background clear, let’s turn to today’s four key points.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: The Example of Jesus — Not Just Speaking, but Doing
sections.html:
“If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:14–15)

Brothers and sisters, notice that the Lord Jesus does not say here, “I am telling you a truth; remember it.” What he says is, “I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.”

sections.heading: 1. The Weight of the Word “Example”
sections.html:
The word for “example” is ὑπόδειγμα (hypodeigma), literally “a sample set out underneath for people to see.” In the old days, when children learned to write, the teacher would write a line of model characters across the top of the page, and the children would trace them stroke by stroke underneath. That line of model writing was a hypodeigma.

So the Lord Jesus is saying: I’m not giving you a theory to recite. I am writing a line of model script right before your eyes, and you are to trace it.

And what was the line he wrote? A bent back, a basin, a towel — the hands of the Son of God washing twelve pairs of mud-caked feet, including the pair that would shortly walk out to betray him.

This is the concrete version of the words in Matthew 20: “Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant” (Matthew 20:27). The word for “bondservant” is δοῦλος (doulos) — not a hired labourer, but a slave belonging wholly to his master, with no rights of his own. Jesus changed the kingdom’s definition of “greatness” from “how many people serve you” to “how many people you serve.”

Brothers and sisters, if Jesus had only spoken those words in Matthew 20, they would be a great teaching. But because in John 13 he actually picked up the towel, those words became a road we can walk.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Knowing Isn’t Enough — You Must Do It
sections.html:
After washing their feet, the Lord Jesus went on to say something we often overlook: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17)

Listen carefully to how that sentence is built. The blessing isn’t in “knowing”; the blessing is in “knowing and doing.” To know and not do brings no blessing at all — it only adds to what we owe.

This fits perfectly with the close of the Sermon on the Mount: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock … Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand.” (Matthew 7:24, 26) Both men “heard.” The only difference lies in one verb — do. In calm weather you can’t tell them apart; but when the day of rain, flood and wind arrives, the foundation is laid bare.

James puts it even more bluntly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) The greatest danger for those who hear but never do isn’t that others will see through them; it’s that they have fooled themselves. They think they have it, when all they have done is hear about it.

sections.heading: 3. An Example from Life: Nobody Learns to Swim from a Book
sections.html:
I know a brother who, wanting to learn to swim, bought three books and watched dozens of instructional videos. He could explain clearly the angle for breathing, the path of the arm stroke, the rhythm of the kick. One day he finally got into the water — and ten seconds later the lifeguard was fishing him out. Back on dry land he said, “So what I learned was ‘about swimming,’ not ‘swimming.’”

Brothers and sisters, our faith is full of “abouts” — about forgiveness, about humility, about service. We can talk about them very convincingly, yet we have never actually got into the water.

Here’s an example closer to home. When you teach a child to tie shoelaces, explaining it a hundred times is worth less than crouching down and doing it once. And more sobering still: we never taught our children “how to swear in a traffic jam,” yet every one of them learned it. Why? Because life is never passed on by instruction; it is soaked up by what they see and hear day after day.

sections.heading: 4. Science Confirms It: We Are Created to Imitate
sections.html:
In the 1990s a team of neuroscientists led by Giacomo Rizzolatti at the University of Parma in Italy discovered a remarkable group of neurons in the premotor cortex of macaque monkeys. When a monkey reached out to grab something, these cells fired. But when the monkey merely “watched” someone else reach out and grab something, without moving at all itself, the very same cells fired too. The team named them “mirror neurons.”

In other words, at the level of the brain there is a natural pathway between “seeing someone else do it” and “doing it yourself.” Although scholars still debate how far the human mirror system’s functions extend, one basic fact is clear: we are created with a strong built-in tendency to imitate.

Brothers and sisters, when God made us, he placed “living by an example” within us. And so God’s way of saving us was this: he didn’t post us an instruction manual; he sent his Son. “The Word became flesh, and lived among us … full of grace and truth.” (John 1:14)

A saying commonly attributed to Albert Schweitzer captures it vividly: “Example is not the main thing in influencing others. It is the only thing.”

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: Jesus is my role model
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, of the Three Foundations of 321, the first is “Jesus is my role model.”

These words carry two layers of meaning, and we often hear only the first — learning what Jesus said. So we read the Bible, memorise verses and listen to sermons. That is good; it is the groundwork. But the second layer is the key: learning how Jesus lived. How he faced being misunderstood. How he treated the man who betrayed him. How, when the crowds thronged around him, he withdrew to the wilderness to pray. How, when the crowds rejected him, he stayed obedient to the very end.

321 says it plainly: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. And Jesus is the one and only person who was completely “selfless” — “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:6–7) “Emptied himself” means pouring out his very self. That act of stooping down and picking up the towel is the most concrete picture of “emptying himself” there is.

So a true disciple is not someone who “is good at hearing sermons” but someone who “does what they say.”

Brothers and sisters, may the Lord this morning put a new question in our hearts: no longer only “What does this passage mean?” but beginning to ask, “How does this passage want me to live today?”

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Doing What Is Right Brings a Victorious Life
sections.html:
“Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:7)

Brothers and sisters, we often pull out the second half of this verse and shout it on its own, while skipping the first half. The result? We shout very loudly, and the devil doesn’t run.

sections.heading: 1. The Order in the Original Cannot Be Reversed
sections.html:
The word for “be subject” is ὑποτάσσω (hypotassō), a military term meaning “to rank under, to be enlisted in the formation, to come under command.” It’s a soldier falling back into line and taking orders from his commander.

The word for “resist” is ἀνθίστημι (anthistēmi), meaning “to stand up against, to stand firm without budging.” Notice James’s order: first fall into line, then you can stand firm. A soldier who has broken ranks and steps out alone to fight dies all the faster. And “flee” means to run away in panic — victory doesn’t come because we chase the devil off; it comes because the devil sees the Commander standing behind us and runs off by himself.

So the message of Key Point 2 today is this one sentence: Jesus overcame Satan not by power, but by the “act of obedience.”

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Route to Victory on the Cross
sections.html:
On the cross he could have called down more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53). He didn’t. Instead he did three things.

First, on the cross he forgave: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” (Luke 23:34)

Second, in humiliation he still obeyed: “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:8)

Third, in suffering he still loved: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” (1 Peter 2:23)

And the result? “Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it.” (Colossians 2:15)

Brothers and sisters, see it clearly: the weapon of victory isn’t a fist; it’s obedience. It isn’t resistance; it’s surrender. Revelation sums up this route beautifully: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.” (Revelation 12:11)

sections.heading: 3. Psychology Bears Witness: The Harder You Suppress, the Harder It Rebounds
sections.html:
Many brothers and sisters fight sin by gritting their teeth and telling themselves, “I am absolutely not going to think about this again!” And the more they struggle, the more they fail.

In 1987 the psychologist Daniel Wegner conducted a well-known experiment. He asked participants, for five minutes, “not to think of a white bear,” and to ring a bell whenever they did. The bells of the group told not to think of it rang constantly. What’s more, in the later stage they thought of the white bear even more often than the group that had never been asked to suppress it. Wegner called this the “rebound effect”: when we deliberately suppress a thought, the brain has to keep checking, “Am I thinking about it?” — and that very checking keeps calling the thought back.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the struggle of Romans 7: “For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice.” (Romans 7:19)

And the Bible’s answer has never been “try harder not to”; it is “turn to Another.” Romans 7 doesn’t conclude with “keep it up!” but with “I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!” (Romans 7:25). It’s like a dark room: you could sweep away furiously with a broom until dawn and never sweep the darkness out. But just switch on the light, and the darkness disappears by itself. You don’t drive out the darkness; you welcome in the light.

sections.heading: 4. Applying the 321 Vision: Selflessness Overcomes Satan
sections.html:
321 states it decisively: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Why? Because the root of Satan’s fall was pride — “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:13–14) Those five “I will”s are the complete definition of the self-centred life: leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, and wanting to take the place of God.

So when we fight Satan with a self-centred heart, we are playing his game on his home ground, and the result is inevitable: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. But when we are “selfless” — laying down our rights, returning to our originally intended position, letting man be man and letting God be God — Satan instantly loses his foothold. He cannot strike a soldier who has already surrendered under the Commander’s banner, because that blow would have to land on the Commander first.

So the 321 formula is very clear: the self-centred life wants control, and the result is defeat; selflessness is willing to obey, and the result is victory.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

The German martyr-pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote in The Cost of Discipleship: “Only those who believe obey, and only those who obey believe.” Faith and obedience are two sides of one and the same thing.

Brothers and sisters, when you are willing to do what God’s word says, you aren’t “fighting for” the place of victory; you are “stepping onto” the place of victory. Because the Lord has already bought that place for you.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Doing What Is Right Brings an Influence of Life
sections.html:
“The things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me: do these things, and the God of peace will be with you.” (Philippians 4:9)

Brothers and sisters, “doing” isn’t only for our own sake; it is even more for the sake of others. This is an important turn in today’s message.

sections.heading: 1. The Words Paul Dared to Say
sections.html:
Paul once said something to the church in Corinth that no one would dare say unless moved by the Holy Spirit: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1) The word for “imitator” is μιμητής (mimētēs), from which the English word “mimic” comes.

But notice the second half — “even as I also am of Christ.” Paul wasn’t telling people to copy him as a man; he was telling them to copy “the way he copied Christ.” He placed himself in between, like a mirror. A mirror gives off no light of its own; it reflects the light on to the next person.

Paul also told Timothy, “Let no man despise your youth; but be an example to those who believe, in word, in your way of life, in love, in spirit, in faith, and in purity.” (1 Timothy 4:12) Here “example” is a different word, τύπος (typos), which originally meant “the impression left by a hammer blow, a mould used for casting.”

Brothers and sisters, your life is a mould. However you live, that is the shape the people around you are poured into.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: A Family Tree of Three Generations
sections.html:
In Paul’s letter to Timothy there is a deeply moving verse: “having been reminded of the sincere faith that is in you, which lived first in your grandmother Lois, and your mother Eunice, and, I am persuaded, in you also.” (2 Timothy 1:5)

Grandmother Lois, mother Eunice, son Timothy — three generations. The Bible records no sermon Lois ever preached and no book Eunice ever wrote. They simply lived out a “sincere faith,” and that faith flowed down through the days to the third generation.

Paul then turns this principle into a formal charge: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)

Count them: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others — a full four generations. This is the heart of discipleship: not teaching more, but living it out so others can see it, and then letting those who have seen it live it out for others to see.

Life is passed on not by talking, but by living.

sections.heading: 3. The Scientific Data: Behaviour Spreads Through Networks of Relationships
sections.html:
In 2007 Nicholas Christakis of Harvard University and James Fowler of the University of California, San Diego, published a study in The New England Journal of Medicine that followed more than twelve thousand people over thirty-two years. They found that human behaviour spreads along the networks of social relationships — and not only to our friends, but on to our friends’ friends, and to our friends’ friends’ friends — what has been called “three degrees of influence.”

Some scholars still debate the statistical methods of studies like this, but it confirms what the Bible said long ago: no one is an island. “A little yeast grows through the whole lump.” (Galatians 5:9)

Brothers and sisters, this is a double-edged sword. Your complaining is contagious, and so is your gratitude; your bitterness is contagious, and so is your forgiveness. You cannot choose not to influence others. You can only choose which direction you influence them in.

sections.heading: 4. An Example from Life: Those Who Plant Trees Seldom Sit in Their Shade
sections.html:
Those who plant trees seldom get to sit in the shade of what they planted; an oak needs more than a hundred years to grow big enough for a roof beam. Brothers and sisters, legacy is just like that. Your obedience today, your forgiveness today, the choices you make today where no one can see — these may not bear fruit in someone else’s life until many years from now.

I knew an elderly sister who never preached a single sermon in her life. She did only one thing: for more than thirty years, early every morning, she prayed for her children and grandchildren and for the young people of the church, by name. When she died, at her memorial service people stood up to give testimony one after another — every one of them someone her prayers had brought into the church.

She left no writings behind. She left a generation.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
sections.html:
321 has a very important order: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Many people get the order backwards: they throw themselves into ministry first, talk about relationships next, and only think about life last. The result is that the bigger their ministry grows, the drier their life becomes and the more their relationships crack. But God’s order is: first life, then influence, then legacy. Change moves from the inside out; it isn’t pressed in from the outside.

So 321 gives us two very concrete practices:

“The 920 practice”: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” Before every “2,” we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life that bears the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Your spouse is your 2; your child is your 2; and that colleague you least want to run into is your 2 as well.

“235 relationships”: first, become a “2” with a selfless person — spiritual companions who support one another; next, build the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; finally, become the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers.” (Ephesians 4:11)

Brothers and sisters, remember: people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things.

When you live out what is right, you aren’t only changing yourself; you are influencing a generation.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: Experiencing God’s Presence in the “Doing”
sections.html:
“teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” (Matthew 28:20)

Brothers and sisters, many people have two stock phrases: “I’ll act once I’m ready,” and “I’ll obey once I have the strength.”

But God’s principle runs exactly the other way: go and do it, and you will experience God.

sections.heading: 1. The Grammar of the Great Commission: As You Go
sections.html:
“Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” (Matthew 28:19–20)

The grammar of this passage deserves attention. “Go” is the participle πορευθέντες, which can be rendered “as you go.” In other words, the Lord’s promise isn’t given to those who are sitting down; it’s given to those who are on the move. The words “I am with you always” are stitched onto the back of “as you go.” His presence is experienced in the course of doing.

This is an enormous comfort: God doesn’t demand that you become perfect before he will walk with you. God wants you to move first, and he will meet you on the road.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Feet Go into the Water First, Then the Water Is Cut Off
sections.html:
In the Old Testament, Israel crossed water twice. The first time was the Red Sea: Moses lifted his staff, the sea parted first, and only then did the people walk across on dry ground (Exodus 14:21–22). That was what God did for a faith still in its infancy. The second time was the crossing of the Jordan, and God’s instruction changed: “It shall be that when the soles of the feet of the priests who bear the ark of Yahweh, the Lord of all the earth, rest in the waters of the Jordan, that the waters of the Jordan will be cut off. The waters that come down from above shall stand in one heap.” (Joshua 3:13)

The Bible goes on to record: “when those who bore the ark had come to the Jordan, and the feet of the priests who bore the ark had dipped in the edge of the water … the waters which came down from above stood, and rose up in one heap a great way off.” (Joshua 3:15–16)

This time God wanted the priests to put their feet into the water first. And the text makes a special note of it: “for the Jordan overflows all its banks all the time of harvest” (Joshua 3:15). Not the dry season — the flood season. The order was: the feet went into the water, and only then was the water cut off. Had they stood on the bank waiting for the water to part first, they would have stood on that bank until they died.

The New Testament is the same. Ten men with leprosy came begging the Lord for mercy. The Lord didn’t heal them on the spot; he simply said, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And the Bible says, “As they went, they were cleansed.” (Luke 17:14) They weren’t cleansed and then went; they were cleansed as they went. Peter was the same: the surface of the water didn’t harden first; it was at the moment his foot stepped onto it that the water held him up (Matthew 14:29).

sections.heading: 3. Psychology Confirms It: Action Comes Before Feeling
sections.html:
Our culture teaches us to “wait until you feel like it,” but research in psychotherapy shows the order is often the reverse. In 1996 the psychologist Neil Jacobson and his team at the University of Washington published a component analysis of treatment for depression. They found that “behavioural activation” on its own — that is, not waiting for your mood to improve, but first scheduling and carrying out meaningful activities — was as effective as the full course of cognitive behavioural therapy.

The conclusion is simple: it isn’t that motivation comes first and then action; very often action comes first and motivation catches up. It’s like a car: when it’s standing still, the steering wheel barely turns; once it’s moving, a light touch changes its direction. Brothers and sisters, God rarely gives directions to a car with the engine off. Start it up first, and then God will turn your steering wheel.

sections.heading: 4. It Is God Who Makes Us Perfect
sections.html:
David says in the Psalms: “the God who arms me with strength, and makes my way perfect” (Psalm 18:32). The Hebrew word for “perfect” is תָּמִים (tamim), meaning “whole, without blemish, complete.” Notice who the subject is — “the God.” It isn’t you making yourself perfect; it is God who enables you to live it out.

So when we go and do, we don’t rely on gritting our own teeth. Philippians puts it in perfect balance: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:12–13)

On one side, “work out”; on the other, “God who works in you.” We are responsible for taking the steps; God is responsible for supplying the strength.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: The Holy Spirit Is My Guide
sections.html:
The third of the Three Foundations of 321 is: the Holy Spirit is my guide.

321 has a saying that cuts to the heart: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled.

Those who rely on the brain and on themselves do their sums before acting: Can I pull this off? What will people think? What if I fail? They calculate and calculate, and then they don’t move. Those who rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit ask first: Lord, what do you want me to do? And then they go. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

Brothers and sisters, when you are willing to act, you will discover something greater than yourself: it isn’t you living after all; it is God living in you.

This is what 321 calls the shift of perspective — from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

Go and love, and you will experience God’s love; go and forgive, and you will experience God’s forgiveness; go and serve, and you will experience God’s presence; go and obey, and you will experience God’s power.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From One Example to a Whole System
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s place today’s four key points within the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Today’s four key points walk right through all three: Key Point 1 is “Jesus is my role model”; Key Points 2 and 3 are “the Bible is my standard” — obeying God’s word and living it out; Key Point 4 is “the Holy Spirit is my guide” — being led by God’s Spirit in the midst of action.

The Two Core Values — let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. When I stoop to wash feet, I let Jesus reign as King over my pride; when I forgive my enemy, I let Jesus reign as King over my wound; when I stop defending myself, the glory naturally goes to him.

The Goal — establish God’s system. One example influencing one person is called being touched; one example reproduced in a whole group of people — that is what we call a system. What God wants isn’t a few especially spiritual heroes; God wants a system of his own that can be passed down from generation to generation.

The five stages of the Path of Serving are: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. Today’s lesson is precisely about carrying “Understanding” into “Life,” and then moving from “Life” toward “Service.” Many people get stuck at “Understanding” — they understand a great deal, yet it never becomes life. “Doing what is right” is the bridge from Understanding to Life.

The fivefold change of 321 is also a road where you can’t skip a grade: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. This morning, what God wants to do is the first step — to replace one old mindset.

The old mindset says: knowing is enough. The new mindset says: now that I know, I must do it. The old mindset says: I’ll obey once I have the strength. The new mindset says: I obey, and the strength comes. The old mindset says: I must beat this person who is attacking me. The new mindset says: I will surrender before God and let God fight for me.

Brothers and sisters, Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. When our focus is right, our actions are right; when our actions are right, our life is seen; and when our life is seen, a legacy begins.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Living a Life That Sets an Example
sections.html:
The lesson has prepared five very practical exercises for us. Let’s take them one at a time and drive them deep using the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Each day, practise living out one aspect of Jesus

Each day, choose just one of the Lord’s examples to live out: today live out humility, or today live out forgiveness, or today live out service.

Don’t try to do too much; focus on living out one thing.

Why not try to do too much? Because practice that grasps at too much often accomplishes nothing at all. Research by the psychologist Phillippa Lally and her team at University College London found that a new habit takes on average sixty-six days to become automatic, with individual differences ranging anywhere from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. So treat yourself gently but firmly: one thing at a time, every single day.

Go deeper with the eight stages: Information — you heard it this morning; Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to show you which one to live out first; Conviction — tell God in your heart, “This is the road I am to walk today”; Implementation — do it once, today; Evaluation — be still for three minutes this evening; Correction — if you didn’t manage it, don’t condemn yourself, just adjust; Repetition — keep it up for a full week; Multiplication — invite your “2” to do it with you.

Practice 2: In difficulty, choose to respond differently

When you are wronged: don’t retaliate — choose to forgive; don’t complain — choose to pray; don’t run away — choose to obey.

These moments are the key to your victory.

Remember: victory doesn’t happen on the smooth days; it happens in the thirty seconds after you’ve been wronged. In those thirty seconds the self-centred life jumps up and says, “Who do they think they are?” Selflessness grows quiet and says, “Lord, you take over.”

Go deeper with the eight stages: Information — “love your enemies … pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you” (Matthew 5:44); Revelation — ask God to show you a name that is still lodged like a thorn in your heart; Conviction — admit that bitterness wounds no one but yourself; Implementation — pray for that name once today; Evaluation — is your heart hard or soft?; Correction — if it’s hard, first ask God to give you a willing heart; Repetition — pray for that person for forty days; Multiplication — lead others to do the same.

Practice 3: Practise loving people through action

Each day do one thing “for someone else”: care for one person, or help one person, or pray for one person.

Let love flow out through action.

John puts it very directly: “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” (1 John 3:18)

This is exactly the 321 “920 practice” — before every “2,” living out the selfless “0” and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions.

Go deeper with the eight stages: Information — love is a verb; Revelation — ask God to lay one person on your heart; Conviction — a small thing is not small in God’s eyes; Implementation — do it today; Evaluation — was it out of love or out of duty?; Correction — ask God to renew your heart; Repetition — twenty-one days in a row; Multiplication — get your small group doing it together.

Practice 4: Develop an awareness that you are an example

Keep reminding yourself: someone is watching my life; someone is learning my ways.

So choose to live out what is right.

An “awareness that you are an example” doesn’t mean living under other people’s gaze — that is pressure. It means living before God while knowing that God has placed certain people behind you. Paul says, “be an example to those who believe, in word, in your way of life, in love, in spirit, in faith, and in purity.” (1 Timothy 4:12) Not one of these is a pulpit gift; every one of them is a character quality of everyday life.

Go deeper with the eight stages: Information — your life is a mould; Revelation — ask God to show you the person who is watching you; Conviction — admit that your influence is real; Implementation — model the right thing once in front of them today; Evaluation — did they see Jesus, or my temper?; Correction — if you got it wrong, apologise honestly; that in itself is the most powerful example of all; Repetition — keep guarding your daily living; Multiplication — invite them to take someone under their wing too.

Practice 5: Depend on God in the midst of action

Before every step of action, pray first: “Lord, I am willing to act, but I need your strength.”

Learn to experience God’s presence in the midst of action.

This prayer is short, yet it gets two things right at once: “I am willing” — that is my part; “I need your strength” — that is God’s part.

“apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), and at the same time, “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13). Only the two together make the whole truth.

Go deeper with the eight stages: Information — God’s presence is experienced on the road; Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to show you the step you’ve been afraid to take; Conviction — believe that God’s power is revealed in action; Implementation — take that step this week; Evaluation — write down one thing you saw God do as you acted; Correction — if you fail, admit it and go again; Repetition — make a habit of praying before setting out; Multiplication — tell others what God has done.

A Gentle Reminder

Don’t just admire Jesus’ power; imitate Jesus’ life.

Don’t just listen to an example; become an example.

Don’t wait until you’re perfect before you act; you are made complete in the acting.

Brothers and sisters, the focus isn’t on “Can I?” The focus is on “Am I willing?”

Because when you are willing, God goes to work.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let Jesus Live Out Through You
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, doing what is right isn’t merely a change of behaviour; it is the revealing of a life.

A change of behaviour is added on from the outside — it gets tired, it puts on an act, it breaks down. The revealing of a life grows from within — it is natural, it lasts, it bears fruit.

When you begin to live out Jesus, your life becomes a message; when you keep on living out Jesus, your life becomes an example.

Paul told the church in Corinth: “you are a letter of Christ, served by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tablets of stone, but in tablets that are hearts of flesh.” (2 Corinthians 3:3)

Brothers and sisters, this generation has far too many letters written in ink. What it truly lacks are living letters, written by the Holy Spirit on tablets of the heart, that can walk out among the crowds.

A life like this brings not only personal victory but revival for the whole community. So from today, let Jesus not only be within you, but live out through you.

I want to issue three calls to you, brothers and sisters —

First, let Jesus reign as King over your pride. The road that requires you to bend down — bend down today.

Second, let Jesus reign as King over your wound. The name you have never been able to let go — hand it to him today.

Third, let Jesus reign as King over your footsteps. The step of obedience you have put off for so long — take it today.

May all the glory go to the Lord Jesus Christ, who stooped to wash our feet and who died for us on the cross.

prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We thank you. You didn’t only tell us how to live; you lived it out yourself first, for us to see. You picked up the towel, you bent down, and on the cross you prayed for those who nailed you there. Lord, you are my role model.
Lord, forgive us. We know so much, yet do so little; we admire your power, yet refuse to walk your way; we struggle in our own strength, yet refuse to surrender before you.

Lord, take away the self-centred life within us. Put on the cross that “me” that wants to control, wants to prove itself, wants to win; teach me to submit to you and resist the devil, and to stand in the place of victory you have already bought.
Lord, give us a life that is an example. Let our families see you; let the next generation see you. Make us not only people who are built up, but people who build others up.
Lord, we are willing to act, but we need your strength. Holy Spirit, lead us today to take that step; as we go, let us experience your presence.
Reign as King over us, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

James says, “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:7) Share one time you fought with willpower and failed, and one time you chose to submit to God and overcame. What made the difference?

blog.title: How You Live Is the Message You Preach

blocks.x: Live Out an Example, Bring Victory and Legacy

Suppose a brand-new believer followed you around for a whole week — not to hear you preach, but simply to tag along quietly: stuck in the same traffic, standing in the same queues, there when that infuriating phone call comes in, there when you get home and speak to your family. After seven days, what kind of Jesus would that person have learned?
The question stings a little, but it is well worth facing honestly. Because we often assume that spiritual influence flows from the pulpit. It doesn’t. It flows from daily living.
1. He Didn’t Only Teach with His Lips; He Showed Us with His Life

On the night before Passover, in an upper room in Jerusalem, there was water, a basin and a towel — but not one person was willing to pick them up. For the disciples were arguing about which of them was considered to be greatest.
Twelve men, each feeling far too great to be washing feet.

And so the greatest One in all the world stood up. He took off his outer garment, tied a towel around his waist, and washed their feet one pair at a time — including the pair that would shortly walk out to betray him.

When he had finished, he said: “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:14–15)
The original word for “example” literally means “a model script set out underneath for people to trace”. The Lord Jesus didn’t toss us a theory; he wrote a line of model script right before our eyes.

He taught humble service, and he bent down to wash feet; he taught love for enemies, and on the cross he prayed for those who persecuted him. Between his teaching and his life there isn’t the slightest gap.

The psychologist Albert Bandura showed in his 1961 research that people learn chiefly not by being taught but by watching and imitating. That is why the Lord chose twelve men “that they might be with him”. Three years later, those twelve men changed the world.
2. Victory Comes Not from Fighting but from Obeying
Many people fight sin by gritting their teeth and telling themselves, “I am absolutely not going to think about this again!” And the more they struggle, the more they fail.
The road the Bible gives is a different one altogether: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:7)

We often shout only the second half and skip the first — and so we shout very loudly, and the devil doesn’t run. The order in the original can’t be reversed: fall into line first, and then you can stand firm.

Jesus overcame Satan not by power, but by the act of obedience. On the cross he forgave; in humiliation he obeyed; in suffering he still loved — and the result was that he triumphed over the powers through the cross.

This is what 321 means: the self-centred life wants control, and the result is defeat; selflessness is willing to obey, and the result is victory. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.
You don’t sweep darkness out with a broom. Just switch on the light, and the darkness disappears by itself.
3. Go and Do It, and You Will Experience God
Many people say: I’ll act once I’m ready; I’ll obey once I have the strength.

But God’s principle often runs the other way. At the crossing of the Jordan, God had the priests put their feet into the water first, and only then was the water cut off — and at that time the river was overflowing its banks. Ten men with leprosy came begging the Lord for mercy, and the Bible says: “As they went, they were cleansed.”
They weren’t cleansed and then went; they were cleansed as they went.
His presence is experienced in the course of doing. God doesn’t demand that you become perfect before he will walk with you; God wants you to move first, and he will meet you on the road.

So from today, choose just one thing to live out: today live out humility, or forgiveness, or service. Don’t try to do too much; focus on one. When you are wronged, don’t retaliate — choose to forgive; don’t complain — choose to pray. Each day do one thing for someone else. Before you act, pray first: “Lord, I am willing to act, but I need your strength.”
For life is passed on not by talking, but by living. However you live, others learn to live; however you walk, others follow.

Doing what is right isn’t merely a change of behaviour; it is the revealing of a life. When you begin to live out Jesus, your life becomes a message; when you keep on living out Jesus, your life becomes an example.
The focus isn’t on “Can I?” The focus is on “Am I willing?” When you are willing, God goes to work.
Question for reflection: This week, what is one thing you “know” but haven’t yet “done”? What small first step are you willing to take today?

Doing Rightly (Part 3)
