blog.title: Do It, Then Understand

blocks.x: It Isn’t That You Don’t Understand — You Just Haven’t Started

There was a man who badly wanted to learn to swim. He bought six books on swimming technique and read everything from the breathing angle for freestyle to the timing of the breaststroke kick. He watched hundreds of instructional videos, until he could even tell you the angle of a swimmer’s palm as it enters the water. Three years went by, and he knew enough to teach a course. But on the day a friend invited him into the water, he stood at the edge of the pool and kept putting it off. When his friend asked him why, he said, “I don’t fully understand it yet.”

We all laugh at him. But very often we are him. We’ve read a great many books, heard a great many sermons and saved a great many Bible-verse picture cards. Our spiritual knowledge is rich, but our spiritual experience is poor. We understand the whole book, yet we’ve never got into the water.
God’s Order Is the Opposite of Ours
Our natural mindset runs in a nice straight line: I figure it out first, then I do it. But the kingdom of God is exactly the opposite.
“Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, ‘If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.’” (John 8:31–32)

Notice the order: remaining comes first; knowing comes after. It isn’t that we know first and then obey; we obey first, and then truly know. The original word for “remain” carries the sense of “settling in to live” — not dropping by for an occasional visit, but moving in for good. And “know” isn’t acquiring information; it is knowledge that has been tasted, walked through and proven.

The Bible gives us two beautiful footnotes. The Lord Jesus said to the man born blind, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam.” He went while he still couldn’t see, and “he went away, washed, and came back seeing” (John 9:7). Ten men with leprosy begged the Lord to heal them, and he told them to go and show themselves to the priests. The text says: “As they went, they were cleansed.” (Luke 17:14)
They weren’t healed and then went; they went, and were healed.
Two Lies That Nail Us to the Spot

The first lie is: “I can’t.” I can’t share the gospel, I can’t serve, I’m not ready yet. It sounds very humble, but very often it’s just pretty wrapping paper around a refusal to begin. Moses too said he was slow of speech, and God’s answer was: “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.” (Exodus 4:12) Look at the order — “Now therefore go” comes first; the words come after. The words were given on the road.

In 1977 the psychologist Albert Bandura put forward his theory of self-efficacy, showing that what builds a person’s confidence most is “mastery experience” — actually having done the thing successfully yourself, once. In other words, confidence is not the precondition of action; confidence is the product of action.

The second lie is more hidden: “I mustn’t fail.” If I do it, I must do it perfectly; I mustn’t fall; I mustn’t make mistakes. And the result is that we don’t dare to begin. But Proverbs says: “for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again” (Proverbs 24:16). The Bible doesn’t say the righteous never fall; it says they rise up again. The difference between the righteous and the wicked isn’t whether they fall but whether they get back up.

Think of Peter. He got out of the boat, and he sank. But of the twelve men in that boat, only he knew what it felt like to walk on water — and only he knew what it felt like when the Lord’s hand reached out and took hold of him.
Stop Waiting to Be Moved

There’s one more obstacle, and it comes dressed in very spiritual clothing: I’m waiting to be moved. But Ecclesiastes says: “He who observes the wind won’t sow; and he who regards the clouds won’t reap.” (Ecclesiastes 11:4) If a farmer waits for perfect weather before going out to his field, all he’ll have this season is an empty barn.

Love others, forgive, share the gospel, serve — God has long since commanded these clearly; they don’t need us to wait for some special prompting. The Holy Spirit’s guidance never tells people to stand still where they are. God said to Philip, “Arise, and go toward the south.” Ahead lay desert, yet Philip arose and went. It was on the road that he understood why God had sent him.
A ship moored in harbour can’t be steered.
Freedom Is Having the Power to Live Out God’s Word

We all long for freedom, yet we are unwilling to take the step of obedience. But real unfreedom has never been “being unable to do what I want”; it’s “being unable to do what I should.” So freedom isn’t doing whatever I like; freedom is having the power to live out God’s word. And this kind of freedom can only be received in the action of obedience.
When you begin to forgive, your heart is set free; when you begin to serve, your life is opened up; when you begin to share the gospel, your faith is built up.

From today, choose one thing God has clearly commanded and give it a time. Don’t write, “I’m going to care for people more”; write, “At three o’clock this afternoon I’m going to phone so-and-so.” You may do it badly, you may fall, but you must begin. Before you act, pray one sentence: “Lord, I am willing, but I need you.”

The breakthrough in spiritual life usually doesn’t lie in understanding more but in beginning to act. When you take the first step, God leads you to the second. Stop living only in your head. Let the truth get into your footsteps.
Reflection: What is one thing God has already clearly commanded that you have kept on waiting to do? On which day, at what time, and towards whom will you begin to act?

brief12.title: From Understand-Then-Do to Do-Then-Understand
notes: “If anyone desires to do his will,
he will know about the teaching” John 7:17
Known by tasting, not by hearsay
Bandura: ability comes from mastery experience
Key points:
1. Quote John 7:17: desiring to do comes first; knowing comes after.
2. Let Scripture interpret Scripture: James 1:22, Matthew 7:24, John 13:17.
3. Psalm 34:8, “Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good” — tasting before seeing; illustration: you can’t fill your stomach by reading the menu.
4. Albert Bandura, Psychological Review, 1977: the theory of self-efficacy, whose strongest source is “mastery experience”.
5. 321 application: change your mindset and your life changes; rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves.

brief12.title: Two Footnotes from the Bible
notes: The blind man washed, then saw: John 9:7
“As they went, they were cleansed”
Luke 17:14
Not healed, then went — went, then healed
Key points:
1. John 9:7: Jesus told him to go and wash first; he went away, washed, and came back seeing.
2. Luke 17:14: the ten men with leprosy “as they went, they were cleansed”.
3. Point out: under Leviticus you went for inspection after you were healed, but the Lord wanted them to set off before they were.
4. Memory line: not healed, then went — went, then healed.

brief12.title: Lie One: “I Can’t”
notes: “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth”
Exodus 4:12
Go first: the words are given on the road
Don’t do it, and you’ll never be able to
Key points:
1. Satan’s first lie: I can’t share the gospel, I can’t serve, I’m not ready yet.
2. Moses: Exodus 3:11 and 4:10; God’s answers are Exodus 3:12, “Certainly I will be with you,” and 4:12, “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth.”
3. Jeremiah 1:6–7: God wouldn’t let him say, “I am a child.”
4. Matthew 25:25: the servant with one talent was afraid and buried it; the problem wasn’t ability but mindset.
5. Philippians 4:13, “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me” — the strength is given when you move.

brief12.title: Lie Two: “I Mustn’t Fail”
notes: “A righteous man falls seven times and rises up again”
Proverbs 24:16
Inside perfectionism there is often pride
Satan wants you stuck at perfect; God wants you in the process
Key points:
1. The second lie: I mustn’t fall, I mustn’t make mistakes — and so we don’t dare to begin.
2. Proverbs 24:16: the difference between the righteous and the wicked isn’t whether they fall but whether they get back up.
3. Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water (Matthew 14:29–31): only he in the whole boat knew what that felt like.
4. Carol Dweck, Mindset (2006): a fixed mindset fears mistakes; a growth mindset treats mistakes as data.
5. 321 application: the subject of perfectionism is “I” — this is the self-centred life; humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan.

brief12.title: Don’t Spiritualise It — Make It Practical
notes: “He who observes the wind won’t sow” Ecclesiastes 11:4
The revealed things are commanded: no need to wait
The Spirit’s guidance moves you, not stops you
Philip arose and went: Acts 8:27
Key points:
1. Deuteronomy 29:29 divides things into the secret things and the revealed things; the revealed things are given us to do.
2. Ecclesiastes 11:4: a Palestinian farmer who waits for perfect weather ends the season with an empty barn.
3. James 4:17: “To him therefore who knows to do good, and doesn’t do it, to him it is sin.”
4. Acts 8:26–27 and 16:10; Galatians 5:25. Illustration: a ship moored in harbour can’t be steered.
5. Peter Gollwitzer, American Psychologist, 1999: “implementation intentions” — make it concrete with a time and place, and follow-through rises markedly.

brief12.title: Experiencing Truth and Freedom in the Doing
notes: “The truth will make you free”
John 8:32
Freedom isn’t doing whatever I like
Freedom is power to live out God’s word
Key points:
1. John 8:34 and 8:36 explain what this freedom is: release from slavery to sin.
2. Romans 7:18–19 and 8:2: real unfreedom is “being unable to do what I should”.
3. Three roads: forgiving (Matthew 6:14–15; Joseph, Genesis 50:20), serving (Mark 10:45), sharing the gospel (Philemon 1:6).
4. Hebrews 5:14, “senses exercised”: γυμνάζω in the original, an athlete’s training; neuroplasticity as corroboration.
5. 321 application: selflessness, obedience, experiencing God; Galatians 2:20; the 920 practice bears the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.

brief12.title: Practices: From Knowing to Doing
notes: Each day, choose one thing: do it first
Allow yourself to begin imperfectly
Stop waiting to be moved; respond to the truth
Remain in the doing; 5. Walk by the Spirit
Key points:
1. Make the first practice concrete: not “I’m going to care for people more” but “At three today I’ll phone so-and-so.” Psalm 119:60.
2. The second practice matches Evaluation and Correction in the eight stages; Matthew 25:21 — the master praises faithfulness, not perfection.
3. The third matches Conviction; Hebrews 11:8 — Abraham went out not knowing where he went.
4. The fourth matches Repetition; the emphasis of the theme verse is on “remain”.
5. The fifth brings us back to the Holy Spirit is my guide; 2 Timothy 1:7, Philippians 1:6. Finally, don’t forget the eighth stage, Multiplication: pass your experience on to one person.

brief12.title: Closing and Call
notes: Breakthrough isn’t understanding more, but beginning to act
Take the first step; God leads you to the second
Stop living only in your head
Let the truth get into your footsteps
Key points:
1. Goethe is commonly credited with saying: knowing is not enough; we must apply. Willing is not enough; we must do.
2. Restate the four-link chain, stressing that we are responsible only for the first link.
3. Call: letting Jesus be King means whatever he says, I do.
4. Invite the congregation to do, before today is over, one thing they didn’t dare to do this morning.

brief12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Lord, I am willing, but I need you
Give me a push today
As I do, I will understand the truth
All glory to Jesus our King
Key points:
1. Lead in confession: we use “I don’t understand, I can’t, I haven’t been moved” as excuses.
2. Name the root as the self-centred life and ask the Lord for humility.
3. Ask the Holy Spirit for a name, a time and a thing to do.
4. Close by giving the glory to Jesus, praying in the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

brief21.title: Do It, Then Understand
notes: The Right Mindset About Doing (Part 1)
Not understand first, then do, but do, then understand
“If you remain in my word”
Key points:

1. Read the full theme verses: “Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, ‘If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.’”
2. Set the tone in one sentence: remaining comes first; knowing comes after.
3. Explain that this is the first talk in the series “The Right Mindset About Doing”.
4. Warm tone; address the brothers and sisters.

brief21.title: Understanding the Whole Book, Never in the Water
notes: Read six swimming books, never got in
Rich in spiritual knowledge, poor in experience
We laugh at him, but very often we are him
Key points:
1. The swimming story: six books bought, hundreds of videos watched, standing by the pool saying, “I don’t fully understand it yet.”
2. Ask the congregation: how many books have we read, how many sermons heard, how many notes taken?
3. Point out the gap: rich in spiritual knowledge, poor in spiritual experience.
4. Wrap up: we understand the whole book, yet we’ve never got into the water.

brief21.title: Fly, Then Understand; Walk, Then Learn
notes: The Wrights’ first flight: 12 seconds, about 36 metres
17 December 1903, Kitty Hawk
Toddlers walk about 2,368 steps an hour
And fall 17 times: Adolph, 2012
Key points:
1. The Wright brothers ran a bicycle shop and had no university degrees, yet they pushed their glider up the sand dunes and crashed again and again.
2. Stress the contrast: plenty of people had more thorough theories than theirs.
3. Karen Adolph and colleagues, Psychological Science, 2012: the data from the study of toddlers learning to walk.
4. Memory line: the child didn’t stand up because they’d figured it out; they slowly figured it out because they stood up again.
5. Preview the four main points.

brief21.title: Theme Verses and Background
notes: Jerusalem, Feast of Booths: to those who believed
Remain: dwelling in the word
Know: experiential knowing, not information
Remain, disciples, know the truth, be free
Key points:
1. Written by the apostle John around AD 85–95 in Ephesus; for his purpose see John 20:31.
2. The setting is the Feast of Booths (John 7:2); the water-drawing ceremony matches John 7:37, the lamp-lighting ceremony John 8:12.
3. John 8:30 says many believed in him; verse 31 is spoken to those who had believed him.
4. “Remain” is μένω, settling in to live; “know” is γινώσκω, experiential knowing; “make free” is ἐλευθερόω, releasing a slave.
5. The four-link chain: the first link can’t be skipped.

brief21.title: Man’s Order and God’s Order
notes: We say: I figure it out, then I do it
God says: go and do it, then truly understand
Remaining first, knowing after
Key points:
1. Draw two opposite arrows: man’s straight line and God’s straight line.
2. Point out that our mindset sounds reasonable and responsible, yet it leaves us stuck.
3. Reread the theme verses, stressing the conditional “if … then …”.
4. 321 application: the starting point of the fivefold change is mindset.

brief21.title: Desire to Do It, and You Will Know
notes: “If anyone desires to do his will,
he will know about the teaching” John 7:17
Taste before see: Psalm 34:8
Greeks ask “What?”; Hebrews ask “How shall I walk?”
Key points:
1. John 7:17: desiring to do comes first; knowing comes after.
2. Let Scripture interpret Scripture: James 1:22, Matthew 7:24, John 13:17.
3. Psalm 34:8, “Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good”; illustration: you can’t fill your stomach by reading the menu.
4. Pilate asked, “What is truth?” (John 18:38), and having asked it, turned and went out.
5. Confucius: “Is it not a delight to learn, and to practise what you have learned at due times?” — learning without practising brings no delight.

brief21.title: The Blind Man and the Ten Lepers
notes: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam”
He went away, washed, and came back seeing
“As they went, they were cleansed”
Luke 17:14
Key points:
1. John 9:7: mud smeared on your eyes only makes you see less, yet the Lord told him to go and wash first.
2. Luke 17:14: under Leviticus you went for inspection after you were healed; the Lord wanted them to set off before they were.
3. Ask: what if they had looked down at their skin and said, “I’ll go once I’m better”?
4. Memory line: not healed, then went — went, then healed.

brief21.title: Lie One: “I Can’t”
notes: I can’t share the gospel; I’m not ready yet
“Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth”
Exodus 4:12
Ability grows in the course of doing
Key points:
1. Satan is the father of lies (John 8:44); his strategy isn’t to stop you believing but to get you to believe and then not act.
2. “I can’t” sounds humble, but very often it’s wrapping paper around a refusal to begin.
3. Exodus 4:10: Moses said he was slow of speech; in 4:12 God’s “Now therefore go” comes first, “I will be with your mouth” after.
4. Matthew 25:25: the servant with one talent was afraid and buried it.
5. Philippians 4:13: the strength is given — and it’s given to you when you move.

brief21.title: Ability Grows Out of Action
notes: Moses, slow of speech: “I will be with you”
Jeremiah, “I am a child”: “you must go”
Bandura 1977: mastery experience builds confidence
Confidence is the product of action, not its precondition
Key points:
1. Exodus 3:11–12: God didn’t say, “You’re very capable”; God said, “Certainly I will be with you.”
2. Jeremiah 1:6–7: God wouldn’t let him say “I am a child” out loud.
3. Albert Bandura, Psychological Review, 1977: the theory of self-efficacy, whose strongest source is mastery experience.
4. Remind: the Bible is our highest standard; psychology is only corroboration.
5. Memory line: confidence is not the precondition of action; it is the product of action.

brief21.title: Lie Two: “I Mustn’t Fail”
notes: “A righteous man falls seven times and rises up again”
Proverbs 24:16
Peter sank, but only he walked on water
Satan wants you stuck at perfect; God wants you in the process
Key points:
1. What lies inside perfectionism is often not holiness but pride; what it fears isn’t offending God but being embarrassed.
2. Proverbs 24:16: the difference isn’t whether we fall but whether we get back up.
3. Matthew 14:29–31: as Peter sank he cried, “Lord, save me!” and immediately Jesus stretched out his hand and took hold of him.
4. Carol Dweck, Mindset (2006): fixed and growth mindsets. Amy Edmondson’s 1999 research on psychological safety.
5. 321 application: the seventh of the eight stages is Repetition; humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan.

brief21.title: Don’t Spiritualise It — Make It Practical
notes: “The secret things belong to Yahweh our God”
Deuteronomy 29:29
Love, forgive, share the gospel: already commanded
No need to wait for a special prompting
Key points:
1. Deuteronomy 29:29 sorts things into two piles: the secret things belong to God, the revealed things to us, “that we may do” them.
2. We so often use the secret things as our excuse for not doing the revealed things.
3. The revealed things: Matthew 22:37–39, 6:14, 28:19.
4. James 4:17: to know what you should do and not do it — the Bible calls that sin, not caution.

brief21.title: Watch the Wind and Clouds, Reap Nothing
notes: “He who observes the wind won’t sow;
he who regards the clouds won’t reap” Ecclesiastes 11:4
Endless preparation, no action
The result: spiritual stagnation
Key points:
1. A Palestinian farmer who waits for perfect weather before going to his field will end the season with an empty barn.
2. List the usual waiting list: when I’m less busy, when I’m in a better mood, when my faith is bigger, when I’ve read the Bible through.
3. Restate μένω: remaining means settling in to live, not passing through.
4. Illustration: nobody gets up each morning and decides all over again whether to live in their own house today.

brief21.title: The Spirit’s Guidance Gets You Moving
notes: “Arise, and go toward the south” — he arose and went
Gollwitzer 1999: turn goals into concrete plans
Heart and Spirit act; brain and self hesitate
Key points:
1. Acts 8:26–27: God gave only a direction, not a reason; ahead lay desert, and Philip arose and went.
2. The “immediately” of Acts 16:10 was the key to the gospel entering Europe.
3. Galatians 5:25 and 5:16: the Spirit’s guidance is guidance on the move. Illustration: a ship moored in harbour can’t be steered.
4. Peter Gollwitzer, American Psychologist, 1999, on implementation intentions; William James is commonly credited with saying: we don’t sing because we’re happy; we’re happy because we sing.
5. 321 application: all Three Foundations come into play — John 4:34, 1 Samuel 15:22, Luke 5:5, “but at your word I will let down the net.”

brief21.title: What Is True Freedom?
notes: “Everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin”
John 8:34
Freedom isn’t doing whatever I like
Freedom is power to live out God’s word
Key points:
1. Illustration: a heavy smoker doesn’t smoke whenever he wants to; he has to smoke even when he doesn’t want to.
2. Romans 7:18–19: desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good.
3. Romans 8:2, John 8:36, Galatians 5:1.
4. Conclusion: freedom can only be received in the action of obedience, never in the speculations of the mind.

brief21.title: Three Roads You Can Walk Today
notes: Forgive others, and your heart is set free
Serve others, and your life is opened up
Share the gospel, and your faith is built up
Truth is no longer knowledge but empowered experience
Key points:
1. Matthew 6:14–15; Joseph, Genesis 50:20 — he didn’t first understand God’s purpose and then forgive.
2. Illustration: bitterness is a pair of handcuffs we lock on ourselves, and the key lies in the act of forgiving.
3. Mark 10:45: many discover only after they start caring for others that they themselves have been healed.
4. Philemon 1:6: faith is built up as it becomes effective.

brief21.title: Senses Exercised to Discern
notes: “By reason of use have their senses exercised
to discern good and evil” Hebrews 5:14
Exercised: an athlete’s repeated training
Selflessness, obedience, experiencing God
Key points:
1. “Exercised” in Hebrews 5:14 is γυμνάζω in the original, the root of “gymnasium”.
2. Spiritual discernment isn’t read into you; it’s trained into you.
3. Neuroplasticity: repeated behaviour strengthens the related neural connections.
4. John 14:21: keeping comes first; revealing comes after.
5. 321 application: Galatians 2:20; John 15:5 uses the same μένω; the 920 practice bears the nine fruits of Galatians 5:22–23.

brief21.title: Practices (1)
notes: Each day, choose one thing: do it first
Allow yourself to begin imperfectly
Replace “I’m going to care for people more”
with “At three today I’ll phone so-and-so”
Key points:
1. The first practice matches Implementation in the eight stages; the chain so often breaks at the fourth link.
2. Make it concrete: time, place, action — echoing Gollwitzer’s implementation intentions. Psalm 119:60.
3. The second practice matches Evaluation and Correction; the eight stages already leave room for failure.
4. Zechariah 4:10; Matthew 25:21 — the master praises faithfulness, not perfection.

brief21.title: Practices (2)
notes: Stop waiting to be moved; respond to the truth
Build a rhythm of remaining in the doing
Depend on the Holy Spirit in action
“Lord, I am willing, but I need you”
Key points:
1. The third practice matches Conviction; Hebrews 11:8 — Abraham went out not knowing where he went.
2. The fourth matches Repetition; recall the toddler data: not practising once a month, but over two thousand steps every hour.
3. 1 John 3:18: in deed and truth.
4. The fifth brings us back to the Holy Spirit is my guide; 2 Timothy 1:7, Philippians 1:6.
5. Finally, the eighth stage, Multiplication: tell one person about your experience — this is the “3” of the 235 relationships.

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
notes: Three Foundations: role model, standard, guide
Two Core Values: Jesus as King, all glory to him
Mindset, life, living, relationships, ministry
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan
Key points:

1. The four obstacles share one root disease: the self-centred life. Understanding first is wanting control; “I can’t” is fear of losing face; “I mustn’t fail” is keeping up an image; waiting to be moved is wanting God to fit in with me.
2. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. 1 Peter 5:5; Matthew 11:29, “Take my yoke upon you.”
3. Romans 12:2: the renewing of the mind comes first; proving God’s will comes after.
4. Shift of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Colossians 3:2; 2 Corinthians 4:18.
5. Life first, then relationships, then ministry; the 235 relationships grow out of working together.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: Breakthrough isn’t understanding more, but beginning to act
Take the first step; God leads you to the second
Stop living only in your head
Let the truth get into your footsteps
Key points:
1. Goethe is commonly credited with saying: knowing is not enough; we must apply. Willing is not enough; we must do.
2. Restate the four-link chain, stressing that we are responsible only for the first link.
3. Matthew 7:21: only he who does the will of the Father in heaven will enter.
4. Call: letting Jesus be King means whatever he says, I do; the glory goes to him.
5. Invitation: before today is over, do one thing you didn’t dare to do this morning.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Lord, I am willing, but I need you
Give me a push today
As I do, I will understand the truth
All glory to Jesus our King
Key points:
1. Lead in confession: we use “I don’t understand, I can’t, I haven’t been moved” as excuses.
2. Name the root as the self-centred life; ask the Lord to take away our pride and give us humility.
3. Ask the Holy Spirit for a name, a time and a thing to do.
4. Declare: from knowing, into doing, into receiving.
5. Pray in the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. Bless the congregation to take that step today.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today’s theme is: Do It, Then Understand. The Lord Jesus said — “Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, ‘If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.’” That’s John chapter 8, verses 31 to 32. Notice the order: remaining comes first; knowing comes after. It isn’t that we know first and then obey; we obey first, and then we truly know.

Brothers and sisters, let me start with a story. There was a man who badly wanted to learn to swim. He bought six books and watched hundreds of videos, until he could explain the angle of a swimmer’s palm as it enters the water. But when a friend invited him in, he stood at the edge of the pool and said, “I don’t fully understand it yet.” We laugh at him. But very often we are him. And the Wright brothers? On 17 December 1903 their first flight lasted just twelve seconds. They didn’t understand first and then fly; they flew, and then they understood. It’s the same with how you and I learned to walk. Research has recorded that toddlers learning to walk take on average over two thousand steps an hour — and fall seventeen times. Not one child stood up because they had figured it out.

Let’s put the passage back where it belongs. These words were spoken in Jerusalem at the Feast of Booths, and the Lord Jesus spoke them to “those who had believed him.” So what he is dealing with is precisely the problem most common among those of us who already believe: we believe, and then we stop there. The original meaning of “remain” is “to dwell in” — not dropping by for an occasional visit, but moving in to live there for good. And “know” isn’t acquiring information; it’s knowing that has been tasted and walked through. Brothers and sisters, there’s a chain of four links here: remain in my word, truly my disciples, know the truth, be made free. Four links joined together, and the first can’t be skipped.

In the chapter just before, the Lord Jesus had already said: “If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I am speaking from myself.” That’s John chapter 7, verse 17. Desiring to do comes first; knowing comes after. Psalm 34, verse 8 says: “Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good.” Tasting comes before seeing. Brothers and sisters, you can’t fill your stomach by reading the menu. In 1977 the psychologist Albert Bandura put forward his theory of self-efficacy, and he found that what builds confidence most is the experience of having actually done the thing successfully yourself, once. Confidence is not the precondition of action; confidence is the product of action.

The Bible gives us two beautiful footnotes. The first: the Lord Jesus said to the man born blind, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam.” He still couldn’t see, but he went. And the text says: “So he went away, washed, and came back seeing.” The second: ten men with leprosy came begging the Lord. The Lord said: go and show yourselves to the priests. And the text says: “As they went, they were cleansed.” Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the timing — they weren’t healed and then went; they went, and were healed. If they had looked down at their skin and said, “I’ll go once I’m better,” they would never have got better as long as they lived.

Satan uses two lies to stop us. The first lie is: I can’t. I can’t share the gospel, I can’t serve, I’m not ready yet. Moses said it too: “I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” And how did God answer? God said: “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.” Exodus chapter 4, verse 12. Brothers and sisters, listen to the order: “Now therefore go” comes first; “I will be with your mouth” comes after. The words were given on the road. If you don’t do it, you’ll never be able to; ability is given by God in the course of doing.

The second lie is: I mustn’t fail. I mustn’t fall, I mustn’t make mistakes, nobody must see my weakness. And the result is that we don’t dare to begin. But the Bible says: “for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again.” Proverbs chapter 24, verse 16. The difference between the righteous and the wicked isn’t whether they fall but whether they get back up. Think of Peter. He got out of the boat, and he sank. But of the twelve men in that boat, only he knew what it felt like to walk on water. Brothers and sisters, what lies inside perfectionism is often not holiness but pride. Satan wants you to stop at perfection; God wants you to enter the process.

There’s one more obstacle, and it comes dressed in very spiritual clothing: I’m waiting to be moved. But Ecclesiastes chapter 11, verse 4 says: “He who observes the wind won’t sow; and he who regards the clouds won’t reap.” If a farmer waits for perfect weather before going out to his field, all he’ll have this season is an empty barn. What God has already clearly commanded doesn’t need us to wait for some special prompting. Love others, forgive, share the gospel, serve. The Holy Spirit’s guidance gets you moving; it doesn’t make you stop. In Acts, God said to Philip, “Arise, and go toward the south.” Ahead lay desert, and Philip arose and went. Brothers and sisters, a ship moored in harbour can’t be steered.

The Lord Jesus’ promise is this: do, and you will know the truth; the truth brings freedom. But what is freedom? A heavy smoker looks as if he smokes whenever he wants to, but in fact he has to smoke even when he doesn’t want to. Real unfreedom isn’t “being unable to do what I want”; it’s “being unable to do what I should.” So freedom isn’t doing whatever I like; freedom is having the power to live out God’s word. When you begin to forgive, your heart is set free; when you begin to serve, your life is opened up; when you begin to share the gospel, your faith is built up. Hebrews says that those whose senses are exercised are able to discern good and evil. Spiritual sensitivity is trained into you.

So we have five practices. First, each day, choose one thing — do it first, talk later. Don’t write, “I’m going to care for people more”; write, “At three today I’ll phone so-and-so.” Second, allow yourself to begin imperfectly. You may fall, you may do it badly, but you must begin. Third, stop waiting to be moved and start responding to the truth. Stop asking whether you’ve been moved, and ask instead when you’ll start doing it. Fourth, build a rhythm of remaining in the doing — one act of obedience every day. Fifth, depend on the Holy Spirit in the midst of action. Before every step, pray: “Lord, I am willing, but I need you.”

Brothers and sisters, the breakthrough in spiritual life usually doesn’t lie in understanding more but in beginning to act. Goethe is commonly credited with saying: knowing is not enough; we must apply. Willing is not enough; we must do. When you take the first step, God leads you to the second; when you keep on doing, the truth becomes your life. The focus isn’t on “Can I?” The focus is on “Am I willing?” When you are willing, God will teach you. From today, stop living only in your head. Let the truth get into your footsteps. This is what letting Jesus be King means — whatever he says, I do.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we confess that we so often stay at knowing and refuse to step into action. We use “I don’t understand yet” as an excuse, “I can’t” as a shield, and “I haven’t been moved yet” as a reason to put things off. Please forgive us and take away our pride. Holy Spirit, give us a push today. Give us a clear name, a clear time, a clear thing to do. Lord, we are willing, but we need you. May all the glory go to you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today’s theme is: Do It, Then Understand. This is the first talk on “The Right Mindset About Doing.” Our theme verses are John chapter 8, verses 31 to 32: “Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, ‘If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.’” Brothers and sisters, listen carefully first to the order: remaining comes first; knowing comes after. It isn’t that we know first and then obey; we obey first, and then we truly know. This one sentence could turn our whole spiritual life around.

Let me start with a story. There was a man who badly wanted to learn to swim. He bought six books on swimming technique and read everything from the breathing angle for freestyle to the timing of the breaststroke kick. He watched hundreds of videos, until he could even tell you the angle of a swimmer’s palm as it enters the water. One day a friend invited him to the pool. He stood at the edge and kept putting off getting in. When his friend asked him why, he said, “I don’t fully understand it yet.” Brothers and sisters, we laugh at him. But very often we are him. We’ve read a great many books and heard a great many sermons. Our spiritual knowledge is rich, but our spiritual experience is poor. We understand the whole book, yet we’ve never got into the water.

Let me tell you two things that really happened. The first: on 17 December 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, the Wright brothers achieved humanity’s first powered flight. That flight lasted only twelve seconds and covered about thirty-six metres. At the time there were plenty of people whose theories were more thorough than theirs, and the Wright brothers just ran a bicycle shop. But they did something others wouldn’t: they pushed their glider up the sand dunes and crashed, again and again. The second: in a 2012 study, the New York University psychologist Karen Adolph and her colleagues found that toddlers learning to walk take on average about 2,368 steps an hour — and fall seventeen times. Brothers and sisters, not one child stood up because they had figured it out; they slowly figured it out because they stood up again.

Let’s put the passage back where it belongs. The Gospel of John was written by the apostle John, around AD 85 to 95, in Ephesus. Chapters 7 and 8 take place in Jerusalem at the Feast of Booths. The Feast of Booths had a water-drawing ceremony, when the priests drew water from the Pool of Siloam and poured it out on the altar; and a lamp-lighting ceremony, when huge golden lampstands were lit in the Court of the Women. Right there, Jesus said, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!” And he said, “I am the light of the world.” Then chapter 8, verse 30 says many believed in him. And verse 31 is spoken to precisely these people — “those who had believed him.”

Brothers and sisters, our natural mindset runs in a nice straight line: I figure it out first, then I do it. It sounds so reasonable, so responsible. But the kingdom of God is exactly the opposite: you go and do it first, and only then do you truly understand. The original word for “remain” means “to dwell, to stay in” — not dropping by for an occasional visit, but moving in to live there for good. The original word for “know” isn’t about acquiring information; it’s knowledge that is experiential and relational. And the original for “make free” means releasing a slave into a free person. This verse is a chain of four links: remain in my word, truly my disciples, know the truth, be made free. Four links joined together, and the only one you are responsible for is the first.

In the chapter just before, the Lord Jesus had already laid down this principle: “If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I am speaking from myself.” John chapter 7, verse 17. Desiring to do comes first; knowing comes after. Psalm 34, verse 8 says: “Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good.” Tasting comes before seeing. Brothers and sisters, you can’t fill your stomach by reading the menu. The Greeks asked, “What is truth?” Pilate asked exactly that as he stood before Jesus — and having asked it, he turned and went out. The Hebrews asked, “How shall I walk in the truth?” Confucius said it too: “Is it not a delight to learn, and to practise what you have learned at due times?” Learning without practising brings no delight.

The Bible gives us two of its most vivid footnotes. The first: the Lord Jesus spread mud on the eyes of the man born blind and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam.” The man had no idea what the point was — mud smeared on your eyes only makes you see less. But the text says, “So he went away, washed, and came back seeing.” The second: ten men with leprosy stood at a distance and begged the Lord. The Lord said: go and show yourselves to the priests. And the text says: “As they went, they were cleansed.” Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the timing. Under the rules of Leviticus, you went for inspection after you were healed; but the Lord wanted them to set off while they were not yet healed. If they had looked down at their skin and said, “I’ll go once I’m better,” they would never have got better as long as they lived.

Satan is the father of lies. His most effective strategy isn’t to stop you believing; it’s to get you to believe and then not act. And he uses two lies most often. The first lie is: I can’t. I can’t share the gospel, I can’t serve, I can’t lead a Bible study, I’m not ready yet. These words sound very humble, but very often they aren’t humility at all — they’re just pretty wrapping paper around a refusal to begin. Moses said it too: “I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” And how did God answer? “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.” Exodus chapter 4, verse 12. Brothers and sisters, notice the order: “Now therefore go” comes first; “I will be with your mouth” comes after.

At Horeb, Moses asked, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh?” God didn’t say, “You’re very capable.” God said, “Certainly I will be with you.” Jeremiah said, “Behold, I don’t know how to speak; for I am a child.” God wouldn’t even let him say it. God said, “You must go to whomever I send you.” And then there was the servant who received one talent. He said, “I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth.” He was rebuked not because he lost money, but because he did nothing at all. In 1977 the psychologist Albert Bandura put forward his theory of self-efficacy, and he found that the source that builds confidence most is the experience of having actually done the thing successfully yourself, once. The Bible said it long ago: confidence is not the precondition of action; confidence is the product of action.

The second lie is more hidden: I mustn’t fail. If I do it, I must do it perfectly; I mustn’t fall; I mustn’t make mistakes. And the result is that we don’t dare to begin. But Proverbs chapter 24, verse 16 says: “for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again.” The Bible doesn’t say the righteous never fall. Think of Peter. He got down from the boat and walked on the water, and then, seeing the strong wind, he began to sink. We often laugh at him. But of the twelve men in that boat, only he knew what it felt like to walk on water — and only he knew what it felt like when the Lord’s hand reached out and took hold of him. Carol Dweck’s research tells us that those who fear mistakes don’t dare to learn. Brothers and sisters, Satan wants you to stop at perfection; God wants you to enter the process.

There’s one more obstacle, dressed in very spiritual clothing: I’m waiting to be moved; I’m waiting until I’m quite sure before I move. In Deuteronomy chapter 29, verse 29, Moses left us a vitally important sentence: “The secret things belong to Yahweh our God; but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law.” Brothers and sisters, the things of life fall into two piles. The secret things are God’s business, and he is under no obligation to tell you in advance. The revealed things are our business — and they are given “that we may do” them. Love God and love others, forgive, share the gospel — God has long since commanded these; they don’t need us to wait for some special prompting. James says: to him who knows to do good, and doesn’t do it, to him it is sin.

Ecclesiastes chapter 11, verse 4 might almost have been written for our generation: “He who observes the wind won’t sow; and he who regards the clouds won’t reap.” If a farmer in Palestine insisted on waiting until the wind was exactly right and there wasn’t a single cloud in the sky before going out to his field, he could forget about a harvest that season. We’re the same. When I’m less busy, I’ll start my devotions; when I’m in a better mood, I’ll go and apologise; when my faith is bigger, I’ll share the gospel; when I’ve read the Bible through once, I’ll start serving. The result is endless preparation and no action at all. This is called spiritual stagnation. Brothers and sisters, the Lord said “remain,” and in the original that means settling in to live. Nobody gets up each morning and decides all over again whether to live in their own house today.

We need to straighten out a mindset: the Holy Spirit’s guidance never tells people to stand still where they are. Open the book of Acts, and every time the Spirit guides, it comes as a verb. The angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Arise, and go toward the south.” Ahead lay desert; God gave only a direction, not a reason — but Philip arose and went. It was on the road that he met the eunuch. Paul says: if we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit. Brothers and sisters, a ship moored in harbour can’t be steered. In 1999 the psychologist Peter Gollwitzer found that when goals are written with a concrete time, place and action, the rate of follow-through rises markedly. “I’m going to forgive him” is a prompting; “At twelve noon today I’m going to make that phone call” is an action.

The Lord Jesus promises: do, and you will know the truth; the truth brings freedom. But what is freedom? People today think freedom means doing whatever I like. But the Lord says: “everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin.” Brothers and sisters, a heavy smoker looks as if he smokes whenever he wants to, but in fact he has to smoke even when he doesn’t want to. Real unfreedom isn’t being unable to do what I want; it’s being unable to do what I should. Paul describes this struggle in words that cut to the bone: desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good. And then he found the way out: the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free. So freedom isn’t doing whatever I like; freedom is having the power to live out God’s word.

There are three roads you can walk today. First, forgive others, and your heart is set free. Joseph was sold into Egypt by his own brothers and thrown into prison for a crime he didn’t commit. Years later he said, “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” He didn’t first understand God’s purpose and then forgive; it was on the road of obedience that he gradually came to see it. Bitterness is a pair of handcuffs we lock on ourselves, and the key lies in the act of forgiving. Second, serve others, and your life is opened up. Many brothers and sisters discover only after they start caring for others that God has been healing them all along. Third, share the gospel, and your faith is built up. Every time you open your mouth to bear witness for the Lord, what you yourself believe becomes a little more real. Then truth is no longer just knowledge but experience full of power.

The writer of Hebrews uses an analogy from the gym: “who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” The original word for “exercised” is the root of the English word “gymnasium” — an athlete’s repeated training. First exercised, then able to discern. Spiritual discernment isn’t read into you; it’s trained into you. Even our bodies bear witness to this: modern neuroscience has confirmed that the brain’s connections are strengthened by repeated behaviour. And the Lord says: one who has my commandments and keeps them is one who loves me, and I will reveal myself to him. Brothers and sisters, keeping comes first; revealing comes after. If God seems very far away to you, it may not be that you haven’t read enough; quite possibly you haven’t done enough.

So let’s practise. First, each day, choose one thing — do it first, talk later. Stop waiting until you fully understand; today, choose one thing God has clearly commanded and go and do it: forgive one person, care for one person, share the gospel with one person. And make it concrete: don’t write, “I’m going to care for people more”; write, “At three today I’ll phone so-and-so.” The psalmist says: I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments. Second, allow yourself to begin imperfectly. You may fall, you may do it badly, but you must begin. The eight stages of changing our mindset already include the two stages of Evaluation and Correction; the path of growth God designed assumes from the very start that you’ll do things badly. What the master praised in his servant was “faithful,” not “perfect.”

Third, stop waiting to be moved and start responding to the truth. Stop asking, “Have I been moved?” and ask instead, “When do I start doing it?” When Abraham was called, he obeyed and went out, and the text says he went out not knowing where he went. The starting point of the father of faith was a departure without knowing the destination. Fourth, build a rhythm of “remaining in the doing.” Don’t be zealous only now and then; take one small step of obedience every day. Remember those toddlers? They don’t practise once a month; every hour they take over two thousand steps. Fifth, depend on the Holy Spirit in the midst of action. Before every step, pray: “Lord, I am willing, but I need you.” We don’t act by willpower — that would crush us; we act by the Holy Spirit — and that sets us free.

Brothers and sisters, today’s four obstacles are really all the same disease: the self-centred life. “I need to understand before I do it” is wanting to keep control; “I can’t” is being afraid of losing face; “I mustn’t fail” is wanting to keep up an image; “I’m waiting to be moved” is wanting God to fit in with my rhythm. The subject of every one of these sentences is “I.” Pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. The order of change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. And it is life first, then relationships, then ministry. The person you need to forgive today, the person you need to care for — that is your “2.” Live out the selfless life with them, and the ninefold fruit of the Spirit will grow.

Brothers and sisters, the breakthrough in spiritual life usually doesn’t lie in understanding more but in beginning to act. We often think what we lack is light; in fact what we lack is footsteps. Goethe is commonly credited with saying: knowing is not enough; we must apply. Willing is not enough; we must do. When you take the first step, God leads you to the second; when you keep on doing, the truth becomes your life. Remember the chain: remain in my word, truly my disciples, know the truth, be made free. You are responsible only for the first link. From today, stop living only in your head. Let the truth get into your footsteps. This is what letting Jesus be King means — whatever he says, I do. The glory doesn’t go to our cleverness but to the Lord who spoke.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. Lord, we confess that we so often stay at knowing and refuse to step into action. We use “I don’t understand yet” as an excuse, “I can’t” as a shield, and “I haven’t been moved yet” as a reason to put things off. Please forgive us. We also confess that the root of all this is our self-centred life. Take away our pride and give us humble hearts. Holy Spirit, give us a push today. Give us a clear name, a clear time, a clear thing to do. Lord, we are willing, but we need you. May all the glory go to you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless every brother and sister to take that step today.

sections.heading: Introduction: No Child Learns to Walk Before Walking
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me ask you to play a short video in your mind. On the living-room floor, an eleven-month-old child pulls himself up by the coffee table. He lets go, wobbles, takes one step, then a second — and then, bump, he sits down hard on the floor. Mum and Dad, close by, are laughing, clapping, filming. The child pauses for a moment, crawls back on his own, pulls himself up by the coffee table again, and walks again.

Let me ask you a question, brothers and sisters: can that child walk?

No. Not at all. His balance is all over the place, his steps are crooked, and he falls several times a minute. If we graded him on whether he can or can’t, he would score zero.

So why does he keep walking? Because he wants to walk. Because his eyes are fixed on that pair of open arms in front of him. Because there is a longing in his heart far bigger than his ability.

A team led by Karen Adolph, a developmental psychologist at New York University, published a study in 2012 in the journal Psychological Science, in which they actually filmed and tracked toddlers learning to walk. Here is what they found: a toddler takes on average more than 2,300 steps an hour, and falls about seventeen times. Seventeen falls an hour. Over a day, that is dozens, even a hundred or more, failures.

But brothers and sisters, have you ever seen a child who, after falling seventeen times, sat down in the middle of the living room, hugged his knees and said, “Forget it — I’m probably not cut out for walking. Crawling is safer”?

No. Not one.

So here is the question. Every one of us got up off the floor just like that — fell our way, walked our way, into walking. So when did we start to care more about whether we can than whether we will? When did we start preferring to sit still and know a great deal, rather than stand up and take a single step?

In the last lesson we said that true “doing” is lived out from within, not performed from without. Today we want to make this even more practical. Because many brothers and sisters have already nodded, already agreed — and still haven’t acted. Why? Because there are two large stones in the heart:

The first is “I can’t.” The second is “It’s too hard.”

This morning, God’s word is going to roll both stones away with its own hand. To the first stone, the Bible answers: the key is not whether you can, but whether you do it from the heart. To the second stone, the Bible answers: his commandments are not grievous.

Brothers and sisters, the title of this lesson is “Do It from the Heart — In Love It’s Not Hard.” May God this morning lift us up from the seat of “knowing,” and walk us out the door.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Books, Three Settings, One Answer
sections.html: We have three key passages today. They have not been thrown together at random. Each stands in a real-life setting of its own, and together they answer our two stones exactly.

sections.heading: 1. 1 Timothy 1:5: A Group of People Who Could Talk Well but Lacked One Thing
sections.html:
1 Timothy is a letter from the apostle Paul’s later years. It is generally thought to have been written between AD 62 and 64, after Paul’s release from his first imprisonment in Rome. It was addressed to Timothy, Paul’s spiritual son, whom Paul had left in Ephesus to shepherd the church there.

Paul states his reason for writing very plainly in verses 3 and 4: “As I urged you when I was going into Macedonia, stay at Ephesus that you might command certain men not to teach a different doctrine, and not to pay attention to myths and endless genealogies, which cause disputes, rather than God’s stewardship, which is in faith” (1 Timothy 1:3–4).

Brothers and sisters, notice those words: “which cause disputes.” A group of people had arisen in the Ephesian church who could talk very well. They had words, they had genealogies, they had systems, they had research. Verse 7 says they were “desiring to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say, nor about what they strongly affirm” (1 Timothy 1:7).

It was against that background that Paul wrote verse 5: “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.”

The word “goal” is the Greek τέλος (telos), meaning end point, aim, destination. Paul is saying: you have talked so much and argued so long — do you know where all of it is meant to end? In love. Not in the heights of knowledge, but in the reality of love.

Brothers and sisters, this is precisely our first stone today. The people in Ephesus did not lack ability; they had too much of it. Their problem was not a shortage of skill but a heart that was wrong. Our problem is often the opposite: our hearts are actually good, but we are trapped by the words “I’m not good enough.” Paul recalibrates the scales: what God weighs has never been your talent. It is your heart.

sections.heading: 2. 1 John 5:3: People Who Claimed to Know God but Did Not Obey
sections.html:
1 John comes from the apostle John’s later years. It is generally thought to have been written around AD 90, very likely from Ephesus itself, to the churches of the province of Asia.

At that time, false teaching had begun to appear in the church in an early form of what would later be called Gnosticism. Its defining feature was to exalt “knowing” to the skies while making light of what the body actually does. They said: salvation comes through special knowledge, and the spiritual person need not care how he lives day to day.

So in chapter 2, verse 4, John names it directly: “One who says, ‘I know him,’ and doesn’t keep his commandments, is a liar, and the truth isn’t in him” (1 John 2:4).

By chapter 5, John completes the thought: “For this is loving God, that we keep his commandments. His commandments are not grievous” (1 John 5:3).

Brothers and sisters, pay special attention to the next verse here, because it is John’s own reason: “For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith” (1 John 5:4).

Look carefully: the reason the commandments are “not grievous” is not that God has lowered the standard. It is that the new life born of God overcomes the world. This is the most important step in letting Scripture interpret Scripture. Some people read “not grievous” and grumble to themselves: of course it isn’t hard for you apostles. No. What John means is this: whether it is hard does not depend on how heavy the commandment is, but on which life inside you is carrying it.

sections.heading: 3. Romans 8:6: An Honest Struggle and a Thorough Answer
sections.html:
Paul wrote Romans around AD 57, while staying in Corinth near the end of his third missionary journey, to the church in Rome, which he had not yet visited in person.

Romans 7 is the most honest struggle in the whole Bible: “For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good” (Romans 7:18). “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24).

Brothers and sisters, isn’t that us? We know we should act, yet we can’t carry it out. We resolve a hundred times and fail a hundred and one.

Chapter 8 is the answer. First Paul states the principle: “For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit” (Romans 8:5). Then he states the outcome: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8:6).

The word “mind” here is the Greek φρόνημα (phronēma). It does not mean an occasional thought; it means the whole orientation of one’s thinking — the steering wheel of a person’s mind. Wherever your steering wheel points, that is where your life goes.

Brothers and sisters, there is one more detail worth noticing. Between Romans 7 and Romans 8 there is an obvious turn: in chapter 7 the word “I” appears with extraordinary density; in chapter 8 the word “Spirit” appears again and again. A person full of “I” knows only wretchedness; only a person full of the Spirit has life and peace.

This is exactly what the 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless. Chapter 7 is the autobiography of the self-centred life; chapter 8 is the freedom of selflessness.

Three books, three settings — and together they make today’s answer: the goal of the command is love (1 Timothy 1:5); the commandment of love is not grievous (1 John 5:3); and the secret of its not being grievous is setting the mind on the Spirit (Romans 8:6).

Brothers and sisters, now let’s walk through this one key point at a time.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: The Key Is Not “Can I?” but “Am I Doing It from the Heart?”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when people don’t dare to act, their reasons usually come down to three sentences: I can’t. I’m not good enough yet. I don’t know how.

Those sentences sound very humble, but hidden inside them is a wrong mindset: I must have the ability first, and only then can God use me.

But the Bible, from beginning to end, never reads that way.

At the burning bush on Horeb, Moses said to God: “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” (Exodus 4:10). And how did God answer? God did not debate his eloquence with him: “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak” (Exodus 4:11–12).

When Jeremiah was called, he said: “Ah, Lord Yahweh! Behold, I don’t know how to speak; for I am a child.” And God said: “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for you must go to whomever I send you, and you must say whatever I command you” (Jeremiah 1:6–7).

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? God has never once answered, “You can.” God’s answer is “Go,” together with “I am with you.”

That is why our key verse says: “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith” (1 Timothy 1:5).

Paul lists three things here. None has anything to do with ability; all have to do with the heart:

A pure heart means motives that are unmixed. A good conscience means no accusation within. A sincere faith means a faith that is real.

The word “sincere” deserves a pause. In Greek it is ἀνυπόκριτος (anypokritos), which literally means “unmasked.” Its root, ὑποκριτής, originally meant an actor in the ancient Greek theatre who performed wearing a mask; it later became the source of the New Testament word for “hypocrite.”

Brothers and sisters, what a vivid picture. God does not want a beautifully acted play. God wants a real face. If your face has sweat on it, dust on it, hesitation on it — that’s fine, as long as it is your real face.

So please engrave this on your heart: what God values is not a perfect action but a genuine motive.

Elsewhere Paul states this principle in no uncertain terms: “For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what you have, not according to what you don’t have” (2 Corinthians 8:12). What God accepts is “according to what you have,” not “according to what you don’t have.” God never demands from you what you do not have.

When the prophet Samuel was in Bethlehem and saw how tall and handsome Eliab was, he thought, surely this is the anointed one. But Yahweh said: “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

Man looks at the outward appearance; God looks at the heart. This verse should hang in the heart of everyone who says “I can’t.”

Let’s go back to the picture of learning to walk. Why does the child learn? Not because he could already do it, but because he wanted to learn, and he kept on walking.

Psychology offers good supporting evidence here. Carol S. Dweck, a professor of psychology at Stanford University, drew on decades of research to distinguish a “fixed mindset” from a “growth mindset.” People with a fixed mindset see ability as fixed, so they fear failure, because failure proves “I’m no good.” People with a growth mindset see ability as something that can grow, so they see failure as part of the process, are willing to try again and again, and in the end really do grow.

Another psychologist, Albert Bandura, put forward his theory of “self-efficacy” in 1977. He pointed out that the strongest source of a person’s belief that they can do something is not other people’s encouragement but “mastery experience” — their own experience of succeeding.

Brothers and sisters, please notice the order here, because it matters enormously: you don’t first have confidence and then act; you act, and then confidence grows.

You have never dared to pray aloud because you have never opened your mouth to pray. You have never dared to share the gospel because you have never shared it. You have never dared to care for someone because you have never yet taken the first step towards anyone. Confidence is not something you sit your way into; it is something you walk your way into.

There is a saying commonly attributed to Mother Teresa that puts it beautifully: we cannot do great things, only small things with great love. Brothers and sisters, God has never asked you to do great things. God simply asks you to do the small thing in front of you with a sincere heart.

I think of a sister like the one found in so many small groups. Whenever it was her turn to pray aloud, she would always lower her head and pass the turn to the person beside her. Asked why, she said, “I don’t know how to pray. I’m afraid I’ll say it wrong.” Then one time a child in the group fell ill. She couldn’t hold back; the tears came, and she managed only one sentence: “Lord, please heal him.” And she couldn’t go on. That day, the whole group wept.

Brothers and sisters, “could” she pray? By human standards she never got out one complete prayer. But that was the most powerful prayer of the day, because it came from the heart.

This is a 321 insight: rely on the heart and your heart is glad; rely on the brain and you’re left with strain.

The person relying on the brain analyses everything: Is this appropriate? What will people think? What if I get it wrong? By the end of all that analysis, they are still sitting in the same place, and their heart is more and more weary. The person relying on the heart dares to act: Lord, I can’t, but I love you, so I’ll go. When it’s done, it isn’t perfect — but the heart is open and glad.

The Bible says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). The wellspring of life flows not from the brain but from the heart.

Brothers and sisters, the 321 vision says the focus is not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances — Jesus is the focal point. “I can’t” has its focus on self. “Others do it better than me” has its focus on others. “The timing isn’t right” has its focus on circumstances. When you move your focus back to Jesus, you’ll find that whether you can or can’t isn’t the point at all — because the one doing the work was never you in the first place.

When you act from the heart, God is pleased even if it isn’t perfect. When you rely on the brain and stay where you are, you may know a great deal, but no life will grow.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: God’s Commands Are Really Not Hard
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the second stone is “It’s too hard.”

Deep down we often carry a secret complaint: being a Christian is exhausting. You have to love people, forgive, be patient, give, serve, deal with your temper. Who can do all that?

But the Bible says: “For this is loving God, that we keep his commandments. His commandments are not grievous” (1 John 5:3).

The word “grievous” is the Greek βαρύς (barys), meaning “heavy, weighty, crushing.” The Lord Jesus used the same word of the Pharisees: “For they bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not lift a finger to help them” (Matthew 23:4).

Brothers and sisters, put the two side by side and the truth comes out: the heavy burdens were put there by the religious system, not by God.

What did the Lord Jesus himself say? “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30).

The yoke is easy; the burden is light. Then why do we still find it so heavy?

Because we try to do it in the flesh.

Let me give you a picture. A car has a fine engine and a full tank, but the handbrake is still on. You press the accelerator and the car does move — but the engine roars, the body shudders, the tyres smoke, and it crawls along with great effort. You wouldn’t say the car is no good. You’d say: the handbrake is still on.

Brothers and sisters, that is many people’s spiritual life. The Holy Spirit is more than enough, grace is sufficient — but the handbrake of the flesh is still pulled up. So the harder you try, the more you smoke.

The lesson gives us the most practical example of all: loving our brothers and sisters.

Let me ask you: which is easier, to love or to hate?

From the standpoint of the flesh, hatred comes more naturally. When we are hurt, our first reaction is always to strike back, to defend ourselves, to remember. Love needs to be reminded; hatred doesn’t need to be taught.

But from the standpoint of life, love is the easy one. Why? Because love walks in the light, and hatred walks in darkness.

The Bible could not be clearer: “He who loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no occasion for stumbling in him. But he who hates his brother is in the darkness, and walks in the darkness, and doesn’t know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:10–11).

What is it like to walk in the dark? You can’t see clearly, you trip easily, and walking is hard work. Every step you have to feel your way; every step your heart is in your mouth.

This is not just a metaphor; it is a physiological fact. When our eyes go from a bright place into darkness, the rod cells of the retina need about twenty to thirty minutes to adapt fully. And even once adapted, in that light we can hardly tell colours apart — we see only blurred outlines. Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what a person living in hatred looks like: the world loses its colour, people become blurred shadows, and every step must be guarded.

As for “weight,” medical research offers a reminder too. In a 2009 meta-analysis published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, Y. Chida and A. Steptoe of University College London reviewed a number of prospective follow-up studies and found that anger and hostility are associated with a raised risk of coronary heart disease.

Hatred really is heavier. It weighs not only on the heart but on the body.

On the other hand, what is it like to walk in the light? Clear, peaceful, steady. “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path” (Psalm 119:105). With light, you dare to walk; with light, you walk steadily.

So the 321 insight is this: setting the mind on the Spirit brings life and peace; setting the mind on the flesh brings death and pain.

Living in God’s word is lightness and freedom; living in the enemy’s words is burden and confusion.

In Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis has a famous piece of advice. Don’t waste time bothering whether you “love” your neighbour, he says; act as if you did. As soon as you start doing that, you will find that the love really comes.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly the teaching of this lesson. Love doesn’t wait for the feeling before it acts; love acts, and then the feeling catches up.

So please remember this sentence: what is truly hard is not obeying God; what is truly hard is leaving God and still trying to live well.

God’s way is not hard — it simply requires you to switch systems. From the system of the flesh to the system of the Spirit; from man’s viewpoint to God’s viewpoint; from the earthly and temporary to the heavenly and eternal. The 321 vision says the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry, and the first step is always mindset. Change the mindset, and the road changes.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Doing Has a Cost, but It Is Full of Worth
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, I need to say something honest here. It is true that God’s commands are not hard; and it is also true that doing them always has a cost.

Not hard doesn’t mean painless. Light doesn’t mean free.

The lesson uses a very beautiful picture: a woman who is pregnant.

Is pregnancy hard? In one sense, not at all, because the life grows by itself; no mother has to teach her unborn baby how to grow a heart. Medicine tells us that the baby’s heart begins to beat around the third week after conception, without the mother having to do a thing.

But in another sense, pregnancy comes at a great cost. It takes time — about forty weeks. It means enduring discomfort — morning sickness, an aching back, sleepless nights, moving about with difficulty. And at the end comes the pain of giving birth.

The Lord Jesus himself used this picture: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her time has come. But when she has delivered the child, she doesn’t remember the anguish any more, for the joy that a human being is born into the world” (John 16:21).

Brothers and sisters, look at the order: first sorrow, then joy; first anguish, then life. And the Lord says that once the child is born, “she doesn’t remember the anguish any more.” The cost has not vanished; it has simply been covered over by the joy of new life.

The lesson maps the spiritual process onto this very clearly:

Seeing and listening are like conception. The truth has come inside.

Thinking and speaking are like the pregnancy. The truth is digested inside, meditated on, spoken out.

Doing is like giving birth. The truth comes out from within and becomes visible life.

And if we don’t do it? Everything stays inside and can never become life.

Brothers and sisters, this is a serious matter. In obstetrics, a baby long overdue is a danger to both mother and child. It is the same spiritually: when we only take in for a long time and never live it out, we can suffer a kind of “spiritual obstructed labour.” You have heard many messages, taken many notes, attended many courses, yet your heart grows heavier and number. Why? Because too much truth has built up inside that has never been brought to birth.

So please remember this: if you don’t do it, truth stays as knowledge; if you do it, truth becomes life.

The Lord Jesus said: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24).

A grain of wheat left in the barn is very safe, very intact — and very alone. It remains a single grain for ever. Fallen into the earth, it must go into darkness, break open, disappear — and then a whole field grows up.

The cost has never been a loss. The cost is the ticket of admission.

This is exactly what the 321 vision says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). The old self is self-centred and clings to itself, and the result is only one grain; the new self is selfless and lets itself go, and the result is much fruit.

Psychology offers an interesting confirmation too. In a study published in 2008 in the journal Science, Elizabeth Dunn of the University of British Columbia in Canada, Michael Norton of Harvard University and their colleagues found that people who spent money on others were happier than those who spent the same money on themselves.

This is the very opposite of the world’s arithmetic, yet entirely in keeping with the Bible. Paul says: “In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive’” (Acts 20:35).

Brothers and sisters, let’s make this “cost” a little more concrete. In real life, living out God’s word usually costs three things.

First, the cost of time. The phone call you need to make to show you care will take half an hour; the person you need to keep company will take an evening.

Second, the cost of face. If you want to apologise to someone, you have to lower your head first. If you want to share the gospel, you have to be ready to be turned down. If you want to admit your weakness, you have to take off your mask first.

Third, the cost of comfort. Going along with the flesh is most comfortable; going against it is least comfortable. Yet the Bible says: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). The Chinese Union Version, following many manuscripts, reads “take up his cross daily,” and that word “daily” tells us this is not a single heroic act but a little denying of self every day.

Not one of these three is paid in vain.

So the 321 insight is this: life does not stay inside; it is lived out.

Brothers and sisters, only those willing to pay the cost will see the fruit of life.

The Bible says: “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up” (Galatians 6:9). Those words “in due season” are for everyone who is enduring right now.

Our Lord himself walked this way: “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God” (Hebrews 12:2). It isn’t that the Lord didn’t know the pain; it’s that he saw the joy beyond the pain.

When you are truly willing to act, you will discover three things: it really was worth it; there really was joy in it; there really was glory in it.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: From “Knowing” to “Doing” to “Receiving”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, many people stop at “knowing,” and so they never “receive.”

God’s principle is actually very simple: know it, do it, receive it.

James puts it most directly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22).

Please notice the words “deluding your own selves.” The greatest danger for those who only hear the word is not that they make no progress, but that they “think they are making progress.” They are moved by what they hear and mistakenly believe they have already changed. Being moved is not being changed; being moved is only being moved.

James goes on: “But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets, but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does” (James 1:25).

Where is the blessing? “In what he does.” Not in what he hears, but in what he does.

The Lord Jesus also said: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” (John 13:17). The Lord didn’t say, “Since you know these things, you are blessed.” He said, “if you do them.” Between knowing and doing lies the whole of the blessing.

The Lord said again: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock” (Matthew 7:24). The one who hears and does not do builds his house on sand. Both men heard the same sermon; the only difference is one word: do.

The lesson gives a most fitting example: sharing the gospel.

If you never go and share it, you will never be able to share it. Once you start sharing, you gradually learn how.

We often wait for a moment when we are “ready.” But brothers and sisters, that moment won’t come by itself. The Lord’s command is: “Go into all the world, and preach the Good News to the whole creation” (Mark 16:15). When does the power come? “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth” (Acts 1:8). Power is received on the road, not waited for at home.

Learning to swim is the same. You can watch every instructional video there is and memorise buoyancy, breathing and the angle of your stroke — but as long as you never get into the water, you will never swim.
