And once you really are in the water, you discover that what the book says and what your body learns are two completely different things. The first time you swallow water; the second time you swallow water again; the third time, suddenly, you float — and what you learn in that moment is something no book could ever teach you.

Brothers and sisters, spiritual things are the same. You only touch grace once you get into the water.

So: doing brings experience; doing brings growth; doing brings power.

Brain science offers solid supporting evidence here. In 1949 the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb put forward a famous principle: neurons that fire together wire together. In other words, every time you actually do something, a pathway in your brain is walked once more. The more often it is walked, the wider, faster and steadier that pathway becomes. Years of research by R. Douglas Fields, a neuroscientist at the US National Institutes of Health, also indicate that repeated neural activity promotes myelination, allowing nerve signals to travel faster and more reliably.

In other words, brothers and sisters, you don’t “wait until you can before you act”; you “gradually become able because you act.”

So how long must you keep at it? Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London followed ninety-six participants, and their results, published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, found that for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit took a median of sixty-six days, with large individual differences — anywhere from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days.

So don’t judge yourself a failure on the strength of three days of obedience. What God gives is a road, not an exam.

The 321 insight is this: change your mindset, step into action, experience God.

And the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset lay this road out very clearly: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. “Knowing” is Information and Revelation; “doing” is Conviction and Implementation; “receiving” is the fruit that comes after Evaluation, Correction and Repetition — and finally it must be passed on to others through Multiplication.

Brothers and sisters, please remember: God isn’t waiting for you to be perfect; God walks with you.

“For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). The willing is God’s doing, and the working is God’s doing too — all you have to do is not stay sitting down.

“being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

The moment you take that step, God begins to work within you.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Doing It from the Heart Is Living Out 321
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s message back into the framework of 321, and you will see it isn’t scattered at all.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. Our Lord was never a teacher who only talked. The Word became flesh and lived among us — that in itself is the greatest “doing” of all. He said: “even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28). The Lord did first, and only then spoke.

The Bible is my standard. A standard isn’t for studying; it’s for walking. James says to be doers of the word, not only hearers. If today we merely find this message “very reasonable,” we have fallen into exactly the fault James describes.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. “The mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8:6). Not gritting our teeth in our own strength, but relying on the Spirit at work. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,” says Yahweh of Armies (Zechariah 4:6).

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King. A person who lets Jesus reign as King no longer asks, “Can I do it?” He only asks, “What does the King want me to do?” A soldier doesn’t debate with the general whether he is qualified; a soldier simply takes his orders.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. This sets you free from two kinds of bondage. When you do well, you needn’t take the credit, because the glory was never yours. When you do badly, you needn’t blame yourself until you can’t get up, because the one who is to receive the glory is him. When the glory goes to the Lord, people are set free.

The Goal

Establish God’s system. God’s system is not established by a few very impressive people; it is established together by many people who are willing to act from the heart.

From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness

Brothers and sisters, we have to face one thing honestly: behind the words “I can’t” there is often not humility but another form of “self.”

What we fear is not doing badly; what we fear is “being seen doing badly.” That is pride. Pride is not only thinking we are very capable; it also includes being overly preoccupied with our incapacity — both have their focus in the same place: self.

The 321 vision puts it precisely: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

When I say, “I can’t, so I won’t,” I am actually deciding on God’s behalf whether he can use me — that is taking God’s place. When I say, “I can’t, but I’ll go, because you are sending me,” I have returned to man’s originally intended position.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

The Fivefold Change and the Order of Service

The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. In today’s lesson what we are changing is our “mindset” — from “first be able, then act” to “act from the heart.” Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; once relationships change, ministry changes.

The 321 vision also reminds us: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

So the “doing” we are talking about today does not begin with rushing out to get things done. It begins with letting God win your heart within you. When the heart is right, doing is life; when the heart is wrong, doing is mere activity.

The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

The 920 practice: everyone who is in a relationship with us is our “2.” Before them we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, the first of today’s practices, “take the initiative to care for someone,” is the 920 at its most practical. You don’t need to wait until you are very mature; you only need, today, to show your “2” some care from the heart.

235 relationships: with a selfless person we become a “2,” spiritual companions; together we build the “3,” a legacy of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and then we become the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. One person acting from the heart grows tired; a group acting from the heart goes far.

A Shift in Viewpoint

From man’s viewpoint to God’s viewpoint: man looks at ability; God looks at the heart.

From the earthly to the heavenly: earth looks at efficiency; heaven looks at obedience.

From the temporary to the eternal: the discomfort before us lasts forty weeks; what is born is an eternal life.

From the worldly to the godly: the world says you need ability before you get a stage; God says you need a sincere heart and then comes grace.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Living Out God’s Word from the Heart
sections.html: Brothers and sisters, the lesson gives us five practices. Please don’t just let them wash over you — pick one of them and start today.

sections.heading: 1. Each Day, Do One Thing with a “Simple Heart”
sections.html:
Don’t overthink it. Today, do one thing that pleases God: take the initiative to care for someone; speak a word of encouragement; pray for someone.

The point is to do it from the heart, not to do it perfectly.

What is one word of encouragement worth? “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver” (Proverbs 25:11). You don’t need eloquence; you only need a heart that means it.

sections.heading: 2. Practise an Obedience That Isn’t Afraid of Mistakes
sections.html:
Tell yourself three things: it’s all right not to do it well; it’s all right to learn; it’s all right to correct course. But don’t stay where you are.

The Lord Jesus told a sobering parable. The servant who had received one talent said: “Lord, I knew you that you are a hard man, reaping where you didn’t sow, and gathering where you didn’t scatter. I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours” (Matthew 25:24–25).

Brothers and sisters, he did nothing wicked; he simply did nothing at all, because he was afraid. What the Lord rebuked was not that he did it wrong, but that he didn’t do it.

sections.heading: 3. Discern Which System You Are Living In Right Now
sections.html:
When you feel pressure, confusion or pain, stop and ask yourself one question: right now, am I setting my mind on the flesh, or on the Spirit?

Then choose to return to God’s word. Don’t argue with your emotions; just switch systems. When your heart grows heavy, you know the handbrake has been pulled up again; release it, and the Lord’s yoke is light once more.

sections.heading: 4. Pay the Cost for Every Act of Obedience
sections.html:
When you want to give up, remind yourself: this is the process of growing in life; this is the cost of bearing fruit.

Then choose to keep going and live it out. Remember the pregnant mother — she doesn’t carry on because it doesn’t hurt; she carries on because she knows a child will be born.

sections.heading: 5. Turn “Knowing” into “Action Right Now”
sections.html:
Every time you finish hearing a message or reading Scripture, write down one thing “I will do today,” and do it that same day.

Don’t write three things; one is enough. Don’t write “I will love people more”; write “Today I will phone so-and-so.” Let the truth touch the ground at once.

Deepening These Five Practices with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

The eight stages of 321 are the complete process for turning “knowing” into “receiving.” Walk through them like this:

Information: Today you have already heard it — God’s commands are not grievous; the key is whether you act from the heart. That is Information.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to turn this word into your own seeing. Ask the Lord to show you which thing you have been hiding from for a long time because “I can’t.”

Conviction: Hand over the old mindset before God. Admit that “first be able, then act” is the world’s arithmetic, not God’s.

Implementation: Do one thing today. Something small is fine — but really do it.

Evaluation: In the evening, be quiet for three minutes and ask yourself: today, did I rely on the heart, or on the brain? Was I in the light, or in the darkness?

Correction: Where it didn’t go well, don’t condemn yourself — just adjust. God wants a real face, not a perfect performance.

Repetition: Keep it up for sixty-six days in a row. Not because psychology says so, but because life is something that grows, not something conjured up.

Multiplication: Once you have walked this road yourself, take someone else along the same road. This is the “3” of 235 — spiritual parents bringing up spiritual children.

A Gentle Reminder

God doesn’t want you to be perfect; God wants you to be real.

God doesn’t look at how well you do; God looks at whether you do it from the heart.

Don’t be afraid of doing badly; be afraid of not doing it at all.

Brothers and sisters, the focus is not on “how well I do it,” but on “whether I do it from the heart.”

When you act from the heart, God goes to work.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, spiritual breakthrough doesn’t begin with “understanding more”; it begins with “doing it more from the heart.”

In this life we will hear countless sermons and read countless verses. But one day, standing before the Lord, he won’t ask us how many times we read the Bible. He will ask: that little I entrusted to you — did you go and do it?

When you act from the heart, God’s word will grow within you; when you keep on acting, life will bear fruit naturally.

So from this morning on, please change the question. Stop asking, “Can I do it?” Ask only one thing:

Am I willing to do it from the heart?

Brothers and sisters, let Jesus be King. When the King has given the order, the servants don’t need to call another meeting. Let Jesus receive all the glory. If it goes well, the glory is his; if it doesn’t go well, the grace is still his.

Look back at that toddler. He fell seventeen times, but he kept looking at that pair of open arms in front of him. Today, those arms are the Lord’s. He doesn’t hurry you; he doesn’t laugh at how slow you are. He says only one thing: come, walk over to me.

Brothers and sisters, stand up, and take a step.

declarations: In the name of the Lord Jesus, I declare:
I will no longer stop because I can’t; I will do it from the heart.
God’s commands are not grievous.
I choose to live in the light, to live in love, to live in the Holy Spirit.
I am willing to pay the cost and live out God’s word.
I move from knowing, into doing, into receiving.
My life will bear fruit and glorify the Lord’s name.
Amen.

Practise an obedience that isn’t afraid of mistakes

prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
Thank you for speaking to us this morning.

Lord, we confess that we often use “I can’t” as our reason for not acting. We are afraid of doing badly, afraid of being seen, afraid of failing. Please forgive us, for that is not humility; it is another form of “self.”

Lord, you said that the goal of the command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith. Give us a pure heart and take away what is mixed in us; give us a good conscience and take away our accusations; give us a sincere faith and take away our masks.

Lord, you said your commandments are not grievous. Holy Spirit, help us to switch systems — no longer straining in the flesh, but setting our minds on the Spirit and receiving life and peace. Teach us to live in the light, to love our brothers and sisters, and to walk in your word.
Lord, we are willing to pay the cost. Let us no longer simply store the truth in our heads, but let the truth be born out of our lives and bear fruit.
Today we place one specific thing into your hands. Give us the courage to do it before this day is over.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: 1 Timothy 1:5 says, “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.” Please share: is there something recently that you know you should do, but have kept putting off because “I can’t” or “I’m not good enough”? What do you think is holding you back — ability, or the heart?

1 John 2:11 says, “But he who hates his brother is in the darkness, and walks in the darkness, and doesn’t know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.” Please share: in which relationship have you experienced the hardship of “walking in the darkness”? How did you find your way back into the light? This week, for whom will you take the first step of love?

blog.title: A Life of Seventeen Falls an Hour

blocks.x: Why God never asks whether you “can”
Brothers and sisters, have you ever watched a child learning to walk?

He pulls himself up by the coffee table, lets go, wobbles two steps — and then, bump, he sits down hard on the floor. In a study published in 2012 in the journal Psychological Science, a team led by Karen Adolph of New York University found that a toddler learning to walk takes on average more than 2,300 steps an hour, and falls about seventeen times.
Seventeen falls an hour. Yet have you ever seen a child who, because he fell, decided he would crawl from now on?
Not one.
So when did we start to care more about whether we can than whether we will?
God Wants Not Perfection but Reality
When people don’t dare to act, their reasons usually come down to three sentences: I can’t; I’m not good enough yet; I don’t know how.

Moses said it too: “I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” (Exodus 4:10). God didn’t debate his eloquence with him; he simply said, “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth.” Jeremiah said he was only a child, and God said, “You must go to whomever I send you.”
Do you see it? God has never once answered, “You can.” God’s answer is, “Go.”
The Bible says: “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith” (1 Timothy 1:5).
Three things — none of them about ability, all of them about the heart. The Greek word for “sincere” literally means “unmasked”; its root is the masked actor of the theatre.
God does not want a beautifully acted play. God wants a real face.

When the psychologist Albert Bandura put forward his theory of “self-efficacy” in 1977, he pointed out that the strongest source of a person’s belief that they can do something is not other people’s encouragement but their own experience of succeeding. Notice the order — you don’t first have confidence and then act; you act, and then confidence grows.
What Is Hard Is Not Obeying God, but Leaving God and Still Trying to Live Well
The second obstacle is: it’s too hard.
But the Bible says: “For this is loving God, that we keep his commandments. His commandments are not grievous.” (1 John 5:3)

Why aren’t they grievous? The very next verse gives the reason: because whatever is born of God overcomes the world. It isn’t that God has lowered the standard; it’s that a different life inside you is now carrying the load.
Then why do we still find it so heavy? Because we try to do it in the flesh.

It’s like a car with a fine engine and a full tank, but the handbrake is still on. The harder you press the accelerator, the more the tyres smoke. You wouldn’t say the car is no good; you’d say: the handbrake is still on.

Which is easier, to love or to hate? From the standpoint of the flesh, hatred comes more naturally; from the standpoint of life, love is the easy one. Because love walks in the light, and hatred walks in darkness. Walking in the dark, you can’t see clearly, you trip easily, and walking is hard work.
Doing Is Giving Birth to the Truth
But let’s be honest: not hard doesn’t mean painless.
Doing always has a cost. It’s like a woman who is pregnant: it takes time, it means enduring discomfort, and only at the end is a new life born.
Seeing and listening are like conception; thinking and speaking are like the pregnancy; doing is like giving birth. If we don’t do it, everything stays inside.
If you don’t do it, truth stays as knowledge; if you do it, truth becomes life.

So God’s principle is very simple: know it, do it, receive it. If you never go and share the gospel, you will never be able to share it; once you start sharing, you gradually learn how. Doing brings experience; doing brings growth; doing brings power.
God isn’t waiting for you to be perfect; God walks with you.
Do One Thing Today
Don’t write three things; one is enough. Don’t write “I will love people more”; write “Today I will phone so-and-so.”
Take the initiative to care for someone. Speak a word of encouragement. Pray for someone.
Do it from the heart, not perfectly.
Spiritual breakthrough doesn’t begin with “understanding more”; it begins with “doing it more from the heart.” Don’t be afraid of doing badly; be afraid of not doing it at all.
Reflection
This week, is there one thing you know you should do but have kept putting off because “I can’t”? If you could do only one thing today, which would it be?

notes: Do It from the Heart — In Love It’s Not Hard
The Right Mindset About Doing (Part 2)
“His commandments are not grievous”
1 John 5:3
Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 145
• Greeting: Brothers and sisters, good morning; today is the second lesson on “doing”.
• Last lesson: living it out from within; this lesson: doing it from the heart.
• Name the two stones: “I can’t” and “It’s too hard”.
• Three theme passages: 1 Timothy 1:5, 1 John 5:3, Romans 8:6.
No one learns to walk before walking
The toddler lets go, wobbles, falls
Can he walk? Not at all
Yet he keeps going forward
Is the question “Can I?” or “Will I?”
• Scene: an eleven-month-old learning to walk in the living room, parents clapping nearby.
• Research: Karen Adolph’s team at New York University, Psychological Science, 2012 — toddlers take on average about 2,368 steps and fall about 17 times an hour.
• Ask: has any child given up after falling seventeen times? No.
• Lead into the theme: when did we start caring more about “Can I?” than “Will I?”
Theme Verses and Background
“The goal of this command is love”
1 Timothy 1:5
“His commandments are not grievous”
1 John 5:3
• 1 Timothy: written in Paul’s later years to Timothy in Ephesus, addressing people whose teaching “cause[d] disputes” (1 Timothy 1:3–4).
• “Goal” is the Greek telos: end point, aim.
• 1 John: written in John’s later years to the churches of Asia Minor, against false teaching that made light of conduct.
• Scripture interpreting Scripture: 1 John 5:4 gives the reason it isn’t grievous — “whatever is born of God overcomes the world.”
• Romans 8:6: “mind” is phronēma in the original, the whole orientation of one’s thinking.
The key isn’t whether you can
I can’t, I’m not good enough, I don’t know how
God never asks you to “be able” first
God only asks you to act “from the heart”
Moses and Jeremiah both said it too
• Moses: “I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” (Exodus 4:10).
• God’s answer: “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth” (Exodus 4:12).
• Jeremiah: “I am a child.” God: “You must go to whomever I send you” (Jeremiah 1:6–7).
• Key point: God never answers “You can”; God answers “Go — I am with you.”
• 2 Corinthians 8:12: “If the readiness is there, it is acceptable.”
Heart brings gladness; brain brings strain
A pure heart, a good conscience
A sincere faith (unmasked)
“Out of it is the wellspring of life”
Proverbs 4:23
• “Sincere” is the Greek anypokritos, literally “unmasked”; its root is the actor of the theatre.
• God does not want a beautifully acted play; he wants a real face.
• 1 Samuel 16:7: “Yahweh looks at the heart.”
• Psychology: Carol Dweck (Stanford) on the growth mindset; Bandura (1977): self-efficacy comes from first-hand experience.
• Illustration: the sister in the small group who never dared to pray, who said only, “Lord, please heal him” — and the whole group wept.
God’s commands really aren’t hard
“His commandments are not grievous”
1 John 5:3
It feels hard because we do it in the flesh
Like driving with the handbrake on
• “Grievous” is the Greek barys: heavy, weighty, crushing.
• Compare: the Pharisees “bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders” (Matthew 23:4).
• The Lord says: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30).
• Illustration: fine engine, full tank, but the handbrake is on — the harder you press the accelerator, the more the tyres smoke.
• The heavy burdens were put there by the religious system, not by God.
Love in the light, hatred in the dark
He who loves his brother remains in the light
He who hates his brother walks in darkness
Romans 8:6: the mind of the Spirit
• Ask: which is easier, to love or to hate? To the flesh hatred is natural; to life, love is easy.
• Science: going from light into darkness, the rod cells need about 20–30 minutes to adapt, and we can hardly tell colours apart.
• Medicine: Chida and Steptoe, Journal of the American College of Cardiology, 2009 meta-analysis — anger and hostility are associated with a raised risk of coronary heart disease.
• C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity: don’t bother whether you love your neighbour; act as if you did.
• Key line: what is truly hard is not obeying God, but leaving God and still trying to live well.
Doing has a cost, but it’s full of worth
Seeing and listening: conception
Thinking and speaking: pregnancy
Doing: giving birth
Don’t do it, and truth stays as knowledge
• Illustration: pregnancy lasts about forty weeks of discomfort, and at the end a life is born.
• John 16:21: a woman in labour has sorrow, but once the child is born she no longer remembers the anguish.
• John 12:24: if a grain of wheat dies, it bears much fruit.
• Three costs: time, face, comfort.
• Research: Dunn, Norton and colleagues, Science, 2008 — spending money on others makes people happier than spending it on themselves; echoes Acts 20:35, “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
Know it, do it, receive it
“Blessed are you if you do them”
John 13:17
Doing brings experience, growth, power
God doesn’t wait for perfect; he walks with you
• James 1:22: be doers of the word, not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
• James 1:25: the blessing comes “in what he does”.
• Example: sharing the gospel — never share and you’ll never be able to; start sharing and you gradually learn (Acts 1:8: power is received on the road).
• Brain science: Hebb (1949), neurons that fire together wire together; Lally and colleagues, European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010 — a new habit takes a median of about 66 days.
• The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Practices for Daily Life
Do one thing with a simple heart
Obey without fear of mistakes
Discern which system you’re in
Pay the cost · 5. Act right now
• Practice 1 is 920 in action: show your “2” care from the heart, bearing the ninefold fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23).
• Practice 2: it’s all right to do it badly, to learn, to correct course — but don’t stay where you are.
• Warning: the servant who buried the talent didn’t do wrong; he did nothing at all because he was afraid (Matthew 25:24–25).
• Practice 3: as soon as it feels heavy, you know the handbrake is on again.
• Practice 5: write just one thing, and make it concrete — not “I will love people more” but “Today I will phone so-and-so.”
Stop asking “Can I?”
Breakthrough doesn’t start with understanding more
But with doing it more from the heart
Don’t be afraid of doing badly
Be afraid of not doing it at all
• Back to the toddler: he isn’t looking at his feet but at his father’s open arms.
• Call: let Jesus be King — when the King has given the order, the servants don’t need to call another meeting.
• Let Jesus receive all the glory: no taking credit when it goes well, no losing heart when it doesn’t.
• Invitation: choose one thing today and do it from the heart.
Prayer of Response and Blessing
Lord, I am willing to do it from the heart
From knowing, into doing, into receiving
Let Jesus be King
All glory to Jesus
• Lead the brothers and sisters in declaring: I will no longer stop because I can’t.
• Pray for a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith.
• Invite each person to settle in their heart the one thing they will do today.
• Blessing: may the Lord’s yoke be easy and his burden light; may the brothers and sisters walk in the light today.

Yet he keeps going forward

Toddlers fall about 17 times an hour
No child gives up walking because of it
Two stones that hold us back:
“I can’t” and “It’s too hard”
• Research: Karen Adolph’s team (New York University), Psychological Science, 2012 — toddlers take on average about 2,368 steps and fall about 17 times an hour.
• Ask: when did we start caring more about “Can I?” than “Will I?”
• Preview: the answer to the first stone is “from the heart”; the answer to the second is “not grievous”.

“The goal of this command is love”
1 Timothy 1:5
“His commandments are not grievous”
1 John 5:3
• 1 Timothy: Paul’s later years (around AD 62–64), to Timothy left in Ephesus, addressing those whose teaching “cause[d] disputes” (1 Timothy 1:3–4).
• “Goal” is the Greek telos, end point or aim; the end point of every command is love.
• 1 John: John’s later years (around AD 90), to the churches of Asia Minor, against false teaching that made light of conduct (1 John 2:4).
• Romans: written around AD 57 in Corinth; chapter 7 is the struggle of the self-centred life, chapter 8 the freedom of the Spirit.
• “Mind” is the Greek phronēma, the steering wheel of one’s whole thinking.
Three Common Sentences
I can’t
I’m not good enough yet
I don’t know how
Behind them: “be able first, then act”
• These three sound humble, but hidden inside is a wrong mindset: I must have the ability first, and only then can God use me.
• The Bible, from beginning to end, never reads that way.
• Preview: Moses and Jeremiah both said the same thing.
God’s Answer Isn’t “You Can”
Moses: “I am slow of speech”
Exodus 4:10
God says: “Now therefore go,
and I will be with your mouth”
• Exodus 4:11–12: Who made man’s mouth? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth.
• Jeremiah 1:6–7: Don’t say, “I am a child”; you must go to whomever I send you.
• Key point: God never answers “You can”; God answers “Go,” together with “I am with you.”
God Looks at the Heart
A pure heart, a good conscience, a sincere faith
“Yahweh looks at the heart”
1 Samuel 16:7
The brain analyses; the heart acts
• “Sincere” is the Greek anypokritos, literally “unmasked”; its root is the masked actor of the theatre.
• 2 Corinthians 8:12: “If the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what you have.”
• Psychology: Carol Dweck (Stanford) on the growth mindset; Bandura (1977): self-efficacy comes from first-hand experience.
• Order: you don’t first have confidence and then act; you act, and then confidence grows. Proverbs 4:23 — out of the heart is the wellspring of life.
• Illustration: the sister in the small group who never dared to open her mouth, who said only, “Lord, please heal him” — and the whole group wept.
The Real Reason It Isn’t Hard
“His commandments are not grievous”
“Whatever is born of God overcomes the world”
1 John 5:3–4
Not a lower standard, but a different life
• The key to letting Scripture interpret Scripture: verse 4 is the reason for verse 3.
• It isn’t grievous not because God lowered the standard but because a different life inside is now carrying the load.
• Answer the inner grumble: easy for the apostles — but for me? The answer lies in the new life.
Where Do Heavy Burdens Come From?
“Grievous”: heavy, crushing
Pharisees laid burdens on people’s shoulders
Matthew 23:4
The Lord says: my burden is light
• “Grievous” is the Greek barys; the same word is used of the “heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne” in Matthew 23:4.
• Matthew 11:28–30: my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
• Conclusion: the heaviness was put there by the religious system, not by God.
• Illustration: fine engine, full tank, but the handbrake is on — the harder you press the accelerator, the more the tyres smoke.
Love in the Light, Hatred in the Dark
He who loves his brother remains in the light
He who hates his brother walks in darkness
The mind of the Spirit is life and peace
• Ask: which is easier, to love or to hate? To the flesh hatred is natural; to life, love is easy.
• Science: going from light into darkness, the rod cells need about 20–30 minutes to adapt, and we can hardly tell colours apart.
• Medicine: Chida and Steptoe, Journal of the American College of Cardiology, 2009 meta-analysis — anger and hostility are associated with a raised risk of coronary heart disease.
• C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity: don’t bother whether you love your neighbour; act as if you did.
• Key line: what is truly hard is not obeying God, but leaving God and still trying to live well.
The Picture of Pregnancy
It takes time: about forty weeks
It means enduring discomfort
It comes at a cost
And at the end, a new life is born
• On one hand: the life grows by itself; the baby’s heart begins to beat around the third week after conception, without the mother doing a thing.
• On the other: forty weeks of discomfort, then the pain of giving birth.
• John 16:21: once the child is born, she doesn’t remember the anguish any more.
• Not hard doesn’t mean painless; light doesn’t mean free.
From Conception to Birth
Seeing and listening: conception
Thinking and speaking: pregnancy
Doing: giving birth
Don’t do it, and everything stays inside
• Don’t do it, and truth stays as knowledge; do it, and truth becomes life.
• Warning: long-term taking in without living out leads to “spiritual obstructed labour” — the more you hear, the heavier and number your heart grows.
• 321 insight: life does not stay inside; it is lived out.
Three Costs
Time, face and comfort
“If it dies, it bears much fruit”
John 12:24
The cost isn’t a loss; it’s the ticket of admission
• Time: half an hour for a phone call, an evening to keep someone company.
• Face: to apologise you must lower your head first; to share the gospel you must be ready to be turned down.
• Comfort: Luke 9:23 — deny yourself and take up your cross daily.
• Research: Dunn, Norton and colleagues, Science, 2008 — spending money on others makes people happier than spending it on themselves.
• Acts 20:35: it is more blessed to give than to receive. Galatians 6:9: we will reap in due season.
Know It, Do It, Receive It
“Be doers of the word, not only hearers”
James 1:22
“Blessed in what he does”
James 1:25
• “Deluding your own selves”: the greatest danger of only hearing the word is thinking you have already changed.
• Being moved is not being changed; being moved is only being moved.
• John 13:17: if you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.
• Matthew 7:24: the one who hears and does is like a man who built his house on a rock.
You Learn It by Doing It
Never share, and you’ll never be able to
Start sharing, and you gradually learn
Power is received on the road
Acts 1:8
• Mark 16:15: Go into all the world, and preach the Good News to the whole creation.
• Illustration: learning to swim — however many videos you watch, you’ll never swim without getting into the water; you swallow water twice before you float.
• Doing brings experience; doing brings growth; doing brings power.
Repeat Until It Takes Shape
Neurons that fire together wire together
A new habit takes a median of 66 days
Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation
Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
• Donald Hebb (1949): neurons that fire together wire together.
• R. Douglas Fields (US National Institutes of Health): repeated neural activity promotes myelination, making signals faster and more reliable.
• Phillippa Lally and colleagues, European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010: a new habit becomes automatic after a median of about 66 days, ranging from 18 to 254 days.
• Don’t judge yourself a failure on the strength of three days of obedience.
• Philippians 2:13: it is God who works in you both to will and to work.
Practices (Part 1)
Do one thing with a simple heart
Obey without fear of mistakes
Discern which system you’re in
Do it from the heart, not perfectly
• Practice 1 is 920 in action: show your “2” care from the heart, bearing the ninefold fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23).
• Practice 2: it’s all right to do it badly, to learn, to correct course — but don’t stay where you are.
• Warning: the servant who buried the talent didn’t do wrong; he did nothing at all because he was afraid (Matthew 25:24–25).
• Practice 3: as soon as you feel heavy or confused, ask — am I setting my mind on the flesh, or on the Spirit?
Practices (Part 2)
Pay the cost for every act of obedience
Turn knowing into action right now
Write down one thing “I will do today”
And do it that same day

• Practice 5: write just one thing, and make it concrete — not “I will love people more” but “Today I will phone so-and-so.”
• Deepen with the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Jesus my role model, the Bible my standard
The Holy Spirit my guide; let Jesus be King
The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless
Mindset, life, living, relationships, ministry
• Three Foundations: the Lord did first, then spoke (Matthew 20:28); the Bible is for walking; rely on the Spirit, not on ourselves (Zechariah 4:6).
• Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — not “Can I?” but “What does the King want me to do?”; let Jesus receive all the glory — no taking credit when it goes well, no losing heart when it doesn’t.

• Life first, then relationships, then ministry; the order of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.
• Shift of viewpoint: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.
Stop asking “Can I?”
Breakthrough doesn’t start with understanding more
But with doing it more from the heart
Don’t be afraid of doing badly
Ask only: am I willing to do it from the heart?
• The Lord won’t ask how many times we read the Bible; he will ask: that little I entrusted to you — did you go and do it?
• Back to the toddler: he isn’t looking at his feet but at his father’s open arms.
• Call: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.
• Invitation: stand up, and take a step.
Prayer of Response and Blessing
Lord, I am willing to do it from the heart
From knowing, into doing, into receiving
Let Jesus be King
All glory to Jesus
