script: Brothers and sisters, good morning.
Today we’re reading the second talk on “The Right Mindset About Doing,” and the title is: Do It from the Heart — In Love It’s Not Hard.

In the last lesson we said that right doing is lived out from within. Today we’ll be even more practical. Many people have nodded, yet still haven’t acted. Why? Because there are two stones weighing on the heart.
The first is “I can’t.” The second is “It’s too hard.”
This morning, God’s word is going to roll both stones away with its own hand.
Brothers and sisters, let me ask you first to play a short video in your mind.
An eleven-month-old child pulls himself up by the coffee table, lets go, wobbles two steps — and then, bump, he sits down hard on the floor.
Let me ask you: can that child walk?
No. Not at all. So why does he keep walking? Because he wants to walk.
In a study published in 2012, a team led by Karen Adolph of New York University found that toddlers learning to walk take on average more than 2,300 steps an hour, and fall about seventeen times.
Seventeen falls an hour. Yet have you ever seen a child who, because he fell, decided he would crawl from now on? Not one.
So when did we start to care more about whether we can than whether we will?
We have two theme passages today.
The first: “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.” 1 Timothy chapter 1, verse 5.
At the time there was a group of people in Ephesus who could talk very well and argue very well. Paul says: the end point isn’t knowledge; it’s love.
The second: “For this is loving God, that we keep his commandments. His commandments are not grievous.” 1 John chapter 5, verse 3.
Why aren’t they grievous? The very next verse tells us: because whatever is born of God overcomes the world.
Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that God has lowered the standard; it’s that a different life inside you is now carrying the load.
Let’s roll away the first stone.
People who don’t dare to act usually say three things: I can’t; I’m not good enough yet; I don’t know how.
Moses said: “I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” And God said: “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth.”
Jeremiah said too: “I am a child.” And God said: you must go to whomever I send you.
Brothers and sisters, do you see it? God has never once answered, “You can.” God’s answer is “Go,” together with “I am with you.”
So what does God look at? God looks at the heart.
“Sincere faith” — that word “sincere” in Greek literally means “unmasked,” and its root is the actor of the theatre.
Brothers and sisters, God does not want a beautifully acted play. God wants a real face.

So many small groups have a sister like this. Whenever it’s her turn to pray she lowers her head and says, “I don’t know how to pray; I’m afraid I’ll say it wrong.” Then one time a child fell ill, and she couldn’t hold back. She managed only one sentence: “Lord, please heal him.” And the whole group wept.
Could she pray? By human standards, no. But that was the most powerful prayer of all.
The Bible says: “out of it is the wellspring of life.” Proverbs chapter 4, verse 23. Rely on the heart and your heart is glad; rely on the brain and you’re left with strain.
Now let’s roll away the second stone: it’s too hard.
The Greek word for “grievous” means heavy, crushing. The Lord Jesus used the same word when he said the Pharisees bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne and lay them on people’s shoulders.
Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: the heaviness was put there by religion, not by God. The Lord himself said: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
Then why do we still find it so heavy? Because we try to do it in the flesh.

It’s like a car with a fine engine and a full tank, but the handbrake is still on. The harder you press the accelerator, the more the tyres smoke. It isn’t that the car is no good; the handbrake is on.
Let me ask you a question, brothers and sisters: which is easier, to love or to hate?
From the standpoint of the flesh, hatred comes more naturally; from the standpoint of life, love is the easy one. Why? Because love walks in the light, and hatred walks in darkness.
The Bible says: he who loves his brother remains in the light; he who hates his brother walks in the darkness, and doesn’t know where he is going. 1 John chapter 2, verses 10 to 11.

Walking in the dark, you can’t see clearly, you trip easily, and walking is hard work. When our eyes go from a bright place into darkness, they need twenty or thirty minutes to adapt. That is exactly what a person living in hatred is like: the world loses its colour, and every step must be guarded.
So brothers and sisters, what is truly hard is not obeying God; what is truly hard is leaving God and still trying to live well.
But let me say something honest: the commands aren’t hard, but doing them always has a cost. Not hard doesn’t mean painless.
It’s like a woman who is pregnant: it takes time, it means enduring discomfort, and at the end a new life is born.
Seeing and listening are like conception; thinking and speaking are like the pregnancy; doing is like giving birth. And if we don’t do it? Everything stays inside.
Brothers and sisters, if you don’t do it, truth stays as knowledge; if you do it, truth becomes life. The cost isn’t a loss; the cost is the ticket of admission.
God’s principle is very simple: know it, do it, receive it.

James says: be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves. The greatest danger for those who only hear the word isn’t that they make no progress, but that they think they’ve already made progress. Being moved is not being changed; being moved is only being moved.
The Lord said: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” John chapter 13, verse 17.
It’s like sharing the gospel. If you never go and share it, you’ll never be able to; once you start sharing, you gradually learn how. Doing brings experience, brings growth, brings power.
Brothers and sisters, God isn’t waiting for you to be perfect; God walks with you.
So today we have five practices.
First, do one thing with a simple heart: care for someone, speak a word of encouragement, pray for someone. Do it from the heart, not perfectly.
Second, practise an obedience that isn’t afraid of mistakes. It’s all right to do it badly, it’s all right to correct course — but don’t stay where you are.
Third, discern which system you are living in. As soon as it feels heavy, ask: am I setting my mind on the flesh, or on the Spirit?
Fourth, pay the cost for every act of obedience.
Fifth, turn knowing into action right now: write down one thing “I will do today,” and do it that same day.
Brothers and sisters, spiritual breakthrough doesn’t begin with “understanding more”; it begins with “doing it more from the heart.”
One day, standing before the Lord, he won’t ask us how many times we read the Bible. He will ask: that little I entrusted to you — did you go and do it?
Don’t be afraid of doing badly; be afraid of not doing it at all.

Look back at that toddler. He fell seventeen times, but he kept looking at that pair of open arms in front of him. Today, those arms are the Lord’s. He doesn’t hurry you; he doesn’t laugh at how slow you are. He says only one thing: come, walk over to me.
Let Jesus be King. When the King has given the order, the servants don’t need to call another meeting.
Let’s pray together.
Dear Lord Jesus, thank you for speaking to us this morning. We confess that we often use “I can’t” as our reason for not acting. Please forgive us.

Lord, give us a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith. Holy Spirit, help us to switch systems — no longer straining in the flesh, but setting our minds on the Spirit. Today we place one specific thing into your hands. Give us the courage to do it before this day is over.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, may the Lord’s yoke be easy on you and his burden light. May you walk today in the light and in love. May all the glory go to Jesus.
Brothers and sisters, good morning.
Today we’re reading the second talk on “The Right Mindset About Doing”: Do It from the Heart — In Love It’s Not Hard.

In the last lesson we said that right doing is lived out from within, not performed from without. Today we want to make it even more practical. Many brothers and sisters have already nodded — and still haven’t acted. Why? Because there are two large stones weighing on the heart.
The first is “I can’t.” The second is “It’s too hard.”
This morning, we’re going to let God’s word roll both stones away with its own hand.
Let me ask you first to play a short video in your mind.

An eleven-month-old child pulls himself up by the coffee table. He lets go, wobbles, takes one step, then a second — and then, bump, he sits down hard on the floor. Mum and Dad, close by, are laughing, clapping, filming. The child pauses for a moment, crawls back up on his own, and walks again.
Let me ask you: can that child walk?
No. Not at all. His balance is all over the place, his steps are crooked. Graded on whether he can or can’t, he scores zero.
So why does he keep walking? Because he wants to walk. Because his eyes are fixed on that pair of open arms in front of him.

In a study published in 2012 in the journal Psychological Science, a team led by the New York University developmental psychologist Karen Adolph filmed and tracked toddlers learning to walk, and found that they take on average more than 2,300 steps an hour — and fall about seventeen times.
Seventeen falls an hour.
But brothers and sisters, have you ever seen a child who, after falling seventeen times, sat down and said, “Forget it — crawling is safer”?
Not one.
So when did we start to care more about whether we can than whether we will?
Let’s look first at the background.

1 Timothy was written in Paul’s later years, around AD 62 to 64, to Timothy, who had been left in Ephesus to shepherd the church. A group of people had arisen there who taught a different doctrine, talked about genealogies and loved to argue. It was against that background that Paul wrote: the goal of this command is love. “Goal” in the original is telos, meaning the end point.

1 John was written in John’s later years, around AD 90. At that time some people were exalting “knowing” to the skies and making light of conduct. That’s why John says: his commandments are not grievous.
Romans was written around AD 57. Chapter 7 is the struggle: desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good. Chapter 8 is the answer: the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.
Now let’s roll away the first stone.
People who don’t dare to act usually say three things: I can’t. I’m not good enough yet. I don’t know how.
Those sentences sound very humble, but hidden inside them is a wrong mindset: I must have the ability first, and only then can God use me.
Brothers and sisters, the Bible, from beginning to end, never reads that way.
At Horeb, Moses said to God: “I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” Exodus chapter 4, verse 10.
God didn’t debate his eloquence with him. God said: “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.”
When Jeremiah was called, he said: “Behold, I don’t know how to speak; for I am a child.” And God said: “You must go to whomever I send you.”
Brothers and sisters, do you see it? God has never once answered, “You can.” God’s answer is “Go,” together with “I am with you.”
So what does God look at? God looks at the heart.
Our theme verse says this love comes out of a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith. None of the three has anything to do with ability; all three have to do with the heart.
“Sincere” in the original is anypokritos, which literally means “unmasked”; its root is the masked actor of the theatre.
God does not want a beautifully acted play. God wants a real face.
Paul says: “If the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what you have, not according to what you don’t have.” God never demands from you what you do not have.
Samuel saw how tall and handsome Eliab was, but God said: “Yahweh looks at the heart.”
Psychology offers good supporting evidence here.

Professor Carol Dweck of Stanford University distinguishes a “fixed mindset” from a “growth mindset.” People with a fixed mindset fear failure, because failure proves “I’m no good”; people with a growth mindset see failure as part of the process, so they’re willing to try again and again.
In 1977 Albert Bandura put forward his theory of “self-efficacy,” pointing out that the strongest source of believing you can do something is your own experience of succeeding.
Brothers and sisters, please notice the order: you don’t first have confidence and then act; you act, and then confidence grows.

So many small groups have a sister like this. Whenever it’s her turn to pray, she lowers her head and passes the turn on, saying, “I don’t know how to pray; I’m afraid I’ll say it wrong.” Then one time a child fell ill, and she couldn’t hold back. She managed only one sentence: “Lord, please heal him.” And the whole group wept.
The Bible says: “out of it is the wellspring of life.” Rely on the heart and your heart is glad; rely on the brain and you’re left with strain.
Now let’s roll away the second stone: it’s too hard.
Deep down we often carry a secret complaint: being a Christian is exhausting. You have to love people, forgive, be patient, deal with your temper. Who can do all that?
But the Bible says: “His commandments are not grievous.”
Pay attention to the next verse, because it is John’s own reason: “For whatever is born of God overcomes the world.”
Do you see it? They aren’t grievous not because God has lowered the standard, but because the new life born of God overcomes the world.
Whether it is hard doesn’t depend on how heavy the commandment is, but on which life inside you is carrying it.
“Grievous” in the original is barys, meaning heavy, crushing.
The Lord used the same word of the Pharisees: “For they bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders.” Matthew chapter 23, verse 4.
Put the two side by side and the truth comes out: the heaviness was put there by the religious system, not by God.
The Lord himself said: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
Then why do we still find it so heavy? Because we try to do it in the flesh.

It’s like a car with a fine engine and a full tank, but the handbrake is still on. You press the accelerator and the car does move — but the engine roars and the tyres smoke. It isn’t that the car is no good; the handbrake is on. That is many people’s spiritual life: the harder they try, the more they smoke.
Let’s take the most practical example of all: loving our brothers and sisters.
Which is easier, to love or to hate?
From the standpoint of the flesh, hatred comes more naturally. Love needs to be reminded; hatred doesn’t need to be taught.
But from the standpoint of life, love is the easy one. Why? Because love walks in the light, and hatred walks in darkness.
The Bible says: “He who loves his brother remains in the light … But he who hates his brother is in the darkness, and walks in the darkness, and doesn’t know where he is going.”

When our eyes go from a bright place into darkness, they need twenty to thirty minutes to adapt, and even then we can hardly tell colours apart. Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what a person living in hatred is like: the world loses its colour, and every step must be guarded.

And hatred really is heavier. A 2009 meta-analysis by researchers at University College London, published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, found that anger and hostility are associated with a raised risk of coronary heart disease.
What is truly hard is not obeying God; what is truly hard is leaving God and still trying to live well.
But I need to say something honest here. It is true that the commands aren’t hard; and it is also true that doing them always has a cost.
Not hard doesn’t mean painless.
The lesson uses a very beautiful picture: a woman who is pregnant.

In one sense it isn’t hard at all, because the life grows by itself: the baby’s heart begins to beat around the third week after conception, without the mother doing a thing. In another sense it comes at a great cost: forty weeks of time, morning sickness, an aching back, sleepless nights — and at the end, the pain of giving birth.
The Lord himself said: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow … But when she has delivered the child, she doesn’t remember the anguish any more.”
First sorrow, then joy; first anguish, then life.
The lesson maps the spiritual process onto this very clearly.
Seeing and listening are like conception — the truth has come inside.
Thinking and speaking are like the pregnancy — the truth is meditated on and spoken out.
Doing is like giving birth — the truth comes out and becomes visible life.
And if we don’t do it? Everything stays inside.

Brothers and sisters, when we only take in for a long time and never live it out, we can suffer a kind of “spiritual obstructed labour.” You’ve heard many messages and taken many notes, yet your heart grows heavier and heavier, because too much truth has built up inside that has never been brought to birth.
If you don’t do it, truth stays as knowledge; if you do it, truth becomes life.
What exactly is the cost? Usually there are three kinds.
The cost of time: that phone call to show you care will take half an hour; keeping that person company will take an evening.
The cost of face: to apologise you have to lower your head first; to share the gospel you have to be ready to be turned down; to admit your weakness you have to take off your mask first.
The cost of comfort: the Lord says, “deny yourself, take up your cross daily, and follow me.” That word “daily” tells us this is not a single heroic act but a little denying of self every day.
The Lord says: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.”
Left in the barn, it’s very safe and very alone — for ever a single grain. Fallen into the earth, it must break open, and then a whole field grows up.

A study published in 2008 in the journal Science found that people who spent money on others were happier than those who spent it on themselves. That is in keeping with the Bible: it is more blessed to give than to receive.
The cost isn’t a loss; the cost is the ticket of admission.
Brothers and sisters, many people stop at “knowing,” and so they never “receive.”
God’s principle is very simple: know it, do it, receive it.
James says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”
Please notice the words “deluding your own selves.” The greatest danger for those who only hear the word isn’t that they make no progress, but that they think they’ve already made progress.
Being moved is not being changed. Being moved is only being moved.
James goes on to say that the one who really does it “will be blessed in what he does.” The blessing is in what he does, not in what he hears.
The Lord also said: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.”
The lesson gives a most fitting example: sharing the gospel.
If you never go and share it, you’ll never be able to share it; once you start sharing, you gradually learn how.
We often wait for a moment when we are “ready,” but that moment won’t come by itself. The Lord’s command is: go into all the world, and preach the Good News to the whole creation.
When does the power come? “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you.” Power is received on the road, not waited for at home.

Learning to swim is the same. Watch as many instructional videos as you like — if you never get into the water, you’ll never swim. The first time you swallow water; the second time you swallow water again; the third time, suddenly, you float — and what you learn in that moment is something no book could ever teach you.
Brothers and sisters, you only touch grace once you get into the water.
Doing brings experience; doing brings growth; doing brings power.
Brain science offers supporting evidence too.

In 1949 the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb put forward a famous principle: neurons that fire together wire together. Every time you actually do something, a pathway in your brain is walked once more; the more often it’s walked, the wider and steadier that pathway becomes.

So how long must you keep at it? Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London followed ninety-six participants, and in research published in the European Journal of Social Psychology they found that for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit took a median of sixty-six days, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days.
So don’t judge yourself a failure on the strength of three days of obedience.
The 321 eight stages of changing our mindset lay this road out perfectly: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
God isn’t waiting for you to be perfect; God walks with you.
The lesson gives us five practices. Please pick one and start today.
First, each day, do one thing with a simple heart: care for someone, speak a word of encouragement, pray for someone. The point is to do it from the heart, not to do it perfectly.
Second, practise an obedience that isn’t afraid of mistakes. Tell yourself: it’s all right not to do it well, it’s all right to learn, it’s all right to correct course — but don’t stay where you are.

The servant who had received one talent said: “I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth.” He did nothing wicked; he simply did nothing at all, because he was afraid. What the Lord rebuked was not that he did it wrong, but that he didn’t do it.

Third, discern which system you are living in. When you feel pressure, confusion or pain, stop and ask: am I setting my mind on the flesh, or on the Spirit? As soon as your heart grows heavy, you know the handbrake has been pulled up again.

Fourth, pay the cost for every act of obedience. When you want to give up, remind yourself: this is the process of growing in life; this is the cost of bearing fruit. That pregnant mother doesn’t carry on because it doesn’t hurt; she carries on because she knows a child will be born.

Fifth, turn “knowing” into “action right now.” Every time you finish hearing a message, write down one thing “I will do today,” and do it that same day. Don’t write three things; one is enough. Don’t write “I will love people more”; write “Today I will phone so-and-so.”

Brothers and sisters, walk it through the eight stages and it’s complete: what you heard today is Information; ask the Holy Spirit for Revelation; handing over the old mindset is Conviction; doing one thing today is Implementation; three quiet minutes in the evening is Evaluation; where it didn’t go well, make a Correction; then Repetition; and finally take someone along the same road — that is Multiplication.
Let’s set today’s message back into 321.

Jesus is my role model — the Word becoming flesh was the greatest “doing” of all. The Bible is my standard — a standard isn’t for studying; it’s for walking. The Holy Spirit is my guide — not gritting our teeth in our own strength.

Let Jesus be King — a person who lets Jesus be King no longer asks, “Can I do it?” He only asks, “What does the King want me to do?” Let Jesus receive all the glory — when you do well you needn’t take the credit, and when you do badly you needn’t blame yourself until you can’t get up.
Brothers and sisters, let’s be honest: behind the words “I can’t” there is often not humility but another form of self. What we fear is not doing badly; what we fear is being seen doing badly.
Pride is not only thinking we are very capable; it also includes being overly preoccupied with our incapacity — both have their focus in the same place: self.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Today what we are changing is our mindset — from “be able first, then act” to “act from the heart.”
Brothers and sisters, spiritual breakthrough doesn’t begin with “understanding more”; it begins with “doing it more from the heart.”
One day, standing before the Lord, he won’t ask us how many times we read the Bible. He will ask: that little I entrusted to you — did you go and do it?
So from today on, change the question. Stop asking, “Can I do it?” Ask only: am I willing to do it from the heart?

Look back at that toddler. He fell seventeen times, but he kept looking at that pair of open arms in front of him. Today, those arms are the Lord’s. He doesn’t hurry you; he doesn’t laugh at how slow you are. He says only one thing: come, walk over to me.
Let’s pray together.

Dear Lord Jesus, thank you for speaking to us this morning. We confess that we often use “I can’t” as our reason for not acting. Please forgive us. Give us a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith. Holy Spirit, help us to switch systems — no longer straining in the flesh, but setting our minds on the Spirit and receiving life and peace. Today we place one specific thing into your hands. Give us the courage to do it before this day is over. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord’s yoke be easy on you and his burden light. May the brothers and sisters walk today in the light, in love and in the Holy Spirit. May all the glory go to Jesus.

sections.heading: Introduction: What Changes You Is Not That One Day, but Every Day
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin with a very simple question: on which day of your life were you shaped into the person you are today?

We often imagine that a changed life is a matter of “one day.” That one conference, that one tearful prayer, that one message that hit home, that one late-night decision. Deep down we hope: if only I could have one more experience like that, I would be different.

But brothers and sisters, we have all been there — that meeting really was on fire, that prayer really was sincere, and yet three weeks later we were back to our old selves. It isn’t that the meeting wasn’t real, or that the prayer wasn’t heard. The problem is this: we mistook being “moved” for being “changed.”

Being moved happens in a day. Being changed happens every day.

There was a brother who wrote down the same three goals at the start of every year: read the Bible every day, exercise every day, stop losing his temper with his wife. He wrote them for eleven years. In the twelfth year he finally understood something: he didn’t lack resolve; what he lacked was “doing.” Every time, he had been waiting for a “day when change would begin,” and he had failed to see that the day of change is today, and the unit of change is not the year but the day.

Brothers and sisters, in this series we have been learning the right mindset about “doing.” In the first lesson we saw that doing is the proof of faith; in the second, that doing must follow God’s heart. Today, in the third lesson, we come to the most crucial and most practical step of all: how does doing become life?

The answer is one word: habit.

Life is not changed in an instant; life is shaped through “repeated choices.” The first choice you make when you open your eyes in the morning, your first reaction at the office to a cutting remark, the screen your finger slides towards late at night when all is quiet — these seemingly trivial things are drawing, stroke by stroke, the outline of your life.

William James, the father of American psychology, devoted an entire chapter of The Principles of Psychology, published in 1890, to “habit.” He put it bluntly: our whole life, so far as it has definite form, is but a mass of habits. He also reminded his readers that every one of our actions leaves its mark on the nervous system; not one of them truly “doesn’t count.”

Brothers and sisters, this is what the Bible said long ago:

“Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians 6:7).

What we sow each day is not only the seed of behaviour, but the seed of life. Today we are going to learn together how to turn “right doing” into “right habits,” and how “right habits” grow into “a new creation.”

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter Written Through Tears
sections.html:
To receive today’s message rightly, we first need to know where our key verse comes from.

The author of 2 Corinthians is the apostle Paul. It was written around AD 56, generally thought to be from Macedonia (both 2 Corinthians 2:13 and 7:5 mention Paul arriving in Macedonia). It was addressed to the church in Corinth — a church that caused Paul both great love and great pain.

Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia and one of the busiest trading ports in the Greek world. Maritime trade, pagan temples, moral corruption — every kind of current churned through that city. The Corinthian church was planted in just such soil: rich in gifts yet riddled with problems, full of zeal yet often lacking the foundation of life.

2 Corinthians is the most personal of Paul’s letters, and the one most full of tears. In it he defends his apostleship, because some were questioning him and looking down on him. But Paul did not use his position to crush anyone; he used the logic of the cross.

Our key verse sits within this utterly glorious passage in chapter 5. Let’s look at its context.

Chapter 5 opens with Paul speaking of our earthly tent — this perishable body — which will be taken down, while God has prepared for us an eternal house in heaven (2 Corinthians 5:1). Then he says:

“For we must all be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ that each one may receive the things in the body according to what he has done, whether good or bad” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

Brothers and sisters, notice this: before Paul speaks of the “new creation,” he speaks of “what he has done.” Our doing will be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ.

Then Paul states the driving force behind this letter:

“For the love of Christ constrains us; because we judge thus, that one died for all, therefore all died. He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15).

“No longer live to themselves” — brothers and sisters, this phrase is the most precise footnote to “selflessness” in the 321 vision. The old self is centred on self; the new self is centred on Christ.

Next comes verse 16: “Therefore we know no one after the flesh from now on.” The viewpoint has changed. And only then comes verse 17 —

“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

The Greek of this verse well repays a closer look.

“New creation” is καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) in the original — literally “a new creation.” The Chinese Union Version renders it “a newly created person,” but in the Greek there is in fact no word for “person.” The word κτίσις means “creation,” “that which is created”; Paul uses the same word in Romans 8:19, where “the creation” waits with eager expectation for the children of God to be revealed. So Paul is not merely saying “you as a person have improved,” but “a new creation has taken place” — a miracle on the same scale as Genesis 1, God saying once again, “Let there be light.”

Even more important is the word “new.” Greek has two words that are both translated “new”: νέος (neos) is new in time — fresh out of the oven, just born; καινός (kainos) is new in nature — a wholly new kind, a wholly new quality. Paul uses καινός. Brothers and sisters, in Christ you are not “a slightly newer old self”; you are “an entirely new kind of person.”

“The old things have passed away” is ἀρχαῖα παρῆλθεν in the Greek. “The old things” refers to the old, original way of things; “have passed away” means gone by, departed. And “have become new” uses the perfect tense, γέγονεν καινά — denoting something that happened in the past whose effect continues into the present.

Brothers and sisters, there is a vitally important order here: first “the accomplished fact,” then “the life to be lived out.” You don’t become a new creation by forming habits; it is because you already are a new creation that, relying on the Holy Spirit, you live this new life out through new habits.

This is where today’s lesson stands. We do not earn new life by our behaviour; we live out, through each day’s doing, the new life that has already been given to us.

sections.heading: 1. Doing Forms Habits; Habits Form a Life
sections.html:
Doing something once is an action; doing it repeatedly is a habit; a long-held habit becomes character

Brothers and sisters, please remember these three steps:

Doing something once is an action. Doing it repeatedly is a habit. A long-held habit becomes character — and character is the shape of your life.

So: those who often obey become obedient people; those who often complain become complaining people; those who often love become loving people. This is not a motivational slogan; it is a law of Scripture:

“Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life” (Galatians 6:7–8).

Between sowing and reaping lies a stretch of time. That is why we so easily deceive ourselves — because what we sow today is not reaped today. But the day of harvest will certainly come.

The Bible gives two beautiful examples of “habit” that deserve to be remembered all our lives.

The first is Daniel. When King Darius’s decree had been issued and the lions’ den lay open and waiting, this is what Scripture records:

“When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before” (Daniel 6:10).

Brothers and sisters, notice the last words: “as he did before.” Daniel did not decide to pray at the moment the crisis struck. Through decades of days without any crisis, he had knelt down three times a day, three times a day. When the crisis came, he didn’t need to make a decision; he only needed to do as he always did.

A habit is the thing you do automatically under pressure.

The second example is our Lord himself:

“He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. He entered, as was his custom, into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and stood up to read” (Luke 4:16).

“As was his custom” is κατὰ τὸ εἰωθὸς αὐτῷ in the Greek, meaning “according to his usual habit.” Brothers and sisters, even the Son of God, in his days on earth, had spiritual habits. Thirty years in Nazareth, every Sabbath, the same synagogue, the same road. When the day of his public ministry came, that habit became the pulpit from which he announced his mission.

Confirmation from Neuroscience: A Path Worn by Walking

Modern brain science also bears witness to this truth. In his 1949 book The Organization of Behavior, the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb put forward the famous Hebbian theory, which later generations have boiled down to one sentence: neurons that fire together wire together. That is, when two groups of neurons are repeatedly active at the same time, the connection between them grows stronger.

In other words, every time you repeat a choice, you are deepening a pathway in your brain.

It is like a patch of grass. When the first person walks across, the grass is merely bent. When a hundred people walk across, the grass begins to lie flat. When a thousand people walk across, a footpath appears. When ten thousand people walk across, that footpath becomes a route you can walk without thinking, with your eyes closed.

Brothers and sisters, the reactions in your life — “the moment I’m angry I say harsh things,” “the moment I’m tense I want to run,” “the moment I’m misunderstood I go cold and silent” — were not born in you; they were worn in by walking. In the same way, “the moment something happens I pray first,” “the moment I’m wronged I bless first,” “the moment I wake I draw near to God first” — these too can be worn in by walking.

There is a saying often attributed to Aristotle: “We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.” On closer inspection, the saying actually comes from the American historian Will Durant’s The Story of Philosophy (1926), as his interpretation of Aristotle’s ethics. But the truth it expresses agrees entirely with the Bible: the quality of a life is hidden in repetition.

A 321 insight: a changed life comes not from one breakthrough but from sustained choices

In the 321 vision we speak of a fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

But notice: between “mindset” and “life” there is a bridge, and the name of that bridge is “Repetition.” The seventh of the eight stages is Repetition. Without repetition, a mindset is mere knowledge; with repetition, a mindset grows into life.

So your life now is the accumulation of past habits; your life in future is the accumulation of today’s choices.

Brothers and sisters, if you want to change your life, start changing your daily “doing.”

sections.heading: 2. Replace “Fighting It” with “Cultivating”
sections.html:
Why “Don’t” Never Seems to Work

Brothers and sisters, let’s be honest about something. Many people try to change their lives by “fighting” — by grappling with their faults:

Don’t get angry. Don’t be lazy. Don’t be negative. Don’t look at those things any more. Don’t say those things any more.

We grit our teeth, cover the walls with notes, make solemn vows. And the result? Usually a great deal of pain, and nothing that lasts. Why?

In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner and his colleagues carried out an experiment that is now very famous. They asked participants to say aloud everything that came into their heads for five minutes, with one condition: they must not think of a white bear, and if they did, they were to ring a bell. The result? Those told “don’t think of a white bear” rang the bell far more often than usual. More striking still, when the ban was lifted and they were allowed to think of white bears, their thoughts of white bears rebounded — they thought of them more often than people who had been allowed to think of white bears from the start. Wegner called this phenomenon “ironic process theory.”

Brothers and sisters, this experiment gives us a very important reminder: mere suppression doesn’t bring freedom; mere prohibition actually increases the weight of that thought in the heart.

Paul saw the spiritual version of this long ago. Speaking of rules that treat the body harshly, he said:

“These things indeed appear like wisdom in self-imposed worship, humility, and severity to the body; but aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh” (Colossians 2:23).

“Not of any value” — what a severe verdict. Fighting the flesh in our own strength looks very spiritual, but it is of no value at all.

God’s Way: Put Off, and Put On

So what is God’s way? To replace wrong doing with right doing.

“that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Ephesians 4:22–24).

Brothers and sisters, look at this set of verbs: put away, be renewed, put on. Paul never stops at “put away.” Nobody takes off dirty clothes and then just stands there naked; you take off in order to put on.

Paul even gives a very concrete example:

“Let him who stole steal no more; but rather let him labor, producing with his hands something that is good, that he may have something to give to him who has need” (Ephesians 4:28).

Notice that this change has three layers. From “stealing” to “steal no more” — that is only stopping. From “steal no more” to “producing with his hands something that is good” — that is replacing. From “producing with his hands something good” to “having something to give to him who has need” — that is turning it right around. Hands that once took from others now supply what others need. This is not suppression; this is transformation.

So: form the habit of rising early to replace rising late; form the habit of thanksgiving to replace complaining; form the habit of obedience to replace rebellion; form the habit of blessing to replace criticising.

“Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).

You Needn’t Chase Out the Darkness — Just Let the Light In

Brothers and sisters, picture a basement that has been lived in for thirty years, dark and damp. How do you drive the darkness out? Sweep it with a broom? Shovel it into bags? Beat it with a stick? Darkness doesn’t leave because you hate it.

But the moment you reach out and switch on a lamp, the darkness vanishes in an instant — not driven out by force, but replaced by light.

“For you were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light” (Ephesians 5:8).

So the secret Paul gives is this:

“But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts” (Romans 13:14).

The order is: first put on Christ, and only then make no provision for the flesh. Put on the light first, and the darkness has nowhere left to stand.

A 321 Insight: Selflessness Is Not Suppressing Yourself but Letting Jesus In

Brothers and sisters, this is the most central — and most often misunderstood — point in the 321 vision.

“Selflessness” does not mean strangling yourself, treating your body harshly, or standing in front of the mirror saying a hundred times, “There is no me.” That is just another form of “relying on self” — using the strength of “self” to fight “self,” and in the end both sides lose.

Selflessness is letting Jesus in, and letting Jesus be King.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

“It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Brothers and sisters, this sentence turns the whole direction around. It isn’t that I strive to become better; it is that Christ lives himself out in me. Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus.

So stop wrestling with yourself alone in the dark. This morning, please switch on the light.

sections.heading: 3. Three Keys to Forming Habits: Quickly, Often, Constantly
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we have seen that to change our lives we must change our habits, and to change our habits we must replace fighting with cultivating. So what do we actually do? Scripture and experience together give us three key words: quickly, often, constantly.

First: Do It Quickly — When God Moves You, Act

“I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments” (Psalm 119:60).

Brothers and sisters, look at these two expressions: “hurry” and “not delay.” The psalmist describes his response to God’s word as being like someone who hears an alarm and springs up at once.

Why quickly? Because a prompting has a shelf life.

When the Holy Spirit prompts us, the heart is soft and the door is open. But if we say “in a minute,” “tomorrow,” “this week is rather busy,” that softness slowly hardens and that door slowly closes. It isn’t that the Holy Spirit has withdrawn the prompting; it is that our hearts have grown dull.

“When you vow a vow to God, don’t defer to pay it; for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay that which you vow” (Ecclesiastes 5:4).

The most frightening thing about procrastination is not that the thing goes undone, but that it trains our hearts into “the habit of disobedience.” Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: procrastination is itself a habit. Every time you say “in a minute” to a prompting, you are deepening that “in a minute” neural pathway.

Conversely, obedience can become a reflex too. I know a sister who set herself a rule: whenever someone’s name surfaces in her heart, within three minutes she prays for that person or sends them a message of blessing. No weighing it up, no hesitating, no waiting until she feels like it. Three years on, she has become the greatest encourager in her whole small group. She says, “I’m not more spiritual than anyone else. I just don’t give myself time to think about it.”

Obedience belongs to the present moment. Because the prompting God gives is prepared for “now.”

Second: Do It Often — Repeat It, and Look for Chances to Do It

“But refuse profane and old wives’ fables. Exercise yourself toward godliness. For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come” (1 Timothy 4:7–8).

The word “exercise” is the Greek γυμνάζω (gymnazō), the root of the English word “gymnasium.” Paul is saying: train in godliness the way an athlete trains the body.

Brothers and sisters, no athlete ever got strong by “understanding the principles.” You can learn every training theory by heart, and your muscles won’t grow by a single gram. Muscle recognises only one thing: repetitions.

The writer of Hebrews uses the same root:

“But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil” (Hebrews 5:14).

“Exercised” here is γεγυμνασμένα in the Greek — the perfect passive participle of “to train,” meaning “having been trained and continuing in a trained state.” The ability to discern good and evil is not an inborn instinct; it is trained.

So “do it often” means not just passively waiting for opportunities, but actively looking for them.

Want to form the habit of blessing people? Then deliberately find three people to bless every day. Want to form the habit of gratitude? Then count five things before you sleep each night. Want to form the habit of sharing the gospel? Then open your mouth at least once a week.

In 1885 the nineteenth-century psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus published his famous research on the forgetting curve. Experimenting on himself, he found that newly learned material, if not reviewed, is lost in large amounts within a very short time; but with each review, the rate of forgetting slows a little. Brothers and sisters, spiritual training is the same. Not because God’s word loses its power, but because our hearts slip away. So it must be often — coming back to the same thing again and again.

Third: Do It Constantly — Without a Break, Keep On Doing It

“He also spoke a parable to them that they must always pray, and not give up” (Luke 18:1).

“Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up” (Galatians 6:9).

The early church gives us a picture of “constantly”:

“They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer” (Acts 2:42).

“Continued steadfastly” — not three months of blazing zeal, but a lifetime of a steady, quiet stream.

Brothers and sisters, the greatest enemy of the spiritual life is often not great sin but short-lived enthusiasm. Ten chapters of the Bible today, none at all tomorrow; two hours of prayer every day this week, not a word the whole of next week. Great highs and great lows look very fervent, but they are the hardest to build anything on.

In a study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, the psychologist Phillippa Lally of University College London and her colleagues followed ninety-six participants for twelve weeks to see how long it takes for a new behaviour to become automatic. They found that the median was about sixty-six days, with huge individual differences — anywhere from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. An even more important finding was this: missing the occasional day did not ruin the whole process of forming the habit.

Brothers and sisters, both points are worth remembering. First, don’t assume that twenty-one days guarantees success; forming a habit usually takes longer than you think — so set your heart for a long campaign. Second, if you miss a day, don’t give up; what is truly fatal is not falling, but not getting up again after you fall.

“for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity” (Proverbs 24:16).

How the Three Keys Divide the Work

Let’s look at the three keys side by side:

Quickly breaks through procrastination. It deals with “the difficulty of starting.”

Often builds skill. It deals with “not knowing how.”

Constantly forms habit. It deals with “not being able to keep it up.”

You can’t do without any of the three. Quickly without often is a passing impulse; often without constantly is a season of zeal; constantly without quickly is a slow, half-hearted going through the motions.

For many years Ann Graybiel, a neuroscientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, has studied the relationship between the brain’s basal ganglia and habit. Her team found that when a sequence of actions is performed repeatedly, the brain packages them into a single “chunk”; after that, a single starting cue is enough for the whole sequence to run automatically. That is why an experienced driver can drive and hold a conversation at the same time — the whole set of actions has already been packaged.

Brothers and sisters, the spiritual life can be packaged in the same way. Once “open my eyes in the morning — sit up — open my Bible” has been repeated until it becomes a single chunk, you no longer need to negotiate with yourself every morning.

A 321 Insight: Change Needs Repetition, and Repetition Brings Stability

In the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — Repetition comes seventh.

Why does Repetition come so late? Because repetition is not the starting point; it is the last stretch of road before the harvest. Many people stop after Implementation, and after a single failure declare that they can’t do it. But Evaluation, Correction and Repetition exist precisely so that we can get back on the road after failing.

Quickly, often, constantly — in the end it comes down to one sentence: let right doing happen in you over and over again, until it no longer takes gritted teeth and has become your very nature.

sections.heading: 4. In Christ, Live Out the Life of a New Creation
sections.html:
What does “in Christ” mean?

Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to our key verse:

“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

The centre of gravity of the whole verse lies in its opening words: “in Christ.” In Greek it is ἐν Χριστῷ (en Christō), a phrase that appears more than a hundred times in Paul’s letters and lies at the very heart of his understanding of salvation.

So what does it mean to be “in Christ”?

It is not an abstract position, nor a mystical feeling. The Lord Jesus himself explained it most clearly:

“Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me” (John 15:4).

“I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

And what, concretely, does “remaining in him” consist of? The Lord goes on to say:

“If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free” (John 8:31–32).

The apostle John puts it even more directly:

“he who says he remains in him ought himself also to walk just like he walked” (1 John 2:6).

Brothers and sisters, so to be “in Christ” is to live in Christ’s word and walk in Christ’s truth.

Walk in the truth, and you are in Christ; leave the truth, and you are not in Christ. This does not mean our salvation can be cancelled by our behaviour. It means that being joined to the life of Christ will always show itself in “doing.” If a branch really is joined to the vine, the sap of the vine will certainly flow into the branch, and the fruit will certainly grow.

A New Creation, Not an Improvement

Brothers and sisters, please distinguish two things: improvement and new creation.

Improvement is taking something old, repairing and patching it, and making it look a little better. New creation is the appearing of an entirely new kind of thing.

Nature offers a wonderful witness. When a caterpillar forms its chrysalis, it does not slowly sprout wings. Biologists have found that inside the chrysalis the tissues largely break down, and the butterfly’s body is then built anew from “imaginal discs” that had lain dormant all along. What emerges from the chrysalis is not a caterpillar that can fly, but a butterfly — a wholly new structure, wholly new organs, a wholly new way of life.

Paul says you are καινὴ κτίσις, a new creation. Brothers and sisters, what God is doing in you is not a renovation project; it is a rebuilding project.

So if we are already a new creation, why are we still weak, still stumbling, still just as we used to be?

Because new life needs new habits to carry it.

Let me give you a picture. A man moves into a brand-new house — new floors, new walls, windows looking out on mountains and light. But he brings with him every broken sofa, mouldy cardboard box and dead appliance from his old home, and piles them into every room. Tell me: is the house new? Yes. Does living there feel like living in a new house? Not in the least.

Brothers and sisters, that is the state of many people who have been believers for years. Their standing is new; their habits are old.

So Paul says, “The old things have passed away.” We must let old habits pass away, let old thinking pass away, let old behaviour pass away — not by gritting our teeth, but by replacing them, one by one, with new choices.

A 321 Insight: The Old Self Is Self-Centred, the New Self Is Selfless

In the 321 vision we say: the old self is “self-centred,” the new self is “selfless.”

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. In the Garden of Eden our first parents wanted to be “like God, knowing good and evil” — that is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place. Pride is the root of every problem.

Selflessness is not having no self; it is no longer making self the centre. It is not being annihilated; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus. Because when I no longer live for myself, Christ lives in me; when my cup is emptied, God’s rivers come flooding in.

So every act of right doing is living out the new self.

When you keep choosing right seeing, right listening, right thinking, right speaking and right doing, you will become more and more like Jesus. Not because you have sculpted yourself well, but because the form of Jesus within you is able more and more to shine out through you.

“But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

“From glory to glory” — brothers and sisters, this is a process, layer upon layer. And the vessel that carries this process is our everyday habits.

sections.heading: 5. The Five Basics: Seeing, Listening, Thinking, Speaking and Doing
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the nurturing of life follows a complete process, which this series calls the five basics:

Seeing is taking in; listening is receiving; thinking is digesting; speaking is confirming; doing is living it out.

Not one of these five steps can be left out. Let’s look at them one by one.

Seeing: Guard Your Eyes

“I will set no vile thing before my eyes. I hate the deeds of faithless men. They will not cling to me” (Psalm 101:3).

David says, “I will set no vile thing before my eyes.” Brothers and sisters, the eyes are the gateway to the heart. In this generation every mobile phone is a door, opened and shut hundreds of times a day. We can’t avoid looking at the world, but we can decide what we allow to stay before our eyes for long.

Listening: Tune Your Ears Rightly

“So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17).

Faith comes by hearing. Whatever you listen to over the long term, you will believe over the long term. If what we feed our ears every day is complaining, fear and criticism, yet we hope faith will grow in our hearts, it simply cannot happen.

Thinking: Set Your Thoughts on the Right Things

“Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things” (Philippians 4:8).

“Think about” means active, sustained meditation. Thinking is the process of digestion — chewing the truth we have heard, absorbing it, making it our own flesh and blood.

Speaking: Say the Truth Out Loud

“For with the heart, one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation” (Romans 10:10).

Speaking is confirming. When you say the truth out loud, it is as if you have signed your name to it before yourself and others. Say something three times, and it begins to become yours.

Doing: Let the Truth Enter Your Life

“But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22).

Brothers and sisters, notice James’s words: “deluding your own selves.” When we only hear and never do, the chief victim is not anyone else but ourselves — because we mistakenly think that “I understand it” means “I have it.”

The Lord Jesus puts it even more solemnly:

“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock” (Matthew 7:24).

That one step between hearing and doing is the dividing line between rock and sand.

In fact, as far back as Joshua’s time, God compressed these five basics into a single verse:

“This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success” (Joshua 1:8).

Shall not depart from your mouth — that is speaking. Meditate on it day and night — that is thinking. Observe to do — that is doing. And “this book of the law” must first be seen and heard. All five basics are there.

Without Doing, Everything Stays in the Head

Brothers and sisters, when this fivefold cycle keeps running, it produces habits; habits produce character; character becomes life.

But if the last step, “doing,” is missing, what happens?

Something very dangerous: we become people who “know a lot but haven’t changed.” The more messages we hear, the harder our hearts become; because every time we hear and do not do, we are training our hearts to “feel nothing at God’s word.”

A 321 Insight: From Mindset to Life, from Life to Daily Living

The fivefold change of 321 is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

Seeing, listening and thinking chiefly change our mindset; speaking and doing carry that mindset into life and daily living. This is not a single moment but a process.

Brothers and sisters, as long as you stay in this cycle, you will certainly change. Because you are not turning this wheel on your own; the Holy Spirit is at work within you.

“For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Let Jesus Be King in the Small Things of Every Day
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s place what we have learned today into the overall blueprint of 321.

The Three Foundations Are Three Daily Habits

Jesus is my role model — so every day I ask: how would Jesus handle this?

The Bible is my standard — so every day I ask: what does God’s word say?

The Holy Spirit is my guide — so every day I ask: what is the Holy Spirit prompting me to do right now?

Brothers and sisters, notice: these three foundations are not three slogans; they are three questions — and questions can become habits. When these three questions become the reaction that surfaces in you automatically every day, the Three Foundations have moved from mindset into life.

The Two Core Values Set the Direction of Every Choice

Let Jesus be King — in every small choice, who has the final say?

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when it is done, who gets the applause?

What makes habits both frightening and precious is that they are automatic. And what is automatic most clearly reveals “who is King.” Because when I have no time to think, my reaction gives away who my real king is.

Brothers and sisters, so forming spiritual habits is really handing over the kingship to Jesus, inch by inch.

The Goal: Establish God’s System

One person’s habits become a family’s culture; a family’s culture becomes a community’s system.

When the people in a small group have grown used to obeying at once, used to blessing one another, used to praying before speaking, that small group is no longer just running activities; it is establishing God’s system.

The Fivefold Change and the Shift in Viewpoint

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Today’s lesson falls right on the seams between three links of that chain: “mindset → life → daily living.” Habit is the conveyor belt that carries mindset into daily living.

Then there is the shift in viewpoint: from man’s to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly.

Brothers and sisters, man’s viewpoint looks at habits and sees only “self-discipline”; God’s viewpoint looks at habits and sees “shaping.” The earthly viewpoint asks, “Is this efficient?” The heavenly viewpoint asks, “Is this like Jesus?” The temporary viewpoint sees only this one time; the eternal viewpoint sees a whole life that will be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ.

The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

The 920 practice reminds us: everyone who is in a relationship with us is our “2”; and before every “2” we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control — which of these nine does not grow in repeated relationships? Patience doesn’t grow in a room where no one provokes you; gentleness doesn’t grow in days when no one contradicts you.

So God puts your “2” beside you not to make things hard for you, but to make you whole. Every time you choose right doing before that “2,” you are bearing fruit.

And 235 relationships remind us: don’t form habits alone. Become a “2” with a selfless spiritual companion, keeping each other company and reviewing together; with spiritual parents leading you and spiritual children following, become a “3”; and finally become part of a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team, building together.

This is also the last of the eight stages — Multiplication. A habit that stays only with you is good; a habit that can be passed on to someone else has become the multiplication of life.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Building Good Spiritual Habits
sections.html: Brothers and sisters, there are five practices today. We will use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to deepen them one by one.

sections.heading: 1. Set One Spiritual Habit, Starting with Twenty-One Days
sections.html:
Choose one habit you want to form: praying every day, reading the Bible every day, blessing someone every day. Practise it for twenty-one days in a row, and lay the foundation first.

Information: Today you have already heard it — doing becomes habit, and habit becomes life.

Revelation: Be quiet for three minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to show you “which habit God most wants me to form in this season.” Don’t choose five at once; choose just one.

Conviction: Write it down as a concrete sentence. Don’t write “I will pray more”; write “Every morning at 6:30 I will pray for fifteen minutes.”

Implementation: Start today. Don’t wait for next Monday.

Evaluation: Each night, put a tick or a cross — just record it, don’t condemn yourself.

Correction: If you miss two days in a row, don’t give up; adjust. Perhaps the time is wrong, or the goal is too big. Cutting fifteen minutes down to five is better than going back to zero.

Repetition: Don’t stop after twenty-one days. As we said earlier, the University College London study found that the median time for a habit to become automatic was about sixty-six days. Twenty-one days is the start, not the finish line.

Multiplication: Invite a brother or sister to do it with you, and report to each other.

sections.heading: 2. Practise Immediate Obedience
sections.html:
When God reminds you: do it straight away — no delaying, no excuses. Let obedience become your reflex.

Brothers and sisters, the key to this practice is shortening the distance between “prompting” and “action.”

Set yourself a rule: within five minutes. Within five minutes, make that phone call; within five minutes, say that apology out loud; within five minutes, pray for the name that has surfaced in your heart.

“I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments” (Psalm 119:60).

sections.heading: 3. Replace Old Habits with New Actions
sections.html:
When an old habit shows up, don’t just stop — replace it straight away with a new action. For example: when you want to complain, give thanks at once.

Prepare a few “replacement plans” for yourself right now:

When you want to complain, count three things you are thankful for.

When you want to criticise, pray one sentence for that person.

When you want to scroll on your phone, open your Bible and read a passage.

When you want to lose your temper, first close your mouth and take a deep breath, then speak a word of blessing.

Brothers and sisters, this is the principle of Ephesians 4:28: steal no more, but rather labour, and give to him who has need. Stop, then replace, then turn it right around.

sections.heading: 4. Build a System of Small Daily Changes
sections.html:
Don’t chase one big change; go a little each day: one right choice, one act of obedience, adding up to a changed life.

Tie your habit to something you already do. For example: after brushing your teeth, pray for three minutes; when you get into the car, say one word of thanks first; before you switch on the computer, read a verse of Scripture.

Because if a new habit has no fixed place, it will always be fighting your busyness for time; once it has a place, it will grow by itself.

sections.heading: 5. Examine Each Day Through 321
sections.html:
Ask yourself each day: was my seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing today of God, or of myself?

Brothers and sisters, I suggest you take two minutes each night before you sleep for a “five questions” self-examination:

What did my eyes see today? What did my ears hear today? What did my mind think about today? What did my mouth say today? What did my hands do today?

Then after each one, ask: was this letting Jesus be King, or letting myself be king?

Don’t condemn yourself; just realign with Christ. Because condemnation makes us hide from God, while his light brings us back before him.

A Gentle Reminder

Habits aren’t formed in a day, but they are being formed every day.

Don’t overlook small choices; small choices determine the big direction.

Don’t wait for change to happen; let change happen every day.

Brothers and sisters, put your focus in the right place: the focus is not on “how good I’m going to become,” but on “whether I made the right choice today.”

Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances.

When you keep on choosing, life naturally changes.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, a changed life comes not from a burst of passion but from daily habits.

When you keep choosing right doing, you are shaping a new you. But please remember — this new you is not built by effort; it is Christ living himself out in you.

We are not building a statue of ourselves; we are moving aside the things that block the light, so that the Lord who lives within us can shine out more clearly with every passing day.

The writer of Lamentations, amid the deepest ruins, saw one thing:

“It is because of Yahweh’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his compassion doesn’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:22–23).

“They are new every morning.” Brothers and sisters, God’s loving kindness comes every morning, so our obedience can come every morning too. He doesn’t ask us to pay the cost of a whole lifetime at once; he only asks us to hand over today, today.

So from today on, through each day’s small obediences, live out a life that is more and more like Jesus.

Let Jesus be King of your mornings, let Jesus be King in your office, let Jesus be King in your home, let Jesus be King in that moment when you are most weary and no one is watching.

May all the glory go to our Lord Jesus Christ.

keyVerses: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)
declarations: In the name of the Lord Jesus, I declare:

I choose right doing and form right habits.

Every day I obey, every day I grow, every day I am renewed.
My life will become more and more like Jesus.
Amen.
practices: Set one spiritual habit (daily prayer, Bible reading or blessing someone) and practise it for twenty-one days in a row.
Practise immediate obedience: when the Holy Spirit prompts you, do it today — don’t wait for next Monday.
Keep company and review together with a spiritual companion, and pass the habit on to someone else.
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
Thank you, because you have already made me a new creation. I did not earn this; you gave it to me freely.
Lord, forgive me for so often waiting for one big breakthrough while despising the small choices of each day; forgive me for fighting myself in my own strength instead of inviting you in to be King.
Help me, from today, to obey you quickly, to train often, and to persevere constantly. When I fall, lift me up, and keep me from losing heart.
Holy Spirit, remind me each day of my seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, so that every one of my habits becomes a vessel that glorifies you.
Lord, may you live in me, and may my life become more and more like you.

Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17) Please share: what “old thing” in your life has God recently been reminding you to let pass away? blog.title: You Don’t Lack Resolve — You Lack a Habit

blocks.x: Form Habits, Live as a New Creation

There was a brother who wrote down the same three goals at the start of every year: read the Bible every day, exercise every day, stop losing his temper with his wife. He wrote them for eleven years. In the twelfth year he finally understood something — he had never lacked resolve; what he lacked was “doing.”
We often imagine that a changed life is a matter of “one day.” That one conference, that one tearful prayer. Yet three weeks later, we are back to our old selves.
It isn’t that the meeting wasn’t real, or that the prayer wasn’t heard. The problem is that we mistook being “moved” for being “changed.”
Being moved happens in a day. Being changed happens every day.
A Habit Is the Thing You Do Automatically Under Pressure
Life is not changed in an instant; life is shaped through repeated choices.

Doing something once is an action; doing it repeatedly is a habit; a long-held habit becomes character. So those who often obey become obedient people; those who often complain become complaining people.

One of the most moving habits in the Bible is hidden in four words. When the king’s decree had been signed and the lions’ den lay open and waiting, Scripture records that Daniel “kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before” (Daniel 6:10).
As he did before. He did not decide to pray at the moment the crisis struck; through decades of days without any crisis, he had knelt down three times a day, three times a day.
You Needn’t Chase Out the Darkness — Just Let the Light In
Many people try to change by “fighting it”: don’t get angry, don’t be lazy, don’t be negative. The result is usually a great deal of pain, and nothing that lasts.

In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner carried out a famous experiment: he asked participants not to think of a white bear for five minutes. Those who were forbidden actually thought of it more — and once the ban was lifted, their thoughts rebounded. He called it “ironic process theory.”
Paul saw the spiritual version of this long ago. He said that rules which treat the body harshly “aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh” (Colossians 2:23).

God’s way is not suppression but replacement: put off the old self, and put on the new. Form the habit of rising early to replace rising late; form the habit of thanksgiving to replace complaining; form the habit of blessing to replace criticising.

Picture a basement that has been lived in for thirty years. How do you drive the darkness out? You can’t sweep it away. But the moment you reach out and switch on a lamp, the darkness vanishes in an instant.

And to make right doing a habit, there are three keys: quickly, often, constantly. Quickly — act as soon as God moves you, because a prompting has a shelf life. Often — do it repeatedly, and actively look for chances. Constantly — without a break, building up day by day. A 2010 study by Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London found that the median time for a new behaviour to become automatic was about sixty-six days — and that missing the occasional day did not ruin the whole process. So if you fall, get up.
The New You Is Christ Living Himself Out
“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)
“New creation” in the original literally means “a new creation.” What God is doing in you is not a renovation project; it is a rebuilding project.

So why do we still so often live like the old self? Because new life needs new habits to carry it. It’s like a man who moves into a brand-new house but brings with him every broken sofa and mouldy cardboard box from his old home. The house is new, but living there doesn’t feel new at all.
Their standing is new; their habits are old — that is the state of many people who have been believers for years.

So from today, just replace one piece of furniture. After brushing your teeth, pray for three minutes; when you want to complain, count three things you are thankful for; when someone’s name surfaces in your heart, pray for them within five minutes.
You don’t become a new creation by forming habits; it is because you already are a new creation that, relying on him, you can live this new life out through each day’s small obediences.
The focus is not on “how good I’m going to become,” but on “whether I made the right choice today.”
Reflection: This week, which habit does God most want you to form? What is the first small step you could take today?
