Context: no longer living to themselves
First the accomplished fact, then the life to be lived out
Key points:
1. Author and date: Paul wrote 2 Corinthians around AD 56 from Macedonia (2:13, 7:5).
2. Recipients and setting: Corinth was the capital of Achaia and a busy trading port; the church was rich in gifts yet riddled with problems.
3. Context: 5:10, receiving before the judgment seat of Christ “according to what he has done”; 5:14–15, “no longer live to themselves”.
4. Original: καινὴ κτίσις is “a new creation”; καινός is new in nature, not νέος, new in time; “have become new” is in the perfect tense.
5. Order: first the accomplished fact, then the life to be lived out — we don’t earn new life by habits; we live out new life through new habits.

brief21.title: Point 1a: Three Steps
notes: Slide text:
Doing it once is an action,
doing it repeatedly is a habit,
a long-held habit becomes character.
Your life now is the sum of past habits.
Key points:
1. Three steps: doing something once is an action, doing it repeatedly is a habit, a long-held habit becomes character.
2. Examples: those who often obey become obedient people; those who often complain become complaining people; those who often love become loving people.
3. Scripture: Galatians 6:7–8, sow to the flesh and reap corruption; sow to the Spirit and reap eternal life.
4. Science: Donald Hebb, The Organization of Behavior (1949) — neurons that fire together wire together.
5. Illustration: a footpath across a patch of grass; once ten thousand people have walked it, it’s a route you could walk with your eyes closed.

brief21.title: Point 1b: As He Did Before
notes: Slide text:
Daniel knelt to pray three times a day,
“As he did before” (Daniel 6:10)
Jesus went to the synagogue “as was his custom”
Luke 4:16
Key points:
1. Daniel 6:10: the decree had been signed, yet he still knelt to pray three times a day, “as he did before”.
2. Key point: the habit was formed through decades without crisis; when the crisis came he didn’t need to decide, only to do as he always did.
3. Luke 4:16: Jesus went to the synagogue “as was his custom”, literally “according to his usual habit”.
4. Application: even the Son of God had spiritual habits on earth; thirty years of habit became the pulpit from which he announced his mission.
5. 321 insight: the bridge from mindset to life is called Repetition, the seventh of the eight stages.

brief21.title: Point 2a: Why “Don’t” Doesn’t Work
notes: Slide text:
Don’t get angry, don’t be lazy, don’t be negative
The more you suppress, the more it rebounds.
“Not of any value against the indulgence of the flesh.”
Colossians 2:23
Key points:
1. Be honest: fighting ourselves with “don’t get angry, don’t be lazy, don’t be negative” is usually painful and doesn’t last.
2. Psychology: Daniel Wegner’s 1987 white bear experiment — those forbidden to think of a white bear thought of it more, and rebounded once the ban was lifted; he called it ironic process theory.
3. Scripture: Colossians 2:23, severity to the body is “not of any value against the indulgence of the flesh”.
4. Conclusion: mere suppression doesn’t bring freedom; mere prohibition increases the weight of that thought.

brief21.title: Point 2b: Put Off, and Put On
notes: Slide text:
Put off the old self, put on the new
Ephesians 4:22–24
No need to keep fighting the darkness;
just let the light in.
Key points:
1. God’s way: Ephesians 4:22–24 — put away, be renewed, put on; you take off in order to put on.
2. Concrete example: Ephesians 4:28 — steal no more (stopping), produce something good with his hands (replacing), give to him who has need (turning it right around).
3. Replacement list: rising early for rising late, thanksgiving for complaining, obedience for rebellion, blessing for criticising.
4. Illustration: the darkness of a thirty-year-old basement can’t be swept out, but vanishes when you switch on a light; Ephesians 5:8, walk as children of light.
5. 321 insight: selflessness is not suppressing yourself but letting Jesus in (Galatians 2:20).

brief21.title: Point 3a: Do It Quickly
notes: Slide text:
When God moves you, act;
no delay, no hesitation.
“I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.”
Psalm 119:60
Key points:
1. Scripture: Psalm 119:60, “I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.”
2. Reason: a prompting has a shelf life; say “in a minute” and the heart slowly hardens.
3. Add: Ecclesiastes 5:4, when you vow a vow to God, don’t defer to pay it.
4. Reminder: procrastination is itself a habit; every “in a minute” deepens that pathway.

5. Illustration: a sister made a rule that whenever someone’s name surfaced in her heart, within three minutes she would pray for them or send a blessing; three years on, she became the greatest encourager in her small group.

brief21.title: Point 3b: Do It Often
notes: Slide text:
“Exercise yourself toward godliness.”
1 Timothy 4:7
“Exercise”: the root of “gymnasium”
Don’t just wait for chances — look for them.
Key points:
1. Scripture: 1 Timothy 4:7–8, “Exercise yourself toward godliness”; “exercise” is γυμνάζω, the root of “gymnasium”.
2. Illustration: no athlete got strong by understanding the principles; muscle recognises only repetitions.
3. Add: Hebrews 5:14, “senses exercised” — in the original, the perfect passive participle of the same root.
4. Data: Hermann Ebbinghaus’s 1885 forgetting curve — without review, much is quickly lost.
5. Application: don’t just wait for chances, look for them — bless three people a day, count five thanks before sleeping.

brief21.title: Point 3c: Do It Constantly
notes: Slide text:
No breaks; build up day by day.
“They must always pray, and not give up.”
Luke 18:1
Not a flash in the pan, but a steady stream.
Key points:
1. Scripture: Luke 18:1, always pray and don’t give up; Galatians 6:9, let’s not be weary in doing good.
2. The early church: Acts 2:42, “they continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching”.
3. Reminder: the greatest enemy of the spiritual life is often not great sin but short-lived enthusiasm.
4. Data: Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London, 2010 — a median of about sixty-six days to become automatic, ranging from 18 to 254; missing a day doesn’t ruin the whole process.
5. Add: Ann Graybiel (MIT) — repeated behaviour is packaged into “chunks” in the basal ganglia and runs automatically.

brief21.title: Point 4a: What Is “In Christ”?
notes: Slide text:
It is living in Christ’s word,
it is walking in Christ’s truth.
“Ought himself also to walk just like he walked.”
1 John 2:6
Key points:
1. The centre of gravity is “in Christ”, the Greek ἐν Χριστῷ, appearing more than a hundred times in Paul’s letters.
2. Scripture interpreting Scripture: John 15:4–5, remain in me; apart from me you can do nothing.
3. John 8:31–32: if you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples.
4. 1 John 2:6: he who says he remains in him ought himself also to walk just like he walked.
5. Conclusion: walk in the truth and you are in Christ; if the branch is truly joined to the vine, the fruit will certainly grow.

brief21.title: Point 4b: New Creation, Not Improvement
notes: Slide text:
Not repairing and patching,
but a wholly new creation.
A new house with old furniture
doesn’t feel like a new house.
Key points:
1. Distinguish improvement from new creation: improvement repairs; new creation is a wholly new kind.
2. Illustration from science: inside the chrysalis the tissues largely break down, and the butterfly is built anew from “imaginal discs” — not a caterpillar that can fly.
3. Illustration: moving into a new house but bringing the broken sofa and mouldy boxes; the house is new, but living there doesn’t feel new at all.
4. Diagnosis: many long-time believers have a new standing but old habits.
5. 321 insight: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; 2 Corinthians 3:18, transformed into the same image from glory to glory.

brief21.title: Point 5a: Seeing, Listening, Thinking
notes: Slide text:
Seeing takes in: no vile thing before my eyes
Listening receives: faith comes by hearing
Thinking digests: think about these things
Philippians 4:8
Key points:
1. Seeing is taking in: Psalm 101:3, “I will set no vile thing before my eyes”; a mobile phone is a door opened and shut hundreds of times a day.
2. Listening is receiving: Romans 10:17, faith comes by hearing; whatever you listen to long-term, you will believe long-term.
3. Thinking is digesting: Philippians 4:8, “think about these things” — active, sustained meditation.
4. Reminder: these three chiefly change our mindset, the first link of the fivefold change.

brief21.title: Point 5b: Speaking and Doing
notes: Slide text:
Speaking confirms: confess with the mouth and be saved
Doing lives it out: be doers, not only hearers
“Deluding your own selves.”
James 1:22
Key points:
1. Speaking is confirming: Romans 10:10, with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation; say something three times and it begins to become yours.
2. Doing is living it out: James 1:22, hearing without doing is “deluding your own selves”.
3. Add: Matthew 7:24, whoever hears and does is like a wise man who built his house on a rock.
4. Joshua 1:8 compresses speaking, thinking and doing into one verse: not depart from your mouth, meditate day and night, observe to do.

brief21.title: Point 5c: From Mindset to Life
notes: Slide text:
Seeing, listening, thinking change the mindset;
speaking and doing carry it into life and living.
Without doing, it all stays in the head;
with doing, truth enters your life.
Key points:
1. As the fivefold cycle keeps running, it produces habits, character and life.
2. Warning: without “doing” we become people who know a lot but haven’t changed; the more we hear, the harder our hearts become.
3. 321: the fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.
4. Encouragement: Philippians 2:13, it is God who works in us both to will and to work — you are not turning this wheel on your own.

brief21.title: Practices (1)
notes: Slide text:
Set one spiritual habit
Pray, read, bless: start with 21 days
Practise immediate obedience
Within five minutes, do it
Key points:
1. Practice 1: choose one habit and write it as a concrete sentence, e.g. “Every morning at 6:30 I will pray for fifteen minutes.”
2. Deepen Practice 1 with the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
3. Reminder: twenty-one days is the start, not the finish line; research shows a median of about sixty-six days.
4. Practice 2: set a “within five minutes” rule to shorten the distance between prompting and action (Psalm 119:60).

brief21.title: Practices (2)
notes: Slide text:
Replace old habits with new actions
Want to complain? Give thanks at once
Build a system of small daily changes
Examine your five basics through 321
Key points:

1. Practice 3: prepare replacement plans — when you want to complain, count three thanks; when you want to criticise, pray for that person; when you want to scroll your phone, read a passage of Scripture.
2. Practice 4: tie the new habit to an existing action — pray after brushing your teeth, give thanks when you get into the car.
3. Practice 5: a two-minute “five questions” self-examination each night — were my seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing letting Jesus be King, or myself?
4. Attitude: don’t condemn yourself; just realign with Christ; condemnation makes us hide from God, while his light brings us back before him.

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
notes: Slide text:
The Three Foundations as three daily questions
Two Core Values: Jesus as King, all glory to him
The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless
Mindset, life, living, relationships, ministry
Key points:
1. The Three Foundations become three daily questions: What would Jesus do? What does God’s word say? What is the Holy Spirit prompting me to do?
2. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; habits are automatic, and what is automatic most clearly reveals who is King.
3. The Goal: one person’s habits become a family’s culture, and a family’s culture becomes God’s system.
4. The 920 practice: live out selflessness before every “2” and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit; patience and gentleness grow in relationships.
5. The 235 relationships: don’t form habits alone; spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, a fivefold-ministry team — leading finally to Multiplication.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: Slide text:
Change comes not from a burst of passion,
but from daily habits.
The new you isn’t built by effort;
it is Christ living himself out in you.
Key points:
1. Return to the lesson’s conclusion: change comes not from a burst of passion but from daily habits.
2. Correct the focus: the new you isn’t built by effort; it is Christ living himself out in you.
3. Scripture: Lamentations 3:22–23, “They are new every morning” — he only asks us to hand over today, today.
4. Call: let Jesus be King of your mornings, your office, your home, and the moments no one sees.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, may I obey quickly, train often,
persevere constantly, and grow more like you.
“They are new every morning.”
Lamentations 3:23
Key points:
1. Lead the brothers and sisters in a prayer of response, in a quiet, warm tone.
2. Confession: we so often wait for one big breakthrough while despising the small choices of each day; we fight ourselves in our own strength.
3. Petition: to obey quickly, train often, persevere constantly; when we fall, ask the Lord to lift us up and keep us from losing heart.
4. Blessing: may the Lord’s loving kindness be new every morning, may your life become more and more like Jesus, and may all the glory go to the Lord.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to the third lesson of “The Right Mindset About Doing”: Form Habits, Live as a New Creation. Our theme verse is 2 Corinthians chapter 5, verse 17: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” Brothers and sisters, we all know this verse well. But today I want to ask a very practical question: if I’m already a new creation, why do I still so often live like the old self? The answer lies in one word — habit.

Brothers and sisters, let me first ask you a question: on which day of your life were you shaped into the person you are today? We often imagine that change is a matter of “one day.” That one conference, that one tearful prayer. But three weeks later? We’re back to our old selves. There was a brother who wrote down the same three goals at the start of every year, for eleven years. Only in the twelfth year did he understand: he didn’t lack resolve; what he lacked was doing. Brothers and sisters, please remember this: being moved happens in a day; being changed happens every day.

2 Corinthians was written around AD 56; Paul wrote it from Macedonia to the Corinthian church, which caused him both great love and great pain. In chapter 5, Paul first says that we must all be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ, to receive according to what we have done; then he says the love of Christ constrains us, so that we “no longer live to ourselves.” Only then comes verse 17. “New creation” in the original means “a new creation” — not “a slightly newer old self,” but an entirely new kind. Brothers and sisters, look carefully at the order: first the accomplished fact, then the life to be lived out. You don’t become a new creation by forming habits; it is because you already are a new creation that you live out, through new habits, the new life he has placed within you.

The first point: doing forms habits; habits form a life. Doing something once is an action; doing it repeatedly is a habit; a long-held habit becomes character. Those who often obey become obedient people; those who often complain become complaining people. Brothers and sisters, remember Daniel? The decree had been issued, the lions’ den lay open, and Scripture says he knelt on his knees to pray three times a day, “as he did before” (Daniel 6:10). He didn’t decide to pray at that moment. Through decades of days without any crisis, he had knelt down three times a day, three times a day. A habit is the thing you do automatically under pressure.

The second point: replace “fighting it” with “cultivating.” Brothers and sisters, we know this approach only too well — don’t get angry, don’t be lazy, don’t be negative. And the result? A great deal of pain, and nothing that lasts. In 1987 the psychologist Daniel Wegner carried out an experiment: he asked people not to think of a white bear. Those who were forbidden actually thought of it more. Paul said long ago that rules which treat the body harshly “aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh” (Colossians 2:23). So what is God’s way? Put off the old self, and put on the new. Brothers and sisters, you needn’t take a broom to sweep away the darkness; you only need to reach out and switch on the light.

The third point: there are three keys to forming habits — quickly, often, constantly. The first is: do it quickly. Psalm 119, verse 60 says: “I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.” Why quickly? Because a prompting has a shelf life. Every time you say “in a minute,” you are practising disobedience. The second is: do it often. Paul says, “Exercise yourself toward godliness” (1 Timothy 4:7). The word “exercise” in the original is the root of “gymnasium.” Brothers and sisters, no athlete ever got strong by understanding the principles. Muscle recognises only one thing: repetitions.

The third is: do it constantly. The Lord Jesus said that we “must always pray, and not give up” (Luke 18:1). The early church “continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching.” Brothers and sisters, the greatest enemy of the spiritual life is often not great sin but short-lived enthusiasm. In 2010 Dr Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London published research showing that for a new behaviour to become automatic took a median of about sixty-six days. But the same study gives us good news too — missing the occasional day does not ruin the whole process. So if you fall, get up. Quickly breaks through procrastination; often builds skill; constantly forms habit.

The fourth point: in Christ, live out the life of a new creation. What does “in Christ” mean? It isn’t a feeling; it’s a way of life. The Lord said: “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples.” John puts it even more directly: he who says he remains in him “ought himself also to walk just like he walked” (1 John 2:6). Walk in the truth, and you are in Christ; leave the truth, and you are not. Brothers and sisters, let me give you a picture: a man moves into a brand-new house but brings every broken sofa and mouldy cardboard box from his old home. Is the house new? Yes. Does it feel new to live in? Not in the least. The standing is new, but the habits are old — that is the state of many of us.

The fifth point: the five basics — seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing. Seeing is taking in, listening is receiving, thinking is digesting, speaking is confirming, doing is living it out. Not one of these five steps can be left out. Joshua 1, verse 8 covers the last three: “shall not depart from your mouth” — that is speaking; “meditate on it day and night” — that is thinking; “observe to do” — that is doing. Brothers and sisters, what happens if the last step is missing? James puts it heavily: those who hear but don’t do are “deluding your own selves.” Without doing, everything stays in the head; with doing, the truth enters your life.

Brothers and sisters, there are five practices today. First, choose one spiritual habit and write it as a concrete sentence — don’t write “I will pray more”; write “Every morning at 6:30 I will pray for fifteen minutes,” and do it for twenty-one days to begin with. Second, practise immediate obedience: give yourself a rule — within five minutes, do it. Third, replace old habits with new actions: when you want to complain, give thanks at once. Fourth, tie the new habit to an old action: after brushing your teeth, pray for three minutes. Fifth, take two minutes each night to ask yourself: today, were my seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing letting Jesus be King, or letting myself be king?

Brothers and sisters, a changed life comes not from a burst of passion but from daily habits. When you keep choosing right doing, you are shaping a new you. But please remember, this new you is not built by effort; it is Christ living himself out in you. Lamentations says: “They are new every morning.” God’s loving kindness comes every morning, so our obedience can come every morning too. He doesn’t ask you to pay the cost of a whole lifetime at once; he only asks you to hand over today, today.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, thank you that you have already made me a new creation. Forgive me for so often waiting for one big breakthrough while despising the small choices of each day. Help me, from today, to obey you quickly, to train often, and to persevere constantly. When I fall, lift me up, and keep me from losing heart. May every one of my habits become a vessel that glorifies you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, may the Lord’s loving kindness be new for you every morning, and may your life become more and more like Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we come together to the third lesson of “The Right Mindset About Doing”: Form Habits, Live as a New Creation. Our theme verse is 2 Corinthians chapter 5, verse 17: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” Brothers and sisters, we all know this verse well; many of us can even recite it. But this morning I want to ask a very practical and very honest question: if I’m already a new creation, why do I still so often live like the old self? The answer lies in one word — habit.

Let me first ask you a question: on which day of your life were you shaped into the person you are today? Brothers and sisters, we often imagine that a changed life is a matter of “one day.” That one conference, that one tearful prayer, that one message that hit home, that one late-night decision. Deep down we all hope: if only I could have one more experience like that, I would be different. But we have all been there — that meeting really was on fire, that prayer really was sincere, and yet three weeks later we were back to our old selves.

So where does the problem lie? Brothers and sisters, the problem is that we mistook being “moved” for being “changed.” I know a brother who wrote down the same three goals at the start of every year: read the Bible every day, exercise every day, stop losing his temper with his wife. He wrote them for eleven years. In the twelfth year he finally understood something: he didn’t lack resolve; what he lacked was “doing.” The father of psychology, William James, wrote in The Principles of Psychology in 1890 that our whole life is but a mass of habits. The Bible said it even earlier: “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians 6:7). So please remember: being moved happens in a day; being changed happens every day.

Let’s look first at the background of our theme verse. 2 Corinthians was written around AD 56, when Paul was in Macedonia, to the Corinthian church that caused him both great love and great pain. In chapter 5, Paul first reminds them: we must all be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ, to receive according to what we have done. Then he states the driving force behind the letter: the love of Christ constrains us, so that we “no longer live to ourselves.” Brothers and sisters, that phrase is the most precise footnote to “selflessness” in 321. Only then comes verse 17. “New creation” in the original literally means “a new creation,” and that word “new” means new in nature, a wholly new kind. So look carefully at the order: first the accomplished fact, then the life to be lived out.

The first point: doing forms habits; habits form a life. Brothers and sisters, remember these three steps: doing something once is an action; doing it repeatedly is a habit; a long-held habit becomes character. So those who often obey become obedient people; those who often complain become complaining people; those who often love become loving people. In 1949 the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb put forward a now-famous principle: neurons that fire together wire together. It’s like a patch of grass: when one person walks across, the grass is merely bent; when ten thousand people have walked across, it becomes a route you can walk with your eyes closed.

The Bible gives two of the most beautiful examples. The first is Daniel. The decree had been signed, the lions’ den lay open and waiting, and Scripture says he still knelt on his knees before God three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks, “as he did before” (Daniel 6:10). Brothers and sisters, notice those words. He did not decide to pray at the moment the crisis struck; through decades of days without any crisis, he had knelt down three times a day, three times a day. The second example is our Lord himself. Luke 4, verse 16 says Jesus went into the synagogue “as was his custom.” Even the Son of God, in his days on earth, had spiritual habits.

The second point: replace “fighting it” with “cultivating.” Brothers and sisters, we know this approach only too well — don’t get angry, don’t be lazy, don’t be negative. We grit our teeth, cover the walls with notes, make solemn vows. And the result? Usually a great deal of pain, and nothing that lasts. In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner carried out a famous experiment: he asked participants not to think of a white bear for five minutes. Those who were forbidden actually thought of white bears more often; and once the ban was lifted, their thoughts rebounded. Paul saw the spiritual version of this long ago, saying that rules which treat the body harshly “aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh” (Colossians 2:23).

So what is God’s way? To replace wrong doing with right doing. Ephesians 4 tells us to put away the old self, be renewed in the spirit of our mind, and put on the new self. Brothers and sisters, nobody takes off dirty clothes and then just stands there naked; you take off in order to put on. Paul even gives a very concrete example: let him who stole steal no more, but rather labour, producing with his hands something that is good, so that he may have something to give to him who has need. Stop, replace, turn it right around — a hand that once took becomes a hand that supplies. So form the habit of rising early to replace rising late, thanksgiving to replace complaining, blessing to replace criticising. You needn’t take a broom to sweep away the darkness; you only need to reach out and switch on the light.

The third point: there are three keys to forming habits — quickly, often, constantly. The first is: do it quickly. Psalm 119, verse 60 says: “I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.” Why quickly? Because a prompting has a shelf life. When the Holy Spirit prompts us, the heart is soft; but as soon as we say “in a minute” or “tomorrow,” that softness slowly hardens. Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: procrastination is itself a habit. I know a sister who set herself a rule: whenever someone’s name surfaces in her heart, within three minutes she prays for that person or sends them a message of blessing. Three years on, she has become the greatest encourager in her small group.

The second is: do it often. Paul says, “Exercise yourself toward godliness” (1 Timothy 4:7). The word “exercise” in the Greek is the root of the English word “gymnasium.” Brothers and sisters, no athlete ever got strong by understanding the principles. You can learn every training theory by heart, and your muscles won’t grow by a single gram. Muscle recognises only one thing: repetitions. Hebrews 5, verse 14 says that the full grown “by reason of use have their senses exercised,” using the same root — the ability to discern good and evil isn’t an inborn instinct; it is trained. So don’t just wait for opportunities; actively go looking for them.

The third is: do it constantly. The Lord Jesus told a parable so that we “must always pray, and not give up” (Luke 18:1). The early church “continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching.” Brothers and sisters, the greatest enemy of the spiritual life is often not great sin but short-lived enthusiasm. In 2010 Dr Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London in Britain published research showing that for a new behaviour to become automatic took a median of about sixty-six days, with individual differences anywhere from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. But the same study brings good news too — missing the occasional day does not ruin the whole process. So if you fall, get up.

The fourth point: in Christ, live out the life of a new creation. What does “in Christ” mean? It isn’t a mystical feeling but a real way of life. The Lord Jesus said: “Remain in me, and I in you.” And he said: “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples.” The apostle John puts it even more directly: he who says he remains in him “ought himself also to walk just like he walked” (1 John 2:6). Brothers and sisters, so to be “in Christ” is to live in Christ’s word and walk in Christ’s truth. Walk in the truth, and you are in Christ; leave the truth, and you are not in Christ.

But we must distinguish two things: improvement and new creation. Improvement is repairing and patching something old; new creation is the appearing of an entirely new kind of thing. Nature offers a wonderful witness: inside the chrysalis, a caterpillar doesn’t slowly sprout wings; its tissues largely break down and are rebuilt, and what emerges is not a caterpillar that can fly but a butterfly. Brothers and sisters, what God is doing in you is not a renovation project; it is a rebuilding project. But let me give you a picture: a man moves into a brand-new house but brings every broken sofa and mouldy cardboard box from his old home. Is the house new? Yes. Does it feel new to live in? Not in the least. The standing is new, but the habits are old.

The fifth point: the five basics — seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing. Seeing is taking in. David says: “I will set no vile thing before my eyes.” Brothers and sisters, the eyes are the gateway to the heart, and today every mobile phone is a door. Listening is receiving. Paul says: “faith comes by hearing.” Whatever you listen to over the long term, you will believe over the long term. Thinking is digesting. Philippians 4, verse 8 says: whatever things are true, honourable, pure, lovely — think about these things. Seeing, listening and thinking chiefly change our mindset.

Speaking is confirming. Romans 10, verse 10 says that with the heart one believes resulting in righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation. Brothers and sisters, when you say the truth out loud, it is as if you have signed your name to it before yourself and others. Doing is living it out. James puts it heavily: those who hear but don’t do are “deluding your own selves.” The Lord Jesus says that everyone who hears his words and does them is like a wise man who built his house on a rock. That one step between hearing and doing is the dividing line between rock and sand.

In fact, as far back as Joshua’s time, God compressed these basics into a single verse: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it” (Joshua 1:8). Shall not depart from your mouth — that is speaking; meditate on it day and night — that is thinking; observe to do — that is doing. Brothers and sisters, without doing, everything stays in the head; with doing, the truth enters your life. And 321 tells us this is the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. You are not turning this wheel on your own, for the Bible says it is God who works in us both to will and to work.

Brothers and sisters, there are five practices today. First, choose one spiritual habit: praying every day, reading the Bible every day, or blessing someone every day. Please write it as a concrete sentence — don’t write “I will pray more”; write “Every morning at 6:30 I will pray for fifteen minutes,” and do it for twenty-one days in a row to begin with. But remember, twenty-one days is the start, not the finish line. Second, practise immediate obedience. Give yourself a rule: within five minutes. Within five minutes, make that phone call; within five minutes, say that apology out loud.

Third, replace old habits with new actions. Please prepare your replacement plans right now: when you want to complain, count three things you are thankful for; when you want to criticise, pray one sentence for that person; when you want to scroll on your phone, open your Bible and read a passage. Fourth, build a system of small daily changes. Tie the new habit to something you already do: after brushing your teeth, pray for three minutes; when you get into the car, say one word of thanks first. Fifth, take two minutes each night to ask yourself five questions: today, were my seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing letting Jesus be King, or letting myself be king? Don’t condemn yourself; just realign with Christ.

Brothers and sisters, let’s place what we’ve learned today into the blueprint of 321. The Three Foundations can become three daily questions: how would Jesus handle this? What does God’s word say? What is the Holy Spirit prompting me to do right now? The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Habits are automatic, and what is automatic most clearly reveals who is King. The 920 reminds us: everyone we relate to is our “2,” and patience and gentleness grow in relationships. The 235 reminds us: don’t form habits alone; find a spiritual companion to walk with you, and in the end multiply it on to others.

Brothers and sisters, a changed life comes not from a burst of passion but from daily habits. When you keep choosing right doing, you are shaping a new you. But please remember, this new you is not built by effort; it is Christ living himself out in you. The writer of Lamentations, amid the deepest ruins, said: “They are new every morning.” God’s loving kindness comes every morning, so our obedience can come every morning too. He doesn’t ask us to pay the cost of a whole lifetime at once; he only asks us to hand over today, today.

Let’s bow our heads and pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, thank you, because you have already made me a new creation. I did not earn this; you gave it to me freely. Lord, forgive me for so often waiting for one big breakthrough while despising the small choices of each day; forgive me for fighting myself in my own strength instead of inviting you in to be King. Help me, from today, to obey you quickly, to train often, and to persevere constantly. When I fall, lift me up, and keep me from losing heart. May every one of my habits become a vessel that glorifies you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, may the Lord’s loving kindness be new for you every morning, may your life become more and more like Jesus, and may all the glory go to him.
